If the murder of the Son of God fell inside the plan, then a threat delivered that morning falls inside it too. Which is why the prayer runs straight on from verse 28 to verse 29 without a pause. The sovereignty is not the conclusion of the prayer. It is the ground they are standing on in order to ask for courage.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: Luke reports the result of the church's generosity in a sentence that echoes the law of Moses: there was not a needy person among them (compare Deuteronomy 15:4). Deuteronomy had held exactly that out as a possibility, attached a condition Israel never met, and admitted in the same chapter that the poor would never cease out of the land. What fifteen centuries of covenant history had not produced, the Spirit produced in Jerusalem inside a year. Now: The particular form belonged to a moment; the open hand does not. And Luke's arrangement is worth attention — he sets the giving immediately beside the preaching, in the same paragraph, so that the community's life and the apostles' message are not two subjects but one.

verseByVerse.quote: When they were released, they went to their friends and reported what the chief priests and the elders had said to them. And when they heard it, they lifted their voices together to God and said, "Sovereign Lord, who made the heaven and the earth and the sea and everything in them,"
verseByVerse.commentary:
When they were released, they went to their friends and reported what the chief priests and the elders had said to them. And when they heard it, they lifted their voices together to God and said, “Sovereign Lord, who made the heaven and the earth and the sea and everything in them,

When they were released, they went to their friends. Two details before the prayer begins, and both are worth having. The first is where they go. Literally, to their own: to the people they belonged to, the church. Released from custody with a formal charge hanging over them, the first place these two men go is to their own people. Nobody scatters. Nobody suggests that association with them has become dangerous, which by any sensible reckoning it now had.

And reported what the chief priests and the elders had said to them. They tell the church everything. There is no pretending the threat was smaller than it was, and no heroics. The church hears the facts and takes them straight to God.

They lifted their voices together to God. The word for together (homothymadon) is a favourite of Luke’s for the early church: with one accord, of one mind, all facing the same way. He uses it of the hundred and twenty waiting in the upper room (1:14) and of the daily meetings in the temple (2:46). Whether the whole company spoke the words in unison or one man led and the rest carried it, Luke does not say and it does not much matter. What he is describing is a room in which nobody is a spectator. Their first response to threats was prayer, together.

Sovereign Lord. Then the address, and it is not the usual one. They call God Despota: the word for an absolute master, the owner of a household with total authority over everyone in it, the word for a master of slaves, and not the ordinary word for Lord that appears on every other page of the New Testament. Luke has used it of God once before, in his first volume, in the mouth of an old man in the temple who had waited his whole life and was now handing it back: Lord, now you are letting your servant depart in peace (Luke 2:29). It is the vocabulary of somebody who has stopped owning himself. They begin their prayer not with their problem, but with God’s sovereignty.

Who made the heaven and the earth and the sea and everything in them. And then, before a single word about the council, four clauses about creation. It is a line out of the Ten Commandments and out of the Psalms (Exodus 20:11; Psalm 146:6), and it is the largest sentence available to them. Here is the thing to see, and it is the most instructive feature of the entire prayer. They have a real emergency. Two of their leaders have spent the night in a cell, the supreme court has issued a formal prohibition, and everyone in the room understands that arrests of this kind escalate. And they spend the opening of the prayer on doctrine: not because they are avoiding the subject, but because they are getting the subject into proportion. The Sanhedrin controls the temple, the treasury and the police. It did not make the sea.

Prayer that begins somewhere else. A reader can run that against his own practice without much difficulty, and most of us will not enjoy the result. Prayer under pressure tends to begin at the pressure and stay there: the diagnosis, the letter, the money, the person, round and round. There is nothing wicked in that; God invites us to bring exactly those things and never once complains about it. But this church begins somewhere else, and by the time the threat is finally raised in verse 29 it has been set inside a universe that has a Maker in it, and it has come down to something like its actual size.

What it does not mean. One guard. This is not a technique for getting prayers answered, and treating it as one would turn a good instinct into a superstition. They did not begin with creation in order to unlock anything. They began there because it was true, and because frightened people need to hear themselves say what is true.

Why does it matter that they went back to the church? Because Christians were never meant to face pressure alone. In trouble, the instinct is often to withdraw, to protect others from our problems or ourselves from their questions. Peter and John did the opposite: they went to their own people, told them everything, and prayed together. That is what the church is for. If you are under pressure, at work, at home, from illness or from opposition, tell some trusted believers and ask them to pray with you. And if you are part of a church, be the kind of friend a frightened brother can come back to.

In a sentence. When released, they went back to the believers and reported what had been said, and together they prayed to the Sovereign Lord who made heaven, earth, sea and everything in them.

On a Tuesday. When you are threatened, start your prayer with who God is. He made everything. Before you name your problem to him tonight, spend a minute saying back to him what is true of him: Maker of heaven and earth, Lord of all, Father in Christ. Then bring the problem, and see what size it is.

For worship. The Sovereign Lord who made the heavens and the earth and the sea and everything in them is the God to whom a threatened little church lifted its voice, and he heard. No council is above him and no threat is outside his house. He is the master of the whole household of creation, and his servants are safe in his hands.

parallels.desc: who made heaven and earth, the sea, and all that is in them

verseByVerse.quote: "who through the mouth of our father David, your servant, said by the Holy Spirit, 'Why did the Gentiles rage, and the peoples plot in vain? The kings of the earth set themselves, and the rulers were gathered together, against the Lord and against his Anointed' —"
verseByVerse.commentary:
who through the mouth of our father David, your servant, said by the Holy Spirit, ‘Why did the Gentiles rage, and the peoples plot in vain? The kings of the earth set themselves, and the rulers were gathered together, against the Lord and against his Anointed’ —

Who through the mouth of our father David, your servant, said by the Holy Spirit. Before the quotation there is a sentence about how Scripture came to exist, and it is dropped in without any fuss at all. Count the agents. God is the speaker. The Holy Spirit is the speaker. David’s mouth is the instrument. Three clauses, one act, and not the faintest sense that these are competing explanations, as Peter had said already (1:16). The people praying this had no difficulty holding together the conviction that David composed a poem out of his own head and heart, and that God said it. And it is worth noticing that the clearest statement about inspiration anywhere in Acts occurs not in an argument about the Bible but in the middle of a prayer, where nobody was trying to prove anything to anyone.

Why did the Gentiles rage, and the peoples plot in vain? Then Psalm 2 itself (Psalm 2:1–2). It is a royal psalm, a coronation psalm, written for the day a son of David was crowned, when the vassal states looked at a new and untested king and began calculating their odds. In vain means empty, hollow, to no purpose. The psalm is not describing feeble opposition. It is describing furious, well-resourced, entirely serious opposition, and calling it empty.

The kings of the earth set themselves, and the rulers were gathered together, against the Lord and against his Anointed. His Anointed is his Christ, his Messiah, and opposition to the Messiah is opposition to God. What the church does with the psalm is the important thing. They are not hunting for a verse that suits their mood. They are reading their own week and finding it already written down: the kings, the rulers, the gathering together, the conspiracy against the Lord and against his Anointed. The Sanhedrin met that very morning, and Psalm 2 has the minutes.

He who sits in the heavens laughs. And they stop the quotation just before the best part, which tells you they knew perfectly well where it goes. A little further on, that psalm says he who sits in the heavens laughs; the Lord holds them in derision (Psalm 2:4). They do not quote it and they do not need to; nobody recites the punchline of something every person in the room has known since childhood. But it is lying underneath the prayer, and it accounts for the extraordinary confidence of what they are about to ask for.

Futile, not harmless. There is a use for that in ordinary Christian life, and it is not the cheap one. The point is not that opposition to God is comic and can be laughed off by his people. Two of the men praying this had been in custody overnight, and within a few years Herod would put one of the apostles to the sword (12:2). The point is that from the only vantage that finally matters, the raging is futile: not harmless, not painless, but futile. The kings of the earth have been setting themselves against the Lord’s Anointed for three thousand years, and that psalm has never once needed rewriting.

How can I pray Scripture like this? Take a passage, especially a psalm, and read it slowly, asking what it says about God and what situation it describes. Then bring your own situation into it, as this church did: name the people and pressures, and pray the psalm’s truths over them. Psalm 2 for opposition, Psalm 23 for fear, Psalm 51 for guilt, Psalm 46 for upheaval, Psalm 121 for travel, Psalm 139 for feeling unseen. You are not twisting the text; you are letting God’s words shape your requests. Over time you will find that Scripture gives you words when you have none, and that it changes what you ask for.

In a sentence. They prayed to the God who spoke by the Spirit through David, asking why the nations rage and peoples plot in vain, and kings and rulers gather against the Lord and his Anointed.

On a Tuesday. Read Psalm 2 today, the whole of it, aloud. Then think of the thing in the world that most frightens you about the future of the church, and read verse 4 again.

For worship. The nations still rage, and still in vain. Christ reigns. The Father has set his King on his holy hill, and given him the nations as his heritage and the ends of the earth as his possession. Every throne that has risen against him has fallen, and his throne stands. Blessed are all who take refuge in him.

parallels.desc: why do the nations rage?

verseByVerse.quote: "for truly in this city there were gathered together against your holy servant Jesus, whom you anointed, both Herod and Pontius Pilate, along with the Gentiles and the peoples of Israel, to do whatever your hand and your plan had predestined to take place."
verseByVerse.commentary:
for truly in this city there were gathered together against your holy servant Jesus, whom you anointed, both Herod and Pontius Pilate, along with the Gentiles and the peoples of Israel, to do whatever your hand and your plan had predestined to take place.

For truly in this city there were gathered together against your holy servant Jesus, whom you anointed. Now the church does something with the psalm that is worth watching closely. They take it apart and put names into it. Jesus is God’s Anointed, his Christ, and the gathering against him happened in truly in this city, a few hundred yards from where they are praying.

Both Herod and Pontius Pilate, along with the Gentiles and the peoples of Israel. Psalm 2 lists four parties: the nations, the peoples, the kings of the earth, and the rulers. The prayer supplies the roster. The kings: Herod, that is Herod Antipas, ruler of Galilee. The rulers: Pontius Pilate. The nations: the Gentiles, the Romans. The peoples: the peoples of Israel. Four slots, four names, and the sum of them is one Friday morning in this city. Jew and Gentile together crucified him. All humanity is implicated. The mention of Herod is a small mark of authenticity, because the meeting between Herod and Pilate over Jesus is recorded by nobody except Luke (Luke 23:6–12), who also notes that the two men, who had been enemies, became friends that day. The prayer of a Jerusalem congregation and the research of a Greek physician are describing the same afternoon.

To do whatever your hand and your plan had predestined to take place. Then the sentence. Predestined (proōrisen) means decided beforehand; it is the word used of election in Romans 8:29–30 and Ephesians 1:5, 11. God’s hand, his power, and his plan, his will, determined it. The greatest crime in history was planned by God. They did what they wanted, wickedly; and they did exactly what God had determined. This is God’s sovereignty over evil without his being its author (2:23).

A doctrine to stand on. The double agency of the cross has already been set out in this book, with all the guards that belong to it, at Peter’s first sermon. What is different here is not the doctrine but the setting, and the setting is the entire point. This is not an argument. Nobody in the room is defending predestination against an objection, or drawing careful distinctions, or fielding the question about whether God is then the author of sin. These are frightened people the morning after a night in custody, and they are using the doctrine: putting their weight on it to see whether it holds. It holds.

The floor they stand on. And the logic they draw out of it is exact. If the crucifixion of the Son of God, the worst single act in the history of the world, carried out by a coalition of everybody, freely, wickedly, with full culpability, was nevertheless inside the hand and plan of God, then what happened in a council chamber that morning is inside it too. Which is why the prayer does not pause here. Verse 28 runs straight on into verse 29 without so much as a breath. The sovereignty is not the conclusion they are working toward. It is the floor they are standing on in order to ask for something.

What it does not mean. It is worth saying what the doctrine is not being used for. Not to make the threat harmless: the threat was real and the flogging came in the next chapter. Not to excuse the men who made it: they were not forced, or less guilty; they plotted freely, and were responsible, and this same prayer calls what they did a gathering against God’s holy servant. God works his perfect will through human sin, not by excusing it. And not as an anaesthetic: nobody here is saying the situation does not matter. They are saying it is not out of hand.

If God predestined the cross, how were Herod and Pilate guilty? Both are true. God ordained the event, and it happened through the free and wicked choices of men who acted from their own motives and were fully responsible. Joseph’s brothers meant evil, and God meant it for good (Genesis 50:20). God is never the author of sin; he governs even sin for good, and holds sinners accountable. The cross is the clearest proof that both truths stand together.

Predestination in its native habitat. Most people meet predestination as a controversy: something to be argued about, usually with somebody who has already decided. Here is its native habitat: a small, frightened, illegal congregation in an occupied city, using it as a place to stand.

How does God’s sovereignty help me when I am suffering? It does not explain every detail; it rarely tells you why. But it tells you that what is happening to you is not random, not out of control, and not outside the care of a Father who did not spare his own Son. If God could take the worst thing ever done and make it the salvation of the world, he can work your trouble together for good, as he has promised to those who love him (Romans 8:28). That does not make the pain less real, and you may still weep and ask him to take it away. But you weep inside a plan, held by a hand that was pierced for you.

In a sentence. In this city Herod and Pontius Pilate, with the Gentiles and the peoples of Israel, gathered against God’s holy servant Jesus, his Anointed, to do what his hand and plan had predetermined.

On a Tuesday. If God was sovereign over the cross, he is sovereign over your trouble. Nothing is outside his plan. Take the thing that has most shaken you this year and say to God, in the words of this prayer: your hand and your plan. Then ask him for what you need to keep going.

For worship. The Father planned the cross before the world began, and the Son walked into it willingly, and Herod and Pilate and the crowds did exactly what they wanted and exactly what God had decided. Every wicked hand at Golgotha served the purpose of redeeming love. There is no power in heaven or on earth that can get outside the hand of the God who turned the murder of his Son into the salvation of his people.
verseByVerse.note: Herod is Herod Antipas.

verseByVerse.quote: "And now, Lord, look upon their threats and grant to your servants to continue to speak your word with all boldness, while you stretch out your hand to heal, and signs and wonders are performed through the name of your holy servant Jesus."
verseByVerse.commentary:
And now, Lord, look upon their threats and grant to your servants to continue to speak your word with all boldness, while you stretch out your hand to heal, and signs and wonders are performed through the name of your holy servant Jesus.

And now, Lord, look upon their threats. Now, at last, the problem. They ask God to look at it. And then, having drawn his attention to it, they ask him for something else entirely. Set out what is not in this prayer, because the omissions are the most striking thing about it. They do not ask for the threats to be withdrawn. They do not ask God to destroy their enemies, or to judge, humble or replace the council. They do not ask for protection, or for the arrests to stop, or for Peter and John to be spared a second night in a cell. They do not even ask for wisdom about proceeding more discreetly. Every one of those would be a perfectly reasonable Christian prayer, and not one of them is here.

And grant to your servants to continue to speak your word with all boldness. What they ask for is to keep doing what they were forbidden to do: more of the exact behaviour that got two of them arrested the previous evening. Not safety, but courage. And two words locate them precisely. At verse 24 they addressed God as Sovereign Lord, the absolute master of a household. Here they call themselves your servants (doulois), and the word is the ordinary one for slaves. Master and slaves. It is not an anxious relationship and it is not a negotiation. A slave does not ask his master to arrange easier work; he asks for what he needs to do the work he has been given.

Asking for what they already had. And the word they choose for boldness is the very word the council had noticed in them at verse 13. They already had it, in a courtroom, without asking for it. They ask anyway. Whatever they were given in the courtroom, they treat as spent, and they come back for more the same day.

While you stretch out your hand to heal, and signs and wonders are performed through the name of your holy servant Jesus. And they ask God to go on stretching out his hand to heal, which is to say, more of the exact thing that started the trouble. Put plainly: the council forbade the name, and the church’s response is to ask God to make the name more conspicuous. They ask God to keep confirming the word with signs, and God did (5:12). These signs belonged to the founding era of the church, accrediting the apostles’ message.

Should we pray for signs and wonders today? This church prayed for boldness first, and for God to confirm the apostles’ word. Continuationist Christians see the prayer as a model for every church. The more likely reading is that the signs accompanying the apostles’ witness belonged to that founding period and are not promised as normal church life; that is the cessationist view, held charitably. What we may always pray for is what they asked first: boldness to speak God’s word, and God’s help for the sick and suffering, as he wills.

What it does not mean. Here a guard is essential, because a passage like this is very easily turned into a rebuke. It would be a serious mistake to conclude that praying for safety is unspiritual. Paul asks the Roman church to pray that he may be delivered from the unbelievers in Judea (Romans 15:31). The church in chapter 12 of this same book prays earnestly for Peter in prison, and God sends an angel to open the door. Jesus himself taught his disciples to pray, deliver us from evil (Matthew 6:13). Nobody reading this passage should come away feeling that asking God to protect his children is a second-class prayer, and a parent praying for a sick child does not need to be told that his praying is insufficiently missionary.

What a prayer reveals. What the passage does show is what these particular people wanted most when they were badly frightened, and that is a different question and a more searching one. A prayer reveals what is actually being protected. It is worth asking, quietly and without theatre, what the last genuinely hard week produced in one’s own praying, and whether any of it would still have been wanted if the whole business had simply been made to go away.

How should I pray for persecuted Christians? Pray as they themselves usually ask to be prayed for, which is very often like this church: not first that the pressure would stop, but that they would stand firm, speak boldly, and love their persecutors. Pray also, rightly, for their protection, release and comfort, and for justice (Hebrews 13:3 tells us to remember those in prison as though in prison with them). Pray for the persecutors to be converted, as Saul was. Learn the names of particular believers or churches from trustworthy organisations, so your prayer is specific. And let their courage shame and strengthen your own.

In a sentence. They asked the Lord to consider their threats and give his servants boldness to keep speaking his word, as he stretched out his hand to heal and do signs and wonders through the name of his holy servant Jesus.

On a Tuesday. Pray this prayer this week, for yourself and your church: not only keep me safe, but make me bold. Then notice what changes in you when you ask for courage instead of escape.

For worship. The Sovereign Lord was asked by his frightened servants not for an easier task but for greater courage to do the dangerous one, and he delighted to give it. The name of his holy servant Jesus, which the council forbade, is the name his people asked to be made more glorious, and God has answered that prayer in every generation since. His hand is still stretched out, and his word still runs.

parallels.desc: pray that words may be given me to open my mouth boldly

verseByVerse.quote: And when they had prayed, the place in which they were gathered together was shaken, and they were all filled with the Holy Spirit and continued to speak the word of God with boldness.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And when they had prayed, the place in which they were gathered together was shaken, and they were all filled with the Holy Spirit and continued to speak the word of God with boldness.

And when they had prayed, the place in which they were gathered together was shaken. The answer arrives before they have got up off the floor. God does not reply in words. He moves the building. In Scripture a shaking of this kind is what happens when God arrives somewhere: the mountain trembling at Sinai (Exodus 19:18), the foundations of the thresholds shaking when Isaiah saw the Lord in the temple (Isaiah 6:4). Here it comes in answer to a prayer that had opened by naming him as the maker of heaven and earth and sea. They had reminded themselves whom they were addressing, and he replied by moving the walls, which is a very short way of saying: correct. The council could threaten; God shakes the building.

And they were all filled with the Holy Spirit. All of them, not the apostles only. And filled once again: the same word used of these same people at Pentecost (2:4), and of Peter twenty-three verses ago. This is not a second Pentecost, and Luke does not treat it as one; the Spirit does not arrive, because he has never left. What this language describes is fresh supply for fresh demand, which is a mercy, since it means the church is not living off a reserve laid down once and steadily running down. Believers who already have the Spirit can be filled again and again for new tasks (Ephesians 5:18).

And continued to speak the word of God with boldness. And then the answer proper. Not felt bold. Spoke. Continued: they kept on doing it, which is the only form courage takes that can actually be measured. Prayer answered exactly. They asked for boldness and got it.

Nerve, not a changed situation. Two things about this answer deserve attention. The first is that it is exactly what was asked for and not one item more. The council was not struck down. The prohibition was not lifted. The danger did not decrease: by the next chapter these men are arrested again and flogged. God supplied precisely what was requested, which was nerve, and left every circumstance standing. That is one of the ways God answers, and it is worth knowing in advance: not by removing the situation but by re-equipping the person who is inside it.

What it does not mean. The second is a caution. A shaking like this comes only rarely in Acts (compare 16:25–26) and never becomes a pattern. Nobody in the New Testament goes looking for it, and no writer anywhere suggests that a prayer without a physical sign has gone unheard. The point of this verse is not the tremor; it is the clause after it. Luke’s evidence that God had answered is not that the walls moved. It is that a roomful of intimidated people went straight back out and said the thing they had been forbidden to say.

Is being filled with the Spirit a feeling? Not essentially. It may come with deep feelings of joy, peace or courage, and sometimes it does. But Luke measures it by what it produces: here, bold speaking of God’s word; elsewhere, wisdom, faith, joy and love (6:3, 5; 13:52). Paul describes it in terms of worship, gratitude and humble submission to one another (Ephesians 5:18–21). So do not judge whether you are filled by the temperature of your emotions on a given day. Ask whether you are yielding to the Spirit’s word and leading, and whether the fruit of Christlikeness and courage for Christ is growing. Ask God to fill you, and then obey him; the filling is often recognised afterwards, in what you found you were able to do.

In a sentence. When they had prayed, the place where they were meeting shook, and they were all filled with the Holy Spirit and kept speaking God’s word boldly.

On a Tuesday. God answers prayer for boldness. Ask him, and then open your mouth. Do not wait for the floor to shake. The evidence of the answer is the next true sentence you say about Jesus.

For worship. The God who shook Sinai shook a house in Jerusalem, not to frighten his children but to tell them he had heard. He filled them again with his Spirit, and sent them straight back into danger with his word on their lips. He is the God who answers his people while they are still on their knees, and who never runs short of what they need for the work he gives.

parallels.desc: the whole mountain trembled

verseByVerse.quote: Now the full number of those who believed were of one heart and soul, and no one said that any of the things that belonged to him was his own, but they had everything in common. And with great power the apostles were giving their testimony to the resurrection of the Lord Jesus, and great grace was upon them all.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Now the full number of those who believed were of one heart and soul, and no one said that any of the things that belonged to him was his own, but they had everything in common. And with great power the apostles were giving their testimony to the resurrection of the Lord Jesus, and great grace was upon them all.

Now the full number of those who believed were of one heart and soul. Luke describes the church here with language his Greek readers would have recognised at once, and it is worth knowing why it would have stopped them. In the Greek world there was a well-worn saying that a friend is a single soul living in two bodies, and an older proverb still that friends hold all things in common. These were the classical ideals of friendship: much quoted, much admired, and universally understood to be out of reach except perhaps between two rare individuals over a lifetime. Luke uses both of them in consecutive clauses and applies them not to a pair of philosophers but to a congregation of several thousand people in an occupied city, most of whom had met one another only in the previous few months. This is deep unity: not uniformity, but shared love and purpose. Jesus had prayed that they may all be one (John 17:21), and here is the answer.

And no one said that any of the things that belonged to him was his own. Then a sentence that is nearly always paraphrased and should not be, because the precision is the whole of it. Read it slowly. It does not say that nobody owned anything. It says that things still belonged to people, for Luke uses the language of possession, and that nobody was saying so. Ownership survived. The claim was dropped. The property register was unchanged and the vocabulary had altered completely. They still owned things, but held them loosely, as belonging to God and available to others.

A change in what people assumed. That distinction does more work than a page of argument. This is not the abolition of private property, and Peter will say as much to Ananias within a few verses. It is something harder and more interior: people who still held the deeds and had stopped speaking as though the deeds settled anything. Anybody can be talked into a scheme. What Luke reports is a change in what people assumed when they were not thinking about it.

But they had everything in common. As in 2:44. What was theirs was available to their brothers.

And with great power the apostles were giving their testimony to the resurrection of the Lord Jesus. And then, dropped straight into the middle of all that, verse 33: the central message. The placing is deliberate and it is easily missed, because chapter headings and sermon habits tend to file these two subjects separately: the church’s inner life over here, evangelism over there. Luke puts the preaching inside the paragraph about the money. The community that had stopped saying mine is the community in which the resurrection was announced with power, and Luke plainly did not consider those to be two different topics.

And great grace was upon them all. The last clause can be read two ways and probably means both. Great grace was the favour of God resting on the whole company, and equally the goodwill of a watching city, which is how Luke used a related phrase two chapters earlier (2:47). Both were true for a season, and the sentence does not need to be made to choose. Generosity and gospel go together.

How can a large church be of one heart and soul? Not by everyone becoming the same, or agreeing on every opinion, but by sharing one Lord, one gospel and one love. The early church held together because the risen Christ mattered more to each of them than their differences or possessions. In practice, unity grows when believers keep the gospel at the centre, pray together, deal quickly and honestly with offences (Matthew 18:15), refuse gossip, bear with one another in love (Ephesians 4:2–3), and actually share life, in small groups, homes and service, so that the large church becomes a family of families. It is the Spirit’s work, and he loves to give it to those who ask.

In a sentence. All the believers were one in heart and soul, and no one claimed his possessions as his own, but they shared everything, while the apostles testified powerfully to the resurrection of the Lord Jesus, and great grace was on them all.

On a Tuesday. Notice how often you say mine this week, aloud or in your head: my car, my evening, my money, my space. Then ask which of those things you would be glad for a brother or sister in Christ to need.

For worship. Open hands and bold witness: that is what grace looks like in a church. The risen Lord made thousands of strangers into one heart and soul, and the ancient dream of friendship came true in a community that had nothing in common except him. Where his resurrection is preached with power, his people stop clutching, because they have been given everything in him.

verseByVerse.quote: There was not a needy person among them, for as many as were owners of lands or houses sold them and brought the proceeds of what was sold and laid it at the apostles' feet, and it was distributed to each as any had need.
verseByVerse.commentary:
There was not a needy person among them, for as many as were owners of lands or houses sold them and brought the proceeds of what was sold and laid it at the apostles’ feet, and it was distributed to each as any had need.

There was not a needy person among them. Luke is echoing the law, and any hearer who knew it would have caught it. In Deuteronomy, God speaks to Israel about the seventh year, when debts were released, and adds a promise: there will be no poor among you. It comes with a condition, if only you will strictly obey the voice of the LORD your God, and seven verses later the same chapter states, flatly and without apology, that there will never cease to be poor in the land (Deuteronomy 15:4–5, 11). The law held out a possibility and in the same breath admitted that Israel would not reach it. And Israel did not. Fifteen centuries of covenant history, with prophets thundering about the neglected widow and the pledged cloak and the corner of the field left unreaped, produced a great deal of legislation and never once produced that sentence. And then Luke, writing about a group of people in Jerusalem perhaps a year after Pentecost, uses it as a plain statement of fact. The new covenant community did, by the Spirit, what Israel was meant to do.

For as many as were owners of lands or houses sold them and brought the proceeds of what was sold. Notice how it came about, because the method is not the one anybody would have designed. Nothing was collected. Nobody was assessed. As needs arose, people who owned land or houses sold them, voluntarily (5:4).

And laid it at the apostles’ feet. That gesture repays a pause. Not handed to the apostles: laid at their feet. Laying gifts at someone’s feet placed them under his authority to distribute; the apostles managed the fund until the seven took it over (6:1–6). And it is the posture of submission and also of anonymity. You put the money down and you walk away. There is no transaction between the giver and the person who receives it, no thanks owed, nobody beholden. The widow eating that week does not know whose field paid for it, and the man who sold the field does not know which widow he fed. The arrangement makes patronage impossible, and patronage is the disease that has attended religious giving in every century since.

And it was distributed to each as any had need. Need, not equality, was the principle.

Was this Christian communism? A word here, since this is sometimes called Christian communism and pressed into political service: it was nothing of the kind. It was wholly voluntary. Peter tells Ananias that the land remained his own while it was unsold, and the money was at his disposal after it was sold (5:4), so private property was kept and giving was free, never compelled. It was love-driven and Spirit-prompted, flowing from hearts made one, not enforced by any state. And it was needs-based generosity, as any had need, not mechanical equalising. This is the very opposite of coercive collectivism: it is the free, glad open-handedness of people whom the Spirit had loosed from the grip of money. The abiding call is that same generosity and care for the needy among us; the particular form was one Spirit-filled moment’s response.

Did this sharing make the Jerusalem church poor? Scripture never calls it a mistake, but neither does it repeat or command it; Ananias was free to keep his property (5:4). The Jerusalem church later needed help from the Gentile churches (Romans 15:26), probably because of the famine (11:28–30) and persecution. The lasting lesson is generosity, not a single economic system.

Would you be willing for the gift to be untraceable? Which suggests a test, and a sharper one than the usual question of whether a person would give if he were asked. Would you be willing for the gift to be untraceable? Not merely for your name to be left off a list, but for the person helped never to discover that it was you, never to be grateful to you, never to know that they owe you anything whatever. That is the arrangement Luke is describing. The money went on the floor at the apostles’ feet, and after that it was nobody’s.

Should all my giving be anonymous? Not necessarily, but most of it can be, and the motive should always be. Jesus said, when you give to the needy, do not let your left hand know what your right hand is doing, so that your giving may be in secret (Matthew 6:3–4). The danger he names is giving in order to be seen. Sometimes it is right for a gift to be known: Barnabas’s gift is recorded in the next verse, and Paul publicly praised the Macedonians’ generosity to stir others (2 Corinthians 8:1–5). But it is wise to give much of what you give through the church or quietly, so that the glory goes to God and the receiver is beholden to no one but him.

In a sentence. No one among them was in need, because those who owned land or houses sold them and laid the money at the apostles’ feet, and it was given to each as needed.

On a Tuesday. Is there need in your church that your abundance could meet? Ask your pastor or deacons whether there is a family in difficulty, and give through them, quietly, this week.

For worship. What the law of Moses held out and Israel could never reach, the Spirit of Christ brought about in a single congregation: there was not a needy person among them. That is what the gospel does when it lands in human hearts. The Lord who became poor for us made his people rich enough to give away their fields, and every time a believer’s need is met in secret by a brother’s gift, he is glorified.
verseByVerse.note: Laying gifts at someone’s feet placed them under his authority.

parallels.desc: there will be no poor among you

verseByVerse.quote: Thus Joseph, who was also called by the apostles Barnabas (which means son of encouragement), a Levite, a native of Cyprus, sold a field that belonged to him and brought the money and laid it at the apostles' feet.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Thus Joseph, who was also called by the apostles Barnabas (which means son of encouragement), a Levite, a native of Cyprus, sold a field that belonged to him and brought the money and laid it at the apostles’ feet.

Thus Joseph, who was also called by the apostles Barnabas (which means son of encouragement). Luke has been describing a pattern. Now he gives it a face, and the face turns out to matter enormously to the rest of the book. The man’s name is Joseph. Almost nobody remembers that, because the apostles gave him a nickname and it stuck so completely that the New Testament uses it more than twenty times while the real name effectively disappears. Son of, in Hebrew idiom, means characterised by, and Barnabas was characterised by encouragement. The word behind encouragement (paraklēsis) is related to the Spirit’s own title, the Helper or Paraclete, the one called alongside (John 14:16). The apostles looked at this man and named him after something the Holy Spirit does.

A Levite, a native of Cyprus. He was a Levite from Cyprus, a large island in the eastern Mediterranean with a big Jewish community, where he would later preach (13:4). Because the tribe of Levi received no territory when the land was divided (Numbers 18:20), some readers have assumed an irregularity in his owning a field. There is probably none. The restriction concerned tribal allotment within Israel; Levites held houses and pasture land; the priest Jeremiah bought a field long before (Jeremiah 32:6–9); and Luke does not tell us where this one was, perhaps in Cyprus. It is a detail to read carefully rather than to press.

Sold a field that belonged to him and brought the money and laid it at the apostles’ feet. What matters is what Luke chose to record about him first, and it is a gift. Before anything else in his biography, before a single word he ever said, the first fact on file about Barnabas is that he sold a field, put the money down, and made no speech about it.

The man who held the New Testament together. Keep him in view, because he is about to do the three things that hold the New Testament together. When Saul of Tarsus came to Jerusalem after his conversion and every Christian in the city was too frightened to go near a man who had been arresting them, one person took him, brought him to the apostles and vouched for him (9:26–27). When the gospel unexpectedly broke out among Greeks at Antioch, Barnabas was sent to look into it, rejoiced at the grace of God he saw there, and then travelled to Tarsus to find Saul and bring him into the work, which is how the apostle to the Gentiles was started on his ministry there (11:22–26). And when Paul refused to take young John Mark on a second journey because he had withdrawn from them earlier, Barnabas took him anyway and lost his partnership with Paul over it (15:37–39). Years later Paul writes from a prison cell asking for Mark, for he is very useful to me for ministry (2 Timothy 4:11). Barnabas had been right about Mark, and Paul lived long enough to say so.

Encouragement began with an open hand. That is the man Luke introduces here with a field and a payment. It is worth noticing that the encouraging of other people, which is what he became famous for, began as a habit of open-handedness in a matter of money; and that the whole Gentile mission of the church runs through a man whose first recorded act was to give something away.

The real thing and the imitation. One last thing, and the chapter break conceals it. The next sentence in Luke’s narrative begins: but a man named Ananias. There is no gap. Barnabas and Ananias are two halves of one paragraph, the real thing and the imitation, set side by side, both selling property and both laying money at the apostles’ feet, and one of them dead the day he brought it (5:1–11). Luke has put the genuine article first so that the reader knows exactly what the counterfeit was copying.

How can I be a Barnabas? Look for the people others are wary of, overlooking or giving up on: the new believer with a bad past, the young person who failed, the newcomer nobody has spoken to, the struggling servant who is about to quit. Go and stand beside them. Speak specific, honest words of encouragement about what God is doing in them; Barnabas saw the grace of God and was glad (11:23). Vouch for people when it costs you something. Give practically, as he did. And be patient with those who have let you down; Mark is in the New Testament partly because Barnabas would not write him off. You will rarely be thanked, but you may be helping to raise the next Paul.

In a sentence. Joseph, a Levite from Cyprus whom the apostles called Barnabas, son of encouragement, sold a field and laid the money at the apostles’ feet.

On a Tuesday. Be a Barnabas: generous and encouraging. The church needs many. Think of one person who needs someone to stand beside them this week, and go and do it. Send the message, make the call, give the gift, say the sentence of encouragement you have been meaning to say.

For worship. The Spirit who is the great Encourager, called alongside God’s people, made an ordinary Levite from Cyprus into a son of encouragement, and through him brought Paul into the church and Mark back into the ministry. Christ’s church is held together not only by apostles and preachers but by quiet givers and faithful encouragers, and every one of them is a gift from the God of all comfort, who comforts us in all our affliction so that we can comfort others.
verseByVerse.note: Cyprus was a large island in the eastern Mediterranean with a big Jewish community.

4.theology: The Sovereignty of God and Mission. The prayer of Acts 4:24–30 is a theology lecture compressed into seven verses. God is addressed as despotēs — Sovereign Lord, absolute Master — who made heaven and earth and everything in them. Herod and Pilate and the nations, in their opposition to Christ, did “whatever your hand and your plan had predestined to take place.” This is not fatalism; it is the Reformed doctrine of providence applied to history’s darkest moment. And the implication for mission is not paralysis but boldness: if God was sovereign over the crucifixion, he is sovereign over every threat to the gospel. The church does not need favourable conditions to advance the kingdom. It needs the Spirit and the Word. God provides both.
4.examples:
Then: A church only weeks old, under arrest, before the same council that crucified their Lord, with no legal protection, no political allies, no plan B — and they prayed for boldness and were given it. The shaking of the place was God’s receipt: prayer received, boldness granted.

Now: The church in every hostile culture faces the same fork: silence or speech, safety or boldness. The prayer of Acts 4 is still available. The God who shook that room has not grown quiet. He is still the Sovereign Lord who made heaven and earth. And he still grants boldness to those who ask for it — not because they deserve it, but because his Word must go out.

5.title: The Fear of the Lord
5.text: <sup>1</sup>But a man named Ananias, with his wife Sapphira, sold a piece of property, <sup>2</sup>and with his wife’s knowledge he kept back for himself some of the proceeds and brought only a part of it and laid it at the apostles’ feet. <sup>3</sup>But Peter said, “Ananias, why has Satan filled your heart to lie to the Holy Spirit and to keep back for yourself part of the proceeds of the land? <sup>4</sup>While it remained unsold, did it not remain your own? And after it was sold, was it not at your disposal? Why is it that you have contrived this deed in your heart? You have not lied to man but to God.” <sup>5</sup>When Ananias heard these words, he fell down and breathed his last. And great fear came upon all who heard of it. <sup>6</sup>The young men rose and wrapped him up and carried him out and buried him. <sup>7</sup>After an interval of about three hours his wife came in, not knowing what had happened. <sup>8</sup>And Peter said to her, “Tell me whether you sold the land for so much.” And she said, “Yes, for so much.” <sup>9</sup>But Peter said to her, “How is it that you have agreed together to test the Spirit of the Lord? Behold, the feet of those who have buried your husband are at the door, and they will carry you out.” <sup>10</sup>Immediately she fell down at his feet and breathed her last. When the young men came in they found her dead, and they carried her out and buried her beside her husband. <sup>11</sup>And great fear came upon the whole church and upon all who heard of these things. <sup>12</sup>Now many signs and wonders were regularly done among the people by the hands of the apostles. And they were all together in Solomon’s Portico. <sup>13</sup>None of the rest dared join them, but the people held them in high esteem. <sup>14</sup>And more than ever believers were added to the Lord, multitudes of both men and women, <sup>15</sup>so that they even carried out the sick into the streets and laid them on cots and mats, that as Peter came by at least his shadow might fall on some of them. <sup>16</sup>The people also gathered from the towns around Jerusalem, bringing the sick and those afflicted with unclean spirits, and they were all healed. <sup>17</sup>But the high priest rose up, and all who were with him (that is, the party of the Sadducees), and filled with jealousy <sup>18</sup>they arrested the apostles and put them in the public prison. <sup>19</sup>But during the night an angel of the Lord opened the prison doors and brought them out, and said, <sup>20</sup>“Go and stand in the temple and speak to the people all the words of this Life.” <sup>21</sup>And when they heard this, they entered the temple at daybreak and began to teach. Now when the high priest came, and those who were with him, they called together the council, all the senate of the people of Israel and sent to the prison to have them brought. <sup>22</sup>But when the officers came, they did not find them in the prison, so they returned and reported, <sup>23</sup>“We found the prison securely locked and the guards standing at the doors, but when we opened them we found no one inside.” <sup>24</sup>Now when the captain of the temple and the chief priests heard these words, they were greatly perplexed about them, wondering what this would come to. <sup>25</sup>And someone came and told them, “Look! The men whom you put in prison are standing in the temple and teaching the people.” <sup>26</sup>Then the captain with the officers went and brought them, but not by force, for they were afraid of being stoned by the people. <sup>27</sup>And when they had brought them, they set them before the council. And the high priest questioned them, <sup>28</sup>saying, “We strictly charged you not to teach in this name, yet here you have filled Jerusalem with your teaching, and you intend to bring this man’s blood upon us.” <sup>29</sup>But Peter and the apostles answered, “We must obey God rather than men. <sup>30</sup>The God of our fathers raised Jesus, whom you killed by hanging him on a tree. <sup>31</sup>God exalted him at his right hand as Leader and Savior, to give repentance to Israel and forgiveness of sins. <sup>32</sup>And we are witnesses to these things, and so is the Holy Spirit, whom God has given to those who obey him.” <sup>33</sup>When they heard this, they were enraged and wanted to kill them. <sup>34</sup>But a Pharisee in the council named Gamaliel, a teacher of the law held in honor by all the people, stood up and gave orders to put the men outside for a little while. <sup>35</sup>And he said to them, “Men of Israel, take care what you are about to do with these men. <sup>36</sup>For before these days Theudas rose up, claiming to be somebody, and a number of men, about four hundred, joined him. He was killed, and all who followed him were dispersed and came to nothing. <sup>37</sup>After him Judas the Galilean rose up in the days of the census and drew away some of the people after him. He too perished, and all who followed him were scattered. <sup>38</sup>So in the present case I tell you, keep away from these men and let them alone, for if this plan or this undertaking is of man, it will fail; <sup>39</sup>but if it is of God, you will not be able to overthrow them. You might even be found opposing God!” So they took his advice, <sup>40</sup>and when they had called in the apostles, they beat them and charged them not to speak in the name of Jesus, and let them go. <sup>41</sup>Then they left the presence of the council, rejoicing that they were counted worthy to suffer dishonor for the name. <sup>42</sup>And every day, in the temple and from house to house, they did not cease teaching and preaching that the Christ is Jesus.
5.overview:
After the bright picture of Barnabas comes a dark one. Ananias and his wife Sapphira sell property and give part of the price while pretending it is the whole, wanting the reputation of generosity without the cost. Peter tells Ananias he has lied not to men but to God, and Ananias falls dead; three hours later Sapphira repeats the lie and dies too. Great fear seizes the whole church, the first time Luke uses that word for the believers. The story echoes Achan, who secretly kept back plunder when Israel entered the promised land (Joshua 7): at the start of a new work of God, sin in the camp is judged severely.

Meanwhile the apostles perform many signs, the sick are carried into the streets in the hope that even Peter’s shadow will fall on them, and multitudes of men and women believe. Jealous, the high priest has the apostles jailed, but an angel opens the doors at night and tells them to go and preach in the temple. Brought before the council again, they answer, “We must obey God rather than men,” and proclaim the risen Jesus as Leader and Saviour. The council wants to kill them, but Gamaliel, the most respected Pharisee teacher of the day, advises caution: movements of human origin fail, as those of Theudas and Judas the Galilean did, but if this is from God they cannot stop it and may find themselves fighting God. The apostles are flogged and released, and leave rejoicing that they were counted worthy to suffer shame for the Name, and they keep teaching every day that Jesus is the Christ.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–16 — Holiness and Power in the Young Church
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: A man named Ananias and his wife Sapphira also sold a piece of property, but with her full knowledge he kept back part of the money and brought the rest to the apostles as if it were the whole. Peter asked him how he had let Satan fill his heart so that he lied to the Holy Spirit and kept back part of the price. The land was his to keep, and after selling it the money was at his disposal. Why had he thought of doing such a thing? He had lied not to people but to God. When Ananias heard this he fell down and died, and great fear came on everyone who heard. The young men wrapped his body, carried him out and buried him. About three hours later his wife came in, not knowing what had happened. Peter asked whether this was the price they got for the land, and she said yes. Peter asked how they could agree to test the Spirit of the Lord, and told her that the men who had buried her husband were at the door and would carry her out too. At once she fell down at his feet and died. The young men came in, found her dead, and buried her beside her husband. Great fear seized the whole church and all who heard. The apostles performed many signs and wonders among the people, and the believers all used to meet together in Solomon’s Colonnade. No one else dared join them, though the people held them in high regard. Yet more and more men and women believed in the Lord and were added to their number. People even brought the sick into the streets on beds and mats so that at least Peter’s shadow might fall on some as he passed. Crowds came from the towns around Jerusalem, bringing the sick and those troubled by impure spirits, and all of them were healed.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Holiness of God and the Danger of Hypocrisy

The deaths of Ananias and Sapphira stand in a recognisable biblical pattern: when God inaugurates something holy, the first sin against it is judged with startling swiftness. Nadab and Abihu at the dawn of the priesthood (Leviticus 10), Achan at Israel's entry into the land (Joshua 7), Uzzah as the ark comes home (2 Samuel 6), and here the first hypocrisy at the birth of the church. These are representative judgements — one public sample of what all sin deserves, set down once. They are not the rule; God's ordinary way is the patient kindness meant to lead to repentance (Romans 2:4), which is precisely why the rest of us are still breathing. A God who never enforced his own holiness would not be holy, and the gospel does not lower that holiness but satisfies it, so that those in Christ may come near to the Holy One with confidence. The second half of the section shows what such a God does with a church that has learned to tremble before him: he fills it, and multiplies it, and heals through it in the open street.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: A church only weeks old discovered that the Spirit who filled it also searched it — and that the same fear which drove off the hangers-on drew in multitudes.

Now: The pattern repeats wherever religious performance stands in for reality: the testimony allowed to run better than the facts, the prayer that warms when others are listening, the struggle described in the past tense because the present tense would cost too much. Two cautions belong with it. This chapter is not a lever for extracting money — Peter says the field and the proceeds were theirs. And the fear here came from what God did, not from what the leaders did; a congregation frightened of its elders has reproduced what this chapter killed, not what it created. The fear of God makes people honest. The fear of men is what made Ananias lie.

verseByVerse.quote: But a man named Ananias, with his wife Sapphira, sold a piece of property, and with his wife's knowledge he kept back for himself some of the proceeds and brought only a part of it and laid it at the apostles' feet.
verseByVerse.commentary:
But a man named Ananias, with his wife Sapphira, sold a piece of property, and with his wife’s knowledge he kept back for himself some of the proceeds and brought only a part of it and laid it at the apostles’ feet.

Meaning first. Acts 5 shows the church threatened from within and from without. From within, by deceit: Ananias and Sapphira lie to the Holy Spirit and die. From without, by persecution: the apostles are jailed, freed by an angel, flogged, and go away rejoicing. In both, God protects his church: by purifying it, and by preserving it. The chapter teaches the holiness of God, the reality of the Spirit’s presence among his people, and the strange joy of suffering for Christ. And it ends with the name the council would not say being spoken in every house in Jerusalem.

But a man named Ananias, with his wife Sapphira. Everything depends on the word Luke opens with. But. The paragraph before this one introduced a Levite from Cyprus called Joseph, whom the apostles nicknamed Barnabas, son of encouragement, who sold a field and laid the money at their feet (4:36–37). Luke names him, and then immediately names two other people who did the identical thing and were not the same at all. He has set them side by side deliberately. The outward act was indistinguishable: the same field sold, the same walk across the room, the same money on the same floor. Even the names are a sad irony. Ananias means the Lord is gracious; Sapphira means beautiful. Names that did not match their deeds.

Sold a piece of property, and with his wife’s knowledge he kept back for himself some of the proceeds. The verb is where this story actually begins. The word for kept back is nosphizomai, and it is not a common one. Outside this chapter the New Testament uses it once, of household slaves pilfering from their masters (Titus 2:10). But in the Greek Old Testament it turns up at one unforgettable place: Joshua 7:1, where Achan takes for himself some of what had been devoted to God at Jericho, hides it in his tent, and stands in the assembly the next morning as though nothing had happened, while Israel is defeated at Ai and nobody knows why. That is not an echo a reader has to strain for. Luke has reached for Achan’s own word. Israel had just crossed into the land, and the first sin inside the new order was a private theft concealed in public. The church has just crossed into its own new order, and here it is again, in the same vocabulary.

What they were really buying. Notice what they were after, because it was not money. They could have kept the whole field and sinned in nothing. They could have sold it and given a tenth openly and been thanked. What they wanted was something the honest options could not supply: the reputation of total surrender, at a price they had negotiated down in private. Barnabas had gone from a nobody to a name in one afternoon, and it is the easiest thing in the world to want that and to want it cheaply. So they arranged an appearance.

And brought only a part of it and laid it at the apostles’ feet. Pretending it was the whole. The laying of the money at the apostles’ feet was a public gesture in front of a watching room, and the gesture was the whole point. They did not steal from the poor. They bought applause with counterfeit currency and had it accepted at face value.

With his wife’s knowledge. It was not a moment’s weakness. Luke will not let that phrase pass, and Peter will come back to it (v. 9). Two people sat down together, discussed a figure, agreed what they would say, and rehearsed a story well enough that she could still deliver it three hours after he was dead. Every private sin has a moment where it could have been stopped by one person saying no. This one had two people in the room and neither of them said it. The marriage that should have been the safest place for an honest word became the place where the lie was made airtight.

The ordinary version. Before anyone comforts himself that this is an extreme case, measure it against the everyday form. The testimony that is allowed to stand a little better than the facts warrant. The prayer that lengthens and warms when other people are listening. The reply “we’ve been praying about that” when the last time you prayed about it was in March. The struggle described to a small group in the past tense because the present tense would cost too much. None of that is a felony, and none of it is what Ananias did on the scale he did it. But it is the same transaction: buying a reputation for a devotion you have not got, and paying in a currency you know to be false.

What it does not mean. This chapter has been misused for money more often than almost any other, and that must be guarded before the passage goes any further. It is not a warning about giving too little. Peter will say in two verses that the field was theirs and the proceeds were theirs, and no one had any claim on either. A church that produces Ananias and Sapphira to loosen a congregation’s grip on its wallet has inverted the passage exactly. The sin here was not withholding; it was pretending. And the pressure to perform generosity is nearer to what killed them than the withholding ever was.

Why would Luke put such an ugly story in the church’s golden age? Because he is an honest historian and a pastor. He has just painted the church at its most beautiful: one heart and soul, no needy person among them (4:32–35). He could have stopped there and left us a legend. Instead he shows that the first serious danger to the church came not from Rome or the Sanhedrin but from inside, from people who sat in the meetings and handled holy things. That is a mercy to us. It tells us not to be shocked when a church we love proves to have hypocrites in it, and not to imagine that any golden age was free of them. It also tells us where to look first when we look for the danger: in our own hearts.

In a sentence. A man named Ananias and his wife Sapphira sold property, and with her knowledge he kept back some of the money and laid only part at the apostles’ feet, as though it were the whole.

On a Tuesday. The temptation to look more generous, more prayerful, more spiritual than you really are is very old, and it is usually small. Catch one instance this week: the story you improved, the impression you let stand, the “I’ll pray for you” you never meant to keep. Put it right in the simplest way available. Correct the impression, keep the promise, or tell the truth next time it comes up. The cure for wanting a reputation you have not earned is to be content with being seen as you are.

For worship. Over against this scene stands the one Man whose outward life and inward heart were one and the same at every moment. Jesus never performed a devotion he did not have. When he gave, he gave the whole: not a portion of a field laid at men’s feet, but himself laid down for his people (Galatians 2:20). He kept nothing back. Blessed be the Son of God, who was exactly what he appeared to be, and who covers with his own wholehearted offering the half-hearted gifts of all who come to him.

parallels.desc: Achan keeps back what was devoted to God

verseByVerse.quote: But Peter said, "Ananias, why has Satan filled your heart to lie to the Holy Spirit and to keep back for yourself part of the proceeds of the land? While it remained unsold, did it not remain your own? And after it was sold, was it not at your disposal? Why is it that you have contrived this deed in your heart? You have not lied to man but to God."
verseByVerse.commentary:
But Peter said, “Ananias, why has Satan filled your heart to lie to the Holy Spirit and to keep back for yourself part of the proceeds of the land? While it remained unsold, did it not remain your own? And after it was sold, was it not at your disposal? Why is it that you have contrived this deed in your heart? You have not lied to man but to God.”

Why has Satan filled your heart to lie to the Holy Spirit? Peter’s Spirit-given discernment exposes the sin at once, and he names it precisely. It was not keeping the money, which was entirely their right. It was the lie: presenting part as the whole, a generosity they were not practising. And Peter means it really and personally: Satan genuinely instigated the sin. The image of being filled is the dark mirror of being filled with the Spirit (2:4; 4:8, 31; Ephesians 5:18). To be filled with the Spirit is not a warm feeling; it is to be so wholly taken up and governed by God that his presence controls one’s words and courage. Here the same idea runs the other way. Satan floods and masters Ananias’s heart, so that his tongue and his deed are ruled toward a lie. The whole church had just been filled with the Spirit (4:31); one man in it had let another tenant in.

Beside Judas. This sets Ananias next to Judas, into whom Satan entered to betray Jesus for money (Luke 22:3; John 13:2, 27). Behind the deceit stood the personal adversary, striking the newborn church from within at the very hour the gospel advanced with power. He had failed to stop it from outside with threats (4:21); he tried from inside with a lie. The echo of Achan, whose secret sin defiled Israel at the threshold of the land, belongs here too (Joshua 7).

Why is it that you have contrived this deed in your heart? Yet Satan’s hand is no excuse. In the same breath Peter asks why Ananias planned it. Both are true at once: Satan filled his heart, and Ananias schemed it in his own. Scripture holds these together everywhere (Luke 22:3 beside 22:22; Genesis 50:20; Acts 2:23). The tempter does not override the will; he inflames a heart already willing. As James says, each person is tempted when he is lured and enticed by his own desire (James 1:14). Ananias’s lie fed on his own covetousness and his craving for praise, and Satan fanned the flame. “The devil made me do it” is no excuse, and Peter offers none. The verb Peter uses means to set or lay down: the deed was put in place in the heart before it was done in the room. It was premeditated.

The world, the flesh and the devil. Is every sin, then, a special act of Satan like this? Scripture sets the proportions. Lying in particular bears his family likeness, for Jesus calls him a liar and the father of lies (John 8:44), which is why his hand is so visible here; and in a broad sense all sin serves his kingdom (Ephesians 2:2; 1 John 3:8). But the ordinary spring of sin is the human heart itself: out of the heart come evil thoughts and deceit (Mark 7:21–23), not, as here and with Judas, a direct filling by Satan. The old shorthand names three sources working together, and Paul gathers all three in a breath (Ephesians 2:2–3): the course of this world, the prince of the power of the air, and the passions of our flesh. The world is not the created order or the people God loves, but the whole system of human life organised against him, its values and applause pulling the heart away (1 John 2:15–16; James 4:4). The flesh is not the body but the fallen self, the inward bent toward sin we carry from Adam, warring against the Spirit (Galatians 5:16–17; Romans 8:7). Behind and through both the devil works. So we neither blame every sin on demons nor pretend he has no hand in it.

While it remained unsold, did it not remain your own? And after it was sold, was it not at your disposal? Their sin was not keeping part of the money but pretending to give it all. They were free to keep the land, or to keep the money. Giving was voluntary, and private property was not abolished (2:45). The church in Jerusalem was not a commune with compulsory pooling; it was a family in which people sold things as needs arose and gave freely. Peter’s two questions protect every Christian’s freedom to own and to give as he decides before God (2 Corinthians 9:7). God loves a cheerful giver, and he has no use for a pretended one.

You have not lied to man but to God. In verse 3 Ananias lied to the Holy Spirit; here, to God. The Holy Spirit is God. This is one of the clearest statements of the Spirit’s deity and personhood in Scripture. You cannot lie to a force or an influence; you lie to a person. And the Spirit dwelling in the church is the living God himself, so to deceive his people in their worship is to lie to him (1 Corinthians 3:16). At the heart of their sin was an attempt to deceive God: to parade a lie of wholehearted devotion before the One who reads the heart, as though he could be fooled. To try to fool God is to mock him, and God is not mocked (Galatians 6:7). He saw through the performance, and judged it. Where the text is silent we will not pretend: Luke tells us that Satan filled the heart and that Ananias contrived the deed, but not how that filling worked. We rest in what is revealed: real satanic instigation, real human guilt, and a holy God.

Can a true Christian be filled by Satan like this? Scripture never speaks of a believer, in whom the Holy Spirit dwells, being owned or possessed by Satan; the Spirit does not share his house as a lodger (1 John 4:4). But believers can certainly be deceived, tempted and used by him for a moment. Peter himself heard the words, get behind me, Satan, within minutes of his great confession (Matthew 16:23), and Paul warns Christians not to give the devil a foothold through unresolved anger (Ephesians 4:26–27). Whether Ananias was a true believer Luke does not say (see on vv. 5–6). The practical point is plain: do not leave a door open. Unconfessed resentment, a secret love of praise, a hidden sin that is being managed rather than fought, these are footholds. Close them by bringing them into the light.

In a sentence. Peter asked Ananias why he had let Satan fill his heart to lie to the Holy Spirit by keeping back some of the money, when the land and the money were his to keep, and told him he had lied not to men but to God.

On a Tuesday. Next time you catch yourself shading the truth to look better, ask Peter’s question of yourself: why? Not why it happened, but what you wanted. Name the desire underneath: approval, safety, being thought generous or spiritual. That desire is the foothold. Then remember who is present. The Spirit who dwells in God’s people hears every word spoken in the church foyer and the house group. Speak as one who knows he is listening.

For worship. The Holy Spirit is God: not a power to be borrowed, but the Lord himself, dwelling among his people and in them. He searches the depths of God (1 Corinthians 2:10), and he searches ours. And this holy, all-seeing Spirit has chosen to make his home in sinners washed by Christ’s blood, to be grieved by them and yet never to leave them (Ephesians 4:30). Glory to the Spirit of truth, who cannot be deceived and who will not abandon his temple.
verseByVerse.note: Their sin was not keeping part of the money but pretending to give it all. Lying to the Holy Spirit is lying to God.

verseByVerse.quote: When Ananias heard these words, he fell down and breathed his last. And great fear came upon all who heard of it. The young men rose and wrapped him up and carried him out and buried him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
When Ananias heard these words, he fell down and breathed his last. And great fear came upon all who heard of it. The young men rose and wrapped him up and carried him out and buried him.

When Ananias heard these words, he fell down and breathed his last. Notice where Luke puts the weight. He does not linger over Ananias; he tells us the effect: great fear came upon all who heard of it. That is the point of the scene. The death is unannounced. Peter pronounces no sentence and calls down no curse; he only exposes the sin. It is God’s act, not Peter’s punishment. And its result is a church that suddenly grasps whom it is dealing with. The Spirit among them is no benevolent force that winks at religious play-acting. He is the holy God himself.

Why so severe? Nearly every liar walks away still breathing. Why this one? Because Scripture shows a pattern: when God inaugurates something holy, the first sin against it is judged with startling swiftness. Nadab and Abihu at the dawn of the priesthood offered unauthorised fire and died (Leviticus 10:1–2). Achan died at Israel’s entry into the land (Joshua 7). Uzzah was struck as the ark came home (2 Samuel 6:6–7). And here is the first hypocrisy at the birth of the church. These are representative judgments: one public sample of what all sin deserves, set down once to stamp God’s holiness on his people and to keep a young, tender church from being poisoned at its core. Among those who are near me I will be sanctified, God said over Nadab and Abihu (Leviticus 10:3). Nearness to God raises the demand for reverence; it never lowers it.

Then why do the rest of us not fall dead at every lie? Because these are the exception, not the rule. God’s ordinary way is patient kindness, meant to lead us to repentance (Romans 2:4; Psalm 130:3). One Ananias, recorded for ever, teaches the whole church age: the lightning flashes once to light up the whole landscape. And for the believer the deepest answer is the cross. The judgment our sin deserves has already fallen on Christ. So the fear Luke records is not the terror that drives us from God but the awe that keeps us from trifling with him: the reverence of a people who have seen, close up, that their God is holy.

The young men rose and wrapped him up and carried him out and buried him. Verse 6 is easy to read past and should not be. Four verbs, no pause, and no funeral. Burial usually took place the same day in that climate, but in a Jewish household a death also set in motion days of formal mourning: the tearing of clothes, the wailing, the seven days of visitors, the family shut in with its grief. None of that happens. He is wrapped where he fell and is in the ground within hours, and the ordinary marks of honour for the dead are simply not given. Luke reports it without comment, which is itself a comment. The church did not stage a scandal, did not hold an inquiry, and did not honour him. It buried him, quietly and fast. And the men who carried him out came back, and three hours later were still there, and had to do it a second time.

Where Christians differ: was Ananias saved? Some think this proves he was never a believer, a false professor exposed like Achan; they point out that Satan had filled his heart (v. 3) and that his sin was a deliberate attempt to deceive the Holy Spirit. Others think a true believer can be disciplined by death without losing salvation, as Paul says of some at Corinth who were sick or had died, judged by the Lord so that they would not be condemned with the world (1 Corinthians 11:30–32; 5:5). Verdict: Scripture does not tell us, and we should not pretend to know. What is clear is that God takes sin in his church seriously, especially hypocrisy, and that he may discipline severely. It is not a pattern to expect in every case; it is a warning written at the church’s beginning.

Does God still strike people dead for sin today? He is free to, and Scripture shows he has done it more than once (Acts 12:23; 1 Corinthians 11:30). But the New Testament never teaches us to expect it, and we should never interpret a particular death, illness or accident as God’s verdict on someone’s hidden sin. Jesus explicitly forbade that kind of reasoning about the Galileans Pilate killed and the eighteen crushed by the tower in Siloam (Luke 13:1–5). His conclusion was not that they were worse sinners, but: unless you repent, you will all likewise perish. That is the right use of Acts 5 too. It is not for diagnosing other people’s funerals. It is for searching your own heart while there is time.

In a sentence. When Ananias heard this, he fell down dead, and great fear came over everyone who heard; and the young men wrapped him up, carried him out and buried him.

On a Tuesday. God is holy, and his grace is not permission to deceive. Walk before him in honesty, and when you sin, run to the light rather than from it. The safest place for a sinner is not hidden but confessed, for if we confess our sins he is faithful and just to forgive us (1 John 1:9).

For worship. The holiness that struck Ananias down is the same holiness that met our sin at Calvary, and there it did not flash once; it fell in full on the Son. The judgment every hypocrite deserves was borne by the one Man who was never a hypocrite. That is why the church still stands, and why sinners can still come near. Holy, holy, holy is the Lord, and holy is the Lamb who was slain, through whom a holy God can dwell among his people without consuming them.
verseByVerse.note: Burial usually took place the same day.

parallels.desc: Nadab and Abihu struck down

verseByVerse.quote: After an interval of about three hours his wife came in, not knowing what had happened. And Peter said to her, "Tell me whether you sold the land for so much." And she said, "Yes, for so much."
verseByVerse.commentary:
After an interval of about three hours his wife came in, not knowing what had happened. And Peter said to her, “Tell me whether you sold the land for so much.” And she said, “Yes, for so much.”

After an interval of about three hours his wife came in, not knowing what had happened. Three hours. Luke times it, and the interval is the most merciful stretch of Sapphira’s life.
