Somewhere in the city she is going about her day, and her husband has been dead for three hours, and nobody has come to tell her. Then she walks in through the door into a room where every person present knows exactly what has happened, and what she is about to say.

Tell me whether you sold the land for so much. Watch what Peter does, because it matters enormously and it is almost always missed. He does not accuse her. He does not tell her that her husband is dead, and he does not say what he already knows. He asks a question, and he makes it as easy to answer truthfully as a question can possibly be made. There is no trap in it. It is a door held open. God did not spring a trap on her. He gave her the last three hours and then he gave her the question.

Yes, for so much. She keeps to the lie. Two words in the Greek, and they are the sound of a rehearsed line. She does not hesitate, does not glance round the room, does not ask why she is being asked. She has the figure ready because they had agreed the figure. And notice the pressure she was not under: her husband was not standing beside her. Nobody was watching her to see whether she would hold the line. She could have broken the agreement at no cost to a marriage that had, unknown to her, already ended. She kept it anyway, alone and freely, which is precisely why Peter’s next words treat her as a principal and not as a wife who was dragged along.

A wife and her husband’s sin. This passage speaks directly to something on which women have been badly counselled, and it is worth saying plainly. A wife is nowhere in Scripture required to follow her husband into sin, and a husband’s headship has never included the authority to make a liar of her. Headship in Scripture is self-giving love modelled on Christ’s love for the church (Ephesians 5:25), and Christ never asks his bride to sin. The principle is the same one the apostles will state to the highest court in the land later in this very chapter: we must obey God rather than men (v. 29). If that holds against a Sanhedrin, it holds against a husband, and it holds in a kitchen. Scripture gives the picture: Abigail went round her husband’s ruinous folly, acted without his knowledge to stop it, and is commended for it in the text and by David himself (1 Samuel 25). Sapphira had the same road open and did not take it. Her tragedy is not that she submitted; it is that she agreed.

The sin only two can commit. A shared lie is far more durable than a private one, because each partner is now the other’s evidence that it is not so bad. Neither has to face it alone, and so neither ever faces it. Whatever conversation Ananias and Sapphira had in the days before this one, it ended with both of them steadier in the deception than either would have been by himself. Three hours were given to break it, and she spent them keeping her side of the bargain.

What if refusing my husband would put me in danger? Then the issue is no longer submission at all but safety, and Scripture never asks a wife to stay in harm’s way. A husband who threatens, intimidates or harms his wife has abandoned the Christ-like headship Scripture describes; abuse is never to be tolerated or covered by a church. If you are afraid of what will happen if you say no, tell someone you trust today: a pastor or elder, a wise friend, and if you are in danger, the police. Getting safe is not rebellion. Abigail acted to save lives, and was praised for it. In ordinary disagreements, a godly wife can refuse to sin respectfully and gently, as Sapphira could have done, and leave the rest with God.

In a sentence. About three hours later his wife came in, unaware of what had happened, and when Peter asked whether they had sold the land for that amount, she said yes.

On a Tuesday. God often gives us a chance to come clean, and it frequently arrives as an ordinary question: did you finish that, did you say that, is that the whole story? When the question comes, treat it as Sapphira’s open door. Answer it truly, even if the truth costs the impression you have spent a long time building. And if you are married, decide now, together, that your marriage will be the one place where a lie cannot live.

For worship. The God of this scene is the God who waits three hours, and three years, and thirty, holding the door open with a question. He is not quick to trap; he is long-suffering, not wishing that any should perish (2 Peter 3:9). Every honest moment in a Christian’s life is the fruit of his patience. Praise him for the questions he still asks us, and for the door that stands open until it is closed.

verseByVerse.quote: But Peter said to her, "How is it that you have agreed together to test the Spirit of the Lord? Behold, the feet of those who have buried your husband are at the door, and they will carry you out." Immediately she fell down at his feet and breathed her last. When the young men came in they found her dead, and they carried her out and buried her beside her husband.
verseByVerse.commentary:
But Peter said to her, “How is it that you have agreed together to test the Spirit of the Lord? Behold, the feet of those who have buried your husband are at the door, and they will carry you out.” Immediately she fell down at his feet and breathed her last. When the young men came in they found her dead, and they carried her out and buried her beside her husband.

How is it that you have agreed together to test the Spirit of the Lord? Her answer is still in the air when Peter names what she has done, and he names it as a partnership. You have agreed together. The verb is symphōneō, to sound together, the word behind our symphony: two instruments in tune. It is one of the loveliest things about a marriage, that two people can come to one mind about something without needing to argue it out, and here it is, working perfectly, in the service of a lie. Whatever else was wrong in that house, they were not at odds. They had harmony, and they had used it to make the deception airtight. A spouse’s calling is to help the other toward God, never away from him.

Testing God. What they had agreed to do, Peter says, was to test the Spirit of the Lord. That phrase unlocks the whole episode, and the English word can mislead. Testing here has nothing to do with examining whether something works, the way a man tests a rope before he trusts his weight to it. The word (peirazō) means to put God to the proof: to presume on him, to dare him, to find out whether he is really watching and will really act. Israel did it at Massah, demanding water and asking, is the LORD among us or not? (Exodus 17:2, 7; Psalm 95:9). It is the one temptation Jesus refused outright on the temple pinnacle, quoting the law back at the tempter: you shall not put the Lord your God to the test (Deuteronomy 6:16; Matthew 4:7). Ananias and Sapphira had, in effect, laid a wager that the Spirit would not notice, or would notice and not mind. They were not sceptics; they had watched the Spirit fall and had seen the healings. They simply did not believe he was paying attention to them. They found that he was.

Behold, the feet of those who have buried your husband are at the door, and they will carry you out. Peter tells her something that no wife should ever have to hear from a stranger, and he tells it in the same breath as her own sentence. She learns she is a widow and that she is about to follow him, in one sentence, standing up, in front of a room. It is worth insisting again on what Peter is and is not doing. He pronounces no penalty. He passes no sentence. He has no power to strike anybody and claims none. He knows by the Spirit what is about to happen and reports it, the way a man reports weather he can see coming. The judgment in this chapter is God’s, twice, and both times the apostle only says out loud what is already true.

Immediately she fell down at his feet and breathed her last. Luke’s last detail is the one that ought to be felt. Go back eight verses and see what happened on that spot: her husband laid the money at the apostles’ feet (v. 2). That was the whole object of the exercise: that square of floor, the public gesture, the watching room. It is the exact spot where she falls. The place they had wanted to be seen is the place she is carried from.

And buried her beside her husband. The young men come back in and do again what they had done three hours earlier. Together in the planning, together in the rehearsing, together in the ground. Luke does not moralise over it, and the tidiness of his sentence is more frightening than any commentary could be. As for why this sin met so immediate a judgment, when sin is not ordinarily repaid on the spot, see on vv. 5–6: God’s normal way is patient forbearance meant to lead to repentance, and this is the exception recorded once so that it need not be repeated.

Terrible but not arbitrary. It is right to find the passage terrible. It would be wrong to find it arbitrary. God was not defending his dignity against an insult; he was defending a church only weeks old against the one thing that kills churches from the inside, which is people who have learned to perform a devotion they do not have and to be admired for it. Everything the early chapters describe, the one heart and soul, the goods held loosely, the apostles’ teaching received as the word of God, depends on the assumption that when a Christian says a thing, it is so. Two people set out to prove that assumption could be exploited. The Lord of the church answered in a way that meant nobody tried it again for a very long time.

What does testing God look like today? Usually it is quiet. It is sinning on purpose because you are sure you will be forgiven afterwards. It is taking a risk God has warned against and daring him to protect you. It is living as though he does not see what happens on a phone at midnight, or in the accounts, or in a marriage behind closed doors. It is also, at the other end, demanding that God prove himself on your terms before you will trust him. The cure is the one Jesus used: answer the temptation with the word of God, and remember that the Lord who sees in secret is the same Lord who loves you. You do not need to test a Father you can trust.

In a sentence. Peter asked her why they had agreed together to test the Spirit of the Lord, and told her that those who had buried her husband were at the door to carry her out; she fell dead at his feet, and the young men buried her beside her husband.

On a Tuesday. Husbands and wives: agree together to honour God, never to deceive him. Ask each other one plain question this week: is there anything we are agreeing not to talk about? Then talk about it. And when one of you proposes something you both know is not right, let the other be the voice that says no. That is love, not disloyalty.

For worship. The Spirit of the Lord is not mocked, and he is not absent. He notices. That is a terror to the hypocrite and the deepest comfort to the believer, because the same Spirit who saw through Sapphira’s rehearsed line also sees every secret prayer, every hidden tear, every unseen act of faithfulness. Nothing done for Christ is lost on him. Glory to the God who sees, and who rewards in the open what was done in secret (Matthew 6:6).

parallels.desc: do not put the LORD your God to the test

verseByVerse.quote: And great fear came upon the whole church and upon all who heard of these things.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And great fear came upon the whole church and upon all who heard of these things.

And great fear came upon the whole church. Twice now Luke has stopped the narrative to tell us the effect rather than the event: great fear came upon all who heard (v. 5), and now great fear came upon the whole church. He is not reporting an atmosphere in passing. He is telling us what the episode was for.

And upon all who heard of these things. He adds a second circle. It did not stay indoors. Jerusalem heard, outsiders as well as believers, and Jerusalem drew its own conclusions about what sort of company this was.

The first time the church is called the church. Notice the word Luke chooses at this exact moment. This is the first time in Acts that he calls the believers the church (ekklēsia): the assembly, the called-out people. In the Greek Old Testament the word was used of Israel assembled before God at Sinai and in the temple; now it is the people of the Messiah. Luke does not use it at Pentecost, with the wind and the fire and the three thousand, nor in the golden paragraph about having all things in common. He uses it here, in the silence after two funerals, in a room that has just learned what it is living with. To be the church is, before anything else, to reckon with the holiness of the God who has moved in. Fittingly, the word appears with fear: the church is God’s holy temple (1 Corinthians 3:16–17).

The soil of the church’s life. This fear is not the enemy of the church’s life; it is the soil of it. Watch what grows in the next three verses: signs and wonders, a people all together in Solomon’s Portico, and more than ever believers added to the Lord, multitudes of men and women. The awe did not freeze the church. It purified it and then filled it. A community that takes God seriously is one the Spirit is pleased to inhabit and the watching world is drawn to: sobered and attracted at the same moment, which is a combination no institution has ever been able to manufacture. A church without the fear of God is not a happier church, but a weaker one.

The man at the hearth. This is not cringing terror that runs from God, nor the thin modern respect that trembles at nothing, but reverent awe that draws near in love and yet will not trifle: the beginning of wisdom (Proverbs 9:10; 2 Corinthians 7:1; Hebrews 12:28–29). Picture a man at his hearth on a winter night. He loves the fire, pulls his chair as close as he can bear, and would not dream of putting his hand into it, because he knows perfectly well what it is. He is not afraid of the fire in the sense of wanting to be further from it. He is nearer to it than anyone else in the house. That is the fear of the Lord, and Luke will later name it as the very mark of a healthy church: walking in the fear of the Lord and in the comfort of the Holy Spirit (9:31). Both, in one sentence, without embarrassment.

Am I Ananias, if I know I am not what I appear to be? There is a particular person who reads Acts 5 and lies awake: who knows he is not what he appears to be in his church, who can name the exaggeration and the unconfessed thing, and who now half expects the floor to open. That fear deserves a straight answer rather than a soothing one. Ananias was not caught out by a God waiting to pounce. He engineered a lie in the presence of God in advance, with a partner, and was given a question at the end of it that he could have answered honestly. So was she. Neither of them wanted to be found out; both wanted to be admired more than they wanted to be true. A man who is trembling because he longs to be genuine and knows he is not yet is describing an entirely different condition, and the trembling itself is the evidence. The Spirit does not produce that ache in people he is about to strike down. He produces it in people he is not going to leave alone. And the door out of it is open and has always been open: say the true thing, to God first and then to whoever needs to hear it, and the whole weight of it goes. No one who confesses his sin and trusts Christ is in their position.

If God is this holy, how can I come near him at all? Only through Christ, and through Christ, with confidence. The fire at the hearth is not safer because you keep your distance; it is safe because someone has made a way to sit beside it. Jesus is the way. His blood has opened a new and living way into the very presence of God, so that we may draw near with a true heart in full assurance of faith (Hebrews 10:19–22). The writer to the Hebrews puts the two together just as Luke does: let us offer acceptable worship, with reverence and awe, for our God is a consuming fire (Hebrews 12:28–29), and let us with confidence draw near to the throne of grace (4:16). Reverence and confidence are not opposites. They are the two hands with which a forgiven sinner holds on to a holy God.

What the church learned that day. What Ananias and Sapphira had lost was precisely this fear, and it is possible to lose it in a room full of miracles. The church, seeing them lose it, learned it. That is the mercy hidden in the hardest paragraph in Acts: two people were the last to learn what the whole church learned that day, and everyone else got it for nothing.

In a sentence. Great fear came over the whole church and over everyone who heard about these things.

On a Tuesday. Before you next walk into a church service, pause at the door for ten seconds and remember whose house you are entering and who is present among his people. Then go in, not stiff and anxious, but glad and careful, the way you would enter the home of someone you love and greatly respect. Let that same awareness follow you home on Monday: the God who is present in the assembly is present at your desk.

For worship. Serve the LORD with fear, and rejoice with trembling (Psalm 2:11). The God who called this people his assembly is the God before whom Israel trembled at Sinai, and he has come nearer than Sinai ever allowed: he has come to dwell in his church by his Spirit. That nearness is the reason for the fear, and it is the reason for the joy. Blessed be the holy God who has made sinners his temple and his assembly, and who keeps his people pure because he loves them.
verseByVerse.note: This is the first time Acts uses the word “church.”

verseByVerse.quote: Now many signs and wonders were regularly done among the people by the hands of the apostles. And they were all together in Solomon's Portico.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Now many signs and wonders were regularly done among the people by the hands of the apostles. And they were all together in Solomon’s Portico.

Now many signs and wonders were regularly done among the people by the hands of the apostles. God answers the prayer of 4:30, where the church had asked him to stretch out his hand to heal and to grant signs and wonders through the name of Jesus. And the words themselves reveal their purpose. A sign points beyond itself; a wonder astonishes. They were never ends in themselves. They were meant to authenticate the message and its messengers: God’s seal on the apostolic gospel. Scripture says so repeatedly. The miracles were the signs of a true apostle (2 Corinthians 12:12). God bore witness to the gospel by signs and wonders and various miracles (Hebrews 2:3–4). The Lord bore witness to the word of his grace, granting signs and wonders to be done by their hands (14:3). Even Jesus’ signs were written so that you may believe (John 20:31). The wonder was the wrapping; the word was the gift. That is why Jesus rebuked those who craved signs for their own sake (Matthew 12:39).

By the hands of the apostles. Luke is careful about whose hands. The signs in these chapters are done by the apostles, and Paul could call them the marks of an apostle precisely because they marked out the men whom Christ had sent. The church prayed; the apostles’ hands were the instruments; the risen Christ was the healer (3:6, 16; 9:34).

Where Christians differ: have the sign gifts ceased? Many Christians, called continuationists, believe that the gifts of healing, tongues and prophecy continue in the church today. They point out that 1 Corinthians 12–14 was written to an ordinary church, that Paul urges believers to earnestly desire the spiritual gifts (1 Corinthians 14:1), and that no verse says plainly that the gifts would cease before Christ returns. The historic Reformed church has held that these apostolic sign gifts have ceased, and its case is drawn from Scripture, not mere observation. The signs marked out the apostles (2 Corinthians 12:12), and the apostles were a foundation laid once: the church is built on the foundation of the apostles and prophets (Ephesians 2:20), and a foundation is laid only once. Their office could not be handed on, for its men had to be eyewitnesses of the risen Christ, and Paul calls himself last of all (1 Corinthians 15:8). The revelation the signs authenticated is complete: the faith once for all delivered to the saints (Jude 3). Once the foundation was laid and the message set down in Scripture, the credentials that attested the foundation-layers had served their purpose, like scaffolding taken down once the building stands. Verdict: the cessationist reading is the more likely one: the apostolic sign gifts, as standing credentials of new revelation, belonged to the foundation age and have ceased. This is held charitably. Our continuationist brothers love the same Christ and the same Bible, and many of them are at least as zealous for Scripture’s sufficiency as we are.

Two honest qualifications. First, no verse says outright that miracles will cease when the apostles die. The certain ground is the purpose of the signs; the timing of their ceasing is a strong inference from that purpose, joined to the close of the apostolic age and the completed canon, not a single proof text. Paul does say that tongues and prophecy will pass away (1 Corinthians 13:8–10), though believers differ over when the perfect comes. Second, this does not mean God no longer works miracles. He remains free to heal and to act wonderfully in answer to prayer, and he often does. What ceased is the apostolic sign gift as a standing credential of new revelation, not God’s power or his nearness.

Does that mean I should not pray for healing? Not at all. Pray, and pray boldly. James tells the sick to call the elders of the church to pray over them, anointing with oil, and promises that the prayer of faith will save the one who is sick (James 5:14–15). God answers such prayers, sometimes with healing that doctors cannot explain, sometimes through medicine, sometimes by giving grace to bear what he does not remove (2 Corinthians 12:8–9). The cessationist conviction is not that God has stopped healing; it is that no one today holds an apostle’s gift to heal at will, and that no new revelation is being added to Scripture. Ask your Father freely, and trust his answer.

And they were all together in Solomon’s Portico. Solomon’s Portico was a long, covered colonnade, a roofed walkway of great columns, along the east side of the temple’s outer court. Tradition linked it to Solomon, though it stood in Herod’s temple. It was a well-known public teaching place: Jesus had walked there (John 10:23), and Peter had preached there after healing the lame man (3:11). That the believers met there all together is striking. They were not huddled in hiding but gathered openly in the most public religious space in Jerusalem, in the temple’s very shadow. The holy, fearless church stood in plain sight.

In a sentence. The apostles regularly did many signs and wonders among the people, and the believers all met together in Solomon’s Portico.

On a Tuesday. Your faith does not rest on a miracle you have seen but on the word the miracles confirmed. When you read the Gospels and Acts this week, read them as God’s attested record: he signed it with signs. And do not hide your faith in corners. The first Christians met where everyone could see them. Let someone at work see you are a Christian, gently and without apology.

For worship. God confirmed his word through the apostles, and their witness is the foundation on which your faith now stands. The risen Christ stretched out his hand through theirs, so that the lame walked and the sick were healed, and then he gave us the account in Scripture, complete and sufficient. Praise the Lord who does not leave his word unattested, and who has built his church on a foundation that will never need to be laid again.
verseByVerse.note: Solomon’s Portico was a covered colonnade on the east side of the temple courts.

verseByVerse.quote: None of the rest dared join them, but the people held them in high esteem.
verseByVerse.commentary:
None of the rest dared join them, but the people held them in high esteem.

None of the rest dared join them. The rest is a fair puzzle. It can hardly mean true believers, who had already gladly joined, yet plain unbelievers would not be joining the church anyway. The word join (kollasthai) means to glue oneself closely. So the rest are best understood as the fringe: the half-hearted, the curious, the would-be hangers-on who in a less sobered moment might have attached themselves to so admired and powerful a movement for the prestige or the perks. After Ananias and Sapphira, no one dared. The community’s fearful holiness (vv. 5, 11) had raised the cost of insincere belonging to terrifying clarity: you do not glue yourself to this people for mixed motives. Commentators differ on the rest, but this reading, straight out of the Ananias episode, is the most natural.

Two sides of one coin. This verse and the next belong together. Verse 13: the nominal and the false no longer dared press in. Verse 14: yet more than ever believers were added. The fear screened out the pretenders while the Spirit kept adding the genuine. The church was purified and multiplied at once.

But the people held them in high esteem. They respected them from a distance. And this is worth pausing over, because the church’s public welcome runs hot and cold through Acts: esteemed here, arrested a few verses on (vv. 17–18), and soon Stephen stoned amid great persecution (chapters 7–8). Is there a pattern? Several, though no rigid formula. First, the fault line often runs between the common people and the authorities: crowds admired the apostles while threatened rulers persecuted them, and the people’s esteem actually shielded them, for the officers dared use no force, afraid of being stoned by the people (v. 26). Early persecution is mostly top down. Second, public favour is real but fickle. The same city can cheer and then turn, as Hosanna became Crucify. Third, both favour and hostility serve God’s purposes and come from his hand. He grants seasons of favour to open doors (2:47) and permits persecution to scatter the seed and spread the word (8:1–4).

Neither intoxicated nor crushed. So the believer should be neither intoxicated by esteem nor crushed by opposition. Scripture holds both. When a man’s ways please the LORD, he makes even his enemies to be at peace with him (Proverbs 16:7); yet all who desire to live a godly life in Christ Jesus will be persecuted (2 Timothy 3:12). Esteem is a gift, to be received humbly and spent for Christ. Persecution is the long-run lot of faithful witness (John 15:20). Both, in God’s hands, advance the same kingdom.

Is it wrong to want my church to be well thought of? No; it is right to want it, as long as you want it on the right terms. Paul wanted elders to be well thought of by outsiders (1 Timothy 3:7), and Peter wanted Christians to live such good lives among unbelievers that they would see their good deeds and glorify God (1 Peter 2:12). What is wrong is buying respect by hiding what is distinctive: softening the gospel, dropping holiness, or becoming so much like the world that nobody could be offended. The esteem in this verse came to a church that was holy, honest and unashamed of Christ. That is the only kind of good reputation worth having, and it is one God may give or withhold as he pleases.

In a sentence. None of the others dared to join them, though the people thought highly of them.

On a Tuesday. A holy church may be respected and even feared before it is joined, and that is better than a church that is joined because it is taken lightly. If you are drifting at the edge of a church, neither in nor out, this verse is a kind invitation to decide. Christ does not want hangers-on; he wants disciples. If you belong to him, belong to his people wholeheartedly.

For worship. The church in this verse is admired and feared at once, and that combination reflects its Lord. Jesus was the most attractive and the most unsettling man who ever lived: crowds pressed to hear him, and many turned back when they understood what he asked. He is both the Lamb and the Lion. Praise the Christ whose holiness makes pretenders keep their distance and whose grace makes sinners run to him.

verseByVerse.quote: And more than ever believers were added to the Lord, multitudes of both men and women,
verseByVerse.commentary:
And more than ever believers were added to the Lord, multitudes of both men and women,

And more than ever believers were added to the Lord. This is the sentence that ought to surprise us and rarely does. Two people have dropped dead in the meeting. The city has heard about it. Nobody outside dares attach himself to this movement casually any more (v. 13). And the result is not decline. More than ever believers were added to the Lord. The comparative is deliberate: more than before the deaths, not fewer. Holiness did not shrink the church; it grew it.

Against modern instinct. Everything in our instinct says that is the wrong way round. We assume a church grows by lowering the temperature: by being easier to belong to, less demanding, less strange, more like the surrounding culture with a religious accent. Luke reports the opposite. When it became unmistakably clear that the God in that room was real and was not to be handled carelessly, the pretenders stopped coming and everyone else started. The two movements in verses 13 and 14 are one movement: the fear screened out the casual and the Spirit kept adding the genuine. A church can be crowded and thin at the same time, and there is a kind of clarity that costs a congregation its hangers-on and gains it a city.

Not a licence for severity. The distinction matters, because it has been abused. The fear in Acts 5 came from something God did, not from something the leadership did. Peter did not strike anyone, threaten anyone, or run a campaign of discipline; he asked two honest questions and God did the rest. A church where people are frightened of the elders, watch their words in the foyer, and cannot admit a struggle without consequences has not reproduced this chapter. It has produced the very thing this chapter killed: a community where everyone performs. The fear of God makes people honest. The fear of men is what made Ananias lie.

Added to the Lord. Then the phrase worth dwelling on: they were added to the Lord. Not to the church, not to the movement, not to a register. Luke could have written either, and wrote neither. What happens when a person is converted is that he is joined to a Person, and membership among the people follows because they belong to him too. Anyone who has ever wondered whether he is in because he signed something, attends something, or is liked by someone has the answer here. The attachment that counts was made to the Lord himself, and it will therefore outlast every congregation any of us ever belongs to. And it was God who did the adding: the Lord added to their number day by day those who were being saved (2:47). The church grows by his gathering, not by its marketing.

Multitudes of both men and women. Luke counts the women. He says it as a matter of course, in a world where a crowd was ordinarily numbered by its men, and he does it repeatedly (8:12; 16:13–15; 17:4, 12). At Pentecost Peter had stood up and read out Joel’s promise that God would pour out his Spirit on sons and daughters, on male and female servants alike (2:17–18). A few weeks later Luke writes the growth figures, and the promise is simply showing in the arithmetic. The gospel was for both alike, and both alike were added to the Lord.

So will a strict church always grow? No, and this verse does not promise it. Churches have been holy and small for generations, and faithful churches have shrunk under persecution. Numbers are in God’s hands, not ours; Paul planted and Apollos watered, but God gave the growth (1 Corinthians 3:6). What this verse forbids is the opposite assumption: that holiness is a hindrance to growth and must be traded away for it. Our task is to be faithful, honest and unashamed of Christ, and to leave the arithmetic to the Lord who adds.

In a sentence. More and more believers were added to the Lord, crowds of both men and women.

On a Tuesday. If you are a Christian, you were added to the Lord himself, not merely enrolled in an organisation. Let that steady you on the days when church life disappoints you. And pray for your church this week, not that it would become easier to join, but that it would become holier and more full of Christ, so that the right people are drawn and the Lord adds whom he will.

For worship. Purity and growth go together in God’s hands, because the one who purifies the church is the same Lord who gathers it. The Good Shepherd knows his sheep and calls them by name, and they come (John 10:3, 16). Every believer in that Jerusalem crowd, every man and every woman, was a sheep he had gone looking for. Praise the Lord of the harvest, who adds to his people day by day, and loses none whom the Father has given him (John 6:39).

verseByVerse.quote: so that they even carried out the sick into the streets and laid them on cots and mats, that as Peter came by at least his shadow might fall on some of them. The people also gathered from the towns around Jerusalem, bringing the sick and those afflicted with unclean spirits, and they were all healed.
verseByVerse.commentary:
so that they even carried out the sick into the streets and laid them on cots and mats, that as Peter came by at least his shadow might fall on some of them. The people also gathered from the towns around Jerusalem, bringing the sick and those afflicted with unclean spirits, and they were all healed.

So that they even carried out the sick into the streets and laid them on cots and mats, that as Peter came by at least his shadow might fall on some of them. The healing ministry has reached a scale that draws the whole Jerusalem region. Ancient people often believed that a person’s shadow carried something of his power. Luke does not say the shadow healed anyone; he reports what people hoped. This is popular faith expressing itself in folk terms, and God was gracious to that imperfect faith, as with the woman who touched the fringe of Jesus’ garment (Luke 8:44) and the handkerchiefs carried from Paul (19:11–12). The power was God’s, not Peter’s shadow.

The people also gathered from the towns around Jerusalem. The word spreads beyond the city, as Jesus said it would: Jerusalem first, then Judea, then Samaria, then the end of the earth (1:8). The ripples are already reaching the villages.

Bringing the sick and those afflicted with unclean spirits. This raises the hard subject of the demonic, and here we should say only what Scripture tells us. Unclean spirits are real, personal, evil spirit beings, what the Gospels equally call demons, using the two terms interchangeably (Mark 5:2, 12–15; 7:25–26). They are not mere symbols, nor simply an ancient label for illness. The New Testament treats them as intelligent beings with will and speech, part of the kingdom of Satan (Matthew 12:24–26), commonly understood as fallen angels (Revelation 12:9; 2 Peter 2:4). Unclean marks their nature: they are defiling, the very opposite of the holiness of God. They can oppress and torment, and at times control a person, with effects both physical, such as muteness, convulsions and unnatural strength (Matthew 9:32–33; Mark 5:3–4; 9:18), and inward, the torment of mind and soul (Mark 5:5). But Scripture does not blame every sickness on demons. It deliberately lists the sick and those afflicted with unclean spirits as two distinct groups, here and in Mark 1:32–34. So we are neither to deny the demonic nor to see a demon behind every illness.

Their relation to Christ. What Scripture stresses above all is how they stand before Jesus. The unclean spirits recognise him and tremble (Mark 1:24; James 2:19). They are utterly subject to his authority and to his name on the lips of his servants (Luke 10:17; Acts 16:18). They flee before the advancing kingdom: if it is by the Spirit of God that I cast out demons, Jesus said, then the kingdom of God has come upon you (Matthew 12:28). At the cross he disarmed the rulers and authorities and put them to open shame, triumphing over them (Colossians 2:15). As for the rest, how exactly a spirit afflicts, the line between oppression and possession, why some and not others, Scripture is reticent, and we will not pretend to know more than it tells us. It gives us enough to take the reality seriously, never to fear it, and to look only to the Conqueror: he who is in you is greater than he who is in the world (1 John 4:4).

And they were all healed. All, as in Jesus’ own ministry (Luke 4:40; 6:19). Luke’s summaries of healing are consistently comprehensive. It was an extraordinary season. The kingdom had arrived, creation was being restored, and a preview of the new creation was visible in the streets of Jerusalem. On the purpose of such healings as signs, given to authenticate the apostolic message, and the question whether these gifts continue, see on v. 12.

Where Christians differ: relics and holy objects. Some have used verses like this to support venerating relics or objects linked with saints. Verdict: Luke reports; he does not prescribe. The healing came from the risen Christ, who was confirming his apostles’ message. The New Testament never teaches believers to seek power through objects, shadows or relics, and the apostles would have been horrified to be venerated (14:14–15). Look to Christ, not to his servants or their belongings.

Should we expect healing through objects or special people today? No. Peter’s shadow is the description of a unique moment, not a method to copy. Prayer cloths sent in the post, anointed water, a celebrity healer whose touch is said to carry power: none of these has a promise behind it, and the danger of superstition, and of people being exploited when they are most desperate, is real. God still heals in answer to prayer, and the ordinary means he has given are prayer, the elders of the church, and medicine received with thanks (James 5:14–15; 1 Timothy 5:23). Bring your sick to Christ directly. You do not need anyone’s shadow.

Can a Christian be possessed by a demon? A true Christian is indwelt by the Holy Spirit and belongs to Christ, bought with a price (1 Corinthians 6:19–20). Scripture nowhere describes a believer being owned or controlled by a demon, and it assures us that the evil one does not touch the one born of God (1 John 5:18). But believers are attacked. They are tempted, accused, and oppressed in their minds, which is why we are told to put on the whole armour of God and to resist the devil, who will flee (Ephesians 6:10–18; James 4:7). If you are troubled by dark fears, do not go looking for a specialist in exorcism. Go to Christ in prayer, fill your mind with Scripture, tell your pastor, and see a doctor as well, because much that feels spiritual is also bodily, and God uses both kinds of help.

In a sentence. People carried the sick into the streets on beds and mats, hoping that at least Peter’s shadow might fall on some of them as he passed, and crowds came from the towns around Jerusalem, bringing the sick and those troubled by unclean spirits, and all of them were healed.

On a Tuesday. God is gracious even to imperfect faith, and that should encourage anyone whose faith feels confused or small. But do not stay there. Fix your faith on Christ himself, not on a method, a place or a person. When you pray for someone sick this week, pray to the Lord who healed through Peter, and leave the outcome in his hands.

For worship. Behind the shadow in the street stood the Lord of all the spirits and all the sicknesses, and none of them could stand before him. Every one of those healings was a small foretaste of the day when he will wipe away every tear, and death shall be no more, neither mourning nor crying nor pain (Revelation 21:4). The demons tremble at his name; the sick are restored at his word. Glory to the risen Christ, who triumphed over every power of darkness at the cross, and who will one day make all things new.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The high priest and his Sadducee allies, filled with jealousy, arrested the apostles and put them in the public jail. But during the night an angel of the Lord opened the prison doors, brought them out and told them to go, stand in the temple courts and tell the people all about this new life. At daybreak they did so. When the high priest convened the full council and sent for the prisoners, the officers found the jail securely locked with guards at the doors but no one inside. While the leaders were puzzling over this, someone reported that the men were standing in the temple teaching the people. The captain went with his officers and brought them, without force, fearing the crowd would stone them. The high priest reminded them of the strict order not to teach in this name, and accused them of filling Jerusalem with their teaching and trying to make the leaders guilty of this man’s blood. Peter and the apostles replied that they must obey God rather than human beings. The God of their ancestors raised Jesus, whom the leaders killed by hanging him on a cross; God exalted him to his right hand as Prince and Saviour, to bring Israel to repentance and forgive their sins. The apostles are witnesses, and so is the Holy Spirit, whom God gives to those who obey him. Furious, the council wanted to put them to death. But Gamaliel, a Pharisee and respected teacher of the law, had the men put outside and warned the council to be careful. Theudas had claimed to be somebody and gathered about four hundred men, but he was killed and his followers scattered; Judas the Galilean led a revolt at the time of the census and he too perished. So they should leave these men alone: if their plan is of human origin it will fail, but if it is from God they will not be able to stop them and may find themselves fighting against God. The council agreed, had the apostles flogged, ordered them not to speak in Jesus’ name, and let them go. The apostles left rejoicing that they had been counted worthy of suffering disgrace for the Name, and day after day, in the temple courts and from house to house, they never stopped teaching and proclaiming the good news that Jesus is the Messiah.
verseByVerse.theology:
Obeying God Rather Than Men

Gamaliel's advice — if it is of man it will fail, if it is of God you cannot overthrow it — is often praised as tolerance. It is not Christian reasoning. It is pragmatic patience that never distinguishes truth from falsehood, only durable movements from short-lived ones, and it allows a man to avoid the one question in the room: did God raise Jesus? He is a providential restraint, not a theological authority. The apostles rest their case on something else entirely. Their principle is not defiance but a hierarchy of obedience: the state's authority is real and derived, and a delegated authority that forbids what God commands has run out of warrant at that point and no further. The same New Testament that records these words commands submission to governing authorities under Nero (Romans 13:1; 1 Peter 2:13-17). And the apostles supply the test that keeps the principle honest — they did not resist arrest, did not raise the crowd that was ready to riot for them, and did not flee. They took the flogging. Biblical civil disobedience characteristically accepts the penalty rather than looking for an escape clause.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: The apostles left the council rejoicing that they were counted worthy to suffer dishonour for the Name — led by the man who, only months earlier, had denied that he knew Jesus to a servant girl beside a fire. What changed was not his temperament.

Now: Suffering for the Name is not masochism and joy in it is not a duty to be manufactured in advance; it was given to those men on the way out of the building. Two things this passage is not: it is not a text to hand a grieving or ill person, since the suffering in view is dishonour incurred for Christ; and it is not a slogan for defying laws one merely dislikes. The question is always whether God is being forbidden what he commands — and whether one is prepared to bear the cost of saying so.

verseByVerse.quote: But the high priest rose up, and all who were with him (that is, the party of the Sadducees), and filled with jealousy they arrested the apostles and put them in the public prison.
verseByVerse.commentary:
But the high priest rose up, and all who were with him (that is, the party of the Sadducees), and filled with jealousy they arrested the apostles and put them in the public prison.

But the high priest rose up, and all who were with him (that is, the party of the Sadducees). The second attack, from outside. A word on who these men were, since they now become the apostles’ chief persecutors. The Sadducees were the priestly aristocracy of Jerusalem: the wealthy, ruling, temple-controlling families, and the high priest himself was their head. The temple and its vast establishment were theirs. They dominated the priestly side of the council and, as the men who profited from the status quo, cooperated closely with Rome to keep their power. Theologically they accepted only the written law of Moses as binding, rejected the oral traditions the Pharisees prized, and, crucially here, denied the resurrection of the dead, along with angels and spirits (23:8). Their name most likely derives from Zadok, Solomon’s high priest (1 Kings 2:35; Ezekiel 44:15), marking them as the party of the old priestly line, though their precise origins are uncertain.

Why the heat. All of that explains their reaction. The apostles were filling Jerusalem with the message of a risen Jesus, the very doctrine of resurrection the Sadducees denied (4:1–2), and were drawing the people’s allegiance away from the temple establishment. The gospel struck at both their theology and their power.

And filled with jealousy. The motive for the second arrest is stated plainly. The word (zēlos) is not petty envy but hot zeal: the burning of men who believe something precious is being taken from them, which is exactly what a religious establishment feels when the people begin listening to somebody else. The apostles were more popular than they were. It is the same motive that handed Jesus over: Pilate perceived that it was out of envy that the chief priests had delivered him up (Mark 15:10). The arrest is a response to success. Every attempt the authorities make to close the church down is prompted by the gospel’s advance.

They arrested the apostles and put them in the public prison. All the apostles this time, not just Peter and John. And the public prison, the common lock-up, not a holding room in the temple. That was a choice. It was meant to be seen, and to be degrading: the men Jerusalem had begun to admire, walked through the streets and put in with the ordinary criminals.

They never investigate the claim. Underneath it all sits the fact that governs this entire chapter. The men now running the case against the resurrection are the party that has staked its theology on there being no such thing. In encounter after encounter, from the guards’ report at the tomb (Matthew 28:11–15) to this morning’s empty cell, not one member of the council is recorded as asking the only question that matters: is it true? They investigate the preachers. They never investigate the claim. It is possible to hold the highest office in the religion of the living God and to have no interest whatever in whether he has done something.

How do I fight envy when God blesses someone else? Name it first, because envy almost never calls itself by its name; it calls itself concern, or discernment, or a sense that something is not quite right about that ministry. Then bring it to God as sin, not as an assessment. Pray, by name, for the person or church whose blessing stings, and ask God to bless them more, until your heart catches up with your prayer. Remember that everything anyone has is a gift (1 Corinthians 4:7), and that the Master of the vineyard is free to be generous to whom he will (Matthew 20:15). And rejoice with those who rejoice (Romans 12:15), even if at first it is an act of obedience rather than a feeling.

In a sentence. The high priest and his Sadducee party, filled with jealousy, arrested the apostles and put them in the public jail.

On a Tuesday. When you hear of God blessing another church, another Christian, another ministry, watch the first flicker in your heart. If it is not gladness, do not justify it. Confess it, and pray for them before the day is out.

For worship. Envy hates the blessing of others, and it put the Son of God on a cross. But the Lord whom they envied did not envy anyone. He emptied himself, and the glory he could have grasped he gave away (Philippians 2:6–7). Now the Father has given him the name above every name, and no jealousy in heaven or on earth can take it from him. Praise the generous Christ, who rejoices to share his own joy with his people (John 15:11).

verseByVerse.quote: But during the night an angel of the Lord opened the prison doors and brought them out, and said, "Go and stand in the temple and speak to the people all the words of this Life."
verseByVerse.commentary:
But during the night an angel of the Lord opened the prison doors and brought them out, and said, “Go and stand in the temple and speak to the people all the words of this Life.”

But during the night an angel of the Lord opened the prison doors and brought them out. Luke spends one clause on the miracle. No description of the angel, no reaction from the apostles, no word about the guards, no drama at all. The escape is not the story. And the humour is not lost: the Sadducees, who denied angels (23:8), are thwarted by one. God mocks their unbelief with the very thing they say does not exist. Angels are ministering spirits sent out to serve for the sake of those who are to inherit salvation (Hebrews 1:14), and here one of them serves with a key.

Go and stand in the temple and speak to the people. What the angel says next is the story, and it is one of the most bracing sentences in the book. Consider what is not said. Not go home. Not lie low until this passes. Not leave Jerusalem, which would have been the obvious counsel and which no reasonable adviser would have withheld. They are told to go straight back to the building owned and policed by the men who had just locked them up, at daybreak, and do precisely the thing they were arrested for doing. Heaven broke into a prison in order to put men back in the place of greatest danger. The rescue was not a rescue from anything; it was a transfer to the front. Release is for mission.

All the words of this Life. The phrase is unusual enough to be worth holding. Not the words about this life, and not the message of eternal life in the abstract. This Life: the thing standing in front of everybody, the life that came out of a sealed tomb and is now visibly loose in Jerusalem, healing people in the street and putting courage into fishermen. It is the new life in Christ that the Sadducees denied. Speak all of it, the angel says. All the words. Not the parts the council will tolerate.

Why does God open this door and not others? A prison that opens raises a question that has to be met honestly, because it is the question a suffering reader will bring, and Acts itself refuses to duck it. Turn forward seven chapters and Luke tells of another night, another angel, another set of chains falling off Peter; and in the same paragraph, James the brother of John is put to death with the sword, and no angel came (12:1–11). One apostle walks out past the guards; the other is buried. Luke sets them side by side without a word of explanation, and he did not have to. He could have left the beheading out. Later in the same book Paul sits in custody for two full years while a governor waits for a bribe (24:26–27), and no angel comes for him either, and the gospel goes on regardless, to a governor and a king (24:24–25; 26:1–29).

No promise for the faithful. So this passage must never be turned into a promise that the door opens for the faithful. The doors that stayed shut in this very book were shut on better men than most of us, and it was never a question of whether they had believed hard enough. What Acts actually teaches is narrower and steadier: God opens what he needs opened for the gospel to go where he intends it to go, and he is under no obligation to explain his selection to anyone. James’s death stopped nothing. Paul’s two lost years put the gospel before a governor and a king.

What have you been let out for? That gives an ordinary Christian a better question than why my door has not opened. Look at what the angel did with these men once they were out. Every deliverance in Acts is for the mission, never for the comfort of the delivered, and this one lasted only a few hours before the same men were arrested again and flogged the same day. Anyone who has been brought out of something, a diagnosis or a debt or a marriage that nearly ended, has a plainer thing to ask than why it happened to him and not to someone else. He can ask what he has been let out for. In this chapter the answer came with the door.

Do angels still rescue people today? God still sends his angels to serve his people; Hebrews speaks of them in the present tense, and some have entertained angels unawares (Hebrews 13:2). But Scripture never tells us to seek angelic visits, to pray to angels, or to expect to see them, and it warns against the worship of angels (Colossians 2:18). Most of their work is unseen, and most of God’s deliverances come through ordinary means: a doctor, a friend, a changed decision. Thank God for his unseen care, and keep your eyes on the Lord of the angels, not on them.

In a sentence. During the night an angel of the Lord opened the prison doors, brought them out, and told them to go and stand in the temple and tell the people the whole message of this new life.

On a Tuesday. When God brings you through something, ask him on the other side what it was for. Then go back to the place you were tempted to avoid, the conversation, the family, the workplace, and speak there, gently and plainly, of the Life who brought you out.

For worship. The Lord Jesus walked out of a sealed tomb, and now his servants walk out of a locked prison, because death and Rome and the Sanhedrin cannot hold what belongs to him. He has the keys of Death and Hades (Revelation 1:18). Whether he opens a door or leaves it shut, he is the Life, and he reigns. Glory to the risen Lord, who commands angels and sends his people into the temple with the words of life.

verseByVerse.quote: And when they heard this, they entered the temple at daybreak and began to teach. Now when the high priest came, and those who were with him, they called together the council, all the senate of the people of Israel, and sent to the prison to have them brought.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And when they heard this, they entered the temple at daybreak and began to teach. Now when the high priest came, and those who were with him, they called together the council, all the senate of the people of Israel, and sent to the prison to have them brought.

They entered the temple at daybreak and began to teach. Simple and stunning: they heard, they went, they taught. By daybreak they are back in the temple, the very building controlled by the men who imprisoned them, teaching exactly what they were imprisoned for teaching. At first light, the earliest hour the gates opened and the first hour of public activity, they were there. They had been let out in the middle of the night, and they went straight there and waited for the doors. There is no interval in the sentence for a discussion about whether the angel had really meant it, or whether it might be wiser to let a day pass. The obedience did not consult anything. This is the pattern of apostolic ministry throughout Acts: when God opens a door, the messengers walk through it without hesitation.

The search for a delay. A great deal of what passes for seeking God’s will is in fact the search for a delay he has not granted. These men had every reason to want one, and they did not take it.

They called together the council, all the senate of the people of Israel. The other half of the verse shows the establishment swinging into action. The council is the Sanhedrin, the supreme ruling court of the Jewish nation: seventy members presided over by the high priest, seventy-one in all, drawn from the chief priests (mostly Sadducees), the elders (the lay aristocracy and heads of leading families), and the scribes (the legal experts, largely Pharisees). It was the highest religious and judicial body in Israel, meeting in the temple precincts, with authority over Jewish law, though under Rome a death sentence still needed the governor’s ratification (John 18:31). The senate (gerousia) is the council of elders, a term with deep roots, for a body of elders had governed the nation for centuries. Luke piles term upon term to stress that they convened the entire official body in its most solemn and formal session.

And sent to the prison to have them brought. Here is the quiet irony Luke means us to feel, and the comedy begins. The full might of the establishment is ponderously assembled, and officers are sent to fetch prisoners who are no longer there. The grandest court in Israel grinds into motion against men God has already set free, and who are, at that very hour, teaching in the temple.

But shouldn’t I pray before I act? Yes, about the things God has not already told you. Prayer for guidance is right when Scripture leaves a real choice open: which job, which city, whom to marry among believers. But when God has already spoken, praying about it can become a pious way of not doing it. The apostles did not need to pray about whether to preach; they had been told. You do not need to pray about whether to forgive, to tell the truth, or to be kind to the colleague who wronged you. Those are settled. Pray for strength to obey, and then obey, today.

In a sentence. They went into the temple at dawn and began teaching, while the high priest and his colleagues called a full session of the council and sent to the prison to have them brought.

On a Tuesday. Think of one thing God has plainly told you in Scripture to do that you have been postponing. Do it before tomorrow’s first light, as the apostles did.

For worship. The council assembled to judge the apostles, who were already free and preaching. He who sits in the heavens laughs (Psalm 2:4). All the dignity of the highest court in the land could not keep pace with the word of the risen Christ. Praise the King whose commands outrun every council, and whose servants are free before their judges have even sat down.
verseByVerse.note: The council is the Sanhedrin.

verseByVerse.quote: But when the officers came, they did not find them in the prison, so they returned and reported, "We found the prison securely locked and the guards standing at the doors, but when we opened them we found no one inside."
verseByVerse.commentary:
But when the officers came, they did not find them in the prison, so they returned and reported, “We found the prison securely locked and the guards standing at the doors, but when we opened them we found no one inside.”

We found the prison securely locked and the guards standing at the doors, but when we opened them we found no one inside. The officers’ report is a small masterpiece, and Luke lets it stand without a word of comment. Everything is exactly as it should be. The prison securely locked. The guards at their posts, awake, doing their job, having seen nothing. And when the door is opened, nobody inside. Every element of the system worked perfectly and the men are gone. There is no human account of it available to anybody in the room, and the officers do not attempt one. They describe what they found and let their superiors make of it what they can.

The signature of the miracle. Notice how God did it, because the manner is a signature. The doors were not blown off their hinges. The guards were not struck down, or blinded, or thrown into a sleep they would have to explain. Nothing was broken and nobody was hurt. The doors were opened and then closed again behind the apostles walking out into the dark. The whole miracle is tidy, and the tidiness is what unnerves: this is not power straining against resistance; it is power to which locked doors are not an obstacle worth damaging.

The same shape as the tomb. Stand back and look at the shape of what these particular men are being asked to explain. A sealed place. Guards posted. An occupant who was certainly there last night. And in the morning, everything secure and the place empty, with nothing but an account nobody can produce. Jerusalem had heard that story once already, about a tomb with guards and a seal (Matthew 27:62–66; 28:11–15), and this council had done its best to keep the lid on it. Now the same shape has turned up in their own jail.

Who is receiving the report. Luke has just told us that the men driving this arrest are the party of the Sadducees (v. 17), the people who say there is no resurrection, nor angel, nor spirit (23:8). An angel has just emptied their prison. They are standing in a room holding a report of an empty cell, delivered by honest witnesses, and the only conclusion available is the one their theology has ruled out in advance. They will spend the rest of the chapter trying to manage the consequences of a fact they have decided cannot happen.

A very modern condition. That is worth carrying out of the passage. It is entirely possible to have all the evidence in hand, in order, from reliable sources, and to be unable to reach the obvious conclusion, not because the evidence is weak but because the conclusion has already been excluded. The officers reported accurately. Nobody disputed the facts. And the council’s next move was not to ask how it had happened; it was to send for the men and tell them to stop talking.

How should I speak to someone whose mind is already closed? Patiently, honestly, and with prayer, because the problem is not finally in the evidence but in the heart, and only God can open a heart (16:14). Give the reasons for your hope when you are asked (1 Peter 3:15), but do not imagine that a cleverer argument will do what only the Spirit can do. Ask gentle questions that help a person notice what he has ruled out in advance: what would you accept as evidence? Live in a way that makes your faith hard to dismiss. And keep praying for him by name. Saul of Tarsus had his mind closed tighter than anyone in this council, and the risen Christ opened it on a road.

In a sentence. The officers did not find them in the prison, and came back to report that it was securely locked with the guards at the doors, but when they opened it no one was inside.

On a Tuesday. No locked door can keep in those God wants out, and no locked heart is beyond his reach. Think of the person you have given up on. Pray for him again today.

For worship. The empty cell points to the empty tomb, and the empty tomb points to the One who walked out of it. He rose without breaking the seal’s dignity or the soldiers’ bodies; he simply was not there, because death had no claim on him. Blessed be the risen Lord, whose power is so great that it does not even need to make a noise.

verseByVerse.quote: Now when the captain of the temple and the chief priests heard these words, they were greatly perplexed about them, wondering what this would come to. And someone came and told them, "Look! The men whom you put in prison are standing in the temple and teaching the people."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Now when the captain of the temple and the chief priests heard these words, they were greatly perplexed about them, wondering what this would come to. And someone came and told them, “Look! The men whom you put in prison are standing in the temple and teaching the people.”

They were greatly perplexed about them, wondering what this would come to. The perplexity is genuine. The word (diēporoun) means at a complete loss, thrown back on nothing: not merely puzzled but out of explanations. And what they are said to be doing with the perplexity is telling: wondering what this would come to. They are not asking what has happened; they are asking where it ends. Men who have felt the ground shift under an institution know that particular anxiety, and it is a more honest reaction than anything they will say for the rest of the day. They have lost control, and they know it.

The captain of the temple and the chief priests. A brief word on the two named here. The captain of the temple was the chief officer of the temple, second in rank only to the high priest: a senior priest who commanded the Levitical temple guard, kept order in the precincts, and held the power of arrest. It was he who helped seize Jesus (Luke 22:4, 52) and the apostles (4:1). The chief priests were the priestly aristocracy at the top of the temple hierarchy: the high priest, former high priests who kept the title and influence, and the heads of the leading priestly families, a small, mostly Sadducean elite. In short, this is the temple’s entire ruling establishment, its head of security and its senior clergy, standing helpless before an empty cell.

The men whom you put in prison are standing in the temple and teaching the people. Then comes one of the finest anticlimaxes in Scripture. Into that silence someone arrives, and Luke gives us his opening word: Look! Not fled. Not hiding. Not across the border. Standing, in the establishment’s own building, a few hundred yards away, doing the very thing at which they were interrupted, while the establishment holds an emergency session about where they might have gone. The cycle of arrest and proclamation is completing its second turn. The word the authorities cannot silence is being proclaimed in the building they control.

Why does Luke make the authorities look so foolish? Not to mock them for sport, but to show us the truth about every power that sets itself against Christ. Psalm 2 had already described it: the kings of the earth set themselves and the rulers take counsel together against the LORD and against his Anointed, and he who sits in the heavens laughs. The church had prayed that very psalm only days before (4:25–28). Luke lets us see the answer to their prayer in the form of a farce. When Christians feel small before powerful opponents, this is the scene to remember. The opponents are not in control, and the comedy is God’s.

In a sentence. The captain and the chief priests were completely baffled, wondering where this would lead, until someone came and told them that the men they had jailed were standing in the temple teaching the people.

On a Tuesday. When the news makes the opponents of the gospel look unstoppable, read Psalm 2 aloud. Then pray for them, as the church in Jerusalem did, and for boldness for yourself.

For worship. The gospel keeps breaking out, and opposition only spreads it. The rulers plan, and their plans dissolve; the Lord speaks, and his word runs. Praise the God who turns the councils of the mighty into perplexity, and who has set his King on Zion, his holy hill (Psalm 2:6).

verseByVerse.quote: Then the captain with the officers went and brought them, but not by force, for they were afraid of being stoned by the people. And when they had brought them, they set them before the council.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Then the captain with the officers went and brought them, but not by force, for they were afraid of being stoned by the people. And when they had brought them, they set them before the council.

Then the captain with the officers went and brought them, but not by force, for they were afraid of being stoned by the people. The captain of the temple goes to fetch them himself, and Luke records the manner in words that carry the whole chapter: but not by force. The head of temple security, with his officers, in his own precinct, arresting men he has the legal right to arrest, does it carefully, almost politely, because he is frightened of the crowd. The men who hold every instrument of power in Jerusalem cannot use any of it, and the reason is given plainly.

Two kinds of fear. Put that beside what Luke has been telling us for twenty verses, because he has built this chapter around one word. Great fear came upon all who heard (v. 5). Great fear came upon the whole church (v. 11). And now fear again, on the other side of the room, in the other party, with a different object. Both groups in this chapter are afraid. The church is afraid of God. The council is afraid of the public. Nobody in the Sanhedrin appears to be afraid of God at all, and that is exactly why they are afraid of everybody else.

The rope round the neck. It is a rule with almost no exceptions. A man who genuinely fears God has one thing to be afraid of and is therefore free of nearly everything; a man who does not ends up managing a long and growing list. The council cannot act on its convictions, cannot speak its mind, cannot follow its own legal judgment, because it has to keep watching the temple courts to see how it is playing. Every decision they take from here to the end of the chapter is shaped by a crowd they despise. That is the price of having replaced conscience with reputation, and it is not paid only by first-century aristocrats. Anyone who has ever softened a conviction because of what a room would think has felt the same rope round the same neck. The fear of man lays a snare (Proverbs 29:25).

And they set them before the council. The contrast with the men being fetched could hardly be sharper. The apostles have just been let out of prison by an angel, are standing in a temple full of people who admire them, and have every opportunity to refuse, to slip away in the crowd, or to let the crowd do what the officers plainly fear it would do. They do none of it. They walk back with the officers and stand before the council. They submit to arrest, and then refuse to submit on the question of preaching. The one group in Jerusalem with real reason to be afraid is the one group behaving as though there were nothing to fear.

A protection with a short shelf life. There is a quiet lesson in the fact that the crowd’s goodwill is what protects them at this moment. It is a real protection, and God is plainly using it. It is also a protection that will not last, and none of these men is leaning on it. Within two chapters the mood of this same city will have turned far enough for Stephen to be stoned. Public favour is a gift to be received and spent, never a foundation to build on.

How do I get free of the fear of what people think? Not by trying to care less about people, but by fearing God more. The fear of man shrinks when God grows large in your sight. Jesus put it with startling directness: do not fear those who kill the body but cannot kill the soul; rather fear him who can destroy both soul and body in hell (Matthew 10:28), and then in the next breath, you are of more value than many sparrows. Fear God, and know that God loves you. Practically, begin small: say the true thing in the next meeting where you would usually stay quiet, and notice that you survive it. Ask what you would do if only God were watching, and do that. He is the only one who is always watching.

In a sentence. The captain and his officers brought them back without force, because they were afraid the people would stone them, and set them before the council.

On a Tuesday. Christians do not use mob power to resist authorities. They submit where they can, and obey God where they must. Notice this week where you are steering by the opinion of a room. Then steer by the fear of the Lord instead, and see how much lighter it is.

For worship. Jesus stood before this same council and was not afraid of it. When they struck him, he did not strike back; when they mocked him, he entrusted himself to him who judges justly (1 Peter 2:23). He feared God perfectly, and so he feared no one else. Glory to the Lord who walked into his trial freely, and whose courage now lives in the men who walk in after him.

verseByVerse.quote: And the high priest questioned them, saying, "We strictly charged you not to teach in this name, yet here you have filled Jerusalem with your teaching, and you intend to bring this man's blood upon us."
verseByVerse.commentary:
And the high priest questioned them, saying, “We strictly charged you not to teach in this name, yet here you have filled Jerusalem with your teaching, and you intend to bring this man’s blood upon us.”

We strictly charged you not to teach in this name. The high priest’s complaint is an inadvertent testimony. And notice that again he avoids saying the name of Jesus. This man, he will say in a moment. The refusal to name Jesus is the first of many failed attempts to suppress him by silence.

Yet here you have filled Jerusalem with your teaching. An unintended compliment. The very thing they were trying to prevent has happened on a city-wide scale. Every word of the sentence is a report of the council’s own failure, delivered in the tone of an accusation. They are complaining, in open session, that the gospel is unstoppable. The prosecution has just entered the defence’s best evidence into the record.

The third filling. One word in the complaint deserves to be traced, because Luke has been laying a thread through this whole chapter and it comes to the surface here. The high priest says the apostles have filled Jerusalem. It is the third filling in twenty-eight verses. Satan filled Ananias’s heart to lie (v. 3). The high priest and his party were filled with jealousy (v. 17). And now the city itself is filled with the message they were forbidden to speak. Luke is showing what happens when the Spirit fills a church: everything in the chapter that sets itself against him is also full of something, and none of it can hold its ground. A heart full of the adversary lasted a morning. A council full of envy could reach no further than a whip. The teaching filled a capital city and has not stopped.

And you intend to bring this man’s blood upon us. The phrase is an old biblical idiom for bloodguilt: to hold someone responsible for a death, to lay the guilt of it at his door (Leviticus 20:9; Joshua 2:19; 2 Samuel 1:16; Ezekiel 33:4). The council fears the apostles are publicly fastening on them the charge of having murdered Jesus, and they are right to fear it, for that is exactly what the apostles have been doing (2:23, 36; 3:15; 5:30). The irony is bitter. At Jesus’ trial the crowd stirred up by this same leadership had cried, his blood be on us and on our children! (Matthew 27:25). They once called the bloodguilt down on themselves; now they are terrified of being held to it.

The accusation and the cure. Notice where their fear is aimed: not at their guilt, but at the men who name it. They want to silence the accusation rather than be cleansed of the blood, and that is their tragedy. For there was a way to be rid of this man’s blood, and it was not to muzzle the preachers but to be washed in the very blood they had shed. The blood that lay upon them as guilt was being held out to them as atonement: repent and be baptised for the forgiveness of your sins (2:36–38). The blood of Jesus speaks a better word than the blood of Abel (Hebrews 12:24). Abel’s blood cried for vengeance; his cries for pardon. The accusation and the cure were one and the same blood.

Were the Jewish people as a whole guilty of Christ’s death? No, not in the way that has so often been claimed. The apostles charge the particular leaders and crowds of Jerusalem who handed Jesus over, and they do it in order to call them to repentance and forgiveness, not to curse a nation. The church itself in Acts prayed that Herod and Pontius Pilate, along with the Gentiles and the peoples of Israel, gathered against Jesus to do what God’s hand had predestined (4:27–28). Jew and Gentile together crucified him, and the deeper truth is that our sins put him there. The centuries in which Christians used Matthew 27:25 to persecute Jewish people were a grievous sin against Christ, who was himself a Jew, and against the apostles, who were all Jews. The right response to this verse is not to point at anyone, but to plead the blood for ourselves.

In a sentence. The high priest said they had been strictly ordered not to teach in this name, yet they had filled Jerusalem with their teaching and meant to make the leaders guilty of this man’s blood.

On a Tuesday. If someone confronts you with a real wrong you have done, notice your first instinct: to silence the accuser, or to deal with the guilt. Go to the blood of Christ with it, and then, where you need to, go and put it right.

For worship. The blood they feared is the blood that cleanses. The very men who shed it were offered pardon through it, and some of them, a great many of the priests (6:7), received it. There is no guilt so close to the cross that the cross cannot reach it. Praise the Lamb of God, whose blood was shed by sinners and is sprinkled on sinners, and who speaks for us before the Father a better word than Abel’s.

verseByVerse.quote: But Peter and the apostles answered, "We must obey God rather than men. The God of our fathers raised Jesus, whom you killed by hanging him on a tree."
verseByVerse.commentary:
But Peter and the apostles answered, “We must obey God rather than men. The God of our fathers raised Jesus, whom you killed by hanging him on a tree.

We must obey God rather than men. They have been arrested twice, held overnight, released by an angel, re-arrested before an assembled Sanhedrin, and formally charged with breaking a court order. And Peter’s reply is a single sentence with no preamble and no apology in it. The verb (dei) is the strong one: it is necessary, it is binding, there is no other course open to us. He is not claiming a right. He is describing an obligation he has no power to set aside. When a human command conflicts with God’s, God wins. It has been the motto of martyrs through the centuries.

Conscience asks first. This is the second time these men have said it to this court. The first was in the previous chapter, softer, framed as a question they invited the council to answer for itself: whether it is right in the sight of God to listen to you rather than to God, you must judge (4:19). The council has now had its answer and repeated its order, and so the question becomes a statement. That is worth noticing about Christian conscience: it does not usually start by shouting. It asks first, and only hardens when the asking has been refused.

Putting the frame back. Because this sentence is quoted so often, and by people in very different situations, it needs its frame put back around it, or it becomes a slogan for whatever a believer happens to want to defy. The New Testament’s ordinary teaching about government is not resistance but submission, and it is stated in the strongest terms by men living under an empire that would shortly execute both of them.
