Let every person be subject to the governing authorities, Paul writes, for there is no authority except from God (Romans 13:1), and he wrote it to Christians in Nero’s capital. Be subject for the Lord’s sake to every human institution, writes Peter; honour the emperor (1 Peter 2:13–17), and he is the man speaking these very words, writing to churches about to feel what that emperor could do. Neither of them regarded obedience to the state as a concession wrung out of them. They regarded it as obedience to God.

Real and derived. So how do the two fit? By recognising that the authority of a government is real and derived. It is genuine authority, and it is held on delegation. A magistrate has his warrant from God, which is why a Christian obeys him in the ordinary run of things without needing to agree with him. But a delegated authority that commands what the one who delegated it forbids has, at that precise point, run out of warrant, and only at that point. Scripture supplies the pattern before Acts ever does: midwives who would not kill the boys (Exodus 1:17), three men who would not bow to a statue and said so without knowing whether they would be spared (Daniel 3:16–18), an old official who kept his windows open toward Jerusalem when praying had been made a capital offence (Daniel 6:10). God alone is Lord of the conscience (Westminster 20.2).

The test. This yields a test an ordinary Christian can actually apply, and it is narrower than most people who quote this verse would like. The question is not whether a law is unwise, unfair, expensive or offensive to me. The question is whether I am being commanded to do what God forbids, or forbidden to do what God commands. The apostles are in the second case: God had told them, that very night and through an angel, to go and speak (v. 20). A tax I resent, a policy I judge foolish, a regulation that inconveniences my church: none of these is Acts 5, and dressing them in this verse cheapens it for the day it is genuinely needed.

The half that is always dropped. Look at what these men do not do. They do not resist arrest, though an angel had just shown that the doors were no obstacle. They do not summon the crowd, though Luke has just told us the officers were afraid of exactly that, and it would have worked. They do not flee the city. They walk in, state their position, take a flogging for it, and go back to work. Biblical civil disobedience is characteristically joined to a willingness to bear the penalty, not to a search for an escape clause. Anyone appealing to this verse who is unwilling to pay the fine, take the sentence or lose the position is appealing to something other than what Peter is doing here.

The God of our fathers raised Jesus. Having refused the court’s authority, Peter immediately preaches to it. He does not merely defend the preaching; he preaches, on the spot, to the men who have him in custody. Every phrase is chosen. The God of our fathers claims continuity: this is not a foreign God or a new religion appearing beside Israel’s, but the God of Abraham keeping his word, and it is the council, not the apostles, who have broken step. Whom you killed is said to their faces, in their own chamber, by a man with no legal standing whatsoever.

Whom you killed by hanging him on a tree. This is the most deliberate phrase of all. Peter could have said crucified; he has said it before. Instead he reaches for the language of Deuteronomy, where a man hanged on a tree is cursed by God, a body to be taken down before nightfall so that the land is not defiled (Deuteronomy 21:22–23). The leaders had meant the cross to prove that Jesus was cursed by God. Peter picks the one description of it most offensive to every man listening, and he picks it because it is the truth about what happened there. The curse was real. It fell. It simply was not his. He was hanged on that tree under a curse he had not earned, in the place of people who had earned it and could not carry it: Christ redeemed us from the curse of the law by becoming a curse for us (Galatians 3:13; 1 Peter 2:24). And the God of their fathers raised him to show the account was settled. There is no gospel that does not go through that sentence, and Peter puts it in front of his judges within a minute of being told to be silent.

What if I am not sure whether a command crosses the line? Then go slowly, and go with others. Ask the test plainly: am I being made to sin, or kept from a clear duty? Search the Scriptures, not your preferences. Seek the counsel of your elders and of mature Christians who will tell you the truth, because one person’s conscience can be either too tender or too hard. Where the matter is genuinely unclear, lean toward submission and courtesy, for Scripture’s default is honour for those in authority. Where it is clear, be respectful in manner and firm in substance, and be ready to bear the cost without bitterness. Daniel served a pagan king faithfully for decades, and still knew exactly where the line was when it came.

In a sentence. Peter and the apostles answered that they must obey God rather than men, and that the God of their fathers had raised Jesus, whom the leaders had killed by hanging him on a tree.

On a Tuesday. At work and at home this week, be the most willing, cheerful and law-abiding person in the room, so that if the day ever comes when you must say no for Christ’s sake, it is plain that you are not saying it from a rebellious spirit. And if that day has come, say it calmly, take what follows, and keep speaking of him.

For worship. Christ hung on the tree under the curse, so that the curse would never fall on those who trust him. The God of Abraham, Isaac and Jacob has kept his promise in the most unexpected way: through a cross, outside the city wall, and an empty tomb in a garden. Blessed be the Son who obeyed God rather than men to the very end, and who became a curse so that we might receive the blessing of Abraham (Galatians 3:14).
verseByVerse.note: Being hung on a tree was under God’s curse in the law.

verseByVerse.quote: "God exalted him at his right hand as Leader and Savior, to give repentance to Israel and forgiveness of sins. And we are witnesses to these things, and so is the Holy Spirit, whom God has given to those who obey him."
verseByVerse.commentary:
God exalted him at his right hand as Leader and Savior, to give repentance to Israel and forgiveness of sins. And we are witnesses to these things, and so is the Holy Spirit, whom God has given to those who obey him.

God exalted him at his right hand as Leader and Savior. The crucified one is now the Leader who blazed the trail through death to resurrection, and the Saviour who offers repentance and forgiveness. Leader renders archēgos (3:15), a word with no tidy English equivalent: it carries the sense of the one who goes first and opens the way, a pioneer who cuts the track others will walk, a founder in whom a whole people begins. Peter is saying that Jesus did not arrange a rescue from a safe distance. He went through death himself, first, and came out the other side, and the road exists because he made it. Nobody who follows him into that country will be going anywhere he has not already been. And Saviour (sōtēr), rescuer, is a title the Old Testament gives to God himself: I, I am the LORD, and besides me there is no savior (Isaiah 43:11). Peter gives it to Jesus without hesitation, before the very court that condemned him for blasphemy.

To give repentance to Israel and forgiveness of sins. Then, quietly, the phrase that ought to stop anybody who has ever tried and failed to repent: God exalted him to give repentance. Repentance is here a thing handed over, not a thing achieved. Not only forgiveness, but repentance itself, is his gift (11:18; 2 Timothy 2:25). That cuts against the way most people instinctively hear the command, as though God stands at a distance requiring a change of heart that we must manufacture before he will look at us. Peter says the exalted Christ dispenses it. Anyone who has wanted to be sorry for something and found that he could only regret the consequences knows the difference between working up remorse and being given a new mind about a thing. The first cannot be done to order. The second is a gift, and the place to go for it is the one who was exalted to give it. And yet we are commanded to repent (3:19). Both are true: God commands what he gives, and gives what he commands.

And we are witnesses to these things, and so is the Holy Spirit. Two witnesses, as the law required (Deuteronomy 19:15), and Jesus had promised exactly this pairing: the Spirit of truth will bear witness about me, and you also will bear witness (John 15:26–27). The apostles are human eyewitnesses of the resurrection. And the Spirit testifies in several joined ways. First, by his very outpouring: the fact that God has poured out the Spirit is itself proof that the crucified Jesus is risen and enthroned, for only the exalted Christ could send him (2:33). Second, by empowering the witnesses themselves, emboldening them and speaking through them (1:8; 4:8, 31). Third, outwardly, in the signs and wonders and in the changed and multiplying church: God bearing witness by gifts of the Holy Spirit (Hebrews 2:4). Fourth, inwardly, pressing the truth home on the conscience, convicting the world concerning sin and righteousness and judgment (John 16:8–11), and bearing witness with the believer’s spirit (Romans 8:16). So the council faces not merely the word of a few fishermen but the testimony of God himself: a witness they can imprison no more than they could keep the prison shut.

Whom God has given to those who obey him. One clause here needs a guard, because it has been misused. Read carelessly, it turns the Spirit into a wage. But the obedience Peter has in mind is not a record of performance. It is the same word he used of himself three verses earlier, when he said we must obey God rather than men, and what he meant there was believing God’s word about his Son and acting on it. That is what the New Testament calls obeying the gospel, or the obedience of faith (6:7; Romans 1:5; 2 Thessalonians 1:8). The Spirit is not the prize for a life already put right. He is the one who puts it right, and he comes to people whose response to the message about Jesus has been surrender rather than management.

If repentance is a gift, do I just wait for it? No. You ask for it, and you act on the light you have. The gifts of God come through the means he has appointed: hearing his word, praying, and turning toward him even when the turning feels weak. Ask Christ plainly: give me a true sorrow for this sin, and a hatred of it, and the strength to leave it. Then take the next step you can see, and confess it, put it right, remove the occasion. If you find any desire at all to repent, that desire is already the gift beginning. The man who says he would like to repent but cannot feel it is not far from the kingdom; he is being drawn.

How can I know I have the Holy Spirit? Not mainly by dramatic experiences, but by what the Spirit always does. He makes Jesus precious to you, so that you confess him as Lord (1 Corinthians 12:3). He bears witness with your spirit that you are a child of God, so that you call God Father (Romans 8:15–16). He makes you hate your sin and fight it (Galatians 5:17). And he grows his fruit in you, slowly, over years: love, joy, peace, patience, kindness, goodness, faithfulness, gentleness, self-control (Galatians 5:22–23). If you trust Christ, the Spirit has been given to you (Ephesians 1:13). You do not have to earn a second blessing; you have to walk in the one you have been given.

In a sentence. God exalted Jesus to his right hand as Leader and Saviour, to give Israel repentance and the forgiveness of sins, and the apostles are witnesses of these things, and so is the Holy Spirit, whom God has given to those who obey him.

On a Tuesday. Ask Christ for repentance; it is his gift to give. Name the one sin you have most often regretted without leaving, and bring it to him today, not with a promise to try harder, but with a request to be changed.

For worship. The Prince of life went first through death and opened the road home. He is the Saviour Isaiah promised, and besides him there is no other. From the right hand of God he gives what we could never produce: a new heart, a true repentance, a full forgiveness, and the Spirit himself. Glory to the exalted Christ, whose hands that were pierced are now full of gifts for the very men who pierced them.

verseByVerse.quote: When they heard this, they were enraged and wanted to kill them. But a Pharisee in the council named Gamaliel, a teacher of the law held in honor by all the people, stood up and gave orders to put the men outside for a little while.
verseByVerse.commentary:
When they heard this, they were enraged and wanted to kill them. But a Pharisee in the council named Gamaliel, a teacher of the law held in honor by all the people, stood up and gave orders to put the men outside for a little while.

When they heard this, they were enraged and wanted to kill them. The council’s response is rage, not refutation, not deliberation, but the visceral fury of men whose authority has been publicly and repeatedly defied. Luke’s word repays a moment: they were enraged (dieprionto), literally they were sawn through, cut in two by what they had heard. Set that beside the day of Pentecost, when the people who heard the same message were cut to the heart and said, brothers, what shall we do? (2:37). Here the same message, delivered by the same man, about the same risen Christ, produces a decision to kill. Stephen will meet the identical reaction, the same word, from this identical body two chapters later, and it will finish the way it wanted to finish here (7:54).

The gospel is never neutral. That is the sober truth about preaching Christ, and it is a comfort as well as a warning. The gospel very rarely leaves people where it found them. It either breaks a man open or hardens him, and the wound feels much the same from the inside at first. Three thousand went one way in chapter 2. This council went the other. Nothing in the message had changed. We are the aroma of Christ, Paul says, to one a fragrance from death to death, to the other a fragrance from life to life (2 Corinthians 2:15–16).

But a Pharisee in the council named Gamaliel. Into that room, at the moment murder is being openly proposed by the supreme court of Israel, God sends a Pharisee. Not an angel this time, not an earthquake, not a miracle of any kind. A respected old teacher stands up and asks for the room to be cleared, and the apostles live. Providence does not always arrive with the doors opening of their own accord. Sometimes it arrives as the one person present whose opinion the others cannot afford to dismiss. The Pharisees were a minority in the council, but they were popular with the people, and the Sadducees could not govern without them.

Who was Gamaliel? Beyond the New Testament, Jewish sources tell us a fair amount about him, though it is best weighed as tradition rather than certified biography. He is remembered as Rabban Gamaliel the Elder, one of the most honoured sages of his age and, by Jewish tradition, a descendant (commonly said to be the grandson) of the famous Hillel and a leader of Hillel’s school. He is traditionally reckoned the first to bear the exalted title Rabban, our master, a rank above Rabbi. The Mishnah pays him a striking tribute: when Rabban Gamaliel the Elder died, the glory of the law ceased, and purity and piety died (Sotah 9:15). Tradition credits him with several rulings for the public good, including protections for women in the law of divorce. And, as Luke notes elsewhere, the young Saul of Tarsus was educated at the feet of Gamaliel (22:3). A much later Christian legend claimed that Gamaliel secretly became a believer; it has no historical foundation and should be set aside.

And gave orders to put the men outside for a little while. A private discussion. The apostles are removed so that the council can speak freely. Luke, of course, knows what was said; perhaps Saul himself, Gamaliel’s pupil, later told it.

Why does the same message soften some and harden others? Because the difference is not finally in the message or the messenger but in the work of God in the hearer. Faith is God’s gift (Ephesians 2:8), and it is the Lord who opens hearts to pay attention to what is said (16:14). Luke says it plainly later: as many as were appointed to eternal life believed (13:48). That does not make the hardened man a puppet; he chooses his rage freely and is responsible for it. But it should humble every Christian. If you were cut to the heart rather than sawn through, it was grace, not your superior openness. And it should free every preacher and every ordinary witness: our task is to speak Christ faithfully; the opening of hearts belongs to God.

In a sentence. When they heard this, they were furious and wanted to kill them, but Gamaliel, a Pharisee in the council and a teacher of the law honoured by all the people, stood up and ordered the men to be put outside for a little while.

On a Tuesday. If you speak of Christ and someone reacts with anger, do not assume you have failed. The same word that angers one person breaks another open. Keep speaking, kindly, and pray that the anger becomes conviction.

For worship. God can raise up an unexpected voice to protect his people, and he rules over councils and kings. The heart of the king is in the hand of the LORD, and he turns it wherever he will (Proverbs 21:1). Praise the sovereign Lord, who held back a murderous court with a Pharisee’s caution, and who opens hearts by his Spirit so that sinners are cut to the heart and live.
verseByVerse.note: Gamaliel was the most respected Pharisee teacher of the day, and Paul’s teacher.

verseByVerse.quote: And he said to them, "Men of Israel, take care what you are about to do with these men. For before these days Theudas rose up, claiming to be somebody, and a number of men, about four hundred, joined him. He was killed, and all who followed him were dispersed and came to nothing."
verseByVerse.commentary:
And he said to them, “Men of Israel, take care what you are about to do with these men. For before these days Theudas rose up, claiming to be somebody, and a number of men, about four hundred, joined him. He was killed, and all who followed him were dispersed and came to nothing.

Men of Israel, take care what you are about to do with these men. Gamaliel opens with a warning, and it is worth registering how serious it is. He is addressing the supreme court of his nation, in session, which has just openly proposed killing the apostles without a trial, and he tells them to be careful. He is the only man in the chamber who says anything of the kind.

For before these days Theudas rose up, claiming to be somebody. His argument is drawn from recent memory. Judea in living recollection had produced a run of men who gathered a following, claimed to be somebody, and came to nothing when they were killed. Josephus says the land was full of them. Gamaliel names one, Theudas, with about four hundred men, and will name a second, and his reasoning is simple: movements of that kind collapse when their leader dies, so let time do the work and keep the council’s hands clean.

A historical note. Josephus mentions a Theudas who led a revolt about AD 44 to 46, about ten years after this speech, and Gamaliel places his Theudas before Judas the Galilean, whose rising came in AD 6. Either Gamaliel refers to an earlier Theudas, a common name in a country full of failed rebels, or Josephus is mistaken in his dating. There is no reason to doubt Luke’s accuracy, which has been confirmed many times elsewhere. The fuller answer is given at vv. 37–38.

He was killed, and all who followed him were dispersed and came to nothing. His movement died with him. As practical advice, Gamaliel’s case is shrewd, and God used it, and the apostles went home alive because of it. As a way of settling what is true, it is worthless, and it is worth being clear about why, because the same reasoning is offered constantly today in a religious voice. Durability is not a test of truth. Plenty of false things last for centuries; Gamaliel was making his case inside a temple that had stood a long time and was forty years from being rubble. Plenty of true things are crushed early and stay crushed for a generation. Applied consistently, his rule would have condemned nearly every prophet Israel ever had, all of whom were dismissed, imprisoned or killed and none of whom looked durable at the time.

A decision not to look. The deeper problem is that Gamaliel’s rule allows a man to avoid the only question in the room. The apostles had not asked the council to predict their movement’s future. They had made a factual claim: God raised Jesus from the dead, and we saw him. That claim can be investigated. It has witnesses, a location, a date, and a tomb whose emptiness nobody in that chamber disputed. Gamaliel proposes instead that they wait and see, which is a decision not to look.

Waiting is itself an answer. That posture is extremely common, and it is always presented as open-mindedness. If Christianity is real it will survive without my verdict; if it is not, my verdict will not have mattered. It sounds humble, and it is in fact the one position that cannot be held. A man deciding whether Jesus rose from the dead is not an observer of the case; he is a party to it. Waiting to see how it turns out is itself an answer, and it is the answer given by everyone who has ever intended to look into it properly later. Gamaliel had the evidence, the intelligence and the standing to settle it, and he chose the one course that required nothing of him.

In a sentence. Gamaliel told them, Men of Israel, take care what you do with these men, for Theudas once rose up claiming to be somebody and gathered about four hundred followers, but he was killed and his movement came to nothing.

On a Tuesday. Many movements claiming to be from God die with their leaders. Christ’s did not, because he rose. If you have been sitting on the fence about him, telling yourself you will look into it properly one day, today is the day to look. Read one of the Gospels through this week, and ask, as you read, whether it is true.

For worship. Every false messiah in Gamaliel’s list stayed dead, and his followers scattered. One Messiah died and did not stay dead, and his scattered followers were gathered again by his own hand and sent into the world. Praise the Lord Jesus, the only leader in history whose death began his movement instead of ending it.
verseByVerse.note: Theudas is otherwise unknown from this period; Josephus mentions a later rebel of the same name.

verseByVerse.quote: "After him Judas the Galilean rose up in the days of the census and drew away some of the people after him. He too perished, and all who followed him were scattered. So in the present case I tell you, keep away from these men and let them alone, for if this plan or this undertaking is of man, it will fail;"
verseByVerse.commentary:
After him Judas the Galilean rose up in the days of the census and drew away some of the people after him. He too perished, and all who followed him were scattered. So in the present case I tell you, keep away from these men and let them alone, for if this plan or this undertaking is of man, it will fail;

After him Judas the Galilean rose up in the days of the census and drew away some of the people after him. Judas the Galilean led a revolt against the Roman census of AD 6, under Quirinius, and Josephus confirms it. He taught that paying taxes to Rome was slavery and that God alone was king, and his movement fed the later Zealots. The mention of it would have resonated deeply with the council; it was better known and more politically charged than Theudas’s movement.

He too perished, and all who followed him were scattered. Another failed messiah. Gamaliel’s principle sounds profound and avoids the actual question: is it of God? His counsel is a deferral, not a judgment. But it serves God’s purpose: the apostles are not killed, the mission continues.

Did Luke get his history wrong? These two names carry a well-known objection, and since Luke’s standing as a historian matters to this whole book, it should be met. Josephus describes a Theudas who led a revolt under the procurator Fadus, about AD 44 to 46, a decade or more after Gamaliel is speaking. And Gamaliel places Judas the Galilean, whose rising came at the census of AD 6, after Theudas. On the face of it Luke has the order backwards and the date impossible, and this is regularly produced as proof that he invented the speech. Two things need saying. First, Theudas was a common name in a country full of failed insurgents. Josephus himself says that after Herod the Great died in 4 BC there were countless disturbances in Judea, and he names several leaders who gathered a following and were cut down. Gamaliel’s Theudas had about four hundred men; the one Josephus dates to the forties drew a great crowd to the Jordan. There is no difficulty in supposing two men of the same name, decades apart, in a generation that produced rebels by the dozen.

The benefit of the doubt. Second, the objection assumes that where Luke and Josephus differ, Josephus is the standard and Luke the suspect. Josephus is a valuable historian and a demonstrably careless one in places, and that assumption has not aged well. Luke was long said to have blundered over the titles of local officials: the city authorities of Thessalonica, the proconsul of Cyprus, the chief man of Malta. Inscription after inscription has since shown him exactly right, in details a forger would have had no way to know. A writer with that record has earned the benefit of the doubt about a rebel’s name.

Keep away from these men and let them alone, for if this plan or this undertaking is of man, it will fail. Gamaliel’s principle: time will tell, for human movements fail. True as far as it goes. But Gamaliel himself is perhaps left wondering whether this movement is different from the ones he named.

Was Jesus a political rebel like these men? No, and the comparison shows the difference. Judas the Galilean said that paying taxes to Caesar was treason against God; Jesus said, render to Caesar the things that are Caesar’s, and to God the things that are God’s (Mark 12:17). Theudas and Judas raised armed followings; Jesus told Peter to put away his sword (Matthew 26:52) and said to Pilate, my kingdom is not of this world (John 18:36). The would-be messiahs wanted a throne in Jerusalem; Jesus took a cross outside it. His kingdom does come, and it overturns every power in the end, but it comes by the word and the Spirit, not the sword. Christians who try to advance it by force or by political domination have misunderstood their King.

In a sentence. Gamaliel said that after Theudas, Judas the Galilean rose up at the time of the census and drew people after him, but he too died and his followers scattered, so they should keep away from these men and leave them alone, for if this plan was of human origin, it would fail.

On a Tuesday. Human plans fail; God’s purpose stands. When you see a cause, a ministry or a leader rise fast and fall hard, do not be shaken. Ask instead whether your own hopes rest on anything that will still stand when every human movement has scattered.

For worship. Human plans fail. My counsel shall stand, God says, and I will accomplish all my purpose (Isaiah 46:10). Revolts rise and are crushed; empires rise and fall; the kingdom of Christ, which came without a sword, has outlasted them all and will outlast whatever comes next. Praise the King whose kingdom cannot be shaken (Hebrews 12:28).
verseByVerse.note: Judas the Galilean led a revolt against the Roman census of AD 6.

verseByVerse.quote: "but if it is of God, you will not be able to overthrow them. You might even be found opposing God!" So they took his advice.
verseByVerse.commentary:
but if it is of God, you will not be able to overthrow them. You might even be found opposing God!” So they took his advice.

But if it is of God, you will not be able to overthrow them. True, and Luke’s whole book proves it. Gamaliel’s last sentence is the sharpest thing said in the chamber all day, and he almost certainly did not know how sharp it was.

You might even be found opposing God! The word he uses (theomachoi, God-fighters) appears nowhere else in the New Testament, and it did not come out of the synagogue. It belonged to the world of Greek tragedy, where the man who sets himself against heaven is destroyed by the attempt, usually while believing he is defending something. Gamaliel raises it as a remote hazard, a possibility worth insuring against. It is the actual position of every man he is speaking to. They have arrested God’s messengers twice, ignored an empty prison reported by their own officers, and just now discussed murdering the apostles for saying that God raised Jesus. The wisest man in the room got nearer to the truth than anyone else present and still treated it as a remote contingency. It is possible to be right about God in the conditional and wrong about him in the indicative.

His best student. There is a further irony that Luke may well intend his reader to catch later. Two chapters from here a young man stands at a stoning, holding the coats, approving; and he tells us himself that he was brought up in this city at the feet of this same Gamaliel (22:3). Saul of Tarsus had this exact warning from his own teacher, and went out and did the very thing it warned against, until a voice on a road asked him why he was persecuting me, and told him it was hard for him to kick against the goads (26:14). Gamaliel’s word turned out to be a prophecy about his best student.

Where Christians differ: is Gamaliel’s test reliable? Some treat it as a sure rule: if something succeeds, it is from God. Verdict: it is wise caution, and true in the long run, but not a full test. False religions have lasted centuries, and God’s work can look as if it is failing for a time. The true test is Scripture and Christ (1 John 4:1–3). Gamaliel’s advice was sensible, but it was neutrality, not faith. Neutrality towards Christ is not enough.

So they took his advice. For now. And the next verse tells you exactly what taking it amounted to. They did not kill the apostles; they had them beaten and repeated the order to be silent. This is what a court does when it has been warned that it may be fighting God: it reduces the sentence and carries on. Gamaliel’s own argument, taken seriously for five minutes, demanded an investigation, because a body told there is a real possibility it is at war with the Almighty cannot rationally respond by doing nothing and waiting. Nobody proposes finding out. They amend the punishment and move to the next item.

Delivered by an argument they did not make. The sentence to carry away from this scene is not about Gamaliel at all. Twelve men who could not defend themselves, in the hands of a court that wanted them dead, were delivered by an argument they did not make, from a man who was not on their side, for reasons that were not the right ones. The church’s survival that morning did not depend on its case being heard, its friends being influential, or its enemies being reasonable. It never has. What Gamaliel offered as a warning against a possibility, the apostles could have offered as a statement of fact: nothing that is of God will be overthrown.

So how do I test a movement or a teacher? By Scripture first, and by Christ at the centre. Does it confess that Jesus Christ has come in the flesh, truly God and truly man, crucified and risen (1 John 4:1–3)? Does it agree with what the apostles taught, as the Bereans checked even Paul against the Scriptures (17:11)? Does it make much of Christ, or of a leader, a method or an experience? And what fruit grows in the lives of its leaders and followers over time: humility, holiness, love, or pride, money and control (Matthew 7:15–20)? Size and success are not on the list. Neither is how moving the meetings are. A small, faithful church preaching Christ crucified passes the test that a famous movement may fail.

In a sentence. Gamaliel said that if it was of God they would not be able to overthrow them, and they might even find themselves fighting against God; and the council accepted his advice.

On a Tuesday. Waiting to see whether Christ is real is not enough. He is. Decide. And if you are already his, take courage from this: the work of God in your life and in your church cannot finally be overthrown, whatever the council of the day decides.

For worship. No one has ever fought against God and won. Pharaoh tried, and the sea closed over his chariots. Saul of Tarsus tried, and was thrown to the ground and raised up an apostle. The Lord does not only defeat his enemies; sometimes he turns them into his servants. Glory to the God whose purpose cannot be overthrown, and whose mercy is strong enough to convert the men who fight him.

verseByVerse.quote: and when they had called in the apostles, they beat them and charged them not to speak in the name of Jesus, and let them go.
verseByVerse.commentary:
and when they had called in the apostles, they beat them and charged them not to speak in the name of Jesus, and let them go.

And when they had called in the apostles, they beat them. The council cannot kill the apostles, for Gamaliel’s counsel has prevented it, but they can punish them, and they do. It is worth knowing what the sentence was, because English translations pass over it in three words. It was probably the synagogue flogging, forty strokes less one: the law permitted forty, and the practice stopped at thirty-nine so that a miscount could not break it (Deuteronomy 25:1–3). The man was stripped to the waist and bent over, and the strokes were laid on with a leather strap, a third of them on the chest and the rest across the back. Men were carried away from it. Paul, who received the same punishment five separate times, thought it worth listing among the things that nearly killed him (2 Corinthians 11:24). This is not a formality or a caution. Jesus had warned them: they will flog you in their synagogues (Matthew 10:17).

And charged them not to speak in the name of Jesus, and let them go. The same command as before, and it will have the same effect. The beating is meant to break the boldness; the charge is meant to silence the proclamation. Neither will succeed.

The incoherence of it. Notice what has just happened, because it is the most damning thing in the chapter. Minutes earlier the council was warned by its most honoured member that it might be found fighting against God. It accepted the advice. Then it had the men beaten and told them again to stop speaking. A body that genuinely thought it might be opposing the Almighty had one reasonable course and did not take it. They kept the verdict and lowered the sentence, which is what men do when they have decided the question already and are only negotiating the cost.

What does it mean to speak in the name of Jesus? In the Bible a name stands for the whole person: his identity, his character and above all his authority. To do or say something in someone’s name is to act on his behalf, as his representative, by his authority, the way an ambassador speaks not his own mind but his king’s, or a constable says stop in the name of the law. So when the apostles spoke in the name of Jesus, they were not merely mentioning him. They were publicly proclaiming who he is, the crucified and risen Lord, and calling people to trust and obey him, as his authorised messengers, backed by his authority and not their own (3:6; 4:12). That is exactly what the council wanted to stop: not idle talk, but the announcement that Jesus is Lord. To forbid the name was to forbid Christ himself.

And what does it mean to pray in Jesus’ name? The same thing, turned toward heaven. Praying in Jesus’ name is not adding a formula to the end of a prayer. It is coming to the Father on the ground of who Jesus is and what he has done, not on the ground of our own worthiness, and asking for what he would want, as people who belong to him (John 14:13–14; 16:23–24). It means we come with confidence, because his name opens the door; and it means we come with humility, because we are asking for his glory and not merely our wishes. When you end a prayer with in Jesus’ name, you are saying, I have no standing of my own here; I come in his.

In a sentence. They called the apostles in, had them flogged, ordered them not to speak in the name of Jesus, and released them.

On a Tuesday. The first apostles bled for the name. Honour them by speaking it. In one conversation this week, mention Jesus by name, not vaguely as God or faith, but as the person he is.

For worship. The backs of the apostles were laid open for the name, and the name was worth it, because the one who bears it was scourged first, and by his stripes we are healed (Isaiah 53:5). He took the lash that we deserved, and now he counts his servants’ wounds as precious. Blessed be the name of Jesus, at which every knee shall bow (Philippians 2:10), and for which his people have gladly suffered in every age.
verseByVerse.note: The beating was probably the synagogue punishment of thirty-nine lashes.

parallels.desc: forty stripes

verseByVerse.quote: Then they left the presence of the council, rejoicing that they were counted worthy to suffer dishonor for the name. And every day, in the temple and from house to house, they did not cease teaching and preaching that the Christ is Jesus.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Then they left the presence of the council, rejoicing that they were counted worthy to suffer dishonor for the name. And every day, in the temple and from house to house, they did not cease teaching and preaching that the Christ is Jesus.

Then they left the presence of the council, rejoicing that they were counted worthy to suffer dishonor for the name. The apostles walk out of the Sanhedrin with their backs opened, and Luke says they were rejoicing. Not resigned. Not composed. Not bearing it well. Rejoicing, on the way home, out loud enough that somebody remembered it. Not because pain is good, but because suffering for Christ is an honour (Matthew 5:11–12; 1 Peter 4:13–16; Philippians 1:29).

Counted worthy to suffer dishonour. The reason Luke gives is a phrase that should not be able to exist. To be counted worthy is to be honoured, singled out, judged fit for something valuable; dishonour is public shame, the thing every man in that culture organised his life to avoid. Luke welds them. Whatever had happened to these men, it had reversed the sign on the whole transaction. They walked into that room as defendants and came out feeling that they had been given something. Not long before, this same group had been arguing on a road about which of them was the greatest (Mark 9:33–34). The argument is over. The prize turned out to be a flogging.

For the name. That is all Luke writes. No qualifier, no possessive, nothing to say whose name is meant. Every Jew reading it would feel the weight of that construction, because in Jewish speech the Name was how you referred to the God of Israel when you would not pronounce the divine name itself. And here is Luke, writing about a carpenter executed only a short time earlier outside the city wall, and he uses the phrase absolutely, as though there could be no confusion about which name is meant. Among these people there was not. Within a few years Christians spoke of the name as a title for Jesus (3 John 7). The council in this very chapter refused to say the name at all, calling him this man (v. 28). The apostles have stopped needing to say it, for the opposite reason.

What it does not mean. A guard is needed here, because this verse has been laid on suffering people as a demand, and it is not one. Three things keep it honest. First, they are not rejoicing in the pain; they are rejoicing in what the pain meant, that the Lord they had abandoned in a garden had now counted them fit to be shamed on his account. Nobody is asked to enjoy a scourge. Second, this is a specific kind of suffering: dishonour incurred for Christ, in the course of obeying him. A diagnosis is not dishonour for the name. Neither is a bereavement, a betrayal, or a depression that will not lift. Those are real, and Scripture speaks to them elsewhere and at length; this verse is not the text to beat a grieving person with. Third, this joy is a thing given, not manufactured. It arrived in them on the way out of that building. It is not a mood that a Christian owes in advance and is failing to produce.

I could never do that. To anyone who reads this and quietly concludes he could never do it, that if it cost him his job, his family’s standing or a beating, he would fold: look at who is walking out of that chamber. The man in front is Peter. Only a short while ago, with nothing at stake but a servant girl’s opinion beside a fire, he said he did not know Jesus, and then went out and wept. Nobody in history has a worse record under pressure than the man leading this procession. What changed was not his temperament. Something was given to him that had not been there in the courtyard, and it is given to people when it is needed and not before. The measure of what you could bear today is not the measure of what you would be carried through tomorrow.

Is it right to want to suffer for Christ? Not to seek it. The apostles did not court the flogging; they obeyed and accepted what came. Jesus told his disciples to flee from one town to the next when persecuted (Matthew 10:23), and Paul used his Roman citizenship to escape unjust punishment (22:25). Some in the early church rushed to martyrdom, and wise pastors rebuked them. What is right is to be willing: to love Christ more than comfort or reputation, so that when faithfulness costs something, you pay it gladly. Do not go looking for the cross. Do not run from it when it is laid on you for his sake.

And every day, in the temple and from house to house. Luke ends the chapter with the council’s order and its answer set side by side. They were charged not to speak in the name of Jesus, and every day they did not cease. Every day: not resumed after a decent interval, but daily, from that day. In the temple, the most public and most dangerous place in the city, belonging to the men who ordered the flogging; and house to house, at kitchen tables, where the church has always done most of its real work. Public and private together, and neither instead of the other. It is the pattern Paul would later describe to the Ephesian elders: teaching you in public and from house to house (20:20).

They did not cease teaching and preaching that the Christ is Jesus. Preaching (euangelizomenoi) is announcing good news, and the heart of it is one sentence: the Messiah is Jesus. All the hopes of Israel, all the promises of the prophets, all the longing of the psalms, have a name and a face, and it is the man the council would not name. They did not cease. It is a strange note to end on, and it is the right one. The whole apparatus of the most powerful religious body in that world had been brought to bear on twelve provincials over two days, arrest, imprisonment, formal trial, flogging, legal injunction, and by the following morning the only measurable result was that the message was being preached in more houses than before. He is worth this, was the verdict of the men with the wounds. Two thousand years later the name they would not stop saying is spoken every hour in every language on earth, and hardly anybody can name a single man who sat on the council that day, except the one who argued for leaving them alone.

Must I go house to house? Not necessarily door to door with leaflets, though some are called to that. But every Christian has a house, and the house is where the gospel has always travelled furthest. Open your home: a meal with a neighbour, a Bible read with your children, a conversation over coffee with a friend who is struggling. Speak of Christ where you already are, naturally and honestly, and support the public preaching of your church with your presence and prayers. The temple and the house belong together. Your pastor preaches in the one; you are sent into the other.

In a sentence. They left the council rejoicing that they had been counted worthy to suffer disgrace for the name, and every day, in the temple and from house to house, they did not stop teaching and proclaiming that Jesus is the Christ.

On a Tuesday. If you are mocked or passed over for Christ today, count it an honour, and then keep speaking of him. And if nothing of the kind has happened to you for a very long time, ask honestly whether anyone around you knows whose you are.

For worship. The Name the apostles carried out of that council chamber is the name above every name. It belongs to the Christ who endured the cross, despising the shame, for the joy that was set before him (Hebrews 12:2), and his joy is the joy that filled them on the road home. He counted it worth it to be shamed for them; they counted it worth it to be shamed for him. Glory to Jesus the Christ, whose name cannot be silenced, whose servants cannot be stopped, and whose praise will fill not only Jerusalem but the whole earth.

5.theology: The Holiness of God in the New Covenant Community. The deaths of Ananias and Sapphira are not anomalies — they have a precise parallel in Leviticus 10, where Nadab and Abihu are struck dead at the founding of the tabernacle worship. At every founding moment of a new covenant expression, God makes his holiness unmistakable. He did it at Sinai. He did it in the wilderness. He does it here, at the birth of the church. The message is the same: I am holy. You are dwelling in the presence of the Holy One. This is not a place for pretence. It is not that God is more severe in the new covenant than the old; it is that the new covenant community lives in an even closer proximity to the Holy Spirit than any previous generation, and proximity to holiness demands purity.
5.examples:
Then: A Jerusalem church only weeks old, discovering that the Spirit who fills them also searches them — and that the God of grace is also the God of holiness. The fear that fell on the church was not paralyzing; a few verses later we are told that believers were added to the Lord in multitudes. Healthy fear of God does not drive people away from him; it drives away the casual, and draws in the sincere.

Now: The contemporary church has largely lost the category of the fear of God. We speak of grace, love, and welcome — and rightly so. But a church that never trembles before the holiness of God has not understood grace; it has domesticated it. Ananias and Sapphira remind every generation that the Spirit cannot be fooled, that the church is not a social club, and that God’s presence is still a consuming fire.

6.title: The Choosing of the Seven
6.text: <sup>1</sup>Now in these days when the disciples were increasing in number, a complaint by the Hellenists arose against the Hebrews because their widows were being neglected in the daily distribution. <sup>2</sup>And the twelve summoned the full number of the disciples and said, “It is not right that we should give up preaching the word of God to serve tables. <sup>3</sup>Therefore, brothers, pick out from among you seven men of good repute, full of the Spirit and of wisdom, whom we will appoint to this duty. <sup>4</sup>But we will devote ourselves to prayer and to the ministry of the word.” <sup>5</sup>And what they said pleased the whole gathering, and they chose Stephen, a man full of faith and of the Holy Spirit, and Philip, and Prochorus, and Nicanor, and Timon, and Parmenas, and Nicolaus, a proselyte of Antioch. <sup>6</sup>These they set before the apostles, and they prayed and laid their hands on them. <sup>7</sup>And the word of God continued to increase, and the number of the disciples multiplied greatly in Jerusalem, and a great many of the priests became obedient to the faith. <sup>8</sup>And Stephen, full of grace and power, was doing great wonders and signs among the people. <sup>9</sup>Then some of those who belonged to the synagogue of the Freedmen (as it was called), and of the Cyrenians, and of the Alexandrians, and of those from Cilicia and Asia, rose up and disputed with Stephen. <sup>10</sup>But they could not withstand the wisdom and the Spirit with which he was speaking. <sup>11</sup>Then they secretly instigated men who said, “We have heard him speak blasphemous words against Moses and God.” <sup>12</sup>And they stirred up the people and the elders and the scribes, and they came upon him and seized him and brought him before the council, <sup>13</sup>and they set up false witnesses who said, “This man never ceases to speak words against this holy place and the law, <sup>14</sup>for we have heard him say that this Jesus of Nazareth will destroy this place and will change the customs that Moses delivered to us.” <sup>15</sup>And gazing at him, all who sat in the council saw that his face was like the face of an angel.
6.overview:
The growing church faces a problem from within. It now contained two groups of Jewish believers: “Hebrews”, who spoke Aramaic and were rooted in the land, and “Hellenists”, Greek-speaking Jews, many born abroad, who had settled in Jerusalem. Many Hellenists were elderly couples who had come to Jerusalem to die near the temple, which left a large number of widows without family support. The church shared food daily with widows in need, and the Hellenists complained that their widows were being overlooked. Prejudice between language groups was threatening the unity of chapter 4.

The apostles do not ignore the problem or try to handle it themselves. They tell the church to choose seven men of good reputation, full of the Spirit and wisdom, to take charge of the distribution, so that the apostles can give themselves to prayer and the ministry of the word. All seven have Greek names, so the church entrusts the matter to the very group that complained. The apostles pray and lay hands on them, and the word of God spreads, even many priests becoming believers. Then Luke turns to one of the seven, Stephen, full of grace and power, who works wonders and debates with Greek-speaking Jews from the Synagogue of the Freedmen. When they cannot answer his wisdom, they bring false witnesses who accuse him of speaking against the temple and the law, and he is brought before the council, where those staring at him see that his face is like the face of an angel.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–7 — The Appointment of the Seven
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: As the number of disciples grew, the Greek-speaking Jewish believers complained against the Aramaic-speaking ones that their widows were being neglected in the daily distribution of food. So the Twelve gathered all the disciples and said it would not be right for them to neglect the ministry of God’s word to wait on tables. The believers should choose seven men from among them who were known to be full of the Spirit and wisdom, and the apostles would put them in charge of this task, while giving their own attention to prayer and the ministry of the word. The proposal pleased everyone. They chose Stephen, a man full of faith and the Holy Spirit, and Philip, Procorus, Nicanor, Timon, Parmenas, and Nicolas, a convert to Judaism from Antioch. They presented these men to the apostles, who prayed and laid their hands on them. So God’s word spread. The number of disciples in Jerusalem increased rapidly, and a large number of priests became obedient to the faith.
verseByVerse.theology:
Word and Service in the Church

The apostles' refusal to give up preaching the word of God to serve tables (v. 2) is about vocation, not about dignity, and the passage guards against the misreading in the very next sentence: the men appointed to the tables must be full of the Spirit and of wisdom, which is not a lower bar. The whole argument turns on a single Greek root that appears on both sides of it — the apostles will not abandon the service of the word in order to serve tables. Waiting on widows and preaching to thousands are not two categories, one menial and one spiritual. They are two forms of one thing, and the only question is which form a particular man is called to. Nor are the Seven junior figures: Stephen is preaching within a paragraph and dead within a chapter, and Philip is still being called an evangelist twenty years later. What the passage protects is not the apostles' status but the church's food supply — a congregation whose teachers are buried in administration will in time be starved of the word, and a congregation whose widows are overlooked has already stopped believing what it preaches.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: The overlooked widows were very likely the kind of women Luke described in chapter 2 — Diaspora Jews, some of whom had come home to Jerusalem to end their days near the temple. Their husbands died, and the widows were left in a city where they had no land, no clan and no relatives, and could not follow the conversation at the distribution. Now: The question every congregation has to keep asking is not whether it would refuse anyone. It is who is currently being looked past — the people whose absence nobody notices, because they were never in the middle of the room to begin with.

verseByVerse.quote: Now in these days when the disciples were increasing in number, a complaint by the Hellenists arose against the Hebrews because their widows were being neglected in the daily distribution. And the twelve summoned the full number of the disciples and said, "It is not right that we should give up preaching the word of God to serve tables."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Now in these days when the disciples were increasing in number, a complaint by the Hellenists arose against the Hebrews because their widows were being neglected in the daily distribution. And the twelve summoned the full number of the disciples and said, “It is not right that we should give up preaching the word of God to serve tables.

Meaning first. Acts 6 shows a third threat to the church: division. A practical problem, the neglect of some widows, threatens to split Greek-speaking and Aramaic-speaking believers. The apostles solve it by appointing seven men to oversee the care, so that they can keep to prayer and the word. The result: the word spreads further, and even priests believe. Then one of the seven, Stephen, becomes the first great witness to suffer death, and his story leads the gospel out of Jerusalem. The chapter that begins with bread for widows ends with a face shining like Moses’ before the highest court in Israel.

Now in these days when the disciples were increasing in number. Luke dates the trouble precisely. The problem is a symptom of the growth. Nothing had gone wrong with the church except that there was more of it than the existing arrangements could see. Growth brings new problems, and a church that is never troubled by them is usually not growing.

A complaint by the Hellenists arose against the Hebrews. Both groups in this quarrel are Jews and both are Christians. The Hellenists were Greek-speaking Jews, mostly born in the lands of the dispersion or returned from them, who read their Scriptures in Greek and thought in a Greek idiom. Many had settled in Jerusalem, some perhaps to die in the holy city. The Hebrews were Aramaic-speaking Jews native to the land, who read the Hebrew text. The line between them is language, culture and accent, not theology, and that is worth registering, because it is the line along which the first Christian conflict actually fell.

The word for complaint. Luke’s word (gongysmos) is grumbling, and it has a hard history: it is the word the Greek Old Testament uses over and over for Israel muttering in the wilderness, and it never once means anything good there. But notice what Luke does not do with it. He does not rebuke the complainers, and neither do the apostles. The grievance was true, it was raised, and it was acted on inside a single meeting. There is a lesson in that for anybody inclined to treat every complaint in a church as a spiritual failure in the person making it. Sometimes the murmuring is right.

Because their widows were being neglected in the daily distribution. Widows in that world had no pension and no state support; the church fed them daily. And the widows on the wrong side of this line are very likely women the book has already told us about. Chapter 2 described Jews from every nation under heaven who were dwelling in Jerusalem, settled residents rather than pilgrims, some of whom had crossed an empire in old age to be buried near the temple. Men like that died, as they had come to do. Their widows were left behind in a city where they owned no land, had no clan to fall back on, no sons in the district, and could not always follow what was being said around them. They were the most exposed people in the congregation, and they were the ones who got missed.

Overlooked, not rejected. Luke’s word is neglected, and it is the mercy of the sentence: overlooked, looked past. Nobody had decided that these women should go without. There was no policy, no vote, no meeting at which the Hellenists were discussed and set aside. In the press of a distribution serving thousands, run by men who spoke a different language at home, the ones without a voice were simply not seen. It was probably oversight, not malice, but it was real. That is how this kind of injustice nearly always happens, and it is why the people responsible are usually genuinely surprised to hear of it.

And the twelve summoned the full number of the disciples. The Twelve do not deal with it quietly. A congregation now numbering many thousands is called together and told there is a problem. They could have adjusted the rota and said nothing. Instead the failure is put in public, in front of the very people who had been neglected.

It is not right that we should give up preaching the word of God to serve tables. The sentence has been misread for centuries, so it needs handling with care. It is not a clergyman declining a menial job. The proof is in the next verse, where the men who are to do that job must be full of the Spirit and of wisdom, which is not a lower standard, and in the event these are the men who go on to preach in synagogues and evangelise Samaria. Serving tables is not beneath the apostles; their calling is the word. If they did everything, the word would suffer. A matter of priority, not of dignity. What the apostles are protecting is the church’s food supply of a different kind: a congregation whose teachers disappear into administration will be starved within a generation, and the widows will still not be fed.

What should I do if I feel overlooked in my church? Say so, gently and to the right people. The Hellenists raised their complaint, and it was heard; that is the pattern. Go to an elder or deacon, describe what has happened rather than accusing anyone of motives, and assume, as is usually true, that it was oversight rather than contempt. Then give the leaders time to act. Avoid the wilderness kind of grumbling, which talks to everyone except the people who can help and nurses a grievance instead of solving it. And if you have been overlooked, you will know better than most how to notice others who are. Become the person who sees them.

Who is being looked past? That leaves a question a reader can put to his own church, and it is sharper than the one usually asked. Not, would we turn anybody away? Almost nobody would. But who is currently being looked past: who is in the building and not in anybody’s line of sight, because they were never in the middle of the room, and because asking would require somebody to find out? The widow who comes alone, the international student, the family whose English is halting, the man with a disability who leaves before the coffee.

In a sentence. As the disciples grew in number, the Greek-speaking Jews complained that their widows were being overlooked in the daily food distribution, and the Twelve gathered all the disciples and said it was not right for them to neglect the word of God to serve tables.

On a Tuesday. Growth brings problems. Deal with complaints honestly and quickly before they divide. And this Sunday, before you speak to your friends, look round the room for the person nobody is talking to, and go and talk to them first.

For worship. The God of this church is the defender of widows (Psalm 68:5), who watches over the sojourner and upholds the widow and the fatherless (Psalm 146:9). Not one of those overlooked women was overlooked by him. The Lord Jesus, from the cross, made provision for his own widowed mother (John 19:26–27), and his church learned to do the same. Praise the Shepherd who sees the sheep at the edge of the flock, and who will not let his people forget them.
verseByVerse.note: The Hellenists were Greek-speaking Jewish believers, many born outside the land; the Hebrews spoke Aramaic. Widows without family depended on the community’s daily food distribution.

verseByVerse.quote: "Therefore, brothers, pick out from among you seven men of good repute, full of the Spirit and of wisdom, whom we will appoint to this duty. But we will devote ourselves to prayer and to the ministry of the word."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Therefore, brothers, pick out from among you seven men of good repute, full of the Spirit and of wisdom, whom we will appoint to this duty. But we will devote ourselves to prayer and to the ministry of the word.

Therefore, brothers, pick out from among you seven men of good repute, full of the Spirit and of wisdom. Look at what the apostles ask for in a man who is going to hand out food. Three qualifications, and not one of them is administrative. Nothing about numeracy, or organisation, or a head for logistics, which is what the work actually called for. Good reputation, filled with the Spirit, wise. The church’s first job description asks for character, the Spirit and wisdom, and then sets the men to work on a food queue. Handling money and caring for vulnerable people requires character before it requires skill, and Paul’s later qualifications for deacons are similar (1 Timothy 3:8–13).

The congregation chooses. Notice also who does the choosing. Pick out from among you: the apostles set the standard and the congregation makes the selection. No slate is presented. The people who had raised the complaint are handed the pen. The congregation chooses; the apostles appoint. Responsibility is shared.

Whom we will appoint to this duty. The word for duty (chreia) is need, task: the practical need that had come to light. The office exists because of a need, not a need because of an office.

But we will devote ourselves to prayer and to the ministry of the word. Then the Twelve state their own limit, and the wording repays attention. The verb for devote is the one Luke used of the whole church at 2:42: to stick at a thing and refuse to be prised off it. And prayer is named first. It is worth sitting with the fact that when the apostles listed the two things they could not afford to be dragged away from, one of them was the thing nobody in the congregation would have noticed them dropping. These are the priorities of pastoral ministry, and both are labour (1 Timothy 4:13; 2 Timothy 4:2). A minister who neglects them for administration fails his flock, however busy he looks.

Service of tables, service of the word. The word for ministry (diakonia) is service, and the verb for serving tables is from the same root. Both halves of the apostles’ sentence use it. That is the whole argument. Waiting on widows and preaching to thousands are not two categories, a menial one and a spiritual one. They are two forms of the one thing, and the only question is which one a particular man is called to.

Where Christians differ: were the seven the first deacons? They are not called deacons here, though the verb serve (diakonein) and the noun (diakonia) are used. Luke never calls these men deacons anywhere; later he simply calls Philip one of the seven (21:8). Verdict: many rightly see here the pattern for the office of deacon, which appears formally later (Philippians 1:1; 1 Timothy 3:8–13): men set apart to oversee practical care so that elders can give themselves to the word and prayer. The two offices, elders and deacons, are the New Testament pattern for church leadership.

Not an administrative committee. Paul’s later requirements for deacons, men of dignity, tested, holding the faith with a clear conscience, plainly grow from the same soil as the qualifications set out here. But do not reduce these seven to a committee. Watch what they actually do next. Stephen is arguing in synagogues within a paragraph and is dead within a chapter. Philip takes the gospel to Samaria, baptises an Ethiopian official on a desert road, and is still called an evangelist twenty years later. Neither of them stayed at the tables. Whatever the church later made of the office, it began with men so full of the Spirit that the job could not hold them.

Does this mean only men may serve as deacons? Luke uses the word for men, and the seven were chosen for a public trust in the church. Christians differ on whether women may hold the office of deacon. Paul calls Phoebe a servant of the church at Cenchreae, using the same word (Romans 16:1), and 1 Timothy 3:11 may speak of women deacons or of deacons’ wives. Many complementarian churches appoint women as deacons, since the office is one of service, not of teaching and ruling, which belong to the elders; others reserve it for men. What is plain is that women served the early church in many ways, and that every church needs their gifts.

What it was actually for. Notice what the church’s first appointment of servants was for. Not a building programme, not a doctrinal commission, not a mission board. Some widows who spoke the wrong language were being missed at the food distribution, and the apostles treated that as serious enough to reorganise the leadership of the church over it. The complaint came from the minority group, and the solution, as the next verse shows, handed the entire operation to seven men with Greek names. They did not manage the grievance; they gave the aggrieved the keys.

How can I help my pastors keep to prayer and the word? By taking up the tasks that do not need them. Every church has a hundred necessary jobs that someone other than the minister can do: the rota, the accounts, the building, the visits, the meals for the new mother, the lifts for the elderly. When you do one of them well and without being asked twice, you are not doing something lesser than preaching; you are serving the word by clearing room for it. And pray for your pastors by name, that their study would be fruitful and their prayers persevering. Then guard their time kindly: not every question needs the pastor.

In a sentence. The apostles told the believers to choose seven men of good reputation, full of the Spirit and of wisdom, to put in charge of this task, while they gave themselves to prayer and the ministry of the word.

On a Tuesday. If you are a leader, ask whether you are spending your best hours on what only you can do. If you are not, ask which task in your church you could quietly take up so that someone else can.

For worship. The Lord Jesus came not to be served but to serve (Mark 10:45). He washed feet and broke bread and fed multitudes, and he also spent whole nights in prayer and taught the word with authority. Both kinds of service meet in him perfectly, and he gives both to his body. Praise the Servant King, who has arranged his church so that the hungry are fed and the word is preached, and who counts no faithful service small.

parallels.desc: Jethro advises Moses to share the load

verseByVerse.quote: And what they said pleased the whole gathering, and they chose Stephen, a man full of faith and of the Holy Spirit, and Philip, and Prochorus, and Nicanor, and Timon, and Parmenas, and Nicolaus, a proselyte of Antioch. These they set before the apostles, and they prayed and laid their hands on them.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And what they said pleased the whole gathering, and they chose Stephen, a man full of faith and of the Holy Spirit, and Philip, and Prochorus, and Nicanor, and Timon, and Parmenas, and Nicolaus, a proselyte of Antioch. These they set before the apostles, and they prayed and laid their hands on them.

And what they said pleased the whole gathering. Unity restored. It is worth marking the moment, because it does not come again so simply: a church with money, a grievance and an ethnic fault line running through it settles the matter in one meeting, by giving the power away.

And they chose Stephen, a man full of faith and of the Holy Spirit. Stephen stands out. He will be the first martyr (chapter 7). But how could anyone tell that a man was full of the Spirit? The apostles told the church to pick out such men (v. 3), so the fullness was no hidden claim but something the congregation could recognise. It shows itself, and over time unmistakably. In character: the fruit the Spirit grows, love, joy, peace, patience, kindness, gentleness, self-control (Galatians 5:22–23), steady enough to earn good repute. In wisdom: how a man speaks and handles matters, and Stephen’s opponents could not withstand his (v. 10). In faith: a settled trust and boldness. The church needed no special revelation. They saw the Spirit in how he lived, spoke and served, by Jesus’ own rule: you will recognise them by their fruits (Matthew 7:16, 20). And note the lovely ordinariness. These Spirit-filled men were chosen to wait tables and settle a food dispute. Fullness of the Spirit is proved first in humble, everyday service.

And Philip. Later Philip the evangelist (21:8), who takes the gospel to Samaria and to the Ethiopian official (chapter 8).

And Prochorus, and Nicanor, and Timon, and Parmenas. Otherwise unknown. Four men, named once in Scripture and never again, trusted with widows’ bread and forgotten by history. They are remembered by God.

And Nicolaus, a proselyte of Antioch. A Gentile convert to Judaism, and then to Christ. He had converted in a Syrian city, and he is now on the body running the welfare of the Jerusalem church. Antioch will become the great centre of the Gentile mission (11:19–26), and here is its first appearance, in a man.

Was this Nicolaus the founder of the Nicolaitans? Revelation condemns a group called the Nicolaitans (Revelation 2:6, 15), and some early writers, from Irenaeus on, linked them with this man. Scripture does not. Luke presents him as a man of good repute, full of the Spirit and of wisdom, chosen by the whole church, and the link is uncertain at best. The name was not rare. It is wise not to blacken a man whom the Bible honours on the strength of a later guess.

All seven have Greek names. Read the list and something jumps out that would have been unmissable to Luke’s first readers. Stephen, Philip, Prochorus, Nicanor, Timon, Parmenas, Nicolaus: there is not a Hebrew name among them. And the last man was not born a Jew at all. Consider what the congregation has just done. A minority group complained that its widows were being overlooked. The majority could have appointed four Hebrews and three Hellenists, which would have been fair and defensible and would have left the Hebrews in control of the money. Instead they handed the whole operation to the people who had raised the complaint. Generous and wise.

These they set before the apostles, and they prayed and laid their hands on them. The Bible uses this gesture several ways, best read against its Old Testament roots: for blessing (Jacob over Ephraim and Manasseh, Genesis 48:14; Jesus over the children, Mark 10:16); for identifying with a sacrifice (the worshipper’s hand on the animal, Leviticus 1:4; the high priest’s on the scapegoat, Leviticus 16:21); and, closest here, for commissioning to an office. The pattern is Moses and Joshua. God told Moses to take Joshua, a man in whom is the Spirit, and lay his hand on him and commission him (Numbers 27:18–23), and afterwards Joshua was full of the spirit of wisdom, for Moses had laid his hands on him (Deuteronomy 34:9). Just so here: the seven are publicly set apart, with prayer that God would equip them by his Spirit. The New Testament keeps the practice for appointing to ministry (13:3; 1 Timothy 4:14; 2 Timothy 1:6).

Not magic. Two things are to be held together. It is never magic: it is always joined to prayer, and it is the prayer that asks God to act, not the hands that transfer power. And it is a public act: the church openly recognising those God has called and entrusting them with a task. Scripture even warns against doing it lightly: do not be hasty in the laying on of hands (1 Timothy 5:22).

How do we heal division in a church? The way this church did. Take the complaint seriously instead of explaining it away. Bring it into the open with the whole church rather than handling it in corners. Look for godly people from the group that feels unheard and give them real responsibility, not a token seat. Pray over the solution together. And keep the gospel at the centre, because the deepest unity in a church is not a compromise between groups but a shared belonging to Christ, in whom there is neither Jew nor Greek (Galatians 3:28). Division usually grows where people feel unseen. It shrinks when they are seen and trusted.

In a sentence. The whole group was pleased and chose Stephen, a man full of faith and of the Holy Spirit, with Philip, Prochorus, Nicanor, Timon, Parmenas and Nicolaus, a convert from Antioch, and set them before the apostles, who prayed and laid their hands on them.

On a Tuesday. When people feel overlooked, give them a voice and a share in leadership; it heals division. And pray this week, by name, for the deacons and helpers in your church, the people whose names no one will remember but God.

For worship. The Spirit who filled Stephen for the work of waiting on tables is the same Spirit who raised Christ from the dead. He does not save his power for platforms. Praise the God who fills ordinary servants with extraordinary grace, who writes the names of Prochorus and Parmenas in his book, and who makes one new people out of Hebrews and Hellenists, Jews and Gentiles, in his Son.
verseByVerse.note: All seven have Greek names, suggesting they came from the Hellenist side. Laying on hands marked commissioning for a task.

parallels.desc: Moses lays hands on Joshua

verseByVerse.quote: And the word of God continued to increase, and the number of the disciples multiplied greatly in Jerusalem, and a great many of the priests became obedient to the faith.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And the word of God continued to increase, and the number of the disciples multiplied greatly in Jerusalem, and a great many of the priests became obedient to the faith.

And the word of God continued to increase. This sentence is doing more work than it looks. Luke uses a formula of this shape several times in Acts (9:31; 12:24; 16:5; 19:20; 28:31), and every time it marks the close of a section and the opening of the next. He is putting a full stop at the end of the church’s Jerusalem years. What follows is Stephen, then persecution, then Samaria, then the world.

The word grows. Notice the odd subject of the clause. Not the church increased: the word of God increased. Luke habitually talks about the message as though it were the living thing and the congregation merely its visible result, a seed with its own vitality, growing in ground that did not manufacture it. It is a small habit of speech with a large theology inside it. God’s word does not return to him empty; it accomplishes what he purposes (Isaiah 55:10–11). Solving the problem freed the apostles, and the word spread.

And the number of the disciples multiplied greatly in Jerusalem. Steady growth, in the city that had crucified Jesus a short while before.

And a great many of the priests became obedient to the faith. The sentence exists for this last clause, and it is startling. It is easy to misread who these men were. This is not the council changing its mind, and it is not the high-priestly families; those men appear in this book only as opponents. The ordinary priesthood was an enormous body, Josephus reckons some twenty thousand, divided into courses that served at the temple for a week or two each year and spent the rest at home in the villages of Judea working an ordinary trade (Luke 1:8–9). Zechariah, the father of John the Baptist, was one of them, and Luke’s Gospel opens with him burning incense on the one occasion in his life that the lot fell to him. These are the rank and file of the temple, often poor, and not part of the Sadducee aristocracy.

The cost of their faith. That makes the cost of what they did very sharp. A priest who confessed Jesus was saying that the sacrifice he assisted at every morning had been fulfilled: that the machinery he had been trained for, the altar his family existed to serve, the whole apparatus that gave his household its identity and its livelihood, had done its work. He was not changing his opinion about a religious question. He was declaring that the shadow had given way to the substance, having watched, perhaps, a man die outside the wall on the afternoon the lambs were being killed. Some of them had very likely been on duty that day. The letter to the Hebrews would later explain at length what they had grasped: Christ has offered for all time a single sacrifice for sins (Hebrews 10:12).

Obedient to the faith. Luke’s phrase is worth keeping. Not persuaded of it, not interested in it: they became obedient to it. The faith is something a man obeys, which is exactly how Paul frames the whole business at both ends of his letter to Rome (Romans 1:5; 16:26). Believing the gospel is obedience to God’s call. In the New Testament, believing is a thing you do with your feet as well as your mind.

The quiet argument of the chapter. Then there is the placing. Luke reports a row about widows and bread, a congregational meeting and the appointment of seven men to a distribution list, and in the very next sentence tells us the word spread and the priests started coming. He does not say the one caused the other, and it would be crude to pretend that sorting out administration produces revival; God is not a mechanism. But he has put the two side by side, and the implication is hard to miss. A church whose Greek-speaking widows go hungry while it preaches that the risen Christ has made one people out of many is making an argument against itself, and everybody watching can hear it. Remove the contradiction and the message can be heard for what it is.

Can people still come to Christ from the heart of another religion? Yes, and this verse is one of the great encouragements to pray for them. These priests had more invested in the old system than anyone: training, income, family identity and the respect of their village. God brought them to Christ anyway. The same God still calls imams, monks, rabbis, priests of other faiths and convinced atheists, often at great personal cost.
