Do not write anyone off as too religious, too devoted or too committed elsewhere to be reached. The word of God increases in the most unlikely soil, and the Spirit who opened the hearts of temple priests can open any heart.

In a sentence. The word of God kept spreading, the number of disciples in Jerusalem increased greatly, and a large number of priests became obedient to the faith.

On a Tuesday. Think of the person you know who seems least likely to become a Christian, perhaps someone deeply committed to another faith or to none. Pray for them by name today, and expect God to be able to do it.

For worship. The word of God grows, and even priests of the old order bowed to Christ, the great High Priest to whom every altar had pointed. He offered himself once for all, and then sat down at the right hand of God, because the work was finished. Praise the Lamb of God, whose one sacrifice made every temple sacrifice complete, and who drew the very men who had served at that altar to kneel before him.
verseByVerse.note: There were many thousands of ordinary priests, serving in rotation.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 8–15 — Stephen: The Man Who Couldn't Be Stopped
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Stephen, full of God’s grace and power, performed great wonders and signs among the people. Opposition arose from members of the Synagogue of the Freedmen, as it was called, Jews from Cyrene and Alexandria as well as the provinces of Cilicia and Asia, who began to argue with him. But they could not stand up against his wisdom or the Spirit by whom he spoke. So they secretly persuaded some men to say they had heard Stephen speak blasphemy against Moses and God. They stirred up the people, the elders and the teachers of the law, seized Stephen and brought him before the council. They produced false witnesses, who said that this man never stopped speaking against the holy place and the law, and that they had heard him say Jesus of Nazareth would destroy this place and change the customs Moses handed down. Everyone in the council looked intently at Stephen, and they saw that his face was like the face of an angel.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Cost of Prophetic Witness

Stephen's arrest follows the shape of his master's with a precision Luke's first readers cannot have missed: suborned witnesses, a charge concerning the temple and the law, a council, a verdict of blasphemy. The accusation that Matthew and Mark record against Jesus (Matthew 26:61; Mark 14:58) is in fact the accusation Luke records against Stephen — the servant is handed the master's charge sheet. Reformed theology has read this as more than a coincidence of circumstance. Where the gospel genuinely threatens entrenched religious power it meets the same resistance in the same order, because the objection is never finally to the argument — the argument had already been lost at verse 10 — but to what conceding it would cost. What Stephen's case adds to the pattern is the sober detail that winning the argument and losing your life are entirely compatible, and that Luke plainly did not consider the second to be a reversal of the first.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: Stephen's opponents could not withstand his wisdom, and rather than yield to it they changed the subject to blasphemy and found men who would swear to it. The gospel does not always win in the short term; sometimes the first thing it wins is a grave. Now: The promise attached to moments of that kind is more modest, and more useful, than it is usually made out to be. A believer put on the spot is promised a mouth, not a result — that he will not be left standing there with nothing to say. Whether he is believed, and what it costs him, are God's business.

verseByVerse.quote: And Stephen, full of grace and power, was doing great wonders and signs among the people.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And Stephen, full of grace and power, was doing great wonders and signs among the people.

And Stephen, full of grace and power. Two verses ago this man’s job was to see that the widows got their share of the bread. Luke now has him working great wonders and signs among the people. And there is a quiet fact underneath what follows. Stephen enters Scripture three verses ago and is dead by the end of the next chapter. In that short space Luke gives him more superlatives than he gives most of the Twelve, and tells us nothing else about him whatever: no home town, no trade, no family, no age, no account of how he came to believe. He has two chapters, one sermon and a shining face.

A man filled with God. Stephen is described as full four times: of the Spirit and of wisdom (v. 3), of faith and of the Holy Spirit (v. 5), of grace and power (here), and of the Holy Spirit as he dies (7:55). He is a man saturated by God. Grace carries two notes that belong together: the favour of God resting richly upon him, his life freely enabled and blessed, nothing of it earned; and the graciousness that such favour produces, the winsome, Christ-like attractiveness of a man shaped by grace (compare the Word, full of grace and truth, John 1:14). Power is the Spirit’s enabling might, the very power Jesus promised: you will receive power when the Holy Spirit has come upon you (1:8).

Grace first, then power. Note the order. The favour and gracious character come first, and the power flows out of a life already full of grace. Power without grace is a dangerous thing, and the church has seen enough gifted men without grace to know it. Stephen had both, in the right order.

Was doing great wonders and signs among the people. Mark who this is: not an apostle, but one of the seven chosen to wait on tables, yet working wonders that Luke had until now reported only of Jesus and the apostles (2:22, 43; 5:12). He is the first non-apostle in Acts to do signs, and it comes after the apostles laid their hands on him (v. 6). Signs went with the apostles and with those they commissioned (8:6, 18).

Stephen was not an apostle, so how does this fit the view that signs belonged to the apostles? Stephen and Philip were among the seven on whom the apostles had laid their hands, and their signs belong to the same foundational ministry. The signs were not given to every believer, but to those closely tied to the apostles as the gospel first spread, and on the cessationist reading, the more likely one, held charitably, they did not continue as standing gifts beyond that generation (see on 5:12). What did continue, and continues today, is what Stephen had first: grace, faith, wisdom and the Spirit. Those are not for a few. They are for every believer.

In a sentence. Stephen, full of grace and power, was doing great wonders and signs among the people.

On a Tuesday. A man appointed to serve tables became a mighty witness. Faithfulness in small tasks prepares for great ones. Do the small task in front of you this week as though Christ himself had handed it to you, because he has.

For worship. Every grace in Stephen was a ray from the One who is full of grace and truth, from whose fullness we have all received, grace upon grace (John 1:16). Stephen was full because Christ is fuller. Praise the Lord Jesus, who pours his own grace and power into ordinary servants, and whose glory shines brightest in men who will soon lay down their lives for him.

verseByVerse.quote: Then some of those who belonged to the synagogue of the Freedmen (as it was called), and of the Cyrenians, and of the Alexandrians, and of those from Cilicia and Asia, rose up and disputed with Stephen.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Then some of those who belonged to the synagogue of the Freedmen (as it was called), and of the Cyrenians, and of the Alexandrians, and of those from Cilicia and Asia, rose up and disputed with Stephen.

Then some of those who belonged to the synagogue of the Freedmen. This is the first mention of a synagogue in Acts, so a word on what it was. The synagogue was the local Jewish assembly and meeting house: not the temple, of which there was only one, in Jerusalem, but a community centre found in every town where Jews lived, for the reading and study of Scripture, prayer and teaching. It arose after the Babylonian exile, when the temple lay in ruins and the people were scattered, and by Jesus’ day it was the heartbeat of Jewish life everywhere (see the fuller note at 13:15). A great city like Jerusalem held many synagogues, often grouped by homeland or language.

Who were the Freedmen? Freed slaves and their descendants. The likeliest background is that these were Jews, or the children of Jews, taken captive when the Roman general Pompey conquered Jerusalem in 63 BC, carried to Rome as slaves, later set free, and forming a distinct community; some settled again in Jerusalem with their own synagogue. An inscription found in Jerusalem records a synagogue built by one Theodotus, with lodging for those coming from abroad, which gives a vivid picture of exactly this kind of community. Whether Luke means one synagogue or several is grammatically uncertain; the number is not the point.

And of the Cyrenians, and of the Alexandrians, and of those from Cilicia and Asia. Greek-speaking Jews from North Africa (Cyrene), Egypt (Alexandria), and Asia Minor (Cilicia and Asia). Notice that these were all Hellenists, the very group Stephen himself belonged to (v. 1). So this first great clash is a debate among fellow Greek-speaking Jews, Hellenist against Hellenist. Stephen went to those he knew best.

Cilicia. One homeland on the list should make the reader sit up. Cilicia’s capital was Tarsus, the home city of Saul (21:39), who appears at the end of the next chapter, standing by and approving Stephen’s death (7:58; 8:1). Scripture does not say outright that Saul was among these disputants, but he was a zealous Cilician Pharisee, present at the scene, and many think it likely he was in the thick of it. The synagogue debate may well be the place where the future apostle Paul first set himself against the name of Jesus.

Rose up and disputed with Stephen. They argued with him, and finding that they could not withstand his Spirit-given wisdom (v. 10), they would soon abandon argument for false witness and violence. This is the arena of the church’s first great public defence of the faith.

How do I start speaking about Christ to people I know? Begin where Stephen did: with your own circle, the people who share your language, background and world. You understand their questions better than an outsider would, and they know you well enough to see whether your faith is real. You do not need to win debates. Ask good questions about what they believe and why, listen properly, and say honestly what Christ means to you and why you believe he rose from the dead. Pray before and after. Be ready for some to argue and some to listen. And remember that the man arguing hardest may, like Saul, be closer to the kingdom than anyone would guess.

In a sentence. Some members of the synagogue of the Freedmen, with Jews from Cyrene, Alexandria, Cilicia and Asia, rose up and began to argue with Stephen.

On a Tuesday. Witness in your own circles. Think of one person from your own background, family or workplace whom you have never spoken to about Christ, and look for an opening this week.

For worship. The God who scattered his people to Rome as slaves gathered their children back to Jerusalem to hear the gospel. Nothing in their history was wasted, not the captivity, not the freedom, not the synagogue. And among those listening, perhaps, stood a young man from Tarsus whom God had set apart before he was born (Galatians 1:15). Praise the Lord of history, who prepares his hearers and his apostles in ways they cannot see.
verseByVerse.note: The Freedmen were descendants of Jews once enslaved and later freed, perhaps taken captive to Rome. Cilicia, in south-east Asia Minor, was Paul’s home province.

parallels.desc: Tarsus in Cilicia

verseByVerse.quote: But they could not withstand the wisdom and the Spirit with which he was speaking.
verseByVerse.commentary:
But they could not withstand the wisdom and the Spirit with which he was speaking.

But they could not withstand the wisdom and the Spirit with which he was speaking. One sentence, and it is a promise being kept word for word. Not long before, in the temple, Jesus had told his disciples what would happen when they were dragged before synagogues and rulers: I will give you a mouth and wisdom, which none of your adversaries will be able to withstand or contradict (Luke 21:15). Luke wrote that sentence in his first volume. He now writes, in his second, that they could not withstand the wisdom and the Spirit with which Stephen spoke. The same verb, the same word for wisdom, the same author. He is showing his reader the promise and then the receipt.

Whom they failed to withstand. Withstand is a strong word: to stand against, to hold a line. These men were not politely unconvinced. They set themselves against him and could not hold the position. And consider whom they failed against. Stephen is not an apostle. He has no training that Luke mentions, no commission to teach, and a job that consists of seeing that widows are fed. He may have been in office only weeks. The men across the room were literate, argumentative, thoroughly at home in Greek, the sort of men who had spent their lives in exactly this kind of dispute. They lost.

What it does not mean. This verse is regularly made to promise something Scripture does not promise. It does not say Stephen’s opponents were persuaded. It says they could not withstand him, and the very next verse tells you what they did instead. He won the argument comprehensively and was dead within a chapter. Any use of this promise which implies that a believer who trusts God will come out of such conversations with the other man conceding is not describing what happened here. What is promised is both better than a debating record and more limited than one. When a Christian is put on the spot for Christ, he will not be left with nothing to say. Not that he will be believed. Not that he will be safe. That he will not be silenced.

The fear of standing there empty. That is worth knowing in advance by anyone who dreads that kind of moment: the family lunch where the subject suddenly arrives, the colleague who wants to know how an intelligent person can believe any of it. Most people’s fear in those moments is not of being argued into a corner. It is of standing there empty. This verse speaks to that fear exactly, and declines to speak to the other one. The mouth is promised; the outcome is not.

Out-argued and unmoved. One further thing should be said plainly, because it explains the rest of the chapter. It is entirely possible to be comprehensively out-argued and completely unmoved. Everyone has done it: the moment when the point lands and, instead of yielding, you change the subject, or turn on the man, or observe that everybody is entitled to an opinion. When you cannot win the argument, you can attack the man. Verse 11 is that same manoeuvre carried out by professionals, with money and perjured witnesses, and it ends in a killing. The distance between the small version and the large one is shorter than most of us would care to measure.

Does this mean I need not prepare to explain my faith? No. The promise is not an excuse for laziness. Peter tells every Christian to be prepared to make a defence to anyone who asks for the reason for the hope that is in you, with gentleness and respect (1 Peter 3:15). Stephen’s wisdom came from the Spirit, but the Spirit had a man soaked in Scripture to work with, as the next chapter shows. So read your Bible, learn the reasons for the resurrection, think through the questions your friends actually ask. Then, when the moment comes and your preparation feels thin, trust the promise. The Spirit brings to mind what you have learned (John 14:26).

In a sentence. But they could not stand against the wisdom and the Spirit with which he spoke.

On a Tuesday. Ask for the Spirit’s wisdom before conversations about Christ, and expect him to give it. And when you lose an argument yourself, about anything, notice whether you yield to the truth or change the subject.

For worship. The Lord Jesus keeps his promises to the letter. He said he would give a mouth and wisdom, and here is the mouth and here is the wisdom, in a table-servant before the scholars of the dispersion. He is the Wisdom of God in person (1 Corinthians 1:24), and his Spirit speaks through his servants still. Praise the faithful Christ, who never leaves his witnesses empty-handed.

parallels.desc: a mouth and wisdom none can withstand

verseByVerse.quote: Then they secretly instigated men who said, "We have heard him speak blasphemous words against Moses and God." And they stirred up the people and the elders and the scribes, and they came upon him and seized him and brought him before the council,
verseByVerse.commentary:
Then they secretly instigated men who said, “We have heard him speak blasphemous words against Moses and God.” And they stirred up the people and the elders and the scribes, and they came upon him and seized him and brought him before the council,

Then they secretly instigated men. The word Luke uses for what they did (hypoballō) occurs nowhere else in the New Testament. It means to suborn: literally, to put a man in underneath, to plant him. They did not find witnesses. They installed them, as false witnesses had been found against Jesus (Mark 14:55–59). Think about what that involves. Somebody had to identify men willing to swear a false oath in a capital case. Somebody had to brief them on what to say. Somebody had to be confident enough of their nerve to stand them up in front of the council. This is not a crowd losing its temper. It is a considered operation, undertaken by religious men against someone they had failed to answer in open debate.

We have heard him speak blasphemous words against Moses and God. The charge carried the death penalty (Leviticus 24:16). And note the order: Moses first. In an accusation drafted to secure a conviction, the name placed first is the one expected to do the work, and here it is not God’s. What they had actually heard Stephen discuss concerned the law and the temple, and they knew perfectly well which half of that would move a room.

And they stirred up the people and the elders and the scribes. This is the hinge of the whole narrative, and it is easily read straight past. Go back over the previous two chapters. When Peter and John were arrested, the council could find no way to punish them because of the people (4:21). When the apostles were seized the second time, the captain brought them in without force, for they were afraid of being stoned by the people (5:26). Twice now the crowd has been the church’s protection and the authorities’ constraint. Here, for the first time, the crowd is turned against the church, and the moment it turns, the church has its first martyr. Peter walked out of that chamber alive. Stephen will not. The variable Luke has been quietly tracking through four chapters has just moved.

And they came upon him and seized him and brought him before the council. The council is the Sanhedrin, the same body that had tried Jesus and flogged the apostles.

When a man cannot be answered, he is re-described. The mechanism deserves naming, because it is the oldest one there is and nobody has improved on it. Nobody in that synagogue set out to prove Stephen wrong a second time. They set out to change what he was accused of, so that the argument would never have to be had again. It works because a crowd cannot check, and because a summary always travels faster than the thing it summarises.

Two warnings for Christians. Two things should be said before a Christian reader settles too comfortably into this passage. The first is that it describes what was done to a man who was genuinely innocent, and it is not a licence to file every criticism under persecution. Some criticism of Christians is accurate, and the reflex that reaches for Acts 6 is a very efficient way of never having to look at it. The second is harder. The church has, over the centuries, run this exact operation on other people: the misquoted opponent, the summarised heretic, the man whose actual words nobody troubled to read. Luke is describing a human technique, not a specifically anti-Christian one, and the people using it here were the religious ones.

What should I do if I am falsely accused? First, take it to God before you take it to anyone else, as Jesus did, who when he was reviled did not revile in return, but continued entrusting himself to him who judges justly (1 Peter 2:23). Second, ask honestly whether there is any truth in it, and own whatever there is. Third, where a false accusation does real harm, it is right to correct it calmly and through proper channels; Paul defended himself repeatedly in Acts, and appealed to Caesar. But do not retaliate, do not slander back, and do not let it make you bitter. God sees, and he will vindicate his servants, sometimes in this life and always on the last day.

In a sentence. They secretly got men to say they had heard him speak blasphemy against Moses and God, stirred up the people, the elders and the scribes, seized him and brought him before the council.

On a Tuesday. Christ’s servants are often falsely accused, as he was. If it happens to you, entrust yourself to the one who judges justly. And if you hear an accusation against someone else this week, check it before you repeat it.

For worship. Before Stephen, there was Jesus: falsely accused by planted witnesses, condemned for blasphemy by the same council, silent like a lamb before its shearers (Isaiah 53:7). He bore the injustice of the world so that he could bear its sin. Praise the innocent Lamb, who knows from the inside what it is to be lied about, and who stands beside every servant of his who is lied about for his sake.
verseByVerse.note: The council is the Sanhedrin.

parallels.desc: false witnesses against Naboth

verseByVerse.quote: and they set up false witnesses who said, "This man never ceases to speak words against this holy place and the law, for we have heard him say that this Jesus of Nazareth will destroy this place and will change the customs that Moses delivered to us."
verseByVerse.commentary:
and they set up false witnesses who said, “This man never ceases to speak words against this holy place and the law, for we have heard him say that this Jesus of Nazareth will destroy this place and will change the customs that Moses delivered to us.”

This man never ceases to speak words against this holy place and the law. Luke gives the verdict before the evidence: they were false witnesses. Then he reports what they said, and the interesting thing about it is how much of it was true. Two charges are brought: against the temple, and against the law.

For we have heard him say that this Jesus of Nazareth will destroy this place. Take the accusation apart. Jesus had spoken about this temple being thrown down, not one stone left on another (Luke 21:6). He had also said something about destroying a temple and raising it in three days, which his hearers misunderstood at the time and which John tells us was about his body (John 2:19–21; Mark 14:58). Stephen probably taught that Jesus is the true temple, and that the Most High does not dwell in houses made by hands, as he will say in the next chapter (7:48). The false witnesses twist the truth into a lie.

And will change the customs that Moses delivered to us. The customs delivered by Moses were indeed going to change: the whole New Testament argues that they did, and one letter spends most of its thirteen chapters on it. Stephen probably taught that the law is fulfilled in Christ (Matthew 5:17), and that its ceremonies were a shadow of the good things to come (Hebrews 10:1). Not against the law, but beyond its shadows to its substance.

They kept the topic and removed the reason. So this is not the case of a blameless man slandered with an invented story. The subject matter is genuinely his. What the witnesses did was subtler and far more effective than invention. Destroy in place of fulfil. Change in place of complete. Nothing about a new covenant; nothing about a temple that had finished the work it was built for; nothing about the one in whom God had come to live among his people. Strip out the framework, keep the residue, and then report the residue accurately. It is the technique of describing a surgeon as a man who cuts people open with a knife. Every word is true. The account is a lie.

Two finishing touches. They add two touches of their own. Never ceases: the suggestion of an obsessive who cannot leave the subject alone, which is a characterisation dressed as a fact. And this holy place, said inside the building, to the men who ran it, so that the offence stops being theological and becomes personal. They are not inviting the council to judge a doctrine. They are telling seventy-one men that their life’s work has been attacked.

Something worth distorting. Now the application, and it cuts in a direction readers may not expect. Christians who are misrepresented, and they are, and it is genuinely painful, reach for this passage very naturally. Before doing so it is worth asking a hard question: is the thing being distorted actually something I said? Stephen’s answer was very probably yes. He says it again at far greater length in the next chapter. He was not misquoted about his views. He was misrepresented about his reasons. That is a considerably better position to be in than the alternative. If a man is going to be misrepresented, let it be because he said something worth distorting.

Did Christianity abolish the law of Moses? It fulfilled it. The moral law, summed up in the Ten Commandments, still shows God’s holy will and guides the Christian life, though it no longer condemns those who are in Christ (Romans 8:1; 13:8–10). The ceremonial law, the sacrifices, priesthood, food laws and temple rituals, pointed forward to Christ and has been fulfilled in him, so we no longer keep it (Colossians 2:16–17). The civil laws of Israel as a nation have expired with that nation, though their general principles of justice remain wise (Westminster 19.3–5). So Stephen did not speak against Moses. He spoke of the one Moses wrote about (John 5:46).

In a sentence. They brought forward false witnesses who said that this man never stopped speaking against the temple and the law, for they had heard him say that Jesus of Nazareth would destroy this place and change the customs Moses handed down.

On a Tuesday. Half-truths are the most dangerous lies. Be careful how you report what others say: before you pass on someone’s words, ask whether you have kept their reasons as well as their topic. Quote people as you would want to be quoted.

For worship. Jesus is the temple where God meets man, the true and final sacrifice, the substance of every shadow Moses drew. He did not destroy the law; he kept it perfectly and bore its curse. Praise the Christ in whom all the customs of Moses find their meaning, and in whom God has come to dwell with his people for ever.

verseByVerse.quote: And gazing at him, all who sat in the council saw that his face was like the face of an angel.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And gazing at him, all who sat in the council saw that his face was like the face of an angel.

And gazing at him, all who sat in the council saw that his face was like the face of an angel. Luke closes the chapter on a sentence he never explains, and the reader is meant to carry it into everything Stephen says next. First the staring. The verb (atenizō) is the fixed, deliberate gaze Luke is fond of, the same word used of Peter looking straight at the beggar at the temple gate (3:4). And it is all who sat in the council: seventy-one men in a semicircle, every one of them looking at the same face, and looking long enough that it was still being described years later. There was, very possibly, a young Pharisee from Cilicia at this trial who would afterwards spend a great deal of time in Luke’s company.

The face of Moses. What they see is the face of an angel. Luke offers no gloss, and the temptation is to take it as a general remark about serenity. It is far more precise than that, and the precision is devastating. Stephen is on trial for speaking blasphemous words against Moses. There is exactly one man in the Old Testament whose face is described as having been altered by nearness to God, and it is Moses. He came down from the mountain carrying the two tablets, and the skin of his face shone because he had been talking with God, and the people were afraid to come near him, and he put a veil over it (Exodus 34:29–35). The court assembled to try a man for defaming Moses looks up and sees the one face in Jerusalem that looks like Moses’ did. They have the charge sheet in front of them and the answer to it in front of them at the same moment, and they proceed with the trial.

They knew what they were looking at. There is a second echo, from this same book. Two chapters ago another council looked at two uneducated men and recognised that they had been with Jesus (4:13). A shining face was, in Israel’s own Scriptures, the recognised mark of a man who had been with God. These were not ignorant men. Calm, radiant and unafraid, Stephen is visibly vindicated by God before he speaks a word.

What it does not mean. Now the pastoral care this verse needs, because it turns into a burden very quickly. It does not establish that a faithful Christian will look radiant under pressure. A great many faithful people have gone to prison, to a diagnosis or to their deaths looking precisely as frightened as they were, and Scripture nowhere treats that as a failure of faith. The Lord himself sweated in a garden and asked for the cup to be taken away. This is not a standard anyone is being asked to meet. It is a gift, given once, to one man, and Luke is careful to report it as something the observers saw rather than something Stephen felt.

What kind of God does this? He does not deliver Stephen. There is no earthquake, no angel opening a prison door as there had been for Peter, no crowd too dangerous to defy. Before long this man will be dragged outside the wall and killed with stones by people who have just heard him preach. What God gives him instead is a face. He is not spared, and he is not left alone. The same glory that met Moses on the mountain comes to rest on a man about to be executed for allegedly slandering him, in the last hour of his life, where every one of his judges can see it. Whatever else this is, it is not the conduct of a God who has lost control of the proceedings. Then Luke lets the sentence hang, and the next thing that happens is that the high priest turns to the shining man and asks him whether these things are so.

Will God give me peace when I face my worst moment? He promises to be with you, and he promises a peace that surpasses understanding to those who bring their requests to him (Philippians 4:6–7). He does not promise that you will feel calm or look radiant. Sometimes his peace is felt as a deep stillness; sometimes it is simply the strength to keep going, one step at a time, while afraid. Both are his gift. Paul says that we all, beholding the glory of the Lord, are being transformed into the same image from one degree of glory to another (2 Corinthians 3:18). That transformation is going on in every believer now, mostly unseen. One day it will be seen in full.

In a sentence. Everyone sitting in the council stared at him and saw that his face was like the face of an angel.

On a Tuesday. The peace of God can rest on a face in the worst moment. Ask him for it before the hard conversation, the hospital appointment, the meeting you dread. And spend time with God today, in his word and in prayer, because faces are changed by the company they keep.

For worship. The glory on Stephen’s face was borrowed light. Its source is the face of Jesus Christ, in whom God has shone the light of the knowledge of his glory into our hearts (2 Corinthians 4:6). Moses saw that glory from behind; Stephen will see it standing at God’s right hand; every believer will see it face to face. Praise the Lord of glory, who lets his light rest on his servants even in the courtroom, and who will one day make every one of his people shine like the sun in the kingdom of their Father (Matthew 13:43).

parallels.desc: the skin of Moses’ face shone

6.theology: Word and Deed, Order and Spirit. Acts 6 is the New Testament’s foundational text on church structure. It establishes that the body has different members with different callings; that no one person can or should do everything; that the criterion for all ministry, however practical, is character shaped by the Spirit; and that when ministry is rightly ordered, the Word — not the institution, not the ministers — is what grows. This is not a management manual; it is a theology of the church as the body of Christ, each member functioning according to its calling, all of it in service of the one mission: that the Word of God would run and be glorified.
6.examples:
Then: A rapidly growing Jerusalem church discovering that love without structure produces injustice — the widows being neglected are real women with real needs — and that structure without love produces dead religion. The seven are the church’s solution: Spirit-filled servants who bring both.

Now: Every growing church faces the tension of Acts 6: how do we care well for people without the leaders becoming so consumed with management that the Word is starved? The answer is not to choose between pastoral care and proclamation; it is to raise up men and women of Spirit and wisdom to share the load — and then to watch what God does with a church that is both devoted to the Word and devoted to its neighbours.

7.title: The Speech of Stephen
7.text: <sup>1</sup>And the high priest said, “Are these things so?” <sup>2</sup>And Stephen said: “Brothers and fathers, hear me. The God of glory appeared to our father Abraham when he was in Mesopotamia, before he lived in Haran, <sup>3</sup>and said to him, ‘Go out from your land and from your kindred and go into the land that I will show you.’ <sup>4</sup>Then he went out from the land of the Chaldeans and lived in Haran. And after his father died, God removed him from there into this land in which you are now living. <sup>5</sup>Yet he gave him no inheritance in it, not even a foot’s length, but promised to give it to him as a possession and to his offspring after him, though he had no child. <sup>6</sup>And God spoke to this effect—that his offspring would be sojourners in a land belonging to others, who would enslave them and afflict them four hundred years. <sup>7</sup>But I will judge the nation that they serve, said God, and after that they shall come out and worship me in this place.’ <sup>8</sup>And he gave him the covenant of circumcision. And so Abraham became the father of Isaac, and circumcised him on the eighth day, and Isaac became the father of Jacob, and Jacob of the twelve patriarchs. <sup>9</sup>“And the patriarchs, jealous of Joseph, sold him into Egypt; but God was with him <sup>10</sup>and rescued him out of all his afflictions and gave him favor and wisdom before Pharaoh, king of Egypt, who made him ruler over Egypt and over all his household. <sup>11</sup>Now there came a famine throughout all Egypt and Canaan, and great affliction, and our fathers could find no food. <sup>12</sup>But when Jacob heard that there was grain in Egypt, he sent out our fathers on their first visit. <sup>13</sup>And on the second visit Joseph made himself known to his brothers, and Joseph’s family became known to Pharaoh. <sup>14</sup>And Joseph sent and summoned Jacob his father and all his kindred, seventy-five persons in all. <sup>15</sup>And Jacob went down into Egypt, and he died, he and our fathers, <sup>16</sup>and they were carried back to Shechem and laid in the tomb that Abraham had bought for a sum of silver from the sons of Hamor in Shechem. <sup>17</sup>“But as the time of the promise drew near, which God had granted to Abraham, the people increased and multiplied in Egypt <sup>18</sup>until there arose over Egypt another king who did not know Joseph. <sup>19</sup>He dealt shrewdly with our race and forced our fathers to expose their infants, so that they would not be kept alive. <sup>20</sup>At this time Moses was born; and he was beautiful in God’s sight. And he was brought up for three months in his father’s house, <sup>21</sup>and when he was exposed, Pharaoh’s daughter adopted him and brought him up as her own son. <sup>22</sup>And Moses was instructed in all the wisdom of the Egyptians, and he was mighty in his words and deeds. <sup>23</sup>“When he was forty years old, it came into his heart to visit his brothers, the children of Israel. <sup>24</sup>And seeing one of them being wronged, he defended the oppressed man and avenged him by striking down the Egyptian. <sup>25</sup>He supposed that his brothers would understand that God was giving them salvation by his hand, but they did not understand. <sup>26</sup>And on the following day he appeared to them as they were quarreling and tried to reconcile them, saying, ‘Men, you are brothers. Why do you wrong each other?’ <sup>27</sup>But the man who was wronging his neighbor thrust him aside, saying, ‘Who made you a ruler and a judge over us? <sup>28</sup>Do you want to kill me as you killed the Egyptian yesterday?’ <sup>29</sup>At this retort Moses fled and became an exile in the land of Midian, where he became the father of two sons. <sup>30</sup>“Now when forty years had passed, an angel appeared to him in the wilderness of Mount Sinai, in a flame of fire in a bush. <sup>31</sup>When Moses saw it, he was amazed at the sight, and as he drew near to look, there came the voice of the Lord: <sup>32</sup>‘I am the God of your fathers, the God of Abraham and of Isaac and of Jacob.’ And Moses trembled and did not dare to look. <sup>33</sup>Then the Lord said to him, ‘Take off the sandals from your feet, for the place where you are standing is holy ground. <sup>34</sup>I have surely seen the affliction of my people who are in Egypt, and have heard their groaning, and I have come down to deliver them. And now come, I will send you to Egypt.’ <sup>35</sup>“This Moses, whom they rejected, saying, ‘Who made you a ruler and a judge?’—this man God sent as both ruler and redeemer, by the hand of the angel who appeared to him in the bush. <sup>36</sup>This man led them out, performing wonders and signs in Egypt and at the Red Sea and in the wilderness for forty years. <sup>37</sup>This is the Moses who said to the Israelites, ‘God will raise up for you a prophet like me from your brothers.’ <sup>38</sup>This is the one who was in the congregation in the wilderness with the angel who spoke to him at Mount Sinai, and with our fathers. He received living oracles to give to us. <sup>39</sup>Our fathers refused to obey him, but thrust him aside, and in their hearts they turned to Egypt, <sup>40</sup>saying to Aaron, ‘Make for us gods who will go before us. As for this Moses who led us out from the land of Egypt, we do not know what has become of him.’ <sup>41</sup>And they made a calf in those days, and offered a sacrifice to the idol and were rejoicing in the works of their hands. <sup>42</sup>But God turned away and gave them over to worship the host of heaven, as it is written in the book of the prophets: ‘Did you bring to me slain beasts and sacrifices, during the forty years in the wilderness, O house of Israel? <sup>43</sup>You took up the tent of Moloch and the star of your god Rephan, the images that you made to worship; and I will send you into exile beyond Babylon.’ <sup>44</sup>“Our fathers had the tent of witness in the wilderness, just as he who spoke to Moses directed him to make it, according to the pattern that he had seen. <sup>45</sup>Our fathers in turn brought it in with Joshua when they dispossessed the nations that God drove out before our fathers. So it was until the days of David, <sup>46</sup>who found favor in the sight of God and asked to find a dwelling place for the God of Jacob. <sup>47</sup>But it was Solomon who built a house for him. <sup>48</sup>Yet the Most High does not dwell in houses made by hands, as the prophet says, <sup>49</sup>‘Heaven is my throne, and the earth is my footstool. What kind of house will you build for me, says the Lord, or what is the place of my rest? <sup>50</sup>Did not my hand make all these things?’ <sup>51</sup>“You stiff-necked people, uncircumcised in heart and ears, you always resist the Holy Spirit. As your fathers did, so do you. <sup>52</sup>Which of the prophets did your fathers not persecute? And they killed those who announced beforehand the coming of the Righteous One, whom you have now betrayed and murdered, <sup>53</sup>you who received the law as delivered by angels and did not keep it.” <sup>54</sup>Now when they heard these things they were enraged, and they ground their teeth at him. <sup>55</sup>But he, full of the Holy Spirit, gazed into heaven and saw the glory of God, and Jesus standing at the right hand of God. <sup>56</sup>And he said, “Behold, I see the heavens opened, and the Son of Man standing at the right hand of God.” <sup>57</sup>But they cried out with a loud voice and stopped their ears and rushed together at him. <sup>58</sup>Then they cast him out of the city and stoned him. And the witnesses laid down their garments at the feet of a young man named Saul. <sup>59</sup>And as they were stoning Stephen, he called out, “Lord Jesus, receive my spirit.” <sup>60</sup>And falling to his knees he cried out with a loud voice, “Lord, do not hold this sin against them.” And when he had said this, he fell asleep.
7.overview:
Stephen’s speech is the longest in Acts. Accused of speaking against the temple and the law, he answers by retelling Israel’s history, and two threads run through it. First, God has never been confined to one land or one building: he appeared to Abraham in Mesopotamia, was with Joseph in Egypt, met Moses in the desert at the burning bush, and was worshipped in a portable tent; Solomon built him a house, but, as the prophets said, the Most High does not live in houses made by human hands. Second, Israel has repeatedly rejected the deliverers God sent: Joseph was sold by his brothers, Moses was pushed aside, the people turned to idols in the wilderness and persecuted the prophets. The pattern ends where Stephen’s hearers stand: they have betrayed and murdered the Righteous One.

Stephen follows the Greek Old Testament and some Jewish traditions of his day, which explains a few details that differ from the Hebrew text, such as seventy-five rather than seventy members of Jacob’s family. His conclusion is a direct charge: they are stiff-necked and resist the Holy Spirit, as their ancestors did. Enraged, the council rushes at him. Stephen, full of the Spirit, sees heaven open and Jesus, the Son of Man, standing at God’s right hand. They drag him out of the city and stone him, laying their cloaks at the feet of a young man named Saul. Stephen dies as his Lord did, committing his spirit to Jesus and praying that this sin not be held against them.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–50 — Stephen's Defense: Israel's History and God's Patience
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The high priest asked whether the charges were true. Stephen began with Abraham: the God of glory appeared to him in Mesopotamia before he lived in Haran, and told him to leave his country for a land God would show him. So Abraham moved to Haran and then, after his father’s death, to Canaan, though God gave him no inheritance there, not even a foot of ground, only a promise that his descendants would possess it, when as yet he had no child. God warned that his descendants would be foreigners, enslaved and mistreated for four hundred years, but God would judge their oppressors and they would come out and worship him. God gave Abraham the covenant of circumcision, and the line ran through Isaac, Jacob and the twelve patriarchs. The patriarchs were jealous of Joseph and sold him into Egypt, but God was with him, rescued him and gave him wisdom and favour with Pharaoh, who made him ruler over Egypt. In a famine Jacob sent the patriarchs to buy grain; on their second visit Joseph revealed himself, and he brought his whole family, seventy-five people, to Egypt. Jacob and the patriarchs died there and were buried in Shechem. As the time of the promise drew near, the people grew in Egypt until a new king arose who did not know Joseph. He oppressed them and forced them to abandon their babies. Moses was born then, a fine child, raised for three months in his father’s house and then adopted by Pharaoh’s daughter. He was educated in all the wisdom of Egypt and was powerful in speech and action. At forty he visited his fellow Israelites, defended one who was being mistreated and killed the Egyptian, thinking his people would realise that God was using him to rescue them; but they did not. The next day he tried to reconcile two Israelites who were fighting, and the one in the wrong pushed him aside, asking who had made him ruler and judge, and whether he meant to kill him as he had killed the Egyptian. Moses fled to Midian and had two sons there. After forty years an angel appeared to him in the flames of a burning bush near Mount Sinai. The Lord’s voice said he was the God of Abraham, Isaac and Jacob, and Moses trembled. God told him to take off his sandals, for the place was holy ground. God had seen his people’s oppression and heard their groaning, and was sending Moses to Egypt. This Moses, whom they rejected, God sent as ruler and deliverer through the angel in the bush. He led them out with wonders and signs in Egypt, at the Red Sea and in the wilderness for forty years. He told Israel that God would raise up a prophet like him from their own people. He was with the congregation in the wilderness, with the angel at Sinai and with their ancestors, and he received living words to pass on. But their ancestors refused to obey him; in their hearts they turned back to Egypt and asked Aaron to make them gods. They made a calf, sacrificed to it and celebrated what their hands had made. So God gave them over to worship the stars, as the prophet Amos says: they did not bring sacrifices to God in the wilderness but carried the shrine of Moloch and the star of the god Rephan, and so God would send them into exile beyond Babylon. Their ancestors had the tabernacle of the testimony in the wilderness, made to the pattern Moses was shown, and brought it in with Joshua when they took the land, until the time of David. David found favour with God and asked to provide a dwelling for him, but it was Solomon who built him a house. Yet the Most High does not live in houses made by human hands, as the prophet says: heaven is his throne and earth his footstool; what house could anyone build for him, or where would his resting place be? Did his hand not make all these things?
verseByVerse.theology:
The Temple and the Transcendence of God

Stephen's climax — the Most High does not dwell in houses made by hands (v. 48) — is not an outsider's attack on the temple. It is the temple's own prophetic self-criticism, read back to the men who ran it. Solomon said it himself on the day he dedicated the building: the heaven of heavens cannot contain God, how much less this house (1 Kings 8:27). Isaiah said it within sight of the same building. God had said it to David before a stone was laid, pointing out that since the exodus he had never once asked anybody for a house of cedar. The problem was never the temple; it was the reduction of God to a location — the belief that having the building in Jerusalem meant having God in a form that could be managed and defended. Reformed theology has read Stephen's argument as the permanent warning against every arrangement in which the sign is kept and the reality quietly replaced by it. And the warning has teeth precisely because Stephen is not against the sign: God designed the tent, God filled the temple, and God was the one who said he would not be confined to either.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: Every institution Stephen's accusers trusted came after the God who made it. Abraham had the covenant and no land; the patriarchs had the promise and a grave; Moses had holy ground in a foreign desert; Israel had a sanctuary that could be packed up in a day. Now: The question the speech puts to a congregation is not whether it values its building, its tradition or its structures — Stephen valued the tabernacle and said God designed it. It is whether it could lose them and still know where to find God.

verseByVerse.quote: And the high priest said, "Are these things so?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
And the high priest said, “Are these things so?”

Meaning first. Acts 7 is Stephen’s defence, the longest speech in Acts, and his martyrdom. Charged with speaking against the temple and the law (6:13–14), he retells Israel’s history. He makes two points. First, God was never confined to the land or the temple: he appeared to Abraham in Mesopotamia, was with Joseph in Egypt, spoke to Moses in Midian, and walked with his people in a tent. Second, Israel always rejected the deliverers God sent: Joseph, Moses, the prophets, and now Jesus. Then Stephen sees Jesus standing at God’s right hand, and dies forgiving his killers. A young man named Saul watches.

Are these things so? Four words, and they hand Stephen the longest speech in the book. The high priest, probably Caiaphas, is following procedure: the charges have been read, and the accused is invited to answer them. It is the formal opening of a trial.

Not a history lesson but a brief. What follows is the passage most readers of Acts quietly skip. It reads, on a first pass, like a man who has been asked a direct question and has responded with a summary of the Old Testament. Fifty verses on Abraham, Joseph, Moses, the tabernacle and Solomon, and not one word of denial, not one appeal for acquittal. It is worth knowing before starting that this is not evasion and it is not rambling. It is the most carefully aimed speech in Acts. Remember the two charges: he is accused of speaking against this holy place, and of saying that Jesus would change the customs Moses delivered. Hold those two in mind and the speech stops looking like a history lesson and starts looking like a brief.

The temple charge answered by geography. God appeared to Abraham in Mesopotamia. God was with Joseph in Egypt. God called a patch of desert holy ground. God designed his own sanctuary as a tent with carrying poles. God told David he had never asked for a building. Isaiah asked what kind of house anyone imagined they could put him in. Stephen does not argue that the temple is bad. He walks his accusers through their own Scriptures and lets them notice that God has spent the entire story refusing to be located.

The Moses charge answered by turning it round. Stephen honours Moses extravagantly: sent by God, ruler and redeemer, receiver of living oracles, worker of signs and wonders for forty years. And in the middle of the tribute he points out that Israel rejected him twice, and made a golden calf while he was on the mountain receiving the law. By verse 53 the man accused of despising the law is telling the court that they received it from angels and did not keep it.

He never asks to be let off. It should be said what Stephen never does with the floor he has been given. He does not produce character witnesses, does not clarify what he actually said, does not seek to establish that the testimony against him was perjured, which it was. He has the undivided attention of the supreme council of his nation, and he spends the whole of it preaching to them. A man is given the last opportunity of his life to save it, and uses it instead on the people who are going to take it.

Why does Stephen hardly mention Jesus until the end? Because he is letting the story do the work. He never names Jesus in the speech itself; he calls him the Righteous One only in verse 52, and names him only in his dying prayer. But Jesus is everywhere in it. Joseph, rejected by his brothers and raised up to save them; Moses, thrust aside and sent back as ruler and redeemer; the prophet like Moses; the true dwelling of God that no hands built. Stephen lays out the pattern so clearly that when he finally says, you have now betrayed and murdered the Righteous One, every man in the room already knows whom he means. It is a lesson in reading the Old Testament: it is Christ’s story from the beginning (Luke 24:27).

In a sentence. The high priest asked Stephen whether these charges were true.

On a Tuesday. When you are asked about your faith, you do not have to begin with yourself. Begin, as Stephen did, with the whole story of God’s dealings with his people, and let it lead to Christ. Learn that story well enough this year that you could tell it at a moment’s notice.

For worship. The God of this speech is the God who has been working one plan from Abraham to Jesus, through famines and slavery, deserts and rebellions, and has never once lost the thread. Every rejection of his messengers he has woven into the rescue of his people. Praise the Lord of history, whose Son is the meaning of the whole story, and whose servant could tell it so clearly on the last day of his life.

verseByVerse.quote: And Stephen said: "Brothers and fathers, hear me. The God of glory appeared to our father Abraham when he was in Mesopotamia, before he lived in Haran, and said to him, 'Go out from your land and from your kindred and go into the land that I will show you.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
And Stephen said: “Brothers and fathers, hear me. The God of glory appeared to our father Abraham when he was in Mesopotamia, before he lived in Haran, and said to him, ‘Go out from your land and from your kindred and go into the land that I will show you.’

Brothers and fathers, hear me. He opens by calling the court that is going to kill him his family, using the respectful address a younger man owes his elders. He is a Jew among Jews. There is no defiance in the first sentence and there will be none until verse 51. It is the same opening Paul uses years later, standing before a mob in this same city (22:1), and both men are doing the same thing: establishing, before anything else, that this is an argument inside the house and not an attack from outside it.

The God of glory appeared to our father Abraham when he was in Mesopotamia, before he lived in Haran. The first clause of the speech is the whole thesis, and every word in it is doing work. The God of glory: the title the psalmist uses (Psalm 29:3), and glory is the temple word. It is what filled the tabernacle when it was finished and the house when Solomon dedicated it, until the priests could not stand to minister (Exodus 40:34–35; 1 Kings 8:10–11). If there is one thing these men believe belongs to their building, it is the glory. Stephen takes the title and attaches it to an event that happened before Israel existed, in what is now southern Iraq, some six hundred miles from the room they are sitting in. God’s presence is not tied to a holy place.

Ur or Haran? He is careful about the timing: before he lived in Haran. Genesis 12:1 records the call in Haran; Stephen follows the earlier summons in Ur, which Scripture itself records: I am the LORD who brought you out from Ur of the Chaldeans (Genesis 15:7; Nehemiah 9:7). Either God called him twice, or the call that began in Ur was renewed in Haran. So the very first appearance of God to the founder of the covenant people happened in a pagan city, in a family that served other gods (Joshua 24:2), to a man with nothing to go on but the voice that spoke to him.

Go out from your land and from your kindred and go into the land that I will show you. Then the command (Genesis 12:1), and it is worth measuring what it asked. In that world those two things were not sentiment; they were survival. Your kindred were the people who fed you in a bad harvest, avenged you if you were wronged, buried you, and remembered your name. Your land held the graves of your fathers. To leave both was not an adventure. It was to make yourself a man with no protection, no insurance and no standing, in a world that had no other kind. And he is not told where he is going. The land that I will show you: future tense, no name, no map. God gives him the leaving in full detail and the arriving not at all. The life of faith begins with leaving.

The ordinary shape of obedience. There is a great deal in that for anyone who has been asked to obey without being shown the destination: the move, the resignation, the relationship ended, the thing put down that cannot be picked up again. Abraham’s instructions consisted entirely of what to leave, plus a promise that there would be somewhere to go. It is the ordinary shape of obedience, and Scripture holds up the man who managed it as the father of all who believe (Romans 4:11; Hebrews 11:8).

Does God still speak to people as he spoke to Abraham? God spoke to Abraham directly because there was as yet no written word. Now he has spoken to us finally in his Son (Hebrews 1:1–2), and that word is recorded for us, complete and sufficient, in Scripture (2 Timothy 3:16–17). So you should not wait for a voice before you obey. The commands you need are already written, and the promises are already given. God still guides his people, through his word, through the wisdom he gives in prayer, through the counsel of mature believers, and through his providence opening and shutting doors. But the voice that called Abraham is now heard whenever the Bible is opened, and it calls us, as it called him, to trust and go.

In a sentence. Stephen began by recalling that the God of glory appeared to Abraham in Mesopotamia, before he lived in Haran, and told him to leave his land and his family for the land God would show him.

On a Tuesday. Is there something God has plainly asked you in Scripture to leave, a habit, a grudge, a comfort that has become an idol, while you wait to be shown what comes next? Abraham left first. Take the first step today, and trust God with the map.

For worship. The God of glory is not confined to buildings. He came looking for an idolater in Ur and made him the friend of God. Before Abraham sought God, God sought Abraham. That is how grace has always worked, and it is how it reached you. Praise the God of glory, who calls sinners out of darkness into his marvellous light (1 Peter 2:9), and who is himself the country we travel toward.
verseByVerse.note: Stephen retells Israel’s story to show that God was never confined to one land or building, and that Israel repeatedly rejected his messengers.

parallels.desc: go to the land that I will show you

verseByVerse.quote: Then he went out from the land of the Chaldeans and lived in Haran. And after his father died, God removed him from there into this land in which you are now living. Yet he gave him no inheritance in it, not even a foot's length, but promised to give it to him as a possession and to his offspring after him, though he had no child.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Then he went out from the land of the Chaldeans and lived in Haran. And after his father died, God removed him from there into this land in which you are now living. Yet he gave him no inheritance in it, not even a foot’s length, but promised to give it to him as a possession and to his offspring after him, though he had no child.

Then he went out from the land of the Chaldeans and lived in Haran. Haran, in northern Mesopotamia, a stopping place on the long road west.

And after his father died, God removed him from there into this land in which you are now living. Two facts sit side by side here, and Stephen wants the collision. God brought Abraham into this land in which you are now living, and gave him no inheritance in it.

Did Terah die before Abraham left? There is a difficulty buried in the clause, and a reader with Genesis open will find it. Genesis appears to say Terah was seventy when he fathered Abram (Genesis 11:26), died at two hundred and five (11:32), and Abram left Haran at seventy-five (12:4). That would leave Terah alive for another sixty years. But look at how Genesis writes these lines. When Terah had lived seventy years, he fathered Abram, Nahor and Haran does not mean all three arrived that year; it means that is when he began having sons. Genesis uses the identical formula of Noah, five hundred years old when he fathered Shem, Ham and Japheth, and nobody imagines triplets there. In both places the sons are listed by prominence rather than birth order, which is why Abram heads a list he may well have come last in. Put Abram’s birth in Terah’s hundred and thirtieth year and every number falls into line: Terah dies at two hundred and five, Abram is seventy-five, and he leaves exactly as Stephen says. Ancient readers noticed the question too: the Samaritan copies of the law give Terah’s age at death as a hundred and forty-five, and Philo agrees with Stephen. Some also suggest Stephen means that Terah, an idolater (Joshua 24:2), was spiritually dead. It does not affect his point, and Stephen, about to die for what he draws out of these Scriptures, knows them better than the men about to stone him.

Yet he gave him no inheritance in it, not even a foot’s length. Take the measurement seriously, because the measurement is the argument. Not a farm, not a field, not the width of a foot. The man to whom the entire country was promised died holding legal title to exactly one thing in it: a cave with his wife buried in it, bought from a Hittite at a price he did not trouble to haggle over (Genesis 23). He lived his whole adult life in tents, as a stranger in a land that was his by promise and nobody else’s by law (Hebrews 11:9), and he never once slept in a house standing on ground he owned. Stephen is saying this to men whose entire case rests on a plot of land and a building on it. The founder of their nation had neither, and the lack of them did not make him less the friend of God. It made him the pattern. God’s promises were never exhausted by the land.

But promised to give it to him as a possession and to his offspring after him, though he had no child. Faith in a promise, without seeing it. Abraham had no land and no child, only God’s word. He was promised offspring when he had none and a country when he owned none, and he believed God, and it was counted to him as righteousness (Genesis 15:6).

Is the land of Israel still promised to the Jewish people? Christians answer differently, and this app presents the views fairly. Some believe God’s promise of the land to Abraham’s physical descendants still stands and will have a future fulfilment, and they point to the unconditional language of the promise and to Romans 11. Others believe the land promise is fulfilled and enlarged in Christ: Abraham was to be heir of the world (Romans 4:13), and the patriarchs themselves were looking for a better country, a heavenly one (Hebrews 11:13–16). All agree on what Stephen shows here: that Abraham’s true hope was never a piece of real estate but God himself and the city he has prepared, and that every Christian shares that hope with him.

In a sentence. Abraham left the land of the Chaldeans and settled in Haran, and after his father died God brought him to this land, though he gave him none of it, not even a foot’s length, but promised it to him and his descendants, though he had no child.

On a Tuesday. Live by God’s promise even when you have nothing to show for it. Abraham did. Name one promise of God you are clinging to with nothing yet in your hand, and thank him for it today as though it were already kept.

For worship. Abraham died owning a grave, and he died rich, because he had God’s word. The God who promised him a land and a seed kept both promises in a way Abraham could hardly have imagined: through the one Offspring, Christ (Galatians 3:16), in whom the meek inherit the earth. Praise the faithful God, who never runs short of time to keep his word, and whose children are heirs of all things in his Son.

verseByVerse.quote: And God spoke to this effect — that his offspring would be sojourners in a land belonging to others, who would enslave them and afflict them four hundred years. 'But I will judge the nation that they serve,' said God, 'and after that they shall come out and worship me in this place.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
And God spoke to this effect — that his offspring would be sojourners in a land belonging to others, who would enslave them and afflict them four hundred years. ‘But I will judge the nation that they serve,’ said God, ‘and after that they shall come out and worship me in this place.’

And God spoke to this effect, that his offspring would be sojourners in a land belonging to others, who would enslave them and afflict them four hundred years. The promise as God actually gave it (Genesis 15:13–14) contained something people rarely notice when they quote it: four centuries of slavery, announced in advance. God did not tell Abraham the land would come quickly or that the road would be short. He told him his descendants would be strangers in someone else’s country, enslaved and mistreated, for four hundred years, and only then would they come out. Abraham was being informed that his great-grandchildren’s great-grandchildren would be born in chains, and that this was not a failure of the plan but part of it.

The gap between word and fulfilment. That is a hard thing to sit with, and Stephen includes it because his hearers need to see how God’s promises actually run. There is a gap between the word and the fulfilment, and God fills it with things nobody would have chosen. The four hundred years are not an interruption in this story; they are the story. Anyone who concludes from four months of silence that God has changed his mind should look carefully at the arithmetic Abraham was handed, and still believed.

Four hundred or four hundred and thirty? Stephen is quoting God’s word to Abraham, which says four hundred. Exodus gives the sojourn as four hundred and thirty years (Exodus 12:40), and Paul uses that longer figure too (Galatians 3:17). There is no conflict. Four hundred is the round number for the affliction, spoken to Abraham in the shape a promise takes rather than a ledger; four hundred and thirty is the precise span, counted from a different starting point. Scripture is quite capable of giving a figure to the year in one place and rounding it in another, exactly as we do.

But I will judge the nation that they serve, said God. The plagues on Egypt, foretold centuries before Pharaoh was born. The oppressor is not out of God’s reach, even when he is out of the oppressed people’s sight.

And after that they shall come out and worship me in this place. Then the clause Stephen is steering toward. Which place? Stephen blends Genesis 15:14 with Exodus 3:12, where God says these words to Moses at the burning bush, and this place means the mountain in the desert where he is standing. The first act of national worship God ever promised his rescued people was to take place at Sinai, several hundred miles from the building these men are prosecuting Stephen to protect. Worship, not land, was the goal of the exodus.

How do I keep trusting when God’s promise seems delayed? Remember that delay is not denial. God told Abraham about the four hundred years in advance precisely so that later generations would not mistake the waiting for abandonment. Fill the waiting with what you know: his character, his past faithfulness, his written promises. Keep obeying in the meantime, as Israel kept having children in Egypt. Bring your impatience honestly to him, as the psalmists did: how long, O LORD? (Psalm 13:1). And remember that the greatest delay in history, the long wait for the Messiah, ended exactly on time, when the fullness of time had come (Galatians 4:4). He is not late with you either.

In a sentence. God told Abraham that his descendants would be strangers in another land, enslaved and mistreated for four hundred years, but that God would judge that nation, and afterwards they would come out and worship him in this place.

On a Tuesday. God redeems his people so that they will worship him. When you wonder what your salvation is for, the answer is here: you were brought out to worship. Begin this week by thanking him for one specific way he has brought you out.

For worship. God redeems his people so that they will worship him. That is why he saved you. He named the slavery before it began and the rescue before it came, and he did both because he had already set his love on a people who did not yet exist. Praise the God who sees the end from the beginning, who judges the oppressor, and who brings his people out to stand before him and adore.

parallels.desc: your offspring will be sojourners, afflicted four hundred years
you shall serve God on this mountain

verseByVerse.quote: And he gave him the covenant of circumcision. And so Abraham became the father of Isaac, and circumcised him on the eighth day, and Isaac became the father of Jacob, and Jacob of the twelve patriarchs.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And he gave him the covenant of circumcision. And so Abraham became the father of Isaac, and circumcised him on the eighth day, and Isaac became the father of Jacob, and Jacob of the twelve patriarchs.

And he gave him the covenant of circumcision. Notice where the covenant sign is given (Genesis 17:9–14). Abraham has no land, no city, and not yet the son of the promise, and God hands him a sign to be cut into his own body. Given before the law, and long before the temple. And Stephen honours it: he is not against Moses or the covenant.

A sign that travels. That is a striking arrangement, and Stephen has set it up carefully. The mark of belonging to God is put on the flesh, not on a plot of ground. It travels. Jacob’s sons carried it down into Egypt, their descendants carried it through slavery and out again, and every Israelite in Babylon carried it through seventy years with no temple to go to. Of all the ways God might have marked out a people, he chose the one thing they could not be separated from and could not leave behind when they were deported.

Why call it the covenant of circumcision? The phrase names the covenant by its sign. The covenant itself was God’s promise to Abraham: a people, a land, and blessing for all nations (Genesis 12; 15; 17). When God formalised it, he gave circumcision as its token: this is my covenant, every male among you shall be circumcised, and it shall be a sign of the covenant between me and you (Genesis 17:10–11). Sign and covenant became so bound together that the whole could be called by the sign. And two things are worth holding. The sign sealed a promise already received by faith: Abraham was counted righteous before he was ever circumcised (Genesis 15:6; 17), so circumcision was a seal of the righteousness that he had by faith (Romans 4:11). The mark never earned the promise; it pointed to it.

And so Abraham became the father of Isaac, and circumcised him on the eighth day. God kept his promise of a son. And Isaac became the father of Jacob, and Jacob of the twelve patriarchs, the heads of the twelve tribes. Three generations in a single sentence, and a nation exists by the end of it. Stephen is moving fast, but he is establishing something no one in that room can dispute: that everything essential to being the people of God was in place and working generations before there was a land to live in or a house to worship in.

Where Christians differ: does baptism replace circumcision? Our paedobaptist brothers in the Presbyterian and Reformed churches see baptism as the new covenant sign that takes the place of circumcision (Colossians 2:11–12), and so give it to the infant children of believers, as circumcision was given to Isaac on the eighth day. They do so out of a sincere conviction about God’s covenant faithfulness to families, and we honour them for it. Credobaptists answer that the new covenant is different in its membership: all its members know the Lord (Jeremiah 31:34; Hebrews 8:11), and its true circumcision is of the heart, by the Spirit (Romans 2:29). In Colossians 2 the circumcision that answers to baptism is the one made without hands, the new birth, and in Acts baptism follows repentance and faith (2:38, 41; 8:12). Verdict: baptism is for those who profess faith in Christ (1689 London Baptist Confession 29.2). Circumcision marked out a physical family through whom Christ would come; baptism marks out those who have been united to Christ by faith. Both sides agree on what matters most here: the sign never saves, and the promise is received by faith alone.

In a sentence. God gave Abraham the covenant of circumcision, and so Abraham became the father of Isaac and circumcised him on the eighth day, and Isaac became the father of Jacob, and Jacob of the twelve patriarchs.

On a Tuesday. God keeps his promises across generations. Trust him for your children and grandchildren, pray for them by name, and teach them the promises. And if you have been baptised, remember this week what it signified: not something you achieved, but your union with Christ in his death and resurrection (Romans 6:3–4).

For worship. The covenant God made with Abraham was always reaching beyond Abraham, toward the blessing of all nations in his Offspring (Galatians 3:8, 16). In Christ, Gentiles who never bore the old sign have been brought near, and given the circumcision of the heart. Praise the covenant-keeping God, who sealed his promise in the flesh of a family, and fulfilled it in the flesh of his Son.

verseByVerse.quote: "And the patriarchs, jealous of Joseph, sold him into Egypt; but God was with him and rescued him out of all his afflictions and gave him favor and wisdom before Pharaoh, king of Egypt, who made him ruler over Egypt and over all his household."
verseByVerse.commentary:
And the patriarchs, jealous of Joseph, sold him into Egypt; but God was with him and rescued him out of all his afflictions and gave him favor and wisdom before Pharaoh, king of Egypt, who made him ruler over Egypt and over all his household.

And the patriarchs, jealous of Joseph, sold him into Egypt. Consider whom Stephen is saying that to. In front of him sits the high priest, and on the high priest’s chest, when he is robed, is a breastpiece set with twelve stones, and on those stones are engraved twelve names: Reuben, Simeon, Levi, Judah and the rest (Exodus 28:21). The founding fathers of the nation, worn over the heart of the man presiding at this trial. Stephen has just described them, accurately and without softening, as men who sold their brother into slavery because they could not stand him. This is the first rejection. The fathers of Israel rejected the one God had chosen to save them, out of jealousy, the same motive as the leaders who handed Jesus over (Mark 15:10; Acts 5:17).

The pattern appears. He does not linger, because he is laying down a pattern rather than scoring a point. But the pattern is now visible for the first time, and it will run through everything that follows: the man his brothers got rid of turns out to be the man they cannot live without. Joseph goes down into Egypt in a slave train and comes up as the only source of food in the world, and the brothers who sold him arrive at his door to beg.

But God was with him. Then the clause that carries the other half of Stephen’s case. Where, exactly? Not in the promised land. Not at a shrine, an altar or a festival. God was with Joseph in a slave caravan, in an Egyptian official’s household, and in a prison cell on a false accusation, for some thirteen years between the pit and the palace. There is no record that Joseph in all that time had a priest, a place of worship, a copy of any Scripture, or a single one of the things his descendants would one day kill a man for defending. And the text says God was with him, in Egypt, outside the land.

And rescued him out of all his afflictions and gave him favor and wisdom before Pharaoh, king of Egypt, who made him ruler over Egypt and over all his household. Note precisely what God’s presence did and did not do. It did not keep him out of prison. God rescued him out of all his afflictions, which means he was in them first, all of them, one after another. The rescue ran through the trouble rather than round it, and at no point during those thirteen years could Joseph have told you that it was working. Then God exalted the rejected one, and the rejected one became the saviour of his brothers: God sent me before you to preserve life; you meant evil against me, but God meant it for good (Genesis 45:5–8; 50:20).

What it does not promise. There is a version of this story preached as a guarantee: hold on, because your Egypt is preparing you for a throne. Scripture does not promise that. Joseph received a visible reward within his lifetime; a great many faithful people do not, and the letter to the Hebrews says plainly of a long list of them that they died still waiting. What this passage does establish is the thing Stephen needs, and it is enough to build a life on: there is no place a believer can be taken, sold, imprisoned, deported, forgotten or simply stuck, where God is not already there ahead of him, and no institution whose absence can put him out of reach.

Is it right to see Joseph as a picture of Jesus? Yes, because Stephen does, and because the shape is unmistakable. The beloved son of his father, hated by his brothers, sold for silver, falsely accused, brought down into the depths, then raised to the right hand of the throne, and from there giving bread to the very people who betrayed him. The Old Testament is full of such patterns, which the New Testament calls types: real events and people that God shaped to point forward to Christ (Romans 5:14; Hebrews 10:1). We should not invent fanciful links, but where Scripture itself draws the line, as here, we should follow it with joy.

In a sentence. The patriarchs, jealous of Joseph, sold him into Egypt, but God was with him and rescued him from all his troubles, and gave him favour and wisdom before Pharaoh, king of Egypt, who made him ruler over Egypt and over all his household.

On a Tuesday. If you are in your own pit or prison this week, the promise is not that you will be out by Friday but that God is with you there. Say it to yourself aloud: God is with me here. Then do the next faithful thing, as Joseph did in Potiphar’s house and in the jail.

For worship. Joseph points to Jesus: rejected by his brothers, exalted by God, the saviour of those who sold him. Jesus went down further than any prison, into death itself, and was raised to the right hand of the Majesty on high, and now he feeds with the bread of life the very sinners who betrayed him. Praise the greater Joseph, who forgives his brothers with tears and says to every one of them, come near to me.
verseByVerse.note: Joseph, rejected by his brothers but raised up by God, is the first of Stephen’s rejected deliverers.

verseByVerse.quote: "Now there came a famine throughout all Egypt and Canaan, and great affliction, and our fathers could find no food. But when Jacob heard that there was grain in Egypt, he sent out our fathers on their first visit."
