verseByVerse.commentary:
Now there came a famine throughout all Egypt and Canaan, and great affliction, and our fathers could find no food. But when Jacob heard that there was grain in Egypt, he sent out our fathers on their first visit.

Now there came a famine throughout all Egypt and Canaan, and great affliction. A famine in the ancient world was not a disruption to the food supply. There were no reserves worth the name, no imports, and nobody to appeal to. A household ate its stores, then its breeding animals, then the seed corn it needed for the next year, and once the seed was gone, next year had been decided as well. After that it moved, or it died (Genesis 41:54–57).

And our fathers could find no food. Notice where this one strikes. The chosen family, standing in the land of promise, holding the covenant, descended directly from Abraham, could find no food. The country God had sworn to give them could not feed them, and the grain was in the pagan empire down the road. The brothers who rejected Joseph are in desperate need. Stephen is still quietly dismantling the same equation. His accusers hold that God’s favour and God’s land belong together, so that possessing one proves the other. He observes that the covenant family’s first great crisis was solved by leaving.

But when Jacob heard that there was grain in Egypt, he sent out our fathers on their first visit. Look at the machinery of it. That is the entire mechanism. A rumour reaches an old man in Hebron that there is wheat for sale in the south, and he sends his sons to buy some. There is no vision, no angel and no word from God recorded anywhere in the transaction. A man hears a piece of market news and acts on it sensibly, and in doing so sets in motion the descent into Egypt, the four hundred years, the exodus, Sinai and the whole national existence of Israel. And on that first visit they did not recognise Joseph (Genesis 42:8).

How providence usually works. That is how providence usually works, and it is worth noticing, because a great deal of Christian anxiety is spent looking for the other sort. Very little of what God does in a life arrives labelled. It arrives as the price of wheat, a conversation that ran longer than expected, a job that fell through, a piece of news somebody happened to mention. Jacob was not being spiritual when he sent his sons to Egypt. He was being practical. He was also, without the faintest suspicion of it, delivering his household into the hands of the son he had spent twenty years mourning.

Not fatalism. One guard, because this can slide into fatalism. That God governs the ordinary does not mean ordinary decisions are unimportant. Jacob still had to weigh the risk and send the boys, and if he had not, they would have starved. What it means is that a man doing the sensible next thing in front of him, with no sense of destiny about it whatever, may be doing something that is still being discussed thousands of years later.

Does God send famines and disasters? Scripture teaches that God governs all things, including famines, storms and pandemics, and that nothing happens outside his wise and holy providence (Westminster 5.1; Amos 3:6). Genesis says plainly that God sent the famine as part of his plan to save many lives (Genesis 45:5–7). But God is never the author of sin, and his purposes in a disaster are usually hidden from us. Jesus forbade us to read a disaster as proof that its victims were worse sinners (Luke 13:1–5). The right response is not to explain other people’s suffering, but to humble ourselves, help the hungry, and trust that the God who governed Joseph’s famine is governing ours for the good of his people.

In a sentence. A famine came over all Egypt and Canaan, bringing great hardship, and their fathers could find no food, but when Jacob heard that there was grain in Egypt, he sent them on their first visit.

On a Tuesday. God uses hunger to bring people to the one they rejected, and your need may be his call. Look back over the last year at one ordinary event, a chance meeting, a closed door, a piece of news, and thank God for the hand you can now see was in it.

For worship. The God of the famine is also the God of the granary. He was ahead of the hunger by seven years, storing grain in Egypt through the son the brothers thought was dead. He is always ahead of his people’s need. Praise the Lord of providence, who feeds the world through the one who was rejected, and who has set his Son over all the bread of heaven.

verseByVerse.quote: "And on the second visit Joseph made himself known to his brothers, and Joseph's family became known to Pharaoh. And Joseph sent and summoned Jacob his father and all his kindred, seventy-five persons in all."
verseByVerse.commentary:
And on the second visit Joseph made himself known to his brothers, and Joseph’s family became known to Pharaoh. And Joseph sent and summoned Jacob his father and all his kindred, seventy-five persons in all.

And on the second visit Joseph made himself known to his brothers. Two visits, and everything turns on the second (Genesis 45:1–4). Stephen says nothing about what that moment cost. Genesis gives it four chapters, a room emptied of Egyptians, and a man weeping so loudly that the household heard it through the wall. Stephen gives it a single clause. He needs the shape rather than the detail. The brother they sold is the one they end up standing before, and the moment he tells them who he is, is the moment their lives are saved. They had assumed for twenty years that they had got away with it. The man they had wronged had in the meantime been put in charge of the only food in the world, and could have done anything he liked with them.

Recognised the second time. Some see a hint here that Stephen means his hearers to catch. On the first visit the brothers did not recognise Joseph; on the second they did. Israel did not recognise Jesus at his first coming, and Stephen is calling these men to recognise him now.

And Joseph’s family became known to Pharaoh. One clause in the middle is easy to skim, and it decides everything that follows. A household of shepherds from the hills was presented at the Egyptian court, and Genesis records the king assigning them the best of the land in Goshen. Israel did not arrive in Egypt as refugees sleeping rough. They came by royal invitation, with a grant of territory, under the protection of the second man in the kingdom. That is exactly why the change of dynasty at verse 18 is such a catastrophe: everything had rested on one man’s standing at court, and courts forget.

And Joseph sent and summoned Jacob his father and all his kindred, seventy-five persons in all. The whole covenant family, counted, packed and moved out of the land of promise into the land of the Nile. On the face of it, it is the end of the story. It is in fact the mechanism of the next act. A household goes down, and a nation comes up.

Seventy or seventy-five? Genesis puts the number at seventy (Genesis 46:27; Exodus 1:5). Stephen follows the Greek Old Testament, which Greek-speaking Jews used everywhere in his day, and which reads seventy-five, counting several more of Joseph’s descendants born in Egypt. A difference in counting between two textual traditions, not an error. Either way Stephen’s point holds.

Will Israel recognise Jesus at a second visit? Christians hold different views about Israel’s future, and this app presents them fairly. Many believe Romans 11 foretells a great turning of the Jewish people to Christ before his return, when all Israel will be saved (Romans 11:25–26). Others read all Israel as the whole people of God, Jew and Gentile, gathered in through the gospel age. All agree that God has not cast away his people, that Jewish men and women are coming to Christ now as they did in Acts, and that the church should pray and long for Jewish people to see in Jesus the brother they did not recognise.

In a sentence. On the second visit Joseph made himself known to his brothers, and his family became known to Pharaoh, and Joseph sent for his father Jacob and all his relatives, seventy-five people in all.

On a Tuesday. Is there someone you wronged long ago and have avoided ever since? Joseph’s brothers found that the one they feared most was the one who forgave most freely. Pray about whether it is time to seek that person out and put it right.

For worship. The one they rejected welcomed them and fed them. That is what Christ does for sinners. He makes himself known to those who sold him, weeps over them, and gives them the best of the land. Praise the brother who is not ashamed to call us brothers (Hebrews 2:11), and who on the day he reveals himself fully will be the joy of all who once did not know him.
verseByVerse.note: Stephen follows the Greek Old Testament, which gives seventy-five; the Hebrew text counts seventy.

verseByVerse.quote: "And Jacob went down into Egypt, and he died, he and our fathers, and they were carried back to Shechem and laid in the tomb that Abraham had bought for a sum of silver from the sons of Hamor in Shechem."
verseByVerse.commentary:
And Jacob went down into Egypt, and he died, he and our fathers, and they were carried back to Shechem and laid in the tomb that Abraham had bought for a sum of silver from the sons of Hamor in Shechem.

And Jacob went down into Egypt, and he died, he and our fathers. A single clause for the death of an entire generation, and Stephen keeps moving. They all died outside the promised land.

And they were carried back to Shechem and laid in the tomb that Abraham had bought for a sum of silver from the sons of Hamor in Shechem. But Stephen stops for one thing, and it is the burial. These men died outside the land, every one of them, patriarchs of a people who had been promised a country, and their bodies were carried back across the desert so that they could lie in ground they had never owned. Joseph made his brothers swear to it on his deathbed, and four hundred years later a nation walking out of Egypt in a hurry took his coffin with them (Genesis 50:25; Exodus 13:19).

A tomb as evidence. Consider that as a piece of evidence. The only real estate any of the patriarchs held in the promised land was a grave and a field. They believed the promise so completely that they arranged their own funerals around it, and so patiently that not one of them expected to see it kept in his lifetime. Stephen’s accusers hold the land, the city and the temple, and are about to kill a man over a building. The founding fathers held a tomb, and held on to God. And notice where Stephen locates them: at Shechem, in Samaria, the region despised by Jerusalem Jews. The patriarchs lie in Samaritan ground.

Two purchases in one clause. A careful reader will stop here, and should. Genesis records two separate transactions: Abraham bought the cave of Machpelah at Hebron from Ephron the Hittite (Genesis 23), and Jacob bought the plot at Shechem from the sons of Hamor (Genesis 33:19). Jacob himself was buried at Machpelah (Genesis 50:13); Joseph’s bones were laid at Shechem, in Jacob’s plot (Joshua 24:32). Stephen has folded two purchases and two burial grounds into a single clause.

If Stephen compressed the history, can I trust the Bible? Yes. The natural explanation is compression. Stephen is racing through more than a thousand years in one speech, on trial for his life, and he telescopes the patriarchal burials into a summary phrase, as speakers often did; he is not filing a title deed. His hearers knew the law better than we do, and they do not challenge a syllable of his history. They rage at his conclusion, not his facts. A few have suggested Abraham made a further, unrecorded purchase at Shechem, where he built his first altar in the land (Genesis 12:6–7): possible, but speculative. And notice what Scripture is doing. Luke’s task is to report the sermon faithfully, and he has. Inspiration guarantees a true record of what Stephen said, as it guarantees a true record of what Job’s friends said. Nothing hangs on this detail. What Stephen came to say, that God was never confined to this land or that building, stands untouched.

Why did the patriarchs care so much where they were buried? Because their burial was an act of faith in God’s promise and, at its deepest, in the resurrection. By faith Joseph, at the end of his life, made mention of the exodus and gave directions concerning his bones (Hebrews 11:22). He wanted to be where God’s promise would be kept, because he expected to share in it. Christians bury their dead with the same hope, not because the place saves, but because the body matters to God and will be raised. A Christian funeral is a statement of faith about the future, made beside a grave.

In a sentence. Jacob went down to Egypt and died there, as did their fathers, and they were brought back to Shechem and laid in the tomb Abraham had bought for silver from the sons of Hamor.

On a Tuesday. The patriarchs died in faith, not having received what was promised (Hebrews 11:13). So may we. Ask yourself what your plans for the end of your life say about your hope, and whether the people who will one day bury you know what you believe about the resurrection.

For worship. The patriarchs lay in a borrowed grave, waiting. Christ lay in a borrowed grave for three days, and then left it empty, and because he lives, those who sleep in him will live also. Praise the risen Lord, who keeps every promise made over a tomb, and who will one day call Abraham, Isaac, Jacob and Joseph, and all who share their faith, out of the dust.
verseByVerse.note: Stephen compresses two purchases: Abraham bought a tomb at Hebron, and Jacob bought land at Shechem from the sons of Hamor, where Joseph was buried.

verseByVerse.quote: "But as the time of the promise drew near, which God had granted to Abraham, the people increased and multiplied in Egypt until there arose over Egypt another king who did not know Joseph."
verseByVerse.commentary:
But as the time of the promise drew near, which God had granted to Abraham, the people increased and multiplied in Egypt until there arose over Egypt another king who did not know Joseph.

But as the time of the promise drew near, which God had granted to Abraham. Stephen has been counting. Four hundred years were named to Abraham back in verse 6, and the clock has been running ever since. God’s clock was moving. It is now nearly up, and what happens as it runs out is not a softening of Israel’s circumstances but a hardening of them.

The people increased and multiplied in Egypt until there arose over Egypt another king who did not know Joseph. Put the two halves together, because Stephen has welded them deliberately (Exodus 1:7–8). The people increased: the promise working, outside the land, God blessing them in a foreign country. Until there arose another king: the terror beginning. Blessing and persecution arrive in the same sentence, and the second is a direct consequence of the first: a rapidly growing foreign population in the delta is precisely what alarms a new dynasty.

Did not know Joseph. Stop a moment on that phrase. A man had once saved the entire country from starvation, reorganised its agriculture and been made second in the kingdom, and within a few generations the palace has no idea who he was. A new dynasty, with no memory of Joseph’s service. It is a small, cold observation about the memory of nations and the shelf life of gratitude. Whatever a man does for a country, the country forgets him faster than he would believe, and his descendants are assessed on their usefulness this year.

The whip and the promise. The harder thing in this passage is what the wider story makes plain, and it should be said carefully. Israel in Egypt before this king was doing well. They had land in Goshen, they were multiplying, they had standing because of Joseph, and they were generations into a country that was not theirs with no recorded sign of wanting to leave it. The promise required them to go. What finally made them willing to go was the whip. That must be handled with care, because it stands one step away from a cruelty. It does not follow that every hardship is God prising somebody loose from a comfort, and it is never a thing to say to a person in the middle of one; a friend who explains your suffering to you has stopped being a friend. What can be said is only what the text says: this particular affliction fell inside a promise made four hundred years before, and the people groaning under it could not see that, were not told it, and found out afterwards. Most people do.

Settled where we were never meant to settle. There is a plainer application, and it cuts close to home for readers in comfortable countries. It is entirely possible to be a member of the covenant people, prospering quietly, in a place you were never meant to settle, for a very long time, with no intention whatever of moving. Christians are sojourners and exiles (1 Peter 2:11), and the danger of comfort is that we forget it.

How do I wait for God’s timing without becoming passive? Waiting on God in Scripture is never idleness. Israel waited in Egypt by having children, working, and keeping the memory of the promise alive; Joseph had made them promise to carry his bones out, so every generation knew they were not home. Wait like that. Do your work well, raise your children in the faith, pray for what God has promised, and hold your present comforts loosely, ready to move when he moves you. Waiting is active trust: doing today’s duty while looking for tomorrow’s fulfilment.

In a sentence. As the time drew near for God to fulfil his promise to Abraham, the people grew and multiplied in Egypt, until another king came to power who did not know Joseph.

On a Tuesday. Ask honestly whether there is anywhere in your life you have settled that God never meant to be home: a comfort, a pattern, a security you would not let go of if he asked. Hold it more loosely this week.

For worship. God’s promises ripen in his time, and they are never late. Kings rise who forget his servants, but God forgets no one: he remembered his covenant with Abraham, with Isaac and with Jacob (Exodus 2:24). Praise the God whose memory does not fail, who counts the years of his people’s waiting, and who brings them out at the appointed hour.

verseByVerse.quote: "He dealt shrewdly with our race and forced our fathers to expose their infants, so that they would not be kept alive. At this time Moses was born; and he was beautiful in God's sight. And he was brought up for three months in his father's house,"
verseByVerse.commentary:
He dealt shrewdly with our race and forced our fathers to expose their infants, so that they would not be kept alive. At this time Moses was born; and he was beautiful in God’s sight. And he was brought up for three months in his father’s house,

He dealt shrewdly with our race and forced our fathers to expose their infants, so that they would not be kept alive. He outwitted them, out-thought them. The persecution was not a spasm of temper. It was policy: drafted, revised when it failed, and escalated by stages (Exodus 1:10, 22). First the forced labour to break them; then a quiet instruction to the midwives; then, when the midwives would not do it, the open decree that every son be thrown into the Nile. It is the coldest thing in the chapter, and it was arrived at in meetings.

Our fathers. Stephen phrases the result in a way that puts the horror exactly where it belongs: Pharaoh forced our fathers to expose their infants. Not soldiers: the fathers. To expose was to abandon a baby to die, a common practice in the ancient world, which Christians later opposed by rescuing abandoned babies from the rubbish heaps of Roman cities. Stephen puts the horror on the parents who were made to give up their own children, which is why a programme of that kind takes something out of a people that a massacre does not.

At this time Moses was born; and he was beautiful in God’s sight. Against all of that: at this time Moses was born. That is God’s answer to the machinery of a superpower, and it is worth pausing over how small it is. No plague, not yet. No army, no uprising. A baby, born to slaves, in the middle of the programme designed to kill precisely him. Beautiful in God’s sight is a Hebrew way of saying exceptionally fine, pleasing to God (Exodus 2:2). God had his hand on him.

And he was brought up for three months in his father’s house. Hidden in a house where one cry at the wrong moment would have finished the whole family. Three months of a household not breathing. The letter to the Hebrews picks up the same detail: by faith Moses was hidden for three months by his parents, because they saw that the child was beautiful, and they were not afraid of the king’s edict (Hebrews 11:23). The first act of faith in the deliverance of Israel was performed by a mother and a father with a basket, and Scripture says their faith left them unafraid of a king.

The other babies. Now the thing that has to be said, because a passage about God’s rescue of a nation is being read by people who know that rescues are not universal. The other babies died. Stephen does not mention them and Exodus does not name them, but they were there: the households who did what they were forced to do, whose sons were not hidden or were found, and for whom the deliverer being born down the street was, at the time, no help at all. Scripture neither explains them nor pretends they were not there. Any reading of this passage that leaves the impression that God protects the children of the faithful as a general rule must be kept well away from anyone who has buried one. What the passage does say is that a state which had decided to end a people could not manage to kill one particular child, and ended up paying for his upbringing. That is not an explanation of the others. It is a statement about who was actually in charge of the outcome, made to a court that was under the impression it was.

What does this say about the value of unborn and newborn children? That every child is precious to God, including the ones the powerful find inconvenient. Each is made in his image and known by him before birth (Genesis 1:27; Psalm 139:13–16). Pharaoh’s policy was condemned by God, and so is every modern equivalent, including abortion and the abandonment of the unwanted. Christians should speak for the voiceless (Proverbs 31:8), and should do it as the early church did, by caring practically for mothers and children. And to anyone carrying the grief or guilt of an ended pregnancy: there is full forgiveness in Christ, whose blood cleanses from all sin (1 John 1:7). The church is meant to be a place of refuge for you, not judgment. And Scripture gives grieving parents real hope: we believe that God in his mercy saves the elect infants who die in infancy (Westminster 10.3; 2 Samuel 12:23).

In a sentence. The king dealt cunningly with their people and forced their fathers to abandon their babies so that they would die, and at that time Moses was born, a child beautiful before God, who was cared for three months in his father’s house.

On a Tuesday. God saw and valued an infant marked for death, and every child is precious to him. Do one concrete thing this month for a child or a struggling parent: a meal, an hour of help, a gift to a pregnancy support centre, a prayer said with them.

For worship. When Pharaoh decreed death for the sons of Israel, God hid his deliverer in a basket. When Herod decreed death for the boys of Bethlehem, God carried his Son into Egypt. The powers of the world have always raged against the child of promise, and they have always lost. Praise the God who watches over the little ones, and who sent his own Son as a child to save us.

verseByVerse.quote: "and when he was exposed, Pharaoh's daughter adopted him and brought him up as her own son. And Moses was instructed in all the wisdom of the Egyptians, and he was mighty in his words and deeds."
verseByVerse.commentary:
and when he was exposed, Pharaoh’s daughter adopted him and brought him up as her own son. And Moses was instructed in all the wisdom of the Egyptians, and he was mighty in his words and deeds.

And when he was exposed, Pharaoh’s daughter adopted him and brought him up as her own son. The rescue is arranged by the daughter of the man who signed the death warrant, and the child is brought up in the palace of the regime that wanted him dead (Exodus 2:5–10). Rescued by the enemy’s own household. Stephen does not comment on the irony. He does not need to.

What it cost him. Look at what it meant. He was brought up as her own son, which means he was taken out of a Hebrew house and raised as an Egyptian prince. He grew up eating at the table of the people who had enslaved his family, speaking their language, wearing their clothes, learning their gods and their arithmetic, and being addressed by a name that was not the one his mother used. Whatever else that childhood was, it was not simple, and he spent forty years inside a court that belonged to his own people’s enemy.

And Moses was instructed in all the wisdom of the Egyptians. Egypt was the great seat of learning in the ancient world, its name a byword for advanced knowledge; even of Solomon it is said that his wisdom surpassed all the wisdom of Egypt (1 Kings 4:30). It embraced mathematics and geometry (the skill behind the pyramids and the re-surveying of fields after each Nile flood), astronomy and the calendar, a famed medicine, architecture and engineering, the scribal art of writing, statecraft and administration, and a large body of moral instruction literature, together with the lore of the priests. As the adopted son of Pharaoh’s daughter, Moses would have received the education of an Egyptian prince. Exodus does not say this; it is the natural inference from his upbringing, preserved also in Jewish tradition, for Philo and Josephus describe his education at length. God prepared him in a pagan court.

And he was mighty in his words and deeds. Moses would later say he was not eloquent (Exodus 4:10), but his words carried power. And Luke’s description is the phrase he had used in his first volume of Jesus of Nazareth, a prophet mighty in deed and word (Luke 24:19). That is precisely Stephen’s point in this stretch, aimed at the temple charge again. God’s man is formed entirely outside the covenant community, in a pagan palace, by a pagan education, at the expense of the pagan state.

Equipped, but not the deliverer. Stephen’s deeper point soon follows. For all his Egyptian learning and natural greatness, Moses’ first attempt to deliver Israel in his own strength failed (vv. 23–29), and he had to wait forty years in the desert for God’s call. The world’s finest wisdom equipped him, but it did not make him the deliverer. God did.

Should Christians pursue a secular education? Yes, with open eyes. Moses learned the wisdom of Egypt, Daniel the literature of Babylon (Daniel 1:4, 17), and Paul quoted pagan poets (17:28). All truth is God’s truth, and learning is a gift to be used for his glory and our neighbour’s good. But neither Moses nor Daniel let the school decide who they were. Daniel resolved not to defile himself; Moses refused to be called the son of Pharaoh’s daughter (Hebrews 11:24). So study hard, and study well, and take your faith into the classroom with you. Learn everything you can, and let God’s word judge it all.

In a sentence. When he was abandoned, Pharaoh’s daughter adopted him and brought him up as her own son, and Moses was educated in all the wisdom of the Egyptians and was mighty in his words and deeds.

On a Tuesday. God prepares his servants in unlikely places, and your training may be his preparation. Look at the job, the course or the experience you think is wasted, and ask how God might use it for his kingdom.

For worship. The Lord used Pharaoh’s own daughter to raise the man who would bring Pharaoh down, and Egypt’s own schools to train the one who would lead Israel out of Egypt. He makes the wrath of man to praise him (Psalm 76:10). Praise the sovereign God, who turns the resources of his enemies into the equipment of his servants, and who formed in Moses a shadow of the one Prophet mighty in deed and word.
verseByVerse.note: Tradition held that Moses received a full Egyptian education.

verseByVerse.quote: "When he was forty years old, it came into his heart to visit his brothers, the children of Israel. And seeing one of them being wronged, he defended the oppressed man and avenged him by striking down the Egyptian."
verseByVerse.commentary:
When he was forty years old, it came into his heart to visit his brothers, the children of Israel. And seeing one of them being wronged, he defended the oppressed man and avenged him by striking down the Egyptian.

When he was forty years old, it came into his heart to visit his brothers, the children of Israel. Something rose in him, and what rose was a decision about who he was. He had been raised as an Egyptian, and a man in that position has eventually to settle which of the two peoples inside him is going to win. Stephen follows a tradition that divided Moses’ hundred and twenty years into three forties: forty in Egypt, forty in Midian (v. 30), forty in the wilderness (v. 36; Deuteronomy 34:7).

A renunciation. The letter to the Hebrews describes the moment as a refusal: he refused to be called the son of Pharaoh’s daughter, choosing rather to be mistreated with the people of God than to enjoy the fleeting pleasures of sin (Hebrews 11:24–26). So this is not a young man’s impulse. He chose to identify with his oppressed people, and it cost him a kingdom.

And seeing one of them being wronged, he defended the oppressed man and avenged him by striking down the Egyptian. And then he kills a man (Exodus 2:11–12). Stephen reports it without a word of condemnation, and without a word of approval either. Exodus supplies two details Stephen leaves out, and they settle the moral question well enough: Moses looked this way and that, and seeing no one, struck down the Egyptian and hid him in the sand. Those are not the movements of a man who believes he is executing justice. They are the movements of a man who knows exactly what he has done.

Right about the cause, wrong about the method. So the honest account is this. The loyalty was right and the hands were his own. God had not sent him; nobody had appointed him; there is no word from God anywhere in these verses. The deliverer who eventually stands before Pharaoh will do it with a staff and a message and no violence of his own at all. Moses was correct about the cause, correct about which side he belonged on, and entirely wrong about the method, and the method cost him forty years. That is a pattern worth recognising, because it is extremely common and it does not look like sin from the inside. A man is genuinely called to something. He is right about the need, right about the injustice, right that somebody ought to do something. And then he does it in his own strength and by his own means, forces the issue, manages the meeting, applies the pressure, and the result is a body in the sand and a career in the desert. The wrongness is not in the caring. It is in the assumption that being right about the cause authorises whatever gets it done.

Forgiven, but not spared. And then the mercy, which should not be hurried. God did not discard him. The man who buried an Egyptian at forty was standing before a burning bush at eighty, and the intervening decades turned out to be preparation rather than punishment. But they were real decades. He lost forty years, a nation waited forty years longer in slavery, and being forgiven was never the same thing as being spared the consequences.

When should a Christian step in to defend someone being wronged? Often, and gladly, by right means. Scripture commands us to open our mouths for the mute and defend the rights of the poor and needy (Proverbs 31:8–9), and Moses’ instinct to stand with the oppressed was right. But we act within the law and through proper channels: we report abuse to the authorities, speak up at work, give evidence, support the vulnerable, and in an emergency we protect life. What we do not do is take private vengeance; vengeance belongs to God and to the authorities he has appointed (Romans 12:19; 13:4). Care deeply, act wisely, and do not let zeal for justice become an excuse for sin.

In a sentence. When Moses was forty, he decided to visit his fellow Israelites, and seeing one being mistreated, he defended him and avenged him by striking down the Egyptian.

On a Tuesday. Moses chose God’s suffering people over Egypt’s comforts. What will you choose? Ask where in your life you are tempted to force God’s work forward by your own methods, and hand it back to him.

For worship. Moses’ attempt to save by his own hand failed. Another Deliverer came, who also refused the treasures of a kingdom, who also chose to suffer with his people, but who struck down no one. He let himself be struck, and by his wounds we are healed. Praise the Lord Jesus, who saves not by violence but by sacrifice, and who succeeded where every human deliverer fell short.
verseByVerse.note: Stephen follows a tradition that divided Moses’ 120 years into three forties.

verseByVerse.quote: "He supposed that his brothers would understand that God was giving them salvation by his hand, but they did not understand. And on the following day he appeared to them as they were quarreling and tried to reconcile them, saying, 'Men, you are brothers. Why do you wrong each other?'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
He supposed that his brothers would understand that God was giving them salvation by his hand, but they did not understand. And on the following day he appeared to them as they were quarreling and tried to reconcile them, saying, ‘Men, you are brothers. Why do you wrong each other?’

He supposed that his brothers would understand that God was giving them salvation by his hand, but they did not understand. Verse 25 is not in Exodus. Stephen is telling us what Moses was thinking, and this is a preacher interpreting, as preachers do; the interpretation is the key that unlocks the whole speech. God was giving Israel salvation (sōtēria), rescue, by Moses’ hand: that is stated as fact, not as Moses’ opinion of himself. What was Moses’ opinion was that they would grasp it. They did not. The deliverer arrived, God was genuinely at work in him, and the people he had come to rescue looked straight at it and saw a palace-raised Egyptian who had killed a man.

The failure is in the seeing. The failure is not in the sending; it is in the seeing. And the phrase Stephen chooses, they did not understand, hangs over everything that follows. Twenty-seven verses later he will tell these men that they have betrayed and murdered the Righteous One. He does not have to draw the line between the two statements. He has already shown them what happened the last time God sent Israel a deliverer and Israel did not recognise him. It is the same pattern as with Jesus: he came to his own, and his own people did not receive him (John 1:11).

And on the following day he appeared to them as they were quarreling and tried to reconcile them. The second scene is harder than the first. Moses finds two Israelites fighting each other, and his first recorded words in Scripture are a peacemaker’s. Notice the progression. Yesterday he stepped between an Egyptian and a Hebrew, which is the easy kind of intervention: there is an oppressor and a victim and everybody knows which is which. Today he steps between two Hebrews, where there is no obvious villain, both men have a grievance, and neither of them wants him there. Anyone who has tried to make peace inside a family or a congregation knows which of those two days is harder, and knows what tends to happen next: the two parties, who agree about nothing else in the world, unite instantly against the man who came to help.

Men, you are brothers. Why do you wrong each other? A plea for unity. The sentence is true, and is the only reason Moses had any business being there, and is precisely the thing that neither of them wished to hear. He came to his own, and his own would not have him; and that sentence has been true of somebody else since.

How should I try to make peace between two people? Carefully, prayerfully and humbly. Begin by praying for both. Go to each privately before bringing them together, and listen far more than you speak. Remind them, as Moses did, of what they share: if they are believers, they are brothers and sisters for whom Christ died. Do not take sides before you understand, and do not carry tales between them. Be ready to be resented; peacemakers often are. And know your limits: serious conflict, especially where there is abuse or law-breaking, belongs with elders and sometimes with the authorities. Blessed are the peacemakers, for they shall be called sons of God (Matthew 5:9).

In a sentence. Moses thought his brothers would realise that God was rescuing them through him, but they did not, and the next day he came upon two of them fighting and tried to reconcile them, asking why brothers would wrong each other.

On a Tuesday. Think of two people in your church, family or workplace who are at odds. Pray for them by name this week, and ask God whether you are meant to be a peacemaker between them.

For worship. Christ came to save his own, and many did not understand. He came as the great Peacemaker, to reconcile brothers to each other and sinners to God, making peace by the blood of his cross (Colossians 1:20). He was thrust aside, as Moses was, and he did not give up. Praise the Prince of Peace, who breaks down every dividing wall and makes enemies into one family.

verseByVerse.quote: "But the man who was wronging his neighbor thrust him aside, saying, 'Who made you a ruler and a judge over us? Do you want to kill me as you killed the Egyptian yesterday?'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
But the man who was wronging his neighbor thrust him aside, saying, ‘Who made you a ruler and a judge over us? Do you want to kill me as you killed the Egyptian yesterday?’

But the man who was wronging his neighbor thrust him aside. The word for thrust aside (apōtheō) is pushed away, rejected, and it is a key word, for Israel will thrust Moses away again (v. 39). The guilty one rejects the peacemaker.

Who made you a ruler and a judge over us? Stephen has included the question for a reason, and the reason arrives eight verses later. At verse 35 he says: this Moses, whom they rejected, saying, Who made you a ruler and a judge, this man God sent as both ruler and redeemer. The question receives its answer in its own words. Israel demanded to know who had made him a ruler. The answer, which took forty years to become visible, was God (Exodus 2:14).

The question asked again. That is the spine of the whole Moses section, and it is worth watching for, because Stephen leaves the third instance of it unspoken. The men in front of him had put the identical question in the temple courts not long before: tell us by what authority you do these things, or who it is that gave you this authority (Luke 20:2; Matthew 21:23). And they had received an answer they did not like from a man they subsequently killed.

Do you want to kill me as you killed the Egyptian yesterday? The second half of the taunt is the sting, and a threat. Moses had looked round and seen nobody. Somebody had seen. And the man who tells him so is one of the two he has just tried to reconcile: the secret is out, and it is out through the people he was trying to help.

Israel had some reason. Two things are worth saying about this rejection, and the second is the fairer. The first is that it establishes the pattern Stephen is building: the rescuer refused by the rescued, and refused specifically on the question of his standing. The second is that Israel had some reason. Consider how it looked from the labour camp. A man who has spent forty years in the palace, who eats Egyptian food and speaks with an Egyptian accent and has never in his life carried a brick, turns up, kills a foreman, and expects to be recognised as the nation’s deliverer. It is not obvious that this is good news. The reprisals would fall on them and not on him. Their failure was genuine and Stephen names it as a failure. But it was not stupidity. It was the ordinary difficulty of recognising a deliverer who does not look like one, which is exactly the difficulty the men listening to this speech had lately failed to overcome with a carpenter from Nazareth.

How do I respond when my help is thrown back at me? First, do not be surprised; Moses was rejected for trying to make peace, and Jesus for far more. Second, examine yourself honestly, as Moses had reason to: was there something in my manner or method that made the help hard to receive? Third, do not retaliate or become bitter; commit the matter to God, who sees. And fourth, do not conclude that you must never help again. Moses was rejected at forty and sent back at eighty. Sometimes the timing was wrong, not the love. Keep your heart soft, and wait to see whether God reopens the door.

In a sentence. The man in the wrong pushed Moses aside, asking who had made him ruler and judge over them, and whether he meant to kill him as he had killed the Egyptian the day before.

On a Tuesday. When the guilty resist correction, do not be surprised. And when you are corrected, notice whether your first response is to ask who gave them the right. Listen before you answer.

For worship. Who made you a ruler and a judge over us? Israel asked it of Moses and the council asked it of Jesus, and God has answered for ever: he has fixed a day on which he will judge the world in righteousness by a man whom he has appointed, and has given assurance by raising him from the dead (17:31). Praise the King whom God has crowned, whom men thrust aside and the Father exalted, and to whom every knee will bow.

parallels.desc: who made you a prince and a judge over us?

verseByVerse.quote: "At this retort Moses fled and became an exile in the land of Midian, where he became the father of two sons."
verseByVerse.commentary:
At this retort Moses fled and became an exile in the land of Midian, where he became the father of two sons.

At this retort Moses fled and became an exile in the land of Midian, where he became the father of two sons. One sentence, and forty years disappear into it. Midian lay east of the Gulf of Aqaba, in north-west Arabia. Exile (paroikos) is a sojourner, a resident alien, like Abraham.

Three forties. Stephen’s arithmetic of Moses’ life is worth laying out, because this speech is the only place in Scripture where it is spelled out. Forty years in Egypt (v. 23). Forty in Midian (v. 30). Forty in the wilderness with Israel (v. 36), bringing him to the hundred and twenty at which Deuteronomy says he died. Two-thirds of that life was over before God said anything to him at all.

What the middle forty contained. He married a Midianite priest’s daughter and kept another man’s sheep in another man’s country. He named his first son Gershom, which Exodus explains as meaning I have been a sojourner in a foreign land (Exodus 2:22; 18:3–4), and a man who names his child after his own homelessness is telling you how the years were going. Life went on outside the land. He had been a Hebrew in Egypt and an outsider; he was now an Egyptian in Midian and an outsider again. Nothing in the record suggests he expected to go back.

God waited for the second man. The contrast between the men at either end of the gap is the point. At forty he was a prince with an education, a position and a plan, convinced that God was going to save Israel by his hand and that everyone would see it. At eighty he was a shepherd standing before a burning bush producing five separate excuses why God ought to send somebody else. God waited for the second man.

The fallow years. This is the passage to hand to a reader in a long fallow stretch: the years after the thing that was supposed to happen did not, the decade of ordinary work with no visible point to it, the ministry that closed, the plan that came to nothing. Scripture shows this shape repeatedly: David between the anointing and the throne, Paul in Arabia and then back in Tarsus for years until Barnabas came looking for him. But a guard is needed, because the pattern is easily turned into a promise it does not make. Not every fallow decade is preparation for something visible, and telling somebody in year twelve that God is getting them ready is a guess dressed up as a word from the Lord. Moses did not know. As far as the record goes he was a man who had failed, had run, and was keeping sheep. What can be said is that the desert was not wasted and that God had not finished, and that nobody in Midian could have told you either thing at the time.

Is it wrong to run from danger? No. Moses fled for his life, and so did David, Elijah, Joseph and Mary with the infant Jesus, and Paul over the Damascus wall. Jesus told his disciples, when they persecute you in one town, flee to the next (Matthew 10:23). Fleeing is not cowardice when it preserves life and does not require denying Christ. What a Christian must not do is run from a clear duty, or deny the Lord to save his skin. Where faithfulness and safety can go together, take the safe road with a clear conscience. Where they cannot, stand.

In a sentence. At this retort Moses fled and lived as a foreigner in the land of Midian, where he had two sons.

On a Tuesday. If you are in a Midian season, do the ordinary work in front of you faithfully, the sheep, the job, the family, and keep your heart open to God. He spoke to Moses in the middle of a working morning.

For worship. God’s servant was rejected and lived in exile for forty years, and God was still preparing him. The Lord is never in a hurry and never late. He takes proud princes into the desert and brings out humble shepherds fit to carry his name. Praise the patient God, who wastes nothing in his servants’ lives, and who was preparing a deliverer while Israel slept and Moses kept sheep.
verseByVerse.note: Midian lay east of the Gulf of Aqaba.

verseByVerse.quote: "Now when forty years had passed, an angel appeared to him in the wilderness of Mount Sinai, in a flame of fire in a bush. When Moses saw it, he was amazed at the sight, and as he drew near to look, there came the voice of the Lord:"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Now when forty years had passed, an angel appeared to him in the wilderness of Mount Sinai, in a flame of fire in a bush. When Moses saw it, he was amazed at the sight, and as he drew near to look, there came the voice of the Lord:

Now when forty years had passed, an angel appeared to him in the wilderness of Mount Sinai, in a flame of fire in a bush. Stephen puts the silence in first. Whatever else the burning bush is, it is the end of four decades in which God said nothing whatever to the man he intended to use (Exodus 3:1–2). In the wilderness, outside the land, far from any temple: God revealed his name there.

What stopped Moses was not the fire. Picture the setting honestly. He is in the Sinai with a flock: bare rock, thorn scrub, the sort of dry bush that catches in a moment and is a handful of ash a minute later. A burning bush in that country is not a marvel. It is a commonplace and a nuisance. Exodus tells us exactly what arrested him: I will turn aside to see this great sight, why the bush is not burned (Exodus 3:3). It was the duration. He looked, and it was still there, and still there, and at some point he understood that he was watching something that was not obeying the rules.

When Moses saw it, he was amazed at the sight, and as he drew near to look, there came the voice of the Lord. Exodus records what came next in an order that repays attention: when the LORD saw that he turned aside to see, God called to him out of the bush (Exodus 3:4). The voice came after the turning aside. God did not speak to a man walking past. He spoke to a man who had stopped. It would be a mistake to make that a technique, as though a sufficiently attentive person could produce revelations by noticing harder; God was in that bush whether Moses looked or not. But it is worth registering how much of what God does is available to anybody prepared to stop and look twice, and how much of a life can be spent walking briskly past. Moses was eighty, in the middle of an ordinary working morning, minding animals that were not his, and the rest of the Bible turns on his deciding to go and have a proper look at something odd.

Was it an angel or God himself in the bush? Exodus says the angel of the LORD appeared, and then that God spoke from the bush, saying, I am the God of your father (Exodus 3:2–6). The angel of the LORD speaks as God and is called God. Many Christians, from the early church onward, have understood him as the Son of God appearing before his incarnation, and that is a reasonable reading. What is certain is that Moses met the living God himself, and that the God who spoke from the bush is the God revealed in Jesus Christ (John 8:58).

In the wilderness. One further detail, and it is Stephen’s real interest. Where does this happen? In the wilderness of Mount Sinai. Not in Egypt, where God’s people were. Not in Canaan, which God had promised them. In a stretch of desert belonging to nobody, on the wrong side of a border, with one man and a flock of sheep for a congregation. Stephen is on trial for saying that God is not confined to a building, and he is walking the court step by step through the places their own Scriptures record him turning up.

Should I expect God to speak to me in a burning bush? No; the bush was a unique moment in the history of redemption, when God was giving new revelation. Now God has spoken to us by his Son, and his word is complete in Scripture (Hebrews 1:1–2). But the lesson of turning aside still holds. God speaks to us whenever we stop and attend to his word, and he often draws our attention through ordinary things: a verse that will not let go, a sermon that lands, a providence that makes us look twice. Do not rush past. Make room in your day to stop, read, and listen.

In a sentence. After forty years an angel appeared to Moses in the wilderness of Mount Sinai in a flame of fire in a bush, and when Moses saw it he was amazed, and as he went closer to look, the voice of the Lord came.

On a Tuesday. God can meet you in the wilderness, in the most ordinary place. Stop and look. Choose one quiet ten minutes this week, put your phone in another room, and read a passage of Scripture slowly, twice.

For worship. The bush burned and was not consumed, because the God who was in it is a fire that gives life rather than destroying it. He came down to a shepherd in a desert, and one day he came down further still, in his Son, to dwell among us. Praise the holy God of the burning bush, who after forty years of silence still knew Moses’ name, and who knows yours.

verseByVerse.quote: "'I am the God of your fathers, the God of Abraham and of Isaac and of Jacob.' And Moses trembled and did not dare to look. Then the Lord said to him, 'Take off the sandals from your feet, for the place where you are standing is holy ground.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
‘I am the God of your fathers, the God of Abraham and of Isaac and of Jacob.’ And Moses trembled and did not dare to look. Then the Lord said to him, ‘Take off the sandals from your feet, for the place where you are standing is holy ground.’

I am the God of your fathers, the God of Abraham and of Isaac and of Jacob. Four hundred years of silence, and the first thing God says is that he is the same (Exodus 3:6). There is no explanation of the delay and no account of where he has been. He identifies himself by the names of three men who had been dead for centuries, and in doing so tells Moses that nothing has been dropped: the promise made in Mesopotamia to a childless man is the promise being kept this morning in a desert. He is the covenant God. And Jesus would later draw out of this very sentence the proof of the resurrection: he is not God of the dead, but of the living, for all live to him (Luke 20:37–38).

And Moses trembled and did not dare to look. Holy fear. Set that beside the man of verse 24. At forty he was ready to take on Egypt single-handed; at eighty he cannot raise his eyes to a bush. Whatever the desert did to him, it did not leave his nerve where it found it, and this is the man God has decided to send.

Take off the sandals from your feet, for the place where you are standing is holy ground. Then the sentence Stephen has been building toward since he opened his mouth (Exodus 3:5). This is the first time in the Bible that any ground is called holy, and it is worth being exact about where it is. A patch of dirt in a foreign desert with a thorn bush on it. There is no altar. No priest. No ark, no tabernacle, no temple, no city; no free Israel either, which does not yet exist as a nation. There is no ceremony and no sacrifice. And when God had finished speaking and Moses walked back to his sheep, it was scrub again. What made it holy was that God was there. Nothing else did, and nothing else ever has.

The sandals. The instruction is more homely than it sounds. In that world a man took his shoes off at the door of a house, because you do not carry the street into somebody’s home; and, by long tradition, the priests served barefoot in the sanctuary for the same reason. God is telling Moses that this hillside is his house. The command is domestic. It assumes he lives there. Now hold that against the charge sheet. Stephen has just shown the court, out of the law they revere, that the first ground God ever called holy was unmarked desert in Midian, and that it was holy for exactly as long as he was standing on it. Not one man in that room can dispute a word of it, because Moses wrote it down.

Is my church building holy ground? Not in itself. No place under the new covenant is holier than another; Jesus said that true worshippers will worship the Father in spirit and truth, not on this mountain or in Jerusalem (John 4:21–24). A church building is a useful room, to be cared for well and used reverently, but it is not a temple. What is holy is the presence of God among his gathered people, and that is why public worship should be reverent: not because of the bricks, but because the Lord is in the midst of his assembly (Matthew 18:20). Wherever God’s people meet in his name, whether a cathedral, a school hall or a living room, take off your sandals in your heart.

In a sentence. God said he was the God of their fathers, of Abraham, Isaac and Jacob, and Moses trembled and did not dare to look, and the Lord told him to take off his sandals, for the place where he stood was holy ground.

On a Tuesday. Wherever God meets you is holy ground. Before you open your Bible or begin to pray today, pause for a moment and remember who you are speaking with. Let reverence and nearness go together.

For worship. The God of Abraham, Isaac and Jacob is the God of the living, and the patriarchs are alive to him now. He makes ground holy by standing on it, and he makes sinners holy by dwelling in them. Praise the faithful, unchanging God, who names himself by his promises, and before whom even Moses could not lift his eyes, yet who calls us to draw near through his Son.

parallels.desc: the God of Abraham, Isaac and Jacob; take off your sandals

verseByVerse.quote: "'I have surely seen the affliction of my people who are in Egypt, and have heard their groaning, and I have come down to deliver them. And now come, I will send you to Egypt.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
‘I have surely seen the affliction of my people who are in Egypt, and have heard their groaning, and I have come down to deliver them. And now come, I will send you to Egypt.’

I have surely seen the affliction of my people who are in Egypt, and have heard their groaning. Three verbs, and they arrive in an order worth following: I have surely seen, and have heard, and I have come down (Exodus 3:7). The first is emphatic in the Hebrew underneath it, the verb doubled: seeing I have seen. Not glanced at, not been aware of. Looked at, steadily, the whole way through. Four hundred years of it. God sees and hears the suffering of his people.

God hears groaning. The second verb is the one to sit with. God says he has heard their groaning, and Exodus, describing the same moment, does not say that Israel prayed. It says they groaned because of their slavery and cried out for help, and their cry rose up to God, and God heard their groaning and remembered his covenant (Exodus 2:23–24). There is no record of a national repentance, no prayer meeting, no petition properly worded. There is a noise made by people at the end of their strength; it goes up; and God treats it as a communication. That is worth knowing by anybody who has been unable to pray properly, who has sat with something so heavy that the words would not come, and concluded that whatever was happening did not count. Paul goes further and says that when we do not know what to pray for as we ought, the Spirit himself intercedes for us with groanings too deep for words (Romans 8:26). Whatever it is that reaches God, it is not the wording.

And I have come down to deliver them. Then the third verb, which is the strangest. Notice what God does not do here. He does not explain. Four hundred years have passed exactly as he told Abraham, and he offers Moses no account of them whatever: no reason for the timing, no theology of the delay, no answer to the question every Hebrew slave for four generations must have asked in the dark. He says he has seen, he has heard, and he has come down. Israel received a rescue and never received an explanation. That is not a comfortable thing to write, and it may be the most useful sentence in the chapter. An enormous amount of Christian energy goes into demanding from God the reason for a silence, and Scripture’s most sustained example of a long silence ends without one being given. What was given instead was God himself, in motion, on the way.

And now come, I will send you to Egypt. The last clause turns the whole thing over. God says he has come down to deliver them, and then sends a man. The coming down and the sending are one act. It is how he has always worked. And the men listening to this speech had lately watched him do it in a form so complete that they killed the messenger, for the true coming down of God was in his Son, and they are about to kill the next messenger too.

How can God come down, if he is everywhere already? God is everywhere present, filling heaven and earth (Jeremiah 23:24). When Scripture says he came down, it means he acted in a new and particular way: he drew near in saving power to a specific people in a specific place. It is language suited to us, but it describes something real. And it reaches its full meaning in the incarnation, when the eternal Son literally came down from heaven and became flesh (John 6:38; 1:14). The God who said, I have come down, in Exodus, said it again in Bethlehem, and this time he stayed.

In a sentence. God said he had surely seen his people’s suffering in Egypt and heard their groaning, and had come down to rescue them, and now he was sending Moses to Egypt.

On a Tuesday. God sees your affliction and hears your groaning. If you cannot find words to pray today, groan before him. He hears that too. And then look for whom he might be sending to help you, or whom he might be sending you to help.

For worship. God sees and hears, and he comes down. He came down to Egypt with plagues and a sea parted, and he came down to us in a manger and on a cross, to deliver us from a slavery worse than Pharaoh’s. Praise the God who does not stay at a distance from his people’s pain, who hears groans that have no words, and who comes down in person to set captives free.

parallels.desc: I have surely seen the affliction of my people

verseByVerse.quote: "This Moses, whom they rejected, saying, 'Who made you a ruler and a judge?' — this man God sent as both ruler and redeemer by the hand of the angel who appeared to him in the bush. This man led them out, performing wonders and signs in Egypt and at the Red Sea and in the wilderness for forty years."
verseByVerse.commentary:
This Moses, whom they rejected, saying, ‘Who made you a ruler and a judge?’ — this man God sent as both ruler and redeemer by the hand of the angel who appeared to him in the bush. This man led them out, performing wonders and signs in Egypt and at the Red Sea and in the wilderness for forty years.

This Moses, whom they rejected. Something changes in the rhythm here, and it is audible even in English. Stephen begins hammering the same word at the head of each sentence: this Moses, this man, this man, this is the Moses, this is the one (vv. 35, 36, 37, 38). He has stopped narrating. He is pointing. This is the heart of the speech: this man, this one. Stephen is drawing a portrait of Jesus.

This man God sent as both ruler and redeemer. What he points at is a contradiction his hearers have never resolved. Israel demanded to know who had made Moses a ruler and a judge. God made him a ruler and a redeemer. The answer comes in the question’s own words. The very office they refused him is the office he was given, and the men who asked the question spent the next forty years being led by the man they had asked it about. The man they rejected was the one God sent to save them. So with Jesus: God has made him both Lord and Christ, this Jesus whom you crucified (2:36); the stone the builders rejected has become the cornerstone (4:11).

Redeemer. The second title is worth a moment: redeemer (lytrōtēs), a word that occurs nowhere else in the New Testament. It is the one who buys a man out of slavery or debt, the deliverer and ransomer, the man with both the right and the resources to pay what you cannot pay yourself. Stephen is describing Moses, and he has chosen a word his hearers will not be able to keep at a comfortable distance.

This man led them out, performing wonders and signs in Egypt and at the Red Sea and in the wilderness for forty years. Verse 36 spreads the vindication over forty years. Signs confirmed him, as they confirmed Jesus (2:22). And it is worth noticing that this is the phrase Luke has been using of the apostles in this book, and used in the previous chapter of Stephen himself (6:8). Moses, the Twelve and the man now on trial are being set in a single line: all sent, all attested, and all disbelieved by the same institution.

The pattern fully drawn. The pattern is now complete, though Stephen still refuses to name it. Joseph, sold by his brothers, became the man who fed them. Moses, thrust aside by his people, became the man who brought them out. Twice God sent Israel a deliverer; twice Israel refused him at first sight; and twice God sent him anyway, and the refusal cost the refusers years they did not have to spare. That leaves one question hanging in that chamber. Every man on the council can hear it. Stephen has not asked it yet.

What does it mean that Jesus is my redeemer? It means you were a slave, and he paid to set you free. Not with silver or gold, Peter says, but with the precious blood of Christ, like that of a lamb without blemish or spot (1 Peter 1:18–19). You were in bondage to sin, under the law’s curse and the fear of death (Galatians 3:13; Hebrews 2:15), and you could not buy yourself out. Christ had the right, as your kinsman in our flesh, and the resources, as the Son of God, and he paid it all. So you belong to him now, not as a slave in fear but as a ransomed child. You are not your own; you were bought with a price (1 Corinthians 6:19–20).

In a sentence. This Moses, whom they rejected by asking who made him ruler and judge, God sent as both ruler and redeemer by the angel who appeared to him in the bush, and he led them out, performing wonders and signs in Egypt, at the Red Sea and in the wilderness for forty years.

On a Tuesday. When someone rejects you for Christ’s sake, remember that rejection by men has never been the final verdict on God’s servants. And when you are tempted to think little of Jesus, say aloud the titles God gave him: Ruler, Redeemer, Lord.

For worship. The rejected one is the redeemer. That is the gospel. Moses was the shadow; Christ is the substance: thrust aside by his own people, sent by the Father as Prince and Saviour, leading his people out of a far greater bondage than Egypt’s. Praise the Redeemer who paid the price no one else could pay, and who leads his ransomed people home.

verseByVerse.quote: "This is the Moses who said to the Israelites, 'God will raise up for you a prophet like me from your brothers.' This is the one who was in the congregation in the wilderness with the angel who spoke to him at Mount Sinai, and with our fathers. He received living oracles to give to us."
verseByVerse.commentary:
This is the Moses who said to the Israelites, ‘God will raise up for you a prophet like me from your brothers.’ This is the one who was in the congregation in the wilderness with the angel who spoke to him at Mount Sinai, and with our fathers. He received living oracles to give to us.

God will raise up for you a prophet like me from your brothers. Stephen now plays what looks like his strongest card, and does something unexpected with it. That promise (Deuteronomy 18:15) is the text Peter preached from in the temple courts (3:22), and the full weight of it belongs there. Stephen means Jesus, as Peter did. What he does with it here goes straight at the second charge against him. He is on trial for saying that Jesus would change the customs Moses delivered. His answer is that Moses himself told Israel to expect somebody else and to listen to him when he came. The man they accuse Stephen of dishonouring is the man who pointed away from himself, beyond himself, to Jesus. To honour Moses is to listen to Jesus.

This is the one who was in the congregation in the wilderness. The description in verse 38 is extravagant. The word for congregation is ekklēsia, the Old Testament’s term for the assembly of Israel and the New Testament’s word for the church. Israel in the wilderness was God’s assembly, the church of the old covenant.

With the angel who spoke to him at Mount Sinai, and with our fathers. Stephen says the law came through angelic mediation, as the New Testament says elsewhere (v. 53; Galatians 3:19; Hebrews 2:2). He is not diminishing the law by saying so. He is about to use it, at verse 53, as the aggravating factor in the charge he brings against them.

He received living oracles to give to us. Weigh that phrase. Living oracles: not a dead code, not a rulebook, not an antique, but life-giving words of God, words with life still in them, still speaking. It is one of the highest things anybody in the New Testament says about the law of Moses, and it is said by the man on trial for despising it. He honours the law. The charge was false. And note the last two words. Stephen does not say Moses received the law to give to you. He says to us. He puts himself among the people the law was given to and claims it as his own inheritance, in the middle of a hearing convened on the charge that he has thrown it away.

A demonstration, not a denial. There is something to learn from that. The instinct under a false accusation is to deny: I never said that. And denial is very nearly useless; it always sounds like a man on the back foot. Stephen denies nothing. He states what he actually believes, at length and in terms so high that the accusation collapses under its own implausibility. The best answer to being misrepresented is usually not a correction but a demonstration.

Is the Old Testament still for Christians? Entirely. It is the Bible Jesus read, quoted and called the word of God, and he said it bears witness about him (John 5:39). Paul says the Scriptures, meaning the Old Testament, are able to make you wise for salvation through faith in Christ Jesus, and that all Scripture is breathed out by God and profitable (2 Timothy 3:15–16). We read it through Christ, so that its sacrifices point us to his cross and its ceremonies are fulfilled in him rather than kept by us. But its stories, laws, psalms and prophets remain living oracles for us. If you have neglected it, start with Genesis, the Psalms or Isaiah, and read looking for Christ.

In a sentence. This is the Moses who told Israel that God would raise up a prophet like him from among their brothers, who was in the assembly in the wilderness with the angel who spoke to him at Sinai and with their fathers, and who received living words to give to us.

On a Tuesday. God’s word is living. Read it as such: not as a duty to tick off, but as a voice speaking to you today. Before you read tomorrow, pray, Lord, speak; your servant is listening.

For worship. Moses received living oracles, and pointed to a Prophet greater than himself. That Prophet has come, and he is himself the living Word, full of grace and truth, whose words are spirit and life (John 6:63). Praise the God who has spoken, by Moses and the prophets, and at last by his Son, and whose word still lives and gives life.
verseByVerse.note: “The congregation” is the same word as “church.”

parallels.desc: a prophet like me

verseByVerse.quote: "Our fathers refused to obey him, but thrust him aside, and in their hearts they turned to Egypt, saying to Aaron, 'Make for us gods who will go before us. As for this Moses who led us out from the land of Egypt, we do not know what has become of him.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Our fathers refused to obey him, but thrust him aside, and in their hearts they turned to Egypt, saying to Aaron, ‘Make for us gods who will go before us. As for this Moses who led us out from the land of Egypt, we do not know what has become of him.’

Our fathers refused to obey him, but thrust him aside. Two verses, and the second half of Stephen’s case lands. First the verb: thrust aside is the identical word he used at verse 27, where the quarrelling Israelite shoved Moses away in the labour camp. He has used it twice deliberately. Israel pushed Moses aside at the beginning, before the exodus, and pushed him aside again at the foot of the mountain, after the sea had opened. They had the living oracles, and refused them. The rescue made no difference to the reflex.

And in their hearts they turned to Egypt. The sentence that does the most work in the chapter. They had been out of Egypt a matter of months. They had walked through a sea on dry ground and watched an army drown behind them. And they wanted to go back (Numbers 14:3–4): not because anybody had persuaded them that slavery was preferable, but because Egypt was familiar and the food arrived. Numbers records what they actually missed, and the list is worth reading aloud: the fish, the cucumbers, the melons, the leeks, the onions and the garlic (Numbers 11:5). They remembered the menu and forgot the whips. The heart turned back before the feet did.

The homesickness of the redeemed. This is the verse a Christian reader should find hardest to walk past, because it is not about somebody else. It is the standard experience of the redeemed life. A man is genuinely delivered: the thing that owned him has been broken, he knows it, and he would not go back if you asked him outright. And there is nevertheless a homesickness in him for the country he was rescued from. Not for the misery of it, but for the familiarity, the predictability, the not having to trust anybody for tomorrow. Egypt fed you every day and asked nothing of you except your life.

Make for us gods who will go before us. The request, and its timing (Exodus 32:1). Spoken while Moses was up the mountain receiving the law on their behalf. They gave him about forty days before replacing him. Idolatry is wanting a god you can see and control, one who goes where you want to go.

As for this Moses who led us out from the land of Egypt, we do not know what has become of him. The phrasing of the complaint is a small masterpiece of contempt. Not our leader; not the man God sent. This Moses.

A trap closing. One guard, because this passage is easily turned into a lash. The people who did this had seen the sea open. They had eaten manna that morning. Whatever else the golden calf demonstrates, it demonstrates that witnessing miracles does not make anybody faithful, and a Christian who assumes he would have done better is precisely the sort of person Stephen has in front of him. Every man on that council would have agreed warmly that their ancestors were a disgrace. That is the trap he is walking them into, and it closes in twelve verses.

What do I do with the longing for my old life? Name it honestly, and do not be shocked by it; Israel felt it, and so do most believers at some point. Then remember accurately. Egypt was not garlic and melons; it was whips and dead babies. Ask God to show you the truth about what you were rescued from. Feed on what he has given now: his word, his people, the manna of each day’s grace. Remove what makes the road back easy. And look forward, as Moses did, to the reward (Hebrews 11:26). The longing for Egypt fades fastest when the heart is fixed on the promised land.

In a sentence. Their fathers refused to obey Moses and pushed him aside, turning back to Egypt in their hearts and asking Aaron to make them gods to lead them, since they did not know what had become of this Moses.

On a Tuesday. Idolatry begins in the heart. Guard yours. Notice this week what you reach for when God seems slow or distant, the comfort food of the soul, and bring that longing to him instead.

For worship. God did not give up on a people who wanted to go back to Egypt within months of the Red Sea. He fed them, forgave them, and brought their children into the land. His patience outlasts our homesickness for sin. Praise the faithful Shepherd who leads his people through the wilderness, and who will not let go of those he has redeemed, even when their hearts look back.

parallels.desc: make us gods who shall go before us

verseByVerse.quote: "And they made a calf in those days, and offered a sacrifice to the idol and were rejoicing in the works of their hands. But God turned away and gave them over to worship the host of heaven, as it is written in the book of the prophets: "'Did you bring to me slain beasts and sacrifices, during the forty years in the wilderness, O house of Israel?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
And they made a calf in those days, and offered a sacrifice to the idol and were rejoicing in the works of their hands. But God turned away and gave them over to worship the host of heaven, as it is written in the book of the prophets: “‘Did you bring to me slain beasts and sacrifices, during the forty years in the wilderness, O house of Israel?

And they made a calf in those days, and offered a sacrifice to the idol and were rejoicing in the works of their hands. Two things in these verses, and the second is easily skipped. The first is a phrase that explains why Stephen dies. They were rejoicing in the works of their hands (Exodus 32:4–6). Hold that expression, because its twin arrives at verse 48: the Most High does not dwell in houses made by hands. They are the same idea, and the word at verse 48 is not neutral. In the Greek Old Testament, made by hands is very largely a word for idols, the contemptuous term for things people carve and then bow down to (Leviticus 26:1; Isaiah 2:18; 46:6). Idolatry is worshipping what we make.

The temple in the same category. So when Stephen applies it to the temple, a Jewish ear does not hear a remark about architecture. It hears the temple put into the same category as the golden calf. That is the offence: not that he disparaged a building, but that he used the vocabulary of idolatry about the house of God, having just established that Israel has a very long history of rejoicing in things it made itself. Even a God-given building can become an idol when it takes God’s place.

But God turned away and gave them over to worship the host of heaven. Then the judgment, and it is the most frightening kind there is. He did not strike them. He let them have it. It is the language Paul uses three times in the first chapter of Romans (Romans 1:24, 26, 28): God gave them up. It describes a judgment which, from the inside, feels like nothing happening at all. A man insists on his idol and God stops arguing with him. The worst thing God does to people determined on a substitute is to withdraw his objection. The host of heaven: the stars, worshipped as gods.

Did you bring to me slain beasts and sacrifices, during the forty years in the wilderness, O house of Israel? The clause that carries the rest of Stephen’s case, quoted from Amos (Amos 5:25). It is a rhetorical question, and an extraordinary thing to ask, because of course they did. The wilderness generation sacrificed constantly; the book of Leviticus is the paperwork for it. Amos is not denying that the ritual happened. He is denying that it arrived. Forty years of offerings, and God asks whether one of them was ever truly brought to him.

Who is hearing this. Stephen is standing before the men who run the sacrificial system, on trial for allegedly attacking the temple, and he quotes a prophet asking whether Israel’s sacrifices were ever for God at all. He is not merely arguing that the building cannot contain God. He is putting the offerings themselves in question, which is a far more dangerous thing to do in that room. And it puts a question to anybody who does religious things. Not whether the activity is happening: it plainly was, for four decades, in enormous quantity, exactly as prescribed. The question is whether it is being brought to God or merely performed in his vicinity. The test is not the volume of it, nor the correctness of it, nor how sincere it felt at the time.

Could God give me over like that? If you are worried that he might, that worry is good evidence he has not. Those whom God gives over do not tremble about it; they rejoice in the works of their hands and want nothing more. The believer who sins and is grieved, who wants to be rid of his idol and cannot yet see how, is being pursued by God, not abandoned. God disciplines the children he loves (Hebrews 12:6), and his discipline hurts precisely because he has not let go. The danger is not in the struggle. It is in the settled, contented refusal to be turned. If you can still hear his objection to your idol, thank him, and listen.

In a sentence. They made a calf, offered sacrifice to the idol and celebrated what their hands had made, so God turned away and gave them over to worship the stars, as Amos wrote, asking whether they had really brought him sacrifices in the wilderness.

On a Tuesday. What have your hands made that you are tempted to worship: career, home, reputation, a family image? And in your religious life, ask Amos’s question: is my worship being brought to God, or only performed near him? Turn from the idol, and bring the next prayer to God himself.

For worship. The living God will not share his glory with a calf, and he will not accept sacrifices that are not brought to him. Yet he provided the one sacrifice that truly arrived: his own Son, the Lamb without blemish, offered once for all and accepted for ever. Praise the God who turned away from idolaters, and then turned toward us in Christ, so that idolaters could be forgiven.
