parallels.desc: did you bring me sacrifices forty years in the wilderness?
the host of heaven

verseByVerse.quote: "'You took up the tent of Moloch and the star of your god Rephan, the images that you made to worship; and I will send you into exile beyond Babylon.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
‘You took up the tent of Moloch and the star of your god Rephan, the images that you made to worship; and I will send you into exile beyond Babylon.’

You took up the tent of Moloch and the star of your god Rephan, the images that you made to worship. The quotation from Amos runs on, and it names what Israel was carrying alongside the tabernacle (Amos 5:26). That is the force of it. Israel in the wilderness had two tents. One was the tent of witness, built to the pattern God showed Moses on the mountain, with the ark inside it and the cloud over it. The other was the tent of Moloch, carried through the same camp, on the same march, by the same people. Instead of carrying God’s tent alone, they carried pagan shrines beside it. Stephen’s accusers have built their whole case on the sanctity of the sanctuary. He is telling them that from the very first generation the sanctuary had a rival travelling beside it in the baggage, and that the golden calf was not a single lapse but the visible part of something the nation never put down. And note the word again: the images that you made.

Who were Moloch and Rephan? Moloch (or Molech) was a pagan deity, named as the abomination of the Ammonites (1 Kings 11:7) and notorious across the region for child sacrifice: children were made to pass through the fire to him (Leviticus 18:21; 2 Kings 23:10; Jeremiah 32:35). The tent of Moloch is a portable idol shrine carried in procession, a grim parody of the tabernacle. Rephan is the star of your god: an astral deity, probably the planet Saturn worshipped as a god. This is star worship, the bowing to the host of heaven that Scripture repeatedly condemns (Deuteronomy 4:19; 2 Kings 21:3–5).

An honest word on the names. Stephen is quoting the Greek Old Testament of Amos 5:25–27, and its wording differs from the Hebrew, which at this point is genuinely obscure. Where the Hebrew has Sikkuth and Kiyyun, probably names of Mesopotamian astral gods (Saturn again), the Greek rendered them Moloch and Rephan. So the exact identifications are the best scholarly reconstruction, not certainty; but the sense is plain, and it is Stephen’s point. Even in the wilderness, the very generation that carried God’s tabernacle was also carrying the shrines of pagan star gods.

And I will send you into exile beyond Babylon. Amos wrote beyond Damascus. Stephen extends it to the exile that actually came, which is not carelessness but the ordinary freedom of a preacher pressing a prophecy to the event it reached. The end of persistent idolatry was exile from the land. The land did not protect them. The judgment threatened by the prophet is the judgment their ancestors received, and Stephen is placing the court he stands in inside the same sentence.

Do people still worship Moloch and the stars? In other forms, yes. Moloch was the god to whom children were sacrificed for the sake of prosperity and security, and every age finds its own ways of sacrificing children to the adult’s comfort, career or convenience. The star of Rephan is the old ancestor of astrology, the belief that our lives are ruled by the heavens rather than by the God who made them. Horoscopes may seem harmless fun, but Scripture treats looking to the stars for guidance as turning from God (Isaiah 47:13–14). The Christian looks past the stars to their Maker, who calls them all by name (Isaiah 40:26), and who holds our times in his hand.

In a sentence. Amos said they had taken up the shrine of Moloch and the star of their god Rephan, the idols they made to worship, and so God would send them into exile beyond Babylon.

On a Tuesday. Is there a second tent in your baggage, something you carry alongside your faith that has never been surrendered? Name it before God today. And if you have dabbled in horoscopes or similar things, set them aside, and trust your future to the Lord.

For worship. Persistent idolatry leads to judgment, and God would have been just to leave Israel in exile for ever. Instead he brought them back, and then sent his Son, who bore the exile of sinners on the cross, cast out of the city so that we could be brought home. Praise the God who alone is worthy of worship, the Maker of the stars, who will have no rival tent beside his own and who has made his dwelling with us in Christ.
verseByVerse.note: Stephen quotes Amos from the Greek Old Testament; Moloch was the god of child sacrifice, and Rephan probably an astral god (Saturn). Amos said “beyond Damascus”; Stephen says “beyond Babylon,” where the exile actually went.

verseByVerse.quote: "Our fathers had the tent of witness in the wilderness, just as he who spoke to Moses directed him to make it, according to the pattern that he had seen. Our fathers in turn brought it in with Joshua when they dispossessed the nations that God drove out before our fathers. So it was until the days of David,"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Our fathers had the tent of witness in the wilderness, just as he who spoke to Moses directed him to make it, according to the pattern that he had seen. Our fathers in turn brought it in with Joshua when they dispossessed the nations that God drove out before our fathers. So it was until the days of David,

Our fathers had the tent of witness in the wilderness, just as he who spoke to Moses directed him to make it, according to the pattern that he had seen. Stephen now turns to the sanctuary itself, and the first thing to notice is that he defends it. God ordered it. God specified it. There is not a syllable of criticism in the sentence, and any reading of this speech which makes Stephen an opponent of Israel’s worship has to get past it first. The tent of witness is the tabernacle, which held the tablets of the law, the testimony (Exodus 25:16; Numbers 17:7). And there is a contrast with the previous verse: the fathers carried the tent of Moloch; God gave them the tent of witness.

A tent. But look at what he calls it. Not a house, not a sanctuary, not a temple: a tent, with pegs and ropes and curtains and poles, and instructions in Numbers specifying which family carried which section on the march. It had no foundation. It could be struck in a morning and standing again by evening. The one dwelling God ever designed for himself was designed to be portable, and every piece of its furniture was fitted with rings so that poles could be run through and men could pick it up and walk. God was not fixed to a place.

According to the pattern. And he adds that it was made according to the pattern Moses had seen. So even the tent was a copy. Moses was shown something on the mountain and told to build a model of it (Exodus 25:40), which means the tabernacle was never the ultimate thing either. It was a copy and shadow of heavenly realities (Hebrews 8:5). It pointed beyond itself.

Our fathers in turn brought it in with Joshua when they dispossessed the nations that God drove out before our fathers. And it kept moving: into Canaan with the conquest, and then round the country for centuries, to Gilgal, Shiloh, Nob and Gibeon. For something like four hundred years after Israel entered the land, the place where God met his people had an address that changed. And for Greek readers there is a glint of something more: the name Joshua in Greek is Jesus (Iēsous). The first Jesus brought the tent into the land; the second would bring the true dwelling of God among men.

So it was until the days of David. That is the hinge, and everything after it concerns what happened when somebody decided the arrangement ought to be permanent. For centuries Israel worshipped God in a tent.

Then should churches not own buildings? They may, and many should; a building is a tool, and a good one. Stephen thought the tabernacle mattered enormously, and God designed it. The question is not whether a church has a building but whether it could lose one and still be a church. The early Christians met in homes, in rented halls (19:9) and in the open air, and the church grew. A congregation that would collapse if its building were taken away has put its weight on the wrong thing. Use your building gladly, keep it modest and useful, and keep your heart in the people and the word.

In a sentence. Their fathers had the tent of witness in the wilderness, made just as God had directed Moses according to the pattern he had seen, and they brought it into the land with Joshua when God drove out the nations, and it remained until David’s time.

On a Tuesday. God moved with his people in a tent, and he still goes with you wherever you go. Ask whether your church, and your faith, could move if God called: whether what you run on is the sort of thing that can be picked up and carried.

For worship. The God who travelled with his people in a tent later pitched his tent among us in the flesh of his Son: the Word became flesh and dwelt, literally tabernacled, among us, and we have seen his glory (John 1:14). Praise the pilgrim God, who did not wait for his people to build him a house before he came to live with them, and who goes with his church to the end of the age.
verseByVerse.note: The “tent of witness” is the tabernacle, which held the tablets of the testimony.

verseByVerse.quote: "who found favor in the sight of God and asked to find a dwelling place for the God of Jacob. But it was Solomon who built a house for him."
verseByVerse.commentary:
who found favor in the sight of God and asked to find a dwelling place for the God of Jacob. But it was Solomon who built a house for him.

Who found favor in the sight of God and asked to find a dwelling place for the God of Jacob. David comes off well here, and Stephen means him to (Psalm 132:5). He found favour in the sight of God, and what he wanted was to build God a house (2 Samuel 7:2). It was a generous impulse in a man who had noticed that he was living in a palace of cedar while the ark of God sat under canvas, and Scripture never suggests the motive was wrong.

But it was Solomon who built a house for him. That but is carrying a great deal, and to feel it you have to know what God said when David proposed the idea. The answer came through the prophet Nathan, and it is one of the most remarkable speeches in the Old Testament. Would you build me a house to dwell in? I have not lived in a house since the day I brought up the people of Israel from Egypt, but I have been moving about in a tent. And then a question to read slowly: did I ever speak a word to any of the judges of Israel, asking why they had not built me a house of cedar? (2 Samuel 7:5–7). God says, in as many words, that since the exodus he had never asked anybody for a building and had never once complained about not having one.

I will build you a house. When David offered, God turned the offer round. You will not build me a house; I will build you a house, a dynasty (2 Samuel 7:11–13). The play on the word is the point of the whole passage: David offered God a building and God gave David a dynasty. And the heir of that dynasty is the one these men had lately helped to nail to a cross outside the city wall.

Even the builder knew. None of which makes the temple illegitimate. God permitted it, filled it with his glory on the day it opened, and Jesus called it his Father’s house. Stephen does not condemn it. And the man who built it said at the dedication, before the whole nation, that heaven and the highest heaven cannot contain you; how much less this house that I have built (1 Kings 8:27). Even the builder knew.

A short and nearly invisible step. What the passage exposes is a very ordinary religious mistake, and sincere people make it almost invariably. David’s desire was good. The impulse to do something substantial for God is good. But there is a step from I want to honour God with this to God requires this, and must be honoured here, and the step is short and very nearly invisible. A thousand years after Solomon, a man is on trial for his life because a building God never asked for had become the thing his people could not imagine him without.

How do I know whether my good plan for God is what he wants? Hold it with open hands, as David did. David told Nathan, and when God said no, he did not sulk; he sat before the LORD and gave thanks for what God would do instead (2 Samuel 7:18–29). So test your plan against Scripture, pray over it, ask the counsel of godly people, and watch how God opens or closes the way. Above all, notice if the plan has become something you cannot imagine God without. That is the sign a good desire is turning into an idol. God may give you something better than you asked: not the house you wanted to build him, but the house he builds you.

In a sentence. David found favour with God and asked to provide a dwelling place for the God of Jacob, but it was Solomon who built a house for him.

On a Tuesday. Think of a good thing you want to do for God. Offer it to him this week with a genuine willingness to hear no, and thank him in advance for whatever better thing he may give instead.

For worship. God builds his house, his people, through David’s greater Son. You are part of it. Christ is the Son of David who builds the true temple, not of cedar and stone but of living stones, his people (1 Peter 2:5), and his kingdom will have no end. Praise the God who answered David’s small offer with an everlasting promise, and kept it in Jesus.

verseByVerse.quote: "Yet the Most High does not dwell in houses made by hands, as the prophet says, 'Heaven is my throne, and the earth is my footstool. What kind of house will you build for me, says the Lord, or what is the place of my rest?'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Yet the Most High does not dwell in houses made by hands, as the prophet says, ‘Heaven is my throne, and the earth is my footstool. What kind of house will you build for me, says the Lord, or what is the place of my rest?

Yet the Most High does not dwell in houses made by hands, as the prophet says. Here is the sentence they kill him for, and two things in it detonate, both deliberately. The first is the phrase made by hands (cheiropoiētos). As at verse 41, this is idol vocabulary: the standard term in the Greek Old Testament for the manufactured objects the prophets pour contempt on. Stephen has already used its twin of the golden calf, and now he fastens it onto the temple. To the men in that chamber this is not an architectural observation. Not that the temple was wrong, but that treating it as the place where God was contained was idolatry. Paul says the same in Athens (17:24).

The Most High. The second is the title he chooses. The Most High is a title for the God of Israel that outsiders often use: it is on the lips of Melchizedek, of Nebuchadnezzar, of a demoniac in the Gospels, and of a fortune-telling slave girl later in this same book (Genesis 14:18–20; Daniel 4:34; Mark 5:7; Acts 16:17). It is the God of Israel described from beyond the boundary, and exactly the right title for a speech about a God who declines to be kept inside one.

Heaven is my throne, and the earth is my footstool. Then, so that nobody can accuse him of inventing the idea, he quotes Isaiah (Isaiah 66:1). Look at the picture rather than skimming it. God is seated with the sky for a chair and the planet under his feet for a stool. God is too great for any building.

What kind of house will you build for me, says the Lord, or what is the place of my rest? Now, says the prophet, describe the building. Give the dimensions. Say where the resting place is to go. It is God asking a builder for a specification, and the question answers itself the moment anybody tries. No house can hold him. Now he dwells in Christ, the true temple (John 2:19–21), and in his people (1 Corinthians 3:16; Ephesians 2:21–22).

The line he leaves out. The most devastating thing about the quotation is what Stephen leaves out, and his hearers knew the passage well enough to supply it. Isaiah’s very next sentence answers the question. Having asked what house anyone imagines they could build him, God says: but this is the one to whom I will look: he who is humble and contrite in spirit and trembles at my word (Isaiah 66:2). So Isaiah does say where God dwells. Not in a structure: in a certain sort of person. Stephen stops one line short of that, and the line is a description of precisely what the men in front of him are not. They are proud of their building, unmoved by their guilt, and about to show what they think of the word of God by killing the man reciting it. He does not need to quote the sentence. Every man in the room can hear it, which is worse.

If God is everywhere, why should I go to church? Because the church is not a building but a people, and God has promised to be present among his gathered people in a special way (Matthew 18:20; 1 Corinthians 14:25). Scripture commands us not to neglect meeting together (Hebrews 10:25), because we need the preached word, the Lord’s Supper, the prayers and the fellowship of the saints. You can pray alone anywhere, and you should. But the living stones are meant to be built together into one house, not scattered across the field. Going to church is not visiting God’s building; it is joining God’s temple.

In a sentence. The Most High does not live in houses made by human hands, as the prophet says: heaven is my throne and earth my footstool; what kind of house will you build me, says the Lord, or where is my resting place?

On a Tuesday. Church buildings are useful, but God does not live in them. He lives in his people. Be his temple: this week, treat your body, your home and your congregation as the places where God has chosen to dwell.

For worship. Heaven is his throne and earth his footstool, and yet this high and lofty One looks with favour on the humble and contrite heart. The God whom no building can contain has made his home in Christ, and through Christ in sinners who tremble at his word. Praise the Most High, too great for any temple and near enough to dwell in yours.

parallels.desc: heaven is my throne, and the earth is my footstool

verseByVerse.quote: "'Did not my hand make all these things?'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
‘Did not my hand make all these things?’

Did not my hand make all these things? Eight words, and they close the argument (Isaiah 66:2). Follow the logic to the end of it. The temple was built by human hands. Human hands were made by God. The stone came out of ground he made, quarried with tools of metal he put in the earth, cut by men whose lungs he kept full while they worked. There is nothing in that building which did not come from him, and therefore nothing in it capable of containing him. A man cannot house his maker in materials his maker supplied. The contrast is complete: houses made by human hands, and the universe made by God’s hand. The Creator cannot be confined by what creatures make.

A question to end on. Stephen ends this whole section with a question rather than a statement. He has been quoting Isaiah for two verses, and the last thing the council hears before he turns and faces them is God’s own voice asking whether they had ever stopped to consider who made the quarry.

Where God dwells now. If God never truly dwelt in the building, where is his dwelling now? The New Testament answers: in Christ first of all. Jesus called his own body this temple (John 2:19–21), and in him the whole fullness of deity dwells bodily (Colossians 2:9). And then, through him, in his people: you are God’s temple and God’s Spirit dwells in you (1 Corinthians 3:16; 6:19; Ephesians 2:21–22). The God too great for any house of stone has chosen to make his home in ordinary believers. Stephen’s point is not that buildings are wrong, but that we must never trap the living God in a place or a thing while missing him where he truly dwells. Isaiah goes on: God’s dwelling is with the humble.

A question to put to oneself. The error Stephen exposes is not confined to men who own a temple. It is entirely possible to know perfectly well that God is not contained in a building, and to have quietly relocated him somewhere just as manageable: a style of service, a set of convictions, an hour of the week, a way of feeling when the music is right. The test is not what a man says about where God lives. It is what he would have left if the thing were taken away from him.

What does it mean to tremble at God’s word? Not to be terrified of the Bible, but to take it with utter seriousness, as the voice of the living God. The one who trembles at God’s word lets it correct him rather than correcting it. He reads it expecting to be addressed, obeys what it says even when it costs, and is moved by its promises as well as its warnings. Josiah tore his clothes when he heard the law read (2 Kings 22:11–19), and God looked on him with favour. Trembling at the word is the opposite of the council’s stopped ears. It is a soft heart that hears God speaking and bows.

In a sentence. God asks whether his hand did not make all these things.

On a Tuesday. God made everything. He does not need our buildings, but he seeks our humble hearts. Ask yourself what you would have left of your faith if your favourite form of it, the music, the building, the routine, were taken away. Then make sure your hope is in God himself.

For worship. The hand that made all things was pierced with nails, and by that hand the true temple was raised on the third day. God, who needs nothing from us, gave everything for us. Praise the Maker of heaven and earth, who will not live in a house of stone, and who has chosen to make his home with the humble and contrite who tremble at his word.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Stephen turned the charge back on his accusers: they were stubborn, with hearts and ears uncircumcised, always resisting the Holy Spirit just as their ancestors did. Their ancestors persecuted every prophet and killed those who foretold the coming of the Righteous One, and now they had betrayed and murdered him. They had received the law through angels and had not kept it. Hearing this, they were furious and ground their teeth at him. But Stephen, full of the Holy Spirit, looked up to heaven and saw God’s glory and Jesus standing at God’s right hand. He said he could see heaven open and the Son of Man standing at God’s right hand. At this they covered their ears, shouted, rushed at him, dragged him out of the city and began to stone him. The witnesses laid their coats at the feet of a young man named Saul. While they stoned him, Stephen prayed, “Lord Jesus, receive my spirit.” Then he knelt down and cried out, “Lord, do not hold this sin against them.” With that he fell asleep.
verseByVerse.theology:
Stephen and the Pattern of Martyrdom

The Greek word for a witness is martys, and it did not come to mean somebody killed for the faith until enough witnesses had been. Stephen is where the shift begins, and the shape of his death is the shape the church has recognised ever since: the truth told without softening, Christ seen at the moment of dying, the killers prayed for. Reformed theology has been careful about what this is and is not. It is not heroism and it is not an achievement that earns anything — Luke states plainly that Stephen was full of the Holy Spirit at the moment he looked up, which is to say that the courage and the vision and the forgiveness were all supplied to him. What this passage exhibits is not a strong man but a sustained one. And it should be added, because the church has periodically forgotten it, that martyrdom is nowhere in the New Testament something to be sought. Stephen did not go looking for this. He was preaching, and it was done to him.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: Stephen's last recorded words asked that God not hold this sin against the men throwing the stones. A few feet away, minding their coats and approving of the execution, stood the man who never, to the end of his life, stopped mentioning that he had been there (22:20; 26:10). Now: Nobody watching that morning could have identified what was actually happening. The church lost its most gifted man and gained nothing visible; the persecution that followed scattered most of the Jerusalem church; and between them those two disasters put the gospel into Samaria, into Antioch and eventually into Rome. It is worth remembering on a day when a loss looks total.

verseByVerse.quote: "You stiff-necked people, uncircumcised in heart and ears, you always resist the Holy Spirit. As your fathers did, so do you."
verseByVerse.commentary:
You stiff-necked people, uncircumcised in heart and ears, you always resist the Holy Spirit. As your fathers did, so do you.

You stiff-necked people. The turn is abrupt, and it can be located in a single pronoun. Again and again in this speech Stephen has said our fathers: our father Abraham, our fathers could find no food, our fathers had the tent of witness. He has been standing inside the family the whole way, arguing as a member of the household about the household’s own history. Then in this verse he says your fathers, and says it again in the next. That is the moment the defence becomes a prosecution, and every man in that chamber will have felt the floor shift.

A farming word. Then three charges, and every one of them is a quotation. Stiff-necked describes an ox that sets its neck against the driver’s hand and will not be turned: not an animal that bolts, but one that simply refuses to go the way the plough needs to go. Stubborn, like an ox that will not bend to the yoke. It is the word God himself used of Israel at Sinai after the golden calf, when he told Moses he would not go up among them, lest he consume them on the way (Exodus 32:9; 33:3, 5).

Uncircumcised in heart and ears. To that audience this is the deepest insult the language holds. He is calling circumcised men uncircumcised: telling the covenant people, in the covenant’s own vocabulary, that the mark cut into their bodies never reached the place it was pointing at. Outwardly circumcised, inwardly pagan. And it is not his coinage. Moses said it, the law said it, and Jeremiah said it twice (Deuteronomy 10:16; Leviticus 26:41; Jeremiah 4:4; 6:10; 9:26). It is the prophets’ language for those who will not listen to God. True circumcision is of the heart (Romans 2:28–29). Stephen is doing here exactly what he has done for fifty verses: quoting their Scriptures at them and letting the Scriptures do the accusing.

You always resist the Holy Spirit. To resist is to fight, to shove back against something coming toward you. The Spirit is the one who spoke through the prophets, against whom Israel rebelled and grieved his Holy Spirit (Isaiah 63:10). And always is the sting: not sometimes, not in the bad generations, but as a continuous habit running from the wilderness into this room.

As your fathers did, so do you. The recital of the last fifty verses turns out not to have been a history lesson. It was the evidence for this sentence. Rejecting Joseph, rejecting Moses, worshipping idols, and now rejecting Jesus: the pattern Stephen has traced.

A word of care. Sentences like this one have been lifted out and used as a weapon against Jewish people for the better part of two thousand years, and that must be named. Notice the speaker and the setting. This is a Jew, in the Jewish council, quoting Moses and the prophets, saying to the leadership of his own nation what Isaiah and Jeremiah had said to the leadership of theirs. It is prophetic speech inside a family, the oldest and most Jewish form of address in the Bible (see on 3:14). A man does not get to borrow Stephen’s sentence unless he is standing where Stephen was standing, and almost nobody who has quoted it has been.

If the Spirit can be resisted, is grace not irresistible after all? Both truths are taught in Scripture, and they fit. The Spirit’s outward call through the preaching of the word comes to many, and those left to themselves resist it, always, as Stephen says; that is what fallen hearts do. But when God effectually calls his elect, he does not merely invite; he gives a new heart that gladly comes (Ezekiel 36:26; John 6:44; Westminster 10.1). The resistance is real, and God overcomes it, not by forcing an unwilling man but by making him willing. The proof is standing at the edge of this very scene, holding coats. Saul resisted the Spirit as hard as any man in Jerusalem, until the risen Christ called him by name, and he could resist no longer.

In a sentence. Stephen said they were a stubborn people, uncircumcised in heart and ears, who always resisted the Holy Spirit, just as their fathers had.

On a Tuesday. The resistance Stephen names is not an ancient national peculiarity. It is the ordinary daily possibility of hearing something true from God and setting the neck against it. Is there a word of God you are resisting? Soften your neck and listen, today.

For worship. The God whom Israel resisted did not stop sending his Spirit, his prophets and at last his Son. He is the God who circumcises hearts (Deuteronomy 30:6), who takes out the heart of stone and gives a heart of flesh. Praise the Holy Spirit, who is resisted by every sinner and overcomes the resistance of every one of his elect, and who makes stiff necks bow gladly to Christ.
verseByVerse.note: “Uncircumcised in heart and ears” is the prophets’ language for stubborn refusal to listen.

parallels.desc: a stiff-necked people

verseByVerse.quote: "Which of the prophets did your fathers not persecute? And they killed those who announced beforehand the coming of the Righteous One, whom you have now betrayed and murdered, you who received the law as delivered by angels and did not keep it."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Which of the prophets did your fathers not persecute? And they killed those who announced beforehand the coming of the Righteous One, whom you have now betrayed and murdered, you who received the law as delivered by angels and did not keep it.

Which of the prophets did your fathers not persecute? A question with no available answer, which is precisely why he puts it as a question. Israel’s history of prophets is a history of men who were ignored, mocked, imprisoned, dropped into a cistern, and by tradition sawn in two, and it was not the pagans who did it. Jeremiah was imprisoned; Isaiah, by tradition, was sawn in two; Zechariah the son of Jehoiada was stoned in the court of the house of the LORD (2 Chronicles 24:21). The men who suffered most at Israel’s hands were the men God sent to Israel. Jesus had said the same (Matthew 23:29–37; Luke 11:47–51).

And they killed those who announced beforehand the coming of the Righteous One. Stephen chooses his title for Jesus with care: the Righteous One. Not Messiah, not Son of God, not the Nazarene. It is the title Peter used in the temple courts (3:14), and the one Paul will hear applied to Jesus at his conversion (22:14), and it reaches back to the righteous Servant of Isaiah (Isaiah 53:11). It is the exact word for what a court exists to protect. The supreme judicial body of the nation is being told that it condemned the one genuinely innocent man in its history, Jesus, the sinless one.

Whom you have now betrayed and murdered. The climax of the pattern. The Greek does not say they committed betrayal and murder; it calls them betrayers and murderers. He has turned the verbs into nouns and hung them round their necks as titles.

You who received the law as delivered by angels and did not keep it. And then the last line, which is the answer to the charge that began all this. Jewish tradition held that angels were present at the giving of the law (Deuteronomy 33:2; Galatians 3:19; Hebrews 2:2). Stephen has been on trial for speaking against the law of Moses. His closing sentence on the subject is that the law came to them by the hand of angels, an honour he described in glowing terms at verse 38, and that they broke it. He never denies the charge. He changes who is being examined. The question in that room is no longer whether Stephen kept the law. It is whether they did.

The most conservative accusation. Notice what he does not say. He does not say the law is finished, or mistaken, or that it never mattered. Every word he has spoken about the law has been high. What he says is that they had it and did not do it, which is the most conservative accusation available and the hardest of all to answer. The last word of the first Christian to die for the faith was not an attack on Israel’s Scriptures. It was a charge that Israel’s leaders had not obeyed them, brought by a man who had just spent fifty verses showing that he knew them better than the court did.

Was Stephen being unloving? No. Love sometimes has to say the hardest thing, and Stephen said it as a member of the family, in the words of the family’s own prophets, to people he wanted to see saved. His last breath proves it: he prayed for these very men. The prophets spoke like this because they loved Israel, and Jesus wept over Jerusalem in the same week he pronounced its judgment (Luke 19:41–44). We should be slow to imitate Stephen’s sharpness, because we rarely have his clarity, his Spirit-filled courage or his love. But when the truth must be spoken, it is not unloving to speak it plainly, as long as we would gladly die for the people we are speaking to.

In a sentence. Stephen asked which prophet their fathers had not persecuted, for they killed those who foretold the coming of the Righteous One, whom they had now betrayed and murdered, though they had received the law delivered by angels and had not kept it.

On a Tuesday. Before you criticise anyone for failing to keep God’s law, ask honestly whether you keep it. And thank God that the Righteous One kept it perfectly in your place.

For worship. The Righteous One was betrayed and murdered, and by his death he makes the unrighteous righteous (Romans 5:19). Every prophet who was persecuted was pointing to him, and every one of them is now vindicated in him. Praise Jesus the Righteous, who kept the law that we broke, who bore the punishment we earned, and who is our advocate with the Father (1 John 2:1).
verseByVerse.note: Jewish tradition held that angels were present at the giving of the law.

verseByVerse.quote: Now when they heard these things they were enraged, and they ground their teeth at him. But he, full of the Holy Spirit, gazed into heaven and saw the glory of God, and Jesus standing at the right hand of God.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Now when they heard these things they were enraged, and they ground their teeth at him. But he, full of the Holy Spirit, gazed into heaven and saw the glory of God, and Jesus standing at the right hand of God.

Now when they heard these things they were enraged, and they ground their teeth at him. Two reactions in one sentence, and they could not stand further apart. The council is enraged: the same word Luke used at 5:33 of this identical body hearing Peter, cut to the quick, sawn through. And they ground their teeth at him, which is not a figure of speech. Grinding the teeth was a sign of fury (Psalm 35:16; 37:12), and Jesus uses the phrase of the lost in outer darkness (Matthew 8:12). It is what a room of men do when fury has gone past the point where words are available: seventy-one of the most dignified figures in the nation, in session, in robes, making a noise with their jaws.

But he, full of the Holy Spirit, gazed into heaven. And Stephen looks up. While they look at him with hatred, he looks up. Luke’s verb is the fixed, deliberate gaze again (atenizō), the very word he used at the end of chapter 6, when this council stared at Stephen and saw a face like an angel’s. Now the staring runs the other way, and what he is looking at is not in the room.

Full of the Holy Spirit. Luke loves the phrase, and has already used it of Stephen (6:3, 5). It means a person so wholly yielded to the Spirit that the Spirit’s presence and power are evident in and through him. Notice what it brings at this moment. First, spiritual sight: the Spirit gives him eyes for the unseen reality, for the Spirit searches everything, even the depths of God (1 Corinthians 2:9–10). Second, strength for the supreme test: this filling comes at the hour of his death, and it makes him able to die like his Lord, committing his spirit to Jesus and forgiving his killers. It is exactly what Jesus had promised his witnesses when dragged before councils: the Holy Spirit will teach you in that very hour what you ought to say (Luke 12:11–12). This is not a first reception of the Spirit, for Stephen was already full, but a fresh filling for a decisive moment, the same pattern as Peter filled with the Holy Spirit before he answered the council (4:8).

And saw the glory of God, and Jesus standing at the right hand of God. The God of glory who appeared to Abraham (v. 2) now appears to Stephen, at the end of the same speech that began with him. And Jesus is at his right hand, the place of honour and power. The speech opened with the glory appearing to the father of the nation in Mesopotamia; it closes with the glory opened to the first martyr outside Jerusalem, and in the middle of the glory, a man.

Can I be filled with the Spirit? Yes; every Christian is commanded to be: do not get drunk with wine, but be filled with the Spirit (Ephesians 5:18). The verb means keep on being filled. It is not a one-off experience for the spiritual elite, but the ordinary Christian life lived under the Spirit’s control. And its truest evidence is not ecstatic feeling but a man who sees Christ clearly and lives and dies like Christ graciously. Paul follows the command with singing, thanksgiving and humble submission to one another (Ephesians 5:19–21). So ask God for it daily, feed on his word, confess sin quickly, and obey what you know. The Spirit did not spare Stephen the stones. He filled him to face them.

In a sentence. When they heard this they were furious and ground their teeth at him, but Stephen, full of the Holy Spirit, looked steadily into heaven and saw the glory of God, and Jesus standing at God’s right hand.

On a Tuesday. When the world grinds its teeth at you, look up. Jesus is there. Before the meeting, the confrontation or the bad news this week, lift your eyes, and remember who stands at the right hand of God.

For worship. While men grind their teeth on earth, heaven is open, and the glory of God is resting on the face of the crucified and risen Jesus. He is not absent from his suffering people; he is enthroned above them and watching over them. Praise the exalted Christ, who fills his servants with his Spirit in their darkest hour, and who lets them see, at the last, the glory they were made for.
verseByVerse.note: Grinding the teeth was a sign of fury.

verseByVerse.quote: And he said, "Behold, I see the heavens opened, and the Son of Man standing at the right hand of God."
verseByVerse.commentary:
And he said, “Behold, I see the heavens opened, and the Son of Man standing at the right hand of God.”

Behold, I see the heavens opened. As at Jesus’ baptism, when the heavens were opened and the Spirit descended (Luke 3:21). The barrier between earth and the throne room is drawn back, and a dying man is allowed to see.

And the Son of Man standing at the right hand of God. Two things about the sentence are extraordinary, and the first concerns a title. Son of Man is how Jesus habitually spoke of himself, some eighty times in the Gospels. What is striking is how nearly nobody else ever uses it. In the Gospels it almost never appears on another speaker’s lips; once a puzzled crowd throws his own phrase back at him (John 12:34). Outside the Gospels this is the only place where anyone calls Jesus the Son of Man, apart from the visions of Revelation. Stephen is very nearly the only man in Scripture who calls Jesus what Jesus called himself, and he does it in the very chamber where Jesus had used it under examination and been condemned for it. Jesus had told this council: from now on the Son of Man shall be seated at the right hand of the power of God (Luke 22:69). Stephen says: I see him. He confirms the very claim for which they condemned Jesus.

Standing. The second is a posture. Every other reference in the New Testament to Christ at the Father’s right hand has him seated. Psalm 110 says sit. Peter preached him exalted at Pentecost. The letter to the Hebrews builds an entire argument on the fact that this priest sat down, because his work was finished (Hebrews 10:12). This is the one exception. Stephen sees him standing. Why? Perhaps to welcome his servant home; or as a witness standing to testify for him in the heavenly court, as Stephen testifies for him on earth; or as a judge rising to pass sentence. All may be true.

Two courts. The setting suggests the strongest answer, and once it is seen it is hard to forget. Two courts are sitting that morning. In the lower one a man is being tried on the evidence of witnesses who were put up to lie, and the outcome was settled before he opened his mouth. In the higher one, at the moment the accused is about to be condemned, his advocate rises to his feet. Jesus had promised exactly this in Luke’s first volume: everyone who acknowledges me before men, the Son of Man also will acknowledge before the angels of God (Luke 12:8). Stephen is acknowledging him before men in the most expensive circumstances imaginable, and Luke shows the promise being kept while it is still being paid for.

The court at three in the morning. There is comfort in that which reaches far past this chapter. Most Christians will never stand before a council, and will nevertheless be judged: by an employer, a family, a professional body, a country, or simply by their own conscience convening a court at three in the morning with the evidence stacked and no defence prepared. This verse says there is another court, that it is in session, and that the one thing it never does is let the testimony go unanswered. Who shall bring any charge against God’s elect? It is God who justifies. Christ Jesus is the one who is at the right hand of God, who indeed is interceding for us (Romans 8:33–34).

What the sentence does to the room. Stephen has just told the Sanhedrin that he can see the man they executed alive, in glory, at the right hand of God. That is precisely the claim Jesus made before this same council, and precisely what they condemned him for. They have now heard it twice, from two different men, in the same chamber. The second time, they do not wait for a verdict.

Will I see heaven opened when I die? Scripture does not promise every believer a vision like Stephen’s, and many faithful Christians die without one, some peacefully and some in confusion or pain. What it promises is better than a vision: presence. To depart is to be with Christ, which is far better (Philippians 1:23); to be away from the body is to be at home with the Lord (2 Corinthians 5:8). Whether your eyes see anything at the end or not, the Lord Jesus will be there to receive you. Stephen was allowed to see beforehand what every believer will see immediately afterwards.

In a sentence. Stephen said, Look, I see the heavens opened, and the Son of Man standing at the right hand of God.

On a Tuesday. When you feel condemned, by others or by your own conscience, remember the other court. Say it aloud: Christ is at the right hand of God, interceding for me. Then go on with your day as one who has an advocate.

For worship. Jesus stands for those who stand for him, and he will welcome you home. The Son of Man whom the council condemned is the Son of Man to whom the Ancient of Days has given dominion and glory and a kingdom that shall not pass away (Daniel 7:13–14). Praise the risen Lord, who rises from his throne for his dying servants, and who will confess before his Father every one who has confessed him.
verseByVerse.note: Elsewhere the Son of Man is seated at God’s right hand; here he stands — perhaps to welcome Stephen or to plead as his witness.

parallels.desc: I will acknowledge him before the angels of God

verseByVerse.quote: But they cried out with a loud voice and stopped their ears and rushed together at him. Then they cast him out of the city and stoned him. And the witnesses laid down their garments at the feet of a young man named Saul.
verseByVerse.commentary:
But they cried out with a loud voice and stopped their ears and rushed together at him. Then they cast him out of the city and stoned him. And the witnesses laid down their garments at the feet of a young man named Saul.

But they cried out with a loud voice and stopped their ears and rushed together at him. Read that as a picture. Seventy-one of the most dignified men in the nation, the supreme council of Israel in session, with their fingers in their ears, shouting so as not to hear what is being said to them. To them it was blasphemy. They would not hear it. It is the behaviour of children, and Luke reports it without comment. It is also the exact fulfilment of the charge Stephen laid against them six verses earlier: he said they were uncircumcised in their ears, and they proceeded to stop them with their hands.

With one accord. The word Luke uses for rushed together (homothymadon) is the word he used of the church’s unity, with one accord in prayer and in the temple (1:14; 2:46). Now it describes a mob’s rage. There is a unity of the Spirit, and there is a unity of the mob, and they look alike for a moment from a distance.

A lynching by a court. What happens next is not an execution. No verdict is recorded, no sentence pronounced, no vote taken. They simply rushed at him. Whether the council even had the legal power to execute is doubtful; Rome reserved capital punishment, and John records them telling Pilate that it was not lawful for them to put anyone to death (John 18:31). It was probably a lynching rather than a legal execution, perhaps in a gap when no Roman governor was watching closely. Luke does not say, and the silence is itself informative. He is describing a proceeding that had stopped being a proceeding.

Then they cast him out of the city and stoned him. Yet the form is kept wherever it suits them. They cast him out of the city, because the law required a stoning to take place outside the camp (Leviticus 24:14). They keep the geography of Leviticus and abandon everything else in it. And like Jesus, he dies outside the city: Jesus also suffered outside the gate (Hebrews 13:12).

And the witnesses laid down their garments. Then a detail that ought to stop a reader cold. Luke mentions the witnesses because the law of Moses required that in a stoning the witnesses throw first (Deuteronomy 17:7), so that any man who had sworn a life away had to be the one to take it. These are the witnesses of chapter 6: the men who were suborned, planted and briefed. The men who lied about Stephen are the men who killed him with their own hands, and they took their coats off in order to do it properly.

At the feet of a young man named Saul. And then, in a single sentence, the New Testament introduces the most important man in its second half. No introduction. No description. Not a hint from Luke that this name will matter. A young man (neanias), perhaps in his twenties or thirties, minding the coats: doing the respectable part, the part that gets no blood on it, the part a man can afterwards tell himself was not really participation. Luke says plainly at the start of chapter 8 that he approved. And Paul himself never let it go. He raises it years later, standing in this same city, describing how he stood by approving and watching over the garments of those who killed Stephen (22:20); elsewhere he admits he did rather more than watch, and cast his vote against them (26:10). Every man in that field who threw a stone is anonymous. The one whose name Luke records is the one holding the coats, and the coats are the detail he would still be talking about decades later. God was about to make the persecutor a preacher.

Is holding the coats really so bad? Yes, and that is why Paul never forgot it. Most of us will never throw a stone, but most of us have held a coat: laughed along with the cruel joke, stayed silent while someone was slandered, approved in our hearts what we would never have done with our hands. Scripture treats approval as participation; Paul says those who give approval to evil share in its guilt (Romans 1:32). The good news is in the same verse. The man who held the coats became the apostle who wrote, Christ Jesus came into the world to save sinners, of whom I am the foremost (1 Timothy 1:15). There is forgiveness for the coat-holders too.

In a sentence. They shouted, covered their ears, rushed at him together, dragged him out of the city and stoned him, and the witnesses laid their cloaks at the feet of a young man named Saul.

On a Tuesday. When something cruel happens near you this week, a mocking conversation, an unjust decision, a person being shut out, refuse to hold the coats. Say a quiet word, or at least decline to approve. And pray for anyone you know who is fighting Christ hard. They may be Saul.

For worship. The young man holding the coats would become the apostle to the Gentiles. No one is beyond God’s grace. On the very day the church lost its first martyr, God had already marked the man who would carry the gospel to the nations. Praise the sovereign Lord, who stands over the stones and the coats alike, and who was already preparing to turn the fiercest persecutor into the greatest missionary.
verseByVerse.note: Stoning took place outside the city; the witnesses threw the first stones. This is the first mention of Saul, later Paul.

verseByVerse.quote: And as they were stoning Stephen, he called out, "Lord Jesus, receive my spirit." And falling to his knees he cried out with a loud voice, "Lord, do not hold this sin against them." And when he had said this, he fell asleep.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And as they were stoning Stephen, he called out, “Lord Jesus, receive my spirit.” And falling to his knees he cried out with a loud voice, “Lord, do not hold this sin against them.” And when he had said this, he fell asleep.

Lord Jesus, receive my spirit. Two prayers, and the order of them is the last thing Luke wants the reader to notice. The first is for himself, and it is a quotation. Psalm 31:5 says into your hand I commit my spirit, and it is addressed to God. Jesus prayed it from the cross, addressed to the Father: Father, into your hands I commit my spirit (Luke 23:46). Stephen prays it to Jesus.

Dying on the assumption of his deity. Consider what that is. A Jewish man, being killed for blasphemy by the highest religious authority in Israel, spends the last moments of his life praying a psalm addressed to the God of Israel, and addresses it to Jesus of Nazareth. He is not constructing an argument for the deity of Christ. He is doing something far more telling: he is dying on the assumption of it. Nobody commends his soul to a creature. The first Christian martyr dies praying to Jesus as Lord. And he expects his spirit to go at once to be with Christ (Philippians 1:23; 2 Corinthians 5:8).

And falling to his knees. Falling to his knees is a decision. A man under a hail of stones does not kneel by accident. Standing, he might have lasted longer; turned away, he might at least have covered his head. He knelt because he was going to pray, and he wanted his whole body to say so.

Lord, do not hold this sin against them. The second prayer is not for himself. And Luke notes that he cried this one out with a loud voice. The request for his own soul was spoken. The request for his murderers was shouted. He spent the last breath he had on the men who were taking it, and he made certain they heard him do it. It is Jesus again: Father, forgive them, for they know not what they do (Luke 23:34). Stephen loves his enemies to the last.

The order reversed. The parallel with the cross is exact, and the order is reversed. Jesus prayed first for his killers and then committed his spirit. Stephen commits his spirit and then, with whatever he has left, prays for his killers. The first Christian death is shaped like the death of Christ, and the disciple takes the sequence the other way round because he was running out of time and would not go without saying it.

What it does not mean. A guard belongs here, because this verse has been used to lay a burden on people that Scripture does not lay. It is not a rule that a Christian must feel forgiving at the moment of injury, or that failure to produce this prayer at the graveside of a murdered child is a failure of faith. Luke has already told us where it came from: Stephen was full of the Holy Spirit. The forgiveness in this verse is not an achievement modelled for imitation by willpower. It is a gift being reported. What is asked of ordinary Christians is that they should want to get there, and be willing to be taken there slowly, which for most people is the work of years and not of minutes.

Must I forgive someone who is not sorry? Stephen prayed for men who were still throwing stones, so the heart of forgiveness does not wait for an apology. It lets go of revenge, hands the wrong to God, and genuinely desires the other person’s good, even their salvation (Romans 12:17–21). But full reconciliation, the restoring of trust and relationship, does require repentance (Luke 17:3–4), and forgiveness never means pretending a wrong was not wrong, or staying exposed to someone dangerous, or not reporting a crime. You can forgive an abuser in your heart and still go to the police. Begin, as Stephen did, by praying for them. The feelings often follow the prayers, slowly.

And when he had said this, he fell asleep. Then Luke’s last word, the gentlest verb in the language attached to the most violent death in the book. A man has just been beaten to death with rocks in a field outside the wall, and Luke writes it as though somebody had nodded off in a chair. That is not a euphemism and it is not sentiment. It is the New Testament’s word for the death of believers (1 Thessalonians 4:13–14; 1 Corinthians 15:18, 20), and it is a statement about what death now is for people who belong to Christ, made by a writer who had every reason to reach for a harsher word and did not. Amid the stones, a quiet word. For the Christian, death is sleep, from which the body will wake in resurrection.

Does fell asleep mean the soul is unconscious until the resurrection? No. Sleep describes the body, which lies in the grave and will be woken. Stephen’s spirit did not sleep. He had just prayed, Lord Jesus, receive my spirit, and the Lord did. Jesus promised the dying thief, today you will be with me in paradise (Luke 23:43). Paul says that to be away from the body is to be at home with the Lord, and that to depart is to be with Christ, which is far better (2 Corinthians 5:8; Philippians 1:23). The souls of believers at death are made perfect in holiness and pass immediately into glory, while their bodies rest in their graves until the resurrection (Westminster 32.1).

The prayer answered. And one thing more, which Luke leaves the reader to assemble. Stephen asked that this sin not be held against them. A few feet away, holding the coats and approving, stood a young man who would be struck down on the road to Damascus, would spend the next thirty years telling anyone who would listen that he was the foremost of sinners, and would write more of the New Testament’s letters than any other man. Augustine is said to have put it this way: if Stephen had not prayed, the church would not have had Paul. The prayer was answered, and it was answered first in the person who, that morning, would have been the very last to expect it.

In a sentence. As they stoned him, Stephen called out, Lord Jesus, receive my spirit, and falling to his knees he cried out with a loud voice, Lord, do not hold this sin against them, and when he had said this, he fell asleep.

On a Tuesday. Learn to forgive like Stephen, who learned it from Jesus. Name one person who has wronged you, and pray for their good today, even if you have to start with a single sentence. And learn to die like him: each night as you lie down, commend your spirit to the Lord Jesus, so that when the last night comes, the words are already familiar.

For worship. Stephen died like his Master because his Master had died for him. The Lord Jesus received his spirit, as he will receive the spirit of every one who trusts him, and the prayer for his killers was answered in Saul of Tarsus. Death has become sleep, because Christ has taken its sting. Praise the Lord Jesus, to whom we may commit our spirits in life and in death, who forgives his enemies and makes them his apostles, and who will wake all who sleep in him on the morning of the resurrection.
verseByVerse.note: Stephen’s last words echo Jesus’ words on the cross. “Fell asleep” is the Christian way of speaking of a believer’s death.

7.theology: The Pattern of Rejection and Vindication. Stephen’s survey of Israel’s history reveals God’s way in the world: the one God sends is always rejected first. Joseph, Moses, the prophets, the Righteous One himself. And in each case, God vindicates the rejected one and uses that rejection as the means of redemption. This is not historical accident; it is divine pattern — the pattern of the cross. The grain of wheat must fall into the ground and die (John 12:24). The stone the builders reject becomes the cornerstone. And the martyr who follows the rejected-and-vindicated Lord shares the same arc: killed by men, received by God, his prayer answered in the conversion of his chief persecutor. Saul of Tarsus is Stephen’s greatest vindication.
7.examples:
Then: Stephen stands before the Sanhedrin in Jerusalem, the city that kills the prophets, and preaches them their own history. He is the first Christian martyr, and he dies as he lived — full of the Holy Spirit, full of faith, his face like an angel’s. His death scatters the seed further than his life could have planted it.

Now: The church in every hostile culture faces Stephen’s question: what do you do when you cannot be silenced by argument and so are silenced by violence? Stephen shows us: you look up, you see the glory of God, you commend your spirit to Christ, and you pray for those who kill you. This is not heroism; it is the overflow of a life lived so close to Christ that even death cannot separate you from him — and cannot stop the gospel.

8.title: The Scattered Gospel
8.text: <sup>1</sup>And Saul approved of his execution. And there arose on that day a great persecution against the church in Jerusalem, and they were all scattered throughout the regions of Judea and Samaria, except the apostles. <sup>2</sup>Devout men buried Stephen and made great lamentation over him. <sup>3</sup>But Saul was ravaging the church, and entering house after house, he dragged off men and women and committed them to prison. <sup>4</sup>Now those who were scattered went about preaching the word. <sup>5</sup>Philip went down to the city of Samaria and proclaimed to them the Christ. <sup>6</sup>And the crowds with one accord paid attention to what was being said by Philip, when they heard him and saw the signs that he did. <sup>7</sup>For unclean spirits, crying out with a loud voice, came out of many who had them, and many who were paralyzed or lame were healed. <sup>8</sup>So there was much joy in that city. <sup>9</sup>But there was a man named Simon, who had previously practiced magic in the city and amazed the people of Samaria, saying that he himself was somebody great. <sup>10</sup>They all paid attention to him, from the least to the greatest, saying, “This man is the power of God that is called Great.” <sup>11</sup>And they paid attention to him because for a long time he had amazed them with his magic. <sup>12</sup>But when they believed Philip as he preached good news about the kingdom of God and the name of Jesus Christ, they were baptized, both men and women. <sup>13</sup>Even Simon himself believed, and after being baptized he continued with Philip. And seeing signs and great miracles performed, he was amazed. <sup>14</sup>Now when the apostles at Jerusalem heard that Samaria had received the word of God, they sent to them Peter and John, <sup>15</sup>who came down and prayed for them that they might receive the Holy Spirit, <sup>16</sup>for he had not yet fallen on any of them, but they had only been baptized in the name of the Lord Jesus. <sup>17</sup>Then they laid their hands on them and they received the Holy Spirit. <sup>18</sup>Now when Simon saw that the Spirit was given through the laying on of the apostles’ hands, he offered them money, <sup>19</sup>saying, “Give me this power also, so that anyone on whom I lay my hands may receive the Holy Spirit.” <sup>20</sup>But Peter said to him, “May your silver perish with you, because you thought you could obtain the gift of God with money! <sup>21</sup>You have neither part nor lot in this matter, for your heart is not right before God. <sup>22</sup>Repent, therefore, of this wickedness of yours, and pray to the Lord that, if possible, the intent of your heart may be forgiven you. <sup>23</sup>For I see that you are in the gall of bitterness and in the bond of iniquity.” <sup>24</sup>And Simon answered, “Pray for me to the Lord, that nothing of what you have said may come upon me.” <sup>25</sup>Now when they had testified and spoken the word of the Lord, they returned to Jerusalem, preaching the gospel to many villages of the Samaritans. <sup>26</sup>Now an angel of the Lord said to Philip, “Rise and go toward the south to the road that goes down from Jerusalem to Gaza.” This is a desert place. <sup>27</sup>And he rose and went. And there was an Ethiopian, a eunuch, a court official of Candace, queen of the Ethiopians, who was in charge of all her treasure. He had come to Jerusalem to worship <sup>28</sup>and was returning, seated in his chariot, and he was reading the prophet Isaiah. <sup>29</sup>And the Spirit said to Philip, “Go over and join this chariot.” <sup>30</sup>So Philip ran to him and heard him reading Isaiah the prophet and asked, “Do you understand what you are reading?” <sup>31</sup>And he said, “How can I, unless someone guides me?” And he invited Philip to come up and sit with him. <sup>32</sup>Now the passage of the Scripture that he was reading was this: “Like a sheep he was led to the slaughter and like a lamb before its shearer is silent, so he opens not his mouth. <sup>33</sup>In his humiliation justice was denied him. Who can describe his generation? For his life is taken away from the earth.” <sup>34</sup>And the eunuch said to Philip, “About whom, I ask you, does the prophet say this, about himself or about someone else?” <sup>35</sup>Then Philip opened his mouth, and beginning with this Scripture he told him the good news about Jesus. <sup>36</sup>And as they were going along the road they came to some water, and the eunuch said, “See, here is water! What prevents me from being baptized?” <sup>38</sup>And he commanded the chariot to stop, and they both went down into the water, Philip and the eunuch, and he baptized him. <sup>39</sup>And when they came up out of the water, the Spirit of the Lord carried Philip away, and the eunuch saw him no more, and went on his way rejoicing. <sup>40</sup>But Philip found himself at Azotus, and as he passed through he preached the gospel to all the towns until he came to Caesarea.
8.overview:
Stephen’s death sets off the first great persecution, led by Saul, who goes from house to house dragging believers to prison. The church in Jerusalem is scattered, except the apostles, and the scattered believers preach wherever they go. So the second stage of Jesus’ plan in 1:8 begins: Judea and Samaria. The Samaritans were descendants of northern Israelites who had intermarried with foreigners after the Assyrian conquest; they accepted only the five books of Moses, worshipped on Mount Gerizim rather than in Jerusalem, and were despised by Jews, and the feeling was mutual (John 4:9). Philip, one of the seven, preaches Christ there with signs, and many believe, including a famous magician named Simon. The apostles send Peter and John, and only when they pray and lay hands on the Samaritans do they receive the Spirit, a sign to everyone that Samaritans and Jews are one church. Simon tries to buy the power to give the Spirit, and Peter sternly rebukes him.

Then an angel sends Philip to a desert road, where he meets a high official of the queen of Ethiopia, the kingdom of Meroë on the Nile far south of Egypt. The man is a eunuch who had come to worship in Jerusalem, and he is reading aloud from Isaiah 53 about the lamb led to the slaughter. Philip explains that the passage is about Jesus, and when they come to water the Ethiopian asks to be baptised. Philip is then taken away by the Spirit, and the Ethiopian goes home rejoicing, the gospel already heading towards the ends of the earth.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–25 — Persecution, Scattering, and the Gospel in Samaria
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Saul approved of Stephen’s killing. That day a great persecution broke out against the church in Jerusalem, and all except the apostles were scattered through Judea and Samaria. Devout men buried Stephen and mourned deeply for him. Saul set out to destroy the church, entering house after house and dragging men and women off to prison. Those who had been scattered preached the word wherever they went. Philip went down to a city in Samaria and proclaimed the Messiah there. When the crowds heard Philip and saw his signs they all paid close attention: impure spirits came out of many with loud cries, and many paralysed and lame people were healed, so there was great joy in that city. A man named Simon had practised sorcery there for some time and amazed the Samaritans, claiming to be someone great; everyone, high and low, called him the great power of God, because he had astonished them with his magic for so long. But when they believed Philip’s good news of God’s kingdom and the name of Jesus Christ, men and women were baptised. Simon himself believed and was baptised, and followed Philip everywhere, astonished by the signs and miracles. When the apostles in Jerusalem heard that Samaria had accepted God’s word, they sent Peter and John, who prayed for the new believers to receive the Holy Spirit, because the Spirit had not yet come on any of them; they had simply been baptised into the name of the Lord Jesus. Then Peter and John laid hands on them and they received the Spirit. When Simon saw that the Spirit was given through the apostles’ hands, he offered them money to give him the same power. Peter told him to take his money to destruction with him for thinking he could buy God’s gift; he had no share in this ministry, because his heart was not right before God. He must repent and pray that the Lord would perhaps forgive him for such a thought, for Peter could see he was full of bitterness and captive to sin. Simon asked them to pray for him that none of this would happen to him. After testifying and proclaiming the Lord’s word, Peter and John returned to Jerusalem, preaching the gospel in many Samaritan villages on the way.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Scattering as Mission Strategy

Reformed theology has read Acts 8 as the clearest narrative demonstration that God's purposes are not merely undamaged by human wickedness but advanced through it. Jesus had said the witness would go from Jerusalem to Judea and Samaria and to the end of the earth (1:8), and for perhaps two years nothing had moved; the church was large, joyful, generous and entirely stationary. It took a murder and a persecution to get it out of the city. The point is not that God needed the persecution, nor that the suffering was anything other than real — Luke records men weeping loudly over a grave in the same breath. It is that the machinery of opposition turned out to be the machinery of expansion, and that the man superintending the destruction was, without the faintest idea of it, dispersing the gospel across two provinces. The kingdom advanced that year in the shape of a defeat.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: Jews had no dealings with Samaritans, and the quarrel was not a misunderstanding — it had a ruined temple on Mount Gerizim in it, pulled down by a Jewish army. The gospel crossed that line before anybody had written a word of argument about whether it should. Now: The barrier a congregation is least likely to cross is never the one it debates. It is the one it has stopped noticing, because everyone it knows is on the same side of it.

verseByVerse.quote: And Saul approved of his execution. And there arose on that day a great persecution against the church in Jerusalem, and they were all scattered throughout the regions of Judea and Samaria, except the apostles. Devout men buried Stephen and made great lamentation over him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And Saul approved of his execution. And there arose on that day a great persecution against the church in Jerusalem, and they were all scattered throughout the regions of Judea and Samaria, except the apostles. Devout men buried Stephen and made great lamentation over him.

Meaning first. Acts 8 is the turning point when the gospel leaves Jerusalem. Persecution scatters the church, and the scattered believers preach wherever they go. Philip takes the gospel to Samaria, where many believe, a sorcerer is exposed, and the apostles confirm the work. Then Philip meets an Ethiopian official on a desert road and leads him to Christ from Isaiah 53. The gospel is moving outward, as Jesus said it would (1:8): to the half-Jewish Samaritans, and to a Gentile from the ends of the earth. The chapter that opens with a grave ends with a man going home rejoicing.

And Saul approved of his execution. The chapter division cuts a sentence in half. This line belongs with the stoning at the end of chapter 7, and Luke wrote it as the last word on that scene. The young man holding the coats was not a bystander who happened to be present. He approved. The word (syneudokōn) means he consented, thought well of it, was pleased; and Paul spends the rest of his life saying so, with shame (22:20).

And there arose on that day a great persecution against the church in Jerusalem. On that day. Stephen’s death was not merely the first casualty; it was the starting gun. This is the first general persecution. Something had been held back until somebody was killed and nothing happened to the killers, and once that line was crossed the whole thing came down at once. Probably the Hellenists, Stephen’s circle, were the main targets.

And they were all scattered throughout the regions of Judea and Samaria, except the apostles. The scattering fulfils Jesus’ plan in 1:8: Judea and Samaria. The church had not left Jerusalem by choice; God used persecution to push them out. The word for scattered (diesparēsan) is a sowing word: seed thrown across a field. And then a detail that has long puzzled readers: except the apostles. The twelve men most obviously identified with the movement, already arrested twice and flogged once, stayed in the city everybody else was fleeing. Whatever else that was, it was not caution. Perhaps they judged that the shepherds should not be the first out of the field, or that Jerusalem had to keep a centre; Luke does not explain. What he makes clear three verses later is the consequence: the people who took the gospel to Samaria were not the apostles. They were the ordinary members who ran.

Devout men buried Stephen and made great lamentation over him. The burial is braver than it looks. Jewish practice held that public mourning was not observed for a man executed by the court; part of the punishment was that his family grieved in silence and he went into the ground without honour. These men did the opposite, loudly, in a city where a persecution had begun that morning and where being associated with Stephen was demonstrably dangerous. They gave a convicted blasphemer a funeral and made sure it was heard. Luke’s word for them is the one he used of old Simeon in the temple and of the pilgrims at Pentecost (Luke 2:25; Acts 2:5). They may have been believers, or devout Jews who had heard the speech or known the man and would not let him be shovelled away. Either way, somebody with something to lose stood at that grave and wept aloud on purpose.

Grief is not a lapse. That is worth taking, because Christians are frequently given the impression that grief is a failure: that a believer with a firm grasp of the resurrection should be able to bury somebody without much noise. The first Christian response to the first Christian martyrdom was a great lamentation. Paul’s instruction to a grieving church is not that they should not grieve but that they should not grieve as others do who have no hope (1 Thessalonians 4:13), which assumes the grief and changes its quality. Stephen had seen heaven opened moments before he died, and they still stood over the body and wept loudly, and Luke records it without a word of correction. Jesus himself wept at a graveside he was about to empty (John 11:35).

Why does God allow his church to be persecuted? Scripture gives us part of the answer, though not all of it. Persecution purifies the church, as fire refines gold (1 Peter 1:6–7). It joins us to Christ, who was persecuted first (John 15:20; Philippians 3:10). And, as here, God uses it to spread the gospel: the seed is scattered and grows in new fields. The church historian’s old saying, that the blood of the martyrs is seed, began in this verse. None of that makes persecution good, and we should pray for persecuted believers and work for their relief (Hebrews 13:3). But it means that no persecution is outside God’s purpose or beyond his power to turn to good.

In a sentence. Saul approved of Stephen’s killing, and that day a great persecution broke out against the church in Jerusalem, scattering everyone except the apostles through Judea and Samaria, while devout men buried Stephen and mourned him deeply.

On a Tuesday. God can use what looks like disaster to spread his word. Trust him in your scattering: the move you did not want, the job you lost, the church that broke up. And when someone you love dies, grieve honestly. Hope does not forbid tears; it gives them a future.

For worship. The God of this chapter turns a grave into a seed-bed and a persecution into a mission. What Saul meant for the destruction of the church, God meant for the salvation of Samaria and Ethiopia. Praise the Lord of the harvest, who scatters his people only to sow them, and who will one day wipe every tear shed over his martyrs.
verseByVerse.note: The scattering fulfils Jesus’ plan in 1:8: Judea and Samaria come next.

verseByVerse.quote: But Saul was ravaging the church, and entering house after house, he dragged off men and women and committed them to prison.
verseByVerse.commentary:
But Saul was ravaging the church, and entering house after house, he dragged off men and women and committed them to prison.

But Saul was ravaging the church. Luke picks a violent word, and he picks it deliberately. Ravaging (elymaineto) is the word the Greek psalm uses of a wild boar getting into a vineyard and wrecking it (Psalm 80:13): an animal in an orchard, tearing at roots, ruining in an afternoon what took years to grow. Luke had a perfectly good word available for official persecution. He used this one instead. Saul later admitted it all (22:4; 26:10–11; Galatians 1:13; 1 Timothy 1:13).

And entering house after house. There were no church buildings; the church met in people’s homes, ate in them, broke bread in them. So persecuting the church meant going through front doors. Someone had to compile the list of addresses, and somebody in the neighbourhood had to supply it. The scene is domestic and squalid: men coming into a kitchen where a family has been praying, and taking people out of it.

He dragged off men and women and committed them to prison. Women too; he spared no one. Luke says it, and Paul confirms it twice in his own words later: he persecuted this Way to the death, binding and delivering to prison both men and women (22:4), and he locked up many of the saints and cast his vote against them when they were put to death (26:10). He does not soften it in the retelling. In one of his letters he calls himself, without qualification, a blasphemer, persecutor and insolent opponent (1 Timothy 1:13). Dragged off is the word Luke will later use of Paul himself being dragged out of a city and left for dead (14:19), a small piece of irony he leaves the reader to find.

The man who wrote about love. Here is the thing about this verse that ought to arrest anybody: it is written about the man who wrote that love is patient and kind, that it does not insist on its own way, that it bears all things (1 Corinthians 13:4–7). There is no way to read the New Testament without holding these two facts together. The most tender pastoral writing in the Bible came from a man who had gone door to door arresting mothers.

Grace did not give him amnesia. He never got over it, and that is the point rather than a biographical curiosity. Thirty years on he is still saying he is the foremost of sinners, in the present tense (1 Timothy 1:15), and still saying he is unworthy to be called an apostle because he persecuted the church of God (1 Corinthians 15:9). Grace did not erase his memory. It gave him a permanent, accurate, unbearable memory that he carried without despair, which is a far more remarkable thing than forgetting.

Not a guarantee. One guard, because this passage is often preached as though it were a promise. It is not a guarantee that the persecutor in your life will be converted. Most of the men who arrested Christians in the first century died as they had lived, and the same is true in every century since. What it is, is a demonstration that nobody is disqualified by the record, which is a different and better thing to know, and which is what Paul himself says it was given for: that in me, as the foremost, Jesus Christ might display his perfect patience as an example to those who were to believe (1 Timothy 1:16).

How should I pray for those who persecute Christians today? As Jesus told us: love your enemies and pray for those who persecute you (Matthew 5:44). Pray for their conversion, by name if you know them, remembering Saul. Pray that God would restrain their violence and protect his people (4:29–30). Pray for justice, for governments to protect religious freedom, and for persecuted believers to stand firm and be comforted. It is not wrong to ask God to stop evil men, as the psalmists did. But let the first prayer be Stephen’s: Lord, do not hold this sin against them. God has answered that prayer before.

In a sentence. But Saul was trying to destroy the church, going from house to house, dragging off men and women and putting them in prison.

On a Tuesday. Think of the person in public life or in your own life whom you find hardest to imagine as a Christian, perhaps someone hostile to the faith. Pray for them today, as for a future brother.

For worship. The worst persecutor of the church became its greatest apostle. The Lord Jesus, who was being ravaged in his people (9:4), was already preparing to meet the ravager on the road.
