Praise the Saviour whose patience outlasts the cruelty of his enemies, and whose grace is greater than the worst record any sinner can bring.

verseByVerse.quote: Now those who were scattered went about preaching the word. Philip went down to the city of Samaria and proclaimed to them the Christ.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Now those who were scattered went about preaching the word. Philip went down to the city of Samaria and proclaimed to them the Christ.

Now those who were scattered went about preaching the word. The most important word in verse 4 is the one carried over from verse 1. Those who were scattered: and we have just been told that everybody was scattered except the apostles. So the people now preaching across two provinces are precisely the ones with no office, no ordination, no training and no commission to do it. Not the apostles, but ordinary believers. The twelve stayed in Jerusalem. The gospel went to Samaria carried by refugees. The scattering became sowing.

The ordinary word. And the verb Luke chooses (euangelizomenoi) is not the formal one for public proclamation. It is the ordinary word for telling good news. What these men and women did was not preach in the sense of standing up before a congregation. They arrived in strange towns with whatever they could carry, and when people asked why they had left Jerusalem, they told them. The first missionary expansion in the history of the church was carried out entirely by amateurs, under duress, with no strategy, because they had been driven out of their homes and could not stop talking about the reason. Every believer a witness.

Philip went down to the city of Samaria. And note who he is. This Philip is one of the seven (6:5), not the apostle: one of the men appointed two chapters ago to make sure the widows were fed. Stephen, another of the seven, has just preached the longest sermon in the book and been killed for it. Whatever the table-servants were supposed to be doing, it is the table-servants who are breaking the boundaries in this book while the apostles hold the centre.

A feud five centuries old. The boundary he breaks is not a small one. Samaria was not simply an unevangelised region; it was the object of a feud five centuries old. After Assyria deported the northern tribes, it resettled the territory with foreign peoples, and the mixed population that resulted claimed the God of Israel, kept only the five books of Moses, and worshipped at a rival temple on Mount Gerizim (2 Kings 17:24–41). About a hundred and fifty years before this, a Jewish army marched north and pulled that temple down. The wound was still open in Jesus’ day, which is why John’s Gospel has to explain that Jews have no dealings with Samaritans (John 4:9), and why a crowd in Jerusalem thought calling a man a Samaritan a serious insult (John 8:48). For a Jewish believer to preach Christ there was a breakthrough.

And proclaimed to them the Christ. Philip walks into that, and he preaches a person. He does not open with an argument about the temple, or about which mountain was the right one, or about whose copy of the law was correct, all of which were live and available. The Samaritans expected a Messiah too, the restorer (John 4:25), and Philip tells them he has come. The quarrel that five hundred years of argument had not settled was left where it was, and something was announced that made it irrelevant.

Am I meant to share my faith if I am not a pastor? Yes. The people in this verse had no office at all, and they spread the gospel across two provinces. Pastors are called to preach and teach publicly, and that is a particular calling (Ephesians 4:11). But every Christian is a witness to what Christ has done, and every Christian can tell someone why he believes. You do not need to preach a sermon. You need to be ready to give a reason for your hope when asked, gently and respectfully (1 Peter 3:15), to invite people to hear the word, and to speak naturally of Christ in the places where life has put you. The gospel has always travelled furthest in ordinary conversations.

In a sentence. Those who had been scattered went about telling the good news of the word, and Philip went down to the city of Samaria and proclaimed the Christ to them.

On a Tuesday. Wherever life scatters you, take the gospel with you. When someone this week asks about your weekend, your values or your hope, tell them honestly, and let Christ be in the answer.

For worship. The Lord Jesus once sat by a well in Samaria and offered living water to a Samaritan woman (John 4). Now his scattered people carry the same water into the same country. He is the Saviour of the world, not of one nation only. Praise the Christ who breaks down every ancient wall of hatred, and who sends ordinary believers to tell his name wherever they are driven.
verseByVerse.note: This Philip is one of the seven, not the apostle. Samaritans were a mixed people despised by Jews; they also expected a coming deliverer.

parallels.desc: Philip the evangelist

verseByVerse.quote: And the crowds with one accord paid attention to what was being said by Philip, when they heard him and saw the signs that he did. For unclean spirits, crying out with a loud voice, came out of many who had them, and many who were paralyzed or lame were healed.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And the crowds with one accord paid attention to what was being said by Philip, when they heard him and saw the signs that he did. For unclean spirits, crying out with a loud voice, came out of many who had them, and many who were paralyzed or lame were healed.

And the crowds with one accord paid attention to what was being said by Philip, when they heard him and saw the signs that he did. With one accord: the phrase Luke used of the hundred and twenty waiting in the upper room (1:14). He now uses it of a crowd of Samaritans, which for a first-century Jewish reader is a small shock, deliberately given. And what he says they did with one accord is worth noticing, because it is not what people usually remember about this passage. They paid attention to what was being said. The signs are in the sentence, and they are in second place. The miracles got him a hearing. What the crowd gave its attention to was the message. Word and signs went together, confirming each other.

For unclean spirits, crying out with a loud voice, came out of many who had them. As in Jesus’ ministry (Mark 1:26). Luke lists the signs in a way that ties Samaria to Jerusalem on purpose: unclean spirits coming out, and the paralysed and the lame healed. It is precisely the list from the earlier chapters, now in a despised half-Jewish city, through a man appointed to hand out bread. There is no reduced edition of the kingdom for people on the wrong side of a border. On what unclean spirits are, see on 5:15–16. Here the point is simply that the same authority that marked the kingdom’s arrival in Jerusalem now appears in Samaria. At the preaching of Christ the unclean spirits cry out and come out.

And many who were paralyzed or lame were healed. The kingdom’s power at work. And notice which conditions he names. Paralysis and lameness are not ailments a man recovers from quietly. They are chronic, visible and permanent, and in a town of that size everybody knew who was carried where. Luke has already shown, at the Beautiful Gate, what happens when God heals the one person whose condition the whole neighbourhood can verify: it becomes an argument nobody can answer (3:1–10; 4:16).

Many, not all. One small honesty in the wording belongs to anybody who has prayed a long time and not been healed. Luke writes that unclean spirits came out of many, and that many were healed. Even in a chapter of undisputed power, at the height of an outpouring, with a Spirit-filled messenger in the town, Luke reaches for a word that may leave somebody still on the mat. He does not explain it and he does not hide it.

Philip was not an apostle, so why could he do signs? Like Stephen, he was one of the seven on whom the apostles had laid their hands (6:6), and his signs belong to the same founding ministry. Even so, the Samaritans received the Spirit only when the apostles came (vv. 14–17), which shows how closely these gifts were tied to the apostles. On the cessationist reading, held charitably, such sign gifts belonged to the foundation age and are not a standing pattern for today (see on 5:12). God still heals in answer to prayer; what has ceased is the apostolic sign gift attesting new revelation.

Why does God not heal everyone I pray for? Scripture does not give us a full explanation, and we should beware of anyone who claims to. It is not because your faith was too small; Paul prayed three times for his own thorn to be removed, and God said no, my grace is sufficient for you (2 Corinthians 12:7–9), and Paul left Trophimus ill at Miletus (2 Timothy 4:20). God heals some now as a foretaste of the new creation, and he will heal all his people in the resurrection, when there will be no more pain (Revelation 21:4). Until then, keep praying, use the means he gives, and trust that his no is never a lack of love.

In a sentence. The crowds all listened intently to what Philip said as they heard him and saw the signs he did, for unclean spirits came out of many with loud cries, and many who were paralysed or lame were healed.

On a Tuesday. When you pray for the sick this week, pray boldly and leave the answer with God. And notice what grips you most in church: the remarkable things that happen, or the message about Christ. Give your attention, as the Samaritans did, to what is being said.

For worship. Christ’s power over demons and disease was shown in Samaria, and his kingdom has come. The paralysed walked in the city that Jerusalem despised, and the unclean spirits fled before the name of Jesus. Praise the King whose kingdom knows no borders, whose word is the true wonder, and who will one day raise every one of his people whole.

verseByVerse.quote: So there was much joy in that city. But there was a man named Simon, who had previously practiced magic in the city and amazed the people of Samaria, saying that he himself was somebody great.
verseByVerse.commentary:
So there was much joy in that city. But there was a man named Simon, who had previously practiced magic in the city and amazed the people of Samaria, saying that he himself was somebody great.

So there was much joy in that city. One of Luke’s markers, and he uses it carefully. Joy in a city, not merely in individuals: something had changed in the public atmosphere of the place. The gospel brings joy (v. 39; 13:52; 16:34). He will use the same note at the end of this chapter of a single man on a desert road, and the two are the same fact at different scales.

But there was a man named Simon, who had previously practiced magic in the city. Then, without a paragraph break, Luke introduces the man who will spend the rest of the section showing what the gospel is not. It is worth being clear about what magic (mageuōn) meant in that world, because the modern word has gone soft. This was not entertainment, and nobody thought it was conjuring. A practitioner claimed genuine access to powers, and people paid him for results: a curse laid on a rival, a charm against illness, a name to invoke to make something happen. Written spells survive from the period, and they are long lists of divine names collected from every religion available, on the principle that one of them might work. The man who could operate that machinery was feared, consulted and rich, and he was the nearest thing that city had to a public authority. Later Christian writers regarded this Simon, often called Simon Magus, as the father of heresies, especially of Gnosticism, and Justin Martyr, himself a Samaritan, wrote that the Samaritans honoured him as the first god.

And amazed the people of Samaria, saying that he himself was somebody great. Luke’s summary of Simon’s message is devastating. That is the entire content. Not a doctrine, not a God, not a promise: a claim about the speaker. Everything Simon offered was ultimately about Simon. Compare Philip, who proclaimed Christ.

The test of a ministry. The collision Luke is setting up is not between power and no power. Philip has just been casting out unclean spirits and healing paralytics. The difference is what the power is pointing at. Simon amazed people, and they concluded that Simon was great. Philip did signs, and the crowds paid attention to what was being said: they ended up listening to a message about somebody else entirely. That test survives translation into any century. It is not whether remarkable things happen around a person. It is what the people who watch end up attached to. If a ministry produces crowds who are knowledgeable about the minister, something has gone wrong that no amount of orthodoxy in the statement of faith will correct.

Is magic real, and is it harmless to dabble? Scripture treats sorcery and the occult as real and as forbidden, not as harmless fun (Deuteronomy 18:10–12; Galatians 5:20). Some of it is trickery and some of it may involve real spiritual powers, and both are dangerous: the one deceives, the other enslaves. So a Christian should have nothing to do with fortune-telling, séances, spells, tarot or any attempt to gain hidden knowledge or power apart from God. If you have been involved, confess it, renounce it, get rid of the objects, as the Ephesians burned their magic books (19:19), and rest in Christ, who has disarmed every power (Colossians 2:15). You do not need to be afraid. You need to be finished with it.

In a sentence. There was great joy in that city, but a man named Simon had been practising magic there, amazing the people of Samaria and claiming to be someone great.

On a Tuesday. Beware of spiritual leaders who proclaim themselves; true servants proclaim Christ. And check your own speaking about your faith: when you talk about what God has done in your life, who comes out of the story looking great?

For worship. Joy filled a Samaritan city because Christ had come to it, and no magician’s wonder had ever produced that. The Lord Jesus does not need to say he is somebody great; he is the great God and Saviour (Titus 2:13), and he made himself nothing for our sake. Praise the humble King whose greatness is shown in his service, and whose name brings joy wherever it is proclaimed.
verseByVerse.note: Later Christian writers regarded this Simon (often called Simon Magus) as an early false teacher; from his name comes “simony,” the buying of church office.

verseByVerse.quote: They all paid attention to him, from the least to the greatest, saying, "This man is the power of God that is called Great." And they paid attention to him because for a long time he had amazed them with his magic.
verseByVerse.commentary:
They all paid attention to him, from the least to the greatest, saying, “This man is the power of God that is called Great.” And they paid attention to him because for a long time he had amazed them with his magic.

They all paid attention to him, from the least to the greatest. Luke means the whole social range: the labourer and the magistrate, the woman at the well and the man who owned the well. Simon’s hold on that city was not confined to the credulous poor, which is the comforting assumption people make about this kind of thing. It reached the top. His influence was enormous.

This man is the power of God that is called Great. They had a formula for him. It is an odd, half-technical phrase, and it tells you that Simon had not merely impressed people; he had supplied them with a theology. They thought he was a divine power, an emanation of God, as pagan religion often spoke of divine powers. There was a doctrine about him in circulation, with a title in it. He was not a street performer with a following. He was an established religious institution with a creed. Simon was worshipped.

And they paid attention to him because for a long time he had amazed them with his magic. Then Luke gives the mechanism, and it is the most useful sentence in the paragraph. Two ingredients, and neither is truth. Amazement: the experience of watching something you cannot account for. And a long time: the sheer weight of years, during which nobody produced a better explanation and everybody grew up with this one. Put those together and you have the anatomy of most religious authority that is not from God. It does not require anybody to be persuaded of anything. It only requires that nobody can explain what is happening, and that this goes on long enough to become normal.

How was anyone to tell the difference? That raises the question a reader is entitled to ask, since Philip’s ministry looks, from outside, remarkably similar: crowds, signs, amazement. Luke answers it in the next verse, and the answer is not about the phenomena. When they believed Philip as he preached good news about the kingdom of God and the name of Jesus Christ. Simon offered an experience and a claim about himself; Philip offered a message about a King, and people believed it. The signs got him a hearing. The content held them, and the content was somebody else’s name. Signs alone do not prove truth; the message must be tested (Deuteronomy 13:1–3).

Not a reason for cynicism. A guard on the other side is needed too, because it is easy to leave this passage as a cynic. The lesson is not that anything remarkable is suspect and the safest ministry is the one where nothing ever happens. Luke has just described genuine healings and genuine deliverances with evident approval, and the joy in that city was real. The test is not whether power is present. It is whose name is left standing at the end of the meeting.

Can Satan really do miracles? Scripture warns that he can produce counterfeit signs and wonders (2 Thessalonians 2:9; Revelation 13:13; Matthew 24:24), though his power is limited and always under God’s control (Job 1:12). That is why a miracle is never enough by itself to prove a message true. Moses told Israel that if a prophet gave a sign that came to pass but led them to other gods, they were not to listen (Deuteronomy 13:1–3). So the question to ask of any wonder is not merely whether something happened, but what it is being used to teach, and whether it leads you to the Christ of Scripture.

In a sentence. Everyone from the least to the greatest followed him, calling him the power of God that is called Great, because for a long time he had amazed them with his magic.

On a Tuesday. Not every wonder is from God, and not every long-standing religious habit is true. Test what you hear, from any pulpit, book or screen, by the plain message of Christ and his word.

For worship. The true power of God is not a magician in Samaria but the crucified Christ, who is the power of God and the wisdom of God (1 Corinthians 1:24). His power is shown supremely in weakness, at a cross, and in an empty tomb. Praise the Lord whose power is truth and love, who sets free those whom counterfeits had held for a long time.

verseByVerse.quote: But when they believed Philip as he preached good news about the kingdom of God and the name of Jesus Christ, they were baptized, both men and women. Even Simon himself believed, and after being baptized he continued with Philip. And seeing signs and great miracles performed, he was amazed.
verseByVerse.commentary:
But when they believed Philip as he preached good news about the kingdom of God and the name of Jesus Christ, they were baptized, both men and women. Even Simon himself believed, and after being baptized he continued with Philip. And seeing signs and great miracles performed, he was amazed.

But when they believed Philip as he preached good news about the kingdom of God and the name of Jesus Christ. Watch what displaces Simon, because it is not a stronger performance. A city held for years by amazement is released by a message. The gospel content is given in two phrases: the kingdom of God, and the name of Jesus Christ. The kingdom has come in Jesus.

What is it to preach the kingdom of God? The kingdom is God’s saving reign, his kingly rule breaking in through Jesus the Messiah to rescue and to rule. Notice that Philip preached the kingdom of God and the name of Jesus Christ in one breath: you cannot proclaim the kingdom without the King. To preach it is to announce that God’s long-promised reign has arrived in Christ, who died, rose and reigns, and to call people to repent, believe and bow to him as Lord, entering his kingdom now and for ever (28:31). Why is the phrase on nearly every page of Matthew, Mark and Luke, and rare in John and the letters? Not because the truth fades, but because the vocabulary shifts. Jesus preached the kingdom to Jewish hearers, steeped in Israel’s hope (Matthew 4:17; Daniel 7:13–14). John says the same thing with a different word, eternal life (John 3:3, 5). The apostles, writing after the resurrection, put the focus on the reigning King: Jesus is Lord (Romans 10:9). Same kingdom throughout.

They were baptized, both men and women. Believers’ baptism: they believed, then were baptised. And both men and women: Luke keeps saying this, the phrase he used of the Jerusalem church and, grimly, of Saul’s arrests nine verses earlier. In a world where a woman’s religious standing generally travelled through her husband, Luke records the women being baptised on their own account, on their own faith.

Even Simon himself believed, and after being baptized he continued with Philip. And then Simon. Luke states it without qualification: he believed, he was baptised, he attached himself to the preacher. Nothing in the sentence is flagged as false, and a reading which has Simon play-acting from the start is reading something Luke has not written. But in what sense did he believe? The rest of the story shows his faith was not saving: Peter says his heart was not right with God and he was still bound by sin (vv. 21–23). Like those in Jerusalem who believed when they saw the signs, to whom Jesus did not entrust himself (John 2:23–25), or the seed on rocky ground that believes for a while (Luke 8:13), he believed something, for a time, without new birth. Baptism did not make him a Christian.

And seeing signs and great miracles performed, he was amazed. The last clause does careful work. Amazement is the word that has followed Simon through this whole passage: he amazed the Samaritans, they were amazed by him, and now he is the one amazed. The amazer is amazed. He has changed places in the sentence without changing his interest. What held him before is what holds him now: something remarkable is happening, and he cannot account for it. He was drawn by power, not by Christ. Five verses later he will try to buy it.

Was Simon truly saved? Luke says he believed and was baptised, and some take him as a true believer who fell into serious sin. But Peter’s words say his heart was not right before God, that he was in the gall of bitterness and the bond of iniquity, and that he had neither part nor lot in this matter (vv. 20–23). The more likely reading is that his faith was the kind that is impressed by miracles but has never turned from self. That fits what Scripture teaches about perseverance: those whom God truly saves, he keeps, and those who finally fall away show that they were never truly his (1 John 2:19).

Can I be baptised and still not be a Christian? Yes, sadly; Simon was. Baptism is the sign of union with Christ, commanded by him, and believers should be baptised. But the water does not save. What saves is Christ himself, received by true faith, which the Spirit works in the heart (Ephesians 2:8–9). So the question is not, was I baptised, but, do I trust Christ, love him, and want to turn from my sin? If you find those things in yourself, however weakly, they are the marks of the new birth. If you do not, do not rely on your baptism. Come to Christ today.

In a sentence. When the people believed Philip as he preached the good news about the kingdom of God and the name of Jesus Christ, both men and women were baptised, and even Simon believed, was baptised, stayed close to Philip, and was amazed by the signs and great miracles.

On a Tuesday. Being baptised and amazed by God’s power is not the same as being born again. Make sure your faith is in Christ himself. Ask yourself one honest question this week: what draws me to church, what God gives, or God himself?

For worship. The kingdom of God has come in the name of Jesus Christ, and that name sets free a city that a magician had held for years. He is the King who welcomes men and women alike into his kingdom by faith, and who knows those who are truly his (2 Timothy 2:19). Praise the Lord Jesus, whose kingdom is entered not by amazement but by trust, and who never loses one whom he has truly made his own.

verseByVerse.quote: Now when the apostles at Jerusalem heard that Samaria had received the word of God, they sent to them Peter and John, who came down and prayed for them that they might receive the Holy Spirit,
verseByVerse.commentary:
Now when the apostles at Jerusalem heard that Samaria had received the word of God, they sent to them Peter and John, who came down and prayed for them that they might receive the Holy Spirit,

Now when the apostles at Jerusalem heard that Samaria had received the word of God, they sent to them Peter and John. News of a breakthrough travels, and the sentence Luke writes is remarkable for what is not in it. There is no debate recorded, no committee, no objection, no summons for Philip to explain himself. A city of Samaritans has believed, and the response is to send two men down to pray for them. The apostles had every reason to be uneasy. Nobody had authorised this. Philip was not an apostle and had been appointed to a food distribution. The people involved were Samaritans, on the far side of a quarrel with five centuries and a demolished temple in it. Any institution presented with an unauthorised expansion into disputed territory has a standard set of reflexes, and Luke records none of them.

Peter and John. Then the names, and they are the best thing in the verse. John. Luke’s own Gospel records that when a Samaritan village refused Jesus hospitality, James and John asked whether they should call down fire from heaven to consume them, and were rebuked (Luke 9:52–55). Now the same man walks down the same road into the same territory, and his errand is to put his hands on Samaritans and ask God to give them the Holy Spirit. Nobody in the narrative comments on it. Luke simply puts the name in, having written the other story himself, and leaves it for anyone paying attention. What the Spirit had done to John in the intervening years is described nowhere. It is visible only in the fact that he made the journey. Grace changes men.

Who came down and prayed for them that they might receive the Holy Spirit. Note what they came to do. Not to inspect, not to regularise, not to take charge of somebody else’s work. Prayer is the first thing. The two senior apostles arrive at a revival they had no part in starting, and their first act is to ask God to give those people more.

How can I lose a prejudice I have had all my life? Probably not by arguing yourself out of it in an afternoon. John’s instinct about Samaritans was to incinerate them. The instinct was not argued away. It was replaced, slowly enough that nobody recorded the process, by walking with Jesus. So bring the prejudice to Christ honestly, as sin. Pray for the people you find it hardest to love. Get to know some of them as people, especially fellow believers from that group. Serve them. And remember that Christ died for them as he died for you, and that they will share heaven with you (Revelation 7:9). Feelings follow faithfulness, and the Spirit who changed John can change you.

In a sentence. When the apostles in Jerusalem heard that Samaria had received the word of God, they sent Peter and John, who went down and prayed for them that they might receive the Holy Spirit.

On a Tuesday. Think of a group of people toward whom you carry a settled contempt: a nation, a class, a political tribe, a kind of Christian. Pray for them by name this week, and ask God to replace the reflex with love.

For worship. The disciple who wanted to burn a Samaritan village came to bless one, and it was the Lord Jesus who changed him. The Son of Man came not to destroy people’s lives but to save them (Luke 9:56, in some manuscripts). Praise the Christ who turns sons of thunder into apostles of love, and who makes former enemies pray for one another to receive his Spirit.
verseByVerse.note: John had once wanted to call down fire on a Samaritan village.

verseByVerse.quote: for he had not yet fallen on any of them, but they had only been baptized in the name of the Lord Jesus. Then they laid their hands on them and they received the Holy Spirit.
verseByVerse.commentary:
for he had not yet fallen on any of them, but they had only been baptized in the name of the Lord Jesus. Then they laid their hands on them and they received the Holy Spirit.

For he had not yet fallen on any of them, but they had only been baptized in the name of the Lord Jesus. Luke states the anomaly flatly and does not soften it. These people had believed. They had been baptised; their baptism was real. And the Spirit had not come. He knows how strange that is, which is why he stops the narrative to say so. Everywhere else in this book the order runs differently, or all at once. Normally the Spirit comes with faith (2:38). In chapter 10 the Spirit interrupts Peter mid-sentence, before anybody has been baptised at all (10:44). Here there is a gap: people who truly believed in the Lord Jesus and were truly baptised went about their business for a time without what believers elsewhere in this book receive at once. Why the delay?

Then they laid their hands on them and they received the Holy Spirit. The answer that best fits Luke’s own narrative is that this was a hinge in the history of salvation rather than a pattern for individuals. After centuries of hatred and rival temples, there was a real danger of two churches: a Jewish one and a Samaritan one. God held back the Spirit until the apostles came, so that the Samaritans received the Spirit through Jewish apostles, and the church remained one. Five hundred years of schism were repaired in public, by two Jewish pairs of hands on Samaritan heads. Something visible probably happened, since Simon saw it (v. 18).

The great crossings. The pattern across Acts supports this. As the gospel crossed each great barrier, God marked the crossing with a visible coming of the Spirit: on Jews at Pentecost (chapter 2), on Samaritans here, on Gentiles in Cornelius’s house (chapter 10), and on the disciples of John at Ephesus (chapter 19). Each was a once-for-all moment in the spread of the one church to all peoples, as Jesus had mapped it: Jerusalem, Judea, Samaria, the end of the earth (1:8).

Where Christians differ: a second blessing, or a sacrament? Pentecostal and charismatic brothers often see here a two-stage pattern: conversion, then a distinct baptism in the Spirit, and they read Acts 19 the same way. Roman Catholics and others see the basis for confirmation, a sacrament in which a bishop’s hands confer the Spirit. Verdict: this was a unique moment in salvation history, as the gospel crossed a great barrier, like the Gentiles in chapter 10 and John’s disciples in chapter 19. It was a once-for-all bridging, not the normal pattern. Romans 8:9 says anyone who does not have the Spirit of Christ does not belong to him. Every believer receives the Spirit at conversion, without a second stage or an apostle’s hands. This is said with real respect for brothers who differ, many of whom love the Spirit and the Scriptures deeply.

The apostles’ hands. The same reading explains why no one today should claim to give the Spirit by laying on hands. The gift came through the apostles because it was the apostles’ foundational work to join each new people into the one church (Ephesians 2:20). That role was not passed on. On the cessationist reading, held charitably, the visible signs that accompanied these moments, very likely tongues or prophetic praise as in chapters 2, 10 and 19, belonged to the foundation age and are not a pattern to seek now (see on 5:12). The regular doctrine of how we receive the Spirit is taught in the letters: when you believed, you were sealed with the promised Holy Spirit (Ephesians 1:13; Galatians 3:2).

Do I need a second experience of the Spirit? No. If you belong to Christ, you already have the Spirit, all of him, from the moment you believed (Romans 8:9; 1 Corinthians 12:13). You are not a half-Christian waiting for a second gift. What you do need, every day, is to walk by the Spirit and be filled with the Spirit (Galatians 5:16; Ephesians 5:18): to yield more of yourself to the one who already lives in you. Many believers have seasons when God makes his presence and love unusually vivid, and those are precious gifts. But they are fresh fillings of the Spirit you have, not the arrival of a Spirit you lacked.

Should I seek to speak in tongues as proof that I have the Spirit? No. Even in the apostolic church, Paul asked, do all speak with tongues? and expected the answer no (1 Corinthians 12:30). The proof of the Spirit’s presence is that you confess Jesus as Lord, cry to God as Father, and bear the Spirit’s fruit (1 Corinthians 12:3; Romans 8:15; Galatians 5:22–23). Many Reformed Christians believe the gift of tongues ceased with the apostolic age; continuationist brothers disagree, and we hold our view charitably. But on any view, no believer should be told that he lacks the Spirit because he has not spoken in tongues.

In a sentence. The Spirit had not yet come upon any of them, for they had only been baptised in the name of the Lord Jesus; then the apostles laid their hands on them, and they received the Holy Spirit.

On a Tuesday. God keeps his church one. Work for the unity of believers across old hostilities: the church down the road with a different style, the Christians of another nation or background. Pray for them this week, and if you can, worship with them once.

For worship. The Spirit came to Samaria through Jewish hands, and two peoples who had hated each other for five hundred years became one body. That is what the Spirit of Christ does. There is one body and one Spirit, one Lord, one faith, one baptism (Ephesians 4:4–5). Praise the Holy Spirit, given to every believer, who binds Jew and Samaritan, Jew and Gentile, into one holy temple in the Lord.
verseByVerse.note: The apostles’ presence tied the Samaritan believers to the church in Jerusalem, with one Spirit in one church.

verseByVerse.quote: Now when Simon saw that the Spirit was given through the laying on of the apostles' hands, he offered them money, saying, "Give me this power also, so that anyone on whom I lay my hands may receive the Holy Spirit."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Now when Simon saw that the Spirit was given through the laying on of the apostles’ hands, he offered them money, saying, “Give me this power also, so that anyone on whom I lay my hands may receive the Holy Spirit.”

Now when Simon saw that the Spirit was given through the laying on of the apostles’ hands, he offered them money. Saw. Whatever happened when Peter and John laid hands on those Samaritans was visible from across the room: an outward effect, perhaps tongues or praise. Luke declines to say what it was, a restraint worth noticing in a writer normally happy to describe wind and fire and buildings shaking. Then the offer, which is the first attempt in Christian history to purchase a spiritual gift.

Give me this power also, so that anyone on whom I lay my hands may receive the Holy Spirit. Look carefully at what he asks for, because it is not what people generally assume. He does not ask to receive the Spirit. He asks for this power: the power to lay his own hands on somebody else and have the Spirit come. Not give me the Spirit, but give me the power to give the Spirit. He is not applying for a blessing. He is applying for a franchise. He wanted to be the dispenser, to be somebody great again (v. 9).

Doing business the only way he knew. What makes the scene so exact is that by the standards of Simon’s old profession the request is entirely reasonable, even courteous. That is precisely how the trade worked: names, formulas and techniques were commodities, bought from a practitioner at the going rate and then used on paying customers. A man who wanted a new capability approached the man who had it and made an offer, and everybody understood the arrangement. Simon is doing business the only way he has ever known, with a product he has just watched being demonstrated. What he has entirely failed to notice is that he has changed worlds. In the one he has walked into there is no going rate, because the thing on offer was never for sale, and the men holding it did not buy it either. Simon thinks the Spirit is a power to be bought and used. But the Spirit is God.

Simony. His name has been attached to the sin ever since. Simony, the buying and selling of church office and spiritual privilege, became one of the great scandals of the medieval church, with bishoprics going to the highest bidder and cathedrals financed by selling assurances about the next life. It took a Reformation to prise it loose, and it has never been a peculiarly Catholic disease; every tradition has since found its own way of putting a price on something God gives away.

The quieter modern shapes. The modern forms are quieter and harder to see, and the general shape is this: treating a relationship as a transaction. The giving that expects a return in blessing. The service undertaken with an eye on what it buys with God, or with the congregation. The prayer offered as a lever. In each case the assumption underneath is Simon’s: that there is a rate, and that a man who pays it is entitled to the result. It is not a stupid assumption. It is how nearly everything else in life works. It is simply not how this works, and Peter’s next sentence explains why not.

Is it wrong to pay ministers, or to give expecting God to bless me? Paying ministers is right: the labourer deserves his wages, and those who preach the gospel should get their living by the gospel (1 Timothy 5:18; 1 Corinthians 9:14). That is support for work, not a purchase of grace. And God does promise to bless generous giving (2 Corinthians 9:6–11). What is wrong is giving as a transaction to obtain spiritual power or material reward, the seed-faith teaching that a gift to a preacher will make God pay you back with money or healing. That is Simon’s error dressed up as faith. Give because God has given to you, freely and cheerfully, and leave the blessing to him.

In a sentence. When Simon saw that the Spirit was given through the apostles’ laying on of hands, he offered them money, asking them to give him this power too, so that anyone he laid hands on would receive the Holy Spirit.

On a Tuesday. Notice this week where you treat God as a vending machine: if I pray this, if I give this, if I serve here, then he owes me that. Repent of the bargain, and thank him instead for what he has given freely.

For worship. The Spirit is God, not a power to use. He blows where he wishes (John 3:8). He is given, not sold; he gives himself, and no one can buy or control him. Praise the Holy Spirit, the free gift of the Father and the Son, who cannot be purchased and will not be possessed, and who dwells in sinners purely by grace.

verseByVerse.quote: But Peter said to him, "May your silver perish with you, because you thought you could obtain the gift of God with money! You have neither part nor lot in this matter, for your heart is not right before God."
verseByVerse.commentary:
But Peter said to him, “May your silver perish with you, because you thought you could obtain the gift of God with money! You have neither part nor lot in this matter, for your heart is not right before God.

May your silver perish with you, because you thought you could obtain the gift of God with money! It is among the harshest things Peter says to anybody in the New Testament. Literally, your silver be with you to destruction. J. B. Phillips rendered it with deliberate bluntness: to hell with you and your money. Peter is horrified. But it is worth being clear what kind of sentence it is. He is not so much laying a curse as naming the direction the man is travelling: your money is going to destruction, and on present course you are going with it. Peter describes the trajectory because he wants it changed, which is what he tells him to do two verses later.

The gift of God. Then the reason, and it is the theology of the whole passage in one clause. The word is gift. It is the same word Peter used at Pentecost: repent and be baptised, and you will receive the gift of the Holy Spirit (2:38). The gift of God is free (Isaiah 55:1; Romans 6:23). And a gift is not a cheap kind of purchase; it is a different kind of thing altogether. The moment a price is paid, whatever changes hands has stopped being a gift, and the man who insisted on paying has not acquired it at a discount. He has destroyed it, and gone home with something else in his pocket. That is why the answer is so severe. Simon has proposed an arrangement under which grace would cease to be grace, and if it were available on those terms, nobody in that room would have had any, Peter included.

You have neither part nor lot in this matter. No share at all. The phrase echoes the law of Moses, where the Levite has no portion or inheritance when the land is divided (Deuteronomy 12:12). Peter is telling Simon that when the ground is measured out, his name is on none of it. He has no part in the gospel, nor in the Spirit.

For your heart is not right before God. Then the diagnosis, echoing Psalm 78:37: their heart was not steadfast toward him. Something in him does not run true. Outward faith, inward crookedness.

Simon believed and was baptised. Could that be me? Verse 13 said Simon believed and was baptised; verse 21 says he has no share in this at all. Scripture is not embarrassed by the category. It says the demons believe, and shudder (James 2:19). It records a crowd who believed when they saw the signs, to whom Jesus did not entrust himself, for he knew what was in man (John 2:23–25). And John, writing to a church that had watched people walk out, says they went out from us, but they were not of us (1 John 2:19). There is a kind of believing which is real as far as it goes and never goes as far as Christ. Simon is its portrait: gripped, impressed, attached to the preacher, and interested from first to last in what he could get. But the reader who finds this passage frightening, who has read verse 13 and thought, that could be me, is displaying the one symptom Simon never displays anywhere in this story. Simon is not worried about his heart. He is worried, as the next verses show, about what might happen to him. A man anxious about whether he truly loves Christ is asking a question that never entered Simon’s head, and the anxiety is itself evidence of an interest Simon did not have. God gives his children assurance through his promises, the inner witness of the Spirit, and the fruit of a changed life (Westminster 18.2).

In a sentence. Peter told him that his money could perish with him for thinking he could buy God’s gift, and that he had no part or share in this, for his heart was not right before God.

On a Tuesday. Grace cannot be bought. Do not try to purchase God’s favour with gifts or good works or religious effort. Receive it freely, and then live as one who has been given everything.

For worship. The gift of God is free because it was infinitely costly to the Giver. It was bought, but not with silver or gold: with the precious blood of Christ (1 Peter 1:18–19). He paid what no sinner could pay, so that the Spirit could be given for nothing to all who believe. Praise the God of all grace, whose gifts are beyond price and given without price.

parallels.desc: Gehazi takes silver for Elisha’s healing
give without pay

verseByVerse.quote: "Repent, therefore, of this wickedness of yours, and pray to the Lord that, if possible, the intent of your heart may be forgiven you. For I see that you are in the gall of bitterness and in the bond of iniquity."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Repent, therefore, of this wickedness of yours, and pray to the Lord that, if possible, the intent of your heart may be forgiven you. For I see that you are in the gall of bitterness and in the bond of iniquity.

Repent, therefore, of this wickedness of yours, and pray to the Lord. Everything about these verses depends on noticing that Peter, having said one of the severest things he ever says to anybody, immediately tells the man what to do about it. Even for Simon there is a call to repent. The door is not shut. The diagnosis was brutal and the prescription follows in the same breath, which is what distinguishes a rebuke from a dismissal. Most people manage one half or the other. Some will say the hard thing and leave the man standing in it. Others will not say the hard thing at all and will call the omission kindness. Peter does both inside two sentences, and the second is the reason for the first.

That, if possible, the intent of your heart may be forgiven you. The phrase that troubles readers. Read carelessly, it sounds as though Peter were unsure whether God would forgive a sin of this size, as though there were a limit somewhere and Simon might have found it. That is not what the sentence is doing, and the distinction matters enormously to anyone carrying something he is afraid is too large. The uncertainty does not attach to God’s willingness. It attaches to Simon. Peter has no way of knowing whether this man will actually turn, and he is honest about it rather than issuing a guarantee he is in no position to give. It is the difference between God may not forgive you and you may not repent, and every difficulty in the verse dissolves once that is seen. His sin was serious.

Pray to the Lord yourself. Notice what Peter tells him to do: pray to the Lord. Not, ask me to pray. The man who has just tried to buy access through an intermediary is told to go directly and ask for himself. In one sentence Peter refuses both the money and the role of broker.

For I see that you are in the gall of bitterness and in the bond of iniquity. The diagnosis is built from two Old Testament phrases, and both are physical. The gall of bitterness reaches back to Moses warning Israel about a root among them bearing poisonous and bitter fruit (Deuteronomy 29:18): a person who turns from God and spreads poison among God’s people, a thing growing underground and out of sight, which is exactly right for a man whose problem nobody could see until money was mentioned. The bond of iniquity is the language of chains, and it turns up in Isaiah in a passage about the fast God actually wants: to loose the bonds of wickedness and let the oppressed go free (Isaiah 58:6). Peter’s picture is of a man not merely doing wrong but tied up by it, still bound, not set free; not a believer who has slipped, but one who was never released. And what he prescribes is not effort but repentance and prayer, because a man in chains cannot untie himself.

Is there any sin too big to be forgiven? No sin is too big for the blood of Christ, which cleanses from all sin (1 John 1:7). Jesus does speak of blasphemy against the Holy Spirit as unforgivable (Mark 3:28–30), but that is the settled, hardened rejection of the Spirit’s witness to Christ, calling his work the devil’s, not a single terrible act a person regrets. Those who have committed it do not fear they have; they do not care. If you are troubled that your sin may be too great, that very trouble shows the Spirit is still at work in you. Do what Peter told Simon: repent, and pray to the Lord. Whoever comes to Christ, he will never cast out (John 6:37).

In a sentence. Peter told Simon to repent of his wickedness and pray to the Lord that, if possible, the intent of his heart might be forgiven, for he saw that Simon was full of bitter poison and chained by sin.

On a Tuesday. If someone needs to hear a hard truth from you, do not say it without also showing the way back. And if you have heard one, do not stand in it. Go straight to the Lord, yourself, today.

For worship. Christ came to break the bonds of iniquity. He was sent to proclaim liberty to the captives (Luke 4:18), and he does not send away those who come to him in chains. If you feel chained, call on him. Praise the Saviour who sets prisoners free, whose mercy is greater than the bitterest root, and who forgives all who truly turn to him.
verseByVerse.note: “Gall of bitterness” echoes Moses’ warning about a root bearing poisonous fruit.

verseByVerse.quote: And Simon answered, "Pray for me to the Lord, that nothing of what you have said may come upon me." Now when they had testified and spoken the word of the Lord, they returned to Jerusalem, preaching the gospel to many villages of the Samaritans.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And Simon answered, “Pray for me to the Lord, that nothing of what you have said may come upon me.” Now when they had testified and spoken the word of the Lord, they returned to Jerusalem, preaching the gospel to many villages of the Samaritans.

Pray for me to the Lord, that nothing of what you have said may come upon me. Simon answers, and the answer is a small masterpiece of missing the point. Two things are wrong with it, and both are quiet. The first is what he asks about. Peter had named a heart that was not straight, a bitterness growing underground, a bond of iniquity. Simon asks about the consequences: that nothing of what you have said may come upon me. He is not asking to be changed. He is asking not to be hit. He fears the consequences, not the sin. That is the difference between a man who is sorry and a man who is frightened, and the two make very similar noises. It is Pharaoh asking Moses to plead with the LORD to take away the frogs (Exodus 8:8).

Whom he asks. The second is whom he asks. Peter had told him to pray to the Lord himself. Simon’s reply is: you pray for me. He is still in his old trade, still assuming that the power belongs to the practitioner and that a layman’s best move is to hire the man who has it. He has been rebuked for treating the Spirit as a commodity, and his instinctive next move is to treat Peter as one.

Luke stops. And then Luke stops. We hear no more of Simon in Scripture. He does not repent and does not refuse to repent. He leaves the narrative on an unfinished sentence, under a question mark. The later church could not bear it and filled the gap enthusiastically; there is a considerable body of legend about Simon Magus, most of it lurid and none of it in Scripture. Luke leaves the man exactly where he found him: a serious warning delivered, a door held open, and no answer recorded. Partly, perhaps, because Luke did not know. But partly because a resolved ending would let the reader off. If Simon repents, the passage becomes a story about the long reach of grace and the reader relaxes. If Simon is damned, it becomes a story about a bad man and the reader relaxes in the other direction. Left where it is, the question stays open, and it was never really a question about Simon.

Now when they had testified and spoken the word of the Lord, they returned to Jerusalem, preaching the gospel to many villages of the Samaritans. Then verse 25, the loveliest note in the chapter. The apostles themselves now evangelise Samaritan villages. They had come down to see what was happening in one city. They went back seeding a whole region, on foot, village by village, having evidently decided that since they were walking that way anyway they might as well. The two men sent to look into a Samaritan revival went home having become part of it. That is what the errand did to them, and one of the two had once wanted the place burned to the ground. The barrier has fallen.

Is it wrong to ask others to pray for me? Not at all. Scripture tells us to pray for one another (James 5:16), and Paul constantly asked churches to pray for him (Romans 15:30; Ephesians 6:19). The problem with Simon was not that he asked for prayer but that he asked for it instead of repenting, and instead of going to God himself. Ask your friends to pray for you, and pray for them. But never let someone else’s prayers become a substitute for your own coming to Christ. No one can repent for you, and no one needs to stand between you and God: there is one mediator between God and men, the man Christ Jesus (1 Timothy 2:5).

In a sentence. Simon asked Peter to pray for him that none of these things would happen to him, and the apostles, having testified and spoken the word of the Lord, returned to Jerusalem, preaching the gospel in many Samaritan villages on the way.

On a Tuesday. Fear of consequences is not repentance. True repentance hates the sin itself. Next time you are sorry for something, ask yourself honestly: am I sorry I did it, or sorry about what it might cost me? Take the real thing to God.

For worship. The Lord who opened Samaria to the gospel did not stop at one city; he sent his apostles through many villages, because his heart is for the whole of a people he loves. Praise the Lord of the harvest, who leaves no village unvisited in his purpose, and who turned the road John once wanted to burn into a road strewn with the good news.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 26–40 — Philip and the Ethiopian Eunuch
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: An angel of the Lord told Philip to go south to the desert road that runs from Jerusalem down to Gaza. On the way he met an Ethiopian eunuch, a senior official in charge of all the treasury of the Kandake, queen of the Ethiopians. He had gone to Jerusalem to worship, and on his way home was sitting in his chariot reading the prophet Isaiah. The Spirit told Philip to go to that chariot and stay near it. Philip ran up, heard the man reading Isaiah and asked whether he understood it. He replied that he could not unless someone explained it, and invited Philip to sit with him. He was reading the passage about one led like a sheep to the slaughter, silent like a lamb before its shearer, humiliated and denied justice, whose life was taken from the earth. The eunuch asked whom the prophet meant, himself or someone else. Philip began with that very passage and told him the good news about Jesus. As they travelled they came to some water, and the eunuch asked what stood in the way of his being baptised. He ordered the chariot to stop, and both went down into the water and Philip baptised him. When they came up out of the water, the Spirit of the Lord suddenly took Philip away, and the eunuch did not see him again, but went on his way rejoicing. Philip appeared at Azotus and preached the gospel in all the towns until he reached Caesarea.
verseByVerse.theology:
Isaiah 53 and the Death of the Servant

Philip began with this Scripture and told him the good news about Jesus, and the Scripture was the last of Isaiah's Servant Songs. It is the passage in the Old Testament that comes nearest to explaining what a cross is for: the Servant is pierced for our transgressions and crushed for our iniquities, the chastisement that brought us peace was upon him, and with his wounds we are healed. Notice the grammar, because the Reformed tradition has always insisted that everything turns on it: the transgressions are ours, the wounds are his, and the exchange is the entire point. He is not merely an instance of innocent suffering, of which the world has always had an ample supply. He is a substitute — the guiltless one bearing what the guilty had coming, so that the guilty go free. That is what Philip preached from. And it is worth noticing that he did not have to argue his way to Christ across a long distance. He started at Isaiah 53 and the road was short.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: A man barred from the assembly by Deuteronomy 23:1 was reading a scroll which, three chapters past where he had it open, promised eunuchs a name in God's house better than sons and daughters. He was reading his own exclusion, and without knowing it his own invitation. Now: The people most certain the door is shut to them are usually the ones who know the rules best. It was not a careless man who needed telling that nothing prevented him. It was the man who had read the regulation and accepted it.

verseByVerse.quote: Now an angel of the Lord said to Philip, "Rise and go toward the south to the road that goes down from Jerusalem to Gaza." This is a desert place. And he rose and went. And there was an Ethiopian, a eunuch, a court official of Candace, queen of the Ethiopians, who was in charge of all her treasure. He had come to Jerusalem to worship
verseByVerse.commentary:
Now an angel of the Lord said to Philip, “Rise and go toward the south to the road that goes down from Jerusalem to Gaza.” This is a desert place. And he rose and went. And there was an Ethiopian, a eunuch, a court official of Candace, queen of the Ethiopians, who was in charge of all her treasure. He had come to Jerusalem to worship

Rise and go toward the south to the road that goes down from Jerusalem to Gaza. This is a desert place. Consider the timing. Philip is in the middle of the most fruitful work of his life: a whole city believing, joy in the streets, the two senior apostles arriving to see it. And an angel tells him to leave and go and stand on a road. From a city revival to a desert road; from crowds to one man. Luke adds a note a modern reader hurries past: this is a desert place. Gaza was the last town on the road to Egypt, and the road ran south-west through empty country. Philip is sent to a stretch of it with nothing on it: no town, no crowd, no synagogue, and no indication of how long he is to wait. He is not being sent to a mission field. He is being sent to a road.

And he rose and went. Five words, and there is not a question in them. Immediate obedience, without explanation. He does not ask what for, or for how long, or whether the Samaritan work will survive without him. Everything that follows depended on a man being willing to leave something that was going extremely well.

Why did God guide so directly then but not now? First, a correction: angelic appearances were never everyday, even in Scripture. They cluster at a few pivotal moments: the patriarchs, the exodus, the prophets here and there, the birth of Christ, the empty tomb, the launch of the church. Most godly saints never saw an angel. Acts is exactly such a turning point, the once-for-all launch of the gospel to Samaria, to Ethiopia, to Cornelius, to the end of the earth, and for that foundational breakout God used extraordinary steering: angels, visions, the Spirit speaking by name (10:3; 13:2; 16:9). Like the authenticating signs (see on 5:12), this belonged to the laying of the foundation (Ephesians 2:20). Today God guides by settled and sufficient means, and we are not less supplied but more: the completed Scripture, a lamp to my feet (Psalm 119:105), able to equip us for every good work (2 Timothy 3:16–17); the indwelling Spirit who illumines it; prayer, wisdom, godly counsel and providence. Scripture even warns against craving angelic encounters (Colossians 2:18; 2 Corinthians 11:14; Galatians 1:8). God has spoken to us by his Son (Hebrews 1:1–2), and to ask for an angel when we hold the word of the Son is to ask for something lesser. Two honest qualifications: angels are not idle, but remain ministering spirits sent to serve the heirs of salvation (Hebrews 1:14), often unseen; and no verse says outright that angels stopped speaking. That they no longer do so as our normal guidance is a fair inference from the foundational character of the Acts era and the sufficiency of Scripture, held charitably.

And there was an Ethiopian, a eunuch. Ethiopia here is the ancient kingdom of Cush, south of Egypt, in modern Sudan, with its capital at Meroë. To Greeks and Romans it was the end of the earth. A eunuch was, plainly, a man who had been castrated. In ancient royal courts such men were deliberately employed, above all to serve the king’s or queen’s household, since a man who could father no children posed no dynastic threat. Far from lowly, eunuchs often rose to the highest posts of trust. The word could also be a looser title for a high official; Potiphar is called a eunuch in the Greek though married (Genesis 39:1). Here, given his office, he is most likely a literal eunuch.

A court official of Candace, queen of the Ethiopians, who was in charge of all her treasure. Candace was a title, like Pharaoh, for the queen mother who ruled Meroë. And this man is her finance minister: powerful, wealthy, trusted with the treasury of a kingdom.

He had come to Jerusalem to worship. And here is the poignancy. Under the law, no one whose male organ is cut off shall enter the assembly of the LORD (Deuteronomy 23:1). A eunuch was, by his very body, barred from full membership in Israel’s worship, however earnestly he sought God. Here is a God-fearing Gentile who has travelled perhaps a thousand miles to worship the God of Israel, only to remain an outsider, probably barred from the inner courts, shut out at the door. Yet he is reading Isaiah, the very book in which God promised that the eunuch who holds fast his covenant would receive a name better than sons and daughters, an everlasting name that shall not be cut off (Isaiah 56:3–5). The gospel Philip is about to preach is that promise fulfilled: in Christ the excluded outsider is brought all the way in.

Why would God take Philip away from a revival to reach one man? Because God values the one as well as the crowd. The Good Shepherd leaves the ninety-nine to go after the one (Luke 15:4). And God sees what we cannot: this one man was the gospel’s door into Africa. We tend to measure ministry by numbers, and God measures it by faithfulness and by his own purposes. If you are called from something fruitful to something small and hidden, it is not demotion. It may be the most important work you will ever do.

In a sentence. An angel of the Lord told Philip to go south to the desert road from Jerusalem to Gaza, and he went, and there was an Ethiopian eunuch, a court official in charge of all the treasure of Candace, queen of the Ethiopians, who had come to Jerusalem to worship.

On a Tuesday. If God has plainly placed a single person in your path, give that one your full attention. Do not despise the conversation that only one person will hear.

For worship. God sent an evangelist into the desert for one man. He seeks the one, as well as the crowd. He saw an excluded eunuch reading Isaiah on the road home, and he would not let him go home without Christ. Praise the God who keeps his promises to outsiders, who gives the shut-out a name better than sons and daughters, and who sends his servants to the end of the earth for the sake of one soul.
verseByVerse.note: Gaza was the last town on the road to Egypt. “Ethiopia” here is the kingdom south of Egypt (in modern Sudan); Candace was the title of its ruling queen. The law barred eunuchs from the assembly, but Isaiah promised them a place.

parallels.desc: to the eunuchs … a name better than sons and daughters
Cush shall hasten to stretch out her hands to God

verseByVerse.quote: and was returning, seated in his chariot, and he was reading the prophet Isaiah. And the Spirit said to Philip, "Go over and join this chariot."
verseByVerse.commentary:
and was returning, seated in his chariot, and he was reading the prophet Isaiah. And the Spirit said to Philip, “Go over and join this chariot.”

And was returning, seated in his chariot, and he was reading the prophet Isaiah. Two details tell us a great deal about this man before he has said a word. The chariot was a covered carriage, moving slowly, with a driver. And he was reading, and Philip could hear him doing it from the roadside. Reading in the ancient world was almost always aloud; silent reading was unusual enough that people remarked on it. So the picture is of a senior official rolling south through open country, reading a Hebrew prophet aloud to himself in a moving carriage.

The scroll. The second is the scroll. A hand-copied scroll of Isaiah was not a thing anybody owned casually. Every letter was written out by a trained scribe over a matter of weeks, and a complete major prophet represented a serious purchase, the sort of item listed in a will. This man is the treasurer of a kingdom, and he has spent real money on the sacred book of a religion that will not fully admit him, probably in Greek, a language not his own. Nobody made him do it. He is going home from a pilgrimage that ended at a barrier, and he has bought the book anyway and is reading it in the desert. He was seeking.

Go over and join this chariot. The angel sent him to the road; the Spirit sends him to the chariot. The verb is stronger than join suggests (kollaō). It means to be glued to something, to attach oneself and stay attached; it is the word used of Saul later trying to attach himself to disciples who were afraid of him (9:26). Philip is not told to strike up a conversation. He is told to fasten on.

The division of labour. Notice how the work is shared, because it is the pattern of every genuine piece of evangelism in Scripture and it takes an enormous weight off the messenger. The Spirit arranged the road, the timing, the scroll and the passage. He had a man reading Isaiah 53 aloud at the exact mile where Philip happened to be standing. What was left for Philip to do was walk over. God arranged the meeting perfectly. Most Christians will never receive an audible sentence like Philip’s, and that is not the ordinary form. But much of Philip’s obedience here consisted of doing something small and mildly awkward with a situation that was already in front of him. There was a chariot on the road. He went over to it. A great deal of what looks in retrospect like guidance turns out, at the time, to have been a nudge toward a conversation that was already available.

How do I know when God wants me to go over to someone? Usually not by a voice, but by an opportunity you can see and a love you already have. Pray each morning that God would put people in your path and give you courage. Then notice the openings: the colleague who mentions a crisis, the neighbour who asks why you go to church, the friend reading something spiritual. Scripture has already told you to love your neighbour and to be ready to speak (1 Peter 3:15). You do not need special guidance to obey that. If an opportunity is in front of you and nothing forbids it, take it. You may be walking toward a man God has been preparing for years.

In a sentence. He was returning home, sitting in his chariot and reading the prophet Isaiah, and the Spirit told Philip to go over and join the chariot.

On a Tuesday. God is preparing people to hear the gospel. Be ready when he says, go over. Pray tomorrow morning, Lord, put someone in my way today, and then keep your eyes open.

For worship. Long before Philip reached the road, the Spirit had been at work in a royal court in Africa, drawing a man to Jerusalem and putting Isaiah in his hands. God is always ahead of his messengers. Praise the seeking God, who prepares hearts before he sends preachers, and who arranges every detail of the meeting between a sinner and his Saviour.
verseByVerse.note: People usually read aloud. A scroll of Isaiah was a costly possession.

verseByVerse.quote: So Philip ran to him and heard him reading Isaiah the prophet and asked, "Do you understand what you are reading?" And he said, "How can I, unless someone guides me?" And he invited Philip to come up and sit with him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
So Philip ran to him and heard him reading Isaiah the prophet and asked, “Do you understand what you are reading?” And he said, “How can I, unless someone guides me?” And he invited Philip to come up and sit with him.

So Philip ran to him and heard him reading Isaiah the prophet. A grown man jogging along a desert road beside a moving carriage, out of breath, trying to keep pace with a state official’s driver. Eager obedience. Luke includes it, and it is not a dignified picture. Philip is not strolling across when it suits him.

Do you understand what you are reading? Then the opening line, one of the best-judged sentences in the book. In Greek it is a play on words: do you understand (ginōskeis) what you are reading (anaginōskeis)? It is light, and precisely calibrated. Not a challenge, not a sermon, not a change of subject. Philip begins with the thing the man is already doing and asks a question about it. That is worth taking seriously by anyone who dreads these conversations, because the dread is nearly always about having to introduce a subject out of nothing. Philip introduces nothing. He notices what is in the man’s hands and asks how he is getting on with it. A simple, direct question: a good way to start a conversation about the Bible.

How can I, unless someone guides me? And the answer is the most teachable sentence anybody speaks in Acts. Consider who says it: a man of rank, in his own carriage, with an escort, replying to a stranger who has just run up out of the desert on foot. He does not bluff. He does not say he has his own view of the passage, or that he was only reading out of interest. He admits at once, to an obvious inferior, that he is out of his depth. The word for guide (hodēgēsei) means to lead on the way, the word Jesus used of the Spirit guiding into all the truth (John 16:13).

Two errors ruled out. Two errors are ruled out here, on opposite sides. The first is the assumption that Scripture is so plain nobody ought to need help with it, and that asking is a confession of weakness. The Ethiopian is intelligent, serious and reading the right book, and he cannot get through Isaiah 53 without somebody to explain it. The God who inspired the text also gave the church teachers (Ephesians 4:11; Nehemiah 8:8), and the two were meant to go together. The second is the opposite error: that Scripture is so difficult ordinary people had better leave it to the qualified. Nobody suggests the eunuch should stop reading. The Bible is clear in its central message, and the answer to his difficulty is not less Bible. It is a man in the carriage.

And he invited Philip to come up and sit with him. An open door, opened by the man himself.

What if someone asks me a question I cannot answer? Say so honestly; the eunuch’s humility is a good model for the teacher as well as the learner. You might say, that is a good question, and I do not know, but I would like to find out with you. Then do: ask your pastor, read a good book, and come back. Most people are not looking for a Christian who knows everything. They are looking for one who is honest and who cares about the truth. And you can always tell what you do know: who Jesus is, what he did, and what he means to you. Philip did not need to answer every question about Isaiah. He needed to get to Jesus.

In a sentence. Philip ran up, heard him reading Isaiah the prophet, and asked if he understood what he was reading, and he replied that he could not unless someone guided him, and invited Philip to come up and sit with him.

On a Tuesday. Be willing to admit you need help understanding Scripture, and ask for it this week: from your pastor, a mature friend, a good commentary. And be ready to sit beside someone else and help them.

For worship. The Lord who wrote Isaiah 53 sent a guide to explain it, and through the guide he himself spoke. He opens the Scriptures and opens minds to understand them (Luke 24:45). Praise the God who does not leave seekers alone with a scroll they cannot read, but comes near through his word and his servants to show them his Son.
verseByVerse.note: A wordplay in Greek: “Do you understand (ginōskeis) what you are reading (anaginōskeis)?”

verseByVerse.quote: Now the passage of the Scripture that he was reading was this: "Like a sheep he was led to the slaughter and like a lamb before its shearer is silent, so he opens not his mouth. In his humiliation justice was denied him. Who can describe his generation? For his life is taken away from the earth."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Now the passage of the Scripture that he was reading was this: “Like a sheep he was led to the slaughter and like a lamb before its shearer is silent, so he opens not his mouth. In his humiliation justice was denied him. Who can describe his generation? For his life is taken away from the earth.”

Now the passage of the Scripture that he was reading was this. Of all the passages he could have been reading. The scroll is open at Isaiah 53:7–8, in the fourth Servant Song, the clearest prophecy of Christ’s suffering in the Old Testament. God’s providence. The wording differs a little from Isaiah 53 in our Old Testament because the eunuch was reading the Greek translation, but the sense is the same: an innocent sufferer led to death and cut off.

Like a sheep he was led to the slaughter and like a lamb before its shearer is silent, so he opens not his mouth. First the picture. Anybody who has watched shearing knows the detail Isaiah is reaching for: the animal is turned over and held, and it stops struggling. It goes completely still, in a way that can look almost like consent. That image is laid beside the other one, the sheep going quietly up the ramp. Silence in both. The prophet is describing a man who did not resist, and the Gospels record exactly that: Jesus was silent before his accusers (Mark 14:61; 15:5), and before Herod, questioned at length, he answered nothing (Luke 23:9). The silent, innocent sufferer.

In his humiliation justice was denied him. A legal sentence: an unjust trial. Not merely that he suffered, but that the courts failed.

Who can describe his generation? For his life is taken away from the earth. The line is genuinely difficult, and readers have taken it two ways: either that nobody could describe the wickedness of the men among whom he lived, or, more probably, that nobody could number his descendants. The second fits the paragraph, because a few lines later Isaiah says of this same Servant that he shall see his offspring (Isaiah 53:10), an extraordinary thing to say of a man just described as cut off and buried. He dies without descendants, and yet he will have countless spiritual children.

His own biography. Now put that before the man in the carriage. He is a eunuch. He will have no children, no descendants, no name carried forward, and in the ancient world that was not a private sorrow but the erasure of a man from the future. The law that shut him out of the assembly had shut him out on precisely that ground. And he is reading aloud, alone, on a desert road, about a man cut off from the land of the living, whose generation nobody could describe, and who would somehow see his offspring after all. It is not hard to see why he stopped. Whether or not he could have put it into words, he was reading his own biography and could not work out whose it was. The question he asks in the next verse is not academic curiosity. It is a man asking who this is, because whoever it is, is standing exactly where he is standing. And just three chapters on, Isaiah promises eunuchs a place in God’s house (Isaiah 56:3–5).

What does Isaiah 53 offer someone who feels cut off? Everything. The Servant was cut off so that the cut-off could be brought in. He was despised and rejected, a man of sorrows, acquainted with grief (Isaiah 53:3), so he knows from the inside what it is to be excluded, shamed and alone. If you feel shut out, by your body, your past, your singleness or childlessness, your illness or your story, look at him. He bore our griefs and carried our sorrows, and by his wounds we are healed (53:4–5). In him you have a family, the church, and a name better than sons and daughters. No one who comes to the Lamb is left outside.

In a sentence. The passage he was reading was this: like a sheep he was led to the slaughter, and like a lamb silent before its shearer, he did not open his mouth; in his humiliation justice was denied him; who can describe his generation, for his life is taken from the earth?

On a Tuesday. Read Isaiah 53 slowly this week, all twelve verses, and every time it says he, put Jesus’ name; every time it says we or us, put your own.

For worship. The Lamb was silent before his shearers, for you. He bore your sins in silence, and was cut off from the land of the living, and he shall see his offspring and be satisfied (Isaiah 53:11). Every believer is one of those offspring. Praise the Lamb of God, silent in his suffering and victorious in his rising, whose generation no one can number.

parallels.desc: like a sheep he was led to the slaughter

verseByVerse.quote: And the eunuch said to Philip, "About whom, I ask you, does the prophet say this, about himself or about someone else?" Then Philip opened his mouth, and beginning with this Scripture he told him the good news about Jesus.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And the eunuch said to Philip, “About whom, I ask you, does the prophet say this, about himself or about someone else?” Then Philip opened his mouth, and beginning with this Scripture he told him the good news about Jesus.

About whom, I ask you, does the prophet say this, about himself or about someone else? It is the right question, and not a naive one. The identity of Isaiah’s Servant was genuinely disputed, and had been for centuries. Jewish interpreters proposed the prophet himself, or Hezekiah, or Israel as a nation, or a faithful remnant within the nation, or a Messiah still to come. The eunuch has read the passage carefully enough to see that it is about a person, and honestly enough to admit that he cannot tell which. The crucial question.

Then Philip opened his mouth. A solemn phrase for an important speech (10:34; Matthew 5:2).

And beginning with this Scripture he told him the good news about Jesus. The method is as instructive as the content. Beginning with this Scripture: he does not change the subject. He does not say that Isaiah is difficult and here is a simpler way of putting things. He produces no outline and no sequence of steps. The man had a question about a text; Philip answers the question about the text, and keeps going until he arrives at Jesus. Philip begins where the man is and leads him to Jesus. It is the same move the risen Christ made on the road to Emmaus, beginning with Moses and all the Prophets and interpreting to two men the things concerning himself (Luke 24:27). The instinct in these conversations is nearly always to steer: to get off whatever the other person asked and onto ground where we know the material. Philip does the opposite.

He gospelled Jesus to him. The phrasing is precise. He told him the good news about Jesus; literally, he announced Jesus as good news. Jesus is not a topic within the message. He is the message. Isaiah 53 is about Jesus: rejected, silent, suffering for the sins of others, dying, and then exalted. It is the gospel in the Old Testament. Jesus himself said it was written of him (Luke 22:37).

How can I be sure Isaiah 53 is really about Jesus? Notice where the question arises. The eunuch is reading the passage and asking who it is about before Philip arrives.
