The text raised the question by itself, in the mind of a foreigner with no Christian instruction, on a road in the desert. Christ is not being imported into Isaiah; he is being identified in it. And the fit is exact: a Servant who suffers not for his own sins but for the sins of many, who is silent before his accusers, who is condemned unjustly, who dies, is buried with the rich, and then sees his offspring and is exalted (Isaiah 52:13–53:12). No one else in history fits. Jesus said it was about him, and the apostles preached it so (1 Peter 2:22–25).

In a sentence. The eunuch asked Philip whether the prophet was speaking about himself or about someone else, and Philip, starting from this Scripture, told him the good news about Jesus.

On a Tuesday. Start where people are and lead them to Jesus. Every part of Scripture can be a starting point. When a friend asks about anything in the Bible, answer the question honestly, and then ask yourself how this passage leads to Christ, and say it.

For worship. The whole Bible is about him. Moses wrote of him, the prophets foretold him, the psalms sang of him, and in Isaiah 53 he is seen as clearly as in any Gospel. Praise the Lord Jesus, the Servant who was pierced for our transgressions and crushed for our iniquities, the one about whom the prophet spoke, the good news himself.

verseByVerse.quote: And as they were going along the road they came to some water, and the eunuch said, "See, here is water! What prevents me from being baptized?" And Philip said, "If you believe with all your heart, you may." And he answered and said, "I believe that Jesus Christ is the Son of God."
verseByVerse.commentary:
And as they were going along the road they came to some water, and the eunuch said, “See, here is water! What prevents me from being baptized?” And Philip said, “If you believe with all your heart, you may.” And he answered and said, “I believe that Jesus Christ is the Son of God.”

And as they were going along the road they came to some water. In a desert, a stream or pool. Providence again.

See, here is water! What prevents me from being baptized? He asks it; Philip does not suggest it. Whatever was said in that carriage had evidently included the fact that people who believe this are baptised, and the Ethiopian has connected it to the water they are passing and raised it himself. And the question he chooses (ti kōlyei) is the one word he has carried his whole life. What prevents me? He knows the answer. He has known it since he was a boy, and had it confirmed at the end of a journey of well over a thousand miles: his own body prevented him, the law said so in as many words, and the temple he had crossed the world to reach would not let him past the outer court. A eunuch, a Gentile, an outsider, who had been prevented from so much. He puts the question to a man who has just spent an hour telling him about Jesus, and what he is actually asking is whether the barrier is still there. Nothing prevents him from Christ.

He is inhabiting Isaiah 56. What makes this scene so charged is where he has been reading. He has the scroll open at chapter 53, the Servant’s suffering and death for others. But just three chapters later Isaiah makes the eunuch a figure of prophetic promise: let not the eunuch say, behold, I am a dry tree; for to the eunuchs who hold fast my covenant I will give in my house and within my walls a monument and a name better than sons and daughters (Isaiah 56:3–5). The very book he is reading contains the prophecy that he, the excluded one, will be gathered. Luke wants his readers to feel the precision of providence: the Spirit sends Philip not just to the right road but to the right man reading the right book at the right passage.

Textual note: verse 37. Your Bible may not have it. Many modern translations print verse 36 and then jump to verse 38, with the exchange about believing with all your heart in a footnote. The ESV notes that some manuscripts add verse 37: Philip says that if he believes with all his heart he may, and the eunuch confesses that Jesus Christ is the Son of God. It is not in the earliest and best manuscripts and was probably added later, perhaps from an early baptismal liturgy, to make the confession explicit. The words are old; Irenaeus quotes them before the end of the second century. They read exactly like the question and answer the early church used at the water’s edge, and a scribe who knew that liturgy by heart would naturally have supplied what looked to him like a missing line. It reflects true early practice, since baptism followed faith, but it was likely not part of what Luke wrote.

Nothing is lost. Nothing is lost if it goes. The eunuch plainly did believe: he asks for baptism himself, and he goes on his way rejoicing. And every word the verse contains is taught openly elsewhere in the same book: repent and be baptised (2:38); they believed and were baptised (8:12); believe in the Lord Jesus, and you will be saved, and he was baptised at once (16:31–33). No doctrine rests on it, and no doctrine is damaged by it. The words may be a later copyist’s. The practice they describe is apostolic.

Does this show that baptism is for believers? Yes. The order here, as in verse 12, is hearing, believing, then baptism, and that is the order in every baptism described in Acts. Christians who baptise infants agree that adult converts must believe first, but hold that the children of believers may also be baptised, and we honour their sincere conviction. The more likely reading, given every example in Acts, is that baptism is for those who have come to faith (1689 London Baptist Confession 29.2).

I was baptised as a baby. Should I be baptised now? On the believer’s baptism view, which this app holds, yes: baptism is the believer’s own confession of faith in Christ, and so it belongs after faith. That is not a criticism of your parents, who very likely acted in love and faith, praying for you, and whose prayers God may well have answered in your conversion. Talk with your pastor, and if you are in a paedobaptist church, do so with humility and a desire for peace. Paedobaptist brothers would say your infant baptism was valid and should not be repeated, and they hold that conscientiously. Whatever you decide, do it out of obedience to Christ, not out of pressure from anyone.

In a sentence. As they went along the road they came to some water, and the eunuch said, Look, here is water; what prevents me from being baptised? (Some manuscripts add that Philip said he could if he believed with all his heart, and that he answered, I believe that Jesus Christ is the Son of God.)

On a Tuesday. If you have believed in Christ and not been baptised, ask the eunuch’s question: what prevents me? Speak to your pastor this week. And if you have been baptised, remember it with thanks, as the day you publicly said you belong to Jesus.

For worship. Nothing in your past or status prevents you from coming to Christ. The barrier that kept the eunuch in the outer court came down when the Lamb of God was cut off for him. Now there is neither Jew nor Greek, neither slave nor free, for all are one in Christ Jesus (Galatians 3:28). Praise the Saviour in whom the excluded are welcomed, the dry tree is given an everlasting name, and nothing stands between a believing sinner and the water.
verseByVerse.note: The ESV notes that some manuscripts add verse 37: Philip says “If you believe with all your heart, you may,” and the eunuch replies, “I believe that Jesus Christ is the Son of God.”

parallels.desc: can anyone withhold water for baptizing?

verseByVerse.quote: And he commanded the chariot to stop, and they both went down into the water, Philip and the eunuch, and he baptized him. And when they came up out of the water, the Spirit of the Lord carried Philip away, and the eunuch saw him no more, and went on his way rejoicing.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And he commanded the chariot to stop, and they both went down into the water, Philip and the eunuch, and he baptized him. And when they came up out of the water, the Spirit of the Lord carried Philip away, and the eunuch saw him no more, and went on his way rejoicing.

And he commanded the chariot to stop, and they both went down into the water, Philip and the eunuch, and he baptized him. In this whole passage the powerful man gives exactly one order, and it is to halt his own carriage in the middle of a desert so that a stranger can baptise him in whatever water they have just come to. He does not ask whether it might wait until Ethiopia, or whether there is a more suitable place, or whether he ought to be further instructed first. Went down into, and in the next verse came up out of, the water: the language suggests immersion, which is the meaning of the word baptizō, to dip or plunge. Baptism pictures burial and resurrection with Christ (Romans 6:3–4).

Where Christians differ: the mode and subjects of baptism. Some sprinkle or pour; some baptise infants. The words down into and up out of could, taken alone, describe a man wading into a stream. Verdict: the pattern here is a believer, confessing faith, baptised by immersion. This is the New Testament norm. Christians who sprinkle or baptise infants hold their views sincerely, and we hold ours with charity, but the credobaptist practice best fits passages like this. Immersion shows most clearly what baptism means: dying to the old life, buried with Christ, and rising to walk in newness of life.

And when they came up out of the water, the Spirit of the Lord carried Philip away, and the eunuch saw him no more. What Luke makes a point of is what happens next. The verb means snatched (harpazō): it is the word Paul uses of a man caught up to the third heaven, and of the church being caught up at the Lord’s coming (2 Corinthians 12:2; 1 Thessalonians 4:17). A sudden removal, like Elijah’s (1 Kings 18:12; 2 Kings 2:16). Whether miraculous transport or simply a sudden leading, Philip’s work there was done. Luke reports it in half a sentence and does not pause over it.

And went on his way rejoicing. Now stand where the Ethiopian is standing. He has been a Christian for perhaps ten minutes. He is wet, on a desert road, and the man who explained everything to him has gone: not travelled on, not said goodbye, gone. Ahead of him is a journey of a thousand miles and more, back to a court where he may well be the only believer. He has no church, no minister, no Bible in his own language, and the scroll he does have is Isaiah. Nobody has taught him to pray or told him what to do on the first Lord’s Day. And Luke says he went on his way rejoicing. Joy again, as in Samaria (v. 8). Whatever he had received in that carriage did not depend on Philip’s continued presence, and he appears to have understood that immediately. He did not need Philip; he had Christ. The joy is not bravery under adverse conditions. It is the ordinary result of the gospel.

Not a case against the church. One guard, because this is occasionally used to argue that a Christian does not really need the church. Luke has spent seven chapters describing a community that ate together, prayed together, sold property for one another and buried its dead with great lamentation, and he is not now quietly withdrawing all of it. The eunuch’s isolation is a circumstance, not a recommendation. What the verse establishes is narrower and more comforting: a believer who has nothing but Christ has enough to be going on with. That is worth knowing by anyone reading this in a hospital, a prison, or a country where the nearest congregation is a very long way off.

Toward the end of the earth. Later tradition holds that this man carried the gospel home and that the Ethiopian church traces itself to him. Luke does not say so and it cannot be established. What can be said is that a man went south that afternoon with the good news about Jesus, in the direction of the end of the earth, exactly as promised in the first chapter of this book. The gospel reached the end of the earth in one man.

What if I am the only Christian where I am? Then you are in the eunuch’s company, and Christ is enough for you. Hold on to him through his word: read it daily, and memorise some of it. Pray, and pray aloud if you can, as this man read aloud. Look for even one other believer to pray with, in person or at a distance. Find a church online to listen to if you have none near, while you pray for one. Live your faith openly and kindly among the people around you; you may be the beginning of a church, as he may have been. And remember that you are never really alone: you belong to a body that spans the earth, and the Lord has promised, I am with you always (Matthew 28:20).

In a sentence. He ordered the chariot to stop, and they both went down into the water, and Philip baptised him, and when they came up out of the water, the Spirit of the Lord took Philip away, and the eunuch saw him no more, but went on his way rejoicing.

On a Tuesday. When someone comes to faith, they belong to Christ, not to you. Let them go on their way rejoicing. And when you feel spiritually alone this week, remember the man in the chariot, and rejoice in the Christ you have.

For worship. The eunuch went home without Philip, without a church and without a name in any human genealogy, and he went rejoicing, because he had been joined to the Servant whose offspring no one can number. Praise the Lord Jesus, who is enough for the lonely believer on the long road home, and whose joy goes with his people to the end of the earth.

parallels.desc: the Spirit of the LORD caught him up

verseByVerse.quote: But Philip found himself at Azotus, and as he passed through he preached the gospel to all the towns until he came to Caesarea.
verseByVerse.commentary:
But Philip found himself at Azotus, and as he passed through he preached the gospel to all the towns until he came to Caesarea.

But Philip found himself at Azotus. Azotus is Ashdod, one of the five old cities of the Philistines, some twenty miles up the coast from Gaza. The gospel arrives in Philistine country by way of a man who did not choose the destination.

And as he passed through he preached the gospel to all the towns until he came to Caesarea. And then, without pausing, he does what he has been doing all chapter. Not one great mission and then a rest: a coastline of towns, one after another, across perhaps sixty miles, all the way to Caesarea, the Roman capital of Judea. Peter will soon preach to Cornelius there (chapter 10). Philip prepared the ground. Then Luke closes the chapter and Philip disappears from the narrative.

Twenty years later. He reappears once, twenty years later and thirteen chapters on, in a single verse: we entered the house of Philip the evangelist, who was one of the seven, and stayed with him (21:8). Two things in that sentence are worth noticing. The first is the word we. The man writing this book was in that house. Luke stayed several days under Philip’s roof at Caesarea, and it is very hard to avoid the conclusion that much of the material in chapters 6 and 8, the appointment of the seven, the Samaritan mission, the desert road, the Ethiopian’s question, the water, came across a table from the man it happened to. This chapter very likely has an eyewitness behind it, and he is in the book.

Still the evangelist. The second is what Philip had been doing in the meantime. He is still called the evangelist two decades on, which is evidently what people in Caesarea called him. And he has four unmarried daughters who prophesied (21:9), which quietly fulfils the promise Peter had quoted from Joel on the first morning of the church, that sons and daughters would prophesy (2:17). He settled in a port city, raised a family, and went on being the man who tells people about Jesus.

The twenty years and the afternoon. That is the note this chapter deserves to end on. Philip’s famous day was the desert road, and it lasted an afternoon. What he actually did with his life was live in Caesarea for twenty years, keep the door open, bring up four daughters in the fear of God, and go on telling people town by town until a doctor came to stay and wrote it all down. Most of a Christian life is the twenty years and not the afternoon. The afternoon is what gets recorded. The twenty years are what made the record possible.

What if my Christian life feels ordinary? Then it may be exactly what God intends. Most of Scripture’s faithful people spent most of their lives doing ordinary things faithfully: working, raising children, opening their homes, speaking of Christ to whoever was near. Philip had one dramatic afternoon and twenty years of ordinary faithfulness, and the twenty years were not the lesser part. God does not grade us by the drama of our stories but by faithfulness (1 Corinthians 4:2). Keep your door open, raise your children in the Lord, speak of him in your town. Nothing done for Christ is ordinary to him.

In a sentence. Philip found himself at Azotus, and as he passed through the region he preached the gospel in all the towns until he reached Caesarea.

On a Tuesday. Philip preached in every town he passed through. Make every place you go a place to speak of Christ. And thank God this week for the ordinary, faithful Christians who opened their homes and told you about Jesus.

For worship. The Lord who sent Philip to a desert road for one afternoon also kept him faithful for twenty years in a port city, and wrote both into his book. He sees the hidden years as well as the famous day. Praise the faithful God, who carries his gospel from town to town through ordinary servants, who fulfils his promises in the homes of his people, and who will one day gather the fruit of every faithful life before his throne.
verseByVerse.note: Azotus is Ashdod, on the coast. Caesarea, the Roman capital of Judea, became Philip’s home.

8.theology: The Gospel Breaks Every Barrier. Acts 8 is the chapter in which the gospel crosses its first major boundary — from Jews to Samaritans, and then from Israel to Africa. This is not accidental; it is the working out of Acts 1:8: Jerusalem, Judea, Samaria, ends of the earth. The Ethiopian eunuch is the first representative of the “ends of the earth” in the book — geographically distant, ethnically foreign, ritually excluded. And the gospel reaches him on a desert road through a text he happened to be reading. This is the Reformed doctrine of effectual calling in action: the Spirit directs the preacher, opens the Scriptures, and draws the seeker. Nothing is left to chance. The God who elects a people from every tongue and tribe and nation uses the ordinary means — a man, a chariot, a scroll — to accomplish his extraordinary purposes.
8.examples:
Then: Scattered believers, fleeing for their lives, who could not stop preaching. A deacon pulled off a city-wide revival and then redirected to one man on a road. An African official who came to Jerusalem seeking God and left having found him in the most unexpected way. The gospel in chapter 8 is gloriously uncontrollable.

Now: The church tends to think of mission in terms of programs and strategies. Acts 8 shows God doing his best work through disruption — persecution that scatters, divine direction that redirects, a Scripture passage that raises exactly the right question. The lesson is not that we should abandon planning, but that we must hold our plans loosely enough that we can hear “go over and join this chariot” when the Spirit speaks it.

9.title: The Road to Damascus
9.text: <sup>1</sup>But Saul, still breathing threats and murder against the disciples of the Lord, went to the high priest <sup>2</sup>and asked him for letters to the synagogues at Damascus, so that if he found any belonging to the Way, men or women, he might bring them bound to Jerusalem. <sup>3</sup>Now as he went on his way, he approached Damascus, and suddenly a light from heaven shone around him. <sup>4</sup>And falling to the ground, he heard a voice saying to him, “Saul, Saul, why are you persecuting me?” <sup>5</sup>And he said, “Who are you, Lord?” And he said, “I am Jesus, whom you are persecuting. <sup>6</sup>But rise and enter the city, and you will be told what you are to do.” <sup>7</sup>The men who were traveling with him stood speechless, hearing the voice but seeing no one. <sup>8</sup>Saul rose from the ground, and although his eyes were opened, he saw nothing. So they led him by the hand and brought him into Damascus. <sup>9</sup>And for three days he was without sight, and neither ate nor drank. <sup>10</sup>Now there was a disciple at Damascus named Ananias. The Lord said to him in a vision, “Ananias.” And he said, “Here I am, Lord.” <sup>11</sup>And the Lord said to him, “Rise and go to the street called Straight, and at the house of Judas look for a man of Tarsus named Saul, for behold, he is praying, <sup>12</sup>and he has seen in a vision a man named Ananias come in and lay his hands on him so that he might regain his sight.” <sup>13</sup>But Ananias answered, “Lord, I have heard from many about this man, how much evil he has done to your saints at Jerusalem. <sup>14</sup>And here he has authority from the chief priests to bind all who call on your name.” <sup>15</sup>But the Lord said to him, “Go, for he is a chosen instrument of mine to carry my name before the Gentiles and kings and the children of Israel. <sup>16</sup>For I will show him how much he must suffer for the sake of my name.” <sup>17</sup>So Ananias departed and entered the house. And laying his hands on him he said, “Brother Saul, the Lord Jesus who appeared to you on the road by which you came has sent me so that you may regain your sight and be filled with the Holy Spirit.” <sup>18</sup>And immediately something like scales fell from his eyes, and he regained his sight. Then he rose and was baptized; <sup>19</sup>and taking food, he was strengthened. For some days he was with the disciples at Damascus. <sup>20</sup>And immediately he proclaimed Jesus in the synagogues, saying, “He is the Son of God.” <sup>21</sup>And all who heard him were amazed and said, “Is not this the man who made havoc in Jerusalem of those who called upon this name? And has he not come here for this purpose, to bring them bound before the chief priests?” <sup>22</sup>But Saul increased all the more in strength, and confounded the Jews who lived in Damascus by proving that Jesus was the Christ. <sup>23</sup>When many days had passed, the Jews plotted to kill him, <sup>24</sup>but their plot became known to Saul. They were watching the gates day and night in order to kill him, <sup>25</sup>but his disciples took him by night and let him down through an opening in the wall, lowering him in a basket. <sup>26</sup>And when he had come to Jerusalem, he attempted to join the disciples. And they were all afraid of him, for they did not believe that he was a disciple. <sup>27</sup>But Barnabas took him and brought him to the apostles and declared to them how on the road he had seen the Lord, who spoke to him, and how at Damascus he had preached boldly in the name of Jesus. <sup>28</sup>So he went in and out among them at Jerusalem, preaching boldly in the name of the Lord. <sup>29</sup>And he spoke and disputed against the Hellenists. But they were seeking to kill him. <sup>30</sup>And when the brothers learned this, they brought him down to Caesarea and sent him off to Tarsus. <sup>31</sup>So the church throughout all Judea and Galilee and Samaria had peace and was being built up. And walking in the fear of the Lord and in the comfort of the Holy Spirit, it multiplied. <sup>32</sup>Now as Peter went here and there among them all, he came down also to the saints who lived at Lydda. <sup>33</sup>There he found a man named Aeneas, bedridden for eight years, who was paralyzed. <sup>34</sup>And Peter said to him, “Aeneas, Jesus Christ heals you; rise and make your bed.” And immediately he rose. <sup>35</sup>And all the residents of Lydda and Sharon saw him, and they turned to the Lord. <sup>36</sup>Now there was in Joppa a disciple named Tabitha, which, translated, means Dorcas. She was full of good works and acts of charity. <sup>37</sup>In those days she became ill and died, and when they had washed her, they laid her in an upper room. <sup>38</sup>Since Lydda was near Joppa, the disciples, hearing that Peter was there, sent two men to him, urging him, “Please come to us without delay.” <sup>39</sup>So Peter rose and went with them. And when he arrived, they took him to the upper room. All the widows stood beside him weeping and showing tunics and other garments that Dorcas made while she was with them. <sup>40</sup>But Peter put them all outside, and knelt down and prayed; and turning to the body he said, “Tabitha, arise.” And she opened her eyes, and when she saw Peter she sat up. <sup>41</sup>And he gave her his hand and raised her up. Then, calling the saints and widows, he presented her alive. <sup>42</sup>And it became known throughout all Joppa, and many believed in the Lord. <sup>43</sup>And he stayed in Joppa for many days with one Simon, a tanner.
9.overview:
The chapter tells the most important conversion in church history; Luke tells it three times in Acts (here, 22:3–16 and 26:9–18). Saul of Tarsus, a brilliant young Pharisee, is so zealous against “the Way”, as the Christian movement was called, that he obtains letters from the high priest to arrest believers in the synagogues of Damascus, about 135 miles to the north-east. Near the city a blinding light flashes from heaven and a voice asks, “Saul, Saul, why are you persecuting me?” It is Jesus. Blind, Saul is led into Damascus and fasts for three days. The Lord sends a frightened disciple named Ananias to lay hands on him, calling Saul his chosen instrument to carry his name to Gentiles, kings and Israel, and to suffer for it. Saul’s sight returns, he is filled with the Spirit and baptised, and at once he preaches in the synagogues that Jesus is the Son of God.

The persecutor becomes the persecuted. After some time, including a period in Arabia (Galatians 1:17), plots in Damascus force him to escape in a basket over the wall. In Jerusalem the believers are afraid of him until Barnabas vouches for him; when Greek-speaking Jews try to kill him, the church sends him home to Tarsus. The church enjoys a season of peace and growth. Luke then returns to Peter, who heals a paralysed man named Aeneas at Lydda and raises a beloved disciple named Tabitha (Dorcas) from death at Joppa, and stays there in the house of a tanner, setting the scene for chapter 10.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Saul, still breathing murderous threats against the Lord’s disciples, went to the high priest and asked for letters to the synagogues in Damascus, so that if he found any who belonged to the Way, men or women, he could bring them as prisoners to Jerusalem. As he neared Damascus, a light from heaven suddenly flashed around him. He fell to the ground and heard a voice say, “Saul, Saul, why do you persecute me?” He asked who it was, and the reply came: “I am Jesus, whom you are persecuting. Now get up and go into the city, and you will be told what you must do.” His companions stood speechless; they heard the sound but saw no one. Saul got up, but when he opened his eyes he could see nothing, so they led him by the hand into Damascus. For three days he was blind and did not eat or drink. In Damascus there was a disciple named Ananias, whom the Lord called in a vision and sent to the house of Judas on Straight Street to ask for Saul of Tarsus, who was praying and had seen in a vision a man named Ananias come and lay hands on him to restore his sight. Ananias protested that he had heard how much harm this man had done to the Lord’s people in Jerusalem, and that he had come with authority to arrest everyone who called on the Lord’s name. But the Lord told him to go, for this man was his chosen instrument to proclaim his name to the Gentiles, their kings and the people of Israel, and the Lord would show him how much he must suffer for his name. So Ananias went, laid his hands on Saul and called him brother, saying the Lord Jesus who appeared to him on the road had sent him so that Saul might see again and be filled with the Holy Spirit. Immediately something like scales fell from Saul’s eyes and he could see. He got up and was baptised, and after eating he regained his strength. He spent several days with the disciples in Damascus and at once began to preach in the synagogues that Jesus is the Son of God. All who heard him were astonished, asking whether this was not the man who had caused havoc among those who call on this name in Jerusalem, and had come to take them as prisoners. Yet Saul grew more and more powerful and baffled the Jews in Damascus by proving that Jesus is the Messiah. After many days the Jews conspired to kill him, watching the city gates day and night, but Saul learned of their plan, and his followers lowered him in a basket through an opening in the wall. When he came to Jerusalem he tried to join the disciples, but they were all afraid of him, not believing he was really a disciple. Barnabas took him to the apostles and told them how Saul had seen the Lord on the road and how he had preached fearlessly in Damascus in Jesus’ name. So Saul stayed with them, moving freely in Jerusalem and speaking boldly in the Lord’s name. He talked and debated with the Greek-speaking Jews, but they tried to kill him. When the believers learned of this, they took him down to Caesarea and sent him off to Tarsus. Then the church throughout Judea, Galilee and Samaria enjoyed peace and was strengthened. Living in the fear of the Lord and encouraged by the Holy Spirit, it increased in numbers.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Sovereignty of Grace in Conversion

Saul's conversion is the purest demonstration in the New Testament of grace that does not wait to be wanted. He was not seeking Christ; he was hunting Christians. He was not wavering, not quietly troubled, not secretly drawn — he was riding to Damascus with an arrest warrant in his bag. Nothing in the account suggests any prior movement toward faith, and Paul himself, looking back, never once describes his conversion as a search that ended. He describes it as being laid hold of. Reformed theology has read it as the pattern rather than the exception: everybody who comes to Christ was, in one degree or another, going the other way when God stopped them, and the difference between Saul and a quieter case is a matter of speed and lighting rather than of mechanism. It is also the passage that makes despair about anybody unreasonable. The church's most violent enemy would go on to write a great part of its Scriptures, and not one person in Jerusalem could have guessed it.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: Ananias was told to go to the man who had done much evil to the saints in Jerusalem and who was carrying a warrant that covered Ananias himself. He said what he thought about it, out loud, to God — and then he went, and the first word out of his mouth was brother. Now: The church's most persuasive argument has always been the existence of people in it who ought, by every reasonable calculation, to be enemies. That is not an argument anybody constructs. It is one a congregation either exhibits or does not.

verseByVerse.quote: But Saul, still breathing threats and murder against the disciples of the Lord, went to the high priest and asked him for letters to the synagogues at Damascus, so that if he found any belonging to the Way, men or women, he might bring them bound to Jerusalem.
verseByVerse.commentary:
But Saul, still breathing threats and murder against the disciples of the Lord, went to the high priest and asked him for letters to the synagogues at Damascus, so that if he found any belonging to the Way, men or women, he might bring them bound to Jerusalem.

Meaning first. Acts 9 tells the most important conversion in church history. Saul, the church’s fiercest enemy, is stopped by the risen Jesus on the road to Damascus, blinded, healed, baptised, and made the apostle to the Gentiles. Luke tells the story three times (here, 22:3–16 and 26:9–18), which shows how much it matters to him. Then Peter heals Aeneas and raises Tabitha, as the gospel spreads along the coast, setting the scene for the Gentile breakthrough of chapter 10. The chapter shows sovereign grace: Christ saves whom he chooses, even his enemies, and he does it in person. The man who set out to put the name of Jesus out of the world ends the chapter as the one who will carry it to the end of the earth.

But Saul, still breathing threats and murder against the disciples of the Lord. Still makes it a condition rather than an episode. The participle empneōn, breathing in, describes what Saul respires, in and out, the atmosphere he lives in: his very breath is hostility. And the second noun is not rhetorical. Murder means murder, and Paul confirms it in his own words years later: when believers were put to death, he says, he cast his vote against them (26:10). Stephen was not the only one.

Went to the high priest and asked him for letters to the synagogues at Damascus. Then the machinery, and it repays attention because it tells you what kind of man this was. He does not gather a mob. He goes through the proper office. Damascus lies about a hundred and thirty-five miles north-east of Jerusalem, a week on foot, and it is outside Judea altogether, a different province under a different administration. The high priest’s authority reached synagogues in the Diaspora by long-standing arrangement, and Rome had historically allowed the Jewish authorities to deal with their own people in religious matters. So what Saul is carrying is not a licence to riot. It is paperwork, obtained through proper channels, enforceable in a foreign city.

Organised, credentialled and sincere. That is worth sitting with, because it is easy to picture the persecutor as a man out of control. He was nothing of the sort. He was organised, funded and legal, and he believed with his whole heart that he was doing God’s work. He says so himself, later, without excusing it: he was zealous for God, and he was wrong (22:3; Galatians 1:13–14).

Why Damascus? Because there was a large and ancient Jewish community there, and because the believers scattered by the persecution of chapter 8 had gone somewhere. Saul is not opening a new front. He is pursuing refugees he had himself created, a week’s journey from home, to bring them back in chains.

So that if he found any belonging to the Way. This is the earliest name the Christians had for themselves, and Luke uses it half a dozen times in this book (19:9, 23; 22:4; 24:14, 22). It is worth pausing on. They did not call themselves a school, a party, a sect or a synagogue. They called themselves a road, hē hodos. Whether the name came from the Lord’s own words, I am the way (John 14:6), or from the prophet’s cry to prepare the way of the LORD (Isaiah 40:3), or from both, the effect is the same: it is a word about travelling, and it describes a manner of life rather than a set of opinions. Christianity is not first a society you join but a road you walk, behind someone who has gone ahead. It is also, as it happens, precisely the wrong kind of thing to try to stamp out. You can shut a building. A road runs.

Men or women, he might bring them bound to Jerusalem. Once more Luke writes men or women. It is the second time he has said it about Saul in two chapters (8:3), and he will not let the reader make this abstract. Whatever else was in those letters, they authorised the arrest of somebody’s mother. That is the last sentence of the paragraph. Then the road, and God interrupts a man in the middle of a journey he had every intention of completing.

How could a man so devout be so wrong? Because sincerity is not the same as truth, and zeal is only as good as what it is aimed at. Paul later said of his own people what had been true of himself: they have a zeal for God, but not according to knowledge (Romans 10:2). Saul knew his Bible, prayed daily, and lived strictly. What he did not know was who Jesus was, and that one error turned all his devotion into a weapon against God. It is a sobering warning for religious people. Being earnest, disciplined and certain does not make us right; only the truth about Christ does. The safeguard is not less zeal but zeal held open to Scripture, and a readiness to be corrected by it.

In a sentence. Saul, still breathing murderous threats against the Lord’s disciples, went to the high priest for letters to the synagogues in Damascus, so that he could bring any followers of the Way, men or women, back to Jerusalem in chains.

On a Tuesday. The first Christians called their faith a Way, and a way is something you are either walking or not. Ask what in this week’s diary is on the road and what is simply parked beside it: the conversation you have put off, the habit you have kept for years, the generosity you mean to start. And if there is anyone in your life who reminds you of Saul on this morning, a person openly hostile to Christ and very sure of himself, do not write him off. This chapter is about to show what the Lord does with such men.

For worship. Saul rode out with the warrants in his bag, and the Lord he hated let him come. Christ was not taken by surprise on the Damascus road. He had set this man apart before he was born and called him by his grace (Galatians 1:15), and he waited until the persecutor was at the height of his fury and nearly at the city gate before he spoke. That is the patience of the Son of God with his enemies: not indifference, but a purpose that had already chosen the day.
verseByVerse.note: Damascus lay about 135 miles north-east of Jerusalem and had a large Jewish community. “The Way” was an early name for the Christian movement.

verseByVerse.quote: Now as he went on his way, he approached Damascus, and suddenly a light from heaven shone around him. And falling to the ground, he heard a voice saying to him, "Saul, Saul, why are you persecuting me?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Now as he went on his way, he approached Damascus, and suddenly a light from heaven shone around him. And falling to the ground, he heard a voice saying to him, “Saul, Saul, why are you persecuting me?”

As he went on his way, he approached Damascus. A week’s journey, and he was almost there. The city was in sight; the arrests were perhaps a few hours away. God does not stop men only at the beginning of their sins. Sometimes he lets them get to the very edge of the thing they meant to do.

And suddenly a light from heaven shone around him. The verb is built on the word for lightning: it did not glow, it flashed, and it enveloped him. When Paul describes it to King Agrippa he adds two details that fix the scene: it happened at midday, and the light was brighter than the sun (22:6; 26:13). This is a Syrian noon, the harshest light in the year, and something outshone it. It was the glory of the risen Christ, the same glory that Isaiah saw filling the temple and that John says was seen in the face of the Word made flesh.

Three tellings of one event. Since Luke tells this story three times in one book, it is worth laying the accounts beside each other here, because the differences are the sort that get produced as evidence of invention, and they repay an honest look. The first is about posture. Here the men with him stood speechless (v. 7); before Agrippa, Paul says we had all fallen to the ground (26:14). The resolution is not clever and does not need to be: everyone went down, and then the escort got up while Saul stayed where he was. Luke’s summary at verse 7 picks them up after they had risen, men on their feet, staring, waiting for the man they were escorting to move. Anybody who has described the same accident twice will recognise the phenomenon.

The commission on the road. The second difference is larger. In this chapter Saul is told simply to go into the city, where he will be told what to do, and the commission arrives later through Ananias. Before Agrippa, the commission is spoken by Christ on the road itself, at length, with the Gentiles named. But notice where Paul is standing when he tells it that way. He is in the dock in front of a king, with a Roman governor listening, and a Jewish disciple’s testimony from a back street in Damascus is worth nothing to that audience. So he compresses, folding what he was told into the encounter that authorised it, which is what any man does when summarising to a king. And in the middle account, before a Jerusalem crowd, Ananias is not merely present but is the point: Paul takes trouble there to describe him as a devout man according to the law, well spoken of by all the Jews in Damascus (22:12), exactly the credential that mattered to that audience. The three tellings are the same event addressed to three rooms. That is not a mark of fabrication. It is how a truthful man talks.

And falling to the ground. The man who had been dragging others to the floor of their own houses is on the floor of the road. Nobody pushed him. When the glory of God comes near, men do not stand and assess it; they go down, as Ezekiel did by the river Chebar and John did on Patmos.

Saul, Saul. Then the voice, and the first word is the man’s name, said twice. Scripture does that sparingly and always at a hinge: Abraham with the knife raised (Genesis 22:11), Jacob on the way down to Egypt (Genesis 46:2), Moses at the bush (Exodus 3:4), Samuel in the dark (1 Samuel 3:10), Martha in her busy kitchen, Simon on the last night. It is the address of somebody who knows the person and is about to change his life. It is tender as well as urgent. And Paul notes, when he tells it later, that it came in the Hebrew language (26:14), so the risen and glorified Christ speaks to him in his mother tongue and uses his Hebrew name, not the Greek one the world would come to know him by.

Why are you persecuting me? And then the question, which is one of the most consequential sentences in the Bible. Saul had never met Jesus of Nazareth. He had never struck him, tried him or voted against him; as far as we know he was not in Jerusalem during the trial. What he had done was drag Christians out of houses. And the voice from the light does not say, why are you persecuting my people, or my church, or those who follow me. It says me.

The body in a pronoun. Everything Paul later wrote about the church being the body of Christ (1 Corinthians 12:12–27; Ephesians 1:22–23) is already lying in that pronoun, and he heard it before he had a theology to put it in. It is the same truth the Lord taught on the Mount of Olives: as you did it to one of the least of these my brothers, you did it to me (Matthew 25:40). It cuts two ways and both of them matter. It means that the way a Christian treats another Christian is not a matter of church politics; Christ files it under his own name. And it means that whatever has been done to a believer, the exclusion, the cruelty, the years of it, the thing nobody else noticed, has not gone unrecorded, because it was not finally done to him alone. The Lord takes it personally, and he says so in the first sentence he ever speaks to Paul.

Does this mean Jesus is still suffering in heaven? No. He is risen and glorified, beyond pain and beyond the reach of any persecutor; death no longer has dominion over him (Romans 6:9). What the word me teaches is union, not fresh suffering. Christ is so joined to his people, the Head to the body, that what is done to them is counted as done to him, and he feels it with them in sympathy. Hebrews says we have a high priest who is able to sympathise with our weaknesses (Hebrews 4:15). So when you are wronged for his sake, you are not suffering in a corner of the universe he has forgotten. The one who reigns at the Father’s right hand regards the wound as his own, and he will answer for it.

In a sentence. As he neared Damascus, a light from heaven suddenly flashed around him, and he fell to the ground and heard a voice asking, “Saul, Saul, why are you persecuting me?”

On a Tuesday. Think of the Christian you find hardest to bear, the one who irritates you at church or who once hurt you badly. The way you speak about that person this week, and to him, Christ files under his own name. And if you are the one who has been mistreated by people who should have known better, take the other edge of the verse: it was noticed, by the only one whose noticing finally matters.

For worship. The Lord of glory, enthroned above every name, looked down on a road in Syria and saw his people being hunted, and he called the wound his own. He is not a distant King who governs his church from a safe height. He is the Head who feels every blow struck at his members, and the Shepherd who knows each of his sheep by name. And he used that name, twice, to stop the man doing the striking, not with a thunderbolt that ended him but with a question that saved him.

verseByVerse.quote: And he said, "Who are you, Lord?" And he said, "I am Jesus, whom you are persecuting. But rise and enter the city, and you will be told what you are to do."
verseByVerse.commentary:
And he said, “Who are you, Lord?” And he said, “I am Jesus, whom you are persecuting. But rise and enter the city, and you will be told what you are to do.”

Who are you, Lord? He says Lord before he has any idea who is speaking. The word kyrios could mean no more than sir, and a man flat on a road addressing a voice out of a light might reasonably reach for it. But this is a vision from heaven, the fall has already done its work, and Saul knows he is facing a divine being. By the end of the answer the word will mean everything it can mean.

I am Jesus, whom you are persecuting. Six words which cost Saul everything he had. Take the two halves separately, because each is a demolition. I am Jesus: so the body is not in the tomb, the disciples were not lying, the movement is not a fraud, and the man Saul thought a deceiver justly hanged on a tree and cursed by God (Deuteronomy 21:23) is alive, glorified and speaking from heaven. Everything Saul has done for the last year has been done to the Messiah of Israel. Gamaliel, his own teacher, had warned the council that they might be found opposing God (5:39). Saul had been doing exactly that. Whom you are persecuting: present tense, still going on, as of this morning. He is not being told about a mistake he once made. He is being interrupted in the middle of it, with the warrants still in his luggage.

But rise and enter the city, and you will be told what you are to do. And then, instead of a sentence, an instruction. Not a word of rebuke, no accounting demanded, nothing about Stephen, no lecture. He is told to get up and go and wait for instructions, like a man who has just been taken into someone’s service. Which is exactly what has happened. Saul now obeys a new Master, and his first act of obedience is to be led somewhere he did not choose.

Where Christians differ: how does conversion happen? Some describe conversion as entirely a human decision, and Saul’s conversion is sometimes set aside as untypical. Verdict: the details were unique, but the pattern is the same for every believer: Christ takes the initiative, overcomes the sinner’s resistance, and makes him willing (Galatians 1:15–16; 1 Timothy 1:13–16). Saul did not decide to follow Jesus; Jesus stopped him. Paul later said God set him apart before birth and called him by grace. This is effectual calling. Every conversion is a Damascus road, whether quiet or dramatic.

Must every Christian have a dramatic conversion like this? No. Saul’s experience was unusual in form, because he was being called as an apostle and witness. But its substance is the same for every believer: Christ seizes a sinner by grace. Many come to faith gradually, like Timothy, who knew the Scriptures from childhood (2 Timothy 3:15), and cannot name a day. What matters is not the drama but whether one now trusts Christ.

Does God force people to believe against their will? No, and the difference matters. God does not drag an unwilling man into the kingdom kicking and screaming. He changes the will itself, so that the man who would not come now wants to come. Saul was not overpowered into a faith he resented; he got up from that road asking what his new Lord wanted of him. The Westminster Confession puts it well: God draws his people to Jesus Christ, yet so as they come most freely, being made willing by his grace (Westminster 10.1). The Second London Confession says the same. Grace does not cancel our freedom. It rescues it from bondage to sin, which is why everyone who has been called this way describes it afterwards not as captivity but as release.

A note on the older Bibles. For anyone reading alongside the King James, it adds a sentence here that modern versions do not print: it is hard for thee to kick against the pricks, along with Saul’s trembling question about what the Lord would have him do. The words are genuine, in the sense that Jesus really did say them, and Luke records them when Paul retells the scene before Agrippa (26:14). But they are not in the Greek manuscripts at this point. A copyist, knowing the fuller version from chapter 26, filled them in here. So nothing has been lost from Scripture; the saying has simply been returned to the place where Luke actually put it. The image itself is worth keeping: a goad was the farmer’s spiked stick, and an ox that kicked back at it only drove the point deeper. Saul had been kicking for a while. Stephen’s face, Stephen’s prayer, the calm of the people he arrested: the goads had been at work on him long before the light.

In a sentence. Saul asked who he was, and the Lord answered that he was Jesus, whom Saul was persecuting, and told him to get up and go into the city, where he would be told what to do.

On a Tuesday. Write down the name of the person you think least likely ever to become a Christian, and pray for him by name this week. Not vaguely, and not with your expectations already lowered. If Christ could stop Saul, he can stop anyone. And if you are a believer who cannot name the day you were converted, stop envying other people’s stories. The question is not how you came to the road, but whose you are now.

For worship. I am Jesus. The whole of the Christian faith turns on the fact that the Crucified is not dead but speaking, and that he speaks first. Saul did not find Christ; Christ found Saul, at noon, at the city gate, with the warrants in his bag. And he did not answer the persecutor’s hatred with a single word of revenge. He said his own name, and gave him something to do. That is the sovereign grace of the risen Lord, and every one of his people has been on the receiving end of it.

verseByVerse.quote: The men who were traveling with him stood speechless, hearing the voice but seeing no one. Saul rose from the ground, and although his eyes were opened, he saw nothing. So they led him by the hand and brought him into Damascus.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The men who were traveling with him stood speechless, hearing the voice but seeing no one. Saul rose from the ground, and although his eyes were opened, he saw nothing. So they led him by the hand and brought him into Damascus.

The men who were traveling with him stood speechless. Now the picture, and Luke draws it without a word of comment. A party of armed men on the Damascus road, standing in the dust with nothing to say, and their leader on the ground unable to see. They came out of Jerusalem as an escort. They go into the city leading a blind man by the hand.

Hearing the voice but seeing no one. This half-verse has been a favourite of sceptics for a long time, and it deserves a straight answer. Luke says here that the men heard the voice. When Paul himself tells the story later in this same book, he says that those with him saw the light but did not hear the voice of the one speaking (22:9, as the King James and the older versions render it). Same author, same book, same event, and on the face of it a flat contradiction, which is why it turns up in every list of Bible errors ever compiled.

A sound, not the words. It dissolves on a careful reading, and not by special pleading. There is a difference between hearing a sound and hearing with understanding, much as we distinguish hearing someone from catching what they said. So the two sentences say precisely what any of us would say about the same afternoon: the men heard a noise but could not make out the words. It is just what happened when the Father spoke from heaven in John 12:29, and the crowd said it had thundered. Modern translations show this openly (the ESV renders 22:9 did not understand the voice), and the difficulty simply disappears. The seeing works the same way. They saw the light, which is why they were struck speechless; they did not see the person who spoke, which is why Luke says they saw no one. The event was real and public. The revelation was for Saul.

Proximity is not reception. Notice the pastoral point sitting underneath the grammar. The men beside him experienced the identical event, the same blaze, the same sound, the same road, and went away with nothing but a story about strange weather. Saul went away with a Lord. Being near revelation is not the same as receiving it, and the difference between the two was not in the light but in whom it was for. People can sit under the same sermon for years, a pew apart, and one hears a noise and the other hears the voice of Christ.

Saul rose from the ground, and although his eyes were opened, he saw nothing. Luke chooses to put it that way round, and the irony is not lost on Paul either, who spent the rest of his life writing about veils and blindness and light shining into hearts (2 Corinthians 3:14–16; 4:4–6). Here was a man who had never in his life been in any doubt about what he was looking at. He knew the law, he knew the tradition, he knew exactly who was in the right, and he could have set out his reasoning at any length required. His eyes are open and there is nothing in them. The man who thought he saw clearly was blind; now, physically blind, he will learn to see.

So they led him by the hand and brought him into Damascus. That is the detail to keep. The last time we saw Saul he was dragging people through doorways. He meant to lead prisoners out of Damascus; he is led into it, helpless, dependent, going wherever somebody else takes him, in the position of the people he came to arrest.

Was the blindness a punishment? It was more a mercy and a sign than a penalty. A punishment would have fitted the crime, and nothing in this chapter does. The blindness was the natural effect of the glory he had seen, and it gave him three days in which the whole world he had lived in could be taken down. It was also a living picture: the man who had been spiritually blind was made to feel his blindness so that he would know his sight, when it came, was a gift. Compare the sorcerer Elymas, who is struck blind for a time as a judgment for opposing the gospel (13:11). Saul was blinded on the way into the gospel, and his sight was given back with the Spirit.

In a sentence. His companions stood speechless, hearing the sound but seeing no one, and Saul got up from the ground but could see nothing, so they led him by the hand into Damascus.

On a Tuesday. Pride is the feeling of seeing perfectly well. If there is a subject on which you are completely certain and have stopped listening to anyone, it is worth asking God whether that is where you are blind. And if he has recently taken something from you, a confidence, a reputation, a plan you could see clearly, do not assume he is finished with you. Sometimes he has to put out the old light before the new one can be seen.

For worship. Christ did not argue Saul out of his blindness; he shone on him, and the man who had seen everything saw nothing. Then the Lord who is the light of the world had him led by the hand into the city like a child. That is how the God who said, Let light shine out of darkness, shines in our hearts to give the light of the knowledge of his glory in the face of Jesus Christ (2 Corinthians 4:6). Paul wrote that sentence. He was remembering this road.
verseByVerse.note: In 22:9 Paul says his companions did not understand the voice; they heard a sound but not the words.

verseByVerse.quote: And for three days he was without sight, and neither ate nor drank.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And for three days he was without sight, and neither ate nor drank.

For three days he was without sight, and neither ate nor drank. Three days of nothing. No sight, no food, and, the detail people skim, no water. Three days without drinking is not a devotional exercise; in that climate it is the edge of what a body will take. This is not a man keeping a fast. It is a man who has stopped functioning, in shock, in repentance, and, as verse 11 will tell us, in prayer.

The room in the dark. Try to picture it. He is in a strange city, in a borrowed house on a street called Straight, in the dark, with an escort outside who do not know what to do with him and a set of arrest warrants in a bag that nobody is going to use. Every certainty he possessed on the morning he left Jerusalem is gone, not weakened but gone, and the one thing he now knows for certain is that the people he was travelling to imprison were right about everything, and that he has spent his best years and his considerable gifts hunting the Messiah of Israel. He had much to think about: everything he had believed about Jesus, and everything he had done to Jesus’ people.

What he did with the time. Verse 11 tells us. He was praying. Not, one imagines, in the confident, well-formed manner of a Pharisee who had prayed every day of his life. Something else, in a room, with no idea what to say.

A death and a rising. The three days are worth noticing for the shape of them. He goes into darkness, everything he was dies there, and on the third day a man comes and he is raised up and washed. It is the shape of Jonah in the fish and of the Lord in the tomb. Paul would spend the rest of his life writing about being buried with Christ and raised with him (Romans 6:4), about the old self having been crucified, and about a new creation in which the old has passed away (2 Corinthians 5:17). He had lived it before he wrote a word of it, on the floor of somebody’s guest room.

For anyone in a collapse of certainty. There is something here for the person whose faith has come apart in his hands, or who has discovered that a thing he built a life on was not true, or who has been shown something about himself he cannot unsee. Saul’s three days were not the end of him, and they did not feel like anything but an end at the time. It is worth knowing that Scripture’s most spectacular conversion has a dark room in the middle of it, and that nobody in the house had the least idea what was going on.

What it does not mean. This sort of passage attracts imitators. Luke is not recommending three-day fasts, and there is no suggestion that Saul’s abstinence achieved anything or earned him his sight. The man was in shock. What the verse describes is a condition, not a technique.

Does God always bring people through darkness before conversion? No. Some, like Saul, are broken before they are healed. Others are drawn quietly: of Lydia Luke says simply that the Lord opened her heart to pay attention to what was said (16:14), and the Ethiopian went on his way rejoicing within an hour of meeting Philip (8:39). The darkness is not a stage that has to be passed through, and nobody should feel his conversion is suspect because it lacked one. What every conversion has in common is that the old self is put to death and a new one is raised by Christ. In some lives that takes three days on a floor; in others it happens over a cup of coffee and an open Bible.

In a sentence. For three days he was blind and neither ate nor drank.

On a Tuesday. If you are in a dark room of your own just now, do what Saul did: pray, even if the prayer has no shape and you do not know what to say. You do not need to understand what God is doing to keep talking to him. And if you know someone in that room, do not rush him out of it with explanations. Be the person who brings food on the third day.

For worship. The Lord who struck Saul down did not leave him on the road, and he did not leave him in the dark for a day longer than he needed to be there. Three days, and then a knock at the door. The God who brought Jonah up from the deep and raised his own Son on the third day was at work in that silent room, taking a man apart in order to make him new. He is still the God who calls light out of darkness, and who never wastes a night.

verseByVerse.quote: Now there was a disciple at Damascus named Ananias. The Lord said to him in a vision, "Ananias." And he said, "Here I am, Lord." And the Lord said to him, "Rise and go to the street called Straight, and at the house of Judas look for a man of Tarsus named Saul, for behold, he is praying,"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Now there was a disciple at Damascus named Ananias. The Lord said to him in a vision, “Ananias.” And he said, “Here I am, Lord.” And the Lord said to him, “Rise and go to the street called Straight, and at the house of Judas look for a man of Tarsus named Saul, for behold, he is praying,

Now there was a disciple at Damascus named Ananias. Luke introduces the most important minor character in the New Testament with six words. No office. No title. He is not an apostle, not one of the seven, not an elder, not a prophet. He is a Christian who lives in the city, and God has decided to hand him the most consequential errand of the first century. (He is not the Ananias of chapter 5; the name, meaning the LORD is gracious, was common.)

A man with something to lose. Paul fills in what Luke leaves out, when he tells the story in Jerusalem years later: Ananias was a devout man according to the law, well spoken of by all the Jews who lived there (22:12). That is a description of a man with a standing in the Jewish community of Damascus, and the errand he is about to be given would end it.

Here I am, Lord. The Lord calls him by name in a vision, and this is the reply. It is the answer Abraham gave on the mountain, and Jacob, and Moses at the bush, and Samuel in the dark, and Isaiah in the temple (Isaiah 6:8). It is not a promise to do the thing; Ananias has not been told what the thing is, and he will argue about it in three verses. It is simply the reply of a man who is available before he knows the assignment, which is a different and rarer disposition than willingness after the details are in.

Rise and go to the street called Straight. Then the directions, and their ordinariness is the point. It was a real road and it is still traceable: the long colonnaded thoroughfare that ran east and west through Roman Damascus, the main street every visitor could find, and it runs through the old city to this day. A precise, verifiable detail.

At the house of Judas look for a man of Tarsus named Saul. A street, a householder, a name and a home town. Tarsus was Saul’s birthplace, a proud university city in Cilicia, no mean city as he would later call it (21:39). God’s guidance in this passage has an address on it.

For behold, he is praying. And then the one piece of information the Lord offers about the man Ananias is being sent to. It is worth noticing what is not said. Not, he is safe now. Not, he has repented and you will find him much changed. Not, I have dealt with him. The single credential given for the most dangerous man in the province is that he is at that moment praying, which from anybody else would be no proof of anything at all. Saul had prayed every day of his life as a Pharisee. Now he prays as a broken man to the risen Jesus. From the Lord who is speaking, that is the whole case. A man who has begun to pray to Christ is a man Christ has already taken hold of.

Does God still guide his people by visions like this? God is free to do as he pleases, and Christians who believe he still sometimes speaks in dreams and visions are our brothers. But even in Acts such visions were rare and came at turning points in the founding of the church, and the more likely reading is that this kind of direct revelation belonged to that apostolic age. Ananias’s vision was not the normal way God guided his people then, and it is not the normal way now. We are guided by Scripture, which is sufficient for everything we need for faith and life (2 Timothy 3:16–17), and by prayer, wise counsel and the ordinary providences that open and close doors. Any impression that pulls against the plain teaching of Scripture is to be refused, however vivid. And the good news is that we do not need a vision to obey. Ananias’s great act was simply going to a house and loving a man. That is guidance anyone can follow today.

In a sentence. There was a disciple in Damascus named Ananias, and the Lord called him in a vision, and he answered, and the Lord told him to go to Straight Street, to the house of Judas, and ask for a man of Tarsus named Saul, who was praying.

On a Tuesday. God uses ordinary believers for extraordinary tasks, and almost always the task is a person at an address. Ask whether there is someone you have been sent to without a vision: the neighbour who has just lost her husband, the colleague who asked a question about church and was never followed up, the young man at the back who has stopped coming. Be ready to say, Here I am, Lord, before you know what it will cost.

For worship. The ascended Christ, who holds the universe together, knew the name of a street in Damascus and the name of the man whose house was on it. He knew which of his disciples lived nearby and what he was afraid of. That is the Lord of the church: not a remote power issuing general policy, but a Shepherd who knows his sheep and the doors they live behind, and who sends one of them to fetch another home.
verseByVerse.note: Straight Street still runs east–west through the old city of Damascus. Tarsus was a major city in Cilicia, known for learning.

verseByVerse.quote: and he has seen in a vision a man named Ananias come in and lay his hands on him so that he might regain his sight."
verseByVerse.commentary:
and he has seen in a vision a man named Ananias come in and lay his hands on him so that he might regain his sight.”

And he has seen in a vision a man named Ananias come in and lay his hands on him so that he might regain his sight. God has been at both ends of this the whole time. While Ananias is being given a street name in one part of Damascus, Saul has already been shown a picture of a man called Ananias coming through a door and putting his hands on him. Neither of them arranged it. Neither of them knew the other existed a week ago. And when Ananias finally walks into that room, the blind man on the other side of it will have been expecting him by name. Two visions, matching, just as God will prepare both Peter and Cornelius in the next chapter.

A kindness to both. It is worth seeing which way it runs. For Saul, three days into the dark with nothing to hold, it is the first concrete thing he has been given: somebody is coming, and here is his name. For Ananias, it means he is not walking in cold. The man he is dreading has been told he is on his way and what he is coming to do. And the sight to be restored is more than physical. It is a sign of the spiritual sight Saul is about to receive.

The door opened from the inside. Notice how the Lord deploys it. This verse is not narration addressed to the reader; it is still part of what he is saying to Ananias, and it is the last thing he says before Ananias objects. In other words, it is offered as a reason. Go, and by the way, he is expecting you, and he already knows your name. The Lord is not simply issuing an order. He is reasoning with a frightened man, and the argument he uses is that the door has already been opened from the inside.

The dreaded conversation. There is an application here for the conversation a Christian is quietly dreading: the apology owed, the subject that has to be raised, the person who needs to be spoken to and will not welcome it. It is very easy to assume one is walking in entirely unprepared, into a room where nothing has been done. Sometimes a great deal has been done, at the other end, by somebody with access to both sides of the door.

What it does not mean. A promise can be manufactured out of this that Scripture does not make. It is not a guarantee that every difficult conversation has been divinely prepared, or that obedience will always turn out to be safer than it looked. Ananias’s errand was genuinely dangerous and he was right to say so. What the verse establishes is narrower: that the God who sends people is already at work on the far side, and that the messenger is very rarely the first one there.

Why did the Lord not simply heal Saul himself? He could have, of course. The light that blinded him could have restored him on the spot. But Christ chose to give Saul his sight, his welcome and his baptism through a member of the church he had been persecuting. Saul needed to receive mercy from the hands of the people he had hunted, and to be taken into their family, not merely converted on his own. That is how the Lord ordinarily works still. He saves people by himself alone, but he brings them to faith through the word spoken by other believers (Romans 10:14), and he gathers them into a church. Nobody is meant to be a Christian by himself.

In a sentence. Saul had seen in a vision a man named Ananias come in and lay his hands on him so that he would see again.

On a Tuesday. If there is a conversation you have been avoiding because you are afraid of how it will go, pray for the other person before you pray for yourself. Ask God to be at work in him before you arrive. Then go. You may find, as Ananias did, that you are expected.

For worship. Christ works on both ends: preparing hearts to hear, and messengers to speak. He was in a dark room on Straight Street and in a believer’s house across the city at the same hour, arranging a meeting that neither man could have imagined. Nothing in his church happens by accident. The one who sits at the right hand of the Father is the Lord of every appointment, and he loves to bring his enemies and his friends into the same room and make them brothers.

verseByVerse.quote: But Ananias answered, "Lord, I have heard from many about this man, how much evil he has done to your saints at Jerusalem. And here he has authority from the chief priests to bind all who call on your name."
verseByVerse.commentary:
But Ananias answered, “Lord, I have heard from many about this man, how much evil he has done to your saints at Jerusalem. And here he has authority from the chief priests to bind all who call on your name.”

Lord, I have heard from many about this man. Ananias argues with God, and God does not rebuke him for it. That is the first thing to notice, and Luke reports the exchange without a syllable of disapproval. He is not being difficult. He is stating the case as any sane member of that congregation would state it. Reports have been coming up the road from Jerusalem for months: houses entered, people taken, a young man from Tarsus at the centre of it. Ananias almost certainly knew names. Some of the refugees who had run to Damascus were sitting in his own meetings, and they had told him what they had seen. Saul’s reputation had arrived well before Saul.

How much evil he has done to your saints at Jerusalem. One phrase in the objection is worth a moment on its own: your saints. It is the first time in Acts that Christians are called this, and it means simply the holy ones, hagioi, the people set apart for God. It is not a special class of especially pious believers; it is the ordinary name for all of them (Romans 1:7; 1 Corinthians 1:2). Your saints: they belong to Jesus, which is why harming them is harming him (v. 4). Ananias uses it of the men and women Saul had been hunting. Within a few years the man he is being sent to will be using the same word in letter after letter to describe ordinary congregations of fishermen and slaves and tradespeople, and once, describing himself, will say he is the very least of all the saints (Ephesians 3:8).

And here he has authority from the chief priests to bind all who call on your name. The second half of the objection is the sharper one. All. Ananias is describing a warrant that has his own name inside it. He is not being asked to visit a difficult man; he is being asked to walk into a house and identify himself, by name and as a Christian, to the officer sent to arrest him. And notice how he describes the believers: those who call on your name. That was the mark of a Christian from the beginning (2:21; Romans 10:13; 1 Corinthians 1:2). They called on Jesus as Lord, and they prayed to him.

Arguing with God. Scripture has a small tradition of people who answered God back at the moment of calling. Moses produced five separate objections at the bush, and God dealt with each. Gideon asked for the fleece twice. Jeremiah said he was too young. What distinguishes Ananias from Jonah is not that he kept his doubts to himself (he did not) but that he raised them in God’s presence and then did what he was told. Jonah raised nothing and went to the harbour.

Fear in better clothes. That is worth taking, because a certain kind of piety teaches people to suppress the objection and calls the suppression faith. It is not faith; it is usually fear wearing better clothes, and it tends to come out sideways later. Ananias tells God exactly what he thinks of the assignment, in plain words, with the reasons, and God answers him with an explanation rather than a reprimand. There is room in that conversation for a man to say what he actually thinks. The Psalms are full of it.

Where Christians differ: who are the saints? Roman Catholic and Orthodox churches use “saints” mainly for specially holy people, canonised after death, whose prayers are sought. Verdict: in the New Testament every believer is a saint, set apart by God in Christ (Ephesians 1:1; Philippians 1:1). Holiness of life should follow, but the title is given by grace, not earned. We pray to God alone, through Christ alone.

Is it right to pray to Jesus himself? Yes. The usual pattern of Christian prayer is to the Father, through the Son, by the Spirit (Ephesians 2:18), and that is how Jesus taught us to pray. But the first Christians also called directly on Jesus, as Stephen did while the stones were falling: Lord Jesus, receive my spirit (7:59). Ananias is talking to Jesus in this very verse. That is one of the clearest signs in the New Testament that the church worshipped Jesus as God, because a devout Jew would never pray to anyone less. So you may speak to the Lord Jesus freely, as to the Father, and you are not praying to a different God when you do. The three persons are one God, and every prayer offered in Christ’s name reaches him.

In a sentence. Ananias answered that he had heard from many people how much harm this man had done to the Lord’s saints in Jerusalem, and that he had come with authority from the chief priests to arrest all who call on the Lord’s name.

On a Tuesday. If you belong to Christ, you are a saint, not because you feel holy but because he has set you apart for himself. Live like one, in the ordinary places where nobody calls you anything. And if you are carrying an objection to something God has plainly asked of you, do not bury it. Bring it to him in so many words. Then, like Ananias, get up and go.

For worship. Christ calls his people his saints, and he calls them that while they are still frightened, still arguing and still very far from finished. He did not wait for Ananias to stop objecting before he answered him; he reasoned with him, patiently, as a friend. That is the Lord we pray to: holy enough to set us apart, and gentle enough to hear our fears in full.
verseByVerse.note: “Saints” means those set apart as God’s holy people — all believers.

verseByVerse.quote: But the Lord said to him, "Go, for he is a chosen instrument of mine to carry my name before the Gentiles and kings and the children of Israel. For I will show him how much he must suffer for the sake of my name."
verseByVerse.commentary:
But the Lord said to him, “Go, for he is a chosen instrument of mine to carry my name before the Gentiles and kings and the children of Israel. For I will show him how much he must suffer for the sake of my name.”

Go, for he is a chosen instrument of mine. God answers the objection, and the answer is not reassurance. It is information. The word for chosen, eklogē, is the word of election, the same that Paul will use of God’s choosing grace in Romans 9 and 11. Saul was chosen by Christ before he knew it, before he was born (Galatians 1:15), and long before he deserved anything except judgment. Not because he was good, but because God chose him: by the grace of God I am what I am, he would write (1 Corinthians 15:9–10).

A chosen vessel. The word behind instrument, skeuos, is the ordinary one for a container or a piece of equipment: a jar, a pot, a vessel, the sort of word that turns up in an inventory. Saul is not being described as a hero, a champion or a great man. He is a receptacle that has been picked out, and the value is entirely in what it is for and who chose it. Paul evidently never forgot the word. Writing to Corinth years later about the ministry he had been given, he says we have this treasure in jars of clay, to show that the surpassing power belongs to God and not to us (2 Corinthians 4:7). He is using the same term about himself, and he had heard it first in a sentence he was not present for.

To carry my name before the Gentiles and kings and the children of Israel. Then the destinations, and they are the table of contents for the rest of the book. The Gentiles are named first, which would have been an extraordinary thing to say in those first years (13:46–48); the kings are Agrippa in chapter 26 and, by the end, Caesar himself; the children of Israel are the synagogue in every city, which is where Paul begins every time. And he is to carry the name, as one carries something precious through a crowd. It is the name, not his own, that he is entrusted with.

For I will show him how much he must suffer for the sake of my name. And then the sentence which is the reason this passage cannot be preached as a success story. It is joined to the commission by a conjunction, not separated from it by a paragraph. The calling and the cost arrive in the same breath, spoken to a third party before the man himself has been told anything. The little word must, dei, is Luke’s word for divine necessity, the word Jesus used of his own suffering (Luke 9:22). And there is an exchange in it that is hard to miss: Saul had spent a year making people suffer on account of that name, and the first thing said about his future is how much he will suffer for it. Not as punishment, because his sins were forgiven, but as the cost of carrying the name of a crucified Lord.

What that meant in practice. It is not left to the imagination, because Paul eventually listed it (2 Corinthians 11:23–28). Five times he received thirty-nine lashes from his own people; three times he was beaten with Roman rods; once he was stoned and left for dead; three times shipwrecked, and a night and a day adrift at sea.
