Add hunger, cold, sleeplessness, and the daily pressure of anxiety for all the churches. That is the career being announced in verse 16, and God announces it as part of the reason he is giving Ananias to persuade him to go.

What it does not mean. A guard is needed, because this can be turned into a formula. Not every calling carries this measure of suffering, and a Christian whose life has been comparatively gentle has not been overlooked or given a second-rate commission. Scripture nowhere makes hardship the proof of authenticity, and men have done real damage by implying it. But the verse is a permanent corrective to a way of speaking about the Christian life that has become almost standard: the presentation of Christ as the route to a better, smoother, more successful version of the life one already has. The Lord’s own summary of what he was calling his greatest servant to was: he will carry my name a very long way, and it will cost him everything he has.

Was Saul chosen only for service, or for salvation too? Both, and they cannot be pulled apart. In this verse the emphasis falls on service: Saul is chosen as an instrument for a task. But Paul himself traced his salvation back to the same choosing grace. God set him apart before he was born and called him by grace (Galatians 1:15), and he received mercy so that Christ might display his perfect patience in him as an example to those who were to believe (1 Timothy 1:16). The same is true of every believer: chosen in Christ before the foundation of the world (Ephesians 1:4), and created in Christ Jesus for good works that God prepared beforehand (Ephesians 2:10). You were not chosen because you were useful. You were chosen in love, and then made useful.

In a sentence. The Lord told Ananias to go, for Saul was his chosen instrument to carry his name before the Gentiles and kings and the people of Israel, and he would show Saul how much he must suffer for the sake of his name.

On a Tuesday. If following Christ is costing you something this week, a friendship, a promotion, a reputation, do not conclude that you have taken a wrong turning. The cost was in the calling from the start, and your Lord said so. And if you have been treating your faith as a way of getting a smoother life, let this verse reset the expectation gently: he promises himself, and his presence in the suffering, not an easy road.

For worship. Christ chooses his instruments by grace, the clay jars nobody else would have picked, and he fills them with a treasure that is not theirs. He chose the man who had shed his people’s blood and made him the herald of his name to the nations. And when he called him to suffer, he was calling him to walk the road he himself had walked first, all the way to the cross. To bear the name of such a Lord is not a burden borne grudgingly. It is the highest honour a sinner can be given.

verseByVerse.quote: So Ananias departed and entered the house. And laying his hands on him he said, "Brother Saul, the Lord Jesus who appeared to you on the road by which you came has sent me so that you may regain your sight and be filled with the Holy Spirit." And immediately something like scales fell from his eyes, and he regained his sight. Then he rose and was baptized;
verseByVerse.commentary:
So Ananias departed and entered the house. And laying his hands on him he said, “Brother Saul, the Lord Jesus who appeared to you on the road by which you came has sent me so that you may regain your sight and be filled with the Holy Spirit.” And immediately something like scales fell from his eyes, and he regained his sight. Then he rose and was baptized;

So Ananias departed and entered the house. Seven words for the bravest thing anybody does in this chapter. Obedience despite fear. He had said what he thought, been answered, and gone.

Brother Saul. Ananias lays his hands on him, and the first word out of his mouth is brother. Two of the most beautiful words in Acts. Stand in the doorway and weigh them. In the room is a blind man from Tarsus who arrived in Damascus with a warrant that covers Ananias by name. Somewhere in that house is a bag containing letters from the high priest. Ananias belongs to a congregation swollen with refugees who ran from this man, and he will have heard over and over what happened in Jerusalem, quite possibly from people who lost somebody. He has every reason to open with a question, or a condition, or at the very least a wary silence. He opens with a family word, and he uses it before Saul has said anything at all. Grace makes enemies family.

The Lord Jesus who appeared to you on the road by which you came has sent me. What follows is careful and generous. Ananias tells him he knows, and specifies the road, so that Saul understands he is not being humoured. He confirms that the one who met him was Jesus. Then the two things he has come for: sight, and the Holy Spirit.

So that you may regain your sight and be filled with the Holy Spirit. It is worth registering who is doing this. Not Peter. Not John. Not an apostle at all, and not anyone we meet again except in Paul’s own retelling (22:12). The man who lays hands on Paul, restores his sight, tells him he will be filled with the Spirit, and very probably baptises him, is a disciple in a provincial city about whom nothing else whatever is known. There is no fixed pattern here requiring an apostle for the Spirit to be given. Paul would insist for the rest of his life that he had not received his gospel from any man (Galatians 1:11–12), and it is perfectly consistent, because what Ananias gave him was not a gospel. It was his eyes, a welcome, and water.

Was this a second blessing after conversion? No. The filling with the Spirit came as part of Saul’s conversion; Ananias came to him within days of the road, and the Spirit came with the restoring of his sight and his baptism. It was not a later stage that every Christian must seek.

And immediately something like scales fell from his eyes, and he regained his sight. The doctor writing this reaches for the nearest physical comparison and marks it as a comparison: something like. Whatever came away, Luke will not pretend to know exactly what it was. We still say the scales fell from my eyes, and we have this verse to thank for it.

Then he rose and was baptized. And then, with his sight barely back, he got up and was baptised. The first thing the man does when he can see again is get into the water. There is no interval, no period of assessment, no probation while the church works out whether it can trust him. He had been in the dark for three days, and the moment the light came back he went and was washed. Baptism follows faith, at once.

Was Saul converted on the road, or at his baptism? He was Christ’s from the road: he called Jesus Lord, he prayed, and Ananias greets him as Brother (v. 17). Baptism was the outward sign and public confession. When Ananias later says be baptized and wash away your sins (22:16), he joins the sign to what it signifies, as Scripture often does; the washing is by faith in Christ, calling on his name.

Should we baptise people as quickly today? In Acts, those who professed faith were baptised promptly, usually the same day (2:41; 8:38; 16:33), and that pattern should shape us: baptism belongs at the beginning of the Christian life, not as a reward at the end of a long course. We hold, with the London Baptist Confession, that baptism is for those who profess repentance toward God and faith in our Lord Jesus Christ (London Baptist Confession 29.2), so a church rightly asks for a credible profession first and takes time to hear it. Our paedobaptist brothers baptise the children of believers as well, and we honour them as faithful Christians while we differ. But no one should be kept waiting for years to prove himself. If you trust Christ and have not been baptised, speak to your pastor this week.

How could God forgive a man like this? Saul had approved of murder and dragged families to prison. Many people quietly wonder whether some sins are too great. Paul answered the question himself: though formerly I was a blasphemer, persecutor and insolent opponent, I received mercy, and Christ Jesus came into the world to save sinners, of whom I am the foremost (1 Timothy 1:13–15). He adds that he was shown mercy precisely as an example, so that no one would ever think himself beyond it (1:16). The blood of Christ is enough for the worst thing you have done. The only sin that is never forgiven is the one never brought to him.

In a sentence. Ananias went into the house, laid his hands on him and called him Brother Saul, saying the Lord Jesus who appeared to him on the road had sent him so that Saul would see again and be filled with the Spirit, and at once something like scales fell from his eyes, he could see, and he got up and was baptised.

On a Tuesday. Is there someone you find it hard to call brother or sister: a person who hurt you, a believer from a background you distrust, a new convert with an ugly past? Grace calls you to say the family word first, before he has proved anything. That does not mean pretending nothing happened or setting aside wise safeguards. It means meeting a person Christ has received as Christ received you.

For worship. Brother Saul. In those two words the whole gospel stands in a doorway. The Lord Jesus had forgiven his persecutor before a single apology was offered, and sent one of the persecuted to say so. The blood that cleanses the sinner also makes him a son, and every son a brother. That is what the risen Christ does with his enemies: he gives them eyes, he gives them his Spirit, and he gives them a family.

verseByVerse.quote: and taking food, he was strengthened. For some days he was with the disciples at Damascus. And immediately he proclaimed Jesus in the synagogues, saying, "He is the Son of God."
verseByVerse.commentary:
and taking food, he was strengthened. For some days he was with the disciples at Damascus. And immediately he proclaimed Jesus in the synagogues, saying, “He is the Son of God.”

And taking food, he was strengthened. Luke has not forgotten that this man has not eaten for three days. Before the theology there is a meal, and somebody in that house made it. The Lord who restored his eyes also cared that he was hungry.

For some days he was with the disciples at Damascus. The people he came to arrest became his family. He sat at their tables, slept under their roofs and learned their hymns, and some of them will have been the very refugees whose names were in his letters.

And immediately he proclaimed Jesus in the synagogues. Then the sentence, and the geography in it is the irony Luke has been setting up since verse 2. Saul had carried letters addressed to the synagogues at Damascus, authorising him to search them for followers of the Way. He now walks into those same synagogues, with the same letters presumably still in his luggage, and preaches the thing he came to stamp out. One imagines the faces. (Paul tells us that at some point in these years he also went away into Arabia, the Nabataean kingdom to the south and east, and then returned to Damascus, Galatians 1:17. Luke compresses the time.)

He is the Son of God. What he preaches is worth weighing, because of how soon it is. Not: this man was a prophet, or a teacher, or even the Messiah; that comes two verses later. The very first recorded sermon of the apostle Paul, preached within days of his baptism by a man who had spent his adult life defending the oneness of God against every blasphemy, is that Jesus of Nazareth is God’s Son. It is the only time in Acts that the title is used in preaching like this (but compare 13:33), and it is exactly the claim for which the council had condemned Jesus (Luke 22:70–71). Whatever else his conversion did, it did not leave him working his way toward that conclusion gradually. He had met the person and drawn the only possible inference on the road (compare Galatians 1:16; 2 Corinthians 5:17).

What did Saul mean by “Son of God”? The title gathers up two streams of Scripture into one confession. First, it is a claim to full deity. To call Jesus God’s own Son, in the unique sense, is to say he shares the very nature of God, which is exactly how his hearers understood it: Jesus was charged with “making himself equal with God” because he called God his own Father (John 5:18; 19:7). “Son” here speaks not of a beginning or of a lesser rank but of sameness of nature and eternal relation: as an earthly son shares his father’s humanity, the divine Son shares the Father’s deity, eternally, of one substance with him, “begotten, not made.” Second, “Son of God” was a royal, messianic title: the promised king of David’s line was called God’s son (2 Samuel 7:14; Psalm 2:7), so to say “Jesus is the Son of God” is also to say he is the Christ, the anointed King, which is just where Saul’s preaching goes next, “proving that Jesus was the Christ” (v. 22). In Christ the two meet: the true Davidic King who is himself truly God.

One guard against misunderstanding. Scripture calls angels and even believers “sons of God” (Job 1:6; John 1:12), but those are sons by creation or by adopting grace. Jesus is the Son, the “only-begotten” (monogenēs, John 3:16), Son by eternal right and by nature, not made a son and not adopted. We become sons only through him. So this short sentence is the gospel in miniature: the man Jesus, crucified and risen, is God the Son and the royal Messiah, worthy of all trust, worship, and obedience, and it is the very confession that saves, “that you may believe that Jesus is the Christ, the Son of God, and that by believing you may have life in his name” (John 20:31; compare 1 John 4:15). And here is the wonder of the moment: the man who had set out to destroy everyone who made this claim is now the first in Damascus to make it.

Should a new believer start speaking about Christ straight away? Yes, in the sense Saul did: telling people who Jesus is and what he has done. You do not need a theology degree to say that Jesus is the Son of God and that he has changed your life; the man born blind in John 9 had been a believer for an afternoon when he said, I was blind, now I see. What a new believer should not do is rush into teaching or leading others, and the next verses show the church keeping that distinction. Speak of Christ freely and early. Take on responsibility slowly.

In a sentence. He ate and regained his strength, stayed some days with the disciples in Damascus, and at once began proclaiming Jesus in the synagogues, saying that he is the Son of God.

On a Tuesday. If someone asked you today who Jesus is, what would your first sentence be? Saul’s was not about himself, his experience or what Jesus could do for his listeners. It was about the person. Practise saying it plainly, in your own words, so that when the moment comes you are not fumbling. And if you have a past that people know about, do not hide from it. A changed life is the loudest sermon in the synagogue.

For worship. Jesus is the Son of God. The Pharisee who had defended the oneness of God against every blasphemy now bowed before the eternal Son, of one nature with the Father, who had come down into David’s line, died under the curse and risen in power. And that confession is the very centre of heaven’s worship: the Son who was with the Father before the world began, who shares his glory, who reigns now as the anointed King. The first words of the converted persecutor are the words every redeemed voice will be singing for ever.
verseByVerse.note: Paul says he also went to Arabia (the Nabataean kingdom) before returning to Damascus.

verseByVerse.quote: And all who heard him were amazed and said, "Is not this the man who made havoc in Jerusalem of those who called upon this name? And has he not come here for this purpose, to bring them bound before the chief priests?" But Saul increased all the more in strength, and confounded the Jews who lived in Damascus by proving that Jesus was the Christ.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And all who heard him were amazed and said, “Is not this the man who made havoc in Jerusalem of those who called upon this name? And has he not come here for this purpose, to bring them bound before the chief priests?” But Saul increased all the more in strength, and confounded the Jews who lived in Damascus by proving that Jesus was the Christ.

Is not this the man who made havoc in Jerusalem of those who called upon this name? All who heard him were amazed, and the synagogue’s reaction is one of the more understandable in Scripture. They know exactly who this is and exactly what he came for, because the letters had been announced in advance and arrangements had presumably been made. And here he is, in the seat, saying the opposite of what he was sent to say. The word they use of his career, porthēsas, is a violent one: made havoc, the language of sacking a city or laying waste to a country. It is not their invention either. Paul takes the same word and uses it of himself, twice, when he writes to the Galatians (Galatians 1:13, 23). He never softened the vocabulary. Whatever else he became, he did not become a man who described his past in careful language.

But Saul increased all the more in strength. Then two verbs describing what he did next, and both are worth having. The first is the one Paul later uses of being strengthened by Christ, the word behind I can do all things through him who strengthens me (Philippians 4:13). He is not describing natural confidence returning. Something was being supplied.

And confounded the Jews who lived in Damascus by proving that Jesus was the Christ. The Greek word for proving, symbibazōn, means to bring things together, to knit or join them side by side; the image is of laying two things next to each other until the fit is obvious. That is precisely what Paul does in every letter and every sermon recorded of him: this text and that event, laid alongside one another, the promise beside the fulfilment, until the listener can see they belong together. The method of a lifetime was operating from the first days after his conversion, because the raw material, a first-class rabbinic training in the Scriptures, had been in place for twenty years and was now pointing the other way. God does not throw away the gifts and training of the people he converts. He turns them round.

Ability arrived at once; deployment did not. There is a caution here that the passage itself supplies if one keeps reading. Saul is formidable immediately, and he is also, within a few years, sent quietly home to Tarsus and not heard of again for the best part of a decade. The New Testament elsewhere warns against putting a recent convert into leadership, lest he become puffed up with conceit (1 Timothy 3:6), and the most gifted convert in the history of the church spent something like ten years in obscurity before anybody came to fetch him. The interval was not an accident.

How can I show someone that Jesus is the Christ? Do what Saul did, on a smaller scale: lay the Scriptures and the facts side by side. Read Isaiah 53 with a friend and ask whom it describes. Read Psalm 22 next to the crucifixion. Show how the promises to Abraham and David land on Jesus, and how the empty tomb is the hinge of it all (1 Corinthians 15:3–8). You do not need to win every argument, and you will not convert anyone by cleverness, because only the Spirit opens blind eyes. But God uses honest explanation of his word, and it is far better to open the Bible with someone than to argue round it.

In a sentence. Everyone who heard him was amazed, asking whether this was not the man who had ravaged those in Jerusalem who called on this name and had come here to take them back as prisoners, but Saul grew more and more powerful and baffled the Jews in Damascus by proving that Jesus is the Christ.

On a Tuesday. God can use your training, your mind and your past for his glory, including the parts of your past you are ashamed of. Write down one skill or piece of knowledge you have that could serve Christ’s people, and offer it to your church. And if you are newly converted and gifted, be patient with those who ask you to wait before you lead. The waiting is part of the training.

For worship. The Christ whom Saul had denied was the one to whom all his Scriptures pointed, and now every text he had memorised as a boy lit up with the face of Jesus. That is the glory of the Old Testament: it is not a collection of separate stories but one long promise, and Christ is its yes and amen (2 Corinthians 1:20). The God who wrote the promise has kept it, and he gave the persecutor eyes to see it fit.

verseByVerse.quote: When many days had passed, the Jews plotted to kill him, but their plot became known to Saul. They were watching the gates day and night in order to kill him,
verseByVerse.commentary:
When many days had passed, the Jews plotted to kill him, but their plot became known to Saul. They were watching the gates day and night in order to kill him,

When many days had passed. Luke’s phrase is doing a great deal of quiet work. Laid against Paul’s own account, those days include a departure into Arabia and a return to Damascus, and the whole stretch comes to about three years (Galatians 1:17–18). Luke is not concealing it; he is writing the story of a movement and moving at the movement’s pace.

The Jews plotted to kill him. The hunter becomes the hunted. Paul describes the same episode in a letter and adds a detail Luke omits: the governor under King Aretas was guarding the city in order to seize him (2 Corinthians 11:32–33). Aretas was the Nabataean king whose territory ran south and east of Damascus, and his official was involved in the watch on the gates. So this was not merely a synagogue quarrel that turned nasty. Within three years of his conversion, Saul’s preaching had become a matter for the civil authority of a neighbouring kingdom. The suffering Jesus promised (v. 16) has begun.

Charge and muscle. The two accounts fit together without strain, and the shape is familiar from this whole book: the complaint comes from one quarter and the force from another. It happened to Jesus in front of Pilate, to Paul again at Philippi and Thessalonica and Corinth. Religious objection supplies the charge; the state supplies the soldiers.

But their plot became known to Saul. They were watching the gates day and night in order to kill him. Damascus was a walled city with a limited number of gates, and a watch on all of them, around the clock, is not a gesture. Somebody was paying for it. The city was sealed. And set this beside chapter 8, three years earlier, and notice what has happened to the man. There, he was the one going house after house. There, he was the one with the authority, the letters and the men. Here he is the one being hunted through a city, unable to use the gates, dependent on a handful of disciples to get him out alive. The exchange was quick and it was complete, and it is the pattern of everything that follows: for the next thirty years Paul is on the receiving end of precisely what he used to administer.

Why did God let his new servant be hunted so soon? Because this is what the Lord had said would happen (v. 16), and because the servant is not above his master (John 15:20). Persecution was not a sign that something had gone wrong with Saul’s conversion; it was a sign that it was real. Notice, too, that the plot became known to Saul. God did not prevent the danger, but he watched over his man in the middle of it and kept him until his work was done. That is how he usually protects his people: not always from trouble, but always through it, and never one day beyond his appointed time.

In a sentence. After many days had gone by, the Jews plotted to kill him, but Saul learned of their plan; they were watching the city gates day and night so that they could kill him.

On a Tuesday. If you are opposed for your faith this week, at work, in your family, online, do not be surprised and do not take it as proof that you have failed. Ask instead whether you have given offence by Christ or only by your manner. If it is by Christ, rejoice quietly. You are in good company.

For worship. The persecutor became the persecuted, and so began to share in the sufferings of the Lord he had hunted. Christ himself was watched, plotted against and handed over by religious men to the soldiers of the state. Every servant who walks that road walks in his footsteps, and the Lord who was raised from the dead watches the gates of every city where his people are hunted. Not one of them is taken a moment before he says.
verseByVerse.note: “Many days” probably covers about three years. Paul adds that the governor under King Aretas was guarding the city.

verseByVerse.quote: but his disciples took him by night and let him down through an opening in the wall, lowering him in a basket.
verseByVerse.commentary:
but his disciples took him by night and let him down through an opening in the wall, lowering him in a basket.

But his disciples took him by night and let him down through an opening in the wall, lowering him in a basket. The most famous escape in the New Testament, and it is entirely undignified. Picture the mechanics. The house is built into the city wall, which was ordinary enough in ancient cities; there is an opening, a window probably. The basket is a large woven hamper, the kind used for carrying produce, big enough to hold a man if he draws his knees up. It is dark. A rope is tied on. And the future apostle to the Gentiles, the man who will stand in front of kings, is folded into a fruit basket and let down over a wall by people who are hoping the rope holds. The great Pharisee, who came with letters of authority, leaves in a basket in the dark, like the spies Rahab let down from her window at Jericho (Joshua 2:15).

The boast of a basket. He never forgot it, and what he did with the memory is the remarkable part. Years later, writing to the Corinthian church about the men who were undermining him with their credentials, he says that if he must boast he will boast of the things that show his weakness, and then he gives a list: labours, imprisonments, beatings, shipwrecks, hunger, the pressure of the churches. And the item he chooses to end on, the climax of the whole catalogue, is the basket (2 Corinthians 11:30–33). Of everything in a life that included being caught up into the third heaven, he selected as his boast the night he was lowered out of a window like a sack of figs.

The destruction of a category. That is not false modesty and it is not a joke. His rivals were competing on the strength of their standing; Paul answers by producing the single most humiliating moment of his career and putting it at the top of his own list of qualifications. He had understood something about how God works that they had not: my power is made perfect in weakness (2 Corinthians 12:9). The basket was where he learned it. God humbles his servants, not to crush them, but so that the glory will go where it belongs.

Is it cowardly to run? One thing should be said plainly, because it releases a great many people from an unnecessary burden. Saul ran away. He did not stay and preach and take what came; he went over the wall at night and left the city. There is no hint of reproach in the text, and the Lord himself had told his disciples that when they were persecuted in one town they should flee to the next (Matthew 10:23). Courage in Scripture is not the refusal to leave. Paul stood his ground on plenty of occasions and left quietly on others, and he seems to have had no rule about it beyond the work continuing.

So when should a Christian flee, and when stay? A rough guide from Scripture: it is right to flee when staying would achieve nothing but your death or imprisonment and the work can go on elsewhere, as here, and as when Jesus himself withdrew from those who sought to kill him before his hour had come (John 8:59; 10:39). It is right to stay when leaving would mean denying Christ, or abandoning people in your care who cannot leave with you; a shepherd who runs and leaves the sheep is a hired hand (John 10:12–13). Between those two, pray, take counsel from your church, and do not despise yourself for choosing life. The Lord wants living witnesses as well as faithful martyrs.

His disciples. And note who did it. He has been a Christian for perhaps three years and there are already people in Damascus who are his, men and women he has won to Christ. They put him in the basket, and they held the rope.

In a sentence. But his disciples took him by night and let him down through an opening in the wall, lowering him in a basket.

On a Tuesday. Think of your most humiliating moment as a Christian, the time you looked weak, foolish or out of your depth. Instead of burying it, thank God for it, and ask what it taught you about his strength. God’s servants are not too proud for the basket. And if someone you know is in danger or distress, be one of the people who holds the rope.

For worship. The Lord who would one day send Paul before Caesar first sent him over a wall in a basket, and both journeys were equally in his hand. Christ’s strength is made perfect in weakness, because he himself came in weakness: born in a borrowed stable, carried out of reach of Herod by night, crucified in shame. The King of glory does not need his servants to look impressive. He needs them to be his, and he holds the rope.

parallels.desc: let down in a basket through a window in the wall

verseByVerse.quote: And when he had come to Jerusalem, he attempted to join the disciples. And they were all afraid of him, for they did not believe that he was a disciple. But Barnabas took him and brought him to the apostles and declared to them how on the road he had seen the Lord, who spoke to him, and how at Damascus he had preached boldly in the name of Jesus.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And when he had come to Jerusalem, he attempted to join the disciples. And they were all afraid of him, for they did not believe that he was a disciple. But Barnabas took him and brought him to the apostles and declared to them how on the road he had seen the Lord, who spoke to him, and how at Damascus he had preached boldly in the name of Jesus.

And when he had come to Jerusalem, he attempted to join the disciples. And they were all afraid of him. It is the loneliest sentence in the chapter. The last time Saul was in Jerusalem he was emptying houses; the people now shutting their doors are the ones who got away, or whose relatives did not. Their fear is not weak faith. It is arithmetic. A man with his record turning up claiming to be one of them is exactly what an informer would do. Was it a trick? Luke says they did not believe that he was a disciple, which is put charitably. They thought he was lying. So here is Saul, three years after the road, no longer welcome in the synagogue and not admitted by the church, with a price on him in Damascus and nowhere at all to stand.

But Barnabas took him and brought him to the apostles. And then one man crosses the room. Took him means took hold of him: he laid hands on the man everybody else was backing away from, walked him in, and vouched for him out loud. Barnabas was a respected believer, a Levite from Cyprus whose name meant son of encouragement (4:36), and it is the second time Luke has shown us this man doing the same kind of thing. The first was a field sold and the money laid down without a speech; this is a reputation put at risk on behalf of somebody with none. If Barnabas was wrong, he had just introduced an assassin to the entire leadership of the church. Years later he would take the same kind of risk on John Mark (15:37–39), and be proved right again.

The door the Gentile mission came through. It is worth saying plainly what the New Testament would look like without this paragraph. Nobody else moved. There is no indication that the apostles sent for Saul, or that the church debated it and came round. One man with no office beyond a nickname decided to believe a story that everybody else found incredible, and the entire Gentile mission came through that door.

And declared to them how on the road he had seen the Lord. Barnabas tells how the Lord had spoken to him, and how at Damascus he had preached boldly in the name of Jesus. He tells the two things that mattered: that Saul had met the risen Lord, and that his life since had matched his claim. A testimony and a track record. That is still the right way to receive a new believer whose past makes people nervous.

The apostles, or two of them? Set this beside Paul’s own account of the same visit and a question surfaces. Luke says Barnabas brought him to the apostles. Paul says that when he finally went up to Jerusalem he saw Cephas, and stayed fifteen days, and saw none of the other apostles except James the Lord’s brother (Galatians 1:18–19). Plural in one, and pointedly not plural in the other. They fit without strain once you see what each writer is doing. Luke is describing Saul’s reception, that the church’s leadership received him, which is the whole point of the paragraph, and uses the collective term for that body, as we might say a man was taken to meet the board when in fact two directors were in the office that week. Paul is under oath, so to speak: he is arguing to the Galatians that he did not get his gospel secondhand from Jerusalem, so he counts heads with deliberate precision and keeps the number as small as honesty allows. His case depends on it having been a short and limited visit; Luke’s case depends on it having happened at all. And notice that Paul’s two names are exactly the two who mattered for the introduction: Peter, the leading apostle, and James, the head of the Jerusalem church. Barnabas got him in front of the men whose word would settle it.

The timing. It fits the same way. Read alone, Luke’s account gives the impression of a swift sequence, and he does not pause to say that three years in Arabia and Damascus lie between the road and this doorway (Galatians 1:17–18; and see v. 30). That is not concealment. Luke is writing the story of a movement and moves at the pace of the movement; Paul is writing his own defence and needs the calendar. Neither of them is telling you something the other denies.

How can I be a Barnabas without being naive? Barnabas did not simply feel generous; he knew the facts. He had evidently heard Saul’s story, checked what had happened in Damascus, and judged it true before he put his name to it. So take time to listen to the person others are wary of, find out what has actually changed, and then speak up for him. At the same time, welcoming a repentant sinner never means ignoring real dangers. Where someone has abused or harmed others, a church must keep proper safeguards in place and protect the vulnerable, while still offering the gospel and fellowship. Grace and wisdom are not opposites. Barnabas had both, and the church was safer for it, not less safe.

In a sentence. When Saul came to Jerusalem and tried to join the disciples, they were all afraid of him, not believing he was a disciple, but Barnabas took him to the apostles and told them how on the road he had seen the Lord, who had spoken to him, and how in Damascus he had preached boldly in the name of Jesus.

On a Tuesday. Be a Barnabas. Think of the newcomer at church whom nobody quite knows what to do with, the person with the awkward history, the believer from a background that makes others uneasy. Find out his story. Sit with him. Introduce him to someone. One person crossing the room can change the course of a life, and occasionally of the whole church.

For worship. Christ has an advocate before the Father for every one of his people (1 John 2:1), and he took the far greater risk. He did not merely vouch for sinners; he put his own name and his own blood on the line for people with records far worse than their reputations. Barnabas walked Saul into a room of frightened apostles. Jesus Christ brings us into the presence of the holy God and says, this one is mine. Every Barnabas in the church is a small picture of him.
verseByVerse.note: Barnabas was a respected believer from Cyprus.

parallels.desc: Paul visits Cephas and James

verseByVerse.quote: So he went in and out among them at Jerusalem, preaching boldly in the name of the Lord. And he spoke and disputed against the Hellenists. But they were seeking to kill him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
So he went in and out among them at Jerusalem, preaching boldly in the name of the Lord. And he spoke and disputed against the Hellenists. But they were seeking to kill him.

So he went in and out among them at Jerusalem, preaching boldly in the name of the Lord. The phrase in and out is an Old Testament way of describing somebody’s ordinary comings and goings (Deuteronomy 28:6; 1 Samuel 18:16). It means he was simply part of the household now, moving about the city with them, no longer at the door. And he was bold. Boldness, parrēsia, plain and fearless speech, is Luke’s mark of the Spirit-filled witness all through this book (4:13, 29, 31).

And he spoke and disputed against the Hellenists. Then Luke names the people he argued with, and the choice ought to stop a reader. These are the Greek-speaking Jews of the Jerusalem synagogues: the same circle Stephen had argued with in chapter 6, who could not withstand the wisdom and the Spirit with which he spoke, and whose response was to plant false witnesses and have him killed. Saul had been at that killing, holding the coats and approving (7:58; 8:1). So he has walked straight back to the room where it happened and taken up the argument that got Stephen stoned, on Stephen’s side, against Stephen’s opponents. Stephen’s mantle has fallen on the man who held the coats. Luke does not comment.

A word on who “the Hellenists” were. Their fuller profile is at 6:1 and 6:9: the term, as the ESV notes, means Greek-speaking Jews, men of the diaspora, raised in the Greek language and culture, many with synagogues of their own in Jerusalem (such as the Synagogue of the Freedmen, 6:9). The word names a person’s language and culture, not his faith: in 6:1 it labels Greek-speaking Jewish believers, whereas here, as with Stephen’s opponents, it means unbelieving Greek-speaking Jews. And there is a sharp irony in Saul disputing with them: a man of Tarsus in Cilicia (6:9), he was himself a Hellenist, very likely once standing with this same circle against Stephen, and now he turns to plead the name of Jesus among his own former camp, and meets the very answer Stephen met.

But they were seeking to kill him. The last clause deserves counting. That is the second organised attempt on Saul’s life in this one chapter, the Damascus gates in verse 24 and now Jerusalem, and he has been a Christian for about three years. He had been warned. What was said to Ananias about him was not that he would be protected but that he would be shown how much he must suffer for the name, and the instalments have started arriving before he has preached outside two cities.

Was Stephen’s death wasted, then? It looked like it at the time: a brilliant young preacher silenced in his first public season, and the church scattered. But Stephen died praying for the men who stoned him, Lord, do not hold this sin against them (7:60), and one of those men is now preaching Stephen’s message in Stephen’s synagogue. Augustine said that if Stephen had not prayed, the church would not have had Paul. Whether or not one can draw the line so straight, the pattern is plain: no faithful witness for Christ is ever wasted, even when it seems to end in failure. God answers prayers in ways the one who prayed may never see this side of glory.

In a sentence. So Saul stayed with them and moved freely about Jerusalem, preaching boldly in the name of the Lord, and he talked and debated with the Greek-speaking Jews, but they were trying to kill him.

On a Tuesday. Is there a place, a family, a workplace, an old circle of friends, where you used to stand on the other side? That may be exactly where God wants you to speak now. Not with a sense of superiority, but as one who knows from the inside what they believe and why. Your history may be the key to their door.

For worship. God raised up a Stephen from the man who watched Stephen die. The prayer of a dying martyr was heard in heaven, and the Lord Jesus, whom Stephen saw standing at the right hand of God, answered it with the conversion of the man at the coat pile. He always finishes his work. He wastes no witness, forgets no prayer, and turns the church’s worst days into the seedbed of its greatest harvests.
verseByVerse.note: The Hellenists were Greek-speaking Jews — the group that had opposed Stephen.

verseByVerse.quote: And when the brothers learned this, they brought him down to Caesarea and sent him off to Tarsus.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And when the brothers learned this, they brought him down to Caesarea and sent him off to Tarsus.

And when the brothers learned this, they brought him down to Caesarea and sent him off to Tarsus. The church takes charge of him and removes him: down to the coast, to the port at Caesarea, onto a boat, and home to Cilicia. It is worth noticing that the man who had just been prepared to argue himself to death in Jerusalem does not appear to have resisted. He went where the brothers put him. Paul later adds that the Lord himself had told him in a vision in the temple to leave Jerusalem quickly, because they would not accept his testimony, and that he would be sent far away to the Gentiles (22:17–21). So the church’s decision and Christ’s command pointed the same way.

The hidden years. And then the narrative simply stops carrying him. Saul does not appear again until chapter 11, when Barnabas travels to Tarsus to look for him and brings him to Antioch (11:25–26), and depending on how the years are counted, the gap is something in the region of eight to ten. Luke covers a decade of the most important life in the early church with half a sentence.

What was he doing? Not nothing. Paul says in his own account that he went into the regions of Syria and Cilicia, and that the churches of Judea kept hearing that the man who used to persecute them was now preaching the faith he had once tried to destroy (Galatians 1:21–23). Several of the beatings in his later catalogue have to fall somewhere, and this is the most likely stretch of road for them; so does the vision he describes as having happened fourteen years before he wrote about it (2 Corinthians 12:2). He was working. Nobody was writing it down.

The arithmetic of a life. Do the sums on the man. He is converted at perhaps thirty. He goes home at about thirty-three, at the height of his powers, the most formidable mind in the movement, freshly commissioned by the risen Christ himself to carry the name to the Gentiles, and he spends his mid-thirties to his mid-forties in his home town, in a province nobody was watching, doing work that has left no record beyond one sentence in somebody else’s letter. That is worth sitting with by anybody whose most laborious years have produced nothing anybody else can see. It is not that the decade was a waiting room; there is no suggestion Paul spent it marking time until the real thing began. He was preaching, and the churches in Judea heard about it, and it counted. It is simply that the part of a life which turns out to matter most is very often the part nobody records, and that if Barnabas had not remembered where he lived, the whole of it would have been all we ever had of Paul.

Was the church wrong to send its best preacher away? No. They were protecting his life, and the Lord himself had told him to go (22:18). There is no failure here, either of courage on Saul’s part or of love on the church’s. Sometimes the wisest thing a church can do for a gifted and endangered young man is to take him out of the spotlight. And if you are the one who has been moved on, out of a role, a city or a ministry you loved, it may not be a demotion. It may be the Lord’s way of preparing you for the work he actually has in mind.

In a sentence. When the believers learned of this, they took him down to Caesarea and sent him off to Tarsus.

On a Tuesday. If you are in a season where nothing you do seems to be noticed, the ministry is small, the work is unseen, the years are passing, do the work in front of you as though Christ were watching. He is. Write down what you are doing for him this week that nobody else will ever know about, and offer it to him alone.

For worship. The Lord who called Paul to the nations also gave him ten quiet years in Tarsus, and both were his good gift. Christ himself spent thirty years in Nazareth before three years of public ministry, and the Father said of those hidden years, this is my beloved Son, with whom I am well pleased. Our Saviour knows the worth of unseen faithfulness. He wastes none of it, and on the last day he will bring into the light every cup of water given in his name.
verseByVerse.note: Caesarea was the port; Tarsus was Paul’s home city.

parallels.desc: the regions of Syria and Cilicia

verseByVerse.quote: So the church throughout all Judea and Galilee and Samaria had peace and was being built up. And walking in the fear of the Lord and in the comfort of the Holy Spirit, it multiplied.
verseByVerse.commentary:
So the church throughout all Judea and Galilee and Samaria had peace and was being built up. And walking in the fear of the Lord and in the comfort of the Holy Spirit, it multiplied.

So the church throughout all Judea and Galilee and Samaria had peace. One of Luke’s hinge sentences, closing a section and opening the next, and there is a quiet irony in its placing. The church gets its peace in the paragraph immediately after its chief persecutor has been converted and shipped home. The man whose arrival scattered it is gone, and the persecution he was driving has gone with him. And notice church, singular: one church across three regions, not a federation of separate movements. Luke sees all the congregations of the land as one people under one Lord.

A target hit. Note the geography as well, because Luke is quietly marking a stage completed. Jerusalem, Judea, Samaria: that is the second and third stage of the commission given in the first chapter of this book (1:8), and it has now happened, largely by accident, through a persecution nobody wanted. Only the end of the earth is outstanding, and the man who will take it there has just gone home to Tarsus to wait.

And was being built up. Peace was not used for idleness. The church was strengthened, edified, built like a house, the word Paul would later use for the growth of the body in love (Ephesians 4:12–16).

And walking in the fear of the Lord and in the comfort of the Holy Spirit, it multiplied. And then the two phrases in which Luke chooses to describe a healthy church. Not its numbers, not its organisation, not its preaching: walking in the fear of the Lord and in the comfort of the Holy Spirit. It is an unexpected pairing, and it is the whole character of the thing.

The comfort of the Holy Spirit. On “walking in the fear of the Lord,” see the fuller treatment at 5:11: the reverent awe that draws near to God in love while never trifling with his holiness (the man at the hearth, who loves the fire and pulls his chair close, yet would never put his hand in it). Here it is worth dwelling on its companion phrase, “the comfort of the Holy Spirit.” The word “comfort” (paraklēsis) is far richer than our modern notion of soothing ease. It belongs to the same family as paraklētos, the name Jesus gave the Spirit, the “Helper” or “Comforter” he promised: “I will ask the Father, and he will give you another Helper, to be with you forever” (John 14:16). The root means to be “called alongside” to give aid, and it sounds three notes at once: to console the troubled, to encourage the faint-hearted, and, as the old word “comfort” (from the Latin for “with strength”) tells us, to make strong. So “the comfort of the Holy Spirit” is no cosy ease; it is the personal presence of God’s own Spirit coming alongside his people to console them in trouble, embolden them to witness, and strengthen them to stand and grow.

Fear and comfort together. And mark the lovely pairing Luke sets down: fear and comfort, side by side, trembling reverence before the holy God, and the strong consolation of his Spirit. They are not rivals but partners; the same church that fears God is upheld by his Helper, and out of the two together it “multiplied.” A church with fear and no comfort becomes harsh and anxious. A church with comfort and no fear becomes careless and soft. A healthy church has both, and it grows. This is another of Luke’s progress reports (6:7; 12:24).

Does a church grow only when there is no persecution? No. The church had grown explosively under persecution too: those who were scattered went about preaching the word (8:4). God uses both seasons. Persecution scatters the seed; peace lets it root and be built up. Neither is a sign of his absence. If your church is in a quiet season, the question is not whether God is at work but whether you are using the peace to be built up in the fear of the Lord and the comfort of the Spirit, or simply to rest.

In a sentence. So the church throughout Judea, Galilee and Samaria enjoyed a time of peace and was strengthened, and living in the fear of the Lord and encouraged by the Holy Spirit, it grew in numbers.

On a Tuesday. Take the two phrases as a check on your own walk this week. Where have you been treating God casually, as if his holiness did not matter? That is a lack of fear. Where have you been carrying anxiety alone, as if there were no Helper beside you? That is a neglect of comfort. Ask the Spirit for both, and pray for your church by name to walk in them together.

For worship. The God who is a consuming fire is also the God of all comfort, and he gives his church both at once: the awe that bows before his holiness, and the Helper who comes alongside to hold us up. The Father sent the Spirit at the Son’s request, to be with us for ever. That is the life of the church in every age: trembling and consoled, humbled and strengthened, and growing, because the Lord of the harvest is in the midst of it.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 32–43 — Peter's Ministry in Lydda and Joppa
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: As Peter travelled about the country, he went to visit the Lord’s people in Lydda. There he found a man named Aeneas, paralysed and bedridden for eight years. Peter told him that Jesus Christ was healing him and to get up and roll up his mat, and Aeneas got up at once. Everyone in Lydda and Sharon saw him and turned to the Lord. In Joppa there was a disciple named Tabitha (in Greek, Dorcas), always doing good and helping the poor. She became ill and died, and her body was washed and laid in an upstairs room. Since Lydda was near Joppa, the disciples sent two men to urge Peter to come at once. When he arrived he was taken upstairs, where all the widows stood around him crying and showing him the robes and other clothing Dorcas had made while she was with them. Peter sent them all out, knelt and prayed. Turning to the body, he said, “Tabitha, get up.” She opened her eyes, saw Peter and sat up. He took her hand and helped her to her feet, then called the believers, especially the widows, and presented her to them alive. This became known all over Joppa, and many believed in the Lord. Peter stayed in Joppa for some time with a tanner named Simon.
verseByVerse.theology:
Resurrection as the Power Behind Healing and New Life

The raising of Tabitha is told in a way that deliberately recalls the raising of Jairus's daughter — the mourners put outside, the taking of the hand, the command to rise, the girl presented back to her people. Peter is not improvising, and he is not exercising a power of his own; he is doing what he had watched being done, in the name of the one who did it and who was himself raised afterwards. That is why he kneels first. Reformed theology has read every healing and raising in Acts as a sign rather than a policy: a working sample of the new creation, offered in advance and on a small scale, of the day when everything sin and death have broken is put right permanently. Which is also why these events are rare rather than routine even in Acts. A sign that happened every time would not be a sign; it would be the arrangement, and the arrangement is still to come.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: When Tabitha died, the widows stood in the room holding up the coats and the dresses she had made, and Luke notes that she had made them while she was with them. That is what her ministry consisted of, and it is what the church had to show for her. Now: It is worth asking what would be held up. Not what would be said at the service, which is a different question and easier — but what could be carried into the room and shown.

verseByVerse.quote: Now as Peter went here and there among them all, he came down also to the saints who lived at Lydda. There he found a man named Aeneas, bedridden for eight years, who was paralyzed.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Now as Peter went here and there among them all, he came down also to the saints who lived at Lydda. There he found a man named Aeneas, bedridden for eight years, who was paralyzed.

Now as Peter went here and there among them all. Luke’s phrase describes a circuit: the apostle out of Jerusalem, going round from congregation to congregation on the coastal plain. It is the first glimpse in this book of what most Christian ministry actually consists of: travelling to see people who are already believers, in unremarkable towns, and staying a while. Peter the fisherman has become Peter the shepherd, doing what his Lord told him on the shore of Galilee: feed my sheep (John 21:17).

Whose churches these were. Peter did not plant them. Lydda and Joppa lie in exactly the stretch of country the scattered believers of chapter 8 ran into, and Philip had preached his way through this plain from Azotus to Caesarea (8:40). The saints Peter is visiting are the fruit of a persecution and of refugees who could not stop talking. He arrives as a visitor to work somebody else began.

He came down also to the saints who lived at Lydda. Lydda is the old town of Lod, about twenty-five miles north-west of Jerusalem, sitting on the main road down to the sea and about eleven miles from the port at Joppa. It was a market town on a trade route, which means that whatever happened there would be discussed by carriers and travellers within a day.

There he found a man named Aeneas, bedridden for eight years, who was paralyzed. He has a Greek name, and Luke does not say that he was a Christian; the phrase is that Peter found him, which is what you say about somebody you were not looking for. Eight years is the detail to hold, because Luke gives numbers of this kind for a reason. It is long enough that everybody in a town that size knows the house, knows the family, and has stopped expecting anything. Whatever hope was expended in the first year had been spent by the third. Somebody had been washing him and turning him and carrying him for eight years, had reorganised a life around it, and had long since stopped mentioning it.

Mercy before confession. One more thing about Aeneas is worth registering because of where this book is going. Luke tells us his name, his condition and the length of it, and says nothing whatever about his faith. He is not called a disciple, not said to have believed, and not recorded as speaking. He is simply a man Peter found. In two verses the mercy will arrive before any confession does, and within two chapters Peter will be standing in a Gentile house watching the same thing happen on a very much larger scale.

In a sentence. As Peter travelled about the country, he went down to visit the saints in Lydda, where he found a man named Aeneas, who was paralysed and had been bedridden for eight years.

On a Tuesday. Visit the sick and the shut-in. Peter went to them. Think of someone in your church or street who has been ill or housebound so long that people have stopped calling, and go this week. And remember the carers too: the person who has been doing the lifting and washing for years without anyone mentioning it. A meal, an afternoon off, or simply asking how they are may be the first kindness anyone has shown them in months.

For worship. The risen Christ notices the man nobody is looking for anymore. Eight years on a mat in a market town, and the Lord of glory sends his apostle down the road to find him. That is how the Good Shepherd works: he goes after the one, and he knows how long each of his creatures has been waiting.
verseByVerse.note: Lydda (modern Lod) lay about 25 miles north-west of Jerusalem, on the road to the coast.

verseByVerse.quote: And Peter said to him, "Aeneas, Jesus Christ heals you; rise and make your bed." And immediately he rose. And all the residents of Lydda and Sharon saw him, and they turned to the Lord.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And Peter said to him, “Aeneas, Jesus Christ heals you; rise and make your bed.” And immediately he rose. And all the residents of Lydda and Sharon saw him, and they turned to the Lord.

Aeneas, Jesus Christ heals you. Peter says the name before he says anything else, and the tense is present: not will heal, not can heal, but is healing you, now, as I speak. Not I heal you: Jesus Christ heals you. Peter is only the messenger. He had learned this at a temple gate years earlier, when a crowd came running to stare at him and he had to tell them it was not by his own power or piety that the lame man walked (3:12–16). He does not wait to be misunderstood a second time.

Rise and make your bed. Then the strangest instruction in the chapter. The Greek can also mean, prepare a meal for yourself, spread your own table, and either way the point is the same. Consider what it means as the first command given to a man who has not stood up since the reign of Tiberius. Not: run, or leap, or go and tell somebody. Make your own bed. Do for yourself what others have done for you all these years. It is an ordinary domestic action, the sort a mother tells a child to do, and it is the exact gesture by which a man who has been ill for eight years signals that the illness is over. There is nothing to arrange around any more. And immediately he rose.

And all the residents of Lydda and Sharon saw him and turned to the Lord. Then Luke widens the shot. Sharon is not a town but the whole fertile coastal plain running north, so this is a district-wide result from one man getting off a mat in a market town on a main road. It should be read as Luke’s summaries generally should: he is describing a movement across a region, many people rather than every person, not conducting a census. But the mechanism is easy enough to see. Everybody within a day’s travel had known about Aeneas for eight years. He was the case that could not be argued with, and he was standing in the street. The sign led to faith, and the faith was in the Lord, not in Peter.

Does Christ still heal like this through his ministers? Christ still heals and answers prayer as he wills. But healings like Aeneas’ and the raising of Dorcas (v. 40) were apostolic signs confirming the gospel as it spread. Many Christians believe such gifts continue; the more likely reading is that they belonged to the apostolic age, and that no minister today may claim them.

A word to the reader still on the mat. A passage like this can be quietly cruel if it is left to speak alone. Aeneas was healed after eight years; a great many faithful people are not healed after eighty. Paul, whom Luke the physician travelled with, left a colleague behind ill at Miletus (2 Timothy 4:20) and carried a thorn in the flesh that was never removed (2 Corinthians 12:7–9). Nothing in this chapter suggests that Aeneas had more faith than anybody else on the plain, or indeed any faith at all; he is not recorded as saying a word. What the passage establishes is not a method but an authority, and the authority has not diminished. The timing is not ours to hold, and the day is coming when the whole plain of Sharon gets up.

Then should I still pray for healing? Yes, and boldly. James tells the sick to call the elders of the church to pray over them (James 5:14–15), and God often heals in answer to prayer, sometimes through doctors and medicine, sometimes beyond them. What we may not do is claim a guarantee, or tell a sick believer that his illness continues because his faith is weak. Pray as Jesus did in the garden: ask plainly for what you want, and add, not my will, but yours, be done. If healing comes, give Christ the glory. If it does not, he has promised grace sufficient for the weakness (2 Corinthians 12:9), and a resurrection body that will never be ill again.

In a sentence. Peter said to him that Jesus Christ was healing him and told him to get up and make his bed, and at once he got up, and everyone who lived in Lydda and Sharon saw him and turned to the Lord.

On a Tuesday. When something good happens to you, a recovery, an answered prayer, a crisis averted, say out loud whose doing it was, as Peter did. Jesus Christ did this. And if you are still waiting on a healing that has not come, keep bringing it to him, and let the church carry you in prayer as Aeneas’s family carried him for eight years.

For worship. Jesus Christ heals. He healed then by a word through his apostle, and he heals now as he wills, in answer to his people’s prayers. And every healing in this age is a down payment on the morning when he will make all things new, when the lame will leap like the deer and there will be no more mourning, nor crying, nor pain. He is the Lord of the body as well as the soul, and he will raise every one of his people whole.
verseByVerse.note: Sharon was the fertile coastal plain.

verseByVerse.quote: Now there was in Joppa a disciple named Tabitha, which, translated, means Dorcas. She was full of good works and acts of charity. In those days she became ill and died, and when they had washed her, they laid her in an upper room.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Now there was in Joppa a disciple named Tabitha, which, translated, means Dorcas. She was full of good works and acts of charity. In those days she became ill and died, and when they had washed her, they laid her in an upper room.

Now there was in Joppa a disciple named Tabitha. Luke does something here that he does nowhere else in the New Testament, and the Greek shows it where English cannot. He calls her a disciple, and he uses the feminine form of the word, mathētria, which occurs in no other verse of the Bible. There was a perfectly serviceable masculine term he could have used, as he does of everybody else. For Tabitha he reached for a form nobody else ever needed. And Joppa, modern Jaffa, is a town with a history: it was the port from which Jonah sailed to flee from God’s call to the Gentiles (Jonah 1:3).

Which, translated, means Dorcas. Her name is given twice because she lived in a port. Tabitha in Aramaic and Dorcas in Greek both mean gazelle, and a woman with a working name in each language is a woman known in both halves of a mixed town.

She was full of good works and acts of charity. Then the description, and it is worth weighing what Luke has decided to say about her. Full of is his own particular phrase, and he has used it in this book of Stephen: full of faith and of the Holy Spirit (6:5), full of grace and power (6:8). He now uses the same construction of a woman whose recorded output is coats. Luke evidently did not consider these to be different orders of achievement. She overflowed with practical kindness: faith working through love (Galatians 5:6; James 2:17).

In those days she became ill and died. Then, in half a sentence, she is gone. No explanation is offered and none is available. She was full of good works and she got sick and died, in the middle of a chapter full of healings, in a town where an apostle was staying eleven miles away. Luke does not soften it and does not account for it. It is worth registering that the New Testament, which is often accused of promising too much, records the sudden death of its most useful woman in eight words and moves on.

And when they had washed her, they laid her in an upper room. The last detail is the one to notice. In that climate burial followed death within the day; washing the body and laying it out was the first act, and interment ordinarily came next. They did the first and stopped. They put her upstairs, and they sent two men down the road. Nobody says why, and everybody knows why. They were hoping.

Why does God take his most useful servants? Scripture does not give us the reason in Tabitha’s case, and it would be presumption to invent one. What it does tell us is that our days are written in God’s book before one of them comes to be (Psalm 139:16), and that usefulness is not a shield against death. Godly people die young, and wicked men sometimes live long. The comfort is not that we can explain it but that the one who holds the days is good, and that for the believer, to die is gain (Philippians 1:21). The church in Joppa grieved as people who loved her, and they were right to. But they did not grieve as those who have no hope.

In a sentence. In Joppa there was a disciple named Tabitha, which in Greek is Dorcas, who was always doing good and helping the poor, but at that time she became ill and died, and they washed her body and laid it in an upstairs room.

On a Tuesday. Be full of good works. Not famous ones, but the kind that can be held up in a room after you are gone: the meal, the coat, the visit, the note. A life of quiet kindness is precious to God. Ask what one thing you could make or do this week for someone who has no one to provide for them.

For worship. Christ sees the needle and thread. The Lord who will judge the world by what was done for the least of his brothers counted every garment Tabitha stitched as made for him. He does not rank his servants by the size of their stage, and he names a seamstress in a port town in the same breath as the first martyr. Our God is the God of small and faithful things, and nothing done in love for him is ever lost.
verseByVerse.note: Joppa (modern Jaffa) was the port from which Jonah sailed. Tabitha (Aramaic) and Dorcas (Greek) both mean “gazelle.”

verseByVerse.quote: Since Lydda was near Joppa, the disciples, hearing that Peter was there, sent two men to him, urging him, "Please come to us without delay."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Since Lydda was near Joppa, the disciples, hearing that Peter was there, sent two men to him, urging him, “Please come to us without delay.”

Since Lydda was near Joppa, the disciples, hearing that Peter was there, sent two men to him. Eleven miles between Lydda and Joppa: a few hours on foot each way, which means the messengers have a long day’s round trip and a body upstairs in a warm climate. They send two men, which is the formal number for a delegation and also the practical number for a road.

Please come to us without delay. The message they carry is six words long. Now notice what it does not say. It does not say what for. It does not ask Peter to raise her; it does not mention prayer, or even name the woman. They have washed a corpse, declined to bury it, and sent for an apostle with an urgent request that says nothing about what they want him to do when he arrives. They had heard of Aeneas. Luke, who could easily have told us what they were thinking, leaves the sentence exactly as short as they sent it.

How people pray at the worst moments. It is one of the truest things in the chapter. Not with a clear petition properly framed, but with an urgent, half-formed sentence that cannot quite bring itself to ask for the thing it wants, partly because the thing is too large to say out loud, and partly because saying it would mean admitting how much is riding on the answer. Come quickly is very often the whole of it. God is not put off by a badly drafted request. He had already told Moses that he heard the groaning of people who had not managed to compose a prayer at all (Exodus 2:23–25), and Paul says the Spirit himself intercedes for us with groanings too deep for words (Romans 8:26). What these disciples had was a dead friend, a road, and a conviction they could not articulate that it was worth fetching the man who knew Jesus. That turned out to be sufficient.

Joppa again. And the town they are calling him to is worth a moment, because Luke’s readers would have known its one famous story. Joppa is the port where a prophet, ordered to go and preach to Gentiles, went down to the harbour instead and took ship in the opposite direction. It is the place from which a man ran away from a call to the nations. Peter is about to spend many days there. And on a roof in that same town he will be told three times to take and eat what he has spent his life refusing, and will say no, before getting up and going to a Gentile house. Luke does not point at the parallel and does not need to. Of all the ports on that coast, the call to the nations comes a second time at Joppa, and this time the man goes. Jesus himself called Peter Simon bar-Jonah, son of Jonah (Matthew 16:17). The new Jonah does not run.

In a sentence. Since Lydda was near Joppa, the disciples, hearing that Peter was there, sent two men to him to urge him to come to them without delay.

On a Tuesday. In your grief, send for help. Do not wait until you can pray properly or explain what you need. Call a friend, call your pastor, call on the Lord with the six words you have. And if you are the one sent for, go without delay, even if you do not know what you will say when you get there.

For worship. The Lord hears the prayer that cannot finish its own sentence. He heard the groaning of Israel in Egypt, the tears of Hannah, the cry of the thief on the cross, and the six words of a frightened church in Joppa. Our Saviour does not wait for us to pray well. He comes to people who simply know he is the one worth sending for.
verseByVerse.note: Lydda was about 11 miles from Joppa.

verseByVerse.quote: So Peter rose and went with them. And when he arrived, they took him to the upper room. All the widows stood beside him weeping and showing tunics and other garments that Dorcas made while she was with them. But Peter put them all outside, and knelt down and prayed; and turning to the body he said, "Tabitha, arise." And she opened her eyes, and when she saw Peter she sat up.
verseByVerse.commentary:
So Peter rose and went with them. And when he arrived, they took him to the upper room. All the widows stood beside him weeping and showing tunics and other garments that Dorcas made while she was with them. But Peter put them all outside, and knelt down and prayed; and turning to the body he said, “Tabitha, arise.” And she opened her eyes, and when she saw Peter she sat up.

So Peter rose and went with them. And when he arrived, they took him to the upper room. He goes, and the scene that meets him upstairs is the most affecting in the chapter.

All the widows stood beside him weeping and showing tunics and other garments that Dorcas made while she was with them. They are holding up the clothes. Not describing them; holding them out for Peter to look at, one after another, while they cry. It is the sort of detail nobody invents, and it is almost certainly what somebody in that room remembered decades later when Luke asked. Her love had been made visible in cloth. Many a church sewing circle since has been named after her.

Who these women were. Consider them. A widow in that world without a son had no income, no legal standing to speak of, and nothing between her and destitution but charity. They are the same class of people whose neglect had caused the first crisis in the church three chapters back, when the Greek-speaking widows were being overlooked in the daily distribution (6:1). Here in a port town a woman had made it her business, personally, with her own hands, and the evidence is being waved in an upper room. Luke recorded the failure. He records the remedy too, and the remedy has a name.

But Peter put them all outside. Then Peter clears the room, and every move he makes is one he has seen before. He put them all outside, as his Lord had done in a house in Galilee where a twelve-year-old girl lay dead and the mourners laughed at him (Mark 5:40). Peter had been there, one of only three disciples allowed in.

Tabitha, arise. He turned to the body and spoke to it. And what he said, very likely in Aramaic, was Tabitha, koum, one letter away from Talitha koum, the two words Jesus had said to Jairus’s daughter with Peter standing in the room (Mark 5:41). He is doing what he watched being done. That is not imitation in any hollow sense; it is a man reaching for the only precedent he has, in the same language, in almost the same words, because he was there when it worked.

And knelt down and prayed. But one thing he does that his Lord did not, and it is the difference between them. Jesus put the mourners out and took the child’s hand and told her to get up; there is no prayer in that account because there did not need to be. Peter has to ask. He kneels on the floor of a room containing a dead woman and requests something he has no power whatever to perform, and only then turns round and speaks. It is a small distinction and the whole of apostolic ministry sits inside it. The words are nearly identical and the authority is entirely borrowed.

And she opened her eyes, and when she saw Peter she sat up. Simple, vivid detail. The first face she sees is not the one she might have expected, and Luke, who loves such touches, lets us see it through her eyes.

In a sentence. Peter went with them, and when he arrived they took him upstairs, where all the widows stood around him weeping and showing him the tunics and other clothing Dorcas had made while she was with them, but Peter sent them all out, knelt down and prayed, and turning to the body said, “Tabitha, arise,” and she opened her eyes, and when she saw Peter she sat up.

On a Tuesday. Before you try to help anyone in a crisis, kneel. Peter, who had seen Jesus raise the dead, still knew he had nothing of his own to give. Whatever room you are walking into this week, a hospital ward, a difficult meeting, a grieving home, pray first and speak second, and remember that every good thing you bring is borrowed.

For worship. The Lord of life works through his servants’ prayers. He is the one who said to a dead girl, Little girl, arise, and to a widow’s son at Nain, Young man, I say to you, arise, and to a friend four days in the tomb, Lazarus, come out. When Peter knelt in Joppa he was kneeling before that Lord. Death has no word that Christ cannot answer, and every resurrection in his name is an echo of his own.

parallels.desc: “Talitha cumi”

verseByVerse.quote: And he gave her his hand and raised her up. Then, calling the saints and widows, he presented her alive.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And he gave her his hand and raised her up. Then, calling the saints and widows, he presented her alive.

And he gave her his hand and raised her up. The last thing Peter does is the most ordinary: she has been dead and is now sitting on a bed, and a man puts out his hand and helps her to her feet, exactly as anyone would. It is what Peter did for the lame man at the temple gate (3:7), and what Jesus did for Peter’s own mother-in-law (Mark 1:31).

Then, calling the saints and widows, he presented her alive. Then he opens the door. They had been put outside a few minutes earlier in tears with an armful of clothes. Luke does not describe what happened next, and there was no need. And the phrase he uses is worth noticing. Presented her alive is the language Luke used of Jesus presenting himself alive to his apostles after his suffering (1:3). It is a picture of resurrection, and of the joy of the last day, when Christ will present his people alive and blameless before the Father.

The hard thing. Now something has to be said, or the passage becomes an instrument of cruelty. Tabitha was raised. Every other Christian who died in Joppa that year stayed dead. Luke records exactly two resurrections in the whole book of Acts (here and Eutychus, 20:9–12) and the deaths of a great many believers, including one of the Twelve, executed by Herod in chapter 12 with no rescue and no explanation, in the same chapter in which the church’s prayer brought Peter out of prison. Whatever this passage is, it is not a description of what God routinely does when his people ask, and no one should be handed it as though it were.

A sign, not the destination. What it is, is a sign, which by definition is not the destination but a board at the roadside with the destination’s name on it. Tabitha herself is the proof of that, because she died again. Whatever year it came, there was a second funeral in Joppa for the same woman, and that time nobody sent to Lydda. What she was given was not immortality. It was a few more years of making coats, and a demonstration, in one upper room on one afternoon, of what the God of the resurrection intends to do universally and at once.

Where the comfort lies. That is where the comfort actually lies, and it is worth reaching for rather than the shallower one. The point is not that God might do this again for the person you have lost. The point is that he has announced, in a room in a port town, in front of witnesses who told a doctor about it, what he means to do for everybody who belongs to him. The widows got their friend back for a while. They will get her back for good.

Will we know our loved ones again? Scripture gives good reason to think so. Paul comforts grieving Christians not with a vague hope but with a reunion: the dead in Christ will rise, and we will be caught up together with them, and so we will always be with the Lord, therefore encourage one another (1 Thessalonians 4:13–18). That comfort would mean nothing if we did not know each other. Moses and Elijah were known on the mount of transfiguration, and the risen Jesus was recognised by his friends. We will be changed, made like Christ, but not made into strangers. The widows of Joppa will hold Dorcas’s hands again, and they will know whose hands they are.

In a sentence. He gave her his hand and helped her to her feet, and then, calling the saints and the widows, he presented her to them alive.

On a Tuesday. If you are grieving a believer who has died, do not let this story become a reproach, as though you had not prayed hard enough. Let it become a promise. Read 1 Thessalonians 4:13–18 aloud this week, and say the name of the one you have lost alongside it. One day Christ will take your hand and raise you, and present you alive to all his people.

For worship. The Lord Jesus presented himself alive after his suffering, by many proofs, and because he lives, we shall live also. The hand Peter held out in Joppa was a picture of a greater hand, the pierced hand of the Son of God, which will reach into every grave where his people lie and raise them up. On that morning he will call the saints and widows of every age and present them alive, all of them together, for ever. Death will be swallowed up in victory, and the God who did it in one upper room will do it for the whole creation.
