verseByVerse.quote: And it became known throughout all Joppa, and many believed in the Lord. And he stayed in Joppa for many days with one Simon, a tanner.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And it became known throughout all Joppa, and many believed in the Lord. And he stayed in Joppa for many days with one Simon, a tanner.

And it became known throughout all Joppa, and many believed in the Lord. The pattern of the whole section: the sign is not the point, the sign gets a hearing, and what people believe in is the Lord rather than the apostle.

And he stayed in Joppa for many days with one Simon, a tanner. And then the last verse of the chapter, which reads like a piece of travel administration and is nothing of the sort. Consider what a tanner was. He took the hides of dead animals and turned them into leather, scraping, soaking and curing them in solutions that included urine and dung. The work brought him into constant contact with carcasses, which under the law of Moses made a man unclean (Leviticus 11:39–40), and the process produced a stench that carried. Later Jewish law codified what everybody already practised: a tannery had to be sited outside the town, and on the side away from the prevailing wind. A tanner’s trade was a social burden on his whole household. A tanner’s house was where the town ended.

Peter moves in. And Peter, an observant Jew who will shortly tell the Lord to his face that he has never in his life eaten anything common or unclean (10:14), moves in and stays for weeks. His scruples were already loosening, perhaps without his noticing.

The house before the roof. Luke has put that sentence at the end of the chapter deliberately, because of what happens at the beginning of the next. On the roof of that house, over that smell, Peter will fall into a trance and see a sheet let down full of every kind of animal, and be told to kill and eat, and will refuse, and be told not to call common what God has made clean. The vision that opens the door to the Gentile world is given to a man who is already, without quite having noticed it, sleeping under a roof no scrupulous Pharisee would have entered. Cornelius’s messengers will find him at exactly this address (10:6). That is generally how God moves people. Not by winning the argument first and relocating them afterwards, but by getting them into the house, and then asking the question, on the roof, at midday, when the answer has already been half-conceded by the address on the letter.

Whose house would you not stay in? It is worth asking. Not in theory, where everybody is generous, but in practice: the address that would need explaining, the household whose habits or history or trade would make it awkward. Peter had not yet worked out his theology of clean and unclean; he had merely accepted an invitation from a man who worked with dead animals. The theology came later, on the roof, and it came to a man who was already in the building.

Does this mean every scruple is just prejudice? No. Some lines are drawn by God’s word, and those we must keep whatever it costs: Christians may not join in idolatry or sexual sin, however welcoming the house. But many of our lines are drawn by custom, class, culture or temperament, and Christ is constantly stepping over them. The test is to ask, honestly and with an open Bible, whether a thing you avoid is forbidden by God or merely unfamiliar to you (Romans 14:1–4, 14). Peter’s food laws had once been God’s command, and in Christ they had been fulfilled and set aside (Mark 7:19). How much more should we hold loosely the barriers that were never commanded at all.

In a sentence. This became known all over Joppa, and many people believed in the Lord, and Peter stayed in Joppa for some time with a tanner named Simon.

On a Tuesday. Accept the invitation you would normally find a reason to decline: the meal with the neighbour whose life is a mess, the coffee with the colleague from a different background, the visit to the household the church tends to forget. You do not need to have worked out a theology of it first. Go in, and let the Lord teach you on the roof.

For worship. God moves his servants step by step past their prejudices, and he does it gently, one house at a time. The Son of God himself was called a friend of tax collectors and sinners; he touched lepers, ate with outcasts, and was born among the animals. He was crucified outside the city wall, where the unclean things were taken, so that he might bring the unclean home (Hebrews 13:12–13). The Lord who led Peter to a tanner’s door is the Lord who made a way for Gentiles like us into the household of God. Blessed be his name.
verseByVerse.note: Tanners handled the skins of dead animals, a trade many Jews regarded as unclean — a hint of the lesson Peter is about to learn.

9.theology: Sovereign Grace in Conversion. The conversion of Saul is the New Testament’s clearest portrait of unconditional election and effectual calling. There is nothing in Saul that would attract God’s grace — he is actively persecuting the church, violently opposed to Christ, supremely confident in his own righteousness (Philippians 3:4–6). God chose him anyway. Not because of anything foreseen in him, but according to his own sovereign purpose — to display the fullness of his grace in the most unlikely vessel imaginable. Paul himself will later write that his conversion was designed to be a pattern, “an example to those who were to believe in him for eternal life” (1 Timothy 1:16). If God can save Saul of Tarsus, he can save anyone. That is the point. The doctrine of election is not a closed door; it is the foundation of missionary confidence.
9.examples:
Then: A church that had watched Saul drag their brothers and sisters to prison now had to welcome him as a brother. Understandably, they were afraid. It took Barnabas — son of encouragement — to stand between the suspicious church and the new apostle and vouch for the reality of his conversion. The church that had prayed for boldness now needed faith to receive the answer.

Now: No one is beyond the reach of sovereign grace. The person who seems most violently opposed to the gospel may be the one God is about to apprehend. This is not a reason for naivety; it is a reason for prayer — the kind of prayer that believes God can stop any Saul on any road at any time. The church’s task is to be ready, like Ananias, to say “brother” when the moment comes.

10.title: The Gospel to the Gentiles
10.text: <sup>1</sup>At Caesarea there was a man named Cornelius, a centurion of what was known as the Italian Cohort, <sup>2</sup>a devout man who feared God with all his household, gave alms generously to the people, and prayed continually to God. <sup>3</sup>About the ninth hour of the day he saw clearly in a vision an angel of God come in and say to him, “Cornelius.” <sup>4</sup>And he stared at him in terror and said, “What is it, Lord?” And he said to him, “Your prayers and your alms have ascended as a memorial before God. <sup>5</sup>And now send men to Joppa and bring one Simon who is called Peter. <sup>6</sup>He is lodging with one Simon, a tanner, whose house is by the sea.” <sup>7</sup>When the angel who spoke to him had departed, he called two of his servants and a devout soldier from among those who attended him, <sup>8</sup>and having related everything to them, he sent them to Joppa. <sup>9</sup>The next day, as they were on their journey and approaching the city, Peter went up on the housetop about the sixth hour to pray. <sup>10</sup>And he became hungry and wanted something to eat, but while they were preparing it, he fell into a trance <sup>11</sup>and saw the heavens opened and something like a great sheet descending, being let down by its four corners upon the earth. <sup>12</sup>In it were all kinds of animals and reptiles and birds of the air. <sup>13</sup>And there came a voice to him: “Rise, Peter; kill and eat.” <sup>14</sup>But Peter said, “By no means, Lord; for I have never eaten anything that is common or unclean.” <sup>15</sup>And the voice came to him again a second time, “What God has made clean, do not call common.” <sup>16</sup>This happened three times, and the thing was taken up at once to heaven. <sup>17</sup>Now while Peter was inwardly perplexed as to what the vision that he had seen might mean, behold, the men who were sent by Cornelius, having made inquiry for Simon’s house, stood at the gate <sup>18</sup>and called out to ask whether Simon who was called Peter was lodging there. <sup>19</sup>And while Peter was pondering the vision, the Spirit said to him, “Behold, three men are looking for you. <sup>20</sup>Rise and go down and accompany them without hesitation, for I have sent them.” <sup>21</sup>And Peter went down to the men and said, “I am the one you are looking for. What is the reason for your coming?” <sup>22</sup>And they said, “Cornelius, a centurion, an upright and God-fearing man, who is well spoken of by the whole Jewish nation, was directed by a holy angel to send for you to come to his house and to hear what you have to say.” <sup>23</sup>So he invited them in to be his guests. The next day he rose and went away with them, and some of the brothers from Joppa accompanied him. <sup>24</sup>And on the following day they entered Caesarea. Cornelius was expecting them and had called together his relatives and close friends. <sup>25</sup>When Peter entered, Cornelius met him and fell down at his feet and worshiped him. <sup>26</sup>But Peter lifted him up, saying, “Stand up; I too am a man.” <sup>27</sup>And as he talked with him, he went in and found many persons gathered. <sup>28</sup>And he said to them, “You yourselves know how unlawful it is for a Jew to associate with or to visit anyone of another nation, but God has shown me that I should not call any person common or unclean. <sup>29</sup>So when I was sent for, I came without objection. I ask then why you sent for me.” <sup>30</sup>And Cornelius said, “Four days ago, about this hour, I was praying in my house at the ninth hour, and behold, a man stood before me in bright clothing <sup>31</sup>and said, ‘Cornelius, your prayer has been heard and your alms have been remembered before God. <sup>32</sup>Send therefore to Joppa and ask for Simon who is called Peter. He is lodging in the house of Simon, a tanner, by the sea.’ <sup>33</sup>So I sent for you at once, and you have been kind enough to come. Now therefore we are all here in the presence of God to hear all that you have been commanded by the Lord.” <sup>34</sup>So Peter opened his mouth and said: “Truly I understand that God shows no partiality, <sup>35</sup>but in every nation anyone who fears him and does what is right is acceptable to him. <sup>36</sup>As for the word that he sent to Israel, preaching good news of peace through Jesus Christ (he is Lord of all), <sup>37</sup>you yourselves know what happened throughout all Judea, beginning from Galilee after the baptism that John proclaimed: <sup>38</sup>how God anointed Jesus of Nazareth with the Holy Spirit and with power. He went about doing good and healing all who were oppressed by the devil, for God was with him. <sup>39</sup>And we are witnesses of all that he did both in the country of the Jews and in Jerusalem. They put him to death by hanging him on a tree, <sup>40</sup>but God raised him on the third day and made him to appear, <sup>41</sup>not to all the people but to us who had been chosen by God as witnesses, who ate and drank with him after he rose from the dead. <sup>42</sup>And he commanded us to preach to the people and to testify that he is the one appointed by God to be judge of the living and the dead. <sup>43</sup>To him all the prophets bear witness that everyone who believes in him receives forgiveness of sins through his name.” <sup>44</sup>While Peter was still saying these things, the Holy Spirit fell on all who heard the word. <sup>45</sup>And the believers from among the circumcised who had come with Peter were amazed, because the gift of the Holy Spirit was poured out even on the Gentiles. <sup>46</sup>For they were hearing them speaking in tongues and extolling God. Then Peter declared, <sup>47</sup>“Can anyone withhold water for baptizing these people, who have received the Holy Spirit just as we have?” <sup>48</sup>And he commanded them to be baptized in the name of Jesus Christ. Then they asked him to remain for some days.
10.overview:
This is one of the turning points of Acts, so important that Luke tells it twice (again in chapter 11) and Peter retells it at the Jerusalem council (15:7–11). The gospel has reached Samaritans and one Ethiopian; now it reaches Gentiles as Gentiles. Cornelius is a Roman centurion stationed at Caesarea, the Roman capital of Judea, a “God-fearer”: a Gentile who worshipped Israel’s God, prayed at the Jewish hours of prayer and gave generously to Jewish causes, but had not become a Jew by circumcision. In a vision at three in the afternoon an angel tells him that God has noticed his prayers and gifts, and that he should send to Joppa for Simon Peter.

The next day at noon, on a flat rooftop in Joppa, Peter sees a sheet let down from heaven full of animals the law of Moses called unclean, and hears a voice telling him to kill and eat. He refuses, and the voice answers: “What God has made clean, do not call common.” This happens three times. As he puzzles over it, Cornelius’s messengers arrive, and the Spirit tells him to go with them. Peter, who earlier would never have entered a Gentile’s house, goes to Caesarea, finds a house full of Cornelius’s relatives and friends, and declares that God shows no partiality. He preaches Jesus: anointed with the Spirit, doing good and healing, killed on a tree, raised on the third day, appointed judge of the living and the dead, and the one through whom everyone who believes receives forgiveness. While he is still speaking, the Holy Spirit falls on the Gentiles, they speak in tongues and praise God, and Peter’s Jewish companions are astonished. Peter asks who could refuse them water for baptism, and they are baptised in the name of Jesus Christ.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–48 — Cornelius and the Gentile Pentecost
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Cornelius, a God-fearing Roman centurion at Caesarea, is told by an angel to send for Peter in Joppa. The next day Peter, praying on a rooftop at noon, sees a sheet full of animals the law called unclean and hears a voice telling him to eat; when he refuses, the voice says three times that he must not call unclean what God has made clean. Cornelius’s messengers arrive, the Spirit tells Peter to go with them, and he travels to Caesarea, where he enters a Gentile home full of people waiting to hear him. Peter declares that God shows no favouritism and accepts people from every nation who fear him. He tells them about Jesus: anointed by the Spirit, doing good and healing, put to death on a cross, raised on the third day, seen by chosen witnesses, appointed judge of all, and the one through whom everyone who believes receives forgiveness. While he is still speaking, the Spirit falls on all the Gentiles listening, to the astonishment of Peter’s Jewish companions, and Peter has them baptised in the name of Jesus Christ.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Clean and the Unclean, and What the Food Laws Were For

The sheet is full of animals and the argument is about people, and Peter himself makes the translation at verse 28: God has shown me that I should not call any person common or unclean. The food laws had never been about digestion. They were about difference — a daily, three-times-a-day mechanism for keeping Israel visibly distinct from the nations around it, and they worked, which is why a devout Jew could not eat at a Gentile table without the whole arrangement collapsing. Reformed theology has read the vision as the retirement of a shadow rather than the repeal of a word: the separation was always temporary, always pointing forward, and its purpose was fulfilled the moment the dividing wall of hostility came down in Christ (Ephesians 2:14). What is striking is the order in which Peter learned it. He did not reason his way from Christology to table fellowship. He was given a command he found repellent, obeyed it under protest, and worked out the theology afterwards — which is worth remembering by anyone who assumes conviction always precedes obedience.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: Peter needed a vision repeated three times, a direct instruction from the Spirit, three men at the gate and the Spirit falling in front of witnesses before he would accept what he had been told plainly at the ascension. And even then the church argued about it for a chapter and a half. Now: The instinct to take the gospel to people like ourselves is not usually held as a conviction; it is held as an assumption, which is why it survives so much preaching against it. Peter did not have an opinion about Gentiles that could be corrected. He had a lifetime of habit, and it took God three goes.

verseByVerse.quote: At Caesarea there was a man named Cornelius, a centurion of what was known as the Italian Cohort, a devout man who feared God with all his household, gave alms generously to the people, and prayed continually to God.
verseByVerse.commentary:
At Caesarea there was a man named Cornelius, a centurion of what was known as the Italian Cohort, a devout man who feared God with all his household, gave alms generously to the people, and prayed continually to God.

Meaning first. Acts 10 is the great turning point of the book: the gospel goes to the Gentiles. God prepares both sides: Cornelius, a Roman officer, through an angel; Peter, a Jewish apostle, through a vision. Peter preaches Christ, the Holy Spirit falls on the Gentiles as he did at Pentecost, and they are baptised. Luke tells the story at length, and Peter retells it twice (11:1–18; 15:7–11), because it settles for ever that Gentiles are welcomed into God’s people by faith in Christ, without becoming Jews first. It is the chapter in which most of the people reading this commentary first come into view, and over the whole of it stands one sentence of Peter’s: Jesus Christ is Lord of all (v. 36).

At Caesarea there was a man named Cornelius. Luke introduces the man carefully, and every detail is chosen to make him the hardest possible case in the best possible way. Caesarea, on the coast, was the Roman capital of Judea, built by Herod the Great with a harbour, a theatre and a temple to the emperor, and named after Caesar Augustus. Pilate governed from there; a stone bearing his name was found in its theatre in 1961. It was the most Roman city in the land.

A centurion of what was known as the Italian Cohort. A centurion commanded a century, nominally a hundred soldiers and in practice about eighty: the professional backbone of the Roman army and the rank at which the empire actually worked. Cornelius is the occupation. Whatever a Jewish reader felt about Rome, the taxes, the standards, the crucifixions, this is the man who enforces it. And yet the centurions of the New Testament are consistently portrayed well: the one whose faith astonished Jesus (Luke 7:2–10), and the one at the cross who said, Certainly this man was innocent (Luke 23:47).

A devout man who feared God with all his household. Then four things which make him, by any measure available to first-century Judaism, an exemplary human being. He is devout. He feared God with all his household, which means he had brought his family and his servants with him into it and not merely adopted a private opinion. He gave alms generously to the people, and the people in Luke’s usage means the Jewish people, so a Roman officer was funding the poor of the nation he was garrisoning, like the centurion of Capernaum who built them a synagogue (Luke 7:5). And he prayed continually to God.

A God-fearer. What he is not is a convert. He belonged to a recognised category: the God-fearer, the Gentile who attached himself to the synagogue, believed in the God of Israel, kept what he could of the moral law and gave to the poor, but had not been circumcised and so remained, formally, outside. There were many such men around the synagogues of the empire, and they occupied an uncomfortable middle ground: too Jewish for their Roman friends, never quite Jewish enough for the congregation.

The best Gentile in the empire. So Luke has assembled him. Sincere, generous, prayerful, respected by the very people he had power over, at the top of his profession, and bringing his whole household along with him. If moral seriousness and religious sincerity were enough, this is the man they would be enough for. And the angel who arrives in the next verse does not tell him he is fine. He tells him to send thirty miles down the coast for a fisherman who has something to say to him. That is the whole argument of the chapter in its opening two verses, and it cuts in two directions at once. Nothing Cornelius had done had earned him anything, and God had noticed every bit of it, and was already moving.

In a sentence. In Caesarea lived Cornelius, a centurion of the Italian Cohort, a devout man who with his whole household feared God, gave generously to the people and prayed to God constantly.

On a Tuesday. God sees those who seek him, even outside the church: the colleague who asks careful questions, the neighbour who says she prays but has never heard the gospel, the decent man who gives more to charity than you do. Do not assume they are fine, and do not assume they are far away. Pray that God will send them the gospel, and be ready to be the one he sends.

For worship. The God of Israel saw a Roman soldier praying in a garrison town and did not despise his reaching. He is the God who made of one blood every nation of men, who is not far from each one of us (17:26–27), and who had already purposed, before the foundation of the world, to gather a people from every tribe and tongue. Cornelius was groping in the half-light. The Lord of all was coming to meet him.
verseByVerse.note: Caesarea, on the coast, was the Roman capital of Judea. A centurion commanded a company of about eighty soldiers. “God-fearers” were Gentiles who worshipped Israel’s God without becoming full converts.

parallels.desc: another centurion who loved the Jewish nation

verseByVerse.quote: About the ninth hour of the day he saw clearly in a vision an angel of God come in and say to him, "Cornelius." And he stared at him in terror and said, "What is it, Lord?" And he said to him, "Your prayers and your alms have ascended as a memorial before God."
verseByVerse.commentary:
About the ninth hour of the day he saw clearly in a vision an angel of God come in and say to him, “Cornelius.” And he stared at him in terror and said, “What is it, Lord?” And he said to him, “Your prayers and your alms have ascended as a memorial before God.

About the ninth hour of the day. Three in the afternoon, which is one of the Jewish hours of prayer: the hour of the evening sacrifice, when the smoke went up in Jerusalem and devout men everywhere turned toward it (3:1). A Roman officer in a Roman garrison town was keeping Jewish prayer times, and the angel arrived while he was doing it.

He saw clearly in a vision an angel of God. Luke is being careful: not a dream, not an impression, not something he thought he saw. And Cornelius’s reaction is not devotional pleasure. He stared at him in terror, the reaction of every person in Scripture who meets an angel, which is worth remembering by anybody whose picture of angels comes from Christmas cards. A professional soldier who had presumably seen a good deal was frightened rigid. He asks what it is, and he calls the messenger Lord.

Your prayers and your alms have ascended as a memorial before God. Then the message, and it is worth reading slowly, because it has been misread in both directions. The vocabulary is taken from the sacrificial system. A memorial, mnēmosynon, was the portion of the grain offering that the priest burned on the altar, the part that went up as smoke: the token by which the whole offering came before God (Leviticus 2:2). So the angel is telling an uncircumcised Roman soldier, who had never brought a sacrifice and could not have carried one past the outer court, that his prayers and his money have gone up like an offering that God has noticed. The psalmist had prayed that his prayer would be counted as incense before God (Psalm 141:2). Cornelius’s had been.

What it does not mean. It does not mean his prayers and alms earned salvation. If they had, he would not need to send for Peter to hear the message by which he would be saved (11:14). The chapter exists precisely because he still needed a preacher. God honoured his seeking by sending him the gospel. Those who seek God sincerely will find him, through Christ (Hebrews 11:6; Jeremiah 29:13).

Nothing is lost. But neither is God indifferent to the groping of an honest man. The prayers of a Gentile who did not know the gospel went up, and were noticed, and were remembered, and God answered them by arranging a journey. There is a great deal in that for anyone praying for a person who is nowhere near the faith, or for anyone who suspects that his own years of half-informed, badly aimed prayer before he understood anything have simply evaporated. Cornelius’s had not. They were on file, and God’s answer to them was to send a man on a thirty-mile journey he did not want to make.

Does God hear the prayers of people who are not yet Christians? The Bible says plainly that no one comes to the Father except through Christ (John 14:6), and that the prayers of the wicked who despise him are an abomination (Proverbs 15:8). But God is not deaf to the cry of a person whom he is drawing to himself, and this verse shows him hearing such a cry and answering it, by sending the gospel. He does not answer it by saving the man without Christ; he answers it by bringing him to Christ. So if you are not yet a believer and have been praying in the dark, keep seeking. The answer God gives to that kind of prayer is himself, in his Son, through his word.

In a sentence. About three in the afternoon he clearly saw in a vision an angel of God come in and call his name, and staring at him in terror he asked what it was, and the angel said his prayers and gifts to the poor had gone up as a memorial before God.

On a Tuesday. Keep praying for the person who seems furthest from God. You may never see the answer arrive, and it may come by a road you would not have chosen, but nothing offered in faith is wasted. And if you have a time of prayer, keep it as Cornelius kept his, even on the days when nothing seems to happen. The angel came at the ninth hour.

For worship. God remembers. The God who counted the tears of David, who heard Hagar in the wilderness and Hannah at the door of the tabernacle, saw the prayers of a Roman soldier rising and kept every one. He answers in his time, and by his gospel, and his answers are always better than the prayers that asked for them. Cornelius asked for light. God sent him Christ.
verseByVerse.note: The ESV notes that the ninth hour was about 3 p.m., the hour of afternoon prayer. A “memorial” offering was one that brought the worshipper to God’s remembrance.

parallels.desc: the memorial portion

verseByVerse.quote: "And now send men to Joppa and bring one Simon who is called Peter. He is lodging with one Simon, a tanner, whose house is by the sea."
verseByVerse.commentary:
And now send men to Joppa and bring one Simon who is called Peter. He is lodging with one Simon, a tanner, whose house is by the sea.

And now send men to Joppa and bring one Simon who is called Peter. An angel is standing in the room, and what he brings is an address. That is worth stopping over, because it is the most theologically loaded thing in the paragraph. Here is a genuine supernatural messenger, in a chapter full of divine intervention, speaking directly to a man who wants God, and he does not preach the gospel. He does not explain about Jesus, or the cross, or forgiveness. He gives a name, a town, a householder and a street.

On human breath. Angels in Scripture announce, warn, guide and rescue. They do not evangelise. The message by which a man is saved is put into the mouths of other men, and it always has been; God’s settled arrangement is that the news travels on human breath, from someone who has it to someone who has not (Romans 10:14). It would have been simpler to let the angel say it. He is already in the room, he has Cornelius’s undivided attention, and there would have been no need for anybody to walk anywhere. Instead the whole apparatus of heaven is deployed to get a fisherman onto a road. We have this treasure in jars of clay (2 Corinthians 4:7). That is a considerable dignity conferred on ordinary Christians, and a considerable responsibility. Nobody else has been given the job.

He is lodging with one Simon, a tanner, whose house is by the sea. Then the detail of the directions, which is almost comic in its specificity. The angel knows that there are two men named Simon in the story and distinguishes them. He knows the second one’s trade. He knows the house is by the sea, which it was, because tanneries needed water and had to keep their smell downwind of the town. God’s guidance in this chapter has a postcode.

Enough to act on. And notice what Cornelius is not told. Not why. Not what Peter will say, or what will come of it, or that this errand will crack open the whole future of the church. He is told to send for a man, and that is all, and he sends. Most obedience arrives in exactly that condition: enough instruction to act on and nothing whatever by way of explanation.

Why did God not just let the angel tell him the gospel? Because God has chosen to spread the news of his Son through people who have received it themselves. A preacher who has been forgiven speaks of forgiveness as no angel can, for angels have never needed a Saviour. And the message binds the church together: the Gentile is brought in by the Jew, the hearer by the speaker, so that no one can boast of having found the way alone. It also means the job is yours. If an angel would not do it in Caesarea, an angel will not do it in your street.

In a sentence. The angel told him to send men to Joppa to bring back Simon called Peter, who was staying with Simon, a tanner, whose house was by the sea.

On a Tuesday. God has given the gospel to people like you to tell. Angels cannot do it for you. Think of one person who may be waiting for exactly what you know, and ask God for an opening to say it this week. You do not need the whole plan; you need the next address.

For worship. The Lord of hosts, who commands myriads of angels, has chosen to send the best news in the universe by fishermen, tentmakers and ordinary church members. He is not short of messengers. He delights to honour weak servants with the greatest errand there is, so that the glory belongs to him and the power is plainly his.

parallels.desc: Simon the tanner

verseByVerse.quote: When the angel who spoke to him had departed, he called two of his servants and a devout soldier from among those who attended him, and having related everything to them, he sent them to Joppa.
verseByVerse.commentary:
When the angel who spoke to him had departed, he called two of his servants and a devout soldier from among those who attended him, and having related everything to them, he sent them to Joppa.

When the angel who spoke to him had departed, he called two of his servants and a devout soldier. And then, immediately, action. Luke does not record any interval. Cornelius does not sleep on it, does not consult anybody, does not wait to see whether the impression fades by morning. The angel goes and he calls for staff.

A devout soldier from among those who attended him. Look at whom he sends: two household servants and a soldier, and Luke troubles to tell us the soldier was devout. That is a small window into what this man’s household was actually like. Verse 2 said he feared God with all his household, and here is the corroboration: one of the men under his command shared his faith, closely enough that Cornelius could pick him for an errand of this kind and know he would understand it.

And having related everything to them, he sent them to Joppa. That is the sentence to notice. He did not send them with an instruction; he sent them with the whole story. The angel, the hour, the message, the fear, all of it, told to two servants and a private soldier before they set off. A senior officer, in a rigidly hierarchical profession, sat his subordinates down and told them what had happened to him while he was praying.

Why it mattered. It is a small thing, and it explains a great deal about the reception Peter gets four days later. When those men arrive in Joppa they are able to give an account of Cornelius that persuades an apostle to travel; and when Peter reaches Caesarea he finds not a curious individual but a room full of relatives and friends who have been assembled and briefed. That happened because a man who had received something extraordinary told the people around him instead of keeping it to himself. The distance to Joppa is about thirty miles down the coast, a day and a half on foot. Cornelius will spend four days waiting on the strength of one conversation with a stranger in bright clothing. Whatever else this is, it is not a man taking a small risk.

In a sentence. When the angel who had spoken to him had gone, Cornelius called two of his servants and a devout soldier from his attendants, told them everything that had happened, and sent them to Joppa.

On a Tuesday. When God speaks to you through his word, do not delay, and do not keep it to yourself. Tell the people closest to you what he has been showing you: your spouse, your children, the colleague who shares your faith. Obedience that is spoken about tends to spread.

For worship. Cornelius obeyed at once, and behind his obedience stood the God who had made him willing. The Lord who sent an angel to a soldier was also at work in his servants and in the devout man under his command, building a household that would be ready for the gospel. He prepares whole families for his grace, and he loves to save them together.

verseByVerse.quote: The next day, as they were on their journey and approaching the city, Peter went up on the housetop about the sixth hour to pray. And he became hungry and wanted something to eat, but while they were preparing it, he fell into a trance
verseByVerse.commentary:
The next day, as they were on their journey and approaching the city, Peter went up on the housetop about the sixth hour to pray. And he became hungry and wanted something to eat, but while they were preparing it, he fell into a trance

The next day, as they were on their journey and approaching the city. Luke does something here that he does all through this chapter: he cuts between the two ends of the story and lines up the timing so the reader can see the machinery. The messengers are perhaps an hour away, and Peter’s vision comes just as they arrive. God’s timing is not approximate.

Peter went up on the housetop about the sixth hour to pray. The roof was the coolest and most private place in an eastern house: flat, reached by an outside stair, used for sleeping in hot weather and for drying things, often shaded with an awning. It was where a man went to be alone. And the sixth hour is noon. The fixed hours of prayer at the temple were the morning and the afternoon sacrifices, but the devout also prayed at midday (Psalm 55:17; Daniel 6:10). Peter has gone up to pray in the middle of the day, as he did most days.

And he became hungry and wanted something to eat. Then the entirely unspiritual detail that Luke, being Luke, refuses to leave out. It is noon, he has been up since dawn, the meal is being cooked downstairs and he can presumably smell it. And in the gap between the hunger and the food arriving, God speaks. It would be easy to make too much of that and it would be a pity to make nothing of it. A man who is hungry, on a roof, waiting for lunch is a man in whose mind the subject of food is already open, and what is about to come down out of the sky is a sheet full of animals with an instruction to kill and eat. The revelation arrives in the vocabulary Peter’s body has just supplied.

But while they were preparing it, he fell into a trance. The word is ekstasis, a state in which ordinary perception is suspended and God communicates directly, as he did with Paul in the temple (22:17). It is worth registering how ordinary the setting is. The most consequential vision in the book of Acts, the one that opens the church to the entire non-Jewish world, is given to a man on a roof, in a borrowed house that smelt of tanning, at midday, while he was waiting for something to eat. Nothing had been arranged. He had simply gone up to pray, and stayed there long enough to get hungry.

In a sentence. The next day, as the messengers were nearing the city, Peter went up on the roof to pray at about noon, and he became hungry and wanted something to eat, and while the food was being prepared he fell into a trance.

On a Tuesday. Peter was praying when God spoke. Keep your times of prayer, especially the unremarkable ones in the middle of a working day. You are not waiting for a vision; you are keeping company with the God who speaks through his word, and he often meets his people in the most ordinary hour.

For worship. The God who rules the timing of the universe arranged that a sheet would come down from heaven over a tanner’s roof at the very hour three Gentiles reached the gate. He works on rooftops and on roads at once. Not a sparrow falls without him, and not a lunch is cooked in Joppa outside his care, and every one of those threads was being drawn toward the cross of his Son and the gathering of the nations.
verseByVerse.note: The ESV notes that the sixth hour was about noon. Flat roofs were used for prayer and rest.

verseByVerse.quote: and saw the heavens opened and something like a great sheet descending, being let down by its four corners upon the earth.
verseByVerse.commentary:
and saw the heavens opened and something like a great sheet descending, being let down by its four corners upon the earth.

And saw the heavens opened. Luke uses that phrase very sparingly and always at a moment when something changes permanently: at the Jordan when the Spirit came down on Jesus (Luke 3:21), and in a council chamber when Stephen looked up and saw the Son of Man standing (7:56). It is not decorative language. It means the boundary has been crossed from the other side. The vision comes from God.

Something like a great sheet descending. And what comes through is a household object. Note the something like, which is Luke’s habitual honesty when a witness is describing an unfamiliar thing by the nearest familiar one. It was not a sheet. It was whatever it was, and a sheet is what it resembled: a large square of cloth, of the sort that would have been lying about on that very roof, or a ship’s sail of the kind Peter could see in the harbour below.

Being let down by its four corners upon the earth. Four corners is a phrase with a history. The prophets speak of God gathering the outcasts of Israel from the four corners of the earth (Isaiah 11:12), and the four corners are a standard way of saying everywhere, from every direction, the whole inhabited world. Peter is watching something being lowered toward him that is held at the four points of the compass, and it will be full of every kind of living creature. The shape of the vision is announcing its subject before a word is spoken: all nations.

It comes down. The direction of travel is the thing to hold. Peter does not go up, is not caught away, is not given a tour of anything. He is on a roof and heaven descends to where he is standing, which is exactly what the rest of the chapter is about: God moving toward people who could not have come to him, and doing it on their own roofs, at lunchtime.

In a sentence. He saw heaven opened and something like a great sheet coming down, being let down to earth by its four corners.

On a Tuesday. When God’s word opens something to you that you did not expect, do not reach first for the reasons it cannot mean what it says. Let it come down to where you are. The vision was not given for Peter to study from a distance; it was let down to his feet.

For worship. Heaven came down. That is the whole movement of the gospel: not man climbing up to God, but God descending to man. The Son came down from the Father’s side, took our flesh, and was lifted up on a cross so that people from the four corners of the earth could be gathered in. What comes down from heaven is from God, and it comes in mercy.

parallels.desc: the heavens were opened

verseByVerse.quote: In it were all kinds of animals and reptiles and birds of the air. And there came a voice to him: "Rise, Peter; kill and eat."
verseByVerse.commentary:
In it were all kinds of animals and reptiles and birds of the air. And there came a voice to him: “Rise, Peter; kill and eat.”

In it were all kinds of animals and reptiles and birds of the air. The three categories are the ones Genesis uses at the creation and Leviticus uses when it draws the lines (Leviticus 11; Deuteronomy 14), and Luke lists them in a way that makes clear the sheet is not a selection. It is the whole zoo. Clean and unclean together, in one cloth, on Peter’s roof: the pig beside the sheep, the vulture beside the pigeon, and creeping things which were unclean without exception and about which there had never been any argument at all. Contact with unclean creatures defiled a Jew; eating them was unthinkable.

Rise, Peter; kill and eat. Then the voice, and it gives an order rather than an invitation. Feel the force of that on a man of Peter’s upbringing. Kill: so it is not merely eat what is put in front of you; it is do the butchering yourself. And it is not eat the clean ones; it is eat from the mixed sheet. He is being told to get up, take a knife, and prepare a meal out of creatures he had been taught before he could walk were an offence to God.

What martyrs had died for. And it was not a marginal scruple. The food laws were where Jewish identity had been defended at the cost of blood, and the nation had not forgotten it. Under the Greek persecution two centuries earlier, mothers had watched their sons killed rather than eat pork; the books that recorded it were read and treasured. To a Jew of the first century, refusing unclean food was not a dietary preference. It was what martyrs had died for, and everybody knew the stories. So the command is not a gentle stretching of a habit. It is an instruction to do the specific thing that faithful Israelites had gone to their deaths refusing to do, and it comes from heaven, in a vision, from a voice Peter will address as Lord. Which is why the next verse contains one of the most understandable refusals in Scripture, and why God has to say it three times.

The animals were the vehicle; the freight was people. One guard, and it needs stating because this passage gets pressed into service for arguments it was not given for. The vision is regularly produced to settle questions about what Christians may eat, and it does bear on that: the New Testament is clear elsewhere that no food is unclean in itself, and Mark says as much in an aside (Mark 7:19). But Peter himself tells us what the vision was for, and he tells us in verse 28, and it is not a menu. God has shown me that I should not call any person common or unclean. So the passage is being used most faithfully not when it is settling a dispute about diet, but when it is dismantling the far more durable habit the food laws existed to enforce: the sorting of human beings into those one can sit down with and those one cannot. That habit long outlived the dietary code, and it has never needed a Bible verse to keep it going.

In a sentence. In the sheet were all kinds of four-footed animals, reptiles and birds, and a voice told Peter to get up, kill and eat.

On a Tuesday. Sometimes God’s word shocks our habits. Listen anyway. Ask yourself which people you instinctively sort into the category of those you would not sit down with: a class, a nationality, a political tribe, a lifestyle, a church tradition. That is where this vision is aimed in your life.

For worship. The God who drew the lines in Leviticus is the God who erased them in Christ, and he is the same God, faithful in both. He gave Israel the food laws to keep her distinct until the promised Seed came, and when Christ had come and died, he lowered a sheet over a roof in Joppa and declared the meaning fulfilled. His purposes run straight through the centuries, and they were always heading for a table with every nation at it.
verseByVerse.note: The sheet held both clean and unclean creatures together, all of which Peter is told to eat.

parallels.desc: clean and unclean animals

verseByVerse.quote: But Peter said, "By no means, Lord; for I have never eaten anything that is common or unclean."
verseByVerse.commentary:
But Peter said, “By no means, Lord; for I have never eaten anything that is common or unclean.”

By no means, Lord. Two words that will not go together. The first is as strong a refusal as can be made: not I would rather not, but absolutely not, under no circumstances. The second is Lord. Peter has said, in a single breath, never and master, and the sentence contradicts itself before he has finished it. He stands where Ezekiel stood when he protested against eating defiled food (Ezekiel 4:14).

A recognisable habit. It is not the first time he has done it, and readers of the Gospels will hear the echo. In a boat on Galilee, after a catch of fish, Peter had begged the Lord to depart from him, for he was a sinful man (Luke 5:8). At a supper table he had said, You shall never wash my feet (John 13:8). On a road to Jerusalem, when Jesus told him what was going to happen there, he took him aside and said, Far be it from you, Lord (Matthew 16:22). He is the disciple who tells Jesus what will not be happening, and who calls him Lord while doing it.

For I have never eaten anything that is common or unclean. And the reason is not stubbornness. Look at what he actually says. Common means ritually unfit, profane, for ordinary use rather than for God. That is a lifetime’s record laid out as evidence, and every word of it is to his credit. He is not saying he does not want to. He is saying that in a lifetime, under pressure, in poverty, travelling, as a fisherman working alongside Gentiles on a lake with a mixed shoreline, he has never once done it. He is defending God’s own law, which he has kept at cost, and he is defending it against God. Even after Jesus had declared all foods clean (Mark 7:19), he had not grasped it.

Holding the scaffolding. That is the situation worth sitting with, because it is more common than it looks. The thing Peter cannot let go of is not a sin. It is an obedience, a genuine one, in a real command, kept faithfully for decades. What has changed is not that God has grown lax; it is that the command had a purpose, and the purpose has arrived, and Peter is holding on to the scaffolding after the building is up. Most Christians who are stuck are not stuck on something disreputable. They are stuck on something that was once right, and was kept at cost, and has quietly become the thing they will not let God touch. Peter’s by no means, Lord is not the sentence of a rebel. It is the sentence of a good man defending a good thing at the exact moment God is moving past it.

How do I tell a good conviction from a scaffold I should take down? Ask where it comes from and what it is for. If a conviction rests on a plain command of Scripture that still applies to Christians, keep it, whatever it costs: no vision overturns the moral law. But if it rests on a custom, a tradition, or an Old Testament ceremony that the New Testament says has been fulfilled in Christ, hold it loosely, and be ready to let it go when it starts to keep people at a distance whom Christ has welcomed. Peter did not change his mind because he felt like it; he changed because God himself spoke. We have the finished word of God for that, not new visions, and the New Testament is clear on which lines have been taken down (Colossians 2:16–17).

In a sentence. Peter replied, “By no means, Lord; for I have never eaten anything that is common or unclean.”

On a Tuesday. You cannot say no and Lord in the same breath for long. Ask whether there is an area of your life where you have been saying both: a good habit that has become a wall, a preference you defend as if it were Scripture, a way of doing church that you will not let anyone question. Bring it to the word of God honestly, and let him be Lord of it.

For worship. The Lord was patient with Peter on the roof as he had been patient with him in the boat, at the supper table and on the road. He did not cast him off for contradicting him; he spoke again, and again, until his servant understood. That is the gentleness of the risen Christ with his stubborn people. He bears with our never, and he is faithful to bring us to his yes.
verseByVerse.note: “Common” means ritually unfit, profane.

parallels.desc: “I have never defiled myself”

verseByVerse.quote: And the voice came to him again a second time, "What God has made clean, do not call common." This happened three times, and the thing was taken up at once to heaven.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And the voice came to him again a second time, “What God has made clean, do not call common.” This happened three times, and the thing was taken up at once to heaven.

What God has made clean, do not call common. Note the tense and the agent. Not what I am now permitting, but what God has made clean: the thing has already been done, elsewhere, and Peter’s part is simply to stop describing it wrongly. He is not being asked to change a rule. He is being told that a fact has altered and his vocabulary is out of date. The food laws, which had separated Israel from the nations (Leviticus 20:24–26), are now set aside, because the separation they symbolised is ended in Christ (Ephesians 2:14–15; Colossians 2:16–17).

Aimed at his mouth. And the correction is aimed at his speech: do not call common. The problem the voice addresses is not only what Peter eats but what he says about people, and within thirteen verses he will have made the translation himself in front of a room full of Gentiles: God has shown me that I should not call any person common or unclean (v. 28). Not food only, but people. Gentiles are not unclean.

Heard but not grasped. Nor is this the law being contradicted. Jesus had already said it, in a sentence Mark records with an editorial note attached: what goes into a man cannot defile him, and in saying so he declared all foods clean (Mark 7:18–19). Peter had been standing there. He had heard it and had not drawn the conclusion, which is worth knowing by anyone who assumes that hearing good teaching is the same thing as being changed by it. He needed it said again, from heaven, three times, with livestock.

This happened three times. It is the same number as a charcoal fire in a courtyard and three questions on a beach, and it is hard to believe Peter missed the resonance. Three times he had denied; three times he had been restored (John 21:15–17); three times now the vision comes and the command is repeated. God appears to know exactly how many repetitions this particular man requires.

And the thing was taken up at once to heaven. Then, abruptly, it is gone, and no explanation is given. It came from God and it went back to him. The vision does not conclude with an application. It simply stops, leaving a man on a roof holding a command he has refused, a sentence he cannot argue with, and no idea what any of it is for. That is where verse 17 finds him, and it is where a great deal of Christian experience actually happens: the instruction has been received and the meaning has not arrived, and the only thing to do is go on standing there until somebody knocks at the gate.

Where Christians differ: are the food laws binding today? Some groups, such as Seventh-day Adventists and some Messianic Jews, still keep the Old Testament food laws. Verdict: Jesus declared all foods clean (Mark 7:19); this vision confirms it; Paul teaches that food is a matter of freedom (Romans 14:14, 20; 1 Timothy 4:3–5). The food laws were shadows fulfilled in Christ. Christians are free to eat anything with thanksgiving, though they should be considerate of the weaker conscience (Romans 14:15).

Then why did God give the food laws at all? Not because pork was wicked or sheep were holy, but to teach and to protect. Day by day, at every meal, the food laws taught Israel that she was set apart for a holy God, and that holiness means distinction (Leviticus 11:44–45; 20:25–26). They also kept her from being swallowed by the nations around her until the Messiah came. When Christ came, the true holiness they pictured arrived in him, and the people of God was no longer to be marked by a diet but by faith in him, gathered from every nation. The laws were not a mistake that God corrected. They were a signpost, and Peter was standing at the place it pointed to.

In a sentence. The voice spoke to him a second time, telling him not to call common what God had made clean, and this happened three times, and the sheet was taken back up to heaven at once.

On a Tuesday. Do not call unclean anyone God has made clean in Christ. Think of a Christian whose background, culture or past makes you uneasy, and ask whether you treat him as a full brother. Then do one concrete thing about it: an invitation, a phone call, a seat beside him on Sunday.

For worship. What God has made clean is clean indeed. The blood of Christ cleanses from all sin, and no one it has washed can ever be called common again. The Father declared it from heaven three times over a tanner’s roof, and he declares it still over every sinner who comes to his Son: clean, accepted, mine. Blessed be the God who does not leave us to define who is fit for him.

parallels.desc: he declared all foods clean

verseByVerse.quote: Now while Peter was inwardly perplexed as to what the vision that he had seen might mean, behold, the men who were sent by Cornelius, having made inquiry for Simon's house, stood at the gate and called out to ask whether Simon who was called Peter was lodging there.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Now while Peter was inwardly perplexed as to what the vision that he had seen might mean, behold, the men who were sent by Cornelius, having made inquiry for Simon’s house, stood at the gate and called out to ask whether Simon who was called Peter was lodging there.

While Peter was inwardly perplexed as to what the vision that he had seen might mean. Thoroughly at a loss, completely unable to see through it. Luke is not describing a man who has grasped a great truth and is savouring it. He is describing bafflement, and he says it twice, because a moment later he adds that Peter was still pondering when the Spirit spoke. That is a useful thing to have on record. The apostle Peter received a direct revelation from heaven, repeated three times for emphasis, and did not know what it meant. He was not being slow. The vision was genuinely opaque, and it was designed to be: it was about food and it was not about food, and there was no way to get from the sheet to the Gentiles by thinking harder. The interpretation was going to arrive by other means.

The men who were sent by Cornelius stood at the gate. And it is already at the gate. Having made inquiry for Simon’s house, they stand outside and call out, asking whether Simon who is called Peter is lodging there. Luke’s timing is exact and he wants it noticed: while the vision is still fresh enough to be unresolved, the answer to it is standing in the street asking for Peter by name. The explanation is knocking at the door.

Understood by obeying. Notice how the meaning is going to be delivered. Not by further revelation, and not by a better idea occurring to Peter on the roof. It arrives as three men with a message, an address, and a request: which is to say, as circumstances. Peter will understand the sheet by obeying the knock, and not before. This is worth holding by anyone who is wrestling with a passage of Scripture he cannot yet see how to apply, or a burden he cannot put down. The temptation is to sit with it until it clarifies. Peter was perplexed on a roof and the explanation was downstairs, and he would never have worked it out up there. Some things are only understood at the point where they are acted on. God often explains his word by his providence.

In a sentence. While Peter was wondering what the vision might mean, the men sent by Cornelius, having asked their way to Simon’s house, stood at the gate and called out to ask whether Simon who was called Peter was staying there.

On a Tuesday. If you are puzzled by something God has plainly told you in Scripture, do not wait until you understand all of it before you obey the part you do understand. Watch for the knock at the gate: the person who arrives, the need that appears, the door that opens. The meaning is often on the other side of the next step.

For worship. The God who spoke on the roof had already sent the answer up the road. He is never late with his explanations and never early with his providences. His word and his works fit together like a key and a lock, because the same Lord governs both, and he is leading his people step by step into purposes far larger than they can see from where they stand.

verseByVerse.quote: And while Peter was pondering the vision, the Spirit said to him, "Behold, three men are looking for you. Rise and go down and accompany them without hesitation, for I have sent them."
verseByVerse.commentary:
And while Peter was pondering the vision, the Spirit said to him, “Behold, three men are looking for you. Rise and go down and accompany them without hesitation, for I have sent them.”

And while Peter was pondering the vision, the Spirit said to him. Three separate parties are being moved in this chapter and none of them can see the others. Cornelius has an angel and an address. The three messengers have a road and an errand. Peter has a sheet full of animals and no idea what it is for. Here, for the first time, the wiring becomes visible. And notice who speaks: not an angel now, but the Spirit himself, a person who directs, sends and commands.

Behold, three men are looking for you. The information is precise: the number (two servants and a soldier, v. 7), the fact that they are searching, and then the instruction.

Rise and go down and accompany them without hesitation. The phrase rendered without hesitation is worth a moment, because it is doing more than steadying his nerves. The Greek, mēden diakrinomenos, can also be rendered making no distinction. The verb means to divide, to discriminate, to sort one thing from another, and it is the same verb Peter uses in his report at Jerusalem (11:12), and the same idea again at the council in chapter 15, where he says God made no distinction between us and them (15:9). So the Spirit’s word to Peter on the stairs is not merely do not dither. It is do not sort these men into a category. The instruction names the exact reflex that was about to operate, and forbids it before it can.

For I have sent them. That last clause is the hinge of the chapter, and Peter never lets go of it. The Spirit sent Gentiles to fetch an apostle. When Peter is called before the Jerusalem church a chapter later to explain what he has done, this is what he produces: the Spirit told me to go with them. He tells the vision too, and what fell on Cornelius’s house, but the hinge is that he was sent.

The whole briefing. And notice the sheer economy of what Peter is given. He is not told who Cornelius is, or what the vision meant, or what is going to happen in Caesarea, or that this afternoon will change the shape of the church for ever. He is told there are three men downstairs, to go with them, and that they were sent. That is the whole briefing, and it turns out to be enough, because the one thing in it that matters is the last clause.

How does the Spirit lead Christians today? Here the Spirit spoke directly to an apostle at a turning point in the founding of the church, and we should not expect such words as our normal guidance. Today the Spirit leads us chiefly through the Scriptures he inspired, which are complete and sufficient (2 Timothy 3:16–17), by opening our understanding of them, by working in our hearts a desire to obey, and by ordering our circumstances in his providence. And the direction he gives in Scripture is unmistakable on this very point: we are to make no distinction among those Christ has received. You do not need a voice on the stairs to know you should welcome the stranger at the gate.

In a sentence. While Peter was still thinking about the vision, the Spirit told him that three men were looking for him, and that he should get up, go down and go with them without hesitation, for the Spirit himself had sent them.

On a Tuesday. When the Spirit, through his word, leads you toward someone different from you, go without hesitation and without sorting. The next person who knocks at your gate, literally or otherwise, may have been sent.

For worship. The Holy Spirit is not a force but the living God, who speaks, sends and directs his church. He moved on the waters at creation, overshadowed the virgin, descended on the Son at the Jordan, and here he sends Gentiles to fetch an apostle. The whole mission of the church is his work, and he never sends his servants anywhere he has not already gone ahead.

verseByVerse.quote: And Peter went down to the men and said, "I am the one you are looking for. What is the reason for your coming?" And they said, "Cornelius, a centurion, an upright and God-fearing man, who is well spoken of by the whole Jewish nation, was directed by a holy angel to send for you to come to his house and to hear what you have to say."
verseByVerse.commentary:
And Peter went down to the men and said, “I am the one you are looking for. What is the reason for your coming?” And they said, “Cornelius, a centurion, an upright and God-fearing man, who is well spoken of by the whole Jewish nation, was directed by a holy angel to send for you to come to his house and to hear what you have to say.”

I am the one you are looking for. What is the reason for your coming? Peter goes down and opens with a flat, practical sentence, and it is worth noticing that he has not been told the reason. The Spirit gave him the instruction and withheld the explanation, and Peter is now going to get it from three strangers at a gate.

Cornelius, a centurion, an upright and God-fearing man. Their answer is a small masterpiece of diplomacy, and every clause is chosen for the man they are talking to. Cornelius, a centurion: they lead with the awkward fact rather than hiding it. An upright and God-fearing man: the two things a Jewish hearer would most want to know, in the right order. Who is well spoken of by the whole Jewish nation: that is, the people you are worried about offending already think highly of him; there are references available, and they are from your own community. And finally the clincher: was directed by a holy angel to send for you. Not, he would like a word. He was told to fetch you, from heaven. These three men have made the case as well as it could be made, which suggests they had rehearsed it on the road, which suggests they knew exactly how unlikely their errand was.

To come to his house and to hear what you have to say. The last phrase of their speech is the one to sit with. That is the whole invitation. Not to be healed, not to be advised, not to be impressed. A household has been assembled thirty miles away and is waiting, and what they want is words. Cornelius needs Peter’s message to be saved (11:14): not his prayers, not his alms, but the gospel. It is not a common request. Most preachers spend their lives trying to get people to listen; here is a man who sent servants on a journey of days to secure a hearing for a message he had not heard yet and could not have described. Whatever Peter was feeling as he came down those stairs, he was walking toward the most willing audience of his life.

In a sentence. Peter went down and told the men he was the one they were looking for and asked why they had come, and they said that Cornelius, a centurion, an upright and God-fearing man respected by the whole Jewish nation, had been told by a holy angel to invite Peter to his house and hear what he had to say.

On a Tuesday. The world around you is often more ready to hear about Christ than you think, and what people need from you is not your opinions but his word. If someone asks you a question about your faith this week, do not change the subject. Say what you have to say, simply and kindly.

For worship. God was gathering an audience for his Son in a Roman officer’s house before Peter had heard of it. The Father has always been drawing people to the Son (John 6:44), in places the church has not thought to look. The harvest is plentiful, and the Lord of the harvest is already at work in the field.

verseByVerse.quote: So he invited them in to be his guests. The next day he rose and went away with them, and some of the brothers from Joppa accompanied him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
So he invited them in to be his guests. The next day he rose and went away with them, and some of the brothers from Joppa accompanied him.

So he invited them in to be his guests. Three things happen in this one verse and two of them are quietly enormous. The first: Peter takes two Gentile servants and a Roman soldier into the house and puts them up for the night. That means beds, and it means a meal, and a meal means a table, which is precisely the thing a devout Jew did not do with Gentiles, and precisely the thing the vision had been about an hour earlier. Luke does not comment. He simply records that the man who had said by no means, Lord before lunch had Gentiles eating in his lodgings by supper. The vision is already at work.

Obedience before understanding. It is worth noticing how fast that went. Peter did not resolve his theology first and then act on it; the theology is not resolved until verse 28, and he says as much. He obeyed a plain instruction, one step at a time, and understood it afterwards. And the first step was not preaching to Gentiles. It was having them in the house.

The next day he rose and went away with them. Not that afternoon. Joppa to Caesarea is about thirty miles and the men had already walked it. He gave them a night’s rest first, which is a small kindness Luke did not have to record and did.

And some of the brothers from Joppa accompanied him. The third is the shrewdest thing anybody does in this chapter. In the retelling at Jerusalem we learn there were six of them (11:12), and we learn it because Peter had them standing beside him when the church demanded an explanation. He knew what was coming. A man does not take six witnesses on a pastoral visit. Peter understood that whatever happened in Caesarea was going to be examined, contested and possibly disbelieved, and that his own word would not be enough, so he arranged, before he set out, for six other men to see it with their own eyes. It is not timidity and it is not politics. It is a leader anticipating the church’s real difficulty and taking the trouble, in advance, to make his account checkable.

Why does it matter that Peter brought witnesses? Because the gospel is not a private experience but public truth, and God wanted the church to receive the Gentiles on the basis of evidence, not on one man’s say-so. The law required two or three witnesses to establish a matter (Deuteronomy 19:15), and Peter brought six. There is wisdom here for any Christian or leader involved in something sensitive: act in the open, bring others with you, keep your conduct checkable. Integrity that welcomes scrutiny protects both the leader and the people he serves.

In a sentence. So Peter invited them in as his guests, and the next day he got up and set out with them, and some of the believers from Joppa went along with him.

On a Tuesday. Hospitality often comes before the gospel. Open your home this week to someone outside your usual circle: a meal, a coffee, a bed for the night. And in any matter where your conduct might later be questioned, bring a trusted brother or sister with you, not out of suspicion, but out of love for the truth.

For worship. The Lord who broke bread with tax collectors and sinners was teaching his apostle to do the same, one guest at a time. Christ himself is the host of the great supper, who sends his servants into the roads and lanes to compel people to come in, that his house may be filled (Luke 14:23). Every Gentile at Peter’s table in Joppa was a foretaste of the marriage supper of the Lamb.
verseByVerse.note: Joppa to Caesarea was a journey of about 30 miles.

parallels.desc: six brothers accompanied me

verseByVerse.quote: And on the following day they entered Caesarea. Cornelius was expecting them and had called together his relatives and close friends. When Peter entered, Cornelius met him and fell down at his feet and worshiped him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And on the following day they entered Caesarea. Cornelius was expecting them and had called together his relatives and close friends. When Peter entered, Cornelius met him and fell down at his feet and worshiped him.

And on the following day they entered Caesarea. Cornelius was expecting them and had called together his relatives and close friends. He has spent four days on this. The angel came; the messengers walked a day and a half; they stayed a night; they walked back. And in the meantime Cornelius has been going round Caesarea inviting people to his house to hear a man he has never met say something he cannot describe.

What it took. He is a serving officer in a garrison town, and he has told his extended family and his friends, probably including brother officers, that an angel appeared to him while he was praying and told him to send for a Jewish fisherman from Joppa. He had no idea what Peter was going to say. If nothing had come of it he would have looked ridiculous in front of everybody whose opinion mattered to him, and would have gone on looking ridiculous for years. That is faith expecting something, and generosity too: he wanted his loved ones to hear.

He filled a room. And notice the instinct. The first thing this man does with something from God is gather a congregation. He does not receive it privately and consider passing it on later; he assumes from the outset that whatever is coming is too large to keep, and he goes and fetches the people he loves. The whole Gentile mission begins in a house full of somebody’s relatives, because a Roman soldier could not think of a reason to hear this alone.

Cornelius met him and fell down at his feet and worshiped him. Then Peter arrives, and Cornelius does the wrong thing. The verb, prosekynēsen, means to bow down, to prostrate oneself in reverence, and it is the ordinary word for worship. It is worth being fair to him. He is not a theologian. What he knows is that four days ago an angel stood in his house and told him to send for this man, and here the man is; and in the world Cornelius grew up in, when something from heaven turns up you get on the floor. Perhaps he took Peter for a divine messenger. His error is an error of enthusiasm and reverence, made by a man who has been waiting four days and does not know quite what he is dealing with. It is corrected in the next verse, immediately and kindly, and Luke does not hold it against him.

In a sentence. The following day they arrived in Caesarea, where Cornelius was waiting for them with the relatives and close friends he had invited, and when Peter came in, Cornelius met him and fell at his feet in worship.

On a Tuesday. Gather your family and friends to hear the gospel. Invite one person this week to come with you to church, or to a meal where Christ will be spoken of. And when you bring them, let them see that you are expecting God to speak.

For worship. The God who gathered a household in Caesarea is the God who sets the lonely in families (Psalm 68:6). He does not save people only one by one, in isolation; he gathers them into homes and congregations, and he delights when the first thing a seeker does is call his loved ones to come and hear. The gospel was always meant to fill a room.

parallels.desc: “You must not do that”

verseByVerse.quote: But Peter lifted him up, saying, "Stand up; I too am a man."
verseByVerse.commentary:
But Peter lifted him up, saying, “Stand up; I too am a man.”

But Peter lifted him up, saying, Stand up; I too am a man. A single sentence, and it is the whole of Christian ministry. Not, you are embarrassing me; not, this is inappropriate. I too am a man: the same kind of thing you are, on the same side of the floor, made of the same material.

He lifted him up. And he does not simply say it. He reaches down, takes hold of a Roman centurion who is lying on the ground in front of him, and puts him back on his feet. The correction is physical and it is instant, and it happens before a word of the gospel has been preached in that house. The first thing Peter does in the first Gentile home to hear the gospel is pick a man up off the floor.

Two scenes in Caesarea. Luke has a habit of setting scenes like this against each other, and the reader is meant to notice. Two chapters later a king in this same city of Caesarea will accept exactly the acclaim Peter has just refused: the crowd will shout that it is the voice of a god and not of a man, and Herod will take it, and Luke records what happened to him in a single unsparing verse (12:21–23). The two scenes are set in the same town, a few years and a few pages apart: a fisherman on his feet saying I too am a man, and a king on a throne saying nothing at all. Paul and Barnabas will refuse worship at Lystra (14:14–15), and the angel in Revelation refuses it from John (Revelation 19:10; 22:8–9).

Harder than it looks. Peter is doing something harder than it looks. Cornelius’s reverence was genuine, and it was directed at a man who had walked thirty miles to help him; refusing it risked chilling the room before anything had begun. There is a kind of false humility that deflects with one hand and enjoys the compliment with the other, and it is much more comfortable than what Peter does here, which is to end the transaction on the spot. Every ministry that lasts is built on this refusal, and every one that collapses has stopped making it somewhere.

What Jesus did not refuse. And notice the difference that shows who Jesus is. The apostles and angels refuse worship. Jesus accepted it: from the disciples in the boat who said, Truly you are the Son of God (Matthew 14:33), and from Thomas, who called him my Lord and my God (John 20:28). He never once said, Stand up; I too am a man. Either he was the most dangerous blasphemer who ever lived, or he is God.

Where Christians differ: veneration of saints and leaders. Some traditions bow before popes, saints or images. Verdict: Peter, whom Rome calls the first pope, refused to let anyone bow before him. No servant of Christ should receive the reverence due to God.

Is it wrong to honour Christian leaders? No. Scripture tells us to respect and esteem those who labour among us and are over us in the Lord, very highly in love because of their work (1 Thessalonians 5:12–13), and to remember our leaders and imitate their faith (Hebrews 13:7). The line is crossed when honour becomes reverence, when a leader is treated as beyond question, his words as equal to Scripture, or his presence as bringing us nearer to God. Healthy honour says, thank God for this man. Idolatry says, I cannot do without him. A good pastor will do what Peter did and lift you back on your feet.

In a sentence. But Peter lifted him up, saying, “Stand up; I too am a man.”

On a Tuesday. Do not put any Christian leader on a pedestal. They are only men and women, and the pedestal is bad for them and worse for you. And if you are the one people look up to, a parent, a teacher, a pastor, notice when you are enjoying it, and lift them up. Point them past yourself to Christ.

For worship. Worship belongs to God alone, and he will not give his glory to another. Peter the fisherman was a man, and said so. But the Son of God received the worship of his disciples, because he is God the Son, worthy of the same honour as the Father (John 5:23). Every knee will bow to him, and not one will bow to any of his servants. The apostle on his feet points us to the Lord on his throne.

parallels.desc: we also are men, of like nature with you

verseByVerse.quote: And as he talked with him, he went in and found many persons gathered. And he said to them, "You yourselves know how unlawful it is for a Jew to associate with or to visit anyone of another nation, but God has shown me that I should not call any person common or unclean."
verseByVerse.commentary:
And as he talked with him, he went in and found many persons gathered. And he said to them, “You yourselves know how unlawful it is for a Jew to associate with or to visit anyone of another nation, but God has shown me that I should not call any person common or unclean.

And as he talked with him, he went in and found many persons gathered. Peter walks in, into a Gentile house, a huge step for a Jew, sees a room full of Gentiles waiting for him, and opens by naming the barrier. That is the remarkable thing about this speech and it is easily missed. He does not pretend the difficulty is not there. He does not begin with something warm and general and hope nobody raises it.

You yourselves know how unlawful it is for a Jew to associate with or to visit anyone of another nation. He says it in the first sentence, to a roomful of people it applies to. They did know. Every person in that house had lived with it, and the God-fearers among them had felt it most: welcome at the synagogue door and not past it. The word athemiton means taboo, against custom, not done.

Two things about the barrier. The first is that the law of Moses nowhere forbids a Jew to enter a Gentile house. What had grown up was a dense hedge of custom and interpretation around the purity laws, hardened by centuries of pressure, until entering such a house was simply not done; strict Jews would not enter Gentile homes or eat with Gentiles (John 18:28; Galatians 2:12). That is why Peter can call it unlawful in ordinary speech and be perfectly understood. The second is that it had a real purpose once. A people surrounded by empires that swallowed nations whole survived by not eating with them.

But God has shown me that I should not call any person common or unclean. And then the pivot, and Peter makes the translation himself. The vision was about animals. Peter says it was about persons, and he had not been told that. Nobody on the roof explained the parable to him; the voice said, what God has made clean do not call common, and left. Between the roof and this doorway, somewhere on thirty miles of coast road with three Gentiles for company, Peter worked out what he had been shown.
