Obedience came first, at the gate in Joppa; the understanding caught up on the journey. No human being is unclean in God’s sight because of race or nation. The dividing wall of hostility has come down (Ephesians 2:14).

Naming the barrier. It is worth asking what a congregation would sound like if it did this: named its own barrier out loud, in front of the people on the other side of it, before saying anything else. Peter’s honesty here is the reason the room believed him. He had not come to tell them the division never existed. He had come to tell them who had ended it.

Does this mean every human being is already clean before God? No. Peter is speaking about race and nation, not about sin. No one is unclean because he is a Gentile, a Roman, or anything else he was born. But every one of us, Jew and Gentile alike, is unclean because of sin, and needs to be washed (Romans 3:23). That is why Peter goes on to preach forgiveness through Christ (v. 43). The barrier of nationality has been removed so that the gospel can reach everyone; the barrier of sin is removed only by the blood of Christ, received by faith. Both truths have to be held together, or we end either with racism or with universalism.

In a sentence. As he talked with Cornelius, Peter went in and found many people gathered, and told them that they knew it was against Jewish custom for a Jew to associate with or visit a foreigner, but God had shown him that he should not call any person common or unclean.

On a Tuesday. Name your own barrier. Is there a group of people you were raised to look down on, or simply to avoid? Say it honestly to God, and then cross the room. In Christ, no one is unclean because of race, class or background. Tear down your walls, starting with the one nearest you.

For worship. The dividing wall that stood for centuries came down at the cross, where Christ made peace by his blood and created in himself one new humanity in place of two (Ephesians 2:14–16). What custom, history and fear had built, he demolished in a single afternoon outside Jerusalem. And he sent a fisherman through a Roman doorway to announce it. Glory to the Lamb, who has ransomed people for God from every tribe and language and people and nation.
verseByVerse.note: The law did not forbid visiting Gentiles, but Jewish custom treated a Gentile home as unclean.

verseByVerse.quote: "So when I was sent for, I came without objection. I ask then why you sent for me."
verseByVerse.commentary:
So when I was sent for, I came without objection. I ask then why you sent for me.

So when I was sent for, I came without objection. It is a straightforward sentence and it is not quite the whole truth, and Peter knows it. Literally it means without saying anything against. He had objected. He had said by no means, Lord, and had gone on saying it until God had repeated himself three times (v. 14). What he means is that once he was actually sent for, once the men were at the gate and the Spirit had spoken, he raised nothing. The arguing was finished on the roof. From the moment the knock came he simply went.

I ask then why you sent for me. Then the question, and it is a good deal more courteous than it looks on the page. He does not walk in and start preaching. He has a vision, an instruction from the Spirit and the full authority of an apostle, and the first thing he does in that house is ask a question and wait for the answer. He is giving Cornelius the floor in his own home, inviting him to say what has happened at his end, in front of the relatives and friends he has assembled, before anything else is said.

Letting his host establish it. What follows is Cornelius’s account of the angel, told out loud to a room that has been waiting four days for it. And the effect of Peter’s question is that when the sermon finally comes, everybody present already knows that this meeting was arranged from heaven at both ends. Peter could have asserted that. Instead he asked, and let his host establish it. There is a small lesson in it for anybody who arrives somewhere with something to say. The apostle with the revelation began by asking the Roman soldier to explain himself, and listened to the answer, and only then opened his mouth.

In a sentence. Peter said that when he was sent for he came without objection, and asked why they had sent for him.

On a Tuesday. When God calls you to cross a boundary, go without objection. And when you arrive, ask before you tell. The next time you have a conversation about faith, begin by asking the other person what has been happening in his life, and listen properly before you speak.

For worship. The Lord who turned Peter’s by no means into without objection is the God who works in us both to will and to work for his good pleasure (Philippians 2:13). He does not merely command; he changes the heart that hears the command. Every objection silenced in his servants is a monument to his patient grace.

verseByVerse.quote: And Cornelius said, "Four days ago, about this hour, I was praying in my house at the ninth hour, and behold, a man stood before me in bright clothing and said, 'Cornelius, your prayer has been heard and your alms have been remembered before God.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
And Cornelius said, “Four days ago, about this hour, I was praying in my house at the ninth hour, and behold, a man stood before me in bright clothing and said, ‘Cornelius, your prayer has been heard and your alms have been remembered before God.’

Four days ago, about this hour, I was praying in my house at the ninth hour. Cornelius tells it back, and Luke lets him, which means the angel’s message appears twice in one chapter, once as it happened and once as the man himself reports it. That is not padding. Luke wants the reader to have it from both ends, and he will give it a third time in the next chapter when Peter recounts the whole affair in Jerusalem. Luke repeats what matters.

A man stood before me in bright clothing. The angel of verse 3, described as a man in shining clothes, as the angels at the empty tomb were (Luke 24:4).

Your prayer has been heard and your alms have been remembered before God. Here and at verse 4, the angel’s message is that Cornelius’s prayers and alms have been remembered before God, and that he should send for Peter. That is all. In chapter 11, reporting to the Jerusalem church, Peter adds the clause the reader has not yet been given: the angel said Peter would declare to you a message by which you will be saved, you and all your household (11:14).

The question the third telling settles. That clause settles the question this chapter otherwise leaves open, and it is the question every thoughtful reader asks about Cornelius. He was devout, God-fearing, generous and prayerful, and his prayers went up before God like an offering. Was he then already saved, and was Peter merely bringing information? The angel’s own words say no. He was told to send for a man who would tell him how to be saved, which means that on the day the angel appeared, with all that piety behind him, he was not.

Hard and kind. It is a hard sentence and it is a kind one, and both need saying. Hard, because it will not allow the comfortable conclusion that sincerity is sufficient and the gospel is an optional refinement for those who like that sort of thing. Kind, because of what God did about it. He did not leave the honest seeker to his sincerity and call it enough. He sent an angel, and a vision, and moved an apostle thirty miles up a coast road against every instinct the man had, in order to get the message to one Roman officer and the people he had gathered into his front room. That is the missionary logic of the whole book in one household. God is not indifferent to the man reaching after him in the dark. He is so far from indifferent that he will rearrange the church to reach him.

In a sentence. Cornelius said that four days earlier, at this very hour, three in the afternoon, while he was praying at home, a man in bright clothing stood before him and told him his prayer had been heard and his gifts to the poor remembered before God.

On a Tuesday. Tell what God has done for you. Your story, told simply and honestly, can open hearts that an argument would close. Practise telling it in two minutes: what you were, how Christ met you, what he has done since.

For worship. God heard a Gentile’s prayer and answered it with the gospel of his Son. He is the God who hears, the God who remembers, and the God who goes to astonishing lengths to bring the seeking sinner to the only Saviour. Cornelius’s story is a single chapter in a much larger one: the Father sending his Son into the far country to bring home the lost.

verseByVerse.quote: "Send therefore to Joppa and ask for Simon who is called Peter. He is lodging in the house of Simon, a tanner, by the sea.' So I sent for you at once, and you have been kind enough to come. Now therefore we are all here in the presence of God to hear all that you have been commanded by the Lord."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Send therefore to Joppa and ask for Simon who is called Peter. He is lodging in the house of Simon, a tanner, by the sea.’ So I sent for you at once, and you have been kind enough to come. Now therefore we are all here in the presence of God to hear all that you have been commanded by the Lord.

So I sent for you at once, and you have been kind enough to come. Gratitude, and a courtesy that a Roman officer did not owe a Jewish fisherman. Cornelius thanks him for coming, which is a recognition that Peter crossed something to get here.

Now therefore we are all here in the presence of God to hear all that you have been commanded by the Lord. The last sentence of Cornelius’s speech is the one to keep, and it is worth learning by heart. Take it in pieces, because each phrase is doing work. We are all here: nobody is missing, the room is full, the invitations were accepted. In the presence of God: they are not primarily aware of Peter; they know whose house this has become. To hear all: not the parts that suit them, not a summary, all of it. That you have been commanded by the Lord: they are not expecting Peter’s opinions. They have assumed from the start that he is under orders and that they are about to hear what the orders were.

A model congregation. No preacher in the history of the world has walked into a better room than that. There is no resistance to overcome, no attention to win, no suspicion to disarm; the congregation has assembled itself, prepared itself, and stated in advance that it intends to obey. Peter’s whole introduction has been taken out of his hands. And it did not happen by accident. Behind that sentence lie four days of a man going round a garrison town telling people what had happened to him while he prayed, and behind that lie the years of praying and giving that Luke set out in verse 2. This room is what the preparation of a heart looks like when it has spread to a household.

Turning the sentence round. It is worth letting it look at us. Most Christians hear preaching on the assumption that some of it will be interesting and some will not, and that the appropriate response is assessment. Cornelius’s household came expecting to be commanded by God through a man, and said so out loud before he opened his mouth, and the Holy Spirit fell on them before he had finished. It is not certain that those two facts are unrelated.

What if the preaching at my church is poor? Then pray for your preacher, and come anyway in the presence of God. Cornelius’s words do not depend on the preacher’s eloquence but on the hearer’s expectation that God will speak through his word. Where a sermon faithfully opens Scripture, God is speaking, even if the delivery is plain. You can help by preparing: read the passage beforehand, pray for the preacher, arrive in time, and listen for what God is commanding rather than for what entertains. If the preaching is not faithful to Scripture, that is a different and more serious matter, to be raised lovingly with the elders. But most of us need to bring more to church before we complain about what we take away.

In a sentence. Cornelius said he had sent for Peter at once and thanked him for coming, and said they were all there in the presence of God to hear everything the Lord had commanded him to say.

On a Tuesday. Come to church like this: in God’s presence, all of you, ready to hear all he has commanded. On Saturday night, pray this sentence for Sunday, and see whether it changes the way you listen.

For worship. Every faithful sermon is a meeting with the living God, because he has chosen to speak through his word preached by men. The Lord who commanded Peter commands his servants still through the Scriptures, and where his word is opened, he is present. What a wonder that the God of heaven should take his seat among an ordinary congregation and speak.

verseByVerse.quote: So Peter opened his mouth and said: "Truly I understand that God shows no partiality, but in every nation anyone who fears him and does what is right is acceptable to him."
verseByVerse.commentary:
So Peter opened his mouth and said: “Truly I understand that God shows no partiality, but in every nation anyone who fears him and does what is right is acceptable to him.

So Peter opened his mouth and said. A solemn beginning, the formula Luke uses for a weighty speech (8:35). This is the first sermon ever preached to a Gentile household.

Truly I understand that God shows no partiality. That is how the sermon opens, and it is an admission. Not, as I have always taught, but, I am now getting it. The first words of the first sermon ever preached to Gentiles are a man saying out loud, in front of the congregation, that he has just changed his mind.

The face-receiver. Then the sentence itself. The Greek word, prosōpolēmptēs, is a vivid compound meaning one who receives the face: who makes a judgment on the strength of who somebody visibly is. It is courtroom language, the term for a judge who decides by looking at the parties, and the Old Testament uses it to describe exactly the sort of magistrate God is not (Deuteronomy 10:17). He does not take the face. And Peter says it while looking at a room of faces he had been raised to sort. That is the force of truly I understand: he is not quoting a principle he learned in the synagogue (he had known the principle all his life); he is saying that he has finally seen where it goes. Paul will build on the same truth: God shows no partiality (Romans 2:11), and in Christ there is neither Jew nor Greek (Galatians 3:28).

But in every nation anyone who fears him and does what is right is acceptable to him. Acceptable, dektos, means welcome. Nationality is no barrier. God welcomes the one who fears him, from any nation.

Where Christians differ: are sincere seekers saved without the gospel? Inclusivists read this verse to mean that people who fear God and do right in any religion are saved, even without hearing of Christ. Verdict: Cornelius was not yet saved: the angel said Peter would bring a message by which he would be saved (11:14). “Acceptable” means acceptable as a candidate, someone God welcomes to hear the gospel, regardless of nation. The verse removes ethnic barriers, not the need for Christ. Peter goes straight on to preach that forgiveness comes through faith in Jesus (v. 43).

One clarification. Since “anyone who fears him and does what is right is acceptable” is sometimes taken to mean that sincere people of any religion are saved without Christ, it should be said that the passage itself rules that out. The point is that God plays no favourites by nation: he welcomes seekers from every people, not Jews only. But “acceptable” does not mean “already saved apart from the gospel”: devout, praying Cornelius still needed to hear and believe, for the angel said Peter “will declare to you a message by which you will be saved” (11:14; 10:43, “everyone who believes in him receives forgiveness”). God “accepted” Cornelius’s God-fearing search by sending him the gospel, not by counting him saved without it. The precious missionary truth here is that the honest seeker in any nation, God will see to it that the gospel reaches him; yet salvation remains through Christ alone, received by faith. (Inclusivists read “acceptable” more broadly; Cornelius’s own story, a seeker who still had to hear and believe, tells against it.)

What about those who never hear? It is the question behind the question, and it is asked with real anguish. Scripture is clear that salvation comes only through conscious faith in Christ (4:12; Romans 10:13–17), and that everyone has enough light in creation and conscience to be without excuse (Romans 1:20; 2:14–15). It also tells us that the Judge of all the earth will do what is right (Genesis 18:25), and that infants dying in infancy who are among God’s elect are saved by Christ through the Spirit, who works when and where he pleases (Westminster 10.3). What Scripture never does is offer the unevangelised as a reason for the church to relax. Its answer to the question is this chapter: God moved heaven and earth to get the gospel to one man. The right response to the question is not speculation but mission.

In a sentence. Peter began by saying he now truly understood that God shows no partiality, but that in every nation anyone who fears him and does what is right is acceptable to him.

On a Tuesday. God shows no partiality. Neither should you. Notice this week whose company you seek out and whose you avoid, whom you listen to with interest and whom you dismiss, and ask whether the face is deciding for you. Then pray for one missionary or gospel work among a people who have little access to the Bible.

For worship. The God who does not receive faces looked on the human race, Jew and Gentile alike, and saw sinners all. And then, without partiality, he sent his Son for people from every nation. He did not choose us because of our faces, our families or our virtues. He chose us in love, and the welcome he extends in the gospel is as wide as the world. Peter only understood it that afternoon. The Father had purposed it from eternity.

parallels.desc: God is not partial

verseByVerse.quote: "As for the word that he sent to Israel, preaching good news of peace through Jesus Christ (he is Lord of all),"
verseByVerse.commentary:
As for the word that he sent to Israel, preaching good news of peace through Jesus Christ (he is Lord of all),

As for the word that he sent to Israel. Peter begins the story where it began, and he does not apologise for it. The gospel came to the Jews first; that is simply the history, and Peter states it in a Gentile drawing room without embarrassment. This message has an address it started from, as Paul would say: to the Jew first and also to the Greek (Romans 1:16).

Preaching good news of peace through Jesus Christ. And what it is, is good news of peace. That phrase is out of Isaiah, where a runner comes over the hills with news that the war is over and God has come back to his people: how beautiful upon the mountains are the feet of him who brings good news, who publishes peace (Isaiah 52:7). Peter is standing in front of a professional soldier and using the vocabulary of a herald announcing the end of hostilities. Cornelius would have understood the picture better than most people in the room. And the peace is double: peace with God, for sinners who were his enemies (Romans 5:1), and peace between Jew and Gentile, who were enemies of each other (Ephesians 2:14–17).

He is Lord of all. Then, dropped into the middle of the sentence like a bracket, the largest claim in the chapter. Four words. Not Lord of Israel, not Lord of the church, not Lord of those who acknowledge him. Of all, and the phrase in Greek puts all first for emphasis, so it lands as: of all, he is Lord. Peter is talking to an officer of the empire whose formal creed was that Caesar is lord, in a city named after Caesar, with a temple to Caesar on the seafront, and he says it in an aside. Paul says the same: the same Lord is Lord of all, bestowing his riches on all who call on him (Romans 10:12).

Why it matters here. But it is not primarily a political sentence, and it is doing something specific in this sermon. Peter has just said that God shows no partiality, and a hearer might reasonably ask on what grounds. Here is the ground. The reason the gospel cannot be kept inside one nation is not that God has become broad-minded; it is that the man at the centre of it owns everything. A local Lord may have a local people. A Lord of all has no outsiders, only subjects who have not yet been told. And it is the sentence that makes sense of what has been happening for two chapters. Peter has been brought up a coast road against his instincts to a house he would never have entered, and the explanation is in the parenthesis: the one who sent him already owned the address.

What does it mean in practice that Jesus is Lord of all? It means there is no part of the world, and no part of your life, outside his rule. He is Lord of the nations, so no people is beyond the reach of the gospel. He is Lord of governments, so rulers are accountable to him and Christians obey them under him, not instead of him (4:19). He is Lord of your work, your money, your body, your evenings and your relationships. The confession Jesus is Lord was the earliest Christian creed (Romans 10:9; 1 Corinthians 12:3), and it was dangerous precisely because it left Caesar no room to be ultimate. It still leaves nothing else room: not career, not comfort, not self.

In a sentence. Peter said that God sent the message to the people of Israel, announcing the good news of peace through Jesus Christ, who is Lord of all.

On a Tuesday. Take one area of your life you tend to keep to yourself, your finances, your screen time, your ambitions, and say aloud, Jesus Christ is Lord of this. Then ask what one change that confession would make this week.

For worship. Jesus is Lord of all: every nation, every person, every throne and every kitchen. The Father has highly exalted him and given him the name that is above every name, that at the name of Jesus every knee should bow (Philippians 2:9–10). He is not a tribal deity or a private religious preference. He is the King of the universe, and he has come preaching peace.

parallels.desc: who publishes peace

verseByVerse.quote: "you yourselves know what happened throughout all Judea, beginning from Galilee after the baptism that John proclaimed: how God anointed Jesus of Nazareth with the Holy Spirit and with power. He went about doing good and healing all who were oppressed by the devil, for God was with him."
verseByVerse.commentary:
you yourselves know what happened throughout all Judea, beginning from Galilee after the baptism that John proclaimed: how God anointed Jesus of Nazareth with the Holy Spirit and with power. He went about doing good and healing all who were oppressed by the devil, for God was with him.

You yourselves know what happened throughout all Judea, beginning from Galilee after the baptism that John proclaimed. Peter is not introducing a stranger, and the assumption is worth noticing: he takes it for granted that a Roman household in Caesarea has followed the story of a Galilean preacher. They had. It had been in every town in the province for three years and had ended in a public execution outside Jerusalem sixty miles away, and news of that kind reaches a garrison. So he starts where the public record starts and gives them the ministry in one sentence. This is the shape of the earliest Christian preaching everywhere in Acts: not a philosophy, but an account of what a particular man did in a particular province within living memory, offered to people who could check it. And Peter’s outline, from Galilee and John’s baptism through the ministry to the death and resurrection, is the very shape of Mark’s Gospel. Early church tradition says that Mark wrote down Peter’s preaching. Here, perhaps, we hear it in miniature.

How God anointed Jesus of Nazareth with the Holy Spirit and with power. The word anointed is the verb behind Christ, so Peter is explaining the title rather than just using it, a courtesy to a room that has not grown up with the vocabulary. Kings and priests were anointed with oil; this one was anointed with the Spirit, at his baptism (Luke 3:22; 4:18). And here again is the Trinity in a single clause: God the Father anointed Jesus the Son with the Holy Spirit.

He went about doing good. And then the summary of a whole life, which is as good a sentence as exists in the New Testament: he went about doing good and healing all who were oppressed by the devil, for God was with him. A beautiful summary of Jesus’ life, and no one who knew him ever contradicted it.

Oppressed by the devil. “All who were oppressed by the devil”: to be oppressed is to be tyrannised, held down under a cruel power. Peter is summing up Jesus’ whole ministry of healing and deliverance as a rescue operation: he was prising people loose from the devil’s grip. The phrase reaches wider than the cases of open demon-possession (on the nature of those “unclean spirits,” and the caution that not every illness is a direct demonic act, see on 5:15–16). It gathers up all whom the devil’s dark dominion held, for behind the whole reign of sickness, bondage, and death in a fallen world stands, ultimately, “the works of the devil,” and “the reason the Son of God appeared was to destroy” them (1 John 3:8). Jesus himself could call a crippled woman one “whom Satan bound for eighteen years” (Luke 13:16).

The great Liberator. So every healing was a liberation, and a preview of total victory. Jesus came as the stronger man who binds the strong man and plunders his house (Mark 3:27), invading the devil’s territory to set the captives free: “if it is by the Spirit of God that I cast out demons, then the kingdom of God has come upon you” (Matthew 12:28). And he pressed it to the very end: at the cross he “disarmed the rulers and authorities” (Colossians 2:15) and through death destroyed “the one who has the power of death, that is, the devil” (Hebrews 2:14). The comfort here is plain: whatever cruel power has held a person down, Jesus is the great Liberator, mightier than the devil, who rescues us “from the domain of darkness” into his own kingdom (Colossians 1:13; Acts 26:18). “He went about doing good,” and the good he did was to break the oppressor’s chains.

For God was with him. The explanation of his power. Peter speaks here of Jesus’ true humanity: a man anointed and empowered by the Spirit, in whom the Father was at work. That is not the whole truth about him, and in the same sermon Peter calls him Lord of all and Judge of all (vv. 36, 42). But it is a real truth. The eternal Son did not lay aside his deity when he became man; he lived his human life in dependence on the Spirit, as the true and perfect man, which is why he can be our pattern as well as our Saviour.

In a sentence. Peter reminded them of what had happened throughout Judea, beginning in Galilee after the baptism John preached: how God anointed Jesus of Nazareth with the Holy Spirit and with power, and how he went about doing good and healing all who were oppressed by the devil, because God was with him.

On a Tuesday. Go about doing good today, as Jesus did. Not grand deeds, but the next good thing: the visit, the repair, the meal, the word of comfort. And if you feel held down by something you cannot shake, a habit, a fear, a darkness, bring it to Christ by name. He came to set captives free.

For worship. He went about doing good. The Son of God walked the dusty roads of Galilee with the Spirit upon him, touching lepers, opening blind eyes, freeing the oppressed, and then went to the cross to break the devil’s power for ever. There has never been a life like his. Every act of mercy he performed was the kingdom of God breaking in, and every one was a promise of the day when the oppressor will be cast down and his people set free completely.
verseByVerse.note: Peter’s outline of Jesus’ life resembles the shape of Mark’s Gospel.

parallels.desc: the Spirit of the Lord God is upon me, because the LORD has anointed me

verseByVerse.quote: "And we are witnesses of all that he did both in the country of the Jews and in Jerusalem. They put him to death by hanging him on a tree, but God raised him on the third day and made him to appear,"
verseByVerse.commentary:
And we are witnesses of all that he did both in the country of the Jews and in Jerusalem. They put him to death by hanging him on a tree, but God raised him on the third day and made him to appear,

And we are witnesses of all that he did both in the country of the Jews and in Jerusalem. Peter says it before he says anything about the cross, and he will say it again in the next verse. Everything in this sermon rests on the claim that the men saying it were there. Eyewitness testimony again, as throughout Acts (1:8; 2:32; 3:15).

They put him to death by hanging him on a tree. Then the death, and the way he puts it would have made a Jewish hearer flinch. He does not say crucified, which is the ordinary word and the one Cornelius would have expected from a Roman perspective. He reaches instead for a phrase out of Deuteronomy, a hanged man is cursed by God (Deuteronomy 21:23): the law about a body left on a tree, which every Jew knew and which was the standing objection to the whole Christian claim. A crucified Messiah was a cursed Messiah, and that was the end of the argument.

The objection as the description. Peter uses the objection as his description. He does not avoid the scandalous word; he puts it in the sermon. Paul later takes the same verse and shows what it is for: Christ redeemed us from the curse of the law by becoming a curse for us (Galatians 3:13). But Peter, years earlier, is already speaking of the cross in the vocabulary of the curse, which means the church had understood from very early on that the worst thing about the crucifixion was the point of it. He bore the curse that was ours.

But God raised him on the third day. One conjunction carries the whole gospel. They put him to death; God raised him. Two subjects, two verbs, and the second reverses the first. And note that the resurrection is consistently something done to Jesus by God in these early sermons. Not only that he rose, though that is true and the New Testament says it, but that God raised him, which is the language of a verdict. A court had ruled; a higher court has set the ruling aside. What men called a curse, God called his Son, and said so by emptying the grave.

And made him to appear. Literally, gave him to become visible. Real appearances, to real people, and that leads directly into the strangest sentence in the sermon.

What does it mean that Jesus became a curse for us? The curse is God’s just sentence on sin, the opposite of his blessing (Deuteronomy 27:26; Galatians 3:10). Everyone who breaks his law is under it. On the cross, Jesus, who had never sinned, took that sentence in our place: God made him to be sin who knew no sin, so that in him we might become the righteousness of God (2 Corinthians 5:21). This is penal substitution: the penalty was real, the substitute was Christ, and the debt was paid in full. So if you trust in him, there is no curse left for you. It fell on him at Golgotha, and the empty tomb is God’s announcement that it has been exhausted.

In a sentence. Peter said the apostles were witnesses of everything Jesus did in the Jewish countryside and in Jerusalem, and though they killed him by hanging him on a tree, God raised him on the third day and made him appear.

On a Tuesday. When you are tempted to think that God is against you because of your sins, look at the tree. Say to yourself, slowly: he became a curse for me. Then live this week as someone who has been blessed instead.

For worship. He hung on the tree under the curse, and rose on the third day. That is the whole gospel in two clauses. The holy Son of God was counted cursed so that cursed sinners might be counted sons, and the Father who laid the curse on him raised him in glory. Blessed be the Lamb who was slain, and the God who vindicated him.
verseByVerse.note: Being hung on a tree was under God’s curse in the law.

verseByVerse.quote: "not to all the people but to us who had been chosen by God as witnesses, who ate and drank with him after he rose from the dead."
verseByVerse.commentary:
not to all the people but to us who had been chosen by God as witnesses, who ate and drank with him after he rose from the dead.

Not to all the people but to us who had been chosen by God as witnesses. It is an odd thing to volunteer, and it is the last thing an inventor of a story would include. If a man is fabricating a resurrection, he does not pause in the middle of the account to concede that the risen figure was not shown to the general public. Peter raises the difficulty himself, unprompted, in front of an audience that had not asked.

Why not to everybody? Scripture does not fully explain it, and it is honest to say so. But the logic is not hard to see. A public appearance in the temple courts would have compelled belief of a kind, the kind a man cannot get out of, and God’s consistent way is to give sufficient evidence to those who will testify rather than overwhelming evidence to those who will not. And there was to be a definite, nameable, countable body of witnesses, so that the church’s claim would rest on people who could be found and questioned rather than on a rumour that everybody had heard from somebody (1 Corinthians 15:5–8). God chose to spread the news by witness, not by spectacle, because faith comes by hearing (Romans 10:17), and blessed are those who have not seen and yet have believed (John 20:29).

Who ate and drank with him after he rose from the dead. Then the detail Peter chooses as his proof, which is not the one anybody would predict. Not: we saw him, we touched him, we heard him teach. We had meals with him. It is the most ordinary evidence available and by some distance the most difficult to explain away. A vision does not ask for something to eat. A hallucination shared by a dozen men does not take bread and hand it round. Luke’s own Gospel records the risen Christ asking whether they had anything to eat, and being given a piece of broiled fish, and eating it in front of them (Luke 24:41–43), and John records breakfast on a beach (John 21:12–13). Ghosts do not eat.

A man at supper. The resurrection Peter is preaching is not a survival of the spirit or a continuing influence or a sense that he is somehow still with us. It is a man who was dead, sitting down to supper. That is what the apostles said they had seen, and it is why they could not be talked out of it, even under the lash and the sword.

Does it matter whether the resurrection was physical? Everything depends on it. If Christ was raised only as a spirit, then death has not been defeated, only survived, and our bodies have no future. But the New Testament insists that the same body that was laid in the tomb came out of it, transformed and glorified, with the marks of the nails still in its hands (John 20:27). That is why Christians bury their dead in hope, and why Paul could say that if Christ has not been raised, our faith is futile and we are still in our sins (1 Corinthians 15:17). Because he rose bodily, we will too.

In a sentence. He appeared not to all the people but to witnesses whom God had chosen beforehand, to us, who ate and drank with him after he rose from the dead.

On a Tuesday. You believe on the testimony of chosen witnesses, and their word is enough. When doubts come, go back to the evidence they gave: read Luke 24 or 1 Corinthians 15 this week, slowly, as testimony from men who had breakfast with the risen Lord.

For worship. The risen Christ ate broiled fish by a lake. The Lord of glory, who has conquered death, sat at a charcoal fire with fishermen and cooked them breakfast. His resurrection body is real, and so is his friendship. And he has promised that we too will sit at table with him in his kingdom, in bodies raised like his, at the marriage supper of the Lamb.

verseByVerse.quote: "And he commanded us to preach to the people and to testify that he is the one appointed by God to be judge of the living and the dead. To him all the prophets bear witness that everyone who believes in him receives forgiveness of sins through his name."
verseByVerse.commentary:
And he commanded us to preach to the people and to testify that he is the one appointed by God to be judge of the living and the dead. To him all the prophets bear witness that everyone who believes in him receives forgiveness of sins through his name.

And he commanded us to preach to the people and to testify. Two sentences follow, and between them they contain the whole of what the church has to say. The first is the harder.

He is the one appointed by God to be judge of the living and the dead. Peter has told them who Jesus was, what he did, how he died and that God raised him, and the conclusion he draws from all of it is that this man will judge the human race (17:31; John 5:22; 2 Timothy 4:1). The living and the dead is a phrase that closes every exit: nobody is too long buried to be included and nobody is too much alive to be exempt. Every person will stand before him. The gospel includes the warning of judgment.

Good news, not only threat. It is worth noticing that this is presented as part of the good news rather than as a threat attached to it. And it is good news, when you consider the alternatives: a universe in which nothing is ever finally called what it is, where the man who arranged the killing and the woman who was killed go into the same silence and nobody ever says which was which. A judgment is the guarantee that the accounts will be settled. What makes it terrifying is not that there is a judge; it is that we are in the dock.

To him all the prophets bear witness. Which is why the second sentence has to come immediately, and does. The whole Old Testament points to Christ (Luke 24:27). So this is not a novelty; it is what Israel’s Scriptures were for.

That everyone who believes in him receives forgiveness of sins through his name. The judge and the Saviour are the same person. That is the whole architecture of the gospel in one movement, and it is the only arrangement under which anybody could survive the first sentence. The one appointed to assess the living and the dead is the one on whose name a man may call and be forgiven, and he is offering it now, in a front room in Caesarea, before the bench is ever taken. This is the climax of Peter’s sermon, and the answer to Cornelius’s prayers.

Every word chosen. Then look at the width of the last sentence, because Peter has chosen every word of it for the people in front of him. Everyone: not every Jew, not every circumcised person, everyone. Who believes in him: not achieves, not qualifies, not is born into; faith alone, not circumcision, not law-keeping, not good works. Receives forgiveness of sins: a gift received, not a wage earned. Through his name: by who he is and what he has done, on his account and not on ours. Peter never gets to say anything else. That word everyone is very nearly the last thing out of his mouth before the Holy Spirit interrupts him, and the interruption is God’s way of saying that the word meant what it said.

Where Christians differ: how are we justified? Some teach that forgiveness comes through faith plus sacraments, or faith plus works. Verdict: Peter says forgiveness is received by everyone who believes, and the Spirit falls before any baptism or work is done (v. 44). This is justification by faith alone, through Christ alone, by grace alone.

How do I know if I have really believed? Believing in Christ is not a feeling to measure but a trust to place. Ask yourself: Do I rely on Jesus alone, and not on my goodness, to be accepted by God? Do I believe he died for my sins and rose again? Am I turning from sin to follow him, however falteringly? If the answer is yes, then the promise of this verse is yours: everyone who believes receives forgiveness. Assurance does not rest on the strength of your faith but on the faithfulness of the one you trust. Weak faith in a strong Saviour saves as surely as strong faith does. And the evidence that it is real will grow: love for Christ, a hatred of sin, and a desire to obey him (1 John 5:13).

In a sentence. Peter said Jesus had commanded them to preach to the people and testify that he is the one appointed by God to be judge of the living and the dead, and that all the prophets testify that everyone who believes in him receives forgiveness of sins through his name.

On a Tuesday. Hold both truths together this week. When you are careless about sin, remember that Jesus is the Judge. When you are crushed by guilt, remember that the Judge is the one who forgives. And if you have never put your trust in him, there is no reason to wait: everyone who believes receives forgiveness.

For worship. Everyone who believes in him is forgiven. Everyone. The Judge of all the earth has become the Saviour of sinners, and the bench before which we must stand is occupied by the one who bore our sentence. There is no condemnation for those who are in Christ Jesus. All the prophets sang of him, and the whole of heaven will sing of him for ever.

verseByVerse.quote: While Peter was still saying these things, the Holy Spirit fell on all who heard the word. And the believers from among the circumcised who had come with Peter were amazed, because the gift of the Holy Spirit was poured out even on the Gentiles.
verseByVerse.commentary:
While Peter was still saying these things, the Holy Spirit fell on all who heard the word. And the believers from among the circumcised who had come with Peter were amazed, because the gift of the Holy Spirit was poured out even on the Gentiles.

While Peter was still saying these things. He is interrupted. The most important sermon of his life is cut off in the middle by the Holy Spirit, and Luke evidently thought the timing worth recording precisely. As soon as they heard that everyone who believes receives forgiveness, they believed, and God sealed it.

The Holy Spirit fell on all who heard the word. It matters because of everything that is not in this account. There is no appeal, no call to respond, no moment of decision announced, no prayer to repeat. Nobody is baptised first; the water does not appear until verse 47, and Peter has to ask for it. Nobody is circumcised, nobody has agreed to keep the law, nobody has been examined by anyone. God simply does not wait. He falls on a room of uncircumcised Gentiles at the point in the sermon where the word everyone has just been spoken, and the effect is to put his own signature under it before the sentence has cooled. Faith comes by hearing (Romans 10:17), and the Spirit with it (Galatians 3:2).

The believers from among the circumcised who had come with Peter were amazed. Then Luke turns the camera on the men Peter had brought with him. These are the six from Joppa: Jewish Christians, brought along as witnesses, who had walked thirty miles for exactly this purpose. And what they feel is not delight. It is astonishment: the word means they were standing outside themselves, knocked out of their own minds. They had believed for some time that Jesus was the Messiah. They had not remotely believed this.

Because the gift of the Holy Spirit was poured out even on the Gentiles. Even on the Gentiles: unthinkable, but undeniable. God accepted them as they were, uncircumcised. It is one of the more honest sentences in the New Testament, and it is a mercy that Luke left it in. The first Christians did not arrive at the inclusion of the Gentiles by reflection, and they did not welcome it warmly when it came. They were shocked. Their own Scriptures had said it would happen, their Lord had told them to go to the ends of the earth, and when God did it in front of them they stood there with their mouths open.

Is this a second experience after conversion? The Spirit fell while Peter was still speaking, the moment they believed; there was no second step. This was the Gentile Pentecost, the moment God showed the church that Gentiles too received the Spirit on believing, and as an event it was unrepeatable. Pentecostal Christians read it as a pattern for a later baptism in the Spirit; but Peter himself later says that God gave them the same gift when we believed in the Lord Jesus Christ (11:17).

Bewildered witnesses. Which should be a comfort to anybody who has watched God do something they had no framework for, and found that their first reaction was not faith but bewilderment. That was the reaction of the six men who had been brought specifically as witnesses. And it did not stop God, and it did not disqualify them; they went back to Jerusalem and told the church what they had seen.

In a sentence. While Peter was still speaking, the Holy Spirit fell on all who heard the message, and the circumcised believers who had come with Peter were astonished that the gift of the Holy Spirit had been poured out even on the Gentiles.

On a Tuesday. Expect God to be at work when his word is spoken, even before the speaker has finished. When you share the gospel, you are not the one who makes it effective; the Spirit is. And if God does something in your church you did not expect, a conversion from an unlikely quarter, a newcomer you would not have chosen, let your astonishment turn into praise.

For worship. The Spirit is poured out on all who believe, whatever their background. The Father kept his promise to pour out his Spirit on all flesh, and the risen Son, exalted to his right hand, poured him out on a Roman household while the preacher was still mid-sentence. Praise God for the Gentile Pentecost, and for the grace that does not wait for us to finish.

verseByVerse.quote: For they were hearing them speaking in tongues and extolling God. Then Peter declared,
verseByVerse.commentary:
For they were hearing them speaking in tongues and extolling God. Then Peter declared,

For they were hearing them speaking in tongues and extolling God. How did anybody know the Spirit had fallen? Luke answers the question directly, because the whole argument of the next five chapters depends on the answer being checkable. The sign is the same sign as the first morning in Jerusalem (2:4, 11), and that is the entire point of it. Not a similar experience, not a comparable enthusiasm, but the same thing, recognisable instantly by a man who had been in the upper room and had spent years telling people about it. When Peter reports this to the Jerusalem church he puts it exactly so: the Holy Spirit fell on them just as on us at the beginning (11:15), and when the council meets in chapter 15 he says God gave them the Spirit just as he did to us, and made no distinction (15:8–9).

The demonstration was for Jerusalem. Consider why God chose to do it this way. He could have converted that household quietly, and nobody in the room would have doubted it: the sermon was believed, the response was genuine, and Peter could have baptised them and gone home. Instead he gave a sign that could not be described in any language except the one already used of Pentecost, in front of six Jewish witnesses who would be required to give evidence. The tongues served as proof, at a turning point in the church’s history. The demonstration was not for Cornelius. It was for Jerusalem.

No two-tier church. And it settled the question before the argument could begin. Once the Spirit had been given on exactly the same terms as at Pentecost, there was no case left to make for a two-tier church: no possibility of Gentile believers as associate members, admitted on probation, conditional on circumcision, seated at a separate table. God had already decided, publicly, and the church spent the following years catching up with a decision it had not been consulted about.

Were these tongues real languages, and is speaking in tongues the evidence of the Spirit? Peter says the Spirit fell on them just as on us at the beginning (11:15), so they were likely the same as at Pentecost. The tongues were a sign for the Jewish believers that God had accepted Gentiles; they are not presented as the proof of the Spirit for every later Christian. Many Christians believe the gift continues today; the more likely reading is that it belonged to those foundational moments.

Extolling God. The other thing worth hearing in the verse is what these people were actually doing with the gift. The word, megalynontōn, means magnifying, making great. As at Pentecost, they declared the mighty works of God. Not analysing it, not asking what it meant, not wondering whether it would last. A Roman officer’s household, five minutes into the Christian faith, was in the middle of its front room magnifying the God of Israel out loud in languages nobody had taught them, and the sermon that produced it had not even finished.

Then how do I know I have the Spirit if I have not spoken in tongues? By the signs Scripture gives every believer, not the special sign given at this turning point. The Spirit is present wherever a person confesses from the heart that Jesus is Lord (1 Corinthians 12:3), cries out to God as Father (Romans 8:15–16), loves other Christians (1 John 4:13), and bears his fruit: love, joy, peace, patience and the rest (Galatians 5:22–23). Paul asks the Corinthians, do all speak with tongues? and expects the answer no (1 Corinthians 12:30). If you trust Christ, you have the Spirit. Anyone who does not have the Spirit of Christ does not belong to him (Romans 8:9), so the reverse is also true: if you belong to him, the Spirit is yours.

Then Peter declared. He sees what this means, and he draws the conclusion at once.

In a sentence. They heard them speaking in tongues and praising God, and then Peter spoke up.

On a Tuesday. The Spirit’s gift always leads to praise of God. If you are a believer, the same Spirit lives in you, so let him do in you what he did in Caesarea: magnify God. Take five minutes today simply to tell God what he has done, without asking for anything.

For worship. The Spirit of God took the tongues of Gentiles and filled them with the praises of the God of Israel. It was a foretaste of the great multitude that no one can number, from every nation, crying out with a loud voice, Salvation belongs to our God who sits on the throne, and to the Lamb. Magnify him today, for the same Spirit has opened your mouth to praise him.

verseByVerse.quote: "Can anyone withhold water for baptizing these people, who have received the Holy Spirit just as we have?" And he commanded them to be baptized in the name of Jesus Christ. Then they asked him to remain for some days.
verseByVerse.commentary:
“Can anyone withhold water for baptizing these people, who have received the Holy Spirit just as we have?” And he commanded them to be baptized in the name of Jesus Christ. Then they asked him to remain for some days.

Can anyone withhold water for baptizing these people, who have received the Holy Spirit just as we have? Peter puts it as a question, and the question is not really addressed to the room. It is addressed to the six men standing behind him, and through them to the church in Jerusalem, and it is unanswerable. Withhold, kōlysai, means prevent, hinder: the same word as the eunuch’s question by the roadside, what prevents me from being baptized (8:36). The argument runs backwards from a fact nobody present can dispute: these people have received the Holy Spirit just as we have. Just as we have: no second-class Gentile believers. Everything else is now a formality. If God has given the reality, who can refuse the sign?

Not more cautious than God. It is worth noticing what Peter does not do. He does not send to Jerusalem for a ruling, though the question is momentous and he will certainly be answering for it later. He does not impose conditions or a probationary period. He does not require circumcision, which is what the whole church will be arguing about for the next several years. He watches what God has plainly done and refuses to be more cautious than God.

And he commanded them to be baptized in the name of Jesus Christ. And then, having asked whether anyone can withhold it, he commanded them to be baptised. Not invited, not offered: the language of an order, which the head of that household would have recognised. The question was for the Jewish witnesses; the command was for the Gentile believers. Baptism follows faith and the Spirit.

In the name of Jesus Christ. “Baptized in the name of Jesus Christ”: the apparent tension with Jesus’ own command to baptise “in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit” (Matthew 28:19) is treated more fully at 2:38 (including why the “Jesus Only” or Oneness reading goes wrong). In brief: Luke is not recording the exact words spoken over the candidate; he is describing the baptism’s character: it was Christian baptism, baptism that belongs to Jesus and marks a person out as now his, as distinct from John’s baptism or any other washing. To be baptised “into the name of Jesus” is to be baptised into the whole triune God, for you cannot have the Son without the Father who sent him and the Spirit he gives, and this very scene proves it, with the Father anointing (10:38), the Son saving, and the Spirit falling on the household (10:44).

The Spirit before the water. These people received the Spirit before they were baptised. That shows that the Spirit and forgiveness come by faith, and that baptism follows as the sign and the Lord’s command, not as the means. Christians who see baptism as the instrument of new birth must explain why these had the Spirit already; Peter’s reasoning is that those who have received the Spirit should not be refused the sign.

And does all his household support infant baptism? The household here were those who heard the word, received the Spirit and spoke in tongues (vv. 44, 46), so all were believers. Christians who baptise infants see in household baptisms a covenant pattern including children; but this household, at least, was made up of believers.

The way we should do it. So, as to “the way we should do it”: we follow Jesus’ own explicit instruction and baptise in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit (Matthew 28:19), the words the Lord himself gave, and the church’s practice from the earliest days (the Didache, around AD 100, already prescribes them). The Acts phrase “in the name of Jesus” does not compete with that formula; it simply names whose baptism it is. The two say one thing from two angles: those baptised belong to Jesus, and to belong to Jesus is to belong to the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit.

Then they asked him to remain for some days. The last clause is easy to skim and is the quiet triumph of the chapter. A Jewish apostle who a few days earlier had never entered a Gentile house stays on as a guest in one, eating at that table, sleeping under that roof, for days. The Jerusalem church will complain of exactly this: you went to uncircumcised men and ate with them (11:3). And the man who had said by no means, Lord across a sheet full of animals had stopped arguing entirely. The wall is truly down.

If baptism does not save, why does it matter so much? Because Christ commanded it, and obedience to him is never optional (Matthew 28:19). Baptism is his appointed sign of union with him in his death and resurrection (Romans 6:3–4), a public confession that you belong to him, and the doorway into the visible fellowship of his church. It does not make you a Christian; it marks you as one. Peter did not treat it as a formality to be skipped once the Spirit had come. He commanded it at once. A believer who has never been baptised is not lost, but he is living in disobedience to a plain command of his Lord, and missing a means of grace by which Christ strengthens faith.

In a sentence. Peter asked whether anyone could withhold water for baptising these people who had received the Holy Spirit just as they had, and he commanded them to be baptised in the name of Jesus Christ, and then they asked him to stay on for a few days.

On a Tuesday. If God has accepted someone, so must you. Welcome every believer as a brother or sister, whatever his background, and refuse to create second-class Christians in your church by look, tone or seating plan. And if you have trusted Christ but never been baptised, do not withhold the water from yourself any longer. Speak to your pastor this week.

For worship. The Father anointed, the Son saved, and the Spirit fell, and a Roman household went down into the water in the name of the triune God. The God who had promised Abraham that in him all the families of the earth would be blessed kept his word that afternoon in Caesarea. And the apostle who had refused to eat what was common sat at a Gentile table for days, because the Lord of all had made them one family. Every believer from every nation who has ever been welcomed into Christ’s church owes something to that house by the sea. Glory to God, who has granted repentance that leads to life even to the Gentiles.

10.theology: Election and the Nations. Acts 10 is the fulfilment of the promise to Abraham: “in your offspring shall all the nations of the earth be blessed” (Genesis 22:18). The blessing always intended to reach the Gentiles; what Acts 10 shows is the mechanism — the proclamation of Jesus Christ, Lord of all, and the sovereign gift of the Holy Spirit to all who believe. The Gentile mission is not an emergency plan devised when Israel rejected the Messiah. It is the ancient plan of the God who chose Abraham in order to bless the world through him. Peter’s visit to Cornelius is, in the deepest sense, the arrival of what Genesis 12 promised. The God who shows no partiality has always intended a people from every nation. Acts 10 is that intention breaking into history.
10.examples:
Then: A Roman soldier who prayed toward Jerusalem and a Jewish fisherman who would never have entered a Gentile home — brought together by two visions, thirty miles apart, orchestrated by the God who wastes nothing and plans everything. The Spirit fell. The barriers fell. The church was never the same.

Now: The church in every generation must resist the temptation to build walls that God has torn down. The divisions that seem most natural — racial, cultural, economic, denominational — are the ones most likely to be the new versions of the Jewish-Gentile divide. What God has made clean, do not call common. The community of the Spirit is wider than our instincts, and deeper than our categories.

11.title: The Church at Antioch
11.text: <sup>1</sup>Now the apostles and the brothers who were throughout Judea heard that the Gentiles also had received the word of God. <sup>2</sup>So when Peter went up to Jerusalem, the circumcision party criticized him, saying, <sup>3</sup>“You went to uncircumcised men and ate with them.” <sup>4</sup>But Peter began and explained it to them in order: <sup>5</sup>“I was in the city of Joppa praying, and in a trance I saw a vision, something like a great sheet descending, being let down from heaven by its four corners, and it came down to me. <sup>6</sup>Looking at it closely, I observed animals and beasts of prey and reptiles and birds of the air. <sup>7</sup>And I heard a voice saying to me, ‘Rise, Peter; kill and eat.’ <sup>8</sup>But I said, ‘By no means, Lord; for nothing common or unclean has ever entered my mouth.’ <sup>9</sup>But the voice answered a second time from heaven, ‘What God has made clean, do not call common.’ <sup>10</sup>This happened three times, and all was drawn up again into heaven. <sup>11</sup>And behold, at that very moment three men arrived at the house in which we were, sent to me from Caesarea. <sup>12</sup>And the Spirit told me to go with them, making no distinction. These six brothers also accompanied me, and we entered the man’s house. <sup>13</sup>And he told us how he had seen the angel stand in his house and say, ‘Send to Joppa and bring Simon who is called Peter; <sup>14</sup>he will declare to you a message by which you will be saved, you and all your household.’ <sup>15</sup>As I began to speak, the Holy Spirit fell on them just as on us at the beginning. <sup>16</sup>And I remembered the word of the Lord, how he said, ‘John baptized with water, but you will be baptized with the Holy Spirit.’ <sup>17</sup>If then God gave the same gift to them as he gave to us when we believed in the Lord Jesus Christ, who was I that I could stand in God’s way?” <sup>18</sup>When they heard these things they fell silent. And they glorified God, saying, “Then to the Gentiles also God has granted repentance that leads to life.” <sup>19</sup>Now those who were scattered because of the persecution that arose over Stephen traveled as far as Phoenicia and Cyprus and Antioch, speaking the word to no one except Jews. <sup>20</sup>But there were some of them, men of Cyprus and Cyrene, who on coming to Antioch spoke to the Hellenists also, preaching the Lord Jesus. <sup>21</sup>And the hand of the Lord was with them, and a great number who believed turned to the Lord. <sup>22</sup>The report of this came to the ears of the church in Jerusalem, and they sent Barnabas to Antioch. <sup>23</sup>When he came and saw the grace of God, he was glad, and he exhorted them all to remain faithful to the Lord with steadfast purpose, <sup>24</sup>for he was a good man, full of the Holy Spirit and of faith. And a great many people were added to the Lord. <sup>25</sup>So Barnabas went to Tarsus to look for Saul, <sup>26</sup>and when he had found him, he brought him to Antioch. For a whole year they met with the church and taught a great many people. And in Antioch the disciples were first called Christians. <sup>27</sup>Now in these days prophets came down from Jerusalem to Antioch. <sup>28</sup>And one of them named Agabus stood up and foretold by the Spirit that there would be a great famine over all the world (this took place in the days of Claudius). <sup>29</sup>So the disciples determined, every one according to his ability, to send relief to the brothers living in Judea. <sup>30</sup>And they did so, sending it to the elders by the hand of Barnabas and Saul.
11.overview:
News that Gentiles have received the word reaches Jerusalem, and when Peter returns, Jewish believers who insisted on circumcision criticise him: he went into the house of uncircumcised men and ate with them. Table fellowship meant full acceptance, and that was the offence. Peter tells the whole story step by step, with six witnesses, and ends with the decisive fact: God gave the Gentiles the same gift of the Spirit he gave the apostles, so who was Peter to stand in God’s way? The critics fall silent and praise God that he has granted repentance leading to life even to the Gentiles.

Meanwhile, believers scattered after Stephen’s death reach Antioch in Syria, the third city of the Roman Empire after Rome and Alexandria, a great trading centre on the Orontes river, with a large Jewish community and a reputation for luxury and loose living. Some of them, from Cyprus and Cyrene, begin preaching the Lord Jesus to Greeks, and many believe. Jerusalem sends Barnabas, who is delighted by what he sees, and fetches Saul from Tarsus to help him; for a whole year they teach the new church, and it is at Antioch that the disciples are first called “Christians”. When the prophet Agabus predicts a severe famine, which came in the reign of the emperor Claudius, the Antioch church sends relief to the believers in Judea by Barnabas and Saul, a first sign of the Gentile churches caring for the mother church.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The apostles and believers in Judea heard that the Gentiles had received God’s word. When Peter went up to Jerusalem, the circumcised believers criticised him for going into the house of uncircumcised men and eating with them. Peter explained everything in order: the vision at Joppa of the sheet with animals, the voice telling him to eat, his refusal, the voice saying three times not to call unclean what God has made clean, and the arrival at that moment of three men from Caesarea. The Spirit told him to go with them without hesitation, and six brothers went with him into the man’s house. The man told them how an angel had told him to send for Peter, who would bring a message through which he and his household would be saved. As Peter began to speak, the Holy Spirit came on them as on the apostles at the beginning, and Peter remembered the Lord’s words that John baptised with water but they would be baptised with the Spirit. If God gave them the same gift he gave those who believed in the Lord Jesus Christ, who was Peter to stand in God’s way? When they heard this they had no further objections and praised God, saying that God had granted even the Gentiles repentance that leads to life.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Gospel's Reach and the Church's Lag

What this passage shows is not a wicked church being corrected but a devout one being overtaken. The men who met Peter at the door were not bigots inventing a rule; they were holding to a boundary God himself had drawn, for reasons he himself had given, which had been kept at enormous cost for centuries. Their difficulty was that the boundary had done its work and been retired, and nobody had told them. Reformed theology has taken the episode as the clearest case in Scripture of the Spirit going ahead of the church's understanding — and of how he settles such questions. Not by a decree, not by a text, and not by an apostolic ruling: by doing the thing in public, in front of witnesses who could be cross-examined, and letting the church draw the conclusion. It is also a warning about the gap between conviction and conduct. The Jerusalem church conceded the principle in verse 18 and was still arguing about the practice at a council several years later, and Peter, who won this argument, later behaved as though he had lost it.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: Peter's answer to a hostile hearing was to narrate what had happened, including the parts against himself, with six men present who had seen it. He produced no proof text and pulled no rank. Now: That is still the strongest thing available in a disputed matter, and the rarest. A man who tells the story straight, admits where he resisted, and brings witnesses is very hard to answer — and a man who says only that God told him, with nothing checkable attached, has said nothing anybody can test.

verseByVerse.quote: Now the apostles and the brothers who were throughout Judea heard that the Gentiles also had received the word of God. So when Peter went up to Jerusalem, the circumcision party criticized him saying,
verseByVerse.commentary:
Now the apostles and the brothers who were throughout Judea heard that the Gentiles also had received the word of God. So when Peter went up to Jerusalem, the circumcision party criticized him saying,

Meaning first. Acts 11 has two halves. First, Peter defends himself in Jerusalem for eating with Gentiles, and the church accepts that God has given the Gentiles repentance that leads to life. Second, the gospel reaches Gentiles in Antioch, the great city of Syria, where a mixed church of Jews and Gentiles grows under Barnabas and Saul, and where believers are first called Christians. Antioch will become the base for the mission to the world. Over both halves stands the same truth: the turning of a sinner to God is God’s own gift, and he gives it to whom he pleases, from every nation, so that his people come to be known simply by the name of his Son.

Now the apostles and the brothers who were throughout Judea heard that the Gentiles also had received the word of God. Two sentences, and a great deal is happening in them. The first is that the news travelled faster than the man. Not just Jerusalem, but the whole province heard. Something like this does not stay in Caesarea; six men had walked home from it with a story, and by the time Peter came up to the city everybody had heard a version.

The circumcision party criticized him. The second is that Luke names a faction. The phrase is literally those of the circumcision, and it is the first time in this book that a group inside the church is identified as a party with a position. They are not outsiders. They are believers, in Jerusalem, who hold that Gentiles must be circumcised and keep the law of Moses to belong to God’s people (15:1, 5). Paul uses exactly the same phrase years later (Galatians 2:12), describing the men whose arrival at Antioch made Peter get up from a Gentile table. So this is not a passing mood. It is a standing party with a policy, and it will run through the next four chapters and out into the epistles. They were believers, but they had not yet understood that the wall was down.

The verb Luke chooses. And then the verb for what they did, which is the sharpest thing in the sentence and is invisible in English. They criticised him, diekrinonto, took issue with him, and the word is the same one the Spirit had used on the stairs at Joppa, when Peter was told to go with the three men making no distinction (v. 12). It is the verb for separating, sorting, discriminating between one thing and another. So the sentence reads, to anyone with the Greek: the Spirit told Peter not to discriminate, and here are the brothers, discriminating. They made the distinction God had removed. Luke does not comment. He simply uses the word twice, ten verses apart, and lets the reader find it.

Being fair to them. It is worth being fair to them before the passage moves on. These men were not inventing a prejudice. They were defending a boundary God had drawn himself, in writing, for reasons he had given, which faithful Israelites had died rather than cross. From where they stood, Peter had done something indefensible, and the fact that it had gone well was not obviously an argument; plenty of wrong things go well. Their instinct to ask him about it was not the instinct of small men. It was the instinct of serious ones who had not yet been told what God had decided.

Is it wrong to question a Christian leader? No, and this passage shows it can be right. The Jerusalem believers did not gossip about Peter behind his back or split the church; they raised the matter with him directly, and he answered them patiently. The Bereans were praised for checking even Paul’s teaching against the Scriptures (17:11). What matters is the spirit and the standard. Question openly, not in whispers. Question by Scripture, not by preference. And be ready, as these men were in the end, to be persuaded and to praise God when you are shown to be wrong.

In a sentence. The apostles and believers throughout Judea heard that the Gentiles too had received the word of God, and when Peter went up to Jerusalem, the circumcision party criticised him.

On a Tuesday. Even true believers can resist what God is doing when it breaks their habits. Be teachable. Ask yourself where you might be defending a good thing past the point where God has moved on, and where your first instinct when something new happens in the church is to look for the fault.

For worship. The word of God had been received by the Gentiles. That is the headline of the chapter, and it is the work of God from first to last. He spoke, they heard, they believed, and no faction in Jerusalem could make it unhappen. The word of the Lord runs swiftly, and it is never bound (2 Thessalonians 3:1; 2 Timothy 2:9).
verseByVerse.note: The circumcision party were Jewish believers who held that Gentile converts must be circumcised and keep the law.

verseByVerse.quote: "You went to uncircumcised men and ate with them."
verseByVerse.commentary:
“You went to uncircumcised men and ate with them.”

You went to uncircumcised men and ate with them. Here is the charge, and the first thing to notice is what it is not. They do not say, you preached to Gentiles. They do not say, you baptised uncircumcised men, which is the far larger question and the one that will dominate the council in chapter 15. They say: you went to uncircumcised men and ate with them. The complaint is about a meal.

Eating as a verdict. That looks trivial to a modern reader and it was nothing of the sort. In the ancient world a shared table was the plainest public statement two people could make about each other. You ate with your own; hospitality created obligation, and eating in a man’s house said, in front of everybody, that you and he belonged to one company. A Jew could trade with a Gentile, employ one, serve under one and argue with one. Sitting down to supper was different, and everybody on both sides understood exactly what it meant. So the circumcision party have gone straight to the real issue, and they have better instincts than they are usually given credit for. Preaching to Gentiles could be a mission. Eating with them is a verdict. If Peter can sit at Cornelius’s table, then the wall is down, and everything else follows. The same objection had been made against Jesus himself: this man receives sinners and eats with them (Luke 15:2).

The same man, later. And now the thing that must be said about this verse, because it makes the whole passage honest rather than triumphant. Peter wins this argument. He wins it completely; the room falls silent and praises God. And some years afterwards, at Antioch, Peter is eating with Gentile believers as a matter of course when men arrive from this same circumcision party, and he gets up from the table. He withdraws, and the other Jewish believers follow him, and even Barnabas is carried along, until Paul confronts him in front of everybody because his conduct was not in step with the truth of the gospel (Galatians 2:11–14). The same man. The same issue. The same party. Having stood in Jerusalem and told them all why the wall was down, he later got up from a table because he was afraid of them.

Where Christian failure lives. There is no comfort in that and there is a great deal of use. A conviction can be argued to a conclusion, defended in public, praised by the church, and still not have reached the part of a man that decides where he sits at dinner. Peter’s theology was right in chapter 11 and his feet were wrong in Galatians, and the gap between the two is where most Christian failure actually lives.

If Peter could fail like that, how can I hope to stand? By the same grace that restored Peter every time he fell. He denied Christ three times and was restored; he withdrew from the Gentiles and was corrected, and he received the correction, for years later he calls Paul our beloved brother (2 Peter 3:15). Your standing does not depend on never failing, but on Christ, who keeps those the Father has given him (John 10:28–29). What you can do is close the gap between belief and practice deliberately: notice where your table, your friendships and your diary contradict what you say you believe, and let a faithful friend tell you when they do.

In a sentence. They accused him of going to uncircumcised men and eating with them.

On a Tuesday. Who would you be uncomfortable being seen eating with? Not in theory, but in your actual town, with your actual friends watching. That is the person to invite.

For worship. Christ welcomes sinners to his table. He ate with tax collectors, received a sinful woman’s tears at a Pharisee’s dinner, and on the night he was betrayed broke bread with the man who would deny him. And now he spreads a table for people from every nation and calls it his own supper. Who could ever be worthy to sit there? None of us. That is why it is grace.
verseByVerse.note: Eating together meant full acceptance; that was the offence.

verseByVerse.quote: But Peter began and explained it to them in order: "I was in the city of Joppa praying, and in a trance I saw a vision, something like a great sheet descending, being let down from heaven by its four corners, and it came down to me."
verseByVerse.commentary:
But Peter began and explained it to them in order: “I was in the city of Joppa praying, and in a trance I saw a vision, something like a great sheet descending, being let down from heaven by its four corners, and it came down to me.

But Peter began and explained it to them in order. The word for in order, kathexēs, is the one Luke used in the preface to his Gospel when he told Theophilus he had decided to write an orderly account (Luke 1:3). It means sequentially, one thing after another, with nothing left out and nothing rearranged. Peter is not making a case. He is giving evidence.

What is absent. That is the most striking feature of this whole defence, once you look for what is absent from it. He does not quote Scripture, though he could have; Isaiah has a great deal to say about the nations. He does not appeal to his office, though he is the leading apostle. He does not invoke the commission to go to the ends of the earth, which every man in that room had heard from the Lord’s own mouth. He does not argue or pull rank. He tells them what God did, in the order it happened.

Why an account works better than an argument. An argument can be met with a counter-argument, and both sides go home unmoved; every man in that room was capable of debating the law with Peter, and some of them would have enjoyed it. But an account of events, given in order, with witnesses present, has to be either accepted or called a lie. Peter narrows the options to two, and one of them is not available, because six men from Joppa are standing there. The best answer to criticism is often a patient, honest account.

I was in the city of Joppa praying. He starts where the story starts. Not, I had been thinking about the Gentile question. He was on a roof at midday doing what he did most days, and the whole thing came down on him from outside. It began with God. That matters to his case. If this had begun with an idea of Peter’s, the circumcision party would be entitled to their objection. It began with a sheet.

Something like a great sheet descending. And he says so with the same phrase Luke used in chapter 10 (10:11). Even under pressure, defending himself in front of a hostile room, Peter will not describe the thing more definitely than he saw it. And he adds one small detail: it came down to me. Heaven came to where he was.

In a sentence. Peter explained everything to them step by step: while praying in the city of Joppa he saw in a trance a vision, something like a great sheet let down from heaven by its four corners, and it came right down to him.

On a Tuesday. When you are criticised, resist the urge to defend yourself with heat or with your credentials. Tell the story patiently and honestly, in order, and let the facts speak. And when you tell anyone what God has done in your life, begin where it actually began: with him.

For worship. Peter’s whole defence was a testimony to the initiative of God. He did not go looking for the Gentiles; God came down to him on a roof. That is the shape of every work of grace: it begins in heaven, comes down to us where we are, and leaves us with nothing to say for ourselves except to tell, in order, what the Lord has done.

verseByVerse.quote: "Looking at it closely, I observed animals and beasts of prey and reptiles and birds of the air. And I heard a voice saying to me, 'Rise, Peter; kill and eat.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
