Looking at it closely, I observed animals and beasts of prey and reptiles and birds of the air. And I heard a voice saying to me, ‘Rise, Peter; kill and eat.’

Looking at it closely, I observed animals and beasts of prey and reptiles and birds of the air. Compare this retelling with Luke’s own account in the previous chapter, and something worth noticing emerges: Peter’s version is harder than the original. Chapter 10 says the sheet held all kinds of animals and reptiles and birds of the air. Peter, reporting to a room full of law-observant Jews who are already angry with him, adds a category: beasts of prey. Wild carnivores, the class of creature furthest from anything a Jew would put on a plate, all of them unclean by the law. He has volunteered the most repellent item on the list.

He studied it. And he adds something else that is not in chapter 10: looking at it closely. He did not glance at the sheet and recoil. He examined it. He looked at what was in there, item by item, and knew exactly what he was being asked to do before he refused.

Making his own case worse. This is a man under examination making his own case worse on purpose, and it is the reason the defence works. Every instinct in that situation is to shade the account: to leave out the beasts of prey, to imply he had been unclear about what was in the sheet, to present the whole thing as more ambiguous and therefore more excusable. Peter does the opposite. He tells them precisely how offensive the command was, because the strength of his case rests entirely on the command having come from God, and a command that has been softened is no longer the command that came. There is a general principle in that, and it applies well beyond first-century food laws. A man defending something God has done does not need to make it more palatable, and every attempt to do so weakens the only thing he has. The offensiveness of the instruction is part of the evidence that it was not his idea.

And I heard a voice saying to me, Rise, Peter; kill and eat. He quotes the words unaltered, including his own name in them. The command he resisted is reported as it came. Whatever else the men in that room concluded, they could not conclude that Peter had drifted into this.

Should we soften the hard parts of the gospel to make it easier to accept? No. The gospel has an offence that cannot be removed without destroying it: the cross is a stumbling block and folly to the world (1 Corinthians 1:23). We should remove every unnecessary offence, our rudeness, our jargon, our cultural baggage, so that the only stumbling block left is Christ himself. But we may not trim what God has said about sin, judgment, the uniqueness of Christ or the call to repent, because it is the very hardness of these truths that shows they did not come from us. People are not won by a gospel made comfortable. They are won by a gospel made clear.

In a sentence. Looking at it closely, he saw four-footed animals, wild beasts, reptiles and birds, and heard a voice telling him to get up, kill and eat.

On a Tuesday. When you speak about your faith this week, resist the temptation to leave out the part you think will offend. Say it kindly, say it carefully, but say it. The truth told whole is more persuasive than the truth made convenient.

For worship. God’s commands sometimes cut across our deepest instincts, and he knows exactly what he is doing. The wisdom of God has always looked like foolishness to men: a sheet of unclean beasts, a crucified Messiah, a church of Jews and Gentiles at one table. And every time, the foolishness of God has proved wiser than men, and his weakness stronger than men.

verseByVerse.quote: "But I said, 'By no means, Lord; for nothing common or unclean has ever entered my mouth.' But the voice answered a second time from heaven, 'What God has made clean, do not call common.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
But I said, ‘By no means, Lord; for nothing common or unclean has ever entered my mouth.’ But the voice answered a second time from heaven, ‘What God has made clean, do not call common.’

But I said, By no means, Lord. And now the shrewdest thing in the speech, and it is not a manoeuvre; it is simply honesty that happens to be devastating. Peter tells them that he refused. For nothing common or unclean has ever entered my mouth. He puts his own objection into the record, in full, in the exact words he used, and they are the words every man in that room would have used. He is telling the circumcision party that when God gave him this command, his first reaction was theirs. He was no quicker to accept this than they were.

What it does to the argument. Consider it. They came to the meeting believing that Peter had gone soft on the law, and here he is testifying that he defended it to God’s face. There is now no version of the story in which Peter is a man with loose views who was looking for an excuse. He was the man who said no. Whatever changed his mind was not in him.

How to move people who disagree. It is worth learning as a habit, because it is one of the few things that actually moves people who disagree. Most persuasion begins by explaining why the other man’s position is inadequate, and most persuasion therefore fails, because a man defending a position hears only that he is being attacked. Peter begins by demonstrating that he held their position, understood the reasons for it, and stated it more strongly than they had. Only then does he say what happened next.

But the voice answered a second time from heaven, What God has made clean, do not call common. And what happened next is the sentence that ends the matter. The word that changed everything. Peter shows his critics that the change came from heaven, not from him.

Does the vision abolish the Old Testament food laws? Its first point is about people: Peter concludes that he should not call any person common or unclean (10:28). But it also reflects what Jesus had already declared (Mark 7:19): the food laws, which separated Jew from Gentile, are fulfilled in Christ (Colossians 2:16–17), and Christians are free to eat any food (Romans 14).

Letting it sit. Note that Peter does not paraphrase or apply it. He simply reports it, and lets it sit in the room. It had been said to him and it is now being said to them, in the same words, by the same voice, and it is exactly as unanswerable the second time. The only reply available to the circumcision party is the one Peter had already tried, and they have just heard how well it went for him.

In a sentence. Peter said he had refused, since nothing common or unclean had ever entered his mouth, but the voice from heaven answered a second time that he must not call common what God had made clean.

On a Tuesday. Admitting your own resistance can help others accept what God is doing. The next time you need to persuade a fellow Christian of something, begin by stating his view fairly and saying honestly where you once stood. Then tell him what changed you.

For worship. The voice from heaven had the last word, and it always will. God does not need our permission to cleanse what he chooses to cleanse, and his declaration over a sinner washed in Christ cannot be overturned by any accuser. Who shall bring any charge against God’s elect? It is God who justifies (Romans 8:33).

verseByVerse.quote: "This happened three times, and all was drawn up again into heaven."
verseByVerse.commentary:
This happened three times, and all was drawn up again into heaven.

This happened three times. Peter is producing it as evidence, and in that room it was strong evidence. A single extraordinary experience can be doubted by the man who had it, and much more easily by everybody else: a dream, a state of mind, something misremembered afterwards. A thing repeated three times, with the same voice, the same command and the same correction, has moved out of the category of impressions. Not a passing dream, but a repeated, deliberate message. Peter is telling the church that God said this to him until it could not be mistaken.

His number. Three is his number and he must have known it. Three denials by a fire. Three questions on a beach. And now a vision three times on a roof, each time with the same command. It is difficult to believe the man who lived through all three did not notice a pattern in how God dealt with him, and there is something almost tender in it. God did not correct Peter once and expect it to take. He said it again. And then he said it a third time.

And all was drawn up again into heaven. Then it stopped. It came from God and returned to him. No interpretation was offered, no application supplied, no instruction about what to do with it. The vision was withdrawn and Peter was left on a roof with a command he had refused and a sentence he could not argue with. That is worth registering by anybody who has been shown something in Scripture with no clear next step attached. Peter’s vision did not come with an application, and it did not need one, because the application was already walking up the road and would be at the gate within the hour. He did not have to work it out. He had to answer the door.

The repetition is the patience. There is a kindness in the arithmetic that should not be hurried past. God did not say it once and hold Peter responsible for having heard. He did not say it twice and let the silence do the rest. He said it three times, to a man who had already been forgiven three denials, and then took the sheet away. Anyone who has needed a thing said to them repeatedly before it went in, and has assumed that the repetition was a measure of God’s patience running out, should read the verse the other way round. It is not that God grew exasperated and raised his voice. It is that he knew exactly how many times this particular man would need to hear it, and said it that many times.

In a sentence. This happened three times, and then everything was drawn back up into heaven.

On a Tuesday. Is there a lesson God keeps teaching you, through sermons, through Scripture, through circumstances, that you keep failing to learn? Do not read the repetition as anger. Read it as love, and this time, act on it.

For worship. God repeats what we are slow to learn. He is the Shepherd who goes after the same wandering sheep again and again, the Father who runs to meet the same prodigal every time he comes home. His mercies are new every morning because we need them every morning. Thank him for his patience, which is longer than our stubbornness.

verseByVerse.quote: "And behold, at that very moment three men arrived at the house in which we were, sent to me from Caesarea. And the Spirit told me to go with them, making no distinction. These six brothers also accompanied me, and we entered the man's house."
verseByVerse.commentary:
And behold, at that very moment three men arrived at the house in which we were, sent to me from Caesarea. And the Spirit told me to go with them, making no distinction. These six brothers also accompanied me, and we entered the man’s house.

And behold, at that very moment three men arrived at the house in which we were. Peter’s whole case rests on timing, and here it is. The sheet has just gone back up. He is standing on a roof with no idea what any of it meant, and at that instant, not an hour later, three strangers are at the door asking for him by name, sent from a city thirty miles away by a man he has never met. Nobody arranged that. Cornelius’s messengers had left Caesarea the day before the vision was given. God’s timing confirmed the vision.

And the Spirit told me to go with them, making no distinction. That phrase is the hinge of the defence, and in Greek, mēden diakrinanta, it is the same verb Luke used in verse 2 of the men now questioning him: they criticised Peter; the Spirit told Peter to make no distinction. Peter is quoting the instruction back to a room full of people doing the very thing it forbade. He does not point it out. He does not have to. The Spirit forbade distinction between Jew and Gentile.

These six brothers also accompanied me. And then the sentence that wins the argument before it is finished. These. They are in the room. Peter did not merely take witnesses to Caesarea; he brought them back to Jerusalem and up to this meeting, and at the critical moment he can turn and indicate six men who saw the whole thing. The law of Moses required two or three witnesses to establish a matter (Deuteronomy 19:15). He has brought double, and with himself they make seven; it has often been noted that in Roman practice an important document was authenticated by seven seals. Here they are, Peter is saying: ask them.

The foresight. It is worth pausing on. On the morning Peter set out from Joppa he had a vision he did not understand and an instruction he had not been given a reason for, and he still had the presence of mind to think: whatever happens at the other end of this road, I will have to account for it, and my word alone will not be enough. So he took six men. That is not timidity and it is not politics. It is a leader who knows that the church will have to be persuaded, that being right is not the same as being believed, and that the honest way to handle a claim nobody wants to hear is to make it checkable in advance. Anybody who has ever had to report something difficult to a body that would rather not hear it could do worse than copy him.

And we entered the man’s house. He does not hide it. The very thing he is accused of, he states plainly, as a fact.

In a sentence. At that very moment three men sent from Caesarea arrived at the house where Peter was, and the Spirit told him to go with them, making no distinction, and these six brothers went with him, and they entered the man’s house.

On a Tuesday. The Spirit makes no distinction among those who believe, and neither should the church. Look around your congregation and ask whether any group is quietly treated as second-class: the poor, the new, the foreign, the young, the old. Then do something to bring them in.

For worship. The Lord of history arranged a knock at a door to the minute. His providence is not vague goodwill; it is the precise, wise, loving government of all things for the good of his people and the glory of his Son. Every step on the road to Caesarea was ordered, and so is every step of ours.
verseByVerse.note: Six brothers made seven witnesses with Peter.

verseByVerse.quote: "And he told us how he had seen the angel stand in his house and say, 'Send to Joppa and bring Simon who is called Peter; he will declare to you a message by which you will be saved, you and all your household.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
And he told us how he had seen the angel stand in his house and say, ‘Send to Joppa and bring Simon who is called Peter; he will declare to you a message by which you will be saved, you and all your household.’

And he told us how he had seen the angel stand in his house. Here Peter supplies Cornelius’s side of the story, and with it the piece of information Luke has twice withheld. The withholding was deliberate. Chapter 10 gave the angel’s message to Cornelius at verse 4, and gave it again in Cornelius’s own words at verse 30. Both times it ran the same way: your prayers and alms have been remembered, send to Joppa for Simon called Peter. Both times it stopped there.

He will declare to you a message by which you will be saved. Now, reporting to Jerusalem, Peter finishes the sentence. That clause is the whole reason Peter can stand in that room. Think about what he is demonstrating with it. Before he ever left Joppa, before the vision on the roof, before the knock at the gate, God had already told a Gentile that a message was coming by which he would be saved. Peter did not go to Caesarea and then decide that Gentiles could be saved. He was sent as the delivery of a promise that had already been made without him.

It settles chapter 10. And it settles the question the story otherwise leaves open, which is why the clause matters far beyond this argument. Cornelius was devout, generous and prayerful, and God had noticed all of it. He was also, on the day the angel came, not saved, because the angel told him a message was coming by which he would be. There is no reading of that sentence which allows his piety to have been sufficient in itself, and there is no reading of it which allows the gospel to have been an optional enrichment for a man already safe. Salvation comes through the gospel (Romans 1:16; 10:14–17).

Hard and kind together. The hard half and the kind half stand together here as they always do. The hard half: sincerity does not save, and God does not pretend it does. The kind half: God’s response to a sincere man was not to leave him with his sincerity, but to dispatch an angel, arrange a vision, override an apostle’s lifelong conviction and move him thirty miles up a coast road, in order to get him the message.

You and all your household. And note the last five words. The promise arrives with a family attached to it, the servants, the soldiers, the relatives Cornelius had gathered, which is how God had been speaking to households since Abraham, and which Peter had already announced at Pentecost when he said the promise was for them and for their children (2:39). The whole household heard and believed (10:44), and household salvation in Acts follows household hearing and believing (16:31–34; 18:8).

Does you and all your household mean that a family is saved together, or support infant baptism? Cornelius’ household heard the word, received the Spirit and spoke in tongues (10:44–46), so they were believing hearers. The verse does not teach that faith passes to children automatically; each was saved by hearing and believing. Christians who baptise infants see a covenant pattern in household baptisms; but the households in Acts are described as hearing and believing.

Can I trust God for my family’s salvation? You can pray for it with great confidence, because God loves to work in families and has often saved whole households. But Scripture does not promise that every member of a believer’s family will be saved, and each person must come to Christ himself. What you can do is what Cornelius did: bring your family under the word, gather them where the gospel is preached, live the faith in front of them, and pray for them by name, every day. Then leave them in the hands of the God who is more willing to save than you are to ask.

In a sentence. Cornelius told them how he had seen the angel standing in his house and telling him to send to Joppa for Simon called Peter, who would declare to him a message by which he and all his household would be saved.

On a Tuesday. Good people still need the gospel. Do not assume your decent friends and relatives are fine without Christ. Think of the most moral unbeliever you know, and ask God for an opportunity to speak to him about the message by which he can be saved.

For worship. God sent an angel to tell a man that a message was coming, and the message was Jesus Christ. There is no other name under heaven given among men by which we must be saved (4:12), and the Father has given that name freely to Jew and Gentile alike. He did not leave the seeker to his seeking; he sent him the Saviour. That is the love of God, which is never content to admire our sincerity from a distance, but comes all the way to save.

verseByVerse.quote: "As I began to speak, the Holy Spirit fell on them just as on us at the beginning. And I remembered the word of the Lord, how he said, 'John baptized with water, but you will be baptized with the Holy Spirit.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
As I began to speak, the Holy Spirit fell on them just as on us at the beginning. And I remembered the word of the Lord, how he said, ‘John baptized with water, but you will be baptized with the Holy Spirit.’

As I began to speak. Peter is being precise, and the precision is his argument. Luke’s account in chapter 10 says the Spirit fell while Peter was still speaking; Peter’s own account says it happened as he began. He felt he had only just started. He wants the room to understand how little of the work was his. He had not finished. He had not called for a response. He had barely got going, and God did not wait for the rest of it.

The Holy Spirit fell on them just as on us at the beginning. Then the comparison that ends the debate. Not something similar. Not a lesser gift, or a partial one, or an unusual religious experience which might be interpreted in various ways. The same thing, and the apostles in that room had been there for the first one and could judge for themselves. Peter calls Pentecost the beginning, which is how the church had come to date itself, the start of a new era, and he is saying that what happened in a Roman officer’s front room was the beginning happening again to different people. The Gentile Pentecost was the same gift.

And I remembered the word of the Lord. And then the loveliest detail in the speech. The theology arrived as a memory. Standing in Cornelius’s house watching Gentiles speak in tongues, Peter did not reason his way to a conclusion; a sentence came back to him, spoken by Jesus on the Mount of Olives in the last conversation before the ascension: John baptized with water, but you will be baptized with the Holy Spirit (1:5). Luke had recorded it in the fifth verse of this book. Peter had heard it, and it had sat in him for years doing nothing, and then it came up at the exact moment it was needed and explained everything he was looking at. The promise applied to the Gentiles too. Scripture, and the words of Jesus, interpret events, and not the other way round.

The worth of memorising Scripture. That is worth taking personally by anybody who wonders whether the slow business of getting Scripture into the memory is worth the trouble. Peter could not have looked it up; there was nothing to look up. What he had was what he had heard and kept. The moment came without warning and the sentence was there. Jesus had promised exactly this: the Spirit will bring to your remembrance all that I have said to you (John 14:26).

What is the baptism with the Spirit? It is Christ’s act of pouring out his Spirit on his people, uniting them to himself and to one another. John the Baptist could only apply water to the outside; Jesus gives the Spirit himself, who cleanses and renews from within. Paul says that in one Spirit we were all baptised into one body, Jews or Greeks, slaves or free (1 Corinthians 12:13). So every believer has been baptised with the Spirit, and the proof is not a particular experience but faith in Christ and a life being changed by him. If you trust in Jesus, the promise of Acts 1:5 has been kept in you.

In a sentence. As Peter began to speak, the Holy Spirit fell on them as he had on the apostles at the beginning, and Peter remembered the Lord’s words, that John baptised with water, but they would be baptised with the Holy Spirit.

On a Tuesday. Learn one verse of Scripture by heart this week, and say it over to yourself each morning. You do not know when you will need it, but the Spirit does, and he works with what you have stored.

For worship. The same Spirit, the same gift, for every believer. There is one baptism of the Spirit into one body, and the risen Christ who promised it on the Mount of Olives kept his word in Jerusalem and again in Caesarea. He does not give his Jewish people one Spirit and his Gentile people another. He gives himself, wholly, to all who believe.

verseByVerse.quote: "If then God gave the same gift to them as he gave to us when we believed in the Lord Jesus Christ, who was I that I could stand in God's way?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
If then God gave the same gift to them as he gave to us when we believed in the Lord Jesus Christ, who was I that I could stand in God’s way?

If then God gave the same gift to them as he gave to us when we believed in the Lord Jesus Christ. The same gift: no difference. The gift came with faith, for Jews and Gentiles alike. Not with circumcision, not with law-keeping. He gave it when we believed; he gave it when they believed. The only variable that has been removed is the one the circumcision party was standing on.

Who was I that I could stand in God’s way? It is the last sentence of the defence, and it is worth noticing what kind of sentence it is not. Peter does not say he was right. He does not say he had authority, or that he had weighed the matter and reached a considered view, or even that he had obeyed. He pleads incapacity. The leading apostle of the church, answering the church, says in effect: what was I supposed to do, stop him? Stand in God’s way is kōlysai, hinder, prevent: the same word as withhold the water (10:47). To refuse those whom God has accepted is to fight God (5:39).

Airtight. The logic is airtight because it has no moving parts. If God has done the identical thing on the identical terms, then the question is no longer whether Gentiles may be admitted. It is whether anybody proposes to overrule God on a matter he has already settled in public. Nobody does. That is why the next verse records silence.

What it does not mean. A guard is needed here, because this verse is quoted in church disputes far more often than it is examined, and in the wrong hands it becomes a way of ending discussion rather than resolving it. Who was I that I could stand in God’s way is not a formula for winning arguments by asserting divine backing. It works in this passage because of everything attached to it: a vision that was repeated three times, an independent vision given to a man thirty miles away, three messengers who arrived at the precise moment, an explicit word from the Spirit, six witnesses who can be questioned, and a public sign identical to the one the apostles had seen at the beginning. Peter is not merely saying, God told me. He has just spent thirteen verses laying out the evidence, and only then does he draw the conclusion. A man who says God told him and produces none of that has said something quite different, and the church has been damaged by people who learned Peter’s last sentence without noticing that it came at the end. And today, with the apostolic witness complete, the test of any claim is the written word of God.

So is the baptism with the Spirit a second stage after conversion? Peter equates what Jesus promised (1:5) with what Cornelius received when he believed: the same gift. Pentecostal Christians point to the Samaritans (8:14–17) and the Ephesian disciples (19:1–7), who received the Spirit after believing. But those were moments when the gospel crossed new boundaries, and Paul teaches that every believer has been baptised in the one Spirit (1 Corinthians 12:13). The more likely reading is that the baptism with the Spirit is given to every believer at conversion.

In a sentence. Peter asked that if God gave them the same gift he gave the apostles when they believed in the Lord Jesus Christ, who was he to stand in God’s way?

On a Tuesday. Do not stand in God’s way. If he has accepted someone, accept him. Ask whether there is a believer you have been holding at arm’s length, not because of his sin, but because he does not fit your expectations, and close the distance.

For worship. The same gift, to all who believe. God does not ration his Spirit by nationality, or measure out his grace by pedigree. The Father who gave his only Son gives with him all things freely, to Jew and Gentile alike, and the gift is nothing less than himself dwelling in us. Who could stand in the way of such a God, and who would want to?

verseByVerse.quote: When they heard these things they fell silent. And they glorified God, saying, "Then to the Gentiles also God has granted repentance that leads to life." Now those who were scattered because of the persecution that arose over Stephen traveled as far as Phoenicia and Cyprus and Antioch, speaking the word to no one except Jews.
verseByVerse.commentary:
When they heard these things they fell silent. And they glorified God, saying, “Then to the Gentiles also God has granted repentance that leads to life.” Now those who were scattered because of the persecution that arose over Stephen traveled as far as Phoenicia and Cyprus and Antioch, speaking the word to no one except Jews.

When they heard these things they fell silent. Silence first, and the order matters. Before there is any praise there is a roomful of men with nothing to say: the objection simply runs out. Luke does not record anyone conceding, or apologising, or explaining how they had come to see it differently. The argument stops because there is no longer anything on the other side of it.

And they glorified God. Then the praise, from criticism to worship, which is the best possible response to correction. And the sentence they produce is remarkably well judged for men who have just lost a debate.

Then to the Gentiles also God has granted repentance that leads to life. Note the verb. Not, the Gentiles have repented, which would be a report, but God has granted. They identify the giver in the same breath in which they concede the point. Repentance is God’s gift (5:31; 2 Timothy 2:25), not something we produce. And what they praise him for is not that a barrier fell but that people were given life, eternal life. The great conclusion: Gentiles are saved the same way as Jews, by God’s grace, through repentance and faith.

One part for the whole. One small but useful lesson in how to read the Bible lies in that phrase, “God has granted repentance.” Notice that only repentance is named here, not faith; yet faith is plainly implied, for these Gentiles had believed the gospel (vv. 17, 21). Scripture constantly speaks this way, naming one part of a thing to stand for the whole (a figure of speech called synecdoche). Repentance and faith are simply the two sides of one single turning to Christ: repentance is turning from sin, faith is turning to the Saviour, and you cannot truly do one without the other. So Scripture sometimes names both, “repent and believe in the gospel” (Mark 1:15), “repentance toward God and of faith in our Lord Jesus Christ” (Acts 20:21); sometimes only repentance (here; Luke 24:47; Acts 3:19); and sometimes only faith (“believe in the Lord Jesus, and you will be saved,” Acts 16:31; John 3:16). Whichever one is mentioned, the other comes with it. The whole gospel response can be summed up under any of its facets: calling on the name of the Lord (Romans 10:13) and confessing that Jesus is Lord (Romans 10:9) all mean the same conversion.

Two cautions. First, never build a doctrine on the absence of a word: it would be a serious mistake to read this verse as though faith were unnecessary, or to read Acts 16:31 as though repentance were. Each statement is to be read in the light of the whole of Scripture, which everywhere joins the two. Second, savour what the verse actually says: God granted repentance. The very turning is his gift, as faith is also called “the gift of God” (Ephesians 2:8; compare 2 Timothy 2:25; Philippians 1:29). So when you read “repent” or “believe” standing alone, you should hear the whole: turn to Christ, from sin and unto the Saviour, and give thanks that even the turning was granted you from above.

Now those who were scattered because of the persecution that arose over Stephen. And then Luke does something abrupt. He drops the scene entirely, goes back several years to the persecution that killed Stephen, and picks up a thread he had left lying in chapter 8 (8:1–4). The scattered believers travelled as far as Phoenicia, the coastal region north of Galilee around Tyre and Sidon, and Cyprus, and Antioch in Syria, the third city of the Roman Empire after Rome and Alexandria, with perhaps a quarter to half a million people and a large Jewish community.

Speaking the word to no one except Jews. Read that immediately after verse 18 and it lands like a cold draught. The church has just agreed, in Jerusalem, in principle, with praise, that God has granted repentance to the Gentiles. And Luke’s very next sentence reports that for years believers had been carrying the gospel across three provinces and telling nobody but their own kind. It is not an accusation, and Luke makes no comment. But he has put the two sentences side by side, and the gap between them is the honest measurement of how long it takes a settled conviction to reach the street. The principle was conceded in a meeting. The practice changed in Antioch, some time later, almost by accident, in the hands of men whose names nobody wrote down.

If repentance is God’s gift, what am I supposed to do? Repent. God’s gift of repentance does not happen around you but in you: he gives it by working in your heart so that you yourself turn from sin, freely and genuinely. You are never told to wait passively until you feel repentant. You are commanded to repent and believe (17:30), and the very desire to obey that command is the first sign that God is granting it. And if you are praying for someone who shows no sign of repentance, this verse is your warrant. You cannot argue anyone into it, but you can ask the God who grants it to grant it to them.

In a sentence. When they heard this, they fell silent and glorified God, saying that God had granted the Gentiles too repentance that leads to life; meanwhile those scattered by the persecution after Stephen had travelled as far as Phoenicia, Cyprus and Antioch, speaking the word only to Jews.

On a Tuesday. Is there a gap between what you believe about the gospel and whom you actually speak to about it? Write down the names of three people outside your usual circle, a different background, a different language, a different generation, and pray for an opening with one of them this week.

For worship. Repentance is God’s gift. If you have it, thank him: the tears you shed over your sin and the turning of your heart to Christ were not your achievement but his mercy. If someone you love lacks it, ask him to grant it. The God who granted life to the Gentiles is still granting it, and his hand is not shortened that it cannot save.
verseByVerse.note: Phoenicia was the coastal region north of Galilee. Antioch in Syria was one of the great cities of the Roman Empire.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Those scattered by the persecution after Stephen’s death travelled to Phoenicia, Cyprus and Antioch, telling the message only to Jews. But some from Cyprus and Cyrene went to Antioch and began speaking to Greeks as well, telling them the good news about the Lord Jesus. The Lord’s hand was with them, and a great number believed and turned to the Lord. When news reached the church in Jerusalem, they sent Barnabas to Antioch. Arriving and seeing what God’s grace had done, he was glad and encouraged them all to remain true to the Lord with all their hearts. He was a good man, full of the Holy Spirit and faith, and a great number of people were brought to the Lord. Then Barnabas went to Tarsus to look for Saul, found him and brought him to Antioch. For a whole year they met with the church and taught great numbers of people. The disciples were first called Christians at Antioch. During this time some prophets came down from Jerusalem to Antioch. One of them, Agabus, predicted through the Spirit that a severe famine would spread over the entire Roman world, which happened during the reign of Claudius. The disciples, each according to their ability, decided to provide help for the believers living in Judea, and sent their gift to the elders by Barnabas and Saul.
verseByVerse.theology:
Antioch and the Shape of a Sending Church

Antioch is the model the New Testament actually gives us for a missionary congregation, and almost nothing about it was planned. It began with unnamed laymen doing the obvious thing; it was recognised rather than authorised; it was established by a year of ordinary teaching; and its first corporate act was to send money to a church that had been suspicious of people like them. Reformed missiology has drawn the pattern out: rooted in the word, generous beyond its own borders, and willing to give away its best men — for within two chapters Antioch will send Barnabas and Saul off on the first missionary journey, which is to say it exported its two finest teachers and kept none of them. A church is not measured by what it gathers. It is measured by what it is prepared to lose.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: The single most important barrier in Christian history was crossed by men from Cyprus and Cyrene whose names nobody recorded. Luke knows their home towns and not their names, which tells you they were never anybody's leadership. Now: The work that turns out to have mattered most in any generation is very often done by people who will not appear in an account of it — who simply spoke to whoever was in front of them, because it did not occur to them to check first whether they were allowed.

verseByVerse.quote: But there were some of them, men of Cyprus and Cyrene, who on coming to Antioch spoke to the Hellenists also, preaching the Lord Jesus. And the hand of the Lord was with them, and a great number who believed turned to the Lord.
verseByVerse.commentary:
But there were some of them, men of Cyprus and Cyrene, who on coming to Antioch spoke to the Hellenists also, preaching the Lord Jesus. And the hand of the Lord was with them, and a great number who believed turned to the Lord.

But there were some of them, men of Cyprus and Cyrene. Everything turns on a small word at the start of the sentence: but. Verse 19 said the scattered believers spoke to nobody except Jews. But there were some of them, and the whole future of the church is in that exception.

Nameless men. Luke tells us where they came from and not who they were. Men of Cyprus and Cyrene: Jews from abroad, Greek-speaking, from an island and from North Africa, used to living among Gentiles and presumably rather less scandalised by them than a man raised in Judea would have been. Not apostles. That is as much as we know. The most consequential thing any believer did in the first century was done by people whose names were not thought worth recording, and Luke, who is a careful historian and names dozens of minor figures elsewhere, evidently could not find out. The first deliberate preaching to Gentiles in a Gentile city was done by ordinary, nameless Christians. God uses ordinary people.

Cyrene again. Cyrene is worth a second look. Men of Cyrene had a synagogue in Jerusalem and were among those who argued with Stephen and could not withstand him (6:9–10). Luke does not say these are the same men, and it would be wrong to assert it. But the city that supplied some of Stephen’s opponents also supplied some of the men who first did the thing Stephen had been killed for pointing toward, and that is at least worth noticing.

Who on coming to Antioch spoke to the Hellenists also. There is a genuine question about the word here. The manuscripts divide between Hellenists, Greek-speaking Jews, and Greeks, meaning Gentiles proper, and your Bible probably has a footnote. The sense of the passage requires Gentiles: verse 19 has just said to no one except Jews, and this sentence is the contrast to it. Whatever the copyists made of the word, Luke’s argument is unmistakable.

Preaching the Lord Jesus. And notice what they led with. To Gentiles, they did not start with Jesus is the Messiah, a Jewish title that would have meant little in a Greek city, but with Jesus is Lord, which every Greek would understand and which claimed everything. Wise evangelism adapts its words, not its message.

No vision, no angel. And notice what is absent. No vision. No angel. No word from the Spirit, no instruction from Jerusalem, no debate, and no record that anybody asked permission. Peter needed a sheet let down from heaven three times before he would enter a Gentile house. These men arrived in a Greek city and started talking to Greeks, apparently because there were Greeks there. They already had their commission (1:8), and they simply obeyed it.

And the hand of the Lord was with them, and a great number who believed turned to the Lord. The hand of the Lord is an Old Testament phrase for God’s power actively at work (Isaiah 59:1). And notice the pairing: they believed and turned, faith and repentance together, as in verse 18. Heaven’s verdict on the initiative of unnamed men was to bless it enormously.

Do I need a special call to tell people about Jesus? No. Every Christian already has one. The command to make disciples of all nations (Matthew 28:19) and the promise of the Spirit for witness (1:8) belong to the whole church, not to apostles alone. Some are called and gifted to preach and to lead, and the church should recognise them. But speaking of Christ to your neighbour needs no ordination. These men had no title, no training we know of and no instructions, and they started the church that evangelised the world.

In a sentence. But some of them, men from Cyprus and Cyrene, came to Antioch and spoke to the Greeks too, preaching the Lord Jesus, and the Lord’s hand was with them, and a great number believed and turned to the Lord.

On a Tuesday. You do not need a title to share Christ. Think of one person you meet regularly who does not know him, and this week tell him one thing about Jesus as Lord: what he has done for you, or what he claims. Leave the results to the hand of the Lord.

For worship. The hand of the Lord was with nameless men in a pagan city, and a great number turned to him. God does not need famous servants to do his greatest works; he delights to use the unknown, so that the glory is plainly his. Their names are not in Acts, but they are written in heaven, and on the last day the Lord Jesus will call them by name.
verseByVerse.note: “Hellenists” here seems to mean Greek-speaking Gentiles.

verseByVerse.quote: The report of this came to the ears of the church in Jerusalem, and they sent Barnabas to Antioch. When he came and saw the grace of God, he was glad, and he exhorted them all to remain faithful to the Lord with steadfast purpose,
verseByVerse.commentary:
The report of this came to the ears of the church in Jerusalem, and they sent Barnabas to Antioch. When he came and saw the grace of God, he was glad, and he exhorted them all to remain faithful to the Lord with steadfast purpose,

The report of this came to the ears of the church in Jerusalem, and they sent Barnabas to Antioch. Jerusalem hears, and Jerusalem sends somebody. It is the second time in three chapters that news of an irregular advance has reached the mother church and produced a delegation: they sent Peter and John down to Samaria (8:14), and now they send a man to Antioch.

The man they chose. And the man they choose settles the outcome. It is worth pausing on how differently this could have gone. There were men available in Jerusalem who would have arrived at Antioch with the circumcision party’s questions in their pocket; the reader has met them at the start of this very chapter. Send one of them, and the first Gentile congregation in history has its foundations examined by somebody looking for a fault. They sent Barnabas. A wise choice: he was from Cyprus, like some of the evangelists, and he was the son of encouragement (4:36).

When he came and saw the grace of God, he was glad. Stop on that. What did he actually see? A room full of Greeks, uncircumcised, with pagan backgrounds and no synagogue training, worshipping the God of Israel in a Syrian city, taught by nobody in particular. There was plenty there for a careful man to be concerned about, and a great deal that would need sorting out, and Barnabas saw the grace of God. He had the eye for it. He looked at an untidy, unauthorised, doctrinally unformed crowd of new Gentile believers and identified the one thing that was actually going on. He did not look for problems, or for what they were doing wrong. He saw God at work and rejoiced.

Glad. And he was glad. Not relieved, not cautiously satisfied: glad, a word from the same family as the grace he had seen (chairō, charis), and the same joy that runs through this book. His name meant son of encouragement and he had earned it twice already, selling a field for the poor and vouching for Saul when nobody else would go near him. Here he does it a third time, simply by being pleased.

And he exhorted them all to remain faithful to the Lord with steadfast purpose. Then he does the work. Exhorted, parekalei, is the root of his nickname: he encouraged them. With steadfast purpose is literally with purpose of heart, a settled inward intention. He does not begin by correcting them. He tells a young church in a pagan city the one thing it will most need, which is to stay put, and he tells them to do it from the inside out. New believers need encouragement to keep going.

Which man was sent. A great many things in church history have turned on which man was sent, and this is the clearest instance of it in Scripture. The Gentile mission survived its inspection because the inspector was a man capable of being delighted.

How do I see the grace of God in other Christians? Look for what only God could have done. A new believer’s doctrine may be muddled and his habits rough, but if he loves Christ, wants to hear the word, is beginning to hate his sin and loves God’s people, you are looking at the grace of God. Name it to him, and thank God for it aloud. Then, when correction is needed, it will come from someone he knows is on his side. Barnabas did not ignore what needed teaching; he and Saul spent a year teaching (v. 26). But he started with gladness.

In a sentence. When news of this reached the church in Jerusalem, they sent Barnabas to Antioch, and when he arrived and saw the grace of God, he was glad and encouraged them all to remain true to the Lord with steadfast hearts.

On a Tuesday. The next time you visit another church, or meet a Christian from a different tradition, look first for the grace of God and say what you see. Then encourage one person this week to keep going with Christ, specifically and by name.

For worship. The grace of God was visible in Antioch, and it is visible wherever sinners are turning to Christ. It is his grace that saves, his grace that keeps, his grace that makes a church out of strangers. And it is a grace so real that a good man could walk into a room of former pagans and see it shining. Thank God for every place where his grace can be seen, and for every Barnabas with eyes to see it.

verseByVerse.quote: for he was a good man, full of the Holy Spirit and of faith. And a great many people were added to the Lord.
verseByVerse.commentary:
for he was a good man, full of the Holy Spirit and of faith. And a great many people were added to the Lord.

For he was a good man. Luke stops the narrative to explain why the previous verse happened, and the explanation is a character reference. Take the first word on its own, because it is easy to skim and it is not a small thing. Good. Not brilliant, not strategic, not a powerful preacher, not well connected: Luke had all those words available and did not reach for any of them. He was a good man. It is the plainest commendation in the New Testament and one of the rarest, and it is offered as the reason an entire city came to Christ. A good man sees good.

No jealousy in him. And notice where Luke has placed the sentence. It sits between Barnabas being glad at what he found and Barnabas going to fetch Saul: that is, in the middle of an account of a man rejoicing over somebody else’s work and then going to get somebody better at teaching than himself. Luke’s portrait of goodness is not abstract. It is a man with no jealousy in him.

Full of the Holy Spirit and of faith. “Full of the Holy Spirit”: a description we rarely hear on people’s lips today, yet it is one of the loveliest things Scripture ever says of anyone. (On how such fullness shows itself, and how the early church could actually recognise it, see the fuller treatment at 6:5.) In brief, Luke uses the phrase not for a momentary “filling” for a single task (Acts has those too, a sudden filling for boldness or speech, 4:8, 31; 13:9) but for a settled, habitual condition: a man so yielded to the Spirit that the Spirit pervades and governs his whole life, his character and words and deeds. It is the same thing said of Jesus himself (“full of the Holy Spirit,” Luke 4:1) and of Stephen (6:5), so to be full of the Spirit is simply to be deeply like Christ. And notice how concrete it is in Barnabas: it is paired with “a good man” and with faith, and we have watched it in action: the generous giver who sold his field (4:36–37), the big-hearted man who vouched for the feared new convert Saul when others would not (9:27), the encourager who “was glad” to see God’s grace in Antioch (11:23). That is what a Spirit-full life looks like: goodness, faith, generosity, courage, and an eye quick to rejoice in grace.

Not a rare distinction. And it is not meant to be a rare distinction reserved for a Barnabas. The New Testament commands every believer, “be filled with the Spirit” (Ephesians 5:18), a continuous filling, sought by yielding to him: letting the word of Christ dwell richly (Colossians 3:16), praying, obeying, walking in step with the Spirit rather than grieving or quenching him (Galatians 5:16; Ephesians 4:30; 1 Thessalonians 5:19). It is a phrase worth recovering, and a thing worth coveting, for the highest compliment that could be paid to you is not that you are clever or capable, but that those who meet you meet something of God, because you are full of the Holy Spirit.

And a great many people were added to the Lord. Added to the Lord, not merely to the congregation; Luke keeps the phrasing careful, as he did at 5:14. Goodness and the Spirit bear fruit. The register that matters is not the one Barnabas was keeping.

Is goodness enough to make a person a Christian? No. Barnabas was good because he was full of the Spirit and of faith, not the other way round. No one is good enough by nature to be accepted by God; Jesus said that no one is good except God alone (Mark 10:18). The goodness Luke praises here is the fruit of grace: the Spirit producing in a forgiven sinner the likeness of Christ. That is why it is open to every believer. You cannot make yourself good by effort. But if you belong to Christ, the Spirit who made Barnabas good is at work in you, and you can ask him daily to fill you.

In a sentence. He was a good man, full of the Holy Spirit and of faith, and a great many people were added to the Lord.

On a Tuesday. Pray to be a good person, full of the Spirit and faith. Character matters more than talent. Ask a trusted friend this week which of the Spirit’s fruits is weakest in you, and ask God specifically to grow it.

For worship. Every good thing in Barnabas came from God. He was good because the Spirit of the good God filled him, and the Spirit filled him because the Son had been glorified and poured him out. There is only one perfectly good man, Jesus Christ, and the goodness of every saint is a reflection of his. Praise him for the good men and women he has given his church, and for making sinners like us into people who can be called good.

verseByVerse.quote: So Barnabas went to Tarsus to look for Saul, and when he had found him, he brought him to Antioch. For a whole year they met with the church and taught a great many people. And in Antioch the disciples were first called Christians.
verseByVerse.commentary:
So Barnabas went to Tarsus to look for Saul, and when he had found him, he brought him to Antioch. For a whole year they met with the church and taught a great many people. And in Antioch the disciples were first called Christians.

So Barnabas went to Tarsus to look for Saul. He had to look for him, which implies that Saul was not simply sitting at an address. The verb, anazētēsai, means to search hard, to hunt up and down. It had been the best part of a decade since the brothers put him on a boat at Caesarea; he had been working somewhere in Syria and Cilicia, and nobody in Antioch knew exactly where. Barnabas made a journey of a hundred miles or so on the strength of remembering a man, and then had to go and look for him. He knew he needed help, and he knew whom God had called to the Gentiles (9:15). He did not try to keep the work for himself.

The second time. This is the second time Barnabas has done this for Saul, and the two acts between them are the reason there is a Pauline half to the New Testament. The first was in Jerusalem, when every Christian in the city was frightened of the man and Barnabas took him by the arm and walked him in to the apostles (9:27). The second is this: a hidden decade ended because one man could not leave him out there.

Making room for a greater man. Consider what Barnabas is doing to himself. He is the recognised leader of the most promising church in the world, sent by Jerusalem, and he goes and fetches a teacher who will eclipse him entirely. Within two chapters Luke’s phrase has changed from Barnabas and Saul to Paul and his companions (13:13), and Barnabas moves to the back of the story. He must have known it was likely. He went anyway. It is the spirit of John the Baptist: he must increase, but I must decrease (John 3:30).

For a whole year they met with the church and taught a great many people. A year in one place, with one congregation, teaching. Not a campaign. It is worth noticing that the church which becomes the launching point for the entire Gentile mission was built by twelve months of ordinary instruction from two men who stayed put. Converts need grounding.

And in Antioch the disciples were first called Christians. And then the sentence everybody remembers. Christianos is a Greek stem with a Latin ending, the form used for the followers or partisans of somebody, on the same pattern by which people spoke of Herod’s men as Herodians (Mark 3:6). It means Christ’s people, Christ’s lot. It was very probably a nickname coined by outsiders, in the street, perhaps in mockery; there is no suggestion the church chose it. The two other times it appears in the New Testament it is in the mouth of a king who is deflecting, perhaps with irony (26:28), and in a letter about suffering for the name (1 Peter 4:16). The believers later wore it gladly.

What the neighbours had concluded. What it tells you is what the neighbours in Antioch had concluded. Not that these people were generous, or strange, or Jewish, or a philosophy, but that they were somebody’s. They were named after a person, by people watching from outside, who could not describe them without using his name. Outsiders noticed they talked about Christ all the time. And a church of Jews and Gentiles needed a new name: neither Jew nor Gentile, but Christ’s.

What makes someone a Christian? Not a family, a culture, a church membership or a moral code, but belonging to Christ by faith. The name means Christ’s person, and that is the heart of it: you are a Christian if you have trusted Jesus Christ as your Saviour and Lord, and he has made you his own. Many people call themselves Christian because of where they were born; the neighbours in Antioch used the name because of how people lived and whom they talked about. The question to ask yourself is not whether you have the label, but whether you have the Lord.

In a sentence. Barnabas went to Tarsus to look for Saul, and when he found him he brought him to Antioch, and for a whole year they met with the church and taught a great many people, and it was in Antioch that the disciples were first called Christians.

On a Tuesday. You bear Christ’s name. Would your neighbours or colleagues think of it if they had to describe you? Let people see why. And think of someone with gifts the church is not using, someone sidelined, overlooked or forgotten, and go and look for him, as Barnabas did.

For worship. They were called by his name. The Son of God has given his name to a people from every nation, and he is not ashamed to call them brothers (Hebrews 2:11). To be a Christian is to be Christ’s, bought with his blood, sealed by his Spirit, named with his name. There is no higher title in the universe, and he gives it freely to sinners.
verseByVerse.note: “Christians” means “Christ’s people” — probably a nickname given by outsiders.

verseByVerse.quote: Now in these days prophets came down from Jerusalem to Antioch. And one of them named Agabus stood up and foretold by the Spirit that there would be a great famine over all the world (this took place in the days of Claudius).
verseByVerse.commentary:
Now in these days prophets came down from Jerusalem to Antioch. And one of them named Agabus stood up and foretold by the Spirit that there would be a great famine over all the world (this took place in the days of Claudius).

Now in these days prophets came down from Jerusalem to Antioch. Prophets travel from Jerusalem to Antioch, and Luke mentions them without explanation, which tells you they were a familiar feature of church life rather than a curiosity. Prophets were a recognised ministry in the early church (13:1; 1 Corinthians 12:28; Ephesians 4:11), part of the foundation era (Ephesians 2:20).

And one of them named Agabus stood up and foretold by the Spirit that there would be a great famine over all the world. Agabus appears again in 21:10–11, foretelling Paul’s arrest. All the world means the Roman world. It is worth saying briefly what such men were doing, since the word carries freight it did not then have. What Agabus supplies is not doctrine but information: a specific, checkable warning about something coming, given so that the church could act. He tells them there is going to be a famine. He does not tell them what to think about God.

This took place in the days of Claudius. Then Luke adds a parenthesis, and it is the sort of thing that makes him worth trusting. He is telling his reader that the prophecy came true and giving the reign in which to look for it. The emperor Claudius ruled from AD 41 to 54, and ancient historians record a series of severe grain shortages in his reign; a famine struck Judea around AD 45 to 48, severe enough that Queen Helena of Adiabene, a convert to Judaism, bought grain in Egypt and had it shipped to Jerusalem, as Josephus tells. Luke is not asking anyone to take his word for it. He is dating the thing, and tying his story to history that can be checked.

What the warning was for. And notice what the warning is for. God does not tell the church at Antioch about the famine so that they can be impressed, or so that they can fill their own storehouses. Read on: the next two verses are a collection. The foreknowledge is given so that a church can get money to people who are about to be hungry, before they are hungry. That is a very characteristic piece of divine economy. A revelation is given about the future, and its entire practical content turns out to be an opportunity to be generous earlier than would otherwise have been possible.

Do men like Agabus exist now? Christians differ about it, and the difference is real and held in good faith on both sides: some hold that gifts of this kind ceased with the apostolic foundation, others that they continue in some form. The first is the better view, and the fuller discussion belongs at 5:12, where the question of the signs is worked out.

The continuationist case and the better reading. Continuationist Christians believe that prophets like Agabus still speak in the church, pointing to 1 Corinthians 14 and to Christ’s giving of prophets in Ephesians 4:11–13. The more likely reading is that New Testament prophecy, as revelation from God, belonged with the apostles to the church’s foundation (Ephesians 2:20), and that what Agabus foretold, the famine, came to pass, as true prophecy always did.

The boundary. What can be said here, and what both sides agree on, is the boundary. Whatever Agabus was, he was not adding to Scripture and nobody treated him as if he were; his contribution was a piece of practical information which the church then acted on with its own judgment. Any claim in any century that would correct, supplement or override what is written is a different thing altogether, and the church has always known how to name it.

How should I respond if someone tells me he has a word from God for me? Kindly, and carefully. Do not mock him, for he may be a sincere brother who holds a different view of the gifts. But test what he says by Scripture (1 Thessalonians 5:20–21; 1 John 4:1). If it contradicts the Bible, reject it. If it simply repeats what the Bible already says, receive it as a reminder of God’s word, not as new revelation. If it claims to tell you something the Bible does not, a person to marry, a job to take, a date something will happen, you are not bound by it. Make your decisions by Scripture, prayer, wise counsel and the providence of God, and you will not go astray.

In a sentence. In those days prophets came down from Jerusalem to Antioch, and one of them named Agabus stood up and predicted by the Spirit that there would be a great famine over the whole world, which happened in the days of Claudius.

On a Tuesday. God warned his church ahead of time so that it could prepare to help. Use your foresight for others’ good. When you see trouble coming for someone, a redundancy, an illness, a hard winter, do not wait until he asks. Move first.

For worship. The Lord of history knows the end from the beginning, and nothing in his world takes him by surprise, not famines, not emperors, not the price of grain in Egypt. And he uses his knowledge of the future for the good of his people. The same God who warned Joseph of seven lean years warned the church at Antioch, and both times the warning became a means of feeding the hungry. He is the provider, and his care reaches to tomorrow’s bread.
verseByVerse.note: The emperor Claudius ruled AD 41–54; ancient historians record severe famines in his reign, including in Judea.

parallels.desc: Agabus again

verseByVerse.quote: So the disciples determined, every one according to his ability, to send relief to the brothers living in Judea. And they did so, sending it to the elders by the hand of Barnabas and Saul.
verseByVerse.commentary:
So the disciples determined, every one according to his ability, to send relief to the brothers living in Judea. And they did so, sending it to the elders by the hand of Barnabas and Saul.

So the disciples determined, every one according to his ability, to send relief to the brothers living in Judea. Watch which way the money goes. Antioch is the new church: Gentile, recently converted, taught for a single year, and still the subject of some anxiety in Jerusalem, where a party had been arguing not long before about whether people like this could properly be admitted at all. Judea is the mother church, the apostolic centre, the place all of this came from. And it is Antioch that sends relief to Judea. The church that had been argued about is the church that pays for the food. Relief is diakonia, ministry, service: the new unity in Christ expressed in money.

Unasked. Nobody instructed them to. There is no request from Jerusalem in the text, no appeal, no apostolic circular. A prophet said there would be a famine, and the Antioch believers worked out for themselves who would be worst hit and did something about it before it arrived. The response to prophecy was not speculation but generosity.

Every one according to his ability. Not a flat rate and not an equal share: each person gave in proportion to what he had, which is the New Testament’s settled pattern for giving (1 Corinthians 16:2; 2 Corinthians 8:11–12) and is a good deal more searching than a fixed figure. A tenth from a man with nothing and a tenth from a man with everything are not the same act, and this arrangement knows it. Not equal amounts, but equal sacrifice. It also means nobody in that congregation was exempt: the poorest members are included in every one, giving according to an ability that was small and real.

And they did so, sending it to the elders. This is the first mention of elders in the Christian church. The Jerusalem church now had elders alongside the apostles (15:2), men entrusted with its care.

By the hand of Barnabas and Saul. And then the two men who carry it. Sit with that for a moment. The money is being taken to the believers in Judea, the very people who had been dragged out of their houses, imprisoned and in some cases killed under the direction of a young man from Tarsus. Saul is walking into Judea carrying famine relief for the families he had broken up. Whatever conversations happened when he handed it over, Luke does not record them. It is also the first joint mission of the partnership that will take the gospel across the empire, and it is not a preaching tour. Barnabas and Saul’s first work together was delivering money to hungry people. And they were trustworthy men to carry it, as Paul would later insist such gifts must be (2 Corinthians 8:20–21).

How does this visit fit with Paul’s account in Galatians 2? The more likely reading is that Galatians 2:1–10 describes this famine visit, a private meeting with the leaders, before the public council of Acts 15. Others equate Galatians 2 with Acts 15. The first fits better, since Paul, arguing about circumcision, never mentions the council’s decision.

The collection never stopped. Paul spends years of his later ministry organising exactly this: a fund gathered from Gentile churches for the poor believers in Jerusalem. He explains the theology of it in a sentence: if the Gentiles have come to share in their spiritual blessings, they ought also to be of service to them in material blessings (Romans 15:27). That whole enterprise, which occupies large parts of three of his letters, began here, with a famine warning and a young church that did not wait to be asked.

How much should I give? Scripture gives no fixed percentage for Christians, but it gives principles that are more searching than any percentage. Give regularly (1 Corinthians 16:2), in proportion to what God has given you (2 Corinthians 8:12), cheerfully and not under compulsion (2 Corinthians 9:7), and sacrificially, as the Macedonians gave beyond their means (2 Corinthians 8:3). Many Christians find a tenth a helpful starting point, and many who can give more should. Give first to your own church, which feeds you, and then to believers in need and to gospel work. And remember that the measure is not the amount but the cost, and the motive is the grace of Christ, who though he was rich became poor for your sake (2 Corinthians 8:9).

In a sentence. The disciples decided, each according to his ability, to send relief to the believers living in Judea, and they did so, sending it to the elders by the hands of Barnabas and Saul.

On a Tuesday. Love crosses every boundary with open hands. Look at your giving this month and ask whether it is according to your ability or according to habit. Then find one believer in need, in your church or in another country, and give something that costs you.

For worship. The church that had once been argued about sent bread to the church that had argued, by the hands of the man who had once persecuted them. Only the grace of Christ could write such a story. He who gave himself for us all has made Jew and Gentile one body, so that the hunger of one is the burden of the other. Give thanks to the Lord Jesus, who became poor that we might be rich, and who teaches his people to open their hands.

parallels.desc: remember the poor

11.theology: Repentance as Gift. Acts 11:18 contains one of the clearest biblical statements of the Reformed doctrine of monergism in conversion: “God has granted repentance that leads to life.” Repentance is not a human achievement that God rewards with salvation; it is itself a divine gift, granted by God to those he is drawing to himself. This does not eliminate human responsibility — the Gentiles in Cornelius’s house genuinely repented, genuinely believed, genuinely turned to Christ. But behind their turning was God’s giving. This is the grammar of all true conversion: God grants, the sinner turns, and God receives the glory. Antioch is not merely a sociological phenomenon — it is a theological one: God giving repentance to people who had no claim on him, because he is the God of all grace.
11.examples:
Then: Anonymous men from Cyprus and Cyrene, whose names are not recorded in Scripture, who crossed the ethnic boundary no one else had thought to cross, and started the church in Antioch. The hand of the Lord was with them. History turned on their obedience.

Now: The church at Antioch is the model of a healthy sending church: multi-ethnic, Spirit-filled, taught by gifted teachers, responsive to need (the famine collection), and willing to send its best people out on mission. Every local church must ask whether it looks more like the fearful circumcision party in Jerusalem or the glad, generous, outward-facing church at Antioch.

12.title: The Prison and the Providence
12.text: <sup>1</sup>About that time Herod the king laid violent hands on some who belonged to the church. <sup>2</sup>He killed James the brother of John with the sword. <sup>3</sup>And when he saw that it pleased the Jews, he proceeded to arrest Peter also. This was during the days of Unleavened Bread. <sup>4</sup>And when he had seized him, he put him in prison, delivering him over to four squads of soldiers to guard him, intending after the Passover to bring him out to the people. <sup>5</sup>So Peter was kept in prison, but earnest prayer for him was made to God by the church. <sup>6</sup>Now when Herod was about to bring him out, on that very night, Peter was sleeping between two soldiers, bound with two chains, and sentries before the door were guarding the prison. <sup>7</sup>And behold, an angel of the Lord stood next to him, and a light shone in the cell. He struck Peter on the side and woke him, saying, “Get up quickly.” And the chains fell off his hands. <sup>8</sup>And the angel said to him, “Dress yourself and put on your sandals.” And he did so. And he said to him, “Wrap your cloak around you and follow me.” <sup>9</sup>And he went out and followed him. He did not know that what was being done by the angel was real, but thought he was seeing a vision. <sup>10</sup>When they had passed the first and the second guard, they came to the iron gate leading into the city. It opened for them of its own accord, and they went out and went along one street, and immediately the angel left him. <sup>11</sup>When Peter came to himself, he said, “Now I am sure that the Lord has sent his angel and rescued me from the hand of Herod and from all that the Jewish people were expecting.” <sup>12</sup>When he realized this, he went to the house of Mary, the mother of John whose other name was Mark, where many were gathered together and were praying. <sup>13</sup>And when he knocked at the door of the gateway, a servant girl named Rhoda came to answer. <sup>14</sup>Recognizing Peter’s voice, in her joy she did not open the gate but ran in and reported that Peter was standing at the gate. <sup>15</sup>They said to her, “You are out of your mind.” But she kept insisting that it was so, and they kept saying, “It is his angel!” <sup>16</sup>But Peter continued knocking, and when they opened, they saw him and were amazed. <sup>17</sup>But motioning to them with his hand to be silent, he described to them how the Lord had brought him out of the prison. And he said, “Tell these things to James and to the brothers.” Then he departed and went to another place. <sup>18</sup>Now when day came, there was no little disturbance among the soldiers over what had become of Peter. <sup>19</sup>And after Herod searched for him and did not find him, he examined the sentries and ordered that they should be put to death. Then he went down from Judea to Caesarea and spent time there. <sup>20</sup>Now Herod was angry with the people of Tyre and Sidon, and they came to him with one accord, and having persuaded Blastus, the king’s chamberlain, they asked for peace, because their country depended on the king’s country for food. <sup>21</sup>On an appointed day Herod put on his royal robes, took his seat upon the throne, and delivered an oration to them. <sup>22</sup>And the people were shouting, “The voice of a god, and not of a man!” <sup>23</sup>Immediately an angel of the Lord struck him down, because he did not give God the glory, and he was eaten by worms and breathed his last. <sup>24</sup>But the word of God increased and multiplied. <sup>25</sup>And Barnabas and Saul returned from Jerusalem when they had completed their service, bringing with them John, whose other name was Mark.
12.overview:
A new persecution comes from the top. Herod Agrippa I, grandson of Herod the Great, had grown up in Rome as a friend of the imperial family; the emperors Caligula and Claudius gave him his grandfather’s whole kingdom, and from AD 41 to 44 he ruled Judea, courting Jewish favour by careful religious observance. To please the Jewish leaders he has James the brother of John executed with the sword, the first apostle to be martyred, and arrests Peter during the Passover festival, intending a public trial afterwards. Peter is chained between two soldiers, with sixteen guarding him in shifts, while the church prays earnestly. On the night before the trial an angel wakes him, the chains fall off, and he walks out past the guards and through the iron city gate, which opens by itself.

Peter goes to the house of Mary, the mother of John Mark, where many are praying. The servant girl Rhoda is so excited to hear his voice that she runs to tell the others without opening the door, and they tell her she is mad, or that it must be his angel. When they finally let him in, Peter tells them what happened, asks them to tell James, the Lord’s brother, and leaves for another place. Herod executes the guards. Then, at Caesarea, while the crowd hails his speech as the voice of a god, he is struck down by an angel and dies, eaten by worms, an event the Jewish historian Josephus also records. The tyrant dies, and the word of God keeps growing.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–25 — Herod's Persecution and God's Deliverance
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: About that time King Herod arrested some who belonged to the church, intending to persecute them. He had James, John’s brother, put to death with the sword. Seeing that this pleased the Jewish leaders, he arrested Peter too, during the Festival of Unleavened Bread. He put him in prison under the guard of four squads of four soldiers each, planning to bring him out for public trial after the Passover. So Peter was kept in prison, but the church was praying earnestly to God for him. The night before Herod was to bring him to trial, Peter was sleeping between two soldiers, bound with two chains, with sentries at the entrance. Suddenly an angel of the Lord appeared and a light shone in the cell. He struck Peter on the side, woke him and told him to get up quickly, and the chains fell off his wrists. The angel told him to put on his clothes, sandals and cloak and follow him. Peter followed, not knowing whether it was real or a vision. They passed the first and second guards and came to the iron gate leading into the city, which opened for them by itself, and when they had walked the length of a street the angel left him. Then Peter came to himself and realised that the Lord had sent his angel to rescue him from Herod and from everything the Jewish people were hoping for. He went to the house of Mary, the mother of John called Mark, where many were praying. When he knocked at the outer gate, a servant named Rhoda came to answer; recognising Peter’s voice, she was so overjoyed that she ran back without opening it and announced that Peter was at the door. They told her she was out of her mind, and when she insisted, they said it must be his angel. Peter kept knocking, and when they opened the door they were astonished. He motioned for silence, described how the Lord had brought him out of prison, asked them to tell James and the other believers, and then left for another place. In the morning there was great commotion among the soldiers over what had become of Peter. Herod searched for him, cross-examined the guards and ordered their execution, then went down from Judea to Caesarea and stayed there. Herod had been quarrelling with the people of Tyre and Sidon; they sought an audience, secured the support of Blastus, the king’s trusted servant, and asked for peace, because they depended on the king’s country for their food. On the appointed day Herod, in his royal robes, sat on his throne and addressed the people. They shouted that this was the voice of a god, not a man. Immediately, because Herod did not give praise to God, an angel of the Lord struck him down, and he was eaten by worms and died. But the word of God continued to spread and flourish. Barnabas and Saul, having completed their mission, returned, taking with them John, also called Mark.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Praying Church, the Sovereign God, and the Grave of James

This chapter is where a theology of prayer either becomes honest or becomes cruel. The church prayed earnestly and Peter was delivered; the church, we may be sure, had prayed for James too, and James was buried. Luke gives no reason, and the Reformed tradition has been right to refuse to supply one. Prayer is not a mechanism that produces outcomes in proportion to fervency — if it were, the only conclusion available about James would be an obscene one. What prayer is, is the appointed way a dependent people bring their case to a sovereign God who answers according to his own purposes and does not explain them. And notice that Luke reports the failure of the church's expectation in the same breath as the success of its prayer: God answered a request offered by people who did not believe it would be answered, which settles for ever the question of whether the power lies in the praying or in the God prayed to.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: Rhoda's announcement was met with you are out of your mind from the very people who had been up all night asking for exactly this. Luke records it without a word of rebuke, and the deliverance stood. Now: A great many Christians pray for things while quietly not expecting them, and then feel like frauds. This chapter is unusually kind to that condition. The answer arrived and stood knocking at the gate while the intercessors argued about whether it could be him.

verseByVerse.quote: About that time Herod the king laid violent hands on some who belonged to the church. He killed James the brother of John with the sword,
verseByVerse.commentary:
About that time Herod the king laid violent hands on some who belonged to the church. He killed James the brother of John with the sword,

Meaning first. Acts 12 sets two kings side by side. Herod kills an apostle, imprisons another, and is worshipped as a god. The church has no weapon but prayer. By the end, Peter is free, Herod is dead, eaten by worms, and the word of God keeps growing. It is a picture of the whole of history: the kingdoms of this world rage against Christ’s church, and fall; the word of God endures. And over the chapter stands the other King, unseen and unnamed in most of its verses, who sends one angel to wake a prisoner and the same angel to strike down a tyrant, and whose word no throne can stop.
