About that time Herod the king laid violent hands on some who belonged to the church. This Herod is Herod Agrippa I, and the family record is worth having in front of you. His grandfather was Herod the Great, who tried to kill the child at Bethlehem. His uncle was Herod Antipas, who beheaded John the Baptist and put a robe on Jesus to mock him. Raised in Rome, a friend of the emperors Caligula and Claudius, he was made king of all Judea in AD 41, ruling the whole kingdom of his grandfather, and he worked hard to please the Jews. Three generations of one family, three attempts on the same movement, and in this chapter this Herod runs out. It is also the first persecution of the church by the state, rather than by the religious leaders.

He killed James the brother of John with the sword. Ten words, and one of the Twelve is dead, probably beheaded, around AD 44. There is no speech, no trial scene, no defence, no vision of heaven opened, no prayer for his killers, no last words of any kind. Luke gave Stephen, a man appointed to hand out food, a chapter and a half, a sermon of fifty verses, a shining face and a dying prayer. He gives James, one of the inner three who went up the mountain at the transfiguration and into the garden at Gethsemane, half a sentence. The brevity is not carelessness. It is the shape of the thing, and Luke wants the reader to feel it.

Was nobody praying for James? Four verses later the church is praying for Peter, and Peter walks free. And the question that raises has to be asked out loud rather than stepped around, because every reader asks it. Luke does not say, but it is impossible to imagine otherwise. This is the same church, in the same city, in the same weeks, and James was an apostle they had known for a decade. They will have prayed for James as earnestly as they prayed for Peter, and James was executed and Peter was delivered, and Luke offers not one syllable of explanation for the difference.

Respecting the silence. That silence must be respected rather than filled. There is no suggestion anywhere in the text that the prayers for James were less fervent, or that his faith was weaker, or that God had a lesson for him that Peter did not need. Every one of those explanations has been offered to grieving people at some point, and all of them are inventions, and this passage does not license any of them.

What can be said. What can be said is smaller and truer. First, that Jesus had told James this was coming. When he and his brother asked for the two best seats, Jesus asked whether they could drink the cup he was about to drink, and they said they could, and he said they would (Mark 10:35–39). James drank it first. John drank it slowly, over sixty years, and died old. The same question, the same answer, and two utterly different lives. Second, that Peter’s deliverance is the exception Luke records, not the rule he is teaching. Peter himself, by the church’s early and consistent tradition, was executed in the end, in Rome (compare John 21:18–19), and no angel came to that cell. The book of Acts contains three prison rescues and a great many funerals. And third, this is the point of putting them in one chapter: a book which recorded only the deliverances would be a lie, and would be useless to most of the people who read it. Luke tells us about the angel and the falling chains. He also tells us, in ten words and without comment, that the church buried an apostle that spring and God did nothing to stop it.

No replacement. And notice what the church did not do. When Judas fell, a replacement was chosen to make up the Twelve (1:21–26). When James dies, nobody is appointed in his place. Judas had abandoned his office; James finished his. The Twelve were witnesses of the risen Lord for a generation, not an office to be handed down, and their foundation, once laid, did not need relaying (Ephesians 2:20).

Why does God rescue some of his people and not others? Scripture does not give us the reasons in particular cases, and we must not invent them. But it tells us enough to trust him. Both James and Peter were equally loved, equally prayed for and equally safe in Christ. God’s purposes for each were different, and both were good: James was taken home to glory, Peter was given more years of work. Neither outcome was a failure of prayer or of love. Precious in the sight of the LORD is the death of his saints (Psalm 116:15), and nothing, not even the sword, can separate them from his love (Romans 8:35–39). When you cannot see why, you can still see who: the Father who did not spare his own Son.

In a sentence. About that time King Herod laid violent hands on some who belonged to the church, and had James the brother of John killed with the sword.

On a Tuesday. Some of God’s servants are delivered; others die. Both are in his hands. If you are grieving someone whose prayers were not answered as you hoped, do not let anyone tell you it was a lack of faith. And if you are facing trouble yourself, ask God for deliverance boldly, and resolve to be faithful either way.

For worship. James drank the cup his Lord had drunk, and was the first of the Twelve to follow him through death into glory. The Lord Jesus did not fail him when the sword fell; he received him. The King who was himself put to death by the powers of this world reigns over every martyr’s death, and none of his people dies a moment before his time or outside his love. To live is Christ, and to die is gain.
verseByVerse.note: This Herod is Herod Agrippa I, grandson of Herod the Great, who ruled Judea as king from AD 41 to 44. James is the first of the Twelve to die for his faith.

parallels.desc: the cup that I drink you will drink

verseByVerse.quote: and when he saw that it pleased the Jews, he proceeded to arrest Peter also. This was during the days of Unleavened Bread. And when he had seized him, he put him in prison, delivering him over to four squads of soldiers to guard him, intending after the Passover to bring him out to the people.
verseByVerse.commentary:
and when he saw that it pleased the Jews, he proceeded to arrest Peter also. This was during the days of Unleavened Bread. And when he had seized him, he put him in prison, delivering him over to four squads of soldiers to guard him, intending after the Passover to bring him out to the people.

And when he saw that it pleased the Jews, he proceeded to arrest Peter also. There is the motive, stated by Luke without embarrassment. Herod did not kill James out of theological conviction, and he did not arrest Peter because he had assessed the Christian claim and found it dangerous. He killed an apostle because it went down well, and moved on to a second for the same reason. A politician acting to please the crowd. It is one of the coldest sentences in the New Testament, and it describes a kind of man every generation recognises. The Jewish people had turned against the church after Stephen, and the news of Peter eating with Gentiles will hardly have helped.

This was during the days of Unleavened Bread. Agrippa had been raised among emperors and knew exactly how to play Jerusalem; he was scrupulous about the law in Judea and considerably less so elsewhere. Arresting Peter during the feast and holding the execution until after it is a piece of religious tact: he will not spoil Passover, and he will have a larger crowd afterwards. It is the same week in which Jesus had been arrested, more than ten years earlier. Peter’s story echoes his Lord’s. And it produces an irony Luke expects his reader to catch. Passover is the festival commemorating the night God brought his people out of a house of bondage, and the king is holding an apostle in one, waiting for the celebrations to finish before killing him.

Delivering him over to four squads of soldiers to guard him. Then the security, and the detail tells you something. Four squads of four soldiers, sixteen men, one squad on each of the four watches of the night. Two chained to the prisoner, two at the door, relieved every three hours. Sixteen men for one fisherman. That is an extraordinary allocation for one middle-aged Galilean, and there is a reason for it: the authorities in this city had put these men in prison before, and had come in the morning to find the cell locked, the guards at their posts and the prisoners gone (5:19–23). Herod is not being paranoid. He is being careful, on the basis of evidence. And Luke sets out the sixteen men and the two chains and the rotating watch in careful detail, so that the reader knows precisely what was in place before the chains fell off.

Intending after the Passover to bring him out to the people. For a public trial and execution, after the feast. The date was set. Everybody in the city knew it.

Should Christians expect hostility from governments? Sometimes, yes. Scripture teaches us to honour and obey the governing authorities as God’s servants for our good (Romans 13:1–7; 1 Peter 2:13–17), and many governments have been kind to the church. But it also warns that rulers may rage against the Lord and his Anointed (Psalm 2:1–3; 4:25–27), and Jesus said his followers would be brought before kings for his sake (Luke 21:12). The Christian’s posture is respectful submission in everything lawful, prayer for those in authority (1 Timothy 2:1–2), and quiet refusal when commanded to disobey God (5:29). We neither idolise the state nor fear it. We fear God.

In a sentence. When he saw that this pleased the Jews, he went on to arrest Peter as well, during the days of Unleavened Bread, and when he had seized him he put him in prison under four squads of four soldiers, intending to bring him out to the people after the Passover.

On a Tuesday. Notice when you are tempted to do something simply because it will please the people around you. Herod’s sin starts very small in all of us. Ask, before you speak or act this week, whom you are trying to please.

For worship. Herod piled up guards. God needed one angel. The King of kings looks down on the arrangements of tyrants with perfect calm, and he who sits in the heavens laughs (Psalm 2:4). Never measure your danger without measuring your God. The sixteen soldiers were real, and so were the chains, and none of them was any obstacle to him at all.
verseByVerse.note: Four squads of four soldiers took turns to guard him through the night watches.

verseByVerse.quote: So Peter was kept in prison, but earnest prayer for him was made to God by the church. Now when Herod was about to bring him out, on that very night, Peter was sleeping between two soldiers, bound with two chains, and sentries before the door were guarding the prison.
verseByVerse.commentary:
So Peter was kept in prison, but earnest prayer for him was made to God by the church. Now when Herod was about to bring him out, on that very night, Peter was sleeping between two soldiers, bound with two chains, and sentries before the door were guarding the prison.

So Peter was kept in prison, but earnest prayer for him was made to God by the church. Everything in this chapter hangs on the smallest word in the verse: but. On one side, sixteen soldiers, two chains, a locked door and a king. On the other side, a conjunction. Luke sets the entire apparatus of the state against a prayer meeting and joins them with but, and by the end of the chapter one of the two is dead and eaten by worms. Herod had soldiers; the church had prayer. Its weapon against the state was not politics or violence, but prayer.

Earnest. The word for earnest, ektenōs, is worth having. It means stretched out, extended at full reach: the word for a muscle under strain or a runner at full stride. Luke uses a form of it of Jesus praying in Gethsemane, more earnestly, in agony (Luke 22:44). It is not the vocabulary of a routine intercession got through before bed. And the praying is corporate: not merely friends of Peter, but the church, continuous, fervent and united, which had already buried James and knew perfectly well what a Herod does with an apostle.

On that very night, Peter was sleeping between two soldiers, bound with two chains. Then Luke turns to the cell, and the sentence he writes there is one of the quietly extraordinary things in Acts. The night before the execution, the last night, Peter was sleeping. God often waits until the last moment. Take in the arrangements first. He is chained by each wrist to a soldier, so that he cannot turn over without waking two men. There are sentries at the door, every human precaution. In the morning he is to be brought out to a Passover crowd and killed, and everybody in the building knows it. And he is asleep, soundly enough that in the next verse an angel has to hit him to wake him up.

Where the peace came from. Luke does not explain that, and it does not really need explaining. This is a man who had already been in a cell once and walked out, who had been told by his Lord how he would eventually die and knew it involved being old (John 21:18), and who had spent something like a dozen years discovering that the outcome was not his department. Whatever it cost him earlier in the evening, by the small hours he had put it down. In peace I will both lie down and sleep; for you alone, O LORD, make me dwell in safety (Psalm 4:8). It is the same peace, in a harder place, that a great many Christians have longed for at three in the morning over something far smaller: the peace of God, which surpasses all understanding (Philippians 4:7). And it is worth noticing where it comes from in this chapter. Not from confidence about the outcome; Peter had no reason whatever to expect an angel, and James had not got one. From somewhere else entirely: from the Lord himself, in whose hands both outcomes lay.

How can I have that kind of peace? Not by persuading yourself that everything will turn out as you want, but by entrusting yourself to the one who holds the outcome. Paul gives the pattern: do not be anxious about anything, but in everything by prayer and supplication with thanksgiving let your requests be made known to God, and the peace of God will guard your hearts (Philippians 4:6–7). Name the fear to God in so many words. Remind yourself of what is true about him: his love, his power, his promises. Remember that your life is hidden with Christ in God (Colossians 3:3), so that the worst that can happen cannot touch what matters most. Then lie down. Peace is not the absence of danger; it is the presence of the Lord in it.

In a sentence. So Peter was kept in prison, but the church was praying earnestly to God for him, and the night before Herod was to bring him out, Peter was sleeping between two soldiers, bound with two chains, with sentries guarding the door.

On a Tuesday. When you can do nothing else, pray, and pray together. Is there a prayer meeting in your church you have been missing? Go this week. And tonight, whatever you are carrying, hand it over by name before you sleep.

For worship. The church prayed, and Peter slept, and both were acts of faith in the same Lord. He neither slumbers nor sleeps, the keeper of Israel (Psalm 121:4), and so his servants can. The one who slept in the stern of a boat in the storm, because he trusted his Father, gives his peace to his people in their prison cells. Not as the world gives does he give it.

verseByVerse.quote: And behold, an angel of the Lord stood next to him, and a light shone in the cell. He struck Peter on the side and woke him, saying, "Get up quickly." And the chains fell off his hands.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And behold, an angel of the Lord stood next to him, and a light shone in the cell. He struck Peter on the side and woke him, saying, “Get up quickly.” And the chains fell off his hands.

And behold, an angel of the Lord stood next to him, and a light shone in the cell. Four things happen in one verse, and each is worth its own look. Luke does not say the angel appeared or descended: he stood next to him, as though he had been there for some time. And a light in a cell in the middle of the night, with two soldiers chained to the prisoner and two more at the door, and none of them wakes. Light in the darkness of the prison.

He struck Peter on the side and woke him. Hold on to that verb, patassō, because Luke uses it exactly twice in this chapter. Here, an angel of the Lord strikes a man to wake him. At verse 23, an angel of the Lord strikes a man and he dies. Same word, same order of being, sixteen verses apart: one blow to rouse a sleeping prisoner and one to end a king who thought he was a god. Luke never draws attention to it. He simply uses the word twice and lets the chapter do the arithmetic. There is also something almost comic in the detail, and Luke, who could have written this scene reverently, chose not to. An angel from the presence of God, in a blaze of light, in a maximum-security cell, and his first act is to give Peter a dig in the ribs, because the man is asleep and the light has not worked.

Get up quickly. Three words, no explanation. There is no time to lose.

And the chains fell off his hands. Not were unlocked, not were struck off: they fell. Whatever was holding them simply stopped holding. Luke has spent the previous verse itemising Herod’s arrangements with some care, and he now disposes of the first of them in a few words, without any suggestion of effort. Without a sound, and without waking the guards.

Free before he knows it. It is worth registering the order, because it is the order God generally works in. The chains come off first, before the guards are passed and before the gate opens, and before Peter has any idea what is happening, while he is, on his own account two verses later, still under the impression that he is dreaming. He is free before he knows it, and he is walking on the strength of somebody else’s certainty. It is a picture of the gospel itself: Christ came to proclaim liberty to the captives (Luke 4:18; Isaiah 61:1), and the sinner is set free by a power not his own, often before he understands what has been done.

Does God still send angels to rescue his people? Scripture says the angels are ministering spirits sent out to serve those who are to inherit salvation (Hebrews 1:14), and the angel of the LORD encamps around those who fear him (Psalm 34:7). So we may be sure that God uses his angels for our protection, mostly unseen and unknown. But visible angelic rescues like this one are rare even in the Bible, clustered at turning points in redemption, and we are never told to expect them, to seek them, or to pray to angels. Pray to God. How he answers, by angels, by people, by ordinary means or by none that you can see, is his business, and every answer is from his hand.

In a sentence. Suddenly an angel of the Lord stood beside him, and a light shone in the cell, and he struck Peter on the side and woke him, telling him to get up quickly, and the chains fell off his hands.

On a Tuesday. Pray for those in chains, literal and spiritual: persecuted Christians in prison today, and friends bound by addictions or despair. Name one of each before God this week, and ask him to strike the chains off.

For worship. Chains fall when God says so. No iron forged by kings can hold the one the Lord has decided to set free. And the greater chains, of sin and death and the devil, fell at the word of the risen Christ, who holds the keys of Death and Hades (Revelation 1:18). He who freed Peter from Herod has freed his people from a far worse prison, and the door he opens no one can shut.

verseByVerse.quote: And the angel said to him, "Dress yourself and put on your sandals." And he did so. And he said to him, "Wrap your cloak around you and follow me." And he went out and followed him. He did not know that what was being done by the angel was real, but thought he was seeing a vision.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And the angel said to him, “Dress yourself and put on your sandals.” And he did so. And he said to him, “Wrap your cloak around you and follow me.” And he went out and followed him. He did not know that what was being done by the angel was real, but thought he was seeing a vision.

Dress yourself and put on your sandals. Read the angel’s instructions and notice how small they are. Dress yourself. Put on your sandals. Wrap your cloak around you. Follow me. A being from the presence of God has just dissolved Roman iron, and he is now telling a middle-aged fisherman to put his shoes on.

God and the practical. It would be easy to hurry past that, and it is one of the most characteristic things in the chapter. Peter is about to walk out into a Jerusalem street in the small hours of a spring night with nowhere to go, and somebody has thought about the cold. The same providence that stopped the chains working also wanted him properly dressed. There is no suggestion anywhere in Scripture that God finds the practical beneath him; the risen Christ cooked breakfast on a beach, and an angel of the Lord in this verse is concerned about footwear. And notice the division of labour. God does the impossible, the chains; he leaves Peter to do the possible, the sandals.

Wrap your cloak around you and follow me. Follow me: the very words Jesus had said to Peter by the lake, at the beginning and again at the end (Mark 1:17; John 21:19). Peter has been following that voice for years, and he follows now.

He did not know that what was being done by the angel was real, but thought he was seeing a vision. Then the sentence that makes this the strangest rescue in the book. Peter is not being obtuse. He had every reason for the mistake: two chapters ago he had gone into a trance on a roof and seen something let down out of heaven (10:10). Visions were a category he now had. So when a light fills a cell and the chains come off and a figure tells him to get dressed, he assumes it is happening in his head, goes along with it, and walks out of a maximum-security prison in a state of complete confusion. It was too good to be true.

Nobody believes it. That is the thread running through this entire chapter, and it is worth watching for. Peter does not believe what God is doing while God is doing it. In a few verses the church will not believe it either, and will tell a servant girl she is raving. The angel is real, the chains are on the floor, the gate is about to open by itself, and every single human being involved is either asleep, dreaming, or arguing. God did it anyway. That is the comfort of the passage, and it is not a small one: the deliverance was not waiting on anybody’s grasp of what was happening.

Does God only act when we have enough faith? No. Faith is the hand that receives God’s gifts, and Scripture calls us to pray believing (James 1:6). But God is not bound to the size of our faith; he answers out of his own goodness. Here nobody, not Peter, not the church, believed the rescue was happening, and it happened. The man who cried, I believe; help my unbelief, received what he asked (Mark 9:24). So do not despair because your faith is weak. Bring the weak faith to a strong Saviour, and let him do far more abundantly than all that you ask or think.

In a sentence. The angel told him to dress and put on his sandals, and then to wrap his cloak around him and follow, and Peter went out and followed him, not realising that what the angel was doing was real, but thinking he was seeing a vision.

On a Tuesday. God’s rescue sometimes seems too good to be real. Follow anyway. And do the small practical thing in front of you: the sandals, the phone call, the form, the next step. God does not despise it, and very often it is the part he has left for you.

For worship. The God who opens prisons also cares about sandals. His greatness does not make him remote from small things; it makes nothing too small for his care. The hairs of your head are numbered. The same Lord who said to Peter by the lake, follow me, led him out through the guards in the dark, and he leads all his people, step by step, into a freedom they can barely believe is real.

verseByVerse.quote: When they had passed the first and the second guard, they came to the iron gate leading into the city. It opened for them of its own accord, and they went out and went along one street, and immediately the angel left him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
When they had passed the first and the second guard, they came to the iron gate leading into the city. It opened for them of its own accord, and they went out and went along one street, and immediately the angel left him.

When they had passed the first and the second guard. Luke walks the reader out of the prison in the order Peter walked it, and dismantles Herod’s arrangements one at a time. The chains went in the previous verse. Now two guard posts, passed unseen and without explanation. Luke does not say the soldiers were blinded or asleep or struck dumb; he simply reports that two guard posts were passed and says nothing about how.

They came to the iron gate leading into the city. It opened for them of its own accord. Then the last obstacle, and it is a serious one. This is the outer door of the fortress, the barrier between the prison and the street, and it is the one thing in the building that no amount of quiet walking gets you through. The Greek word for of its own accord, automatē, is the one our word automatic comes from, and the New Testament uses it only twice: here, and of the earth in the parable that produces a crop by itself (Mark 4:28). Nobody touched it. There is no lock picked and no guard overpowered; the gate simply behaves as though it had been asked. Every barrier gave way.

And they went out and went along one street, and immediately the angel left him. And then the detail that is easy to miss and is the most instructive thing in the verse. One street. The angel stays exactly as far as is necessary and not a step further, and then he is gone: no farewell, no instructions, no accompaniment to a safe house, no explanation of what to do next. Peter is standing alone in the dark in a city where a king wants him dead, with his cloak on, entirely free and entirely on his own.

Exact help. That is worth having in mind by anybody who has watched God do something remarkable and then found the extraordinary help withdrawn while the situation was still difficult. The angel was not sent to look after Peter. He was sent to get him through a gate, and the moment the gate was behind them the errand was finished. God is not sparing with his help; he is exact with it. He gives what the moment requires, and it very often stops at the point where ordinary walking will do. God does not do for us what we can do ourselves.

Why does God sometimes seem to leave us just when we need him? He does not leave us, though his extraordinary help may be withdrawn. The angel left Peter, but the Lord did not: Peter’s first thought in the next verse is that the Lord had rescued him, and his feet took him straight to the house where the church was praying. God often gives remarkable help to bring us through a crisis and then returns us to the ordinary means: our own legs, our own judgment, the fellowship of other believers. That is not abandonment. It is the Father treating us as sons who can walk. He has promised, I will never leave you nor forsake you (Hebrews 13:5).

In a sentence. When they had passed the first and second guards, they came to the iron gate leading into the city, which opened for them by itself, and they went out and along one street, and at once the angel left him.

On a Tuesday. If God has brought you through something remarkable and now seems quieter, do not panic. Walk the next street. Go to the people of God, as Peter did, and keep doing the ordinary things faithfully.

For worship. No gate is too strong for God. He is the one who opens and no one will shut, who shuts and no one opens (Revelation 3:7). The iron gate of Herod’s prison swung open at his word, and so did the far heavier gate of the tomb on the first Easter morning. Our God is the Lord of every door, and he goes before his people and makes the way.

verseByVerse.quote: When Peter came to himself, he said, "Now I am sure that the Lord has sent his angel and rescued me from the hand of Herod and from all that the Jewish people were expecting." When he realized this, he went to the house of Mary, the mother of John whose other name was Mark, where many were gathered together and were praying.
verseByVerse.commentary:
When Peter came to himself, he said, “Now I am sure that the Lord has sent his angel and rescued me from the hand of Herod and from all that the Jewish people were expecting.” When he realized this, he went to the house of Mary, the mother of John whose other name was Mark, where many were gathered together and were praying.

When Peter came to himself. In the cool night air, he realises it is real. The phrase is a close echo of the one Luke used of a young man sitting among pigs in a far country who suddenly saw his situation for what it was (Luke 15:17). It means the moment the fog clears. Peter has been moving through this entire episode convinced he was dreaming, and standing in an empty street with the prison behind him he understands, all at once, that it happened.

Now I am sure that the Lord has sent his angel and rescued me from the hand of Herod. Now I am sure is an admission that until this moment he was not. And notice how he describes what has occurred. He does not say he escaped. He does not describe his own part in it, because he did not have one; he was asleep for the beginning and confused for the rest. The whole sentence has one subject, and it is not Peter. He gives all the credit to the Lord.

And from all that the Jewish people were expecting. They had expected an execution, and a festival crowd had been promised one. The Lord had other plans.

He went to the house of Mary, the mother of John whose other name was Mark. Then he goes to a house, and Luke tells us whose. Several things are packed into that. Mary owns a house substantial enough to have a gateway and a servant, and she is named in her own right rather than as somebody’s wife, which suggests a widow of means who had put her property at the church’s disposal. A great many early congregations met in rooms belonging to women like her. Many have thought this is the same house with the upper room in it, where the Last Supper was held and the hundred and twenty waited for Pentecost; it cannot be proved, and it is a reasonable guess. And her son is John Mark, a cousin of Barnabas (Colossians 4:10), who will join the first missionary journey in the last verse of this chapter, will desert it, will cause the sharpest quarrel in the New Testament, and will end up writing a Gospel. Church tradition says Mark wrote it from Peter’s preaching, and Peter calls him my son (1 Peter 5:13).

Where many were gathered together and were praying. What matters most is what was happening in that house at the time. It is the middle of the night in Passover week. Peter is under sentence and James is freshly buried, and being known to associate with either of them is demonstrably dangerous. And the church is in a house in the dark, in numbers, still praying, which took nerve, and which is the reason Peter knew exactly which door to knock on.

In a sentence. When Peter came to himself, he said he now knew for sure that the Lord had sent his angel and rescued him from Herod’s hand and from all the Jewish people were expecting, and realising this, he went to the house of Mary, the mother of John called Mark, where many were gathered together praying.

On a Tuesday. Open your home for prayer. Great things happen in houses where people pray. If you have a room and a table, offer them to your church for a prayer meeting or a small group, and be the Mary of your street.

For worship. Now I am sure that the Lord has rescued me. Every Christian will one day say that sentence with the fog cleared for ever, standing in the light of the eternal city with every prison behind him. Our salvation from first to last is the Lord’s doing: he sent, he struck the chains, he opened the gate, he brought us out. And he brings his rescued people home to the household of faith, where the church is praying.
verseByVerse.note: John Mark later wrote the Gospel of Mark; he was a cousin of Barnabas. His mother’s house was large enough to hold a gathering.

parallels.desc: God sent his angel

verseByVerse.quote: And when he knocked at the door of the gateway, a servant girl named Rhoda came to answer. Recognizing Peter's voice, in her joy she did not open the gate but ran in and reported that Peter was standing at the gate.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And when he knocked at the door of the gateway, a servant girl named Rhoda came to answer. Recognizing Peter’s voice, in her joy she did not open the gate but ran in and reported that Peter was standing at the gate.

And when he knocked at the door of the gateway, a servant girl named Rhoda came to answer. Luke names her. That is the first thing to notice about this scene, and it is not a small thing. He does not give us the names of the sixteen soldiers, or of the two men chained to Peter, or of most of the church praying in that room. He gives us the name of a slave girl who answered a door. Rhoda means rose. Somebody remembered it, and told him, and it has been read aloud in churches for two thousand years: a servant of no standing whatever in a house she did not own, whose one recorded action was to make a mistake. Luke remembered small people.

Recognizing Peter’s voice. She knew it through a closed door, without seeing him, at night. That tells you she had heard him a great deal: that a household slave had been in the room often enough while the apostle taught to know his voice from anyone else’s. The church that met in Mary’s house evidently did not send the staff out.

In her joy she did not open the gate. It is the most human sentence in the book of Acts and one of the very few in Scripture that is straightforwardly funny. She is so pleased that she forgets the one thing she has actually been sent to do. The most wanted man in Jerusalem, fresh out of a maximum-security cell in the middle of the night, with a search about to start at dawn, is left standing in the street outside a locked gate, because the girl who found him was too happy to let him in. An angel opened the iron gate; a joyful girl kept the wooden one shut.

But ran in and reported that Peter was standing at the gate. Luke reports it with obvious affection and not a word of criticism. Nobody in the passage tells Rhoda off, and the narrative does not treat her as the failure of the scene; the people who actually come off badly in the next verse are the ones who were praying. And there is a familiar pattern here. The first witness of his release, like the women at the empty tomb, was a woman, and she was not believed (Luke 24:10–11).

The one who believed and was glad. There is something worth keeping in her. Joy that forgets the practical step is a real thing, and it is not the worst fault a person can have. She is the only one in the entire chapter who both believed it was Peter and was glad (the prayer meeting managed neither), and her error was one of excitement. Of all the things to get wrong on the night God answered, hers is the one to be caught doing.

Does God notice people as ordinary as Rhoda? He notices nobody else. Every person in God’s story is ordinary until he notices them, and Scripture is full of servants, widows, children and slaves whom the world never named and God did. Rhoda was a slave in someone else’s house, and her name is in the Bible. If you feel invisible in your church or in your life, remember that the Lord who numbered the hairs on Peter’s head knew the name of the girl who answered his door. Your faithfulness in small places is seen, and your joy in his works delights him.

In a sentence. When he knocked at the door of the gateway, a servant girl named Rhoda came to answer, and recognising Peter’s voice she was so overjoyed that instead of opening the gate she ran in and reported that Peter was standing at the gate.

On a Tuesday. When God answers a prayer, let yourself be glad, out loud and unembarrassed, and tell someone. And notice the Rhodas of your church, the people who serve unseen, and learn their names.

For worship. Joy at answered prayer can make us forget our heads, and God smiles at it. The Lord whose own heart rejoices over his people with gladness (Zephaniah 3:17) gave a slave girl the first joy of Peter’s deliverance. He loves to give his best news to the least, and to let the humble be glad first.
verseByVerse.note: Rhoda means “rose.”

verseByVerse.quote: They said to her, "You are out of your mind." But she kept insisting that it was so, and they kept saying, "It is his angel!" But Peter continued knocking, and when they opened, they saw him and were amazed.
verseByVerse.commentary:
They said to her, “You are out of your mind.” But she kept insisting that it was so, and they kept saying, “It is his angel!” But Peter continued knocking, and when they opened, they saw him and were amazed.

You are out of your mind. That is what they said to her, and it is what you say to somebody who is not making sense. And it is said by a room full of people who have spent the night asking God for precisely the thing the girl has just announced. They were praying for Peter, and when the answer came, they did not believe it. Like us.

But she kept insisting that it was so. Then it gets worse, and Luke’s verbs are merciless. She kept insisting: she would not be put down, and stood her ground against a room of her betters. And they kept saying, over and over: it is his angel.

It is his angel! That was a current belief, and Luke reports it without endorsing it: the idea that a person had a guardian spirit which might appear looking and sounding like him, and which might turn up at the moment of a death. So the prayer meeting has produced, on the spot, a theological explanation for why the answer to their prayers cannot be the answer to their prayers. It is easier to believe in a spectral double than in a released prisoner.

Do believers have guardian angels? Scripture says angels serve those who are to inherit salvation (Hebrews 1:14), and Jesus says of his little ones that in heaven their angels always see the face of my Father (Matthew 18:10). But no text clearly teaches that each person has one assigned angel, and Luke records the disciples’ belief without endorsing it. We may be sure that God sends his angels for his people, and we are never to pray to them.

But Peter continued knocking. And while the argument continues, and this is the detail Luke will not let go of, Peter is still out there. The church is inside debating angels, and the apostle they are praying for is standing in the street in the dark, persistent and probably nervous, in a city about to start hunting for him, knocking, and knocking, and knocking.

Not casual people. It would be very easy to be contemptuous about this and it would be a mistake, because these were not casual people. They had buried James. They were meeting at night, in numbers, during Passover week, at genuine risk, to pray for a condemned man. Whatever was wrong with their faith, it was not that they could not be bothered. Their problem is the one most Christians have and very few will admit to: they prayed without expecting. The asking was sincere and the anticipation was absent, and the two had been running on separate tracks for so long that when the answer knocked they had a category for everything except that.

And when they opened, they saw him and were amazed. And here is the thing to take from the passage, which is far kinder than the rebuke this scene usually gets turned into. God answered anyway. The deliverance did not wait on the quality of their expectation, was not proportioned to their confidence, and was not withdrawn when they told the messenger she was mad. Peter was already out before the debate began. Their faith was real but weak, and God answered their prayers beyond their faith, as he is able to do far more abundantly than all that we ask or think (Ephesians 3:20). Anyone who has prayed for years about something while privately suspecting nothing will come of it, and has felt a fraud for it, should notice what this chapter does with such people. It does not shame them. It puts the answer on their doorstep and lets them be amazed.

Is it wrong to pray when I do not really expect an answer? It is far better to pray weakly than not to pray at all, and this church is proof that God hears such prayers. But we should ask him to grow our expectation, because he invites us to come boldly (Hebrews 4:16). One practical help is to keep a record of what you ask and how God answers, so that your memory of his faithfulness grows. Another is to pray Scripture’s promises back to him, so that your expectation rests on what he has said rather than on how you feel. Expectation is not presumption: it is trusting that God hears and will answer in his way and time, even if the answer is not the one you pictured.

In a sentence. They told her she was out of her mind, but she kept insisting, so they said it must be his angel, while Peter went on knocking, and when they opened the door, they saw him and were amazed.

On a Tuesday. Pray expecting answers. Write down one thing you are asking God for this week, and look back at it in a month. And when the answer comes, open the door.

For worship. God answers the prayers of people who do not quite believe he will. He is better than our faith, kinder than our expectations, and greater than our prayers. The church prayed for Peter and argued with the answer, and God gave them Peter anyway, standing on the doorstep in the dark. That is the God we pray to: the Father who gives good things to those who ask him, and gives them more generously than we ever dared to hope.
verseByVerse.note: Many Jews believed each person had a guardian angel.

verseByVerse.quote: But motioning to them with his hand to be silent, he described to them how the Lord had brought him out of the prison. And he said, "Tell these things to James and to the brothers." Then he departed and went to another place. Now when day came, there was no little disturbance among the soldiers over what had become of Peter.
verseByVerse.commentary:
But motioning to them with his hand to be silent, he described to them how the Lord had brought him out of the prison. And he said, “Tell these things to James and to the brothers.” Then he departed and went to another place. Now when day came, there was no little disturbance among the soldiers over what had become of Peter.

But motioning to them with his hand to be silent. The room has erupted, and a fugitive standing in a courtyard in the dead of night has to quieten a houseful of astonished people before somebody in the street hears them.

He described to them how the Lord had brought him out of the prison. The subject of that sentence is the point of it. He does not tell them how he got out. He tells them what the Lord did, which is the only version of the story he is in a position to give, since he slept through the start of it and thought the rest was a dream. Again, the Lord did it.

Tell these things to James and to the brothers. This is not the James who was killed fifteen verses ago; that one is dead. This is James the Lord’s brother, the man who did not believe in Jesus during his ministry (John 7:5), who saw the risen Lord (1 Corinthians 15:7), and who wrote the letter of James. He is now, without any explanation from Luke, the man you send word to when something happens in Jerusalem. Peter’s instruction is the quiet marker of a change of leadership. From here on it is James who presides at the council and James to whom Paul reports (15:13; 21:18; Galatians 1:19; 2:9).

Then he departed and went to another place. And then eight words that shut a door on half the book. Luke does not say where, perhaps to protect him; he never does. Peter appears once more in Acts, at the council in chapter 15, and we glimpse him later in Antioch (Galatians 2:11) and perhaps in Corinth (1 Corinthians 1:12). After that he leaves the narrative of Acts entirely: no death scene, no farewell, no account of the years in which he wrote two letters and, by every early tradition, died in Rome. The man who has been the leading figure for eleven chapters walks off into an unnamed place before dawn, and Luke’s spotlight swings away and follows somebody else. It is a strange piece of authorship and it is deliberate. This book is not the story of Peter. From chapter 13 it will not even be mainly the story of Jerusalem. It is the story of the word of the Lord.

Where Christians differ: did Peter go to Rome? Some Roman Catholic tradition says Peter went to Rome at this point and was bishop there for twenty-five years. Verdict: there is no evidence that Peter went to Rome now; he is in Jerusalem a few years later (15:7). Paul’s letter to the Romans, written around AD 57, greets many people in Rome but never mentions Peter. Peter probably did go to Rome late in his life and died there under Nero, as early tradition says. But the New Testament never presents him as bishop of Rome or head of the church.

Now when day came, there was no little disturbance among the soldiers over what had become of Peter. Then daylight, and Luke’s driest sentence. No little disturbance is understatement: he means there was uproar. Sixteen men, a locked cell, an untouched door, two chains lying on the floor, and a prisoner due before the king in a few hours.

Why tell the story to the church? Because what the Lord does for one of his people belongs to all of them. Peter could have slipped away without a word; instead, at real risk, he stopped to tell the praying church what God had done and to send word to James and the brothers. Testimony strengthens faith, answers prayer publicly, and gives God the glory. The Psalms are full of it: come and hear, all you who fear God, and I will tell what he has done for my soul (Psalm 66:16). When God answers your prayers, tell the people who were praying with you. It is part of the answer.

In a sentence. Peter motioned to them with his hand to be quiet, described how the Lord had brought him out of prison, told them to report this to James and the brothers, and then left and went to another place; and when day came there was great commotion among the soldiers about what had become of Peter.

On a Tuesday. Tell others what the Lord has done for you. Think of one answered prayer from the past year and tell it to someone this week, especially someone who prayed with you about it.

For worship. The Lord brought him out. Peter vanishes from the story, but the Lord who rescued him does not. Leaders come and go; apostles walk off into unnamed places; even the greatest servants of Christ are only servants. The church does not rest on Peter. It rests on the Rock he confessed, Christ the Son of the living God, who reigns over every change of leadership and builds his church through them all.
verseByVerse.note: This James is the Lord’s brother, who became leader of the Jerusalem church.

verseByVerse.quote: And after Herod searched for him and did not find him, he examined the sentries and ordered that they should be put to death. Then he went down from Judea to Caesarea and spent time there.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And after Herod searched for him and did not find him, he examined the sentries and ordered that they should be put to death. Then he went down from Judea to Caesarea and spent time there.

And after Herod searched for him and did not find him. Herod could not find Peter. God hides his own. The king who had controlled every movement of the prisoner the night before cannot locate him in his own capital the next morning.

He examined the sentries and ordered that they should be put to death. This verse has a shadow in it that ought not to be hurried past, because Luke does not hurry past it and neither should a reader. Under Roman practice a guard was answerable for his prisoner: a man who lost one could expect the penalty the prisoner would have received (16:27; 27:42). So Herod, having failed to find Peter, does the thing the system provided for, and men die because an angel opened a gate.

The shadow in the verse. Luke reports it in half a sentence and offers no comment, and it would be dishonest to supply the comfort he withholds. Peter’s deliverance cost other men their lives. That is in the text, and a reading of this chapter which celebrates the falling chains and skips verse 19 has read half of it. Two things can be said, and neither is a full resolution. The first is where the moral weight actually sits. God opened a door; Herod gave the order. The king who had already killed an apostle because it was popular now executes his own soldiers to cover an embarrassment, and Luke has arranged this chapter so that four verses later God deals with him. The blood of those guards is on the account of the man struck down at Caesarea in the twenty-third verse. This is the kind of king he was. The second is that this is what the world is like, and Scripture will not pretend otherwise. Deliverances happen inside a fallen system, and the system exacts a price somewhere. The Bible reports it rather than tidying it, which is one of the reasons it can be trusted about the rest. A book written merely to encourage the church would have ended verse 19 after the words did not find him.

Then he went down from Judea to Caesarea and spent time there. And then the last clause, which reads like an administrative detail and is in fact the end of a man. Herod leaves Jerusalem for his coastal capital, and never comes back. His final recorded act in the holy city, the place where he had been so careful to appear devout, was to have his own men executed for something none of them had done.

Was God unjust to let the guards die? No. God did not kill the guards; Herod did, and Herod answered for it. God is under no obligation to prevent every evil act of wicked men, and he often allows them to show what they are before he judges them. His ways in such things are often hidden from us, and Scripture does not invite us to explain them all. But it assures us that the Judge of all the earth will do what is just (Genesis 18:25), that no innocent blood is forgotten by him, and that every tyrant will give account. The cross itself is the ultimate proof: the most unjust act in history, done by wicked men, was the means by which God saved the world, and the men who did it will answer to him.

In a sentence. When Herod had searched for him and could not find him, he cross-examined the guards and ordered them to be executed, then went down from Judea to Caesarea and stayed there.

On a Tuesday. Cruel power destroys even its own servants. Pray for those who live under such rulers today, and for those who serve them in fear. And pray for rulers themselves, that they would come to fear God before it is too late.

For worship. The God who hides his own also sees everything done in the dark by those who hate them. He is not mocked. The blood of James and the blood of sixteen soldiers cry out to him, and he hears. And the blood of his own Son speaks a better word than all of them, offering pardon even to the violent, while the unrepentant tyrant runs out of time.
verseByVerse.note: Under Roman practice a guard who let a prisoner escape could suffer the prisoner’s penalty.

verseByVerse.quote: Now Herod was angry with the people of Tyre and Sidon, and they came to him with one accord, and having persuaded Blastus, the king's chamberlain, they asked for peace, because their country depended on the king's country for food. On an appointed day Herod put on his royal robes, took his seat upon the throne, and delivered an oration to them.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Now Herod was angry with the people of Tyre and Sidon, and they came to him with one accord, and having persuaded Blastus, the king’s chamberlain, they asked for peace, because their country depended on the king’s country for food. On an appointed day Herod put on his royal robes, took his seat upon the throne, and delivered an oration to them.

Now Herod was angry with the people of Tyre and Sidon. Luke turns to a piece of provincial diplomacy, and the reason he includes it becomes apparent two verses later. Tyre and Sidon are the two Phoenician ports up the coast. The quarrel itself is not explained, and we do not know why he was angry, but the leverage is plain: their country depended on the king’s country for food. Those cities sat on a narrow strip between mountains and sea with almost no farmland, and had imported their grain from the fields of Galilee since Solomon’s day (1 Kings 5:11; Ezekiel 27:17). Herod could not conquer them. He could starve them, and they knew it.

Having persuaded Blastus, the king’s chamberlain. So they come to terms, and Luke records how it was arranged. The chamberlain was the man in charge of the king’s private rooms, controlling access to the royal bedchamber and therefore to the king, and persuaded is doing a certain amount of work; men in that position were not usually persuaded by argument alone. Probably a bribe. Two ancient cities had to win over a courtier, very possibly with money, in order to get permission to eat.

On an appointed day Herod put on his royal robes, took his seat upon the throne, and delivered an oration to them. Then the day itself: power on display. It is worth knowing that we have a second account of this occasion from outside the New Testament. The Jewish historian Josephus, writing for a Roman audience some fifty years later and with no interest whatever in defending Luke, describes Agrippa at Caesarea at games held in honour of the emperor, coming into the theatre at daybreak in a robe woven entirely of silver, so that when the early sun struck it the garment blazed and the onlookers were dazzled, and then flatterers in the crowd calling out to him as a god. He records that the king was seized almost at once with violent pain in his belly, was carried out, and died after five days.

Two independent witnesses. Two writers, working independently and for different readerships, describe the same king, in the same city, on the same public occasion, in the same royal display, receiving the same acclamation and dying of the same sudden illness. Luke says an angel of the Lord struck him and Josephus does not, which is exactly the difference one would expect between the two. On everything a historian can check, they agree.

Why does it matter that Josephus confirms Luke? Because the Christian faith rests on things that really happened, not on myths or private visions. Luke told Theophilus he had written so that he might have certainty concerning the things he had been taught (Luke 1:4), and he wrote as a historian, naming rulers, cities and dates that could be checked. Again and again, outside sources and archaeology have confirmed his accuracy in detail. That does not prove every miracle, but it shows that Luke was a careful and truthful witness, and it gives good reason to trust him when he tells us what only the eyewitnesses saw: an empty tomb, an angel in a cell, and a church that turned the world upside down.

In a sentence. Herod was angry with the people of Tyre and Sidon, and they came to him together, and having won over Blastus, the king’s chamberlain, they asked for peace, because their country depended on the king’s country for food, and on an appointed day Herod put on his royal robes, took his seat on the throne and delivered a speech to them.

On a Tuesday. Notice how much of your life depends on things you cannot control: food, health, employment, the decisions of powerful people. Thank God this week for daily bread, and remember that every earthly supply comes ultimately from his hand, not from any king’s.

For worship. The world’s power dazzles for a moment. Herod’s silver robe blazed in the morning sun, and within a week he was in the grave. Christ’s glory is for ever. His face shines like the sun in its strength, his garments are white as light, and his throne is established for ever and ever. The kingdoms of this world are lit by borrowed light. The Lamb is the lamp of the city of God.
verseByVerse.note: Tyre and Sidon, on the coast, depended on Galilee’s farmland for grain.

verseByVerse.quote: And the people were shouting, "The voice of a god, and not of a man!" Immediately an angel of the Lord struck him down, because he did not give God the glory, and he was eaten by worms and breathed his last.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And the people were shouting, “The voice of a god, and not of a man!” Immediately an angel of the Lord struck him down, because he did not give God the glory, and he was eaten by worms and breathed his last.

The voice of a god, and not of a man! The crowd kept shouting it. It is flattery from men who had just won over a courtier and needed the grain to keep coming, and Herod knew exactly what it was worth. Ancient rulers were often hailed as gods. That is not the point. The point is what he did with it, which was nothing. He did not correct it.

Two scenes in Caesarea. Set that beside a scene two chapters earlier in this same city of Caesarea. A Roman centurion fell at Peter’s feet, out of genuine reverence rather than calculation, and Peter reached down and pulled him up and said, Stand up; I too am a man (10:26). Same town, same kind of moment, and the two men in it do opposite things. Luke has put them a few pages apart on purpose, and only one of them is alive at the end of this chapter. Paul and Barnabas will do as Peter did at Lystra (14:14–15).

Immediately an angel of the Lord struck him down. And there is the verb again, the one Luke used at verse 7, when an angel of the Lord struck Peter on the side to wake him. Two blows in one chapter from the same order of being: one to rouse a prisoner who was about to die, and one to end a king who thought he was a god. Luke never remarks on it. He simply uses the word twice.

Because he did not give God the glory. Now the reason given, and it is not the one a reader expects. Not because he executed James. Not because he imprisoned Peter, or killed his own guards, or played politics with people’s lives to keep a crowd happy. All of that stands on the record, and none of it is cited. The charge God brings against Herod Agrippa is that a man let himself be called divine and did not hand the honour back. I am the LORD; that is my name; my glory I give to no other (Isaiah 42:8).

The sin underneath the others. That is worth sitting with, because it rearranges most people’s instinctive scale of sins. The murders were real and will be dealt with. But the thing named in the indictment is the theft of something that belongs to God alone, which is, when you think about it, the sin underneath all the other ones. A man who is willing to be worshipped will do anything at all to the people underneath him.

And he was eaten by worms and breathed his last. Josephus, independently, records five days of agonising pain in his belly before his death in AD 44. Luke gives it a single sentence. The grandson of Herod the Great, in silver, on a platform, with a crowd calling him a god, and within the week a burial. The man who was hailed as a god was eaten by worms. Pride goes before destruction (Proverbs 16:18), as Nebuchadnezzar learned when he boasted on his palace roof and was driven out to eat grass like an ox until he acknowledged that the Most High rules (Daniel 4:30–37).

What it does not mean. One guard is needed, and it matters. This is not a template for reading illness or sudden death as divine judgment, and it has been misused that way with great cruelty. Luke tells us the reason here because it was disclosed to him. In almost every other case nobody has been told anything, and the man who claims to know why somebody is ill has appointed himself to a bench he has not been called to. Jesus himself warned against the assumption that those who suffer disaster were worse sinners than others (Luke 13:1–5).

How do I give God the glory when I am praised? Receive the kindness graciously, without false modesty, and then turn it quickly toward God, in your heart and, where it is fitting, in your words. You might say, thank you, God has been very kind, or, I am grateful it helped. More important is what happens inside: remind yourself that every gift you have was given (1 Corinthians 4:7), and refuse to feed on the praise in private afterwards. Herod’s danger was not that people admired him but that he kept what belonged to God. The test is whether, when praised, you feel larger, or more grateful.

In a sentence. The people kept shouting, “The voice of a god, and not of a man!” and at once an angel of the Lord struck him down because he did not give God the glory, and he was eaten by worms and died.

On a Tuesday. When praised, give God the glory. Quickly. And watch the subtler forms of Herod’s sin: the secret pleasure in being thought indispensable, the irritation when someone else gets the credit. Bring them to God as soon as you notice them.

For worship. To God alone belongs the glory. He will not share it with kings in silver robes, nor with apostles, nor with angels, nor with us. And yet the eternal Son, who alone deserves the worship Herod stole, humbled himself to the death of the cross, and therefore God has highly exalted him. The crowd at Caesarea gave a man the honour due to God. One day every tongue will give it to the right Man: Jesus Christ is Lord, to the glory of God the Father.
verseByVerse.note: The historian Josephus also records Agrippa’s sudden death at Caesarea after being hailed as a god, in AD 44.

parallels.desc: my glory I give to no other

verseByVerse.quote: But the word of God increased and multiplied. And Barnabas and Saul returned from Jerusalem when they had completed their service, bringing with them John, whose other name was Mark.
verseByVerse.commentary:
But the word of God increased and multiplied. And Barnabas and Saul returned from Jerusalem when they had completed their service, bringing with them John, whose other name was Mark.

But the word of God increased and multiplied. Put that sentence immediately after the one before it and feel the size of the contrast. A king in cloth of silver, hailed as divine by two cities, is dead and buried. And the next thing Luke writes is a sentence about a message spreading, with a but in front of it, as though the death of a king were the sort of thing that might have been expected to slow it down and did not. This is the point of the whole chapter. Herod killed, imprisoned, persecuted, and was worshipped; now he is dead. The word of God grows.

The language of living things. The verbs are the ones used of living things: increased and multiplied, the language Genesis uses of creatures filling the earth (Genesis 1:22). Luke has used this kind of progress report before, at the end of the Jerusalem years (6:7) and after the conversion of Saul (9:31), and each time it marks the close of a movement and the opening of the next. Here it is doing something more pointed. To most readers today Herod Agrippa is known for one thing: he appears in this chapter. The movement he set out to destroy wrote him into its records as an illustration. The grass withers, the flower falls, but the word of our God will stand for ever (Isaiah 40:8; 1 Peter 1:24–25).

And Barnabas and Saul returned from Jerusalem when they had completed their service. Then the last verse, which is housekeeping and is also the assembling of a team. The famine money from Antioch has been delivered (11:29–30), and the two of them turn for home. Some manuscripts read to Jerusalem, but from Jerusalem, back to Antioch, fits the story.

Bringing with them John, whose other name was Mark. He is Mary’s son, and Mary’s house is where the prayer meeting was. Which means that on the night Rhoda left Peter standing at the gate, this young man was very likely in that house. He had watched the church pray all night for a man, and had watched it refuse to believe the man was at the door.

The boy in the luggage. He is now going to Antioch, and from Antioch he will go out on the first missionary journey (13:5), and at Pamphylia he will turn back and go home (13:13), which will cause the sharpest quarrel recorded between two Christians in the New Testament and split Paul from Barnabas (15:37–39). And years later Paul will write from a prison cell asking for him, because he is useful to him for ministry (2 Timothy 4:11). And somewhere in those years, by the church’s earliest tradition, he wrote down the recollections of Peter, and the church has been reading them as the Gospel of Mark ever since. All of which is in front of a young man who, at the end of this chapter, is simply a name added to somebody else’s luggage. Luke closes an account of an executed apostle, a miraculous deliverance and the death of a king by mentioning, almost in passing, a young man going along with his cousin, and it turns out to be one of the most consequential sentences in the paragraph.

If a Christian has failed badly, can God still use him? Mark is the answer. He deserted the mission, became the cause of a painful split, and might easily have been written off for good. Barnabas did not write him off, and in the end neither did Paul, who came to count him useful. And God used him to write the earliest Gospel. Failure is not the end of usefulness for a believer who repents and keeps going. The same is true of Peter, who denied his Lord and was restored to feed his sheep. If you have failed, confess it, receive Christ’s forgiveness, accept the consequences humbly, and get back to work. The Lord is not finished with you.

In a sentence. But the word of God kept increasing and spreading, and Barnabas and Saul returned from Jerusalem when they had finished their service, bringing with them John, also called Mark.

On a Tuesday. When the news is full of powerful people doing terrible things, read Acts 12 again, and remember who has the last word. Then do something small for the word of God this week: give to a missionary, invite a friend to church, teach a child a verse. That is the work that outlasts every king.

For worship. Tyrants die, but the word of God grows. Herod is dust, and the gospel he tried to silence has gone to the ends of the earth and is still increasing and multiplying in every nation. The kingdom of our Lord is not shaken by the rage of rulers or the death of apostles. Christ reigns, and he must reign until he has put all his enemies under his feet. Take heart. The word of the Lord endures for ever, and so does every soul it has made alive.

12.theology: Providence, Prayer, and the Sovereignty of God over Kings. Acts 12 is a meditation on what it means to live under the providence of a God who governs kings and councils, who opens prison gates and strikes down tyrants, and who is not moved by the calculations of the powerful. James dies; Peter lives — both by divine appointment. The church prays; the answer comes — and still takes them by surprise. Herod grasps at divine honour; he is given worms and silence. This is the world the New Testament describes: not a world where God occasionally intervenes, but a world where God is always governing — every chain, every gate, every angel, every worm. The appropriate response is not to explain his ways, but to pray, to trust, and to keep speaking the Word that outlasts every king.
12.examples:
Then: A church under a murderous king, with no political recourse, no legal protection, and no army — meeting in a house and praying with everything they had. Their prayers opened a prison door a few streets from where they sat. They did not know it would happen that way. They prayed because there was nothing else to do, and because the God they prayed to had not changed.

Now: The church in every hostile political environment must learn the same calculus: Herod has soldiers; God has angels. Herod has chains; God has the Word. The appropriate response to power arrayed against the gospel is not despair and not political calculation — it is earnest, persistent, expectant prayer to the Sovereign Lord who made heaven and earth. And then, when the knock comes at the door, to open it.

13.title: The First Missionary Journey Begins
13.text: <sup>1</sup>Now there were in the church at Antioch prophets and teachers, Barnabas, Simeon who was called Niger, Lucius of Cyrene, Manaen a lifelong friend of Herod the tetrarch, and Saul. <sup>2</sup>While they were worshiping the Lord and fasting, the Holy Spirit said, “Set apart for me Barnabas and Saul for the work to which I have called them.” <sup>3</sup>Then after fasting and praying they laid their hands on them and sent them off. <sup>4</sup>So, being sent out by the Holy Spirit, they went down to Seleucia, and from there they sailed to Cyprus. <sup>5</sup>When they arrived at Salamis, they proclaimed the word of God in the synagogues of the Jews. And they had John to assist them. <sup>6</sup>When they had gone through the whole island as far as Paphos, they came upon a certain magician, a Jewish false prophet named Bar-Jesus. <sup>7</sup>He was with the proconsul, Sergius Paulus, a man of intelligence, who summoned Barnabas and Saul and sought to hear the word of God. <sup>8</sup>But Elymas the magician (for that is the meaning of his name) opposed them, seeking to turn the proconsul away from the faith. <sup>9</sup>But Saul, who was also called Paul, filled with the Holy Spirit, looked intently at him <sup>10</sup>and said, “You son of the devil, you enemy of all righteousness, full of all deceit and villainy, will you not stop making crooked the straight paths of the Lord? <sup>11</sup>And now, behold, the hand of the Lord is upon you, and you will be blind and unable to see the sun for a time.” Immediately mist and darkness fell upon him, and he went about seeking people to lead him by the hand. <sup>12</sup>Then the proconsul believed, when he saw what had occurred, for he was astonished at the teaching of the Lord. <sup>13</sup>Now Paul and his companions set sail from Paphos and came to Perga in Pamphylia. And John left them and returned to Jerusalem, <sup>14</sup>but they went on from Perga and came to Antioch in Pisidia. And on the Sabbath day they went into the synagogue and sat down. <sup>15</sup>After the reading from the Law and the Prophets, the rulers of the synagogue sent a message to them, saying, “Brothers, if you have any word of encouragement for the people, say it.” <sup>16</sup>So Paul stood up, and motioning with his hand said: “Men of Israel and you who fear God, listen. <sup>17</sup>The God of this people Israel chose our fathers and made the people great during their stay in the land of Egypt, and with uplifted arm he led them out of it. <sup>18</sup>And for about forty years he put up with them in the wilderness. <sup>19</sup>And after destroying seven nations in the land of Canaan, he gave them their land as an inheritance. <sup>20</sup>All this took about 450 years. And after that he gave them judges until Samuel the prophet. <sup>21</sup>Then they asked for a king, and God gave them Saul the son of Kish, a man of the tribe of Benjamin, for forty years. <sup>22</sup>And when he had removed him, he raised up David to be their king, of whom he testified and said, ‘I have found in David the son of Jesse a man after my heart, who will do all my will.’ <sup>23</sup>Of this man’s offspring God has brought to Israel a Savior, Jesus, as he promised. <sup>24</sup>Before his coming, John had proclaimed a baptism of repentance to all the people of Israel. <sup>25</sup>And as John was finishing his course, he said, ‘What do you suppose that I am? I am not he. No, but behold, after me one is coming, the sandals of whose feet I am not worthy to untie.’ <sup>26</sup>Brothers, sons of the family of Abraham, and those among you who fear God, to us has been sent the message of this salvation. <sup>27</sup>For those who live in Jerusalem and their rulers, because they did not recognize him nor understand the utterances of the prophets, which are read every Sabbath, fulfilled them by condemning him. <sup>28</sup>And though they found in him no guilt worthy of death, they asked Pilate to have him executed. <sup>29</sup>And when they had carried out all that was written of him, they took him down from the tree and laid him in a tomb. <sup>30</sup>But God raised him from the dead, <sup>31</sup>and for many days he appeared to those who had come up with him from Galilee to Jerusalem, who are now his witnesses to the people. <sup>32</sup>And we bring you the good news that what God promised to the fathers, <sup>33</sup>this he has fulfilled to us their children by raising Jesus, as also it is written in the second Psalm, ‘You are my Son, today I have begotten you.’ <sup>34</sup>And as for the fact that he raised him from the dead, no more to return to corruption, he has spoken in this way, ‘I will give you the holy and sure blessings of David.’ <sup>35</sup>Therefore he says also in another psalm, ‘You will not let your Holy One see corruption.’ <sup>36</sup>For David, after he had served the purpose of God in his own generation, fell asleep and was laid with his fathers and saw corruption, <sup>37</sup>but he whom God raised up did not see corruption. <sup>38</sup>Let it be known to you therefore, brothers, that through this man forgiveness of sins is proclaimed to you, <sup>39</sup>and by him everyone who believes is freed from everything from which you could not be freed by the law of Moses. <sup>40</sup>Beware, therefore, lest what is said in the Prophets should come about: <sup>41</sup>‘Look, you scoffers, be astounded and perish; for I am doing a work in your days, a work that you will not believe, even if one tells it to you.’” <sup>42</sup>As they went out, the people begged that these things might be told them the next Sabbath. <sup>43</sup>And after the meeting of the synagogue broke up, many Jews and devout converts to Judaism followed Paul and Barnabas, who, as they spoke with them, urged them to continue in the grace of God. <sup>44</sup>The next Sabbath almost the whole city gathered to hear the word of the Lord. <sup>45</sup>But when the Jews saw the crowds, they were filled with jealousy and began to contradict what was spoken by Paul, reviling him. <sup>46</sup>And Paul and Barnabas spoke out boldly, saying, “It was necessary that the word of God be spoken first to you. Since you thrust it aside and judge yourselves unworthy of eternal life, behold, we are turning to the Gentiles. <sup>47</sup>For so the Lord has commanded us, saying, ‘I have made you a light for the Gentiles, that you may bring salvation to the ends of the earth.’” <sup>48</sup>And when the Gentiles heard this, they began rejoicing and glorifying the word of the Lord, and as many as were appointed to eternal life believed. <sup>49</sup>And the word of the Lord was spreading throughout the whole region. <sup>50</sup>But the Jews incited the devout women of high standing and the leading men of the city, stirred up persecution against Paul and Barnabas, and drove them out of their district. <sup>51</sup>But they shook off the dust from their feet against them and went to Iconium. <sup>52</sup>And the disciples were filled with joy and with the Holy Spirit.
13.overview:
The third stage of Acts 1:8, “to the end of the earth”, begins in earnest. The church at Antioch, led by a strikingly mixed group of prophets and teachers, is worshipping and fasting when the Holy Spirit tells them to set apart Barnabas and Saul for a special work. With prayer and the laying on of hands they send them off, with John Mark as their assistant. They sail to Cyprus, Barnabas’s home island, preach in synagogues from Salamis in the east to Paphos in the west, and there meet the Roman governor, the proconsul Sergius Paulus, and a Jewish sorcerer and false prophet, Elymas, who tries to turn him from the faith. Saul, from now on called by his Roman name Paul, rebukes Elymas, who is struck blind, and the proconsul believes.

They sail to Perga on the south coast of modern Turkey, where Mark leaves them, and travel inland over the Taurus mountains to Pisidian Antioch, a Roman colony on the high plateau. In the synagogue Paul is invited to speak and gives the first of his sermons recorded in Acts: God chose Israel, brought them out of Egypt, gave them the land, judges and kings, and from David’s line has brought the promised Saviour, Jesus. The people of Jerusalem condemned him, but God raised him, as the psalms foretold, and through him forgiveness is proclaimed and everyone who believes is freed from everything the law of Moses could not free them from. The next Sabbath nearly the whole city gathers. Jealous Jewish leaders oppose Paul, and he and Barnabas announce that they are turning to the Gentiles, quoting Isaiah’s words about a light for the nations. The Gentiles rejoice, and as many as were appointed to eternal life believe. Opposition drives the missionaries out, and they shake the dust off their feet, while the new disciples are filled with joy and the Holy Spirit.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–12 — The First Missionary Journey Begins
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: In the church at Antioch there were prophets and teachers: Barnabas, Simeon called Niger, Lucius of Cyrene, Manaen, who had been brought up with Herod the tetrarch, and Saul. While they were worshipping the Lord and fasting, the Holy Spirit told them to set apart Barnabas and Saul for the work to which he had called them. After more fasting and prayer, they laid their hands on them and sent them off. Sent out by the Spirit, the two went down to Seleucia and sailed to Cyprus. At Salamis they proclaimed God’s word in the Jewish synagogues, with John as their helper. They travelled through the whole island to Paphos, where they met a Jewish sorcerer and false prophet named Bar-Jesus, who was an attendant of the proconsul, Sergius Paulus. The proconsul, an intelligent man, sent for Barnabas and Saul because he wanted to hear the word of God. But Elymas the sorcerer, as his name was translated, opposed them and tried to turn the proconsul from the faith. Then Saul, also called Paul, filled with the Spirit, looked straight at Elymas and called him a child of the devil, an enemy of everything right, full of deceit and trickery, who would not stop perverting the Lord’s right ways. The Lord’s hand was against him, and he would be blind for a time. Immediately mist and darkness came over him, and he groped about for someone to lead him by the hand. When the proconsul saw what had happened, he believed, for he was amazed at the teaching about the Lord.
verseByVerse.theology:
Missionary Call and Corporate Discernment

The Spirit does not speak to Barnabas and Saul privately and send them to inform the church. He speaks in the assembly, to the assembly, about two men who are standing in it — and the church then fasts, prays, and lays hands on them before letting them go. Reformed ecclesiology has taken this as the pattern: an individual sense of call confirmed by a congregation, and a congregation's judgement confirmed by the Spirit, with neither operating alone. Notice also what the sending cost. Barnabas had been sent to build up that church and Saul was its finest teacher, and Antioch gave away both on the strength of one sentence in a prayer meeting.
