A prophet named Agabus came down from Judea. Agabus we have met. He came down from Jerusalem to Antioch years before and foretold a great famine over all the world, and Luke adds drily that it took place in the days of Claudius (11:28). He has a track record, and it is a verified one.

He took Paul’s belt and bound his own feet and hands. What he does now is not a sermon. He crosses the room, takes the long cloth belt from round Paul’s waist, the working man’s girdle that held up his tunic, and ties his own ankles and wrists with it in front of the whole household. This is prophecy in the old manner, and Israel had seen it for centuries. Isaiah walked barefoot and stripped for three years as a sign against Egypt (Isaiah 20:2–4). Jeremiah buried a loincloth by the Euphrates and wore a yoke on his neck through the streets (Jeremiah 13; 27:2). Ezekiel drew Jerusalem on a brick and laid siege to it on the floor of his house (Ezekiel 4). God has always known that a thing seen goes deeper than a thing heard. Everyone in that room would forget the sentence. Nobody would forget the belt.

Thus says the Holy Spirit. This is the line to slow down for. Thus says the LORD is the standing prophetic formula, hundreds of times over, the phrase that marks the difference between a man’s opinion and the speech of the covenant God. Agabus takes that formula unaltered and puts the Holy Spirit’s name in it. He is not being loose. This is a Jewish prophet, in a Jewish house, using the most weighty words in his vocabulary, and he attaches them to the Spirit as naturally as breathing. The doctrine of the Trinity was not invented by a council centuries later; it is lying in the floorboards of the church’s earliest speech, because the men who spoke it could not tell the difference between the Spirit speaking and God speaking. The Spirit is God.

This is how the Jews at Jerusalem will bind the man who owns this belt and deliver him into the hands of the Gentiles. Two things about it. First, notice what Agabus does not say. He does not say do not go. He says this is what will happen. That is the whole difference between him and the well-meaning disciples at Tyre, and it is why Luke has placed the two side by side. Second, the wording is deliberately the wording of the passion. Jesus said of himself, on the way to this same city, that he would be delivered over to the Gentiles (Luke 18:32; 9:44). Luke is telling the reader which story Paul has now walked into. The servant is not above his master, and the road to Jerusalem has only one ending for those who take it.

Did the prophecy come true, when it was the Romans who bound him? Yes, and the answer is ordinary biblical speech. When it happens, the Jews are trying to lynch Paul and it is the Romans who put on the chains (vv. 30–33). But Scripture routinely credits an act to the person who caused it rather than the hands that carried it out. Peter tells Jerusalem that they crucified and killed Jesus by the hands of lawless men (2:23); no Jew drove a nail, and Peter still says they did it. And there is a witness who settles it, because he was the man in the chains. Years later, in Rome, Paul sums up the whole affair to the Jewish leaders by saying that he was delivered as a prisoner from Jerusalem into the hands of the Romans (28:17). That is Agabus’s prophecy, quoted back almost word for word, by the man best placed to complain if it had not come true.

Where Christians differ: do prophets like Agabus still speak today? Many Christians believe the gift continues, and they love the Lord and his word. Verdict: the more likely reading is that New Testament prophecy, as revelation from God, belonged with the apostles to the foundation of the church (Ephesians 2:20), and ceased with the completion of Scripture. Agabus’s words came true in every particular, as true prophecy always did. We hold this charitably toward brothers who see it differently, and we expect the Spirit to speak to his church today through the Scripture he has given, which is sufficient for everything we need for life and godliness.

In a sentence. During their many days there, a prophet named Agabus came from Judea, took Paul’s belt, tied his own feet and hands with it, and said the Holy Spirit declared that the Jews in Jerusalem would bind the owner of this belt like this and hand him over to the Gentiles.

On a Tuesday. When God tells you in his word that following Christ will cost you, believe him the first time. Do not be surprised when the cost arrives in the shape he described. The New Testament does not hide the price: all who desire to live a godly life in Christ Jesus will be persecuted (2 Timothy 3:12). A Christian warned in advance is a Christian who can say, when the belt is tied, that this is exactly what my Lord said would happen.

For worship. The Spirit of God told the truth about chains, as he tells the truth about everything. And the road he described for Paul was the road the Son of God had already walked: bound by his own people, handed over to the Gentiles, and led out to die. But there is this difference. Paul’s binding would carry the gospel to Rome. Christ’s binding carried our sins away. He let himself be tied so that we could go free, and the cords that held him in the garden were the price of every loosed captive since.
verseByVerse.note: Agabus acts out his prophecy as the Old Testament prophets often did.

verseByVerse.quote: "When we heard this, we and the people there urged him not to go up to Jerusalem."
verseByVerse.commentary:
When we heard this, we and the people there urged him not to go up to Jerusalem.

When we heard this, we and the people there urged him not to go up to Jerusalem. Read the pronoun. We. Luke is in the room, and Luke is on the wrong side. He is writing this years later, with the whole outcome in front of him. He knows Paul was right and the room was wrong. He could have written that the Caesarean believers urged him and quietly left himself out of it. Instead he puts himself in the crowd of people who tried to talk the apostle out of obeying God. Historians who invent do not do that. Men who have been forgiven do.

The pressure of love. Notice how total the pressure has become. Disciples at Tyre for seven days. Now the whole household at Caesarea. Now Philip, who knows what persecution costs. Now the travelling companions who have crossed the sea with him. Now the doctor who will be at his side to the last letter he ever writes (2 Timothy 4:11). Every Christian in the building is telling him not to go. It is like Peter trying to stop Jesus going to the cross (Matthew 16:22): natural, loving, and wrong. We prepare ourselves for opposition from enemies, and enemies are not usually the problem. The strongest force ever applied against your obedience will be the affection of people who love you and cannot bear what obedience will cost you. They are not wicked. They are weeping. And their tears can do what threats never could.

Two guards. Both are in this verse. First, their love is not an argument. It is real, it is precious, it should be received warmly, and it settles nothing about what God has said. Second, their love is not an enemy either. Paul does not rebuke them, accuse them of unbelief, or lecture the room. He tells them their weeping is breaking his heart (v. 13), and goes anyway.

How do I know when to listen to people who love me, and when to disappoint them? Ask what their counsel rests on. If they are pointing you to Scripture, to a clear duty you are neglecting, or to wisdom you have not weighed, listen hard; Proverbs says there is safety in many counsellors (Proverbs 11:14), and most of the time the people who love you are right. If they are asking you to step back from something God has plainly called you to, because the cost frightens them, thank them and stay the course. And if you are the one urging, as Luke was and as most of us mostly are, ask honestly whether you want someone to be careful because God has spoken, or because you cannot face losing them.

In a sentence. When they heard this, Luke and the others and the local believers begged Paul not to go up to Jerusalem.

On a Tuesday. Love can try to stop someone obeying God. Be careful your love does not hold others back from God’s call: the missionary son, the daughter marrying into hardship for Christ, the friend taking a stand that will cost him his job. Tell them you will miss them, and then help them pack.

For worship. There was one man whom no tears could turn aside. His mother stood at the cross, his friends tried to keep him from Jerusalem, and Peter drew a sword to stop the arrest, and he went on, because his love for his Father and for us was stronger than his love for his own life. We are saved because Jesus would not be persuaded. His face was set like flint toward the city, and when we were the ones holding him back, he went anyway, for our sake.

verseByVerse.quote: Then Paul answered, "What are you doing, weeping and breaking my heart? For I am ready not only to be imprisoned but even to die in Jerusalem for the name of the Lord Jesus." And since he would not be persuaded, we ceased and said, "Let the will of the Lord be done."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Then Paul answered, “What are you doing, weeping and breaking my heart? For I am ready not only to be imprisoned but even to die in Jerusalem for the name of the Lord Jesus.” And since he would not be persuaded, we ceased and said, “Let the will of the Lord be done.”

What are you doing, weeping and breaking my heart? He is not made of stone, and this verse exists to stop us thinking he was. The word translated breaking (synthryptō) means to crush, to pound something soft to pieces, like a woman beating washing on a stone; it appears nowhere else in the New Testament. Their crying is not glancing off him. It is grinding him down, and he says so. Which means that Paul in this room is under two pressures at once, and only one of them is chains. The prospect of a Roman prison he can face. The thing that is actually crushing him is the sound of people who love him, sobbing. That is what he has to walk through to get to Jerusalem.

For I am ready not only to be imprisoned but even to die in Jerusalem for the name of the Lord Jesus. Then the sentence that ends the argument. Ready is a settled word: not braced, not resigned, but prepared, the way a soldier is prepared. Not reckless, but resolved, like his Lord, who set his face to go to Jerusalem (Luke 9:51). And notice the ladder: not only imprisoned, but even to die. He has already priced the worst outcome and paid for it in advance, which is exactly why the weeping cannot move him. You cannot threaten a man with something he has already agreed to. This is the same man who would write from a cell that it was his eager expectation that Christ would be honoured in his body, whether by life or by death, for to him to live is Christ, and to die is gain (Philippians 1:20–21). What we are watching here is the doctrine going through his own body. And see what he is ready to die for: not a cause, not a project, not the collection in his luggage, but the name of the Lord Jesus. Persons are worth dying for in a way that projects never are.

Is it right to want to die for Christ? Paul is not seeking death, and Scripture never praises those who throw their lives away. He had escaped over the Damascus wall in a basket (9:25) and would shortly use his Roman citizenship to avoid a flogging (22:25). What he has done is settle in advance that his life is not his own, so that if obedience costs him his life, he will not hold it back. That is what every Christian is called to: not a death wish, but a heart that has already handed everything over. Most believers will never be asked to die for Christ. All of us are asked to live as people who would.

And since he would not be persuaded, we ceased and said, Let the will of the Lord be done. It may be the quietest great moment in Acts. Notice what did not happen. They were not convinced. Luke does not write that they came round, or that God gave them peace about it. They ran out of arguments in front of a man who would not move, and they stopped. And the sentence they said when they stopped is the one from the garden: not my will, but yours, be done (Luke 22:42), and behind that, the prayer the Lord taught them all, your will be done (Matthew 6:10). This is Gethsemane in a front room in Caesarea, prayed by ordinary Christians over a friend they expect to lose.

The real article. Anyone can say let the will of the Lord be done about a matter still open, where the will of the Lord might yet turn out to be the thing they wanted. This room says it having just lost the argument, about a man they will very likely never see again. That is not resignation. Resignation gives up on the outcome; these people are handing it to a Person. They can say the will of the Lord because they know whose will it is. There comes a moment in most Christian lives when the praying stops being about changing the verdict and starts being about trusting the Judge. It usually arrives in a room, with people in it, after the arguing has run out. When it comes, this is the sentence to have ready.

Is saying “Let the will of the Lord be done” giving up on prayer? No. These believers had prayed and pleaded, and they were right to; the Lord Jesus himself asked in Gethsemane that the cup might pass. Asking God boldly for what we long for and submitting to what he decides belong together in the same prayer. What changes at the end is not that we stop caring but that we stop insisting. We hand the outcome to a Father who is wiser than we are and who loves the person we are praying for more than we do. That is not defeat. It is the deepest kind of trust.

In a sentence. Paul asked why they were weeping and breaking his heart, for he was ready not only to be bound but to die in Jerusalem for the name of the Lord Jesus, and when he would not be dissuaded, they gave up and said, The Lord’s will be done.

On a Tuesday. Is there something you are asking God for, perhaps for years, where you have not yet been able to say these words? Keep asking. But practise the second half of the prayer as well, out loud, about that very thing: your will be done. Say it first through gritted teeth if you must. The Lord who taught you the prayer will teach you to mean it.

For worship. The prayer the Caesarean church managed through its tears had already been prayed perfectly, in the dark, by a man sweating blood with nobody awake to hear him. In a garden across the valley from the city Paul is travelling toward, the Lord Jesus asked that the cup be taken away, and then said, not my will, but yours. No angel came with a reprieve. The cup was not taken away, and he drank every drop of it. The will of the Lord was done, in his body, on a hill outside the walls, and that is the only reason there was a church in Caesarea to pray it at all.

parallels.desc: not my will, but yours

verseByVerse.quote: After these days we got ready and went up to Jerusalem. And some of the disciples from Caesarea went with us, bringing us to the house of Mnason of Cyprus, an early disciple, with whom we should lodge.
verseByVerse.commentary:
After these days we got ready and went up to Jerusalem. And some of the disciples from Caesarea went with us, bringing us to the house of Mnason of Cyprus, an early disciple, with whom we should lodge.

After these days we got ready and went up to Jerusalem. The verb behind got ready (episkeuazomai) is the ordinary word for packing baggage and loading animals. There is no drama in it. After days of tears and prophecy, a group of men strap their bags to the pack animals and set off on a walk of some sixty-five miles up from the coast to the ridge. Obedience, once the argument is over, mostly looks like luggage. Went up is right in both senses: Jerusalem stands about 2,500 feet above the plain, and every Jew in the world spoke of going up to Jerusalem the way we speak of going home.

What is in those bags? Luke does not tell you here, and that is one of the great restraints of Acts. For years Paul had been organising a relief fund among the Gentile churches for the poor believers in Jerusalem. He gave Corinth detailed instructions about it (1 Corinthians 16:1–4). He devoted two chapters of a letter to persuading them to finish it (2 Corinthians 8–9). He told the Romans he was going to Jerusalem with aid for the saints, and asked them to pray that it would be acceptable (Romans 15:25–31). It was the great labour of his later ministry, a tangible proof that the Gentile churches and the mother church were one body. Luke gives it a single passing mention in the whole book, and not until Paul is on trial: he had come to bring alms to his nation (24:17). There is a lesson in the silence for anyone who handles money in the church, or quietly funds it. The thing Paul travelled for years to deliver gets no paragraph. The evangelist who never left Caesarea gets a verse and a title. Luke is not measuring by what a thing cost to arrange, and neither, in the end, is God.

Bringing us to the house of Mnason of Cyprus, an early disciple, with whom we should lodge. The lodging is not an accident. Some of the Caesarean believers walk the sixty-five miles too, and they have arranged in advance where the party will sleep. Look at who was chosen. Mnason is a Greek name. He is a Cypriot, like Barnabas (4:36). And Luke calls him an early disciple, literally an ancient one, a believer from the beginning, perhaps from Pentecost itself. Put those facts together and the logistics tell you something the story has not yet said out loud. Paul is arriving with uncircumcised Gentiles in a city where thousands of believers are zealous for the law (v. 20), and the host is both a disciple of long standing and a Greek-speaking Jew from Cyprus, at home with Gentiles: a man who can put Trophimus the Ephesian in his spare room without the neighbours calling it a scandal. Thoughtful hospitality, arranged ahead of time. Another quiet, faithful servant, named once in Scripture.

The first generation still opening its doors. Here is the encouraging half. Paul is not walking into Jerusalem as a stranger or a novelty. He is coming back to the community where the whole thing started, to sleep in the house of a man who was following Jesus before he was. The trouble that will explode in a few verses has already been anticipated by whoever booked the rooms, and the old saint has said yes.

What does Christian hospitality look like when my home is small or my life is busy? It looks like Mnason: an open door to the person who needs one, at the moment they need it. It does not need a large house, a polished meal or a tidy kitchen. It needs a willingness to make room, and some thought about who would be uncomfortable elsewhere: the newcomer, the overseas student, the believer from a different background, the person whom others hesitate to have. Scripture makes hospitality a duty for every Christian, not a gift for a few (Romans 12:13; 1 Peter 4:9), and older believers are often its best practitioners. A bed, a bowl of soup and a welcome can be the most strategic thing in the whole mission.

In a sentence. After this they got ready and went up to Jerusalem, with some disciples from Caesarea who took them to stay with Mnason from Cyprus, one of the early disciples.

On a Tuesday. Faithful hosts like Mnason make God’s work possible. Open your home this month to someone who would not otherwise have a place at a Christian table, and think ahead, as the Caesarean believers did, about who would be most at ease where.

For worship. The Lord goes ahead of his servants and prepares a room. He did it for Paul in the house of an old disciple from Cyprus, and he did it for his disciples on the last night, when they found the upper room furnished and ready. And he is doing it still. In my Father’s house are many rooms, Jesus said, and I go to prepare a place for you (John 14:2). The one who arranged lodging for an apostle in a hostile city has arranged our lodging for eternity, and the door is already open.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The believers in Jerusalem welcome Paul warmly. Next day he visits James with all the elders and reports in detail what God has done among the Gentiles, and they praise God. But they tell him that many thousands of Jewish believers, all zealous for the law, have heard that he teaches Jews abroad to give up Moses and not circumcise their children. They advise him to join four men who have taken a vow, go through the purification rites with them and pay for their offerings, so that everyone will see he keeps the law. As for Gentile believers, the earlier letter stands. Paul does so. When the seven days are nearly over, Jews from Asia spot him in the temple and seize him, shouting that he teaches against the people, the law and the temple, and has defiled it by bringing Greeks in; they had seen him in the city with Trophimus of Ephesus. The whole city is in uproar; Paul is dragged out and the gates are shut. As they try to kill him, the commander of the Roman garrison rushes down with troops, and the beating stops. He arrests Paul, binds him with two chains and asks who he is, but cannot get a clear answer through the shouting, and orders him taken to the barracks. The crowd is so violent that soldiers have to carry Paul up the steps while the mob yells, “Away with him!” At the door Paul asks in Greek to speak. Surprised, the commander asks if he is the Egyptian rebel who recently led four thousand terrorists into the desert. Paul says he is a Jew of Tarsus, citizen of an important city, and asks to address the people. Given permission, he stands on the steps, signals for silence, and speaks to them in Aramaic.
verseByVerse.theology:
Liberty, Accommodation, and the Line That Does Not Move

Paul in the temple, paying for sacrifices, is the most severely tested case of Christian liberty in the New Testament, and it is not a contradiction of Galatians but its application. The gospel had freed him from the law as a way of standing before God; that freedom is precisely what allowed him to keep the customs without fear. A man who needed the ritual could not have afforded to perform it. Only a justified man can shave a head, pay for a lamb, and mean nothing by it before God while meaning a great deal by it before his brothers. To the Jews I became as a Jew, in order to win Jews (1 Cor. 9:20).

The line, then, is not drawn at the act. The same razor and the same offering can be innocent or fatal, and what settles it is what the act is made to mean. When men demanded Titus be circumcised as a condition of fellowship, Paul did not yield in submission even for a moment, so that the truth of the gospel might be preserved (Gal. 2:5). Here nothing is required of any Gentile, and James says so out loud before anyone can misread the week. That is the discipline Reformed churches inherit: bend as far as love can bend on matters of culture and conscience, and not one inch on the ground of acceptance with God — and say plainly, in advance, which one you are doing.

And then the harder lesson, which is that this wise and humble course failed. The plan is what put Paul in the temple to be seen and seized. Faithfulness is not a technique for producing outcomes; it is obedience, and the outcomes belong to God, who used this failure as the road to Rome (23:11).
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: An apostle with a Roman citizenship in his pocket that could have ended the whole ordeal, standing chained at the door of a fortress, spending his one request not on rescue but on permission to preach to the mob that had just beaten him. And a pagan officer, who bought his citizenship for a large sum and had no idea whom he was serving, ordering the soldiers to hold the stairs so the prisoner could speak.

Now: Two things to take home. First, God's rescues rarely arrive in the uniform we were watching for; the church of tens of thousands is nowhere in this scene, and a Roman cohort is everything. Second, the platform we are given is almost never the platform we asked for. Paul wanted an unmolested week in the temple and a cleared name; he got a beating, a chain and a staircase — and from that staircase he preached to a larger Jewish crowd than he had faced in years. What has happened to me has really served to advance the gospel (Phil. 1:12) was written by a man remembering days exactly like this one.

verseByVerse.quote: "When we had come to Jerusalem, the brothers received us gladly. On the following day Paul went in with us to James, and all the elders were present."
verseByVerse.commentary:
When we had come to Jerusalem, the brothers received us gladly. On the following day Paul went in with us to James, and all the elders were present.

When we had come to Jerusalem, the brothers received us gladly. Gladly: relief as much as pleasure, the welcome you give when something you had been anxious about turns out well. And there had been real anxiety. Months earlier Paul had written to Rome asking for prayer about this very arrival: that he might be delivered from the unbelievers in Judea, and that his service for Jerusalem might be acceptable to the saints (Romans 15:31). He was not sure the mother church would take what he was bringing, and he had asked Christians fifteen hundred miles away to pray about the reception in this room. The first half of that prayer would be answered in an unexpected way. The second half is answered in this verse.

On the following day Paul went in with us to James, and all the elders were present. Luke marks a change of gear that is easy to read straight past. The warm welcome is one thing; the formal meeting is another, and it happens the next day, by appointment, with the full leadership assembled. James is the Lord’s brother, leader of the Jerusalem church (15:13; Galatians 2:9). There are no apostles in the room. The Twelve, who filled the first chapters of this book, are gone from the narrative; Peter had long before left Jerusalem for another place (12:17), and they may have been away on mission. The church in the mother city is governed by James, presiding, with a body of elders, all of them present. The earliest church did not run on personalities. It had ordinary appointed men, meeting together, and a chairman. When the greatest missionary of the age arrives, he does not summon them. He goes in to them, with his delegation, and reports.

A delegation with a bag. Went in with us: Luke is there, and so, presumably, are the delegates named at 20:4, a Berean, two Thessalonians, a man from Derbe, Timothy, and two from Asia including Trophimus the Ephesian. Men from several Roman provinces, most of them uncircumcised Gentiles, walk into the leadership meeting of the Jerusalem church carrying a large sum collected for Jewish believers they have never met. Paul delivered the collection, probably here (24:17). That is the picture he had worked for years to produce. He wanted the unity of the church to stop being only a doctrine and become a delegation standing in a room with a gift. Whatever happens in the next twenty verses, this happened first, and it happened gladly.

Why does it matter how a church is governed? Because Christ is the head of his church and he has given it an order. In the New Testament, local churches are led by a plurality of elders, who are also called overseers and shepherds (20:17, 28; Titus 1:5–7), with deacons serving alongside them (Philippians 1:1). Christians differ over the details, whether congregations are bound together under wider assemblies or govern themselves, and those views deserve a fair hearing. But every faithful view agrees on what this verse shows: leadership is shared, accountable and humble, and even an apostle submits his work to the brothers.

In a sentence. When they arrived in Jerusalem, the believers welcomed them warmly, and the next day Paul went with them to see James, with all the elders present.

On a Tuesday. If you serve in a church, report to those who lead it, and do it gladly. If you lead, receive the people who come to you, especially those from far away and from different backgrounds, as Jerusalem received these Gentiles: with gladness first, and with questions after.

For worship. Love crosses distance and difference, and the Lord delights to make it visible. Gentiles who had once been far off came carrying gifts to Zion, as the prophets foresaw when they spoke of the wealth of the nations coming to Jerusalem (Isaiah 60:5). But the true fulfilment is greater than any purse. The nations come to Christ himself, the true Temple, and lay before him the only gift he wants: themselves, made one body in him, by the blood that has brought near those who were far off (Ephesians 2:13).
verseByVerse.note: James is the Lord’s brother, leader of the Jerusalem church.

verseByVerse.quote: "After greeting them, he related one by one the things that God had done among the Gentiles through his ministry. And when they heard it, they glorified God. And they said to him, 'You see, brother, how many thousands there are among the Jews of those who have believed. They are all zealous for the law,"
verseByVerse.commentary:
After greeting them, he related one by one the things that God had done among the Gentiles through his ministry. And when they heard it, they glorified God. And they said to him, “You see, brother, how many thousands there are among the Jews of those who have believed. They are all zealous for the law,

He related one by one the things that God had done among the Gentiles through his ministry. One by one: item by item, each in its turn. This was not a summary and it was not brief. Picture what is on the list: Cyprus, Pisidian Antioch, Iconium, Lystra, Derbe, Philippi, Thessalonica, Berea, Athens, Corinth, Ephesus. The jailer and his household at midnight. Lydia. Crispus. The slave girl at Philippi. Eutychus alive on the floor at Troas. Years of work, told out in detail to men who had not seen any of it.

The grammar of a servant. Now look at how Paul tells it, because it is the whole man. He does not relate what he had accomplished. He relates the things that God had done among the Gentiles through his ministry. God is the subject of every sentence. Paul is a preposition: through him. He is not being modest for the room; this is simply how he has learned to see, and it is why he could survive both the applause at Lystra and the stoning that followed it. He had said the same at Antioch when he first returned (14:27), and he would write it to the Romans: I will not venture to speak of anything except what Christ has accomplished through me (Romans 15:18).

And when they heard it, they glorified God. It is not the first time in Acts that a report of Gentile conversion has produced praise in Jerusalem (11:18), and the reflex is healthy. They did not congratulate Paul; they worshipped. No jealousy. A church that can hear about work it did not do, in places it will never see, and respond by praising God rather than measuring itself, is a church in good health.

You see, brother, how many thousands there are among the Jews of those who have believed. And then, in the same breath, the problem. Thousands understates it. The word is myriades, tens of thousands, the largest number Greek had for a crowd. The Jerusalem church has not withered while the Gentile mission flourished; it has become enormous. That is the first thing the elders say, and it is said with joy. And they call Paul brother. Whatever is coming, the relationship is not in question. They are not interrogating an opponent; they are briefing a member of the family about a fire in the house.

They are all zealous for the law. The word is zēlōtai, zealots, the same root as the party name. These are Jewish believers who keep the law of Moses as their way of life, not as their way of salvation: the Sabbath, the circumcision of their sons, the feasts, the food laws, and they love doing it. It is their culture and their identity. Tensions were rising in these years, with Jewish nationalism building toward the war with Rome that would come within a decade, and a zeal for the law could easily turn into suspicion of anyone who seemed to loosen it. Notice what neither James nor Luke does. Nobody rebukes them. The Jerusalem Council had settled that Gentiles are not to be put under the law; it never said that Jews who believe must abandon it, and Paul never taught that either. What we have is one gospel producing two cultures, which is a triumph and a tinderbox in the same sentence.

Should Jewish believers keep the law today? Paul himself kept Jewish customs where they did not compromise the gospel (to the Jews I became as a Jew, 1 Corinthians 9:20), and a Jewish Christian is free to keep them as a matter of heritage and witness. What no one may do is make them necessary for salvation or impose them on Gentile believers (15:19–20; Galatians 2:14–16). The sacrifices and the temple are another matter: they were shadows fulfilled in Christ, and when the temple fell in AD 70 God himself brought that part of the old order to its end (Hebrews 8:13).

In a sentence. After greeting them, Paul reported in detail what God had done among the Gentiles through his ministry, and when they heard, they praised God, and told him there were many thousands of Jewish believers, all zealous for the law.

On a Tuesday. Give an account of your last year of Christian service, out loud, in Paul’s grammar. Not what you managed, not what you built, not what your church achieved, but the things God did, through you. Most of us find the sentences will not go together, and the discovery is worth having. Then rejoice when God works through others, in ways different from yours.

For worship. Every one of those stories on Paul’s list had the same author. It was God who opened Lydia’s heart, God who shook the jail at Philippi, God who called a people for himself in Corinth before Paul ever arrived (18:10). The gospel advances not because servants are clever but because the Lord is gathering his sheep from every nation, as he promised: I have other sheep that are not of this fold, and I must bring them also (John 10:16). He is bringing them still, and every report of it is a reason to glorify him.

verseByVerse.quote: "'And they have been told about you that you teach all the Jews who are among the Gentiles to forsake Moses, telling them not to circumcise their children or walk according to our customs. What then is to be done? They will certainly hear that you have come.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
and they have been told about you that you teach all the Jews who are among the Gentiles to forsake Moses, telling them not to circumcise their children or walk according to our customs. What then is to be done? They will certainly hear that you have come.

They have been told about you that you teach all the Jews who are among the Gentiles to forsake Moses. The verb is katēcheō, and it is not the word for gossip. It is the word for instruction, the word from which we get catechism, used elsewhere for being taught the faith thoroughly (Luke 1:4; 18:25; Galatians 6:6). What has been happening to Paul’s reputation in Jerusalem is not idle talk over a wall. Someone has been teaching this about him, persistently, to tens of thousands of people, and Luke’s passive quietly declines to say who.

An accusation nobody could check. Look where the offence is said to have happened: among the Jews who are among the Gentiles. Not here. Out there, in Antioch, Iconium, Thessalonica, Corinth and Ephesus, places most of those hearing it will never see. It is an accusation about a man’s conduct hundreds of miles away, in synagogues nobody in the room has attended, and so nobody present can disprove it. That is what gives it its grip.

Telling them not to circumcise their children or walk according to our customs. The two specifics are not chosen at random. What you do to your newborn son, and how your household lives its week. Not abstract doctrine but the cradle and the calendar. The charge is that Paul is dissolving Jewish family life one diaspora congregation at a time. Say that about a man in a city of law-zealous believers and you have not merely damaged him; you have made him dangerous.

Was the rumour true? As stated, no; but it grew from a seed of truth, and it is worth seeing both halves. What was false: Paul never taught Jews to forsake Moses or to stop circumcising their children. He kept the customs himself, freely and gladly. He took a vow (18:18), circumcised Timothy (16:3), hurried to keep Pentecost (20:16), worshipped in the temple, and is about to join four men in their vow to show it. He told the Corinthians that a man called when circumcised should not try to undo it (1 Corinthians 7:18). The word in the charge is apostasia, rebellion, abandonment, and of that Paul was simply innocent; he called the law holy, and the commandment holy and righteous and good (Romans 7:12).

The seed of truth. Here is what made the rumour believable. Paul really did teach something radical: that nothing, not circumcision, not law-keeping, makes anyone right with God; that justification is by faith in Christ alone (Galatians 2:16; Romans 3:28); that Gentile believers need not keep the law at all (15:19; he refused to circumcise Titus, Galatians 2:3–5); that the ceremonial law is a shadow fulfilled in Christ (Colossians 2:16–17); and that the believer has died to the law as a way of standing before God (Romans 7:4–6). He taught that the customs are not required and count for nothing as the ground of salvation, and that Jew and Gentile are one in Christ. In the heat of controversy and hostile retelling, that got stretched into Paul tells everyone to forsake Moses. The rumour took you are free from the law and twisted it into you must abandon the law, and that gap is the whole point. Paul preached freedom, not apostasy: a Jewish believer is free to keep his customs as heritage and witness, free not to, and never to trust them for salvation.

What then is to be done? They will certainly hear that you have come. A real pastoral problem. Certainly: no possibility of a quiet visit. Jerusalem is filling for Pentecost, the church numbers tens of thousands, and Paul has walked in with a band of Gentiles and a purse. The news is already moving through the city while the meeting is in progress.

Living your way back. Notice what the elders do not propose. They do not say, we will explain. They do not draft a statement or call an assembly so Paul can clear his name. These are experienced pastors and they know something we are slow to learn: a reputation is rarely repaired by explanation. Once a man is widely believed to be a certain kind of man, words about him, even true words, even his own, are heard as a defence and filed accordingly. So they look for something he can do instead. Not a claim but a fact; not a denial that can be disputed, but a week of conduct in public view. Whether the plan was wise is the question of the next verses. That the instinct was right is hardly in doubt.

What should I do if false things are being said about me? First, ask honestly whether any of it is true, as Paul’s case shows there is often a seed. Repent of what is yours and put it right. Then, where the charge is false, say so plainly once, to those who need to hear it, without bitterness. After that, let your life answer. Peter told believers slandered by their neighbours to keep their conduct honourable, so that those who speak against them would see their good deeds and glorify God (1 Peter 2:12). You will not usually talk your way back; you can sometimes live your way back, slowly, in front of witnesses. And commit your name to God, who judges justly, as Christ did when he was reviled (1 Peter 2:23).

In a sentence. They said these believers had been told Paul taught all Jews living among Gentiles to abandon Moses, not to circumcise their children or follow their customs, and they asked what should be done, since they would certainly hear he had come.

On a Tuesday. False rumours can hurt good servants of God. Do not pass on what you have not checked. When you hear a damaging report about a Christian leader, ask where it came from, whether it has been tested, and whether you have any business repeating it. See how easily a faithful teacher’s true message is twisted by exaggeration, as Paul had warned the Ephesian elders it would be (20:30), and refuse to be a link in that chain.

For worship. Paul was not the first to be falsely accused of destroying Moses. The Lord Jesus came not to abolish the Law or the Prophets but to fulfil them (Matthew 5:17), and he was condemned as a lawbreaker by men who did not understand that the whole law was pointing to him. He kept it perfectly, every jot and tittle, and then bore its curse for those who had broken it (Galatians 3:13). That is why Paul could be free from the law and still honour it: the law had been fulfilled in the obedience and death of his Saviour.
verseByVerse.note: The rumour was false; Paul opposed circumcision only when it was treated as necessary for salvation, especially for Gentiles.

verseByVerse.quote: "'Do therefore what we tell you. We have four men who are under a vow; take these men and purify yourself along with them and pay their expenses, so that they may shave their heads. Thus all will know that there is nothing in what they have been told about you, but that you yourself also live in observance of the law.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Do therefore what we tell you. We have four men who are under a vow; take these men and purify yourself along with them and pay their expenses, so that they may shave their heads. Thus all will know that there is nothing in what they have been told about you, but that you yourself also live in observance of the law.

Do therefore what we tell you. The plan is specific and it is public. Four men in the congregation are near the end of a vow. Paul is to attach himself to them, undergo purification with them, and settle their bill at the temple, and be seen doing it, for a week, in the busiest place in the Jewish world at the busiest season of the year.

We have four men who are under a vow. These men were ending a Nazirite vow, which required costly offerings at the temple (Numbers 6:13–21): a lamb, a ewe, a ram, and grain and drink offerings, for each man. Paying for poorer men’s offerings was considered an act of great piety. The vow itself (Numbers 6) is entirely foreign to most of us, so it is worth explaining. A Nazirite vow was a voluntary dedication to the LORD for a set period, and it involved three abstentions: no wine or anything from the vine, not even grapes or raisins; no razor on the head, the uncut hair being the visible sign of consecration; and no contact with a dead body, even of a parent, as strict a purity rule as the high priest’s. At the end, the Nazirite came to the temple and brought the prescribed offerings, a burnt offering, a sin offering and a peace offering, with grain and drink offerings; his head was shaved and the hair burned in the fire under the peace offering. The whole process was costly in time, money and public visibility, and sponsoring it was a recognised form of piety: Josephus records that King Agrippa I paid for many Nazirites to be shaved when he came to Jerusalem.

Take these men and purify yourself along with them. Paul, returning from Gentile lands, would need ritual purification before entering the temple. A man coming back from the lands of the nations was probably reckoned unclean as though by contact with the dead, and the remedy took seven days, with sprinkling on the third day and the seventh (Numbers 19:11–13). That is very likely where the seven days of verse 27 come from. Paul is not sponsoring a ceremony from the sidelines; he is inside the rite himself, on the clock, with a completion date lodged with the priests.

And pay their expenses, so that they may shave their heads. The end of the vow. And consider who is paying: Paul is settling that bill four times over. It is the gesture of a wealthy patron, made by a man who had told the Ephesian elders, holding up his hands, that these hands had provided for his own needs and for those with him (20:34). He had spent his evenings at a tentmaker’s bench rather than take a church’s money, and now he spends it on four strangers’ lambs and rams.

Thus all will know that there is nothing in what they have been told about you, but that you yourself also live in observance of the law. A public demonstration that Paul respected the law. Is James asking Paul to put on an act? Read the purpose clause and the answer is no. The vow is not a performance designed to create a false impression; it is evidence designed to display a true one, and it only works because it is true. Paul had taken a vow himself at Cenchreae and cut his hair for it (18:18). He had circumcised Timothy (16:3). He had hurried across the sea to keep Pentecost (20:16). He is not being asked to pretend to be a law-keeping Jew. He is being asked to stop being invisible.

The line he will not cross. When men demanded that Titus be circumcised as a condition of fellowship, Paul did not yield to them even for a moment, so that the truth of the gospel might be preserved (Galatians 2:3–5). The difference is not the act; the same knife, the same razor, the same offering can be either. The difference is what the act is made to mean. If a ceremony is required for salvation or imposed on Gentiles, Paul will fight it to the death. If it is a free man’s courtesy to his own people, he will pay for it out of his own pocket and thank God for the chance. To the Jews he became as a Jew, in order to win Jews (1 Corinthians 9:20). That verse is not a theory. This is what it looked like in practice.

Where Christians differ: was this a compromise? Some think Paul compromised the gospel here, since temple offerings point to sacrifice already fulfilled in Christ. Verdict: Paul taught that the law was not the means of salvation; he did not forbid Jewish believers from keeping customs as an expression of devotion. He became a Jew to the Jews (1 Corinthians 9:20). The offerings that closed a vow did include a sin offering (Numbers 6:14), and that is the hard part. But Paul did not offer them as the ground of his acceptance with God, which rested on Christ alone (Hebrews 10:14). They were the ceremonial ending of a vow, Jewish custom kept while the temple still stood, as he had circumcised Timothy for the sake of Jews who knew his family (16:3). It was an act of love for weaker brothers, not a denial of grace. That it ended in his arrest doesn’t prove it was wrong; God used it to send him to Rome.

But how could a sin offering mean anything after the cross? The answer lies in what the old sacrifices ever did. Even in Moses’ day it was impossible for the blood of bulls and goats to take away sins (Hebrews 10:4). They were shadows and signs, given by God to point forward to the one sacrifice that would. A godly Israelite who brought a sin offering was trusting the God who had promised that sacrifice, not the animal. So a shadow kept after the substance has come adds nothing to Christ’s work and takes nothing from it, as long as no one trusts it. Paul knew that his sins had been carried away once for all at the cross. While the temple still stood, he could take part in its customs for the sake of his brothers, as a man might keep an old family custom whose meaning has been fulfilled. What he could never do was rely on it, and he did not.

In a sentence. They told him to join four men who had taken a vow, purify himself with them and pay their expenses so they could shave their heads, so everyone would know the reports about him were false and that he himself kept the law.

On a Tuesday. Be willing to go the extra mile to remove stumbling blocks for weaker believers, as long as the gospel is not compromised. In practice that means asking, before you insist on your liberty, what it will cost a brother with a tender conscience: the drink you will not order at his table, the custom you will keep for his sake, the preference you will lay down. And it means knowing just as clearly where to stop: the moment anyone says that the custom is needed to be right with God, love itself requires you to refuse.

For worship. Every lamb, ewe and ram those four men brought to the altar was a picture, and the picture had already been fulfilled. The Lamb of God had been offered outside those same walls, once for all, and by that single offering he has perfected for all time those who are being sanctified (Hebrews 10:14). Paul could walk into the temple without fear because he was already standing in a better one, clothed in a righteousness no ceremony could add to or take away. The freedom that let him pay for the shadows was bought by the substance, and it was bought with blood.
verseByVerse.note: These men were ending a Nazirite vow, which required costly offerings; paying for them was a recognised act of piety.

parallels.desc: the offerings when the days of separation are complete

verseByVerse.quote: "But as for the Gentiles who have believed, we have sent a letter with our judgment that they should abstain from what has been sacrificed to idols, and from blood, and from what has been strangled, and from sexual immorality." Then Paul took the men, and the next day he purified himself along with them and went into the temple, giving notice when the days of purification would be fulfilled and the offering presented for each one of them.
verseByVerse.commentary:
But as for the Gentiles who have believed, we have sent a letter with our judgment that they should abstain from what has been sacrificed to idols, and from blood, and from what has been strangled, and from sexual immorality.” Then Paul took the men, and the next day he purified himself along with them and went into the temple, giving notice when the days of purification would be fulfilled and the offering presented for each one of them.

But as for the Gentiles who have believed, we have sent a letter with our judgment. Stop on the word but. James is in the middle of asking a Jewish apostle to walk into the temple and keep a Jewish vow, and he interrupts himself to say, unprompted, that none of this touches the Gentiles at all. James reassures Paul: the agreement of chapter 15 stands. Gentiles are not under the law. This arrangement concerns Jewish believers only.

A document still on file. This is the third time in Acts that the Jerusalem decree has been stated, and the three are worth laying side by side. In the council debate James proposed abstaining from things polluted by idols, from sexual immorality, from what has been strangled, and from blood (15:20). The letter the church actually sent put them in a different order: idols, blood, what has been strangled, sexual immorality (15:29). And here, years later, James quotes not his own speech but the letter, in exactly that order. He is not reciting a memory of what he once said. He is citing a document. Sent, past tense, settled business, and still binding. That council was perhaps seven or eight years earlier. In the meantime the Gentile mission had spread across several provinces, and nothing had been added to the terms. Nobody had renegotiated them once the Gentiles were numerous enough to be inconvenient. The freedom granted to the nations at Jerusalem was not a temporary concession that quietly expired; it was a judgement that held.

Saying what an action does not mean. Notice where James puts it. He builds the fence before anyone has had the chance to climb it. If Paul is about to be seen in the temple paying for sacrifices, some observer is bound to conclude that the Gentile churches must be next. James closes off that inference in the same breath as he makes the request. Wise leadership says out loud, in advance, what an action does not mean, while it can still be heard.

Does that decree still bind us? Its permanent parts, avoiding idolatry and sexual immorality, are moral commands repeated throughout the New Testament (1 Corinthians 6:18; 10:14). Its food rules, about blood and strangled meat, were for love’s sake in that setting, so that Jewish and Gentile believers could share a table, and Paul later treats food offered to idols as a matter of conscience and love rather than law (1 Corinthians 8; 10:25–33). For the fuller explanation, see the notes at 15:19–20.

Then Paul took the men, and the next day he purified himself along with them and went into the temple. Paul agreed. Humble, willing to accommodate. No argument is recorded, no delay, no conditions, no request for time to think. The next day. The man who wrote to the Galatians that if they accept circumcision Christ will be of no advantage to them (Galatians 5:2), and to the Romans that a person is justified by faith apart from works of the law (Romans 3:28), takes four men to the temple and submits to the purification. He can do it precisely because he believes what he wrote. A ceremony that cannot save him also cannot endanger him. It is free. And because it is free, he can spend it on his brothers.

Giving notice when the days of purification would be fulfilled and the offering presented for each one of them. Seven days. He puts his name on a list at the temple and agrees to pay a bill for blood sacrifices. Did the plan work? No. It failed completely. The vow put Paul in the temple, in public, at the one moment when Jews from Asia who knew him by sight were in the city for the feast, and being in the temple is what got him seen, seized and nearly killed. The advice of the wisest men in the Jerusalem church, offered in love and accepted in humility, was the immediate cause of his arrest.

Was the plan a mistake, then? Some think so, since it led to his arrest. The more likely reading is that Paul acted in good conscience to remove a false charge and keep peace with Jewish believers, and that God used even the riot to bring him to Rome, as he had promised (23:11). Most of us carry a private theology that says if we take the humble course, seek counsel and pay the cost ourselves, it ought to come out right. Here it does not. James was not foolish and Paul was not weak, and the plan blew up in their faces. Yet two nights later, in a Roman barracks, the Lord stood by Paul and told him to take courage, for as he had testified in Jerusalem, so he must testify in Rome (23:11). The failed plan was the road. Wisdom is not a guarantee of outcomes; it never was. It is faithfulness in the choosing, and God takes responsibility for the rest.

In a sentence. As for Gentile believers, they had written their decision that they should avoid food sacrificed to idols, blood, strangled meat and sexual immorality, and the next day Paul took the men, purified himself with them, and went into the temple to give notice of when their purification would be completed and the offering made for each.

On a Tuesday. Unity in the church sometimes costs personal preference; pay it gladly, as Paul did. And when you have made a careful, prayerful decision with good counsel and it still goes wrong, do not conclude that God has abandoned you or that you must have sinned. Look for what he is doing through it. Paul’s worst week in Jerusalem was his passage to Rome.

For worship. The Lord rules over our wisest plans and our failed ones alike. He let the counsel of godly men end in a riot, and he turned the riot into the road to Caesar’s household. So it was at the cross: the wisest plans of men to be rid of Jesus became the very means by which God accomplished salvation, according to his definite plan and foreknowledge (2:23). Nothing defeats his purpose. Not our mistakes, not our enemies’ schemes, not even our good intentions gone wrong. He works all things together for good for those who love him (Romans 8:28), and he has never yet wasted a chain.

verseByVerse.quote: "When the seven days were almost completed, the Jews from Asia, seeing him in the temple, stirred up the whole crowd and laid hands on him, crying out, 'Men of Israel, help! This is the man who is teaching everyone everywhere against the people and the law and this place. Moreover, he even brought Greeks into the temple and has defiled this holy place.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
When the seven days were almost completed, the Jews from Asia, seeing him in the temple, stirred up the whole crowd and laid hands on him, crying out, “Men of Israel, help! This is the man who is teaching everyone everywhere against the people and the law and this place. Moreover, he even brought Greeks into the temple and has defiled this holy place.”

When the seven days were almost completed, the Jews from Asia, seeing him in the temple. Almost completed. The plan was five or six days through a seven-day rite. Another day or two and Paul would have walked out of the temple with his name cleared before the whole city, and Acts would be a different book. And notice who ends it. Not the Jerusalem believers, who were supposedly inflamed against him. The Jews from Asia: pilgrims from Ephesus and its province, in for Pentecost like everyone else. It was in Ephesus that some became stubborn and continued in unbelief, speaking evil of the Way before the congregation, so that Paul withdrew from the synagogue (19:9). Those men know his face. They know his companions’ faces too, as the next verse shows. A three-year-old grievance from six hundred miles away bought a festival passage, and it is standing in the temple court when he walks past.

Stirred up the whole crowd. The verb (syncheō) is the one for throwing something into total confusion. They do not lodge a complaint with the temple authorities, who are standing right there. They work the crowd.

This is the man who is teaching everyone everywhere against the people and the law and this place. Set that beside the charge sheet from earlier in this book. False witnesses stood up against Stephen and said that he never ceased to speak words against this holy place and the law, and that Jesus would destroy this place and change the customs of Moses (6:13–14). Against the people, the law and this place. It is the same accusation, in the same city, in almost the same words, and behind both lies the charge against Jesus himself, that he would destroy the temple (Mark 14:58). And the young man standing at the edge of Stephen’s crowd, minding the coats and approving the execution, was Saul of Tarsus (7:58; 8:1). He knows it. Before the next chapter is half over he will say to this very crowd that when the blood of Stephen was being shed, he himself was standing by and approving (22:20). The charge he once helped to prosecute is now the charge against him. There is no revenge in this; God is not settling a score. It is something better: the persecutor has been so completely joined to the people he hunted that he now stands where they stood.

Moreover, he even brought Greeks into the temple and has defiled this holy place. This is the clause that turns a shouting match into a death sentence. The temple mount had an outer court that anyone could enter. Inside it, around the sacred courts, ran a low stone barrier, and at its openings stood notices warning foreigners away. Two of those stones have been found, in Greek: a complete one discovered in 1871, now in Istanbul, and a fragment found in 1935. The wording is preserved: no foreigner may enter within the barrier and enclosure around the sanctuary, and whoever is caught will have himself to blame for the death that follows. Josephus records that Rome, which jealously kept the power of execution to itself, allowed the Jews this one exception, even against a Roman citizen. So this is not an insult. It is a capital charge, shouted in a crowded court, and everyone who hears it knows the law permits them to carry out the sentence on the spot. That is why the chapter goes from accusation to attempted murder inside two verses.

The wall that was already down. Hold on to that barrier, because of what happens next in Paul’s own writing. The arrest that begins here becomes an imprisonment, and out of that imprisonment comes a letter to Ephesus, the city these accusers came from, which says that Christ has broken down in his flesh the dividing wall of hostility, and that Gentiles once far off are no longer strangers and aliens but fellow citizens with the saints and members of the household of God (Ephesians 2:14, 19). Whether or not Paul had this very stone in mind, he had stood in front of it, and he was arrested for supposedly breaching it. The wall the mob was defending had already been demolished by the cross; they simply had not been told. And the letter announcing the demolition was written from the chain their shouting produced.

Why did God put up the wall in the first place? Strictly, the stone barrier of Herod’s temple was a later Jewish arrangement, but it expressed something God had built into the old covenant: a holy God dwelling among a sinful people, with courts and curtains marking how far each could come. Those boundaries taught that sinners cannot simply walk into the presence of God. They were never meant to be permanent. From the beginning God promised that all nations would be blessed through Abraham’s offspring (Genesis 12:3), and that his house would be called a house of prayer for all peoples (Isaiah 56:7). The wall kept the distance visible until the one came who could close it.

In a sentence. When the seven days were nearly over, some Jews from Asia saw him in the temple, stirred up the whole crowd and seized him, shouting for help, saying this was the man who taught everyone everywhere against the people, the law and this place, and had even brought Greeks into the temple and defiled it.

On a Tuesday. Ask whether you still keep any walls in your own heart that Christ has torn down: a kind of Christian you would rather not sit beside, a background you quietly think of as further from God. And if you yourself feel like the outsider, the one who has always stood beyond the barrier, hear Ephesians 2 as addressed to you. You are not a guest in God’s house. You are family.

For worship. Consider how that wall came down. Not by decree, not by a quiet change of policy in heaven, not by the slow erosion of an old rule. Christ broke it down in his flesh: Paul’s phrase, and a violent one. The barrier that held the nations at a distance from God was not lifted off its footings and carried away. It was taken into a body and killed there, so that he might create in himself one new man in place of the two. Every Gentile who has ever drawn near to God has come in through a torn body and a poured-out life. And the stone with its warning sits in a museum under glass, an exhibit, out of work for two thousand years.
verseByVerse.note: Inscriptions have been found from the temple’s barrier, warning Gentiles not to go beyond it on pain of death.

parallels.desc: the dividing wall of hostility

verseByVerse.quote: "For they had previously seen Trophimus the Ephesian with him in the city, and they supposed that Paul had brought him into the temple. Then all the city was stirred up, and the people ran together. They seized Paul and dragged him out of the temple, and at once the gates were shut."
verseByVerse.commentary:
For they had previously seen Trophimus the Ephesian with him in the city, and they supposed that Paul had brought him into the temple. Then all the city was stirred up, and the people ran together. They seized Paul and dragged him out of the temple, and at once the gates were shut.

For they had previously seen Trophimus the Ephesian with him in the city, and they supposed that Paul had brought him into the temple. Luke stops the story to tell you that the charge is false and to show you, step by step, how it was manufactured. It is one of the most useful paragraphs in the New Testament for anybody who has been on either end of an accusation. Take it apart. First, a true observation: they had seen Trophimus with Paul in the city. Perfectly accurate. Trophimus is a real man, an Ephesian, one of the delegates carrying the collection (20:4). Second, an inference: they supposed that Paul had taken him inside. Nobody saw it. No witness is produced then or at any of the hearings that follow. The gap between what was seen in the street and what is alleged about the sanctuary is filled entirely by an assumption. Third, certainty. By verse 28 the supposition has hardened into a shouted fact, and note the plural: one man they thought they saw has become Greeks. Fourth, a crowd, and after that nothing can be undone, because a crowd cannot be shown evidence.

Sincerity is not a safeguard. Here is the sobering thing, and the reason Luke bothers: these men need not be lying. They very likely believe it. They are defending the holiest place on earth from a defilement that never happened, and they will nearly kill an innocent man out of what they think is reverence. How much harm is done by assuming the worst.

Then all the city was stirred up, and the people ran together. The city goes up. Pentecost crowds, packed with pilgrims, and people running toward the noise from every direction, most of them with no idea what has happened, which is exactly the state the tribune will find them in at verse 34.

They seized Paul and dragged him out of the temple, and at once the gates were shut. The gate-shutting is the detail to sit with. Part of the reason is crowd control. But part of it is this: a killing inside the sacred courts would defile them, so the man must be got outside before he is beaten to death. The doors are shut to keep the blood off the pavement. It is the same reflex as the men who would not enter the governor’s headquarters, so that they would not be defiled and could eat the Passover, on the morning they arranged a crucifixion (John 18:28): meticulous about the floor, indifferent about the murder.

The last door. And there is a picture in it that Luke, who wrote a Gospel first, will not have missed. This is the last time Paul is ever recorded inside the temple. The final act of that building toward the apostle to the Gentiles is a door closing behind him. Within little more than a decade there would be no doors and no temple. The gospel had moved on.

How do I avoid becoming one of those who supposed? Practise saying the word. When you find yourself repeating something about somebody, stop and say out loud which part you saw and which part you supposed. It is astonishing how much of what we are certain about will not survive being spoken in that form. Then follow the rule Scripture gives the church: a charge is established by the evidence of two or three witnesses (Deuteronomy 19:15; 1 Timothy 5:19), and love believes the best until the facts say otherwise (1 Corinthians 13:7). Before you share, forward or post, ask whether you know it, or only assume it. Most mobs today begin with a screenshot.

In a sentence. They had seen Trophimus the Ephesian with Paul in the city and assumed Paul had taken him into the temple, so the whole city was aroused, people came running, and they seized Paul, dragged him out of the temple, and immediately the gates were shut.

On a Tuesday. Do not assume the worst about others. Check the facts. And if you are the one falsely suspected, remember that Paul was too, by sincere men, in a holy place, and that God had the last word.

For worship. They shut Paul out of a building, but those doors had already stopped being the way in. Luke had written in his first volume that as Jesus died the curtain of the temple was torn in two (Luke 23:45). While the priests were bolting the gates against one man, the way into the true holy place stood open: the new and living way that Christ opened for us through the curtain, that is, through his flesh (Hebrews 10:19–20). No one could shut Paul out of the presence of God, and no one can shut you out, because the door is a Person, and he has said, I am the door; if anyone enters by me, he will be saved (John 10:9).

verseByVerse.quote: "And as they were seeking to kill him, word came to the tribune of the cohort that all Jerusalem was in confusion. He at once took soldiers and centurions and ran down to them. And when they saw the tribune and the soldiers, they stopped beating Paul."
verseByVerse.commentary:
And as they were seeking to kill him, word came to the tribune of the cohort that all Jerusalem was in confusion. He at once took soldiers and centurions and ran down to them. And when they saw the tribune and the soldiers, they stopped beating Paul.

As they were seeking to kill him. A lynching. Not threatening to kill him: seeking to. This is an execution in progress on the pavement of the outer court, carried out by hand, and the only reason it does not finish is a piece of Roman administration.

Word came to the tribune of the cohort that all Jerusalem was in confusion. The tribune commanded the cohort of Roman soldiers stationed in the Antonia Fortress, nominally about a thousand men. The fortress stood at the north-west corner of the temple platform, built to overlook it, with stairs running down into the outer court. Josephus records that at the great feasts soldiers were posted along the roofs of the colonnades above the crowd, because Rome had learned that festivals and riots came as a pair. So there were soldiers already on duty, watching, for exactly this. The tribune is Claudius Lysias, though Luke will not give us his name until a letter in chapter 23 (23:26), and we learn later that he had not been born a citizen but bought his citizenship for a large sum (22:28). A self-made provincial who purchased his way up, and God uses him to preserve the apostle to the nations.

He at once took soldiers and centurions and ran down to them. Centurions, plural: at least two centuries, so well over a hundred men, perhaps two hundred. And Luke says they ran: down the stairs, into the court, at speed, in armour.

And when they saw the tribune and the soldiers, they stopped beating Paul. Read that slowly, because of what it does not say. They did not stop when someone’s conscience woke up, or because a bystander appealed to the law, or because the temple authorities intervened, or because anyone remembered that no witness had been produced. They stopped when armed men appeared. That is the honest teaching of Scripture about human beings in a mass: restraint arrives from outside, or it does not arrive. Rescued by pagan soldiers. God used Rome to protect his servant, as he would later promise him directly (23:11).

The doctrine comes down the steps. This is exactly why God gave the sword to the magistrate. Only months before, wintering in Corinth, Paul had written to Rome that the governing authority is God’s servant for your good, that he does not bear the sword in vain, and that he is the servant of God to carry out his wrath on the wrongdoer (Romans 13:4). The ink was barely dry. And now the doctrine came down the fortress steps in hobnailed boots and saved the man who wrote it.

Where was the church? There is a quiet rebuke in the scene, and it should not be softened. Jerusalem contained tens of thousands of believers (v. 20). Not one of them appears in this paragraph. Perhaps they could have done nothing against a mob; perhaps some were afraid. Luke does not say. But the church is absent and the pagan garrison is everything. Sometimes the help God sends is not the help we would have chosen, does not come from the people we would have expected, and is still from God.

Should Christians thank God for the police and the courts? Yes. Paul tells us to pray for kings and all in authority, so that we may lead a peaceful and quiet life (1 Timothy 2:1–2). Government is a gift of God’s common grace, given to restrain evil in a fallen world, even when those who hold office do not know him. That does not mean every ruler is just or every act of government right: the same Rome that rescued Paul would one day execute him, and Christians must obey God rather than men when the two conflict (5:29). But where the law protects the weak and stops the mob, we should give thanks, pray for those who enforce it, and support them in doing it justly.

In a sentence. As they were trying to kill him, news reached the commander of the Roman troops that all Jerusalem was in uproar, and he immediately took soldiers and centurions and ran down to them, and when the crowd saw them, they stopped beating Paul.

On a Tuesday. Pray this week, by name if you can, for those who keep order where you live: police officers, judges, magistrates, local councillors. And look for ways your church can be present when others are in danger, so that the rescue of the vulnerable is not left to the garrison alone.

For worship. God’s protection can come from unexpected places, and he is Lord of all of them. He holds the hearts of kings and tribunes in his hand and turns them wherever he will (Proverbs 21:1). He placed a garrison above the temple courts, posted guards on the roofs at Pentecost, and sent a self-made officer running down the stairs at the very moment the blows were falling. The God who preserved Paul in a riot is the God who had already raised his Son from a grave that Rome had sealed. No power on earth can lay a hand on his servants one moment before he allows it, or keep them one moment after he calls them home.
verseByVerse.note: The tribune commanded the cohort of Roman soldiers stationed in the Antonia Fortress, which overlooked the temple courts.

verseByVerse.quote: "Then the tribune came up and arrested him and ordered him to be bound with two chains. He inquired who he was and what he had done."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Then the tribune came up and arrested him and ordered him to be bound with two chains. He inquired who he was and what he had done.

Then the tribune came up and arrested him and ordered him to be bound with two chains. Agabus’s prophecy fulfilled (v. 11). Two chains probably means a wrist shackled to a soldier on either side. Luke has described that arrangement once before: Peter was sleeping between two soldiers, bound with two chains (12:6). That night an angel came, the chains fell off Peter’s hands, the iron gate opened by itself, and he walked out into the street. Nothing of the kind happens here. Paul’s chains stay on. From now to the end of Acts, Paul is a prisoner.

One loosed, one left. Two men, the same chains, the same God, opposite outcomes, and Luke reports both with the same steady voice, without a syllable of explanation or apology. That is one of the great honesties of Scripture. It refuses to teach that faith always produces release, and it equally refuses to teach that suffering is the mark of the truly spiritual. It simply tells us that the Lord loosed one man’s chains and left the other man’s on, and that both men were his.

Why does God rescue some believers and not others? Scripture does not give us his reasons in each case, but it does give us his character and his purpose. James was killed by the sword in the same chapter in which Peter was set free (12:2, 7). Hebrews 11 lists those who escaped the edge of the sword and, in the same breath, those who were sawn in two. Neither group had more faith; both are commended. God’s purpose in each life is his glory and our good, and sometimes that is served by rescue and sometimes by endurance. So if your chains have not fallen off, do not conclude that your faith is too small or that God has forgotten you. Paul’s stayed on, and through them the gospel reached Rome.

A bound man already. Follow one word backwards, because Luke has been laying a track. The verb for binding is deō, and this is its fifth appearance in two chapters. At Miletus Paul said he was going to Jerusalem bound in the Spirit (20:22). At Caesarea Agabus bound his own feet and hands and said the Jews would bind the owner of the belt (21:11). In the front room Paul said he was ready to be bound (21:13). Now the tribune orders him bound with two chains. The Spirit’s chain came first. By the time Rome puts iron on this man, he has been a bound man for months, and willingly. What the tribune does at the top of these steps does not make Paul a prisoner; it only confirms, in metal, a captivity Paul had already accepted from God. That is why there is no panic in him, and no sense anywhere in the rest of the book that something has gone wrong. It also explains the name he gives himself afterwards. Writing from custody he calls himself a prisoner of Christ Jesus (Ephesians 3:1; Philemon 1, 9) and a prisoner for the Lord (Ephesians 4:1). Never once does he call himself Caesar’s prisoner. The chain changed owner the moment it was fastened.

He inquired who he was and what he had done. He assumed the victim was the criminal. Arrest first, investigate second: poor justice, and here it saves a life. Those two questions open a legal process that will run through the Sanhedrin, two Roman governors, a Herodian king, an appeal to Caesar, a shipwreck and a rented house in Rome. Chapters 22 to 28, a quarter of the book of Acts, are the answer to a soldier’s routine enquiry at the top of a staircase.

In a sentence. The commander came up, arrested him, ordered him bound with two chains, and asked who he was and what he had done.

On a Tuesday. Paul’s chains were part of God’s plan, and your hardships may be too. Name the chain you are wearing: the illness, the caring duty, the job you cannot leave, the limitation you did not choose. Then ask whose prisoner you are. If you belong to Christ, the answer is not the illness or the boss or the circumstance. It is him, and he does not waste his prisoners.

For worship. Back in Caesarea, in Philip’s house, a prophet had used Paul’s own belt only days before to show a room full of weeping friends exactly what would happen, and it happened exactly so. The Lord who tells the end from the beginning is never surprised by our chains. And he wore chains himself. The Son of God was bound in Gethsemane and led to Annas, and bound again and led to Pilate (John 18:12, 24; Mark 15:1), and he went without resisting, because his binding was our release. Every prisoner of Christ wears iron that his Master has already worn, and wears it for a little while, on the way to a glory that will make it look like nothing.

verseByVerse.quote: "Some in the crowd were shouting one thing, some another. And as he could not learn the facts because of the uproar, he ordered him to be brought into the barracks. And when he came to the steps, he was actually carried by the soldiers because of the violence of the crowd,"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Some in the crowd were shouting one thing, some another. And as he could not learn the facts because of the uproar, he ordered him to be brought into the barracks. And when he came to the steps, he was actually carried by the soldiers because of the violence of the crowd,

Some in the crowd were shouting one thing, some another. Luke has written this sentence before. At Ephesus some cried out one thing, some another, for the assembly was in confusion, and most of them did not know why they had come together (19:32). Two riots, two cities, two religions, one anatomy. A crowd can be entirely united in fury and completely unable to say what the charge is. Mobs do not think. That is the standing signature of a mob, and it is worth knowing how to spot, because mobs have not gone out of fashion; they have only moved indoors and online.
