The test is not how many people are angry or how certain they sound. It is whether any two of them, asked separately, would give the same account of what the accused actually did.

And as he could not learn the facts because of the uproar. The tribune is trying to do his job. He wants a charge; he asks for one; and thousands of people cannot produce a single coherent answer between them. The first casualty of an outraged crowd is the truth it believes itself to be defending.

He ordered him to be brought into the barracks. The Antonia Fortress: out of the court, out of reach.

And when he came to the steps. Steps led from the temple courts up into the fortress, and Josephus describes them.

He was actually carried by the soldiers because of the violence of the crowd. It is the most physically humiliating sentence written about Paul anywhere in Scripture. Carried: lifted off his feet like a load. The press at the foot of the stairs is so violent that the soldiers cannot get their prisoner up on his feet, so they lift him bodily, beaten, bleeding, clothes torn, hands chained, and haul him above the crowd like a piece of baggage. The greatest missionary in the history of the church goes up the last flight of stairs with his feet off the ground, held by pagan soldiers, unable to help himself in any particular.

When you are carried. Some Christians will read that and recognise it immediately, because they are living in it. There are seasons in which you do not walk; you are carried, by other people’s arms, in a direction you did not choose, to a place you would not have picked, with no say in any of it and no dignity left to protect. Luke does not treat that as a failure of faith. He treats it as an ordinary afternoon in the life of a faithful man. And notice whose arms they are. Roman soldiers, who thought they were suppressing a disturbance, were in fact carrying the word of God up a staircase, and in a moment their prisoner will ask them to stop at the top so that he can preach.

What if I feel helpless and humiliated, unable to do anything for myself? Then you are in good company, and you are not outside God’s care. Illness, old age, disability, a breakdown, a long hospital stay: all of them can leave a believer carried by others and stripped of dignity. Scripture never measures your worth by your independence. The Lord says to his people that even to their old age and grey hairs he will carry them; he has made, and he will bear (Isaiah 46:4). Let others help you without shame, and pray even from the stretcher. Paul’s most helpless moment was a minute from his greatest sermon in Jerusalem.

In a sentence. Some in the crowd shouted one thing and some another, and since the commander could not learn the facts because of the uproar, he ordered Paul taken into the barracks, and when they reached the steps the soldiers had to carry him because of the violence of the mob.

On a Tuesday. Before you join any crowd, physical or online, ask the tribune’s question: what exactly is the charge, and who saw it? If nobody can tell you, step out. And if this is a season in which you are being carried, give thanks for the arms that carry you, even if they are not the ones you would have chosen.

For worship. When the crowd rages, God carries his servants through. The Lord who bore Israel on eagles’ wings out of Egypt (Exodus 19:4), who carries the lambs in his arms (Isaiah 40:11), carried Paul up those stairs in the arms of Roman soldiers. And underneath every rescue are the everlasting arms (Deuteronomy 33:27), the arms of a Saviour who once let himself be lifted up, not to safety, but onto a cross, so that he could carry us all the way home.
verseByVerse.note: Steps led from the temple courts up into the fortress.

verseByVerse.quote: "for the mob of the people followed, crying out, 'Away with him!'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
for the mob of the people followed, crying out, “Away with him!”

For the mob of the people followed, crying out, Away with him! Two words in Greek: aire auton. Now open Luke’s first volume, to the trial before Pilate: they all cried out together, Away with this man (Luke 23:18), and John records the same cry (John 19:15). Luke wrote both books for the same reader (1:1), and he knows exactly what he is doing. He has kept the cry until the last verse of the riot and set it down without comment. Paul shares his Lord’s rejection, in the same city, perhaps within a few hundred yards of where Jesus was condemned.

The passion beneath the arrest. It is the fourth time in this chapter that Luke has laid the passion of Jesus underneath the arrest of Paul, and once you see the pattern you cannot unsee it. Agabus: the Jews will bind him and deliver him into the hands of the Gentiles (v. 11), echoing what Jesus said of himself on the road to this city (Luke 18:32). The room at Caesarea: let the will of the Lord be done (v. 14), the prayer of Gethsemane (Luke 22:42). The charge in the temple: against the people, the law and this place (v. 28), the accusation brought against Stephen and against the Lord himself. And now the crowd’s cry.

What it does not mean. Be careful what we take from that, because a wrong step here would be serious. Paul is not a second saviour, and Luke is not suggesting he is. Nothing Paul suffers atones for anybody. He is not carrying sin; he is carrying a message. The parallel is not redemptive but family likeness: the features of the Father’s firstborn appearing in another son. Jesus had said it plainly: a servant is not greater than his master; if they persecuted me, they will also persecute you (John 15:20). And he had said it about this man in particular, on the day he called him: I will show him how much he must suffer for the sake of my name (9:16). That promise, spoken to Ananias in Damascus about a blind man more than twenty years earlier, is being kept on this staircase.

Being answered. Here is the part that searches us. Paul had asked for this. Writing later from prison, he set out what he wanted more than anything: to know Christ and the power of his resurrection, and to share his sufferings, becoming like him in his death (Philippians 3:10). We are happy to pray the first half. The second half is being answered here, in the form of a mob screaming at him the words they once screamed at his Lord. We ask to be made like Jesus and are surprised at the shape the answer takes. But there is only one Jesus to be made like, and he was despised and rejected, and the road he walked to glory went through a crowd exactly like this one. If we are given even a little of it, we are not being punished. We are being answered.

Does every hardship I face count as suffering for Christ? Not every hardship, but more than we think. Peter makes the distinction: suffering as a murderer or a thief or a meddler is no honour, but if anyone suffers as a Christian, let him not be ashamed but glorify God in that name (1 Peter 4:15–16). The mockery you receive because you will not join in, the promotion lost because you would not lie, the family coldness because you follow Christ: these are sharing in his rejection. Other troubles, sickness and loss and grief, are not persecution, but Christ is with you in them too, and he uses them to make you like himself (Romans 8:28–29). What matters is not to bring suffering on yourself by foolishness, and not to be ashamed of it when it comes for his name.

In a sentence. The crowd followed, shouting, Away with him!

On a Tuesday. To share Christ’s rejection is to share his honour. Do not be ashamed of it. If someone mocks you this week for Christ’s sake, do not retaliate or sulk. Pray for them by name, and thank the Lord quietly that he has counted you worthy to bear a little of the reproach that he bore (5:41).

For worship. When that cry was raised against the Lord Jesus, he had the answer in his hand and would not use it. Twelve legions of angels were within call, and he said so (Matthew 26:53), and then he let the sentence stand. Away with this man, and he went: out of the city he had wept over, past the crowd he had come to save, carrying the beam of his own execution, and he did not open his mouth. The silence of the Lamb of God on that road was not weakness. It was the strongest thing that has ever happened in this world. Paul walked a road his Master had already walked to the end, and the one difference is the one that matters: Paul was pulled out at the top of the stairs, and Christ was not, because there was nobody else who could go the whole way.

verseByVerse.quote: "As Paul was about to be brought into the barracks, he said to the tribune, 'May I say something to you?' And he said, 'Do you know Greek? Are you not the Egyptian, then, who recently stirred up a revolt and led the four thousand men of the Assassins out into the wilderness?'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
As Paul was about to be brought into the barracks, he said to the tribune, “May I say something to you?” And he said, “Do you know Greek? Are you not the Egyptian, then, who recently stirred up a revolt and led the four thousand men of the Assassins out into the wilderness?”

May I say something to you? Consider where that sentence is spoken. Paul is at the top of the barracks stairs, seconds from being swallowed by a Roman fortress. He has been beaten by a mob, chained between two soldiers, and carried up the last flight because he could not walk. And he turns to the officer and asks, in courteous, educated Greek, for permission to speak. Remarkable composure.

Do you know Greek? The tribune is astonished, and his astonishment is the comedy of the scene. He had assumed he was dragging an illiterate agitator out of a temple brawl. One well-formed sentence and his whole assessment of the man collapses.

Are you not the Egyptian, then, who recently stirred up a revolt and led the four thousand men of the Assassins out into the wilderness? This is a real man and a recent manhunt. The historian Josephus tells the story twice: a false prophet from Egypt gathered a following in the wilderness, led them round to the Mount of Olives, and promised that at his command the walls of Jerusalem would fall so they could take the city. The governor Felix sent troops; the movement was cut to pieces; and the Egyptian himself escaped and was never caught. It had happened within the last few years, and the file was still open. So when an unidentified man is pulled out of a temple riot, the tribune reaches for the obvious hypothesis. That tells you what he thought he had in his hands, and explains the two chains. He believed he was holding a terrorist leader with followers somewhere in the hills.

Luke’s accuracy. This verse is a small window onto whether Luke can be trusted. Josephus gives two different figures for the Egyptian’s following: thirty thousand in one work, and in the other an affair in which four hundred were killed and two hundred captured. Luke says four thousand, a sober figure, and he gives them their proper name: the Assassins, sikarioi, the dagger-men, who carried short curved blades under their cloaks and mingled with festival crowds to stab a man and disappear before he fell. Josephus describes them in these very years. That is not a word a later writer, romancing about a period he never lived in, would happen to know. It is the vocabulary of somebody who was in Judea at the time. Luke’s history matches Josephus, and this is his habit everywhere: he gets the ranks right, a proconsul on Cyprus, politarchs at Thessalonica, Asiarchs at Ephesus, a town clerk, and here a tribune. The man who is this careful about the size of a rebel band is the same man who tells you that a tomb outside Jerusalem was empty on the third day, and he expects to be read the same way in both places.

Why should historical details like this matter to my faith? Because Christianity is not a set of timeless ideas that would be just as true if nothing had happened. It rests on events: a man who was crucified under Pontius Pilate, rose on the third day, and appeared to witnesses (1 Corinthians 15:3–8). Luke tells us at the start of his Gospel that he investigated everything carefully so that his reader might have certainty (Luke 1:3–4). When he proves reliable in small things that we can check, it gives us good reason to trust him in the great things we cannot. Your faith rests finally on God’s word, which the Spirit confirms in your heart, but God has given his word in history, and it stands up when the historians come to look.

In a sentence. As he was about to be taken into the barracks, Paul asked the commander if he might say something, and the commander asked if he spoke Greek, and whether he was not the Egyptian who had recently led a revolt and taken four thousand terrorists into the desert.

On a Tuesday. God’s servants are often mistaken for troublemakers. Let your life and your words show who you really are: courteous when you are mistreated, calm when you are misjudged, and ready with a reasoned answer when someone asks (1 Peter 3:15). A misunderstanding is often the doorway to a conversation.

For worship. The mistaken identity was the opening God used. Because the tribune had him wrong, he asked a question; because he asked, Paul answered; because Paul answered, the conversation began that ended with permission to preach. The Lord rules over misunderstandings as surely as over storms. And the true Messiah was mistaken for a rebel too. The crowd chose Barabbas, the man who had been thrown into prison for an insurrection in the city (Luke 23:19), and sent the Prince of Peace to the cross in his place. The guilty rebel walked free while the innocent one died, and that exchange is the gospel Paul is about to preach.
verseByVerse.note: The historian Josephus describes an Egyptian false prophet who led followers to the Mount of Olives a few years earlier and escaped when the Romans attacked. The “Assassins” were extremists who stabbed opponents with hidden daggers in crowds.

verseByVerse.quote: "Paul replied, 'I am a Jew, from Tarsus in Cilicia, a citizen of no obscure city. I beg you, permit me to speak to the people.' And when he had given him permission, Paul, standing on the steps, motioned with his hand to the people. And when there was a great hush, he addressed them in the Hebrew language, saying:"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Paul replied, “I am a Jew, from Tarsus in Cilicia, a citizen of no obscure city. I beg you, permit me to speak to the people.” And when he had given him permission, Paul, standing on the steps, motioned with his hand to the people. And when there was a great hush, he addressed them in the Hebrew language, saying:

I am a Jew, from Tarsus in Cilicia, a citizen of no obscure city. That is a beautifully judged sentence. No obscure city is understatement of the kind an educated Greek speaker would recognise at once as good manners, and it happens to be true. Tarsus was a proud and prosperous city, famous for learning; the geographer Strabo, writing a generation earlier, said its people were so devoted to philosophy and education that they surpassed even Athens and Alexandria. In one clause Paul has told the tribune: I am not your Egyptian, I am a Jew, and I am a man of standing.

What he does not say. Far more striking is what he leaves out. He does not say he is a Roman citizen. He is (22:25). It is the most powerful fact about him in that fortress, and in the next chapter, when the soldiers have stretched him out for a flogging, he will produce it in one quiet question and the tribune will be afraid (22:25–29). He is holding it. He is not asking to be rescued. He is asking for something else.

I beg you, permit me to speak to the people. The people. Look at who that is. A few minutes ago they had him on the ground and were beating him to death. They are still packed at the foot of the stairs, still howling for his blood. A man with a legal trump card in his pocket, standing at the door of safety, uses his one request to ask whether he can go back out and talk to them. Beaten, chained, nearly killed, and his first wish is to preach to those who attacked him. Paul’s whole life had been reorganised around one longing: that his own people might be saved. He wrote that he had great sorrow and unceasing anguish in his heart, and could wish that he himself were accursed and cut off from Christ for the sake of his brothers (Romans 9:1–3). He meant it, and this staircase is the proof.

Paul, standing on the steps, motioned with his hand to the people. Permission is given, and Luke slows everything down for the last picture of the chapter. It is the speaker’s gesture, the one Paul used in the synagogue at Pisidian Antioch (13:16) and will use again before a king (26:1), except that this hand is bruised and chained to a soldier. The prisoner, in chains, on the steps, facing the mob.

And when there was a great hush, he addressed them in the Hebrew language. Thousands of people who were screaming for a lynching a moment before fall silent because a beaten man lifted his hand. Luke lets the silence sit in the sentence. Then a last detail, and it is a courtesy. The Hebrew language here is very probably Aramaic, the language of the street and the kitchen and the bedtime story among the Jews of the land. He could have used Greek and been understood perfectly well. He chooses their mother tongue instead, and it lands: when they heard him speaking it, they became even more quiet (22:2). The last thing he does before he tells them about Jesus is honour them.

Stand back and look. James’s plan has failed. The vow ended in a riot. The collection is not even mentioned. Paul is under arrest, beaten, chained, and has just been carried up a flight of stairs like luggage. Every single thing he had arranged has come apart. And by the last verse he is standing above the largest Jewish crowd he has addressed in years, in total silence, with official Roman permission, about to tell them how he met Jesus of Nazareth on the Damascus road. He did not get the platform he might have asked God for. He got the barracks steps. Years later, from another cell, he wrote the sentence that explains this chapter: what has happened to me has really served to advance the gospel (Philippians 1:12). Luke ends the chapter, in effect, with a colon. Nothing is finished; the page simply turns.

How can I love people who have hurt me badly? Not by pretending the hurt did not happen, and not in your own strength. Paul’s love for this crowd came from somewhere: he had himself once been the one shouting, and Christ had loved him anyway. The more clearly you see how much you have been forgiven, the more room there is in you for those who wrong you (Luke 7:47; Ephesians 4:32). Begin by praying for them, honestly, even if the first prayers are short. Then look for one concrete good you can do or say to them, as the Lord commands (Luke 6:27–28). Love for enemies does not mean trusting the untrustworthy or staying where you are in danger. It means wanting their salvation more than your vindication.

In a sentence. Paul answered that he was a Jew from Tarsus in Cilicia, a citizen of an important city, and asked permission to speak to the people, and when it was given, he stood on the steps and motioned to the crowd, and when they were silent, he spoke to them in Hebrew.

On a Tuesday. Name the people who have most recently hurt you. Then ask honestly what your instinct toward them is: a wall, or a hearing? Love those who hate you, and look for every chance to tell them of Christ, in a language they can hear: their words, their interests, their world. And when your plans have all come apart, look for the steps God has put you on instead.

For worship. This is the love of Christ, showing through a chained man’s raised hand. The Lord Jesus wept over the city that would reject him (Luke 19:41), and on the cross he prayed for the men who were killing him, Father, forgive them, for they know not what they do (Luke 23:34). Paul learned that love from him, on the road where Christ stopped him in mid-persecution and made him a brother. The same mercy that silenced Saul’s rage on the Damascus road now silences a crowd on the temple steps, so that it can hear the name it hated. Christ is still doing this: stilling the noise of his enemies so that they can hear him speak, and saving them.
verseByVerse.note: Tarsus was a proud and prosperous city, known for learning. The “Hebrew language” was probably Aramaic, the everyday language of Jews in Judea.

21.theology: The Will of God and the Path of Suffering. Acts 21 presents with unusual clarity the Reformed conviction that the will of God is not always comfortable, and that knowing it does not mean avoiding what it contains. Paul knows chains await. He goes anyway. His companions know Paul knows. They submit anyway. “Let the will of the Lord be done” is not fatalism — it is the active, willing submission of people who have learned that God’s purposes are worked out through suffering, not around it. This is the theology of Romans 8:28 embodied in a house in Caesarea: all things — including imprisonment, beatings, and the howling of a mob — work together for good for those who love God and are called according to his purpose. Paul’s chains will take him to Rome. God knew this. Paul submitted to it. Rome receives the gospel.
21.examples:
Then: A man walking knowingly toward chains, accompanied by weeping friends who have said everything they can say and now can only pray. A church in Jerusalem that receives the Gentile mission report with joy and then watches its guest arrested in the temple court. The will of the Lord, being done — at great cost, with great grief, toward a great purpose that none of them can yet see fully.

Now: The church in every age must learn the grammar of “let the will of the Lord be done.” It is learned most deeply in the moments when the will of the Lord leads into what we would not choose — illness, loss, rejection, persecution. Paul goes to Jerusalem not because it is easy or because he can see the outcome, but because the Spirit has said go and the Lord has said trust. This is the faith that follows a Lord who himself prayed “not my will, but yours.”

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Paul addresses the crowd as brothers and fathers, and when they hear him speak in their own tongue they grow quieter. He tells them he is a Jew born in Tarsus, raised in Jerusalem and trained precisely in the ancestral law under Gamaliel, as zealous for God as they are. He hunted the Way to the death, arresting men and women, with the authority of the high priest and the council. On the road to Damascus at midday a blinding light flashed round him; he fell and heard a voice asking why he was persecuting him. He asked who was speaking, and the voice answered that it was Jesus of Nazareth. His companions saw the light but did not grasp the voice. Told to go into Damascus to learn what he must do, he was led there blind. Ananias, a devout and respected keeper of the law, came and restored his sight, and told him the God of their fathers had chosen him to know his will, see the Righteous One and be his witness to all people. He urged him to be baptised and have his sins washed away, calling on his name. Later, praying in the temple in Jerusalem, Paul fell into a trance and saw the Lord, who told him to leave quickly because they would not accept his testimony. Paul protested that they knew how he had persecuted believers and had approved Stephen’s death. But the Lord replied that he was sending him far away to the Gentiles.
verseByVerse.theology:
Sovereign Grace, and a Commission Older Than the Convert

Ananias's word for what God did to Saul is appointed — chosen and designated (22:14) — and Paul never forgot it, writing later that God had set me apart before I was born (Gal. 1:15). The light at noon was not God changing his mind about Saul of Tarsus. It was God keeping an appointment made before Saul existed. Nothing in the account belongs to the convert: Christ sought him, struck him down, named him in his mother tongue, blinded him, and told him what he would do. Paul did not find Jesus; Jesus took Paul.

Two guards keep this from being abstract. First, on the timing of the new birth Scripture is deliberately reticent, and we should be too — regeneration is the Spirit's secret work, known by its fruits and not by a stopwatch (see the note at vv. 9–10). Second, on wash away your sins (v. 16), the sign is spoken of in the language of the thing signified, as Scripture habitually does; the blood of Christ does the washing and baptism seals and publishes it, which is exactly how Paul afterwards handled circumcision as a seal of a righteousness already had by faith (Rom. 4:11).

And the chapter's summit is what grace does with a specific, named, unforgettable sin. The man who guarded the garments at Stephen's stoning is sent to the ends of the earth with Stephen's message. That is not grace overlooking a small thing. It is the blood of the Righteous One proving stronger than the blood that was shed.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: A frightened disciple in Damascus was given the address of the man holding warrants for his arrest, and went. He knew his own name was probably on the list. He knocked, walked into the one house in the city where a Christian could be seized on the spot, and said two words before anything had been proved about the blind man sitting there: Brother Saul.

Now: Picture the person whose arrival in your church on Sunday would be hardest to absorb — not a stranger, but someone with a history, and a history with you. Somebody who did real damage and knew what they were doing. Now suppose the Lord has laid hold of them. How long, in practice, before anyone says brother, and means it, and stops watching the door? Ananias managed it in three days, before any evidence of change had been produced, because he understood that the church does not decide who its family is. It recognises whom the Lord has already taken in.

verseByVerse.quote: "'Brothers and fathers, hear the defense that I now make before you.' And when they heard that he was addressing them in the Hebrew language, they became even more quiet. And he said:"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Brothers and fathers, hear the defense that I now make before you. And when they heard that he was addressing them in the Hebrew language, they became even more quiet. And he said:

Meaning first. Acts 22 is Paul’s first defence, spoken to the Jerusalem crowd from the steps of the fortress. He tells his own story: a zealous Jew, trained by Gamaliel, a persecutor of the Way, until Jesus met him on the Damascus road. He stresses everything that would connect with his hearers. They listen, until he says the word Gentiles. Then the riot erupts again. Paul is about to be flogged, and claims his Roman citizenship. Personal testimony, honestly told, is one of the gospel’s great tools; and the chapter shows that Paul’s mission to the Gentiles came from Christ himself. Above all it shows the risen Lord of glory, who calls himself by the name of a despised village, stopping his fiercest enemy on a road and sending him with mercy to the ends of the earth.

Brothers and fathers, hear the defense that I now make before you. Four words in, and he has done something the crowd will not have expected. Brothers and fathers is how Stephen began his defence before the council (7:2), and the young man holding the coats that day was Saul of Tarsus. He is opening his own trial with the dead man’s opening line, and before he finishes he will say Stephen’s name out loud (v. 20). Respectful, even to the mob that just beat him.

A defence that is a story. The word for defence is apologia, the term for a formal answer to a charge, the word that gives us apologetics, a reasoned defence of the faith (1 Peter 3:15). And notice what Paul’s apologia turns out to be. Not a rebuttal of the temple accusation. Not a legal argument, though he has a good one. Not a proof of the resurrection from Scripture, though he could give one. He tells them what happened to him. The most rigorously trained mind in the early church, given one chance to speak to people who have just tried to kill him, gives his testimony.

When they heard that he was addressing them in the Hebrew language, they became even more quiet. Luke measures the room. They were already quiet; chapter 21 ended with a great hush (21:40). Now the silence deepens. Why would the language do that? Because of what they had assumed about him. Paul was known as a Jew from abroad, from Tarsus in Cilicia, and the standing suspicion about such men was that they had gone half Greek. Then he opens his mouth and out comes the Aramaic of the street and the kitchen, fluent and native: their heart language. Their theory about the man dies in the first three syllables. Whatever else he is, he is one of them.

Speaking so they can hear. That courtesy cost Paul nothing and bought him twenty verses of silence from a crowd that had been beating him ten minutes earlier. He could have used Greek, which the tribune would have preferred and which every educated person present could follow. He chose the language they dream in. There is a whole doctrine of communication in that choice, and it is not a technique. Paul is about to ask these people to hear the hardest thing they will ever hear. The gospel does not need to be softened. But the man carrying it can decide whether he will make it as easy as possible to hear, or as hard.

Do I need a dramatic story to give my testimony? No. Paul’s story was dramatic, but what made it a testimony was not the drama; it was that it was true and that it pointed to Christ. A testimony is simply an honest account of what Jesus has done for you: what you were like, how he showed you your need, how you came to trust him, and what has changed. For many believers raised in Christian homes the honest story is quiet: I cannot remember a day when I did not know about Jesus, but I remember when he became mine, and I can tell you what he has been to me since. That is a real testimony, and God uses it. Keep it short, keep Christ at the centre, and keep yourself out of the spotlight.

In a sentence. Paul asked his brothers and fathers to hear his defence, and when they heard him speaking in Hebrew, they became even quieter.

On a Tuesday. Speak to people in a way they can understand, with respect, even when they oppose you. Think of one person who is hostile to your faith, and ask what their language is: what they care about, what words they use, what they fear. Then pray for the chance to tell them, in that language, what Christ has done for you.

For worship. The God who stilled this crowd is the God who stills the raging of the nations (Psalm 65:7). He gave his servant a hearing on the steps of a fortress, in the language of the people’s homes, because he is the God who speaks to sinners where they are. He did it supremely in his Son. The eternal Word took flesh and spoke Aramaic in Galilee, so that we could hear God in a human voice. The Lord does not shout at us from a distance. He comes near and speaks our language, and calls us by name.
verseByVerse.note: Paul’s first defence, to the Jerusalem crowd.

parallels.desc: Stephen’s same opening

verseByVerse.quote: "'I am a Jew, born in Tarsus in Cilicia, but brought up in this city, educated at the feet of Gamaliel according to the strict manner of the law of our fathers, being zealous for God as all of you are this day. I persecuted this Way to the death, binding and delivering to prison both men and women,'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
I am a Jew, born in Tarsus in Cilicia, but brought up in this city, educated at the feet of Gamaliel according to the strict manner of the law of our fathers, being zealous for God as all of you are this day. I persecuted this Way to the death, binding and delivering to prison both men and women,

I am a Jew, born in Tarsus in Cilicia, but brought up in this city. Note the tense first. Not I was a Jew, but I am. More than twenty years after the Damascus road, in front of a crowd that has just accused him of apostasy, the first thing Paul says about himself is in the present tense. Nothing in what follows is a farewell to his people. Then a standard rabbinic biography in three verbs: born, brought up, educated. And the weight falls in the middle. Born abroad, raised in Jerusalem from youth (26:4): this city, the one we are standing in. He is dismantling the assumption underneath the charge, that he is an outsider legislating for Jerusalem from a distance.

Educated at the feet of Gamaliel according to the strict manner of the law of our fathers. At the feet is literal: pupils sat on the floor while the rabbi taught from a raised seat, and Paul is naming the most respected teacher of the age, Gamaliel the Elder, grandson of Hillel, a man this crowd revered. Paul had the best Jewish education available. And Luke has already introduced Gamaliel to us. In chapter 5, when the council wanted the apostles dead, it was Gamaliel who stood up and told them to leave these men alone, for if this plan is of man it will fail, but if it is of God they will not be able to overthrow it, and might even be found opposing God (5:34–39). Paul’s own teacher had told the highest court in Israel to consider that this movement might be from God, and his best student went out with warrants. It is possible to sit at the feet of a wise man for years, absorb his method, honour his name, and miss the one sentence he said that mattered.

Strict. The word means exactness, precision. It is the vocabulary Paul uses of himself in Philippians: as to the law, a Pharisee; as to righteousness under the law, blameless (Philippians 3:5–6; Galatians 1:14). Whatever went wrong in Saul of Tarsus, it was not slackness.

Being zealous for God as all of you are this day. Then the sentence that shows what kind of man is speaking. He credits them. He does not say you think you are zealous, or your so-called zeal. He looks at a mob that has just tried to lynch him and says, in effect: your zeal is real, and it is for God, and I know because it was mine. A gracious point of contact: he does not mock them; he says, I was like you. This is the man who wrote of these same people that they have a zeal for God, but not according to knowledge (Romans 10:2), which is the kindest and the most devastating sentence ever written about religious sincerity, and he could write it because he had been the case study.

I persecuted this Way to the death. Then, without a pause, verse 4: binding and delivering to prison both men and women. To the death: not to the courts, not to the point of inconvenience. And he adds a detail nobody asked for, men and women. Luke said it of him at 8:3, and Paul says it here again. He keeps saying it because it is the detail that indicts him. A man making a real confession does not round the number down. The dreadful thing about this paragraph is that his audience is hearing a list of qualifications. He means it as a charge sheet. Both readings are accurate, and the gap between them is the whole speech.

Is sincerity enough before God? No, and Paul is the proof. He was utterly sincere, disciplined and devout, and he was fighting God. Sincerity tells us how earnestly a person holds a belief; it cannot tell us whether the belief is true. Jesus warned that the hour would come when whoever killed his disciples would think he was offering service to God (John 16:2). What saves is not the strength of our zeal but the object of our faith: Christ himself. That should humble every earnest Christian too. The safeguard is not less zeal but zeal kept open to Scripture, and a readiness to be corrected by it.

In a sentence. Paul said he was a Jew, born in Tarsus but raised in Jerusalem, trained by Gamaliel in the strict law of their fathers, as zealous for God as they were, and had persecuted the Way to the death, arresting and imprisoning men and women.

On a Tuesday. Could you describe the people who are most wrong about Christ in words they would recognise as fair? Paul can, and it is not a debating tactic; it is what a man sounds like when he remembers what he used to be. Before your next conversation with someone who opposes the faith, find one thing about them you can honestly credit, and say it.

For worship. Zeal without knowledge of Christ can do terrible harm, and the Lord in his mercy does not leave the zealous to it. He took the most devout persecutor in Israel and made him the apostle of grace, so that no one could ever say that God saves the worthy. Paul would write that he received mercy as the foremost of sinners, so that in him Jesus Christ might display his perfect patience as an example to those who were to believe (1 Timothy 1:16). The patience that waited for Saul is waiting still for the zealous who do not yet know him, and it is mighty to save.
verseByVerse.note: Gamaliel was the most respected Pharisee teacher of the day; students sat at their teacher’s feet.

verseByVerse.quote: "'as the high priest and the whole council of elders can bear me witness. From them I received letters to the brothers, and I journeyed toward Damascus to take those also who were there and bring them in bonds to Jerusalem to be punished. As I was on my way and drew near to Damascus, about noon a great light from heaven suddenly shone around me.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
as the high priest and the whole council of elders can bear me witness. From them I received letters to the brothers, and I journeyed toward Damascus to take those also who were there and bring them in bonds to Jerusalem to be punished. As I was on my way and drew near to Damascus, about noon a great light from heaven suddenly shone around me.

As the high priest and the whole council of elders can bear me witness. Paul does something here that anyone inventing a story avoids: he names living witnesses who could contradict him. The high priest’s office and the council keep records. He is telling the crowd that his account of his own past is checkable this afternoon, by men who have no reason to protect him. Verifiable facts.

From them I received letters to the brothers, and I journeyed toward Damascus. The brothers here are the Jews of Damascus; Paul still calls his people brothers. And letters is the detail to sit with, because it makes Saul of Tarsus something worse than a hothead. Damascus lay outside Judea, and the only way to reach believers there was through the synagogues, by warrant and correspondence. So Saul applied. Somebody drafted the documents. Somebody sealed them. A journey of about a hundred and forty miles was funded and planned. This was not a riot. It was a filing system. Some of the worst things done to the church in this book are done on paper, in office hours, by men who believed they were serving God and kept proper records of it, which should make every religious institution, including ours, read this verse slowly.

To take those also who were there and bring them in bonds to Jerusalem to be punished. In bonds. Saul travelled to Damascus to put chains on people. He is telling this story from inside a Roman chain, and a chapter ago Agabus tied his own hands with Paul’s belt to show what was coming. Here is where the thread began: the man who set out to bind is bound.

About noon a great light from heaven suddenly shone around me. Then everything stops. Chapter 9 does not mention the hour; Paul supplies it here, and before Agrippa adds that the light was brighter than the sun (26:13). He is not decorating. In Syria at midday the sun is overhead and merciless. Whatever flashed around Saul on that road, it was not the low sun at dawn, not heat-shimmer, not a dream. He was awake, on a road, at noon, on business. Paul names the hour because it closes every ordinary explanation before anyone can offer one. And there is a deeper thing in it. God is light, and in him is no darkness at all (1 John 1:5). The man who believed he was defending the light of Israel met the actual light on a public highway at the brightest hour of the day, and it put his eyes out.

What if I cannot point to a moment like this in my own life? Then you are like most Christians. Paul’s conversion was unique because his calling was unique: he was made an apostle, a witness of the risen Christ (1 Corinthians 15:8). God does not promise lights from heaven to the rest of us, and the absence of one is no sign that he has not called you. Lydia’s heart was opened quietly while she listened by a river (16:14); Timothy learned the Scriptures from childhood (2 Timothy 3:15). The question is not how vividly you remember the beginning, but whether you trust Christ now. The same Lord who flashed around Saul shines in every believer’s heart to give the light of the knowledge of the glory of God in the face of Jesus Christ (2 Corinthians 4:6).

In a sentence. The high priest and council could confirm it, since he got letters from them to the Jews in Damascus and went to bring the believers there back to Jerusalem in chains for punishment, but as he neared Damascus around noon, a great light from heaven suddenly blazed around him.

On a Tuesday. Christianity rests on facts that can be checked; your faith is not a fairy tale. When someone tells you that faith is just a feeling, tell them about a man who named his witnesses, gave the hour, and was ready to be cross-examined. And examine your own paperwork: is there anything you are doing, sincerely and properly and in office hours, that sets you against Christ’s people?

For worship. The light that met Saul was the glory of the risen Lord, the same glory Isaiah saw filling the temple, now shining out of the face of a man. Christ did not wait for his enemy to come looking for him. He came down into the noon of a Syrian road and blazed around a persecutor with warrants in his bag, and the light that blinded him was the beginning of his sight. That is how the Lord saves: he shines into hearts that never asked for him, and says, as at creation, let there be light.

verseByVerse.quote: "'And I fell to the ground and heard a voice saying to me, "Saul, Saul, why are you persecuting me?" And I answered, "Who are you, Lord?" And he said to me, "I am Jesus of Nazareth, whom you are persecuting."'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
And I fell to the ground and heard a voice saying to me, ‘Saul, Saul, why are you persecuting me?’ And I answered, ‘Who are you, Lord?’ And he said to me, ‘I am Jesus of Nazareth, whom you are persecuting.’

Saul, Saul, why are you persecuting me? As in 9:4. Take the doubled name first. When God says a name twice in Scripture it is never filler. Abraham, Abraham, with the knife raised (Genesis 22:11). Moses, Moses, at the bush (Exodus 3:4). Samuel, Samuel, in the dark (1 Samuel 3:10). Martha, Martha (Luke 10:41). Simon, Simon, Satan has demanded to have you (Luke 22:31). It is the address of someone who knows the person and means to stop them where they stand. And it is the Hebrew form of the name, spoken, as Paul tells Agrippa, in the Hebrew language (26:14). The risen Lord of heaven, speaking out of a light brighter than the sun, addresses a man in his mother tongue, which is exactly what Paul is doing for this crowd as he tells the story. He learned it from the Lord who did it to him.

Why are you persecuting me? The question is one of the most theologically loaded sentences in the New Testament. Not why are you persecuting my people, or my church. Me. Jesus had been at the right hand of the Father for some years. Saul had never been one of his followers. And Jesus says: me. Every door Saul kicked in, every woman he dragged out, every prison sentence he arranged, was laid on the body of the Lord of glory as personally as the nails. This is the seed from which much of Paul’s theology grows. He would spend his life writing that the church is the body of Christ, that we are members of one another, that no one ever hated his own flesh but nourishes and cherishes it as Christ does the church (1 Corinthians 12:12–27; Ephesians 5:29–30). He did not construct that doctrine in a study. It was handed to him in one question on a road, and it cost him his sight.

Does Jesus really feel what happens to his people? Yes. He is in heaven, glorified, beyond suffering in his own body, but he is united to his people so closely that what is done to them is done to him. He said the same of the last day: as you did it to one of the least of these my brothers, you did it to me (Matthew 25:40). Two things follow. If a believer in your church is being mistreated, overlooked, gossiped about or frozen out, Christ takes it personally, and he does not grade the offence by how important the person is. And if you are the one suffering, you are not suffering alone or unnoticed. Before Saul had finished his question, heaven had registered every name.

Who are you, Lord? The word can mean no more than sir, and on Saul’s lips at that instant it may have meant little more. But you cannot ask that question of that light and keep the word small. The answer will fill it up.

I am Jesus of Nazareth, whom you are persecuting. Compare the tellings. In chapter 9 the answer is simply I am Jesus (9:5), and before Agrippa the same (26:15). Only here, to a Jerusalem crowd, does Paul include the extra words: of Nazareth. He includes them because that is the name with the sneer in it. Nazareth was a nowhere village in the north, the place that prompted the question whether anything good could come out of it (John 1:46), and Nazarene was the label these very people used for the sect (24:5). The despised man from Nazareth, whom Jerusalem had crucified, is the Lord of glory speaking from heaven. He did not shed his humanity at the ascension, and he is not embarrassed by the village. The man on the throne is the man from Nazareth, and he says so.

In a sentence. He fell to the ground and heard a voice asking why he was persecuting him, and when he asked who it was, the voice said, I am Jesus of Nazareth, whom you are persecuting.

On a Tuesday. Treat every believer you meet this week as Christ treats them: as part of himself. Be slow to criticise, quick to defend, and careful with what you say about Christians who are not in the room. And if you are being mistreated for following him, say it to him in prayer: Lord, they are doing this to you. He already knows.

For worship. Consider him on that road. He had every reason to announce himself by the titles now indisputably his: the Lord, the Son of God, the one seated at the right hand of the Majesty on high, before whom every knee will bow. And out of that light he said: Jesus of Nazareth. The village name. The name that had been a joke. He kept it. He carries the marks of the nails still, and he answers to the name of the town they sneered at, and he will answer to it for ever. Heaven’s glory has a carpenter’s address, and the Lamb who was slain is not ashamed of a single scar.

verseByVerse.quote: "'Now those who were with me saw the light but did not understand the voice of the one who was speaking to me. And I said, "What shall I do, Lord?" And the Lord said to me, "Rise, and go into Damascus, and there you will be told all that is appointed for you to do."'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Now those who were with me saw the light but did not understand the voice of the one who was speaking to me. And I said, ‘What shall I do, Lord?’ And the Lord said to me, ‘Rise, and go into Damascus, and there you will be told all that is appointed for you to do.’

Now those who were with me saw the light but did not understand the voice of the one who was speaking to me. This is the verse people bring as a contradiction, and it deserves a straight answer. Luke, narrating in chapter 9, says the men stood speechless, hearing the voice but seeing no one (9:7). Paul, testifying here, says they saw the light but did not understand the voice. Read carelessly, it looks like a collision. Read carefully, it is two halves of one experience. Take the seeing first: they saw no one, and they saw the light. There was a blaze of light that everyone saw, and inside it a Person whom only Saul saw. Then the hearing. The Greek verb akouō can mean to hear a sound or to understand speech, and with a slight difference of construction Luke uses it both ways. They heard, but did not understand. You do not need Greek to know the difference. Stand next to someone on a phone call: you hear a voice perfectly well, and not a word of what it says. Everyone on the Damascus road heard something. One man heard words.

Inside the light and hearing only weather. Now stay with the picture, because the resolution is not the point. There were several men in that light. They all saw the brightness and heard the sound. They were close enough to catch Saul as he went down and to lead him by the hand into Damascus. And nothing whatever happened to them. Not one is named. Not one is heard of again. Nearness to revelation is not revelation. You can sit in the same pew, under the same preaching, singing the same words, close enough to touch someone whom God is at that moment laying hold of, and hear only a noise. He who has ears to hear, let him hear, and the reason that is a warning rather than a truism is standing on the Damascus road, holding Saul’s arm.

What shall I do, Lord? Then Saul speaks a sentence he had never spoken before. The question of a new disciple: total surrender. Lord: he has a new master. Here was a man who had known exactly what to do for years. He had a programme, a mandate, letters in his bag, a route, a list of names, and the backing of the highest religious authority in the world. In one question all of it is handed over. He does not ask what has happened, or whether the letters are still valid. He asks for orders.

There you will be told all that is appointed for you to do. Look at the answer, because it is deliberately not enough. Rise, go into Damascus, the city he had come to raid, and wait to be told. Appointed: his task was already set by God. But he is not given the plan: not the journeys, not the letters, not Rome. That is very nearly always the arrangement. God gives the next step and withholds the itinerary, and the withholding is not stinginess. Had Saul been handed his whole assignment on that road, shipwrecks and beatings and cells included, he would have received it as information. Instead he received it as obedience, one instruction at a time, from a Lord he was learning to trust.

Was Paul born again at this moment? We are not told, and we should not pretend to know what Scripture does not say. Luke tells Paul’s conversion as a connected whole: the encounter on the road, three days of blindness and prayer (9:9, 11), then Ananias, the filling with the Spirit, and baptism (9:17–18; 22:16). Regeneration is the Spirit’s secret work, known with certainty only to God; we see its fruits, not its moment. What we can see is that by verse 10 Paul calls Jesus Lord, surrenders his whole programme, asks for orders and obeys, and soon is found praying, all marks of a heart already being turned by grace. Since the new birth produces faith and repentance, it is reasonable to think the Spirit was already at work beneath that submission. What Scripture leaves unclear, the when, it more than makes up for in what it makes blazingly clear, the who. Christ sought the persecutor, struck him down, named him, and summoned him. Paul did not find Jesus; Jesus seized Paul.

In a sentence. His companions saw the light but did not understand the voice speaking to him, and he asked what he should do, and the Lord told him to get up and go into Damascus, where he would be told all that had been appointed for him.

On a Tuesday. Ask each day: what shall I do, Lord? Then do the next thing he has plainly shown you in his word, without waiting for the whole map. And if you have spent years near the light, in Christian homes and churches, ask honestly whether you have heard words or only weather. Pray that he would speak to you, not only near you.

For worship. Only the Lord could do what happened on that road. He took a man whose whole life was a programme against him and, in a single question, turned him into a servant asking for orders. That is the sovereign mercy of Christ, who has mercy on whom he has mercy (Romans 9:15), and who does not wait to be found. He had appointed Saul’s work before Saul existed, and he would see every part of it done. The Lord who gives his servants the next step has already walked every step of the road ahead of them.
verseByVerse.note: His companions saw the light and heard a sound but could not make out the words.

verseByVerse.quote: "'And since I could not see because of the brightness of that light, I was led by the hand by those who were with me, and came into Damascus. And one Ananias, a devout man according to the law, well spoken of by all the Jews who lived there,"
verseByVerse.commentary:
And since I could not see because of the brightness of that light, I was led by the hand by those who were with me, and came into Damascus. And one Ananias, a devout man according to the law, well spoken of by all the Jews who lived there,

I could not see because of the brightness of that light. Blinded by glory. Then Luke’s word: led by the hand (cheiragōgoumenos), the verb for guiding a small child or a blind beggar through a crowd. Read that against what Paul has just told us he was doing. He was on his way to Damascus to bring believers back in bonds. He arrives in Damascus led by the hand, helpless, unable to find a door. He had come to make people dependent, and he entered the city more dependent than any of them. Chapter 9 fills in what these verses pass over: three days without sight, without food or drink, in a stranger’s house, praying (9:9, 11). Everything Saul had relied on, his learning, his warrants, his standing, his certainty, was taken off him in an afternoon, and what was left sat in the dark and prayed.

And one Ananias, a devout man according to the law, well spoken of by all the Jews who lived there. Watch how Paul introduces him to this audience. When Luke introduced the same man in chapter 9 he called him simply a disciple at Damascus (9:10). Paul, standing before a Jerusalem crowd that believes he abandoned Moses, stresses Ananias’s Jewish piety rather than his Christian discipleship: devout, law-observant, and well spoken of by all the Jews who lived there. Not by the church. By the synagogue, by neighbours who did not share his faith. A law-keeping Jew, respected by Jews, brought God’s message to him.

Same story, different rooms. Paul is shaping his testimony for the room he is in. The story is the same each time, but before a king in chapter 26 he leaves Ananias out altogether, because a provincial holy man means nothing to Agrippa; here he makes him the hinge, because to this crowd he means everything. Truthful preaching is not the same as identical preaching. Wise testimony stresses what connects with its hearers, without changing a single fact.

Is it dishonest to tell my story differently to different people? No, as long as everything you say is true. Paul never changed the facts. He chose, from among true things, the ones that would help a particular audience understand. We all do this: you explain your work one way to a child and another to a colleague. What would be dishonest is inventing details, hiding what you believe in order to be accepted, or telling one group what you would deny to another. Paul became all things to all people (1 Corinthians 9:22), but he never became a liar. Ask of every version of your testimony: is it true, and does it point to Christ?

A good name outside the church. Notice the standard Paul reaches for. The qualification he cites is not Ananias’s gifts or his courage or his visions, all of which he had. It is his reputation among people outside the church. Paul would later write that an overseer must be well thought of by outsiders (1 Timothy 3:7), and perhaps here is where he learned it: the first Christian ever to lay hands on him was a man whose unbelieving neighbours had nothing bad to say about him.

In a sentence. Blinded by the brilliance of the light, he was led by the hand into Damascus, where a man named Ananias, devout in keeping the law and highly respected by all the Jews there, came to him.

On a Tuesday. Be thoughtful in how you tell your story, and stress what helps your hearers. And ask what your unbelieving neighbours would say about you if someone asked. Ananias’s good name opened a door for the gospel; so can yours, in the small honesties of paying bills, keeping promises and treating people kindly.

For worship. The Lord humbles before he lifts up. He led the proud persecutor into Damascus by the hand like a child, and in that darkness Saul began to see. That is the gracious way of our God, who brings the blind by a way they do not know and turns the darkness before them into light (Isaiah 42:16). And he chose an ordinary, devout, frightened man to be the instrument. The Lord delights to use quiet servants with good names, so that the glory goes to him alone.

verseByVerse.quote: "'came to me, and standing by me said to me, "Brother Saul, receive your sight." And at that very hour I received my sight and saw him.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
came to me, and standing by me said to me, ‘Brother Saul, receive your sight.’ And at that very hour I received my sight and saw him.

Brother Saul, receive your sight. The tender greeting (9:17). They are the first words the church of Jesus Christ ever addressed to the apostle Paul, and they are worth standing still for. Consider what it took to say them. Chapter 9 records what Ananias said when the Lord first gave him the address: that he had heard from many how much evil this man had done to the saints in Jerusalem, and that he had authority to bind all who call on the Lord’s name (9:13–14). Ananias knew who was sitting in that house. He knew about the letters, and that his own name was very likely on them. To knock on that door was to walk into the one place in Damascus where a Christian could be arrested on the spot.

Brother. He came anyway. And the first thing out of his mouth was not a caution, not a condition, not an interview, not a probation. Brother. Think about the Christian voices Saul had silenced, beginning with Stephen’s, outside Jerusalem, praying for the men who were killing him. That was the church’s last word to Saul: a dying man asking God not to hold this sin against them. And the next word the church says to him, three days into his blindness, is brother. Between those two words there is no negotiation, no restitution, no proving period. Ananias calls him brother because the risen Christ has claimed him, and that settles it. The church does not decide who its family is; it recognises whom the Lord has already taken in.

How quickly should a church trust a notorious sinner who professes faith? Welcome and trust are not the same, and Scripture gives us both. Ananias welcomed Saul at once as a brother, because the Lord had told him plainly that Saul was his chosen instrument (9:15). The Jerusalem church, without that word, was afraid of him until Barnabas vouched for him (9:26–27). Today we have no vision to tell us, so the church receives a professing believer warmly, as a brother, while positions of trust, leadership or access to the vulnerable wait for the fruit of a changed life (1 Timothy 3:6, 10). Where someone has abused others, wise safeguards are an act of love for everyone, including him. But the greeting should not wait. Say brother, and mean it.

And at that very hour I received my sight and saw him. Instant. And the first thing Saul’s restored eyes rest on is the face of a man he had come to Damascus to put in chains. He is looking at his intended victim, and his intended victim is calling him family. He had been blind for three days. He had been blind a good deal longer than that: a man of formidable learning who could not see the one at the centre of his own Scriptures. Both blindnesses ended in the same room, and an ordinary, obedient disciple was the instrument of it.

In a sentence. Ananias stood beside him and said, Brother Saul, receive your sight, and at that moment he could see him.

On a Tuesday. A kind word can open blind eyes; speak one today. Picture the person whose arrival in your church on Sunday would be hardest to absorb: not a stranger, but someone with a history, and a history with you. Now imagine the Lord has laid hold of them. Ananias said brother in three days, to the man who had come to arrest him. Pray that you would be ready to do the same.

For worship. Brother. It is the word Christ himself is not ashamed to say to us. He who sanctifies and those who are sanctified all have one source, and that is why he is not ashamed to call them brothers (Hebrews 2:11). He said it first, to people who had betrayed him, on the morning of his resurrection: go to my brothers (Matthew 28:10). Every welcome the church gives a forgiven enemy is an echo of the welcome the Son of God gave us, when we were the ones with warrants against him.

verseByVerse.quote: "'And he said, "The God of our fathers appointed you to know his will, to see the Righteous One and to hear a voice from his mouth; for you will be a witness for him to everyone of what you have seen and heard."'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
And he said, ‘The God of our fathers appointed you to know his will, to see the Righteous One and to hear a voice from his mouth; for you will be a witness for him to everyone of what you have seen and heard.

The God of our fathers appointed you. Ananias’s first phrase, and Paul repeats it to this crowd because it is the hinge of his whole defence. Not a new God, but Israel’s God: the God of Abraham, Isaac and Jacob, the phrase Peter used at Solomon’s Portico (3:13) and before the council (5:30), and Stephen at the bush (7:32). The charge against Paul is apostasy. His answer is that the God who commissioned him is the God his accusers were named after. Appointed (procheirizomai): chose beforehand, selected. Sovereign choice. Paul never forgot it; he wrote that God had set him apart before he was born and called him by his grace (Galatians 1:15). The light at noon was not God changing his mind about Saul. It was God keeping an appointment made before Saul existed, which is worth knowing if your own conversion looked, from the inside, like an accident.

To know his will, to see the Righteous One and to hear a voice from his mouth. The Righteous One is a title for the Messiah, and Paul had heard it before. Peter used it in the temple: you denied the Holy and Righteous One (3:14). And Stephen used it in the last speech of his life, in the sentence that got him killed: they killed those who announced beforehand the coming of the Righteous One, whom you have now betrayed and murdered (7:52). Saul heard him say it. That title went into his ears from a dying man he was helping to execute, and the next time he heard it, it was being given to the one who had just spoken to him from heaven. Grace is not tidy about how it gets a word into a man.

Seeing and hearing. Those two verbs are the foundation of Paul’s apostleship. Am I not an apostle? Have I not seen Jesus our Lord? he would ask (1 Corinthians 9:1), and last of all, as to one untimely born, Christ appeared also to him (1 Corinthians 15:8). His authority does not rest on his intellect, his zeal or his results. It rests on the fact that he saw the risen Christ with his own eyes and heard him speak, which is what an apostle is.

For you will be a witness for him to everyone of what you have seen and heard. A witness, martys, the word that came to mean martyr, partly because of the man Paul watched die. A witness in court is not asked what he thinks or what he finds meaningful. He is asked what he saw and heard. That is the whole job, and it is why the least articulate Christian can do it. And listen to one word, because Paul is being deliberate and the crowd has not noticed yet. To everyone: not just Jews. Not a syllable about Gentiles, not yet. The scope is already total, said in the widest and softest form available, and they let it go by. He will say it again, six verses from now, in the word they cannot bear. He is telling them the same thing twice: once so that they can hear it, and once so that they cannot.

Are there apostles today? Not in the sense Paul was one. An apostle in this full sense had to have seen the risen Lord and been sent by him personally (1:21–22; 1 Corinthians 9:1), and Paul calls himself the last to whom Christ appeared (1 Corinthians 15:8). The apostles laid the foundation of the church once, and we build on it through their writings in the New Testament (Ephesians 2:20). Missionaries and church planters are sometimes loosely called apostles, meaning sent ones, but no one today carries the authority of Peter or Paul. That is not a loss. It means the voice of the apostles still speaks, unchanged, every time we open the Bible.

In a sentence. Ananias said the God of their fathers had chosen him to know his will, see the Righteous One and hear him speak, for he would be his witness to everyone of what he had seen and heard.

On a Tuesday. You too are a witness to everyone of what you have seen and heard of Christ: in Scripture, in answered prayer, in his patience with you. Nobody will cross-examine you on systematic theology, and if they do, you may say you do not know. What you have seen and heard is yours to give. Give one piece of it to someone this week.

For worship. The Righteous One. Stephen died saying the name, and the persecutor who heard it was brought to see the one it named. He is the only righteous man who ever lived, righteous in every thought and deed, and he was betrayed and murdered by the unrighteous, and then rose to make the unrighteous righteous. For our sake God made him to be sin who knew no sin, so that in him we might become the righteousness of God (2 Corinthians 5:21). The God of our fathers appointed Saul to see that face. One day all his people will see it, and his name will be on their foreheads.
verseByVerse.note: “The Righteous One” is a title for the Messiah.

verseByVerse.quote: "'And now why do you wait? Rise and be baptized and wash away your sins, calling on his name.' When I had returned to Jerusalem and was praying in the temple, I fell into a trance"
verseByVerse.commentary:
And now why do you wait? Rise and be baptized and wash away your sins, calling on his name.’ When I had returned to Jerusalem and was praying in the temple, I fell into a trance

And now why do you wait? Urgency. You have sat in this dark room for three days, Ananias is saying. That is long enough. Stop being a secret.

Rise and be baptized and wash away your sins, calling on his name. In Greek: having risen, be baptised, and wash away your sins, calling on his name. This is one of the sentences people are given when someone wants to persuade them that the water itself does the saving, so it needs answering carefully. Start with what the sentence does not say. It does not say the water washes. It holds four things together, and the last clause is not decoration: calling on his name is what the whole sentence hangs on. The washing of sins is linked with calling on his name. It is faith, calling on Christ, that receives forgiveness (2:21; Romans 10:13); baptism is its outward sign and seal.

Where Christians differ: does baptism wash away sins? Some take this verse to teach that the water of baptism itself removes sin. Roman Catholic, Lutheran and some other Christians read it this way, pointing also to Peter’s words at Pentecost (2:38) and to the statement that baptism now saves you (1 Peter 3:21). Verdict: Saul had already met the risen Lord, called him Lord, and been addressed as brother before his baptism. Sins are washed away by the blood of Christ (1 John 1:7; Revelation 1:5), received by faith; baptism is the God-given picture and seal of that washing (1 Peter 3:21: not the removal of dirt from the body, but the appeal to God for a good conscience). Baptism should not be delayed, but it is not the cause of forgiveness.

Let Paul interpret Paul. Our best interpreter here is the man who obeyed this very command. If anybody had reason to believe his sins went down a Damascus drain, it was Saul of Tarsus. What did he write afterwards? That Abraham received circumcision as a sign and seal of the righteousness he had by faith while he was still uncircumcised (Romans 4:11): the sign certifies a righteousness already given; it does not manufacture it. That Christ did not send him to baptise but to preach the gospel (1 Corinthians 1:17), an impossible sentence for a man who thought baptism washed sins away. And that he could barely remember whom he had baptised in Corinth (1 Corinthians 1:14–16), which is not how anyone speaks about the thing that saves. Luke’s own book agrees. In Cornelius’s house the Holy Spirit fell on Gentiles while Peter was still speaking, and only afterwards did anyone bring water (10:44–48). And the dying thief, who could never be baptised, was promised paradise that day (Luke 23:43).

The sign and the thing signified. So what is Ananias saying? Scripture often speaks of the sign in the language of the thing signified, because God does not mean the two to be pulled apart. Baptism is the God-appointed sign of a washing that only the blood of Christ performs, and to be baptised is to be publicly and visibly joined to the one who did the washing. Ananias is not telling Saul how to get clean. He is telling a man who has been made clean to go and say so, in water, before witnesses. And notice the order: Saul believed, and then was baptised. That is the pattern throughout Acts, and it is why we baptise those who profess faith in Christ, while gladly honouring paedobaptist brothers who read the covenant signs differently and love the same Saviour.

I believe in Christ but have never been baptised, so does it matter? Yes, it matters, though not because your salvation hangs on the water. Christ commanded his disciples to be baptised (Matthew 28:19), and every believer in Acts was baptised promptly after believing, often the same day. Baptism is the Lord’s appointed way for you to confess him publicly, to be marked as belonging to his people, and to receive the strengthening of faith he gives through it. Staying unbaptised is like keeping a wedding ring in the drawer: the marriage is real, but you are hiding it. Speak to your pastor or elders this week. For a Pharisee trained under Gamaliel, baptism was the point of no return. It is meant to be that for us, too.

When I had returned to Jerusalem and was praying in the temple, I fell into a trance. Then Paul moves the story to a place his accusers will not expect. Read that before this crowd. He is on trial for defiling the temple. And he tells them that his commission, the one they are about to riot over, was given to him inside that building, while he was praying. Not in Damascus, not among Gentiles. In the temple, in the middle of Jewish devotion, doing exactly what a devout Jew does. He had not abandoned it; he honoured it. A vision, given to a man at prayer. It is the most disarming thing he could have said, and it is simply true. The God they think he has abandoned met him in their own house.

In a sentence. Ananias asked what he was waiting for, and told him to get up, be baptised and wash his sins away, calling on the Lord’s name; and when Paul returned to Jerusalem and was praying in the temple, he fell into a trance.

On a Tuesday. If you believe and have not been baptised, why wait? And if you have been, ask whether there is anything else in your following of Christ that you have kept unofficial: not unbelieved, but unannounced. A faith your colleagues have never had to notice, a repentance nobody has been told about, an obedience still pending because going public would cost something. Ananias’s question is the whole application.

For worship. Saul’s sins were not vague. He had faces in his memory, people whose doors he had broken, and Stephen’s blood, and he was told that the whole account could be washed. Not managed, not offset by a life of service, but washed, until the stain could not be found. That is what the blood of Jesus Christ does. It does not negotiate with sin or file it somewhere out of sight. It removes it. The man who guarded the coats at a murder was made as clean as if he had never touched them, by the blood of the Righteous One whose people he had been hunting. There is nothing in the universe like that blood. It has never met a stain it could not lift, and it never will.

verseByVerse.quote: "'and saw him saying to me, "Make haste and get out of Jerusalem quickly, because they will not accept your testimony about me." And I said, "Lord, they themselves know that in one synagogue after another I imprisoned and beat those who believed in you."'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
and saw him saying to me, ‘Make haste and get out of Jerusalem quickly, because they will not accept your testimony about me.’ And I said, ‘Lord, they themselves know that in one synagogue after another I imprisoned and beat those who believed in you.

Make haste and get out of Jerusalem quickly, because they will not accept your testimony about me. The Lord’s instruction is blunt, and it is negative: they will not have it, so go. Jesus himself told Paul to leave Jerusalem. This is a new detail; Acts 9 tells us that the believers sent him away because of a plot against his life (9:29–30). Both are true. Luke gives the human side there; Paul gives the divine side here.

Lord, they themselves know that in one synagogue after another I imprisoned and beat those who believed in you. And Paul argues. That is worth noticing, because it is not what we expect from a man in a trance in the temple. He does not fall on his face and say yes. He puts a case, and it is a good one. His argument is that his testimony is uniquely credible in this city, because here they know what he was. Anywhere else, a preacher claiming that Jesus rose is a man making a claim. In Jerusalem, the man saying it is the man they hired to stop it. They have the paperwork. If a change of that size, in that man, before the people who commissioned him, will not persuade them, what could? He thought his conversion would convince them. The Lord says no.

A good plan refused. Hold on to that, because this is one of the great uncomfortable passages about guidance. Paul’s reasoning is not selfish. Jerusalem is the most dangerous city on earth for him, and he knows it. He is offering the Lord the most strategically intelligent use of his own conversion, and the answer is: get out, quickly. So the no is not a verdict on the quality of the plan. Sometimes God’s refusal has nothing to do with whether your reasoning was sound. He has a different map, a larger one, and you are not being shown it. And watch where the refusal took him: to Tarsus, Antioch, Cyprus, Galatia, Macedonia, Achaia, Asia, and in the end, in chains, to Rome. The whole Gentile mission flows from a no that Paul argued against.

Is it wrong to argue with God in prayer? Not if it is the honest pleading of a child who will still obey. Abraham pleaded for Sodom (Genesis 18:22–33), Moses argued for Israel (Exodus 32:11–14), and the psalms are full of complaint and reasoning. God invites us to bring him our reasons and our longings. What makes Paul’s prayer godly is what he does next: when the Lord answers, he goes. Arguing becomes sin when it turns into refusal, or into the sulking assumption that God owes us an explanation. Pour out your case; then say, as Paul effectively did, your will be done, and pack your bags.

The experiment, run at last. One more thing makes this speech remarkable. What Paul is doing right now, on the barracks steps, is making that same argument. He has told this crowd about Gamaliel, about the letters, about the imprisoning and the beating. His whole case is the one he put to the Lord in the trance, being tried at last before the very audience the Lord said would not accept it. Twenty years later the experiment is finally being run. Three verses from now we find out who was right.

In a sentence. In the vision, the Lord told him to leave Jerusalem quickly, because they would not accept his testimony, and Paul answered that they knew he had gone from synagogue to synagogue imprisoning and beating believers.

On a Tuesday. There is an ache most Christians know and few say aloud: the good thing you were not permitted to do. The ministry you were suited for and were not given. The person you were sure you could reach, from whom God moved you away. Name it before the Lord. Then look at where his no has taken you instead, and thank him for the larger map you cannot yet see.

For worship. Our hopes for how God will use us are not always his plans, and his plans are always better. The Lord who said no to Paul in the temple was sending him to the nations, to us. Every Gentile believer in every century owes something to that refusal. And behind it stands the Father who once said no to his own Son’s prayer that the cup might pass, because a greater salvation was coming through the cross. Our God does not refuse us because he is careless with our desires. He refuses us because he is bringing many sons to glory, and he knows the way.

verseByVerse.quote: "'And when the blood of Stephen your witness was being shed, I myself was standing by and approving and watching over the garments of those who killed him.' And he said to me, "Go, for I will send you far away to the Gentiles."'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
And when the blood of Stephen your witness was being shed, I myself was standing by and approving and watching over the garments of those who killed him.’ And he said to me, ‘Go, for I will send you far away to the Gentiles.’

And when the blood of Stephen your witness was being shed. He is still arguing his case to the Lord, and this is the evidence he offers. Not his training. Not his zeal. The worst thing he ever did. Witness (martys): the ordinary courtroom word, the same one used of Paul’s own calling five verses ago (v. 15). Only later did the church use it to mean someone killed for his testimony, and it came to mean that because of days like this one. Stephen was the first.

I myself was standing by and approving and watching over the garments of those who killed him. Luke gives three verbs and Paul does not soften one of them. Standing by: present, close enough to see it. Approving: not swept along, not silently appalled, but agreeing. Watching over the garments: he held the coats. It is the smallest job at the scene, the one that needs no strength and takes no aim, and it is the one he names. A man managing his own guilt reaches for the version of the story in which his part was marginal. Paul does the opposite. He understands that the man who holds the coats is not on the edge of the stoning. He is in it, making it easier, wanting the outcome. Paul never forgot it (1 Corinthians 15:9; 1 Timothy 1:13). Grace does not erase memory, but it removes guilt.

If God has forgiven me, why do I still remember what I did? Because forgiveness is not amnesia. God promises to remember our sins no more (Hebrews 8:12), meaning he will never hold them against us; he does not promise that we will forget. Paul remembered Stephen for the rest of his life, and the memory did not crush him.
