These are the custodians of the law that says you shall not murder and you shall not bear false witness, and their recorded response is silence and then cooperation.

Not the blow but the memo. Notice what the council is asked to contribute. Not the ambush or the weapon, but a letter: a perfectly ordinary official request that Paul be brought down for further questioning, accurate in form, innocent on paper, and fatal. That is how respectable people take part in evil, and it is nearly always how. Not the blow, but the memo. Not the lie, but the phrasing that lets the lie work. The offer never comes labelled. It comes as a small administrative favour for people who feel strongly about something.

How might I be complicit in wrong without realising it? By the small things that make someone else’s wrong possible. Signing off a report you know is misleading. Wording a reference to hide what you know. Staying silent in a meeting where someone is being treated unjustly. Forwarding a rumour. Looking away from abuse because raising it would be awkward for the organisation. Scripture holds us responsible not only for what we do but for the evil we enable or excuse (Proverbs 24:11–12; Ephesians 5:11). Ask the Lord to show you any piece of paper you have signed, sentence you have worded, or silence you have kept that made something possible you would never have done with your own hands. Then put it right if you can.

In a sentence. More than forty men were in this plot, and they went to the chief priests and elders and told them they had sworn a solemn oath not to eat until they had killed Paul.

On a Tuesday. In the next meeting you sit in, at work, at church, in a committee, listen for the small requests that would make something wrong possible. Be the elder who walks out, or the one who says, gently and plainly, this is wrong.

For worship. Forty men vowed to kill Paul; one promise from Christ kept him alive. The Lord laughs at the plots of the wicked, for he sees that their day is coming (Psalm 37:13). And he had already turned the greatest plot of these same chief priests, the plot against his Son, into the salvation of the world. What they meant for evil, God meant for good. Our God is not outnumbered by forty, or by four thousand. One word from his mouth outweighs every oath sworn against his people.

parallels.desc: Saul’s rash oath

verseByVerse.quote: "'Now therefore you, along with the council, give notice to the tribune to bring him down to you, as though you were going to determine his case more exactly. And we are ready to kill him before he comes near.' Now the son of Paul's sister heard of their ambush, so he went and entered the barracks and told Paul."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Now therefore you, along with the council, give notice to the tribune to bring him down to you, as though you were going to determine his case more exactly. And we are ready to kill him before he comes near.” Now the son of Paul’s sister heard of their ambush, so he went and entered the barracks and told Paul.

Give notice to the tribune to bring him down to you, as though you were going to determine his case more exactly. A trap, using a fake legal hearing. The forms of justice are being used as the bait for murder.

And we are ready to kill him before he comes near. An ambush in the narrow streets between the fortress and the council chamber.

Now the son of Paul’s sister heard of their ambush. Out of nowhere, Paul has family. This is the only mention of Paul’s immediate family in the New Testament, and it lasts seven verses. He had a sister. She had a son. They were in Jerusalem. That is the whole of it: no names, no explanation, and after verse 22 the young man walks out of Scripture. We know nothing else about his sister or nephew. We do not know whether the boy was a believer, or how he heard the plan: whether he was in the wrong room at the right moment, or whether his family’s standing meant plotters spoke freely in front of him. And there is a shadow over the scene from Paul’s own letters. He told the Philippians that for Christ’s sake he had suffered the loss of all things (Philippians 3:8). For a Pharisee of his pedigree, that often meant a family. Perhaps his family had not wholly disowned him; perhaps this boy crossed Jerusalem to save an uncle his household had cast off.

So he went and entered the barracks and told Paul. Brave: he risked the conspirators’ anger. What he did could not be more ordinary: he heard something, walked to the barracks, and said it aloud to the right person. Now weigh the two sides, because Luke has arranged them for exactly that. On one side: forty men, a sworn oath, the cooperation of the chief priests and elders, the machinery of the Sanhedrin. On the other: one unnamed young man who overheard a conversation. The young man wins, not narrowly but completely. The plot never gets near Paul.

Is God really involved in small coincidences like this? Yes. Nothing happens by chance. Scripture teaches that God governs all his creatures and all their actions, down to the fall of a sparrow and the hairs on our heads (Matthew 10:29–30; Westminster 5.1). Usually he does it not by miracles but through ordinary means: someone in a particular room at a particular hour, and then having the nerve to speak. That is what providence looks like from the inside. So when you happen to hear something, or notice something, or find yourself near enough to help, do not dismiss it as coincidence. Ask whether this is the moment God has placed you for, and act.

In a sentence. The plotters asked the council to request the commander to bring Paul down, pretending to examine his case more carefully, while they waited to kill him on the way, but Paul’s nephew heard of the ambush, went into the barracks and told Paul.

On a Tuesday. God uses ordinary people, even young ones, to fulfil his promises; be ready to be used. Most Christians quietly believe their life is too small to matter. Almost nobody gets to be Paul. Nearly everybody gets to be the nephew: the one who knows something, or is standing near enough to act, and has about a minute to decide whether to get involved. Decide now that you will.

For worship. The whole back half of Acts, Caesarea, the appeal to Caesar, the voyage, the two years preaching in Rome, and humanly speaking the letters written in that custody, runs through one boy’s decision to walk across a city. That is how our God works. He hides his great purposes in small faithful acts, so that the glory belongs to him. He chose a manger in Bethlehem and a boy’s five loaves, and he chose an unnamed nephew in Jerusalem. The Lord who promised Rome kept his word through a young man who was never named, and whose name is written in heaven.
verseByVerse.note: This is the only mention of Paul’s family in Jerusalem.

verseByVerse.quote: "Paul called one of the centurions and said, 'Take this young man to the tribune, for he has something to tell him.' So he took him and brought him to the tribune and said, 'Paul the prisoner called me and asked me to bring this young man to you, as he has something to say to you.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Paul called one of the centurions and said, “Take this young man to the tribune, for he has something to tell him.” So he took him and brought him to the tribune and said, “Paul the prisoner called me and asked me to bring this young man to you, as he has something to say to you.”

Paul called one of the centurions. Read what Paul does not do, because it is as instructive as what he does. He has in his pocket the most extraordinary assurance any man in that building could hold. Twelve hours earlier the risen Lord stood beside him in the dark and told him he would testify in Rome. Paul knows that forty men with knives are wasting their time. He could reasonably have done nothing: thanked the boy, sent him home, and waited for God to keep his word. Plenty of Christians have mistaken that for faith. Instead he calls a centurion, working the chain of command like a man who knows how a garrison runs: not to the tribune, which a prisoner cannot do, but to the duty officer, with a short, calm request.

God ordains the means as well as the end. Paul trusts God’s promise, and uses ordinary means. This is the man who, on a sinking ship, having been told by an angel that every soul aboard would survive, saw the sailors lowering the lifeboat and told the centurion that unless these men stayed in the ship, they could not be saved (27:31). He believed the promise absolutely, and he also spoke up. Faith in God’s sovereignty does not mean doing nothing. God promised Rome; Paul still acted wisely. The promise of God is not an alternative to sensible action; it is what makes sensible action possible without panic. A man who truly believes he cannot fail is free to be thoroughly practical, because he is no longer trying to save himself by his competence.

If God is sovereign, why should I bother taking precautions or making plans? Because the God who decides the end also decides the means, and our actions are among his means. He promised Hezekiah fifteen more years and also told him to put a fig poultice on his boil (Isaiah 38:5, 21). He has appointed that the hungry are fed through work, that the sick are healed through doctors and medicine, that sinners are saved through preaching. Trusting God means doing the wise thing and then leaving the outcome to him, without either panic or presumption. Lock your door, see your doctor, plan your budget, and pray, and you will find that faith and prudence are not rivals but friends.

Paul the prisoner. The centurion’s phrase is unintended testimony. He identifies Paul by his status, the prisoner, and in the same breath reports that the prisoner gave him an instruction and he carried it out. An officer of the Roman army has just run an errand for a man in chains, and does not seem to notice anything odd about it. There is an authority that has nothing to do with position, and it tends to show itself when position has been stripped away. Paul later called himself a prisoner of Christ Jesus (Ephesians 3:1; Philemon 1): not Rome’s prisoner, but Christ’s.

In a sentence. Paul called a centurion and asked him to take the young man to the commander, since he had something to tell him, and the centurion did, saying Paul the prisoner had asked him to bring the young man.

On a Tuesday. Trusting God and acting wisely go together; use the means he gives. Is there something you have been leaving to God that he has put within your power to act on: a conversation to have, a letter to write, a precaution to take? Do it today, calmly, and trust him with the rest.

For worship. Look at the calm of it. There is no panic in these verses, no drama, no pleading, no announcement that God spoke to him in the night. Just: take this young man up; he has something to say. The prisoner is the calmest man in the barracks, because his Lord has spoken. That is the peace of God that surpasses all understanding, guarding hearts and minds in Christ Jesus (Philippians 4:7). It does not come from knowing that everything will be easy. It comes from knowing whose prisoner you are.

verseByVerse.quote: "The tribune took him by the hand and going aside asked him privately, 'What is it that you have to tell me?' And he said, 'The Jews have agreed to ask you to bring Paul down to the council tomorrow, as though they were going to inquire somewhat more closely about him.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
The tribune took him by the hand and going aside asked him privately, “What is it that you have to tell me?” And he said, “The Jews have agreed to ask you to bring Paul down to the council tomorrow, as though they were going to inquire somewhat more closely about him.

The tribune took him by the hand and going aside asked him privately. Luke did not have to keep that detail, and the fact that he did tells you he thought it worth keeping. Claudius Lysias commands a thousand men. He has spent two days dealing with riots and is exposed to a charge that could end his career. A frightened young man is brought to him with a story, and he takes him by the hand and walks him aside. A kind, almost fatherly touch. It is the gesture you use with a child, and Luke’s word for the nephew allows a wide range of ages; the young man may have been a boy. Somewhere in that hard professional soldier was an instinct that here was someone out of his depth who needed to be made less afraid before he could speak.

Privately. That is not sentiment; it is competence, and protection. If it became known who had informed, the boy’s life would be in danger. The tribune understands at once and manages the whole disclosure so that no one in the barracks can see who told what. He handled it wisely and discreetly.

The Jews have agreed to ask you to bring Paul down to the council tomorrow. He tells the plan, and the report is a good one: brief, specific, and honest about what he is describing. He does not claim to have seen knives. He gives the shape of the request that is coming and why it is a lie, and lets the officer draw the conclusion.

God uses him as he is. Luke is quietly setting a pagan Roman’s conduct beside that of the chief priests, a few verses after they were told about a murder and said nothing. The tribune has no interest in the God of Israel. His motives are mixed at best: he is protecting a Roman citizen he has already wrongly chained, and he knows what happens to officers who lose prisoners to lynch mobs. God uses him anyway, exactly as he is, without improving him first. The Lord who promised Paul Rome the night before is keeping the promise through a nervous officer’s self-interest and a small kindness to a frightened boy.

Does God use unbelievers to help his people? Yes, constantly, and Scripture is full of it. He used Pharaoh’s daughter to save Moses, Cyrus the Persian to send Israel home (Isaiah 45:1–4), and Roman soldiers to rescue Paul three times in two days. The kindness of unbelieving doctors, teachers, neighbours and officials is part of God’s common grace, his goodness to all people and through all people. That should make us grateful rather than suspicious toward those outside the church who do us good, and it should make us pray for them, that the God who is using them would also save them.

In a sentence. The commander took him by the hand, drew him aside and asked privately what he had to say, and he said the Jews had agreed to ask him to bring Paul before the council tomorrow, pretending to look into his case more carefully.

On a Tuesday. Kindness from unexpected people is God’s grace too; thank him for it. And when someone younger, weaker or frightened comes to you with something hard to say, do what the tribune did: take them aside, make it safe for them to speak, and protect them afterwards. That is especially true when a child or vulnerable person tells you about harm.

For worship. The Lord rules over every heart, believing and unbelieving alike. He can use a Roman officer’s gentleness and a Roman officer’s fear in the same afternoon, and neither the officer nor the plotters know what he is doing. He requires nothing from his instruments at all. He simply uses them, and they go home at the end of the shift with no idea what they have done. Our God is never at the mercy of the people around us. They are always, though they do not know it, at his service.

verseByVerse.quote: "'But do not be persuaded by them, for more than forty of their men are lying in ambush for him, who have bound themselves by an oath neither to eat nor drink till they have killed him. And now they are ready, waiting for your consent.' So the tribune dismissed the young man, charging him, 'Tell no one that you have informed me of these things.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
But do not be persuaded by them, for more than forty of their men are lying in ambush for him, who have bound themselves by an oath neither to eat nor drink till they have killed him. And now they are ready, waiting for your consent.” So the tribune dismissed the young man, charging him, “Tell no one that you have informed me of these things.”

But do not be persuaded by them. Bold advice from a young man to a Roman officer.

And now they are ready, waiting for your consent. That is the sentence the whole plot hangs on, and the boy has understood exactly what he is describing. Urgent: it was planned for tomorrow. Forty armed men are in position. The oath is sworn. The chief priests are willing. The ambush point is chosen. Every part of the machine is assembled, and the whole thing is waiting on one signature from one Roman officer who is about to refuse. They needed him to say yes, and they had no way to make him. That is the story of the plot against Paul, and in a sense of every plot against the purposes of God: enormous preparation, total commitment, and one small permission that never comes.

Tell no one that you have informed me of these things. Protecting the boy, and the secret. It is the last thing anyone says to Paul’s nephew in the Bible. He is told to keep quiet, he goes home, and that is the end of him in the record. He does not watch the escort assemble at nine that night. He is not told that his information has been acted on. As far as he knows, he told a Roman officer something and was ordered to be quiet about it.

What if I never see what came of my faithfulness? Then you will be in the company of most of God’s servants. The nephew never knew, unless someone told him later, that his walk across Jerusalem helped carry the gospel to Rome. Hebrews says of the faithful that they died not having received the things promised, but having seen and greeted them from afar (Hebrews 11:13). God does not owe us a report on the results of our obedience, and much of what we do for him will only be shown to us at the last day. Then the Lord will bring to light the things now hidden, and each one will receive his commendation from God (1 Corinthians 4:5). Do the one thing you can do, and leave the report with him.

The board at the end of the section. Stand back and look. The plot is known completely to the one man with power to stop it, and unknown to the plotters, who are at this moment taking up their positions and going hungry. They think they are hunting. They are being managed. They will spend the night waiting for a prisoner who left under armed guard at nine in the evening, in the opposite direction.

In a sentence. He urged the commander not to agree, since more than forty men were waiting in ambush, sworn not to eat or drink until they had killed Paul, and were ready, awaiting his consent, and the commander sent him away, telling him not to tell anyone he had reported this.

On a Tuesday. Do the one faithful thing in front of you this week, whether or not anyone thanks you or tells you what came of it. A word of warning, a phone call, a prayer, a meal. Then let it go, and trust that it has been noticed where it matters.

For worship. Plots against God’s people often fail through small, hidden means; God is never outwitted. Not one of those forty men knew that the outcome had been fixed the night before, in a cell, by a Lord who does not consult councils. He sits in the heavens and does all that he pleases (Psalm 115:3). The kings of the earth set themselves against the Lord and his Anointed, and he has already set his King on his holy hill (Psalm 2:2, 6). No consent the wicked need will ever be given without his leave.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The commander calls two centurions and orders two hundred soldiers, seventy cavalry and two hundred spearmen to be ready to leave for Caesarea at nine that night, with horses for Paul, to bring him safely to Governor Felix. He writes a letter: Claudius Lysias greets His Excellency Felix. The Jews had seized this man and were about to kill him when he rescued him with his troops, having learned he was a Roman. Wanting to know the charge, he brought him before their council and found it concerned disputes about their law, nothing deserving death or prison. Told of a plot against the man, he has sent him at once and instructed his accusers to bring their case to Felix. The soldiers take Paul overnight as far as Antipatris; next day the cavalry go on with him while the rest return. In Caesarea they deliver the letter and hand Paul over. Felix reads it, asks his province, and on hearing Cilicia says he will hear the case when the accusers arrive. He orders Paul kept under guard in Herod’s palace.
verseByVerse.theology:
Providence Wearing a Uniform

Nothing in this section is miraculous, and that is the theological point. The God who opened the Philippian jail with an earthquake here uses a boy's ears, an officer's fear of a court-martial, a standard troop deployment, and a piece of self-serving correspondence. Scripture is entirely comfortable with both, and Christians who will only recognise God's hand in the spectacular will miss most of what he does.

Two guards keep this from turning into fatalism. First, providence does not excuse the wickedness it employs: the chief priests who agreed to supply the pretext for a murder are guilty of it, and Lysias's falsified report is a lie, and Luke's silence is not approval. Second, providence does not promise comfort. This chapter's happy ending is a two-year detention under a governor angling for a bribe. God's certain purposes and a believer's real losses run down the same road, at the same time, and Scripture never asks anyone to pretend otherwise.

The pattern is Joseph's: you meant evil against me, but God meant it for good (Gen. 50:20). The forty men were, without knowing it, working for the One they were trying to thwart — and so was the empire, which spent a great deal of money that night keeping alive a man it would one day execute.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: The tribune's letter told the governor a true story arranged to flatter its author. He did not invent a single fact. He moved one clause — putting the discovery of Paul's citizenship before the rescue instead of after it — and let his superior draw a generous conclusion. Luke set the letter down beside the events of the previous chapter and left it there.

Now: Take the story you tell most often about a hard episode — why the job ended, why the friendship cooled, how the argument went. You have told it enough times that it runs smoothly now. Every detail in it probably happened. Then lay it beside a transcript, the way Luke lays this letter beside chapter 22, and ask the narrower question: is the sequence right, and is the motive you imply the motive you actually had? Most of us are not liars. Most of us are editors, and the edit is nearly always in our own favour.

verseByVerse.quote: "Then he called two of the centurions and said, 'Get ready two hundred soldiers, with seventy horsemen and two hundred spearmen to go as far as Caesarea at the third hour of the night. Also provide mounts for Paul to ride and bring him safely to Felix the governor.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Then he called two of the centurions and said, “Get ready two hundred soldiers, with seventy horsemen and two hundred spearmen to go as far as Caesarea at the third hour of the night. Also provide mounts for Paul to ride and bring him safely to Felix the governor.”

Get ready two hundred soldiers, with seventy horsemen and two hundred spearmen. Do the arithmetic, because Luke expects it: 470 soldiers to protect one prisoner from forty assassins, moving out at night to escort him some sixty miles. That is nearly half the Jerusalem garrison. A cohort was nominally a thousand men, and the tribune has committed most of his infantry and all his usable cavalry to one overnight transfer, leaving the fortress thin in a city that has rioted twice in three days. He does it for two reasons, and Luke lets both stand. The threat is real: forty men sworn to die trying. And his own neck is on the line, because he has already wrongly chained a Roman citizen, and a dead one in his custody would finish him. Rome took the protection of a citizen seriously, and the tribune was not taking chances. God’s promise kept Paul; Rome supplied the escort. The word for the third group (dexiolaboi) is so rare that its meaning is uncertain; it may mean something like right-hand men, and it is usually taken as light-armed troops or spearmen.

To go as far as Caesarea at the third hour of the night. The ESV notes that the third hour of the night was about 9 p.m. Under cover of darkness.

Also provide mounts for Paul to ride. More than one: perhaps for changes of horse so the pace never had to drop, or for his companions.

And bring him safely to Felix the governor. The verb is diasōzō, to bring through danger to safety, and Luke will use it again of every soul reaching land from the wreck (27:44; 28:1). Felix was governor of Judea about AD 52–59, a former slave, freed by the emperor’s family. The historian Tacitus said he exercised royal power with the mind of a slave. The tribune wants his prisoner delivered alive to a governor. The Lord wants his witness delivered alive to Caesar. For one night those two intentions run on the same road, and only one of them knows the destination.

Why does God protect some Christians so dramatically and not others? We are not always told, and we should not pretend to know. This same Lord let James be killed by the sword (12:2) and let Stephen be stoned, and he would one day let Paul be executed in Rome. What we know is that no believer dies one moment before his work is done, and none is kept alive one moment after God calls him home. Paul himself wrote that to live is Christ and to die is gain (Philippians 1:21). God’s protection in this world is real and often wonderful, but it is not the whole of his care. His deepest protection is that nothing, not even death, can separate us from his love in Christ.

In a sentence. Then he called two centurions and ordered them to prepare two hundred soldiers, seventy horsemen and two hundred spearmen to leave for Caesarea at nine that night, and to provide horses for Paul and take him safely to Governor Felix.

On a Tuesday. God’s protection of his servants almost never arrives in the form we would design. It comes as a rota, a phone call, a colleague who owes someone a favour, a rule that turns out to work in your favour. Look back over the past year and name three such protections you hardly noticed at the time. Then thank him for each one.

For worship. Twenty-four hours after the Lord said Rome, this is what the promise looked like when it started to be kept. No angel. No earthquake; the God who once shook open a Philippian jail (16:26) does nothing of the kind here. Just a worried officer filling in a duty roster and detailing 470 men who were on the payroll anyway. The empire spent a great deal of military effort that night keeping alive a man it would one day execute. The Lord of hosts commanded the legions of Rome without their knowing his name, because the angels of heaven and the armies of earth are alike his servants.
verseByVerse.note: The ESV notes that the third hour of the night was about 9 p.m. Felix, a former slave, was governor of Judea from about AD 52 to 59.

verseByVerse.quote: "And he wrote a letter to this effect: 'Claudius Lysias, to his Excellency the governor Felix, greetings.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
And he wrote a letter to this effect: “Claudius Lysias, to his Excellency the governor Felix, greetings.

And he wrote a letter to this effect. To this effect: Luke gives the substance, perhaps from a copy read out at the trial. A prisoner did not normally read his escort’s covering letter, but its contents would have been disclosed at the hearing. Luke is doing what a careful historian does and giving his reader the document.

Claudius Lysias. The commander finally gets a name, and it is the name he bought. Claudius Lysias probably took the emperor’s name when he bought his citizenship (22:28). Lysias was his Greek name. His own signature is a receipt.

To his Excellency the governor Felix, greetings. Excellency (kratistos): the same title Luke uses for Theophilus (Luke 1:3). A formal Roman letter: sender, recipient, greeting.

The man Paul is being sent to. Felix will hold Paul for two years, so it is worth knowing who he was. Antonius Felix was a freed slave. His brother Pallas was the powerful freedman secretary of the emperor Claudius, and that connection, not merit, raised Felix to the governorship of Judea, an almost unheard-of post for a former slave. He was cruel and corrupt, and he put down disturbances with a brutality that made things worse. He was married to Drusilla, a Jewish princess, daughter of the Herod Agrippa who killed James (12:1–2), whom he had persuaded to leave her husband. She will sit beside him in the next chapter while Paul reasons about righteousness, self-control and the judgment to come (24:24–25). Not a neutral magistrate, then, but an official with a stolen wife and a bad record, who would keep an innocent man in custody for two years hoping for a bribe (24:26). And it is into that man’s jurisdiction that the Lord Jesus Christ is sending his apostle, on purpose, under armed guard.

Why would God send Paul to a man like Felix? For the same reason he sent Moses to Pharaoh and Jesus ate with tax collectors: because wicked rulers need the gospel too. Felix would hear Paul speak of faith in Christ Jesus, and he would tremble (24:25). He did not repent, as far as we know, but he was given the chance, and a corrupt governor heard the truth from the one man in his province who could not be bribed. God often puts his people in front of the hardest hearts, not by accident but by appointment. If you work for, live with, or answer to someone like Felix, you may be the only clear witness to Christ they will ever meet.

In a sentence. He wrote a letter: Claudius Lysias to His Excellency Governor Felix, greetings.

On a Tuesday. Pray this week for the most powerful unbelieving person you deal with: a manager, a landlord, an official. Ask God to give you a word for them, and the courage to speak it without fear or flattery.

For worship. God’s plans unfold even through official letters and bureaucracy. He is Lord of the paperwork too. The covering letter of a self-made Roman officer to a corrupt governor became part of Holy Scripture, read in every century since, because the God who rules history wanted his people to see how carefully he was moving his servant toward Rome. Kings and governors come and go, and their letters are forgotten. The word of our God stands for ever, and it wrote even this letter into his book.
verseByVerse.note: Claudius Lysias probably took the emperor’s name when he bought his citizenship.

parallels.desc: “most excellent”

verseByVerse.quote: "'This man was seized by the Jews and was about to be killed by them when I came upon them with the soldiers and rescued him, having learned that he was a Roman citizen.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
This man was seized by the Jews and was about to be killed by them when I came upon them with the soldiers and rescued him, having learned that he was a Roman citizen.

This man was seized by the Jews and was about to be killed by them when I came upon them with the soldiers and rescued him. True. Every word so far is accurate.

Having learned that he was a Roman citizen. And this clause turns the whole sentence. Lysias leaves out that he had nearly flogged a Roman citizen, and implies he rescued Paul because he was a citizen. Lay the letter beside the record, because Luke plainly intends us to check. What actually happened: he intervened because a riot was in progress, and riots are a tribune’s problem (21:31–32). He then chained Paul and ordered him stretched out and examined under the scourge. He learned of the citizenship at the last moment, from Paul himself, tied to the post, and his reaction was fear at having chained a citizen (22:25–29). The letter reverses the order of events and turns a near-disaster into a commendation. A small, self-serving twist of the facts. Notice how small and how ordinary. He invents nothing. He simply moves one clause and lets the reader assume a motive.

An honest historian. Luke includes it and says nothing: no indignation, no aside about pagan dishonesty. He records the official document and trusts the reader who has just read chapter 22 to notice the seam. Luke, the careful historian, preserves both versions honestly. That is one of the quiet reasons to trust him: a man inventing a case for Paul does not leave discrepancies lying about in his own evidence.

The mirror. The tribune’s account is accurate in every detail and false in its effect. He has arranged true facts so that they flatter him. Most of us are fluent in this. It is the version of an argument you give a friend, in which everything you report really happened. It is the sentence about a colleague that is technically correct. It is the account of why a relationship ended, or why you left a job, in which nothing is invented and the shape is still wrong.

Is it lying if everything I say is true? It can be. Truthfulness is not only avoiding false statements; it is not deceiving. The ninth commandment forbids not only outright lies but anything that prejudices the truth, including misleading arrangement of facts and leaving out what would change the picture (Westminster Larger Catechism 145). If you intend someone to believe something false, the accuracy of each sentence does not make you honest. Ask: what will my hearer conclude from what I have said, and is that conclusion true? Christ is the truth (John 14:6), and his people are called to speak the truth in love (Ephesians 4:15), not merely to avoid technical falsehood.

In a sentence. He wrote that this man had been seized by the Jews and was about to be killed when he came with soldiers and rescued him, having learned that he was a Roman citizen.

On a Tuesday. It is tempting to tell the story so we look good. Tell the truth, even when it is unflattering. Take the story you have told most often about a difficult episode in your life, the one that has smoothed out with retelling, and imagine it laid beside a transcript. Is the order right? Is the motive you imply the one you actually had? If not, tell it straight next time.

For worship. There is one in whom no self-serving word was ever found. Christ committed no sin, and no deceit was found in his mouth (1 Peter 2:22). He never arranged facts to flatter himself; he told the truth when it cost him his life. And because he is the truth, he can bear the whole truth about us. We need not edit our story before him. He has read the transcript, every clause, and he loved us anyway, and died to make liars into truthful children of God.
verseByVerse.note: Lysias leaves out that he had nearly flogged a Roman citizen.

verseByVerse.quote: "'And desiring to know the charge for which they were accusing him, I brought him down to their council. I found that he was being accused about questions of their law, but charged with nothing deserving death or imprisonment.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
And desiring to know the charge for which they were accusing him, I brought him down to their council. I found that he was being accused about questions of their law, but charged with nothing deserving death or imprisonment.

I found that he was being accused about questions of their law. Religious disputes, as Gallio said (18:15). That is what the empire saw. A Roman officer sat in that chamber, watched the supreme court of Israel tear itself in half, heard a man say his whole case turned on the resurrection of the dead, and filed it as a technical dispute about Jewish regulations. Not dangerous, not interesting, a local matter. He was looking straight at the most important claim ever made and could not see it.

But charged with nothing deserving death or imprisonment. A Roman official declares Paul innocent. Luke records such verdicts repeatedly. The tribune could not learn the facts in the riot (21:34); now his official finding is that there is no crime. Festus will say the accusers brought no charge of the evils he expected (25:18, 25), and Agrippa will say this man could have been set free if he had not appealed to Caesar (26:31–32). Official after official, examination after examination, and each time nothing. Paul, like Jesus, was innocent under Roman law. That mattered for Theophilus, and for the church’s standing in the empire. Luke is building a legal case in the pages of a history, and he never once tells the reader what to conclude.

Is Christianity just a private religious matter, as the tribune thought? No. The resurrection of Jesus is either the hinge on which everything turns or it is nothing, and the one thing it cannot be is a question of religious law. If a crucified man walked out of a tomb in Jerusalem, then death has been beaten on its own ground, every grave is provisional, and the risen one holds the keys of Death and Hades (Revelation 1:18). That makes Christ Lord of public life as well as private devotion: of work, politics, money, family and the future of the world. The world has often treated the gospel as a harmless local matter. It is the news that the King has come.

In a sentence. Wanting to know the charge, he brought him before their council and found that the accusation concerned questions of their law, with no charge deserving death or imprisonment.

On a Tuesday. Christians should live so that even unbelieving authorities find no fault in them (1 Peter 2:12). Pay your taxes, keep the law, do your work honestly. And when the world dismisses your faith as a private hobby, do not be offended; gently tell someone why the resurrection is not a hobby but the news that changes everything.

For worship. Claudius Lysias had the resurrection in front of him, in writing, in his own report, and called it a local dispute, and the God who raised his Son from the dead used the report anyway, sent it on, and moved his witness one stage nearer Rome. He is not hurried by being underestimated. He has never needed the world’s assessment of what he is doing in order to do it. The stone the builders rejected has become the cornerstone, and it is marvellous in our eyes (Psalm 118:22–23).

verseByVerse.quote: "'And when it was disclosed to me that there would be a plot against the man, I sent him to you at once, ordering his accusers also to state before you what they have against him.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
And when it was disclosed to me that there would be a plot against the man, I sent him to you at once, ordering his accusers also to state before you what they have against him.

When it was disclosed to me that there would be a plot against the man, I sent him to you at once. Passing the problem upwards, and doing two things in the process. First, it puts the plot on the official record. From now on the conspiracy is not a rumour but a documented fact in the provincial archive.

Ordering his accusers also to state before you what they have against him. A proper Roman trial would follow. And this is the hinge: it moves the venue. With one administrative sentence the trial of Paul is lifted out of Jerusalem and out of the Sanhedrin’s reach, and placed in a Roman provincial court. Follow what that unlocks. In Caesarea, Paul will stand before Felix, then Festus, and before Festus he will do what no man could do before the Sanhedrin: appeal to Caesar (25:11). A Roman citizen’s appeal compels the state to carry him, at its own expense and under guard, to Rome.

The plot that carried him to Rome. Now set that beside the forty men. They swore an oath to stop Paul, the chief priests agreed to help, and the whole apparatus produced exactly one result: it frightened a Roman officer into moving Paul to a court from which he could appeal to the emperor. The plot to keep Paul from Rome is the means by which Paul reaches Rome. This is Luke’s theology of history, and he has shown it before. The scattering meant to destroy the church spread it (8:1–4). The stoning of Stephen preceded Saul’s conversion. The imprisonment at Philippi converted the jailer. Joseph said it first and best: you meant evil against me, but God meant it for good (Genesis 50:20).

Does this mean the evil done to me does not hurt, or does not matter? No. Paul would spend two years in a cell as a direct result of this letter, and it hurt. God never calls evil good, and he will judge those who do it. The comfort is not that opposition will fail to wound. It is that opposition cannot get outside God’s use of it. There is no hostile act available to your enemies that God has not already given a purpose. That allows you to grieve honestly over what has been done to you, to seek justice where it is right, and still to trust that your Father is weaving even this into good for you and glory for himself (Romans 8:28).

In a sentence. When he learned of a plot against the man, he sent him at once to Felix, and ordered his accusers to present their case before him.

On a Tuesday. God uses governments to provide due process; pray for just courts. And look at the opposition you are facing now. Ask not only how to get out of it, but what God may be doing through it. Write down one way he has used past opposition for good in your life.

For worship. The greatest plot ever laid against God’s purposes was the plot to kill his Son, and it became the salvation of the world. Herod and Pontius Pilate, with the Gentiles and the peoples of Israel, gathered together to do whatever God’s hand and plan had predestined to take place (4:27–28). After that, no plot can frighten the people of God. The forty men were, without knowing it, working for him. So is every enemy of the church, until the day when every knee bows.

verseByVerse.quote: "So the soldiers, according to their instructions, took Paul and brought him by night to Antipatris. And on the next day they returned to the barracks, letting the horsemen go on with him."
verseByVerse.commentary:
So the soldiers, according to their instructions, took Paul and brought him by night to Antipatris. And on the next day they returned to the barracks, letting the horsemen go on with him.

Brought him by night to Antipatris. Look at the map, because the logistics are the point. From Jerusalem the road drops out of the hill country through narrow passes and ravines: perfect ambush country, where forty men could stop a column and cavalry is nearly useless. It comes out on to the plain at Antipatris, a town Herod the Great built and named after his father, about 35 miles from Jerusalem. The road beyond ran through open, mostly Gentile country, safer from ambush. A forced march through the night. They set out at nine and do not stop, because the plan depends on being clear of the hills by daylight. Once on the plain, there is nowhere to hide, and seventy horsemen can outrun anything on foot.

And on the next day they returned to the barracks, letting the horsemen go on with him. The foot soldiers went back to a city short of troops; the cavalry took him the last 25 miles to Caesarea at speed. A professional, well-judged operation, and Luke describes it with the flat precision of a man reporting facts he has checked.

The fulfilment, unfelt. That flatness is worth noticing, because of what it describes. This is the night God kept his promise. The sentence spoken in a cell, you must testify also in Rome, is being carried out by 470 men on a road in the dark, most of them tired, none of them praying, all of them simply doing their job. There is no glow in this passage. No one senses anything. The Lord who stood beside Paul the night before is not named in these verses, and he is doing everything in them.

Why does God feel absent when I most need him? Feelings are not a reliable gauge of his presence. Here he was keeping his promise through every mile of road, and nothing in the scene felt holy. The psalmists knew nights when God seemed far away (Psalm 13:1; 88:14), and they kept praying into the silence. God has promised to be with his people always (Matthew 28:20), and his presence does not depend on our sense of it. When you feel nothing, hold on to what he has said, keep to the ordinary means he gives, his word, prayer, the Lord’s Supper, the fellowship of his people, and expect that one day you will look back and see that he was carrying you the whole way.

In a sentence. The soldiers followed orders, took Paul by night to Antipatris, and the next day returned to the barracks, leaving the cavalry to go on with him.

On a Tuesday. If you are in a stretch of life that feels entirely ordinary and entirely unaccompanied, remember this road. The night march is not the gap between the promise and its fulfilment. The night march is the fulfilment, in progress, unfelt. Keep walking.

For worship. God’s escort brought Paul safely through the night; he brings his people through every dark road. Even though I walk through the valley of the shadow of death, I will fear no evil, for you are with me (Psalm 23:4). The Shepherd who led David leads us still, through passes where enemies wait and over plains where nothing seems to happen, and he does not sleep. He who keeps Israel neither slumbers nor sleeps (Psalm 121:4), and by morning his sheep are where he meant them to be.
verseByVerse.note: Antipatris was about 35 miles from Jerusalem; the road beyond was safer, running through mostly Gentile country.

verseByVerse.quote: "When they had come to Caesarea and delivered the letter to the governor, they presented Paul also before him."
verseByVerse.commentary:
When they had come to Caesarea and delivered the letter to the governor, they presented Paul also before him.

When they had come to Caesarea and delivered the letter to the governor. Caesarea, on the coast, was the Roman capital of Judea. Paul would be held here for two years (24:27), and from here he would sail for Rome. The order is correct and bureaucratic: paperwork first, then the man. Roman custody is a chain of documented handovers, and Luke records this one too. Paul has been in Caesarea before. He stayed on the way up in the house of Philip the evangelist, and it was there that Agabus took his belt and bound his own hands and feet (21:8–11). Everything Agabus said would happen has happened. Paul has been bound by the Jews in Jerusalem and handed over to the Gentiles, and he is back in the same city, in chains, as foretold.

They presented Paul also before him. One step closer to Rome. Paul is now, formally and finally, out of the council’s jurisdiction. From this verse to the end of the book he will be tried, guarded, transported and shipwrecked with Romans. The men who wanted him dead will have to travel to Caesarea and argue in a Gentile court, and they will lose. The high priest who had him struck in the mouth will next appear as a plaintiff, coming down in person with a hired advocate (24:1), and the advocate will lose too.

The men still waiting. Meanwhile, sixty miles away, forty men are still waiting on a Jerusalem street for a prisoner who has been gone since the previous night: hungry, under an oath they cannot keep, watching a road nobody is coming down. Luke never tells us what became of them. He simply left them a dozen verses back, waiting for a consent that never came.

A real loss and a door. About twelve days earlier (24:11) Paul had walked into Jerusalem hoping to be welcomed by the church and heard by his own people. He leaves under armed guard at night, rejected by his nation. It is a real loss, and Luke does not dress it up. But the door that shut behind him in the temple (21:30) turned out to be a door he was meant to be on the other side of.

In a sentence. When they reached Caesarea, they delivered the letter to the governor and handed Paul over to him.

On a Tuesday. Each step, even into custody, brought Paul closer to God’s purpose, and so with you. If a door has shut behind you, a job, a church, a relationship, a city, grieve it honestly. Then look at where you are standing now, and ask what God has brought you there to do.

For worship. The word of the Lord through Agabus came true to the letter, because the Lord’s word always does. Not one of his good promises has ever failed (Joshua 21:45). The servant who was handed over to the Gentiles walked the road of his Master, who was also handed over, and whose handing over became the salvation of Jew and Gentile alike. Paul came back to Caesarea in chains, and the chains were carrying the gospel to the ends of the earth.
verseByVerse.note: Caesarea, on the coast, was the Roman capital of Judea.

verseByVerse.quote: "On reading the letter, he asked what province he was from. And when he learned that he was from Cilicia, he said, 'I will give you a hearing when your accusers arrive.' And he commanded him to be guarded in Herod's praetorium."
verseByVerse.commentary:
On reading the letter, he asked what province he was from. And when he learned that he was from Cilicia, he said, “I will give you a hearing when your accusers arrive.” And he commanded him to be guarded in Herod’s praetorium.

He asked what province he was from. Felix’s first question is not about God, or the resurrection, or even the riot. It is a check on jurisdiction: is this case legally mine? Cilicia was then under the governor of Syria, Felix’s superior, so Felix could hear the case rather than pass it on; and since the accusers were from Judea, he kept it. A small procedural moment, and it decided where Paul would spend the next two years of his life.

I will give you a hearing when your accusers arrive. Roman law required the accused to face his accusers (25:16). A reasonable ruling from an unreasonable man. He will hold the hearing, find nothing, and then leave Paul in custody anyway, partly to please the Jewish leaders, partly in hope of a bribe (24:26–27).

And he commanded him to be guarded in Herod’s praetorium. Herod’s praetorium was the palace Herod the Great had built at Caesarea, by the sea, now the governor’s residence. Paul was a prisoner in a palace: not in a common cell, but held under guard in the governor’s headquarters, and later Felix would order that he have some liberty and that his friends be allowed to care for him (24:23).

The chapter from end to end. Look where the chapter has arrived. It opened with a man struck on the mouth by order of the high priest, in the supreme court of his own nation, before he had finished a sentence. It ends with him under guard in a Herodian palace by the sea, alive, formally recorded as charged with nothing, his accusers summoned to a Roman court, and the whole machinery of the empire slowly turning toward the place the Lord named in a barracks two nights before. And yet nothing is resolved. He is still a prisoner, well over a thousand miles from Rome, and two years are about to disappear in this palace: two years of a mission-driven man’s life with no journeys, no new churches, no visible fruit.

What do I do with long seasons of waiting? Hold both halves together, because this is where most Christian lives are actually lived. The promise is certain and the waiting is long. Paul did not waste his two years: he spoke with Felix and Drusilla about faith in Christ, received his friends, and was being prepared for Rome. Use your waiting the same way. Keep the means of grace, serve whoever is in front of you, pray for the work you cannot yet do, and refuse to call the time wasted. Those who wait for the Lord shall renew their strength (Isaiah 40:31). Waiting is not God’s absence from your life. It is often where he does his deepest work in you.

In a sentence. Felix read the letter, asked what province Paul came from, and learning he was from Cilicia, said he would hear his case when his accusers arrived, and ordered him kept under guard in Herod’s palace.

On a Tuesday. If you are in a season of waiting, write down the one sentence from God’s word that you are standing on, and put it where you will see it each morning. Then do one useful, faithful thing today in the place where you are being made to wait.

For worship. Whether in a palace or a prison, Paul was in God’s hands, and so are you. Paul did not know that Luke would be with him, or that the voyage was coming, or that he would preach without hindrance in the capital of the world at the end of it. He knew one sentence, spoken in the dark by someone who stood beside him: take courage. On some days that is the whole visible foundation of a Christian life, and it holds, because of who said it. The Lord Jesus is faithful, and the one who calls you is faithful; he will surely do it (1 Thessalonians 5:24).
verseByVerse.note: Herod’s praetorium was the palace Herod the Great had built at Caesarea, used as the governor’s residence.

23.title: The Plot and the Providence
23.text: <sup>1</sup>And looking intently at the council, Paul said, “Brothers, I have lived my life before God in all good conscience up to this day.” <sup>2</sup>And the high priest Ananias commanded those who stood by him to strike him on the mouth. <sup>3</sup>Then Paul said to him, “God is going to strike you, you whitewashed wall! Are you sitting to judge me according to the law, and yet contrary to the law you order me to be struck?” <sup>4</sup>Those who stood by said, “Would you revile God’s high priest?” <sup>5</sup>And Paul said, “I did not know, brothers, that he was the high priest, for it is written, ‘You shall not speak evil of a ruler of your people.’” <sup>6</sup>Now when Paul perceived that one part were Sadducees and the other Pharisees, he cried out in the council, “Brothers, I am a Pharisee, a son of Pharisees. It is with respect to the hope and the resurrection of the dead that I am on trial.” <sup>7</sup>And when he had said this, a dissension arose between the Pharisees and the Sadducees, and the assembly was divided. <sup>8</sup>For the Sadducees say that there is no resurrection, nor angel, nor spirit, but the Pharisees acknowledge them all. <sup>9</sup>Then a great clamor arose, and some of the scribes of the Pharisees’ party stood up and contended sharply, “We find nothing wrong in this man. What if a spirit or an angel spoke to him?” <sup>10</sup>And when the dissension became violent, the tribune, afraid that Paul would be torn to pieces by them, commanded the soldiers to go down and take him away from among them by force and bring him into the barracks. <sup>11</sup>The following night the Lord stood by him and said, “Take courage, for as you have testified to the facts about me in Jerusalem, so you must testify also in Rome.” <sup>12</sup>When it was day, the Jews made a plot and bound themselves by an oath neither to eat nor drink till they had killed Paul. <sup>13</sup>There were more than forty who made this conspiracy. <sup>14</sup>They went to the chief priests and elders and said, “We have strictly bound ourselves by an oath to taste no food till we have killed Paul.” <sup>15</sup>Now therefore you, along with the council, give notice to the tribune to bring him down to you, as though you were going to determine his case more exactly. And we are ready to kill him before he comes near.” <sup>16</sup>Now the son of Paul’s sister heard of their ambush, so he went and entered the barracks and told Paul. <sup>17</sup>Paul called one of the centurions and said, “Take this young man to the tribune, for he has something to tell him.” <sup>18</sup>So he took him and brought him to the tribune and said, “Paul the prisoner called me and asked me to bring this young man to you, as he has something to say to you.” <sup>19</sup>The tribune took him by the hand, and going aside asked him privately, “What is it that you have to tell me?” <sup>20</sup>And he said, “The Jews have agreed to ask you to bring Paul down to the council tomorrow, as though they were going to inquire somewhat more closely about him. <sup>21</sup>But do not be persuaded by them, for more than forty of their men are lying in ambush for him, who have bound themselves by an oath neither to eat nor drink till they have killed him. And now they are ready, waiting for your consent.” <sup>22</sup>So the tribune dismissed the young man, charging him, “Tell no one that you have informed me of these things.” <sup>23</sup>Then he called two of the centurions and said, “Get ready two hundred soldiers, with seventy horsemen and two hundred spearmen to go as far as Caesarea at the third hour of the night. <sup>24</sup>Also provide mounts for Paul to ride and bring him safely to Felix the governor.” <sup>25</sup>And he wrote a letter to this effect: <sup>26</sup>“Claudius Lysias, to his Excellency the governor Felix, greetings. <sup>27</sup>This man was seized by the Jews and was about to be killed by them when I came upon them with the soldiers and rescued him, having learned that he was a Roman citizen. <sup>28</sup>And desiring to know the charge for which they were accusing him, I brought him down to their council. <sup>29</sup>I found that he was being accused about questions of their law, but charged with nothing deserving death or imprisonment. <sup>30</sup>And when it was disclosed to me that there would be a plot against the man, I sent him to you at once, ordering his accusers also to state before you what they have against him.” <sup>31</sup>So the soldiers, according to their instructions, took Paul and brought him by night to Antipatris. <sup>32</sup>And on the next day they returned to the barracks, letting the horsemen go on with him. <sup>33</sup>When they had come to Caesarea and delivered the letter to the governor, they presented Paul also before him. <sup>34</sup>On reading the letter, he asked what province he was from. And when he learned that he was from Cilicia, <sup>35</sup>he said, “I will give you a hearing when your accusers arrive.” And he commanded him to be guarded in Herod’s praetorium.
23.overview:
Paul stands before the Sanhedrin, the council he once served. The hearing is a disaster as a trial and a triumph of providence. The high priest Ananias, a notoriously greedy and violent man, has Paul struck for claiming a clear conscience; Paul flares up, then apologises when told who gave the order, citing the law. Seeing the council split between Sadducees and Pharisees, he declares that he is on trial for the hope of the resurrection, and the council dissolves into a shouting match, some Pharisees even defending him. The tribune has to rescue him a second time.

That night the Lord stands by Paul: he must testify in Rome as he has in Jerusalem. Next morning more than forty men swear not to eat or drink until they have killed him, but Paul’s nephew hears of the plot and warns him, and the tribune sends Paul by night under an escort of 470 soldiers to the governor Felix at Caesarea, with a letter that states Paul has done nothing deserving death or chains. God’s promise is kept through a boy’s ears, a centurion’s errand and a Roman army. Paul is now in Roman custody, which will last more than four years and bring him, as promised, to Rome.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Five days later the high priest comes down with elders and a lawyer, Tertullus. After flattering Felix, Tertullus charges Paul with being a troublemaker who stirs up Jews everywhere, a ringleader of the Nazarene sect, and one who tried to desecrate the temple. The Jews back him up. Paul replies calmly: he went up to worship only twelve days ago and started no disturbance anywhere, and they cannot prove their claims. He admits that he worships the God of their fathers as a follower of the Way, believing the Law and the Prophets and sharing their hope that God will raise both righteous and wicked; so he strives for a clear conscience. He came bringing gifts for the poor and was found in the temple ritually pure; the Asian Jews who caused the trouble are not even here, and the council found nothing except his cry about the resurrection. Felix, who knows about the Way, adjourns the case and keeps Paul under guard with some freedom. Later he and his wife Drusilla hear Paul on faith in Christ; when Paul speaks of righteousness, self-control and judgment, Felix grows afraid and sends him away until a convenient time. Hoping for a bribe, he often sends for him. After two years Festus succeeds Felix, who leaves Paul in prison to please the Jews.
verseByVerse.theology:
Almost Persuaded: the Sin of the Postponed Decision

Felix is the most quietly terrifying figure in Acts, because nothing about him is dramatic. He does not oppose the gospel. He is interested in it. He understands it accurately (v. 22), he sends for the preacher repeatedly (v. 26), and on the first hearing it frightens him badly enough to end the meeting. He is the nearest thing in this book to a man under conviction — and he dies outside of Christ, so far as Scripture records, with nothing standing between him and the kingdom except a word: later.

Scripture never treats delay as neutral ground. Today, if you hear his voice, do not harden your hearts (Heb. 3:15); behold, now is the day of salvation (2 Cor. 6:2). The reason is visible in this very chapter: Felix felt more at the first conversation than at any of the many that followed. Repeated exposure without submission does not keep the heart tender; it callouses it. The second hearing of a truth is always easier to survive than the first.

This is why the Reformed tradition has insisted that conviction is not conversion. Felix's fear was real and it was the Spirit's work on his conscience — and a frightened conscience saves nobody. What God requires is not to be moved but to be surrendered. Grace is sovereign and grace is free, and the same doctrine that says no one comes unless the Father draws him says also that whoever comes will never be cast out (John 6:37, 44). The only sane response to a conviction you can feel is to act on it while you can still feel it.

Alongside Felix stands Paul, and the contrast is the chapter's argument. One man is free and cannot decide; the other is in chains and settled to the point of cheerfulness (v. 10). One postpones; the other has already been told he must testify at Rome and simply waits. Circumstance is a poor guide to who in a room is actually at liberty.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Paul was asked, by the man who could have freed him with a sentence, to speak about faith in Christ Jesus. He was a prisoner, entirely in that man's power, and the governor's known weaknesses were a court that could be bought and a wife he had taken from another man. Paul chose righteousness, self-control, and the coming judgment. He did not trim one of the three, and he stayed in prison for two more years.

Now: Most Christians will never address a governor, and nearly all of us will at some point have something true to say to somebody who holds an advantage over us — an employer, a relative whose goodwill we need, a friend whose reaction we fear. The pressure is not usually to lie. It is to select: to say the two things that will land well and leave out the third, and to call the omission tact. Ask what your version leaves out, and then ask why it is always the same one. Paul's three subjects took ten seconds to choose and cost him two years, and Luke thought them worth recording precisely because he did not shorten the list to two.

verseByVerse.quote: "And after five days the high priest Ananias came down with some elders and a spokesman, one Tertullus. They laid before the governor their case against Paul. And when he had been summoned, Tertullus began to accuse him, saying: 'Since through you we enjoy much peace, and since by your foresight, most excellent Felix, reforms are being made for this nation,'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
And after five days the high priest Ananias came down with some elders and a spokesman, one Tertullus. They laid before the governor their case against Paul. And when he had been summoned, Tertullus began to accuse him, saying: “Since through you we enjoy much peace, and since by your foresight, most excellent Felix, reforms are being made for this nation,

Meaning first. Acts 24 is Paul’s trial before the Roman governor Felix. A professional lawyer accuses him of being a plague and a ringleader of the Nazarenes. Paul answers calmly with facts: he caused no riot, he worships the God of his fathers, believes the Law and the Prophets, and hopes in the resurrection of the just and the unjust. Felix delays the verdict. Later, Paul speaks to Felix and his wife about righteousness, self-control and the coming judgment, and Felix trembles, but sends him away to wait for a convenient time, which never comes. Paul stays in prison for two years. It is a chapter about two kinds of delay: a corrupt man putting off God, and God, who is never late, keeping his promise to bring his servant to Rome in his own time.

And after five days the high priest Ananias came down with some elders and a spokesman, one Tertullus. Read that sentence as a measure of how badly they want this. Ananias is the high priest of Israel. Caesarea is sixty miles from Jerusalem, and it is a Gentile city, Herod’s showpiece, with a temple to Augustus on the hill. He goes anyway, with a delegation of elders, and he hires a professional. This is the man who a week ago ordered Paul struck on the mouth before he had finished a sentence (23:2). Now he has come down from the chamber where he was the law, to stand in a Roman hall as a plaintiff and pay an advocate to speak for him, because here his office counts for nothing. Tertullus was a professional advocate hired to present the case in Roman legal style, perhaps a Greek-speaking Jew, or a Roman.

Since through you we enjoy much peace. Tertullus begins where every trained speaker began, with an opening designed to win the judge’s goodwill before a single fact is mentioned (the captatio benevolentiae). Flattery, the customary opening of a speech to a governor, and mostly false. Felix had governed Judea for about five years, and the province had rarely been less peaceful. He had crushed the revolt of the Egyptian prophet, the man the tribune took Paul for (21:38), and crucified rebels in numbers, but his rule provoked more unrest than it ended. Josephus records that he arranged the murder of the former high priest Jonathan, who had been urging him to govern better, by hiring assassins to mingle with a festival crowd. Under Felix the dagger-men became a fixture of Jerusalem life. Tacitus and Josephus describe him as cruel and corrupt, and the Jews later complained of him to Rome. So the high priest of Israel sits and listens while his paid advocate thanks a murderer for the peace. Luke writes the flattery out in full and adds no comment. Seven verses later he lets us hear Paul begin, and the difference between the two men is audible in their first sentences.

Why is flattery so dangerous? Because it is not a compliment but a transaction. It is offered because the flatterer wants something and judges that you will pay for it in goodwill. Felix took the payment. He let a delegation from a nation he had bled thank him for their tranquillity, and did not correct them. Scripture warns that a flattering mouth works ruin (Proverbs 26:28) and that a man who flatters his neighbour spreads a net for his feet (Proverbs 29:5). The deeper danger is to the one who swallows it. Every time we accept praise we know is false, we lose a little of our ability to hear the truth from anybody, including God. So give honest encouragement freely, but be suspicious of praise that is useful to the giver, and be most suspicious of the praise you most enjoy.

In a sentence. Five days later the high priest Ananias came down with some elders and a lawyer named Tertullus, who presented their case against Paul to the governor, beginning with flattery about the peace and reforms Felix had brought.

On a Tuesday. Beware flattery, in giving and receiving it. Honest words are better than smooth ones: whoever rebukes a man will in the end find more favour than he who flatters with his tongue (Proverbs 28:23). This week, when you want something from someone, notice whether you reach for praise you do not mean. Say something true instead, or say nothing.

For worship. God cannot be flattered. He searches the heart and tries the mind (Jeremiah 17:10), and no smooth word has ever bought his favour. That is terrifying to the flatterer, and it is the best news in the world to the sinner, because the God who cannot be bought has given freely what no one could pay for. We do not win him with fine speeches. We come with nothing, and he receives us for the sake of his Son, whose mouth had no deceit in it and who never spoke a word he did not mean.
verseByVerse.note: Tertullus was a professional advocate hired to present the case. Opening with flattery of the judge was standard courtroom style; Roman historians remember Felix’s rule as harsh and corrupt.

verseByVerse.quote: "'in every way and everywhere we accept this with all gratitude. But, to detain you no further, I beg you in your kindness to hear us briefly.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
in every way and everywhere we accept this with all gratitude. But, to detain you no further, I beg you in your kindness to hear us briefly.

In every way and everywhere we accept this with all gratitude. More flattery, the last note of the opening.

But, to detain you no further, I beg you in your kindness to hear us briefly. A formula so standard it was almost furniture: the promise of brevity, the appeal to the great man’s patience. Kindness (epieikeia) is gentleness, clemency, the quality of a judge who does not press the law to its harshest edge. Ironic, of Felix. Two sentences of praise, and then Tertullus turns and asks the court to destroy a man.

Respectable persecution. What is worth noticing is how ordinary it all is. There is nothing lurid about this machinery. No conspiracy in a cellar, no forty men under an oath; that failed. This is the second attempt, and it is entirely respectable: a lawful summons, a professional advocate, a formal hearing, correct procedure, courteous language. The forty assassins could not lay a finger on him. The lawyers very nearly did. Persecution rarely arrives dressed as persecution. It comes as a properly constituted committee, a correctly worded complaint, a hearing in the right tone by people who are unfailingly polite. Everyone in the room is behaving well. That is what makes it work. And Luke lets the other side’s best speaker go first, uninterrupted. A book nervous about its case does not do that.

We and I. One more thing before the charges land. Tertullus says we throughout: we accept this, we beg you, we have found this man. He is a hired speaker from outside the community, in the case a matter of days, and the we is a professional’s fiction. Paul, when his turn comes, will say I: I went up to worship, I take pains, this I confess. He has no delegation behind him and no advocate beside him. That is very often the shape of it. Opposition arrives as a body, with a spokesman and the comfort of numbers. Faithfulness usually has to be done in the first person singular, by someone standing up alone.

What should I do when I have to stand alone for Christ? Remember that you are not as alone as it feels. Paul had no advocate in that hall, but he had the Lord’s word from the barracks (23:11), and later he would write that at his first defence no one came to stand by him, all deserted him, but the Lord stood by him and strengthened him (2 Timothy 4:16–17). When you are the only one at work, in your family or in your class who will speak for Christ or refuse to join in wrong, speak calmly, speak for yourself, and do not pretend to a crowd you do not have. Then find fellowship afterwards: tell your church, ask for prayer, and let others stand with you next time.

In a sentence. Tertullus said they gratefully welcomed this in every way and everywhere, and asked Felix kindly to hear them briefly so as not to weary him.

On a Tuesday. Truth needs no flattery; speak plainly and honestly. And watch for wrong that comes dressed in good manners: the polite email, the well-run meeting, the reasonable policy that quietly sets someone up to be harmed. Courtesy is a virtue. It is not a proof of innocence.

For worship. The Lord Jesus was tried this way too: by respectable men, in proper session, with witnesses and procedure, and condemned. He stood alone, with no advocate, while his friends fled. And because he stood alone for us, we never stand alone again. We have an advocate with the Father, Jesus Christ the righteous (1 John 2:1), who pleads for his people in the highest court of all, and whose case has never once been lost.

verseByVerse.quote: "'For we have found this man a plague, one who stirs up riots among all the Jews throughout the world and is a ringleader of the sect of the Nazarenes. He even tried to profane the temple, but we seized him.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
For we have found this man a plague, one who stirs up riots among all the Jews throughout the world and is a ringleader of the sect of the Nazarenes. He even tried to profane the temple, but we seized him.

For we have found this man a plague. The flattery is over and the indictment lands. There are four charges, and the construction is expert. First, the man himself. Plague (loimos): pest, pestilence. A personal attack. Not this man is troublesome, but this man is a disease. It is the language you use of something to be stamped out rather than answered, and it is always the first move: before you can do something terrible to a man, you have to stop describing him as one.

One who stirs up riots among all the Jews throughout the world. Second, sedition, the political charge: the most serious accusation before a Roman governor, under an emperor nervous of Jewish unrest. The word for riots is stasis, insurrection, civil disorder. Rome did not much mind what you believed; it minded a province that would not stay quiet. And notice the reach: throughout the world. And here is what makes the charge so hard to answer: it is built on a true fact with a false cause attached. Riots really did follow Paul: at Pisidian Antioch, Iconium, Lystra, Philippi, Thessalonica, Ephesus, and the temple days ago. Tertullus takes that pattern and reverses the arrow: trouble happens where Paul goes, so Paul makes the trouble. Whether the preacher is the arsonist or the man who turned the lights on is exactly the question the charge is built to skip.

And is a ringleader of the sect of the Nazarenes. Third, the sect. Ringleader (prōtostatēs) is the man in the front rank of the line. Sect (hairesis) means a party or school, like the Pharisees or Sadducees (5:17; 15:5); it does not yet mean heresy in the later sense, but here it suggests an unlicensed splinter group. Nazarenes: followers of Jesus of Nazareth, a Jewish name for Christians, still used for them in Hebrew and Arabic. It is the only time in the New Testament that Christians are called this, and it is meant as a sneer: the followers of a nobody from nowhere, from a village that prompted the question whether anything good could come out of it (John 1:46).

The name heaven answers to. Which is the truth, and it is glorious, and no one in that hall had the faintest idea. The carpenter’s town is the address heaven answers to. The risen Lord named himself by it from the middle of a light that outshone the noon sun: I am Jesus of Nazareth (22:8). Men still use it as an insult. He wears it as a name.

He even tried to profane the temple, but we seized him. Fourth, the temple: the religious charge, and false (21:28–29). It is the one charge with teeth in both legal systems, since Rome allowed the Jews to execute even a citizen for going beyond the barrier. It is also the charge that has quietly shrunk. In the temple it was a flat assertion that he had brought Greeks in and defiled the place (21:28). Here it is that he tried. They have had days to find a witness, and the charge has already begun to soften. And we seized him is a polite description: they were trying to kill him.

Textual note. The ESV notes that some manuscripts add at the end of verse 6 and in verses 7–8 that they would have judged him by their own law, but Lysias took him away with violence. It is probably a later addition, shifting the blame onto Lysias. The earliest and best Greek manuscripts lack it, and it looks like a scribe’s attempt to explain how Paul came to be in Roman custody. Notice the irony in what it says: it has Tertullus complain that Lysias snatched Paul out of their hands with great violence, when their hands were at that moment beating him to death (21:31–32). A scribe’s tidying accidentally records the prosecution’s view of a rescue: how dare the Romans stop us.

What should I do when Christians are called a danger to society? First, check whether there is any truth in it, and repent of it where there is: Christians have sometimes deserved criticism. Then answer calmly, with facts, as Paul is about to do. Peter told believers to keep their conduct among unbelievers honourable, so that when they speak against them as evildoers, they may see their good deeds and glorify God (1 Peter 2:12). Notice that the gospel does disturb things: a quiet town gets loud when the light is turned on, because sin does not like to be seen. That is not the same as causing a riot. Do not be ashamed of disturbing darkness; be ashamed only of disturbing it unlovingly.

In a sentence. Tertullus said they had found Paul a troublemaker who stirred up riots among the Jews all over the world, a ringleader of the Nazarene sect, who even tried to desecrate the temple, so they seized him.

On a Tuesday. Followers of Jesus may be called a plague; let your life prove the charge false. Be the kind of neighbour, worker and citizen about whom slander will not stick: honest, kind, peaceable, generous. And be careful of the language you use about people you oppose. If you would not say it about them to their face, or to God, do not say it at all.

For worship. They called his people Nazarenes as an insult, and he made it a crown. The Lord of glory chose the despised village, the despised manger, the despised cross, so that no one could ever boast before him (1 Corinthians 1:28–29). Every insult thrown at his name has only shown how low he stooped to save us. And one day the same name they sneered at will be the name before which every knee bows: Jesus of Nazareth, King of the Jews, Lord of all.
verseByVerse.note: The ESV notes that some manuscripts add at the end of verse 6 and in verse 7 a complaint that Lysias had taken Paul away by force. “Nazarenes” was a name for Jesus’ followers.

verseByVerse.quote: "'By examining him yourself you will be able to find out from him about everything of which we accuse him.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
By examining him yourself you will be able to find out from him about everything of which we accuse him.

A verse with no number. Open an ESV at this page and you will notice that the text runs from verse 6 to verse 8. That is not a printing error. The verse numbers in our Bibles are not part of Scripture; they were added in 1551 by a Paris printer, Robert Estienne, working from the Greek text then available, which was based on late manuscripts. Far older copies have been found since, and they lack the words that once made up verse 7. Translators follow the older evidence but keep the old numbering, so that four centuries of commentaries and cross-references still work. The result is a number with nothing under it.
